Russian Investment Falls 4.6% as Kremlin's New Tax Plans Spark Business Alarm
Russia’s largest business association has demanded revisions to the Kremlin’s proposed tax increases, warning that additional financial pressure could accelerate capital flight and deepen an investment downturn, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) reported on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Alexander Shokhin, president of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), appealed to Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin to amend the tax bills before their final reading. According to Ukrainian intelligence, the association argued that the measures would increase the burden on companies and violate the government's pledge to maintain stable taxation through 2030.
One major point of contention is a proposed 30% tax on windfall profits in the mining industry, expected to generate approximately $8.3 billion between 2027 and 2029, according to the SZRU. Instead, the RSPP proposed temporarily increasing the corporate profit tax rate from 25% by 0.5–1 percentage point, potentially generating between $5.9 billion and $11.9 billion.
The association also demanded an increase in the federal investment tax deduction ceiling from 3% to 10–12%. The intelligence service noted that investment in Russia's economy declined by 4.6% in real terms during the first half of 2026.
Another major concern involves taxation of passive income. According to the SZRU, the RSPP estimates that the combined tax burden on corporate profits and distributed dividends could reach 42%, making Russian financial instruments less attractive and increasing the risk of capital outflows.
Business representatives proposed limiting higher tax rates to three years, preserving exemptions for bank deposits and long-term investments, and adjusting tax thresholds for inflation.
The association also opposed a proposed 15% tax on investment funds. With profitability levels of 20–30%, the new levy could consume between 50% and 75% of profits, the intelligence service reported. The RSPP instead proposed taxing income at the investor level or postponing implementation.
Russian businesses additionally requested tax relief for companies protecting their facilities against drone attacks. As detailed by the SZRU, proposed measures include property tax exemptions for protective structures and double deductions for mandatory expenses related to safeguarding critical infrastructure.
The business lobby's pushback comes as Moscow pursues a broader tax overhaul to cover record military spending and a widening budget deficit. The planned measures are expected to extract nearly $44 billion from individuals and businesses through 2029, with the maximum rate on passive personal income rising to 22% for about four million people.
Analyst estimates put Norilsk Nickel's additional payments at roughly $592 million, with aluminum producer Rusal facing about $462 million. The revenue drive coincides with plans to spend $202.6 billion on defense in 2027, 27% above the previously budgeted level and the highest since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Esra Tekin
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Turkish, Bulgarian, and Romanian defense ministers on Wednesday reiterated the significance of the Black Sea for international trade and the supply of grain, fertilizers, and energy in a joint statement.
The statement came after the Türkiye-Bulgaria-Romania Meeting of Defense Ministers and Chiefs of General Staff held in Sofia.
Turkish National Defense Minister Yasar Guler, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, and Romanian Defense Minister Stefan-Radu Oprea attended the meeting.
The ministers “strongly condemned” attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
“We wish to reaffirm the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security. Disruptions to maritime traffic threaten global supply chains, food and energy security, particularly in vulnerable regions of Africa, the Middle East, and Asia,” the statement said.
“We call on all parties to refrain from any further actions that could endanger commercial vessels, maritime infrastructure and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
"We deeply regret the loss of innocent seafarers who have lost their lives in these attacks. We emphasize our full solidarity with the states whose citizens and vessels have been affected by these attacks,” it added.
The statement urged all parties to obey international law, including the Montreux Convention and applicable international humanitarian law, in order to safeguard security in the Black Sea, preserve regional stability, and facilitate safe maritime activities.
The statement noted that Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye, as NATO allies, contribute to meeting the region’s security needs. It also expressed appreciation for NATO’s support in the areas of deterrence and defense.
The three countries agreed to take appropriate measures, in coordination with NATO where necessary, to increase information and intelligence sharing, strengthen maritime situational awareness, and improve early-warning capabilities in pursuit of these objectives.
The statement further noted that cooperation and coordination between the three countries’ armed forces would continue to be strengthened to support security and stability in the Black Sea.
It also stated that consultations, information exchanges and the identification of practical measures contributing to regional security and stability would be facilitated.
The next round of consultations is scheduled to take place in Ankara and Bucharest.

On Tuesday, Ukraine’s parliament voted to raise the corporate income tax on bank profits from 25% to 50% in 2027, pressing ahead despite objections from the central bank – the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) – and the banking industry.
A total of 265 lawmakers backed bill No. 15262 in the first reading, 39 votes more than the 226 required.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Lawmakers have turned to the bank profits levy for the fourth time since 2023, with the central bank opposing earlier rounds, warning that the tax is starting to eat into the capital that fuels lending.
However, Tuesday’s vote was only the first reading. Lawmakers must now make amendments to the bill and vote on it again in the second reading, which can then be passed down to the president for approval.
“This is the fourth time we have made such a decision, and the previous three were quite successful, because we managed to attract additional funds to the budget from the banking system, which receives super profits even during wartime,” Interfax-Ukraine quoted Danylo Hetmantsev, co-author of the bill, chair of parliament’s tax committee, and a lawmaker from the Servant of the People Party.

Zelensky: Ukraine’s Data Center Strikes ‘Hurt Russia More’
The vote moves forward despite the NBU previously warning that it comes at the cost of lending, which independent economists see as an easier route than reforms which remain stalled in parliament.
The draft 2027 state budget already counts Hr.38.5 billion ($845 million) in additional revenue from keeping the 50% rate, according to Hetmantsev. The sum compares with the NBU’s estimate of Hr.20 billion ($439 million) that banks will pay in windfall tax in 2026.
High profits and opposition
Lawmakers first imposed a 50% tax on banks’ 2023 profits in a law passed in November 2023 – applied retroactively, in breach of Ukraine’s tax code, which requires at least six months’ notice – and set a permanent 25% rate for 2024 onward, while also setting a permanent 25% rate from 2024.
Neither banks nor the NBU pushed back, as lending was subdued and banks earned record profits largely from government securities.
“We could clearly see that the banks were generating tax revenue and weren’t really using it,” First Deputy Governor Serhiy Nikolaichuk told Kyiv Post at the June 30 briefing.
The 50% rate returned for 2024 despite the IMF recommending against it, and again for 2026. Banks paid Hr.95.9 billion ($2 billion) at the 50% rate in 2024, roughly a third of all corporate income tax collected that year, according to Kyiv Post in July.
                                                                                                                                                                         Data provided and calculated by the National Bank of Ukraine, based on data from the State Treasury of Ukraine and bank data.                             
“The NBU was postponing the implementation of bank capitalization plans, all to spread the impact of this tax and avoid hindering the resumption of lending,” Pervin Dadashova, director of the Financial Stability Department, told Kyiv Post during the June briefing.
The NBU has since raised the alarm that paying the tax more than twice is no longer a war-related excuse, but an unsustainable policy. NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyi described the central bank as “categorically opposed” to the levy at a June 18 briefing.
“The Ukrainian economy needs a banking system that can sustain it, meaning that the banking system, which is ten times smaller in terms of capital than that of neighboring Poland, must grow. If levied permanently, the extra tax would eliminate room for such growth,” the NBU wrote in an official statement condemning the bill.
Loans to businesses rose 30% year-on-year in 2025 and loans to households about 36%, according to NBU estimates.
Comparatively, banks’ capital adequacy ratio has declined from 17.3% to 16.4%. However, independent economists did not rush to defend them.
Concorde Capital estimated their return on equity at 29.9% in 2025, against an EU average of 9.4% in 2024, according to Oleksandr Parashchiy, head of the company’s analytical department, who shared the estimates with Kyiv Post.

For Israel's Arabs, record turnout may bring political clout
NAZARETH, Israel, Oct 28 - Israel's Palestinian citizens appear set to secure a record number of seats in parliament and could emerge as kingmakers after strong turnout in Tuesday's election, galvanized by what they describe as the racist policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government.
But while they may have helped block an outright win by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, parties representing Israel's 21% Arab minority have so far been shunned by the prime minister's main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, who has no clear path to power without them.
Vote tallies show the two main Arab parties on course to win around 19 of parliament's 120 seats, nearly double their current representation in the Knesset. Netanyahu's coalition bloc is on track for 53 seats, short of the 61 needed for a majority, with Eisenkot's grouping expected to win 48 seats.
'GETTING RID OF NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENT'
Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Arab-dominated Joint List, told Reuters his party would seek to use its projected 12 seats "to facilitate getting rid of Netanyahu's government and hopefully helping to change the political situation in Israel."
Jabareen said the Joint List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel's military campaign in Gaza and occupation of southern Lebanon.
But he left open the possibility of bolstering Eisenkot's bloc from the outside, propping up a minority government that could survive confidence votes.
"We have our demands to protect our community, to advance the rights of our community and to promote equality for our community," said Jabareen, speaking from his home in the Arab town of Umm al-Fahm.
He said the priorities were tackling soaring crime, boosting funding and opportunities in Arab communities, and reopening peace talks on a Palestinian state.
The second main Arab party, Ra'am, is led by Mansour Abbas, who joined Naftali Bennett's government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.
This time, Abbas, a dentist-turned-politician, has sought to make Ra'am a more attractive coalition partner, adding a Jewish former police official to its slate and saying he would join an Eisenkot-led government.
Speaking to Israeli television after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Ra'am chief Mansour Abbas said: "I believe we can overcome the difficulties ... and I think that most voters for the (Eisenkot) bloc do want to see (a) government with the Ra'am party."
He said senior members of Eisenkot's bloc had discussed a possible deal with him even before the election.
Eisenkot ruled out forming a government with Arab parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.
In remarks to supporters after exit poll results were published on Tuesday night, Eisenkot said he would work to form a "stable Zionist government that serves all Israeli citizens."
Ameer Fakhoury, a political sociologist at Jerusalem's Van Leer Institute, said that Arab votes may block Netanyahu and make an alternative government possible.
"But arithmetic is not legitimacy. The Jewish opposition may need Palestinian votes while refusing Palestinian partners. That is the central paradox," he said.
ARABS FRUSTRATED BY RIGHT-WING RHETORIC
Israel's Arab minority is mostly descended from Palestinians who lived under Ottoman and British colonial-era rule and who remained inside the borders of what became the modern state of Israel in 1948.
Throughout the elections campaign, Israel's far-right have demonized Palestinian citizens of Israel and branded Arab political participation as a threat to the state.
Ahead of the vote, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich proposed a plan to "Judaize" areas around Nazareth and in southern Israel where many Arabs live, comparing it to Jewish settlement expansion in the West Bank.
Pollsters had predicted high Arab turnout, and, on election day, Netanyahu, Smotrich and far-right partner Itamar Ben-Gvir repeatedly warned that Arabs were voting in large numbers, appealing to their own supporters to turn out.
Mohamed Abbas, 19, speaking in Nazareth, said he and many others in his generation were driven to vote by what he described as rising racism toward Arab Palestinian citizens.
"We want equality...we do not want displacement laws or preference given to Jewish people," Abbas said. REUTERS

Ukrainian Christmas Drop: Weave a centuries-old tradition at home with Kyiv Independent and Pavuk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:16:58 UTC
01:16:58 KST

Ukrainian Christmas Drop: Weave a centuries-old tradition at home with Kyiv Independent and Pavuk
The Kyiv Independent has teamed up with Ukrainian brand Pavuk on a limited-edition Christmas drop built around one of Ukraine's oldest holiday traditions: weaving a pavuk, a delicate mobile made of rye straw.
The collection includes two sets created specially for the Kyiv Independent community in collaboration with Pavuk. Each set contains everything you need to make a pavuk, a hanging mobile woven from rye straw, alongside handmade Christmas ornaments. All handmade in Ukraine, with details in the Kyiv Independent's signature blue.
Only 150 sets were made, and the Kyiv Independent community got first access to pre-order them. The drop resonated with members: one of the two sets — the Winter Diamond and Snowflakes Set — sold out in the first few hours.
The Christmas Star and Surprise Ornaments Set is still available. If you'd like to bring a piece of Ukrainian tradition into your home this Christmas, there's still time to get yours. Presale is open now at the Kyiv Independent Store, and sets begin shipping on Nov. 11.
For centuries, Ukrainian families have woven pavuks, which literally means "spider," and used them to decorate their homes at Christmastime. Hung from a ceiling beam or in a window, the pavuk turns with the slightest draft, casting shadows on the walls, and its gentle movement was believed to protect the home and everyone living in it. Pavuks were made across Ukraine, from Polissia and Kyiv Oblast to Bukovyna and the Carpathians. With this collection, the Kyiv Independent set out to bring that tradition into readers' homes, wherever they live.
From a grandmother's table to homes around the world
Pavuk's founder, Tetiana Poddubna, learned to weave pavuks as a child, at her grandmother Kateryna's table in the village of Novi Kryvotuly in western Ukraine. As an adult, she set out to revive the tradition and share it with others. Then she learned that one of her grandmother's pavuks had been kept in the village's house of culture for more than 20 years. Tetiana recreated it with the Pavuk team and the village community, adding a new chapter to the family story.
"We grow the rye for our pavuks ourselves," said Tetiana. "The whole journey of each piece matters to us: from the sown grain to an object made by hand. Through our pieces and kits, we aim to pass on the way we care for natural materials and a sense of the land's strength, and to introduce the world to Ukraine through its living culture, family stories, and the experience of making things together."
A blue starry night
The Kyiv Independent Store had been talking to Pavuk about creating something special for Kyiv Independent supporters for a while. During one of those discussions, Tetiana had the idea of adding deep blue tassels to the traditional pavuks to match the Kyiv Independent's signature color.
"The idea of blue tassels came almost immediately, when I started working on a pavuk for the Kyiv Independent," she says. "I imagined the blue starry sky of a bright Christmas night. I remembered the words of a song based on a poem by Mykhailo Starytsky: 'What a moonlit night, so starry and clear, you could even gather needles by its light.' That was exactly the mood I wanted to convey."
The tassels are tied by hand by Pavuk craftswoman Olha, and the same blue thread is used to hand-stitch the envelopes that hold each kit's straws.
Two sets, limited to only 150 pieces
The Christmas Star and Surprise Ornaments Set includes everything needed to make the "Christmas Star" pavuk. It also comes with two handmade Christmas ornaments, chosen at random from six designs: two different angels, a star, a bell, and two spinning cones, and a surprise when the box is opened. Only 100 boxes were made, and fewer than 40 are left.
The Winter Diamond and Snowflake Set, now sold out, includes a kit for making a diamond-shaped pavuk inspired by the geometric patterns of Ukrainian embroidery, and five handmade straw snowflake stars.
The ornaments and stars are made by Inna, a straw-weaving craftswoman from Volyn with more than 20 years of experience.
"My mission is to preserve and popularize Ukrainian straw weaving, pass it on to the next generations, and show that every straw holds a special beauty," Inna says.
No experience is needed to make either pavuk. Each set includes step-by-step instructions, video tutorials, and spare straws in case any break, and it takes about 1.5 hours for one person to make a pavuk. Every set arrives in a gift box with a postcard.
The remaining Christmas Star and Surprise Ornaments Sets are available for pre-order now on the Kyiv Independent Store.
About the collaborator
Pavuk is a Ukrainian brand founded in 2023 by Tetiana Poddubna to revive and popularize the craft of the straw pavuk. Alongside rye for its pavuks, the brand grows wheat and other grains for straw decorations and didukhs, the traditional Christmas sheaves that symbolize the harvest, prosperity, and the memory of ancestors. Pavuk creates handmade decorations and DIY weaving kits, runs workshops, and makes photo and video tutorials, so that anyone, anywhere, can make a pavuk of their own.
One of the Kyiv Independent's founding missions is to serve as a bridge between Ukraine and the world. Collections like this one give readers another way to discover Ukrainian culture and traditions while supporting independent journalism. To become a regular supporter of the Kyiv Independent, consider becoming a member.

Canadian advocates, academics urge reassessment of refused study permits for Palestinian students from Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:16:01 UTC

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Rights advocates, academics and a Canadian party leader urged the government on Wednesday to reassess refused study permit applications from Palestinian graduate students accepted into Canadian universities, warning that promises of fair treatment have not been kept.
Speaking at a news conference in Ottawa on behalf of the Palestinian Students and Scholars at Risk Network (PSSAR), Baher Abdulhai said: "Despite repeated assurances from government officials, students from Gaza are receiving refusals, rather than the fair resolutions they were promised."
"What began as a crisis of endless processing times and delays turned into a crisis of fairness and accountability. Unfortunately, the government’s commitments have not translated into results," he said.
Abdulhai said that of 37 students outside the Gaza Strip whom the network is tracking, about 30 have reportedly received refusals or remain without substantive decisions.
"To be frank, we are particularly concerned by reports of students undergoing extensive, aggressive, interrogative immigration interviews, only to receive refusals at the end questioning their credibility or alleged affiliations," he said.
He noted that countries including Spain and the UK have evacuated Palestinian students from Gaza and waived their biometrics. "Canada must demonstrate comparable urgency," he said, urging a temporary mobile biometrics unit in Gaza.
Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, who sits on the executive of the Canada Palestinian Parliamentary Friendship Group, said the students have "already been scrutinized and accepted by leading universities in Canada."
"These students being treated like this makes me ashamed to be Canadian," she said.
Aaron Shafer, a professor at Trent University, said that "well over 100 Palestinian graduate students" have earned admission to leading Canadian universities. "But for over two years, the Canadian government has ignored their files.”
He noted that Palestinian students in Cairo faced lengthy interviews involving repeated questions about Hamas activity at their schools.
"Students should not be collectively penalized for receiving an education in Gaza," he said, adding that security assessments "must be based on individual evidence, not assumptions about an entire population."
He also urged a reassessment of all rejected Cairo applications and timely decisions on outstanding cases.
Corey Balsam, national coordinator of Independent Jewish Voices, said the group was appealing as Jewish Canadians because Jewish safety "has too often been invoked" as a reason against welcoming Palestinians from Gaza.
"We unequivocally reject that premise, which is rooted in anti-Palestinian racism, not reality," he said.
Balsam, who studied and worked at Birzeit University in the occupied West Bank, said: "With every single university in Gaza now in ruins, the absolute least our government can do is to allow Palestinian students already accepted to Canadian universities to pursue their education, their dreams, and their lives."
Firaaz Azeez of the Humaniti Foundation said that "behind every application is a life, a life that’s on hold."
He said humanitarian work should focus not only on survivability but on "stability and about the future," and that "Canada must be held to the same standard."

Knife attacker shot dead outside Israeli Embassy in Belgrade (VIDEO)
Serbia has raised the terrorism alert to the highest level after a knife-wielding minor attacked a guard outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade on Wednesday, the government said.
The attacker was shot dead at the scene of the incident, which took place at around 12:15 AM local time.
“A minor, whose identity has not yet been established… attacked a member of the Gendarmerie with two knives while shouting ‘Allahu Akbar,’” caretaker Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said in a government press release, adding that the suspect was believed to be from the western Serbian town of Sabac. “The Gendarmerie officer neutralized the attacker in self-defense and sustained minor injuries in the process.”
According to the Belgrade Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office, the attacker opened the door of the guard booth and threw a knife that struck the officer’s left cheek. The guard fired several shots, killing the attacker.
The embassy was the site of a similar attack in June 2024, when a crossbow-wielding attacker wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the compound before being shot dead.
Israel ordered tighter security at its embassies last May, after a man shot two embassy employees dead in Washington. The suspect reportedly said he did it “for Palestine” and “for Gaza” during his arrest.
Israeli embassies have faced heightened threats since the Gaza war began in October 2023, amid international condemnation of Israel’s military operation, which has killed nearly 75,000 Palestinians, according to the enclave’s health authorities.
Reported anti-Semitic incidents have also remained above prewar levels. Last year, anti-Semitic attacks killed 20 people worldwide, the highest toll in more than three decades according to Tel Aviv University’s annual report published in April.
The Belgrade attack also came as Israel counted votes from Tuesday’s parliamentary election, which had the highest voter turnout in decades. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who led Israel during the Gaza war and conflicts with Iran, is seeking another term. However, neither his bloc nor the main opposition grouping has secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority as counting continued Wednesday.

The protests come ahead of nationwide demonstrations planned for Saturday, with more than 145,000 students and young people already registered online, according to the organizers.
The initiative Gen Z steht auf, or Gen Z stands up, said it would hold its main demonstrations in Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt and Cologne, with additional protests planned in 27 other cities.

Germany brigade in Lithuania to monitor Kaliningrad, Belarus with electronic warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:11:08 UTC
01:11:08 KST

Germany brigade in Lithuania to monitor Kaliningrad, Belarus with electronic warfare
PALUKNYS AIRFIELD, Lithuania, Oct 28 - Germany's permanent brigade in Lithuania will use electronic warfare capabilities to provide early warning of military activity in Kaliningrad and Belarus, the military's cyber chief said.
The brigade, due to be fully deployed next year, will also collect data on Russian and Belarusian military emitters and radar systems to update electronic-warfare databases used by German and allied forces, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum told Reuters.
"If anything happens, these units will identify that", he said.
"We'll put (the data) into electronic warfare databases which will then inform all our systems if there is a new radar on the Belarusian side."
Daum said Russian activities in parts of Europe had reached what he called "phase two, where the intent is to hurt" below the threshold of armed conflict.
"The cyber-information domain is not yet at war, but it's no longer peace", he said.
He said an earlier phase had focused on covertly penetrating Western networks through cyber attacks and establishing footholds inside systems.
Germany's cabinet in August approved measures, which must still be approved in parliament, to grant intelligence services new powers to hack communications and disrupt foreign adversaries' operations to counter what officials say is a growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks.
The German army is currently testing electronic-warfare systems in Lithuania, such as drone-detection tools, signal interceptors, jammers and sensors designed to relay battlefield data to remote analysts.
Before the war in Ukraine, the German military could barely convince commercial companies to supply it with such systems, said Patrick Jeschke, who heads the Bundeswehr's cyber innovation hub.
The challenge has shifted from finding suppliers to selecting the most promising technologies from a flood of proposals, he said.
"Over the last decades, we have not invested too much money into new capabilities. We've used what we had because we were focused on missions abroad, in Afghanistan and other places," said Daum.
"Now... there is a need to improve our capabilities." REUTERS

The first findings about the accident in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha are likely to revive questions about rail safety in Spain after another high-speed collision in January killed 46 people.

A train operated by state company Renfe restarted and travelled 25km until it collided with a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo, at a speed that could have reached “up to 200 kilometres per hour”, Puente added.
“It is clear that, in the control centre, the decision was taken to restart, and then they had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it,” Puente said. AFP

Wild maral deer spotted at Almaty Nature Reserve

Wild maral deer spotted at Almaty Nature Reserve
A maral deer (Cervus elaphus), one of the largest and most graceful inhabitants of Kazakhstan's mountain forests, has been captured on camera at the Almaty State Nature Reserve, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Maral deer can weigh up to 300 kilograms and are found throughout the reserve at elevations of 1,200 to 3,500 meters above sea level. According to the Forestry and Wildlife Committee of Kazakhstan's Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, they inhabit mixed and coniferous forests, as well as subalpine and alpine areas.
"The most distinctive feature of male maral deer is their large, branching antlers. They shed their old antlers every year in March and April, after which new ones begin to grow. Females do not have antlers," the committee said.
With its impressive appearance and natural habitat among towering mountains and dense forests, the maral is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful representatives of Kazakhstan's wildlife.
Previously, Qazinform reported that a rare ermine had been spotted in Kazakhstan's Kaindy Gorge.

Lawyers for ‘King of the South’ Try to Chip Away at U.S. Drug Trafficking Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:09:00 UTC
01:09:00 KST

Attorneys for alleged South American drug trafficker Sebastián Marset have asked a federal judge to halt the search of a potentially pivotal cellular phone until the U.S. government explains how it took control of the device from Bolivia.
Marset, a Uruguayan national and self-proclaimed “King of the South,” was arrested in March in a pre-dawn raid in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. Soon after his arrest, he was expelled to Peru and then whisked to the U.S. where he faces money laundering, drug trafficking and narco terrorism charges.
Law enforcement officers in Bolivia seized three phones from the house where they arrested Marset. However, it has emerged that they seized a fourth phone from an adjacent house.
Defense lawyers say in their motion — dated October 23 — that “it is impossible” for them to “be certain as to the timing of the search and whether it was done at the behest of the DEA [Drug Enforcement Administration] or was otherwise valid under Bolivian law.”
They argue that they weren’t notified about the fourth phone, which was a potential key piece of evidence for months, hampering their efforts and raising questions about the integrity of the operation.
The phone was sent to the DEA in mid-April, but didn’t appear in any court documentation shared with the defense team until late July.
“No contemporaneous report of the chain of custody appears to have been prepared,” Marset’s defense team wrote to U.S. District Judge Rossie Alston Jr., who presides in the Eastern District of Virginia.
The DEA confirmed to the defense team, the filing said, that it had extracted data from the phone without a court order. The agent "theorized that the search did not require a court order because the defendant had previously ‘consented’ to the search of his other devices."
The lead prosecutor did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication. The DEA said it “does not comment on allegations.”
The prosecution has alleged that the four phones were used by Marset to access cryptocurrency accounts.
Crypto accounts have featured prominently in pre-trial disputes. Marset’s legal team alleges that DEA agents tried to trick his elderly mother into handing over passphrases for accounts that hold his digital currency, and later asked him to “donate” his $4 million in crypto assets.
“A seizure does not require asking the detainee’s mother for a photo of a notebook containing access phrases, which are used to move funds, not to secure them. Such contradictions warrant an explanation, which has yet to be provided,” Santiago Moratorio, Marset’s Uruguayan attorney, told OCCRP.
In a September court proceeding, the lead DEA agent denied the allegation that they had asked for a donation.
The Marset case is being closely watched across South America because of his connections to Colombia, and allegations that he had protection in Paraguay and Bolivia where more than a dozen officials were recently detained under suspicion that they had ties to Marset.
The State Department recently revoked visas for 12 Bolivian government, police, and political figures. It cited the need to defend against corruption and narco-trafficking, and said another unidentified nine Bolivians would be denied visas.
Marset’s lawyers argue that the initial charge of money laundering is invalid because it involved a single wire transfer between Portugal and China that did not involve the servers of a U.S. bank. The lawyers say Marset never trafficked drugs to the U.S. and the narco terror groups cited in court were not designated as such at the time of his dealing with them.
In pre-trial conferences, Marset’s defense team has challenged several elements of the case, trying to get the judge to strike down portions of the indictments and weaken the prosecution. Alston has said he would rule on these motions by November 6.

Israeli soldier visiting UK faces war crimes complaint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:06:17 UTC
01:06:17 KST

Israeli soldier visiting UK faces war crimes complaint
The Hind Rajab Foundation files complaint against an active Israeli soldier, escalating its global accountability campaign.
The Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a criminal complaint in the United Kingdom against Lidor Dafna, an Israeli reservist believed to be visiting the country, over alleged war crimes committed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Dafna, who served in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion, is accused of participating in the demolition of a flour-producing facility in May 2025 at a time when Israel’s blockade of Gaza was leading to widespread starvation.
The foundation said footage posted by Dafna on social media shows an Israeli military bulldozer demolishing wheat silos in southern Gaza.
The filing is the latest move by the Brussels-based organisation, named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old girl killed alongside her relatives when Israeli forces fired on their vehicle in Gaza City in January 2024.
By transforming self-published digital content into evidence for criminal complaints, the foundation is testing whether legal systems in other countries may be used to hold Israeli soldiers accountable for alleged crimes.
Natacha Bracq, head of litigation at the foundation, explained the urgency of the UK filing to Al Jazeera.
“If the authorities let him leave, he [Dafna] will go back and commit more crimes. When a state waves a suspect through its airport, knowing what is documented, it is breaching its obligations to prevent and punish genocide.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to the UK’s Metropolitan Police for comment on the case but has yet to receive a response.
For the families of victims in Gaza, the pursuit of justice through international channels is a response to the failure of internal Israeli accountability mechanisms.
Speaking from Gaza, the 45-year-old grandmother and namesake of Hind dismissed internal Israeli military investigations.
“The occupation [Israel] claims that it opens criminal justice or an investigation for their soldiers, [but] we are certainly not very interested in this topic,” she stated. “They just justify their positions to the world, … but actually on the ground, I don’t think anything happens.”
The foundation’s broader goal resonates deeply with families seeking justice for children killed during the war.
“Hind is not the first child in Gaza. Hind means surely there are many crimes like hers and more,” her grandmother added. “We support anyone who speaks in the name of childhood [and always supports] the Palestinian child.”
Turning social media posts into evidence
The Hind Rajab Foundation’s methodology relies heavily on material published by Israeli soldiers themselves.
“Our starting point is simple: Israeli soldiers documented their own crimes. They’ve posted tens of thousands of photos and videos from Gaza and Lebanon on TikTok, Instagram, X and Telegram, often with their faces and names attached,” Bracq said.
This digital footprint requires rigorous processing to become potentially admissible in legal cases.
“Our collection and analysis follow the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations. Then the real work starts: verification. We geolocate every frame against satellite imagery, matching buildings, roads, water towers, destruction patterns,” Bracq said, noting that investigators then cross-reference military sources to tie a suspect to a documented act.
The Berkeley Protocol, developed by the Human Rights Center at the University of California in Berkeley and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, sets out standards for collecting, verifying, analysing and preserving digital material.
Khaled al-Shouli, an international lawyer registered with the Jordanian Bar Association who represents Palestinian victims before the International Criminal Court (ICC), said social media material could be valuable evidence.
“Its value does not decrease simply because it is a post on the internet, nor does it become decisive simply because it has spread,” al-Shouli said.
He stressed, however, that answering fundamental questions about the source, time and place is essential.
“The crucial difference is the transition from proving the occurrence of the crime to proving the responsibility of a specific person for it as the appearance of a soldier in a place does not alone prove his commission of the crime,” he said.
Legal action across borders
The foundation’s complaints have prompted authorities in several countries to question Israeli military personnel.
Bracq pointed to a significant breakthrough in Belgium, where a complaint filed by the foundation led federal police to detain and question two Israeli soldiers. Both were subsequently released.
“That arrest matters beyond the two individuals involved. It demonstrated that universal jurisdiction is not a theoretical instrument but one that puts suspects in a police station within hours, and the Belgian federal prosecutor has since referred the case onward to the International Criminal Court,” she stated.
Similar actions have disrupted travel for an Israeli in North America. In Canada, former combat soldier Guy Hochman was detained and interrogated for six hours at Toronto Pearson Airport after a complaint was filed accusing him of war crimes and incitement to genocide. He later said his Canadian visa had been revoked.
“These are ruptures in a system of impunity: the moment Israelis calculate that travelling abroad carries a real legal risk,” Bracq emphasised.
Al-Shouli clarified the legal architecture supporting these moves, distinguishing between national courts and the ICC.
“The Palestinian case relies on a set of matters that fall under the category of territorial jurisdiction over crimes committed in the Palestinian territories and not on absolute universal jurisdiction,” he noted. “This distinction is important because the multiplicity of paths expands the opportunities for accountability and does not leave it hostage to one institution.”
Limits of legal action
A Hind Rajab Foundation complaint in Brazil highlighted both the potential and the limitations of filing cases against Israelis in the courts of other countries.
In January 2025, Brazilian authorities issued an urgent order to arrest and investigate an Israeli soldier accused of planting explosives and systematically demolishing entire civilian neighbourhoods in Gaza.
While the case attracted international attention, al-Shouli cautioned against overstating its significance. Although a Brazilian judge ordered an investigation after the foundation’s complaint, the Israeli soldier left the country with the assistance of Israeli authorities before he could be detained or questioned.
The case, he explained, highlighted “the gap between opening an investigation and the ability to secure the suspect’s attendance to the justice of the court in practice”.
Political climates heavily influence these legal instruments. Bracq acknowledged that “political will does determine whether a warrant is executed” but countered that “international crimes carry no statute of limitations.” She noted that relentless documentation ensures “no future window of opportunity finds the evidence missing.”
Al-Shouli viewed government transitions pragmatically. “Changing governments opens practical windows for accountability through improving judicial cooperation,” he noted. “But we prefer to describe them as windows to activate the law, not as loopholes in it.”
Expanding the targets
The foundation is actively expanding its legal efforts beyond individual soldiers to companies and individuals involved in supplying weapons to Israel.
“Our focus has already expanded well beyond front-line soldiers because the strategy must evolve with the genocide itself and with our evidence,” Bracq stated. “We now target the suppliers of the tools of the crime, including companies involved in producing weapons for Israel.”
She cited a recent criminal complaint in Poland against a state-owned TNT producer. “No one gets impunity, from the trigger-puller to the decision-maker to the supplier,” she declared.
For the legal teams, managing the expectations of devastated families remains paramount.
“My professional responsibility begins with not selling false hopes and fake hopes to the victims. It is not permissible for me to tell a family that lost its children that depositing a file has restored its right,” al-Shouli stated. “What we ask for is not sympathy alone but rights that can be proven, claimed and accounted for, and justice will be done.”
“Universal jurisdiction is our instrument, not our objective. Our objective is justice and accountability,” Bracq concluded.
“The generation that posted their own atrocities online now has to live with the knowledge that those posts are forever evidence and that a complaint may be waiting in the next country whose border they cross.”

Kryvyi Rih authorities urge ArcelorMittal owner to reconsider plant shutdown
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:06:05 EET
01:06:05 KST

Acting Kryvyi Rih Mayor and City Council Secretary Yuriy Vilkul has sent ArcelorMittal Executive Chairman Lakshmi Mittal an open appeal, backed by city council members, urging him to reconsider plans to shut down ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih (AMKR, Dnipropetrovsk region), preserve production and jobs, and prevent a potential man-made and environmental disaster.
According to a statement published on the official website of the Kryvyi Rih City Council and its executive committee on Wednesday, the appeal initiated by Vilkul was supported by council members at a session held the same day.
The appeal says the city council, representing the entire Kryvyi Rih community, is responding to reports that AMKR intends to halt all production and subsequently mothball its industrial assets. It expresses particular concern that the city authorities learned of the plans through the media, without prior communication from the company about the possible environmental, industrial safety and socioeconomic consequences.
The appeal warns that a complete shutdown could have severe socioeconomic consequences. Before privatization, the plant employed about 57,000 people, compared with approximately 17,000 today. Further large-scale staff cuts would deprive thousands of families of income and heighten social tensions. During Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, the consequences could affect not only the stability of the Kryvyi Rih community but the country as a whole, the appeal says.
It also highlights industrial and environmental risks associated with a complete shutdown. Metallurgical and coke production processes use and generate hazardous substances, including phenolic and ammonia-containing wastewater, hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid. Halting production could create risks of widespread environmental pollution and threaten the lives and health of a population of 800,000 across Kryvyi Rih and its wider urban agglomeration, according to the appeal.
Another concern is the potential interruption of proper maintenance at hydraulic facilities operated by the mining division and mine management. Tailings storage facilities, dams and drainage systems require continuous technical supervision and maintenance, while the inflow of mine water continues regardless of whether production is operating. The appeal cites the emergency breach of the Central Tailings Storage Facility dam in 2021, whose consequences were contained at the time, and warns that the risk of a recurrence could rise significantly if the plant shuts down and staffing and funding for maintenance are reduced.
The city council argues that a complete halt is not the only option. The appeal says partial operation of the metallurgical complex remains technically possible, subject to safety measures for employees, despite missile attacks. It also points to continued domestic demand for metal products for construction and infrastructure reconstruction.
The appeal separately stresses that the mining division could continue operating. Despite restrictions on Black Sea port use, iron ore concentrate could be transported by rail to ArcelorMittal plants in Europe at volumes of up to 300,000 tonnes per month, as the company had done over the past 20 years. This would help sustain production, preserve jobs and maintain economic activity, the appeal says.
In view of these circumstances, the city council calls on Lakshmi Mittal to intervene personally and ensure a review of the plans for a complete shutdown, with a view to preventing an industrial and environmental disaster, preserving production capacity and retaining as many jobs as possible.
" We are convinced that supporting the enterprise, its employees and the local community during this exceptionally difficult period for Ukraine would demonstrate the responsibility of an international investor and solidarity with the Ukrainian people as they resist military aggression," the appeal says.
As reported, AMKR has begun preparations to place the plant into cold shutdown following four destructive missile attacks that killed six employees and injured more than 18 others. Primary metallurgical production has already been halted, and the company has started implementing the cold-shutdown process.
The company said the process would take place over the following two months, covering preparations for a safe shutdown and its implementation, followed by the mothballing of industrial assets with the aim of resuming operations after hostilities end.
AMKR CEO Mauro Longobardo said cold shutdown was more than a production stoppage. It was a precautionary measure to ensure business sustainability and manage significant risks at the level of each asset. The company's top priority was to protect its people and industrial assets so that operations could resume at the earliest possible opportunity.
Longobardo said ArcelorMittal was not leaving Ukraine. Based on the company's current assessment, safe operations were impossible while the war continued. Once the war ended and conditions allowed, the company would begin discussions with the Ukrainian government and reassess whether operations could be resumed safely and sustainably.
Since the start of the war, ArcelorMittal has provided more than USD 700 million in financial support, while AMKR has invested about USD 500 million from its own cash reserves to support the business and maintain operational continuity.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine's largest producer of rolled steel, specializing in long products, including reinforcing bar and wire rod. ArcelorMittal also owns several smaller Ukrainian companies, including ArcelorMittal Beryslav.

Global cyber incidents hit record high in 1st half of 2026: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:03:18 UTC
01:03:18 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
 Serious cyber incidents worldwide reached a record high in the first half of 2026, with researchers warning that artificial intelligence could further increase the scale and speed of attacks, ANSA reported Wednesday, citing Italy’s information security association Clusit.
The association’s updated 2026 report, presented in Verona, recorded 4,911 serious incidents globally in January-June, up 71% from the same period last year and 105% from the preceding six months.
The figure represented 93% of all incidents recorded in 2025, with an average of 819 incidents per month.
In Italy, known incidents fell to 245 from 280 in the first half of 2025, accounting for about 5% of the global total. However, incidents classified as having “high” severity rose by nearly 20 percentage points to 57% of the country’s total.
Manufacturing became Italy’s hardest-hit sector as financially motivated cybercrime against businesses increased and hacktivism, hacking intended to advance political, social, or ideological causes, declined.
Malware accounted for 43% of incidents in Italy, compared with 22.7% in 2025.
Clusit researchers said improved security procedures and defenses following Italian cybersecurity legislation and the EU's NIS2 rules could partly explain the decline in hacktivism.
The report also highlighted early signs of “agentic hacking,” in which AI agents perform attack tasks with increasing autonomy.
Researchers warned that coordinated groups of AI agents could eventually carry out fully automated attacks, adapting their strategies and combining techniques to exploit vulnerabilities in organizations’ systems.
They called for clearer responsibilities, adaptive governance and defenses capable of responding rapidly and automatically to AI-driven threats.
“The data tells us that the nature of risk is changing,” Clusit President Anna Vaccarelli said.
She urged organizations to treat cybersecurity as essential to business continuity and a shared responsibility supporting national resilience.

What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors? More of the same is expected, with some small positives predicted.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:03:00 UTC
01:03:00 KST

What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
October 28, 2026
As Israeli politicians begin to try to build a coalition government, after an election that saw no clear winner, response from politicians in surrounding Arab countries has been muted or non-existent.
This may be because, for the time being anyway, it remains unclear as to whether the new Israeli government will continue with "business as usual" under incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether a new government headed by Netanyahu's opponents will take what is expected to be a more moderate domestic course.
Whatever the eventual outcome, the consensus is that there is unlikely to be a huge change in Israel's foreign relations with neighboring countries like Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt, and, further afield, the Gulf states. Nor is it likely to produce very different policies toward Palestinians, which many Arab populations in the region feel strongly about.
Both Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot "are two sides of the same coin," Egyptian politician Mostafa Bakry wrote on X after exit polls seemed to indicate an Eisenkot victory (something that's increasingly contested) and Israeli-Arab parties had displaced Netanyahu's far-right allies. "Arab joy at Netanyahu's near-failure to form the government does not mean that what is to come … differs greatly from his predecessor."
"An Eisenkot government would likely be politically fragile, limiting its room for maneuver," Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a commentary last week. "The biggest differences from the current government would be at home: It would halt the judicial overhaul, open a state commission of inquiry into October 7th and pass a conscription law."
However, Oppenheim explained, "when it comes to foreign policy, there would not be a fundamental transformation. Netanyahu's post-October 7th security doctrine — pre-empting threats, operating far beyond Israel's borders and holding 'buffer zones' in neighboring territories — has been embraced by nearly all Jewish Israeli parties."
Palestinian Territories: No two-state solution
One of the election campaign posters for Netanyahu's Likud party bore a stark message — "The right or Palestine" — the message being that if voters did not choose Netanyahu and his right-wing allies, his opponents would be too accommodating toward Israel's Arab-led political parties and would be open to the establishment of a Palestinian state.
But observers believe that message is exaggerated, and that the two-state solution is already dead.
"Support for Palestinian statehood has collapsed across most of the Jewish political spectrum, and permanent Israeli control over Palestinians has become normalized," Oppenheim pointed out. With the exception of one party, "all mainstream Jewish parties support, or at least acquiesce in, the settlement enterprise in some form and publicly oppose a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines."
In August this year, Eisenkot himself said that, "there is no Palestinian state, and no Palestinian state will be established under the government we form."
An Eisenkot-led government would, however, cooperate with more left-wing Israeli parties, which have previously supported a two-state solution. Any new coalition may also need the backing of Israel's Arab-led parties, who are currently thought to have increased their seats in parliament to around 19.
But as Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group, told the news agency Associated Press this week, "At best, [a new government] would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself."
A less extreme government would tone down religious messaging, might be less demanding when it came to conditions on disarming Hamas in Gaza, and could potentially move forward with the next stage of the Gaza ceasefire, agreed to in late 2025, but barely implemented. It might also do more to contain settler violence in the West Bank.
"That's because [settler extremism] is a phenomenon that doesn't enjoy the support of the majority of Israelis, damages Israel's international reputation, and suppressing it is feasible," Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Policy Council, explained on social media.
"[A new Israeli government] would keep expanding the settlements and Palestinian statehood would remain taboo," Oppenheim wrote. "Without a diplomatic track with the Palestinians, further flare-ups of violence in the West Bank and Gaza are inevitable, destabilizing the region — and normalization with Saudi Arabia will remain off the table."
Saudi Arabia: Could anti-Netanyahu bloc bring normalization?
After the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and Israel's ensuing military campaign, which has resulted in at least 70,000 Palestinians killed and Gaza devastated, Saudi Arabia's conditions for normalization with Israel have hardened.
The country, hugely influential in the Muslim world, has put out several statements saying there could be no path to normalizing relations with Israel without some progress on Palestinian statehood.
Last week, at a meeting of foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, the Saudis co-signed a communique in which the four countries said Israel was "the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond."
But there is some cooperation between the two countries behind the scenes. Analysts say that if a government less hardline than Netanyahu's gets into power in Israel, it will be easier for countries like Saudi Arabia — but also the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and Egypt, which all have varying levels of backchannel cooperation and contact with Israel — to admit to this kind of behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
Syria: Security agreement revived?
According to a study published last week by Syrian think tank, Etana, Israeli troops have come as far as 1,160 kilometers (721 miles) into Syria from the two countries' disputed border, occupied Syrian land as far as 400 kilometers from it and carried out 1,996 ground operations in southwest Syria between January and September this year.
Before elections this week there was no chance of any kind of withdrawal from Syria because it would have been seen as "defeat," Ksenia Svetlova, an associate fellow at Chatham House and a former member of the Israeli parliament, told online publication Syria in Transition this month. But if the anti-Netanyahu bloc gets into power, that could change, she suggested.
"A security agreement with Syria will become more probable, as many potential stakeholders [in a new, more centrist Israeli government] have spoken favorably about it in the past," noted Svetlova, who is also director of the Tel Aviv-based Regional Organization for Peace, Economics and Security, which works on Israeli-Palestinian-Arab partnerships. "However I do expect that it will take time as this government will be constantly attacked by the extreme right."
For months this year, Israel and Syrian diplomats negotiated a security agreement under the US' stewardship. But it came to nothing in late 2026 after Israel apparently refused to withdraw back to boundary lines established under a 1974 disengagement agreement.
Lebanon: More diplomacy wanted
Observers and media commentators in Lebanon say the Lebanese government would prefer to have Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc in power.
Lebanon and Israel are continuing to negotiate an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where the Israelis claim they have established a "buffer zone" to facilitate their fight against Lebanese militia group, Hezbollah. The Lebanese argue the Israelis have in fact invaded their country.
And when it comes to negotiations around disarming Hezbollah and withdrawing Israeli troops, there's a perception in Lebanese political circles that Eisenkot would be easier to deal with than Netanyahu and his extremist allies.
This is despite the fact that Eisenkot is widely seen as the inventor of the so-called "Dahiyeh Doctrine," a military strategy that calls for asymmetric warfare in areas like Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah is based, to pressure both militants and their civilian support base.
A similar strategy is thought to be being implemented in southern Lebanon now, where whole villages continue to be razed by the Israeli military, even as active fighting has subsided.
Lebanese commentators are also optimistic that Eisenkot, former commander of the Israeli army, would have something in common with their own president, Joseph Aoun, who used to head Lebanon's armed forces.
"When Netanyahu was ousted from power between 2021 and 2022 by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid [now members of the camp led by Eisenkot], we were able to negotiate and conclude the maritime agreement," a Lebanese official told Lebanese daily, L'Orient Today, referring to a 2022 deal to share offshore territory.

MSF urgently calls on the authorities and all parties involved to spare civilians and ensure access to healthcare facilities for all the wounded and sick, without distinction.
Heavy gunfire and drone explosions have increased in the Plaine de Cul-de-Sac area, in the northeastern part of Port-au-Prince, following the disappearance, on 18 October 2026, of several members of the Gang Suppression Force during an attack on their vehicle by members of armed groups.
Between 18 and 26 October, 30 people injured by gunfire or drone explosions were admitted and treated at MSF hospitals in Tabarre and Cité Soleil.
“We are very concerned about this surge in violence in multiple densely populated neighbourhoods of the capital,” says Davina Hayles, MSF head of mission in Haiti. “Among the victims, we have admitted multiple women and children — it is shocking to see them arriving at our hospitals, wounded by gunfire or explosions.”
Among the victims, we have admitted multiple women and children — it is shocking to see them arriving at our hospitals, wounded by gunfire or explosions.
Davina Hayles, MSF head of mission in Haiti
“We fear that this armed conflict will claim even more victims, and displace even more people in the coming days, particularly with the arrival of additional international security forces,” says Hayles. “Some of our locally based colleagues have themselves been forced to leave their homes and take refuge in MSF accommodations. It is imperative that civilians be protected and spared.”
Due to the ongoing conflict, MSF has also observed that multiple patients have faced serious difficulties accessing healthcare facilities.
“Some patients with gunshot wounds took several hours to reach our hospitals in Tabarre and Cité Soleil,” says Hayles. “Roads and bridges are blocked, and any travel is extremely risky. In a capital city where the healthcare system has collapsed and many facilities are closed, it is essential to ensure there is access to functioning healthcare facilities like ours.”
In the various neighbourhoods affected by armed conflict, MSF has also been forced to suspend our mobile clinics and distributions of treated water. 
“This is a double blow for our patients and for people who lack access to treated water in these neighbourhoods of the capital,” says Hayles. “At any moment, they could become direct or collateral victims, and on top of that, they find themselves deprived of access to healthcare and water. This situation is dreadful.”

How QR codes can make medical PDF resources easier to access

Healthcare organizations often distribute guides, research summaries, and educational documents that may be difficult to fit into printed materials. When a clinic or hospital uses a PDF to QR code link, patients and visitors can open the full document from a poster, leaflet, appointment sheet, or information card without typing a long web address.
Connecting Printed Medical Materials with Digital Documents
A QR code can connect a compact printed message with a longer digital PDF. This can be useful for preparation instructions, facility information, patient education, or general reference materials approved by the healthcare organization.
The printed item can remain simple, while the PDF provides more detailed content. If the document is updated online, a dynamic link can help organizations avoid reprinting every physical copy.
QR Codes for Patient Guides, Research, and Educational PDFs
A QR code generator can support access to different types of medical and educational documents. The key is to use clear labels so people know what they will open after scanning.
Useful applications include:
- patient guides linked from appointment materials;
- research summaries connected with conference posters;
- educational PDFs placed on waiting-room displays;
- preparation instructions linked from reminder cards;
- general facility information connected with visitor materials.
These uses are most appropriate for informational content. Sensitive personal or medical data should remain within systems that meet applicable privacy and security requirements.
Making Important Medical Resources Easier to Access
Digital PDFs can make longer resources available without requiring organizations to print extensive documents repeatedly. A QR code maker can connect each physical touchpoint with the document most relevant to that setting.
Accessibility should remain part of the planning process. Important information should not depend solely on scanning, especially when some users may not have a compatible device or reliable internet access.
How to Convert a PDF into a QR Code
The usual process begins by placing the PDF at a stable online destination. An online QR code generator can then create a code that directs users to that document, after which the finished graphic should be tested before printing.
ME-QR is an international platform for generating, managing, and analyzing QR codes, with dynamic links, scan analytics, bulk creation, API integrations, branding options, and centralized management. Its dynamic functionality can be useful when a medical PDF changes and the organization wants to keep the same printed code. The service supports users worldwide, offers an interface in 28 languages, and reports more than 20 million generated QR codes, over 300 million scans, and more than 500,000 users globally. Before distribution, the code should be tested on the final material and at the intended size. Healthcare teams should also confirm that the linked PDF remains current, accessible, and hosted in an appropriate environment.
FAQ
Can a QR code link directly to a medical PDF?
Yes. It can direct users to a PDF hosted online, provided the document is accessible through the linked destination.
Can the PDF be updated without changing the printed code?
Yes, when a dynamic QR code is used and the destination is managed accordingly.

They can appear on appointment sheets, posters, visitor materials, educational leaflets, conference materials, and other printed resources.

Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:01:04 UTC
01:01:04 KST

Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) with Cesar Chavez and fought legislators and powerful growers in the US to improve the lives of a previously powerless constituency, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, her family said in a statement.
Huerta was one of the foremost women in US labor history, serving the UFW as chief negotiator, strike organizer, lobbyist and reformer during its heyday in the 1960s and '70s in California's agriculture-rich Central Valley.
Thanks to the contracts the UFW negotiated, farmworkers won job security, healthcare, retirement plans, a credit union and job-specific benefits such as guaranteed rest periods, toilets in the fields, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides.
Huerta was credited with giving the UFW its slogan "Si, se puede," the loose translation of which, "Yes, we can," was later used by Barack Obama during his successful 2008 presidential campaign.
She remained a regular on the college lecture circuit into her 90s, speaking out against the immigration policies of President Donald Trump. During elections she traveled the country, endorsing candidates and registering voters.
UFW co-founder Chavez, who died in 1993 and was the face of the organization, was a seventh-grade dropout and former grape picker with a man-of-the-soil appeal who espoused the non-violent philosophies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King, with a nod to Emiliano Zapata, a leader of Mexico's peasant revolution in the early 20th century.
But Chavez had a dark side. In 2026, Huerta was one of a number of women who came forward with accounts of how they had been sexually assaulted by him, in some cases when they were minors. Huerta said that he had pressured her into having sex one time, and another time raped her. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, and Huerta said she arranged for the babies to be raised by others.
OUT OF THE SPOTLIGHT
While Chavez was recruiting, going on well-publicized hunger strikes and being embraced by liberal lawmakers and celebrities, the diminutive, college-educated Huerta handled negotiating with growers, lobbying legislators and other business for the UFW.
She was arrested more than 20 times, subjected to death threats and other harassment. She suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen when beaten by baton-wielding San Francisco police in a 1988 protest against the policies of George H.W. Bush during his presidential campaign.
In an interview with PBS in 2012, before the assault accusations against Chavez came to light, Huerta said she had been fine with him taking the spotlight as she wanted to focus on helping people rather than gaining fame.
"He said, 'One of us is going to have to be the spokesperson. Are you all right if I'm the spokesperson?' Of course, I said yes."
STANDING UP
Huerta was born in Dawson, New Mexico, to a Mexican immigrant family, and spent much of her youth in Stockton, California, after her parents divorced. Her father was a miner, laborer, union activist and state lawmaker; her mother raised three children while buying and running a hotel for low-income people in Stockton.
Huerta's mother instilled a spirit of activism in her daughter. Huerta was into her second marriage when she became a schoolteacher, but that career did not last long.
"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."
She registered voters in Stockton and founded the Agricultural Workers Association before meeting Chavez and joining him in starting the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 they began a series of strikes and boycotts that would last five years against various California grape growers and eventually spread to lettuce growers.
During that period the organization evolved into the United Farm Workers and picked up support from King and New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy. Not eating a grape — unless it had a union label — became a political statement in the United States.
The boycotts and strikes sometimes became contentious. In addition to industry opposition, the UFW found itself up against California Governor Ronald Reagan, who denounced the UFW as immoral and made a point of eating grapes on television.
COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
One by one, growers began signing contracts with the UFW and in 1975 Huerta's work also helped bring about another victory — passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first law in the US that gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.
Huerta said that being a woman gave her an edge at the negotiating table with growers.
"They really didn't know how to respond because they couldn't do the usual forceful type of thing," she told PBS. "And when you would bring up to them and show them the conditions that the workers were working under, and they were kind of embarrassed, actually."
In 2012, Obama presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian award.
Her life was the basis of the award-winning film "Dolores" that was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017.
While the UFW's influence abated, Huerta's activism did not. In 2002 she established the Dolores Huerta Foundation for community activism with her daughter Camila Chavez as its executive director. She pushed for changes in immigration laws, voter registration, women's rights and Obama's healthcare reform.
Huerta, who said she remained close to the two children she had with Chavez, also had two children from her first marriage, five from her second and four from a long-term relationship with Richard Chavez, brother of Cesar and another key UFW figure, who died in 2011. REUTERS

Jetten calls for tougher sanctions against Russia ahead of talks
Gordon Darroch
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten has called for Europe to present a united front and step up sanctions against Russia in order to force Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine.
Jetten told reporters at a joint president with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in The Hague that economic pressure was needed to persuade Putin to give ground.
His remarks came after Polish president Donald Tusk said the US, Ukraine and Russia had provisionally agreed to hold ceasefire talks in Abu Dhabi on November 4.
European leaders will not be present, but Tusk said Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had held a call with Putin after consulting Zelenskyy and the American side.
Zelenskyy told reporters in The Hague that it was “very important” for Europe to show unity “because Russia is focusing on how to divide us”.
“Russia is losing,” he said. “The American side is asking to find a balance and a compromise. If they need a compromise, we say: Russia is not winning. But what is very clear is they are not ending the war.
No Russian gas
“That is the problem. That’s why we need to work step by step and move Russia to end this war.”
Jetten also ruled out restarting supplies of Russian gas to Europe, an idea reportedly raised by Donald Trump’s peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during talks with Zelenskyy at the weekend.
“It is clear that we need to push Putin to take the negotiations seriously,” he said.
“The way forward for Europeans, but also for Americans and others, is to put more sanctions on the Russian regime, not less. So buying Russian energy is a very stupid idea. I can assure you that there is no European leader who is willing to buy Russian gas in the next few years.
“What we want is for Russia to stop this war, and as long as they don’t we will hit them hard in their pockets with sanctions.”
Aid packages
The Dutch government announced on Wednesday it was spending another €1.2 billion on non-military aid to Ukraine over the next three years, as well as €500 million on military support in the form of air defence and drones.
The non-military aid, announced by foreign trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma on a visit to Kyiv, will address “the most urgent needs” such as energy, drinking water, humanitarian aid, healthcare and medicine, as well as operations to clear landmines.
“Russia is hoping to break Ukraine’s morale, its society and its economy,” Jetten said.
“But they will not succeed. Firstly because of the great courage and resilience of the Ukrainians themselves, but also because we as allies realise that we must not let up on giving our support.”

Britain’s military presence in the South Atlantic is at the appropriate level for the defence of the Falkland Islands, and the absence of an ice patrol ship does not change that, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what assessment has been made of the potential impact on Argentine posture in the region of having no ice patrol ship available.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence is committed to maintaining a defensive military presence in the South Atlantic to ensure the protection of the Falkland Islands and South Atlantic Islands. Our defences in the South Atlantic are robust, consisting of air, land, and maritime forces with a strong permanent presence on the Falkland Islands. I am confident that our military presence is at the appropriate level for the defence of the Islands, and we keep this under constant review.”
British forces in the South Atlantic are based around Mount Pleasant Complex on East Falkland, where Typhoons of 1435 Flight hold quick reaction alert, supported by a Voyager tanker, an A400M and Sky Sabre ground based air defence. A River class offshore patrol vessel is forward deployed to the region and the islands are garrisoned by a roulement infantry company.
HMS Protector carries out survey and inspection work under the Antarctic Treaty and has no combat role, though her presence has long been part of the pattern of British activity in the South Atlantic. She last deployed south in the 2024-25 season and will miss a second consecutive Antarctic season this year.
