Diets high in fat and sugar are linked to impulsiveness in people with borderline personality disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

A study of adults with borderline personality disorder in the Chicago area found that those who ate more foods high in both saturated fat and added sugar tended to report greater motor impulsiveness, a tendency to act without thinking. Higher saturated fat intake was also linked to more risk-taking on a gambling task, but diet was not associated with the overall severity of borderline personality disorder symptoms. The paper was published in Nutritional Psychiatry.
Borderline personality disorder, or BPD, is a mental health condition characterized by intense emotions, unstable relationships, difficulties with self-image, and impulsive behavior. People with BPD often struggle to regulate their emotions and may engage in risky behaviors, such as excessive spending, substance misuse, or binge eating. Although specialized psychotherapy can help, about half of adults with BPD do not respond to it, highlighting the need for additional approaches.
One potentially important but largely overlooked factor is nutrition. Research has linked diets high in saturated fat and added sugar, which are common in processed foods, to greater impulsivity. Such foods may also influence the brain’s reward system and inflammatory processes, potentially affecting how people experience and manage emotions.
At the same time, people may turn to highly palatable foods in response to stress or negative emotions, suggesting that the relationship between diet and psychological functioning could work in both directions. Research on diet in BPD is limited, but one study found that women with BPD ate fewer omega-3 fatty acids and fewer foods typical of a Mediterranean diet than healthy controls. In two clinical trials, omega-3 supplements combined with the medication valproic acid appeared to reduce some BPD symptoms, particularly anger.
Study authors Sophie Boutouis and Jon E. Grant of the University of Chicago wanted to examine the relationship between saturated fat and added sugar consumption and BPD symptoms, as well as differences in diet across demographic groups. They hypothesized that higher intake of saturated fat and added sugar would be associated with more severe BPD symptoms, more co-occurring psychiatric disorders, poorer decision-making, and greater impulsivity.
The participants were adults from the Chicago area who enrolled in a clinical trial testing the antipsychotic lumateperone as a treatment for BPD. To take part, they had to be between 18 and 65 years old, have a primary diagnosis of BPD, and have symptoms above a set severity threshold; people with schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder, or moderate or severe substance use disorders were excluded. The analysis used data collected at the trial’s first visit, before treatment began.
Of 60 eligible participants, 57 completed the diet questionnaire and were included in the analysis. Their average age was 32, about 72% were women, and about half identified as white.
Participants reported how often they had eaten various foods high in saturated fat and added sugar over the past year using the Dietary Fat and Free Sugar – Short Questionnaire, which produces separate scores for foods high in saturated fat, foods high in added sugar, and foods high in both. They also completed the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale and the Cambridge Gambling Task, a computerized test of decision-making in which risk-taking is measured by how many points participants bet. Clinicians assessed co-occurring psychiatric disorders and suicidal thoughts using the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview and rated the severity of BPD symptoms over the past week.
After accounting for age, race, depression, and suicidal thoughts, participants who ate more saturated fat tended to bet more on the gambling task, indicating greater risk-taking. After accounting for age, those who ate more foods high in both saturated fat and added sugar tended to report greater motor impulsiveness. Added sugar intake on its own was not linked to any of the impulsivity, decision-making, or symptom measures.
Contrary to the main hypothesis, diet was not associated with the overall severity of BPD symptoms, other aspects of impulsivity, or other aspects of decision-making. The authors note that diet was measured over the past year while symptom severity was measured over the past week, which may help explain why no link emerged.
The researchers also found demographic differences. Black participants reported eating more saturated fat than participants from several other groups, and people who ate more foods high in both fat and sugar tended to be older. Participants without depression or recent suicidal thoughts reported eating more saturated fat than those with these conditions, and those with a substance use disorder reported eating less added sugar.
“Saturated fat and added sugar consumption in the past year may be associated with domains related to BPD (i.e., impulsivity, risk-taking behavior). As causality cannot be inferred due to the cross-sectional design of this study, future research should examine whether improvements in nutrition may lead to reductions in BPD symptoms,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of BPD. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a relatively small group of participants seeking treatment in a clinical trial, and results in other groups may differ. The study also did not examine participants’ medication or psychotherapy status, and, as the authors noted, its cross-sectional design does not allow causal inferences.
Because of this, it remains unknown whether high intake of fat and sugar contributes to impulsiveness or whether impulsiveness leads people to eat more of these foods. Other factors not measured in the study, such as body mass index or physical activity, could also play a role. Diet was self-reported over a full year, which can be difficult to recall accurately, and participants may have underreported unhealthy foods.
The paper, “Associations between dietary fat and sugar intake and impulsivity in adults with borderline personality disorder,” was authored by Sophie Boutouis and Jon E. Grant.

Dua Lipa's literary takeover at London Literature Festival 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:59:30 UTC
00:59:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Dua Lipa is making reading cool again at this year's London Literature Festival
Pop star, activist, skincare entrepreneur and founder of an editorial platform (among her many ventures), Dua Lipa has long championed manifestation, from writing down her goals and using her song Training Season to manifest her ideal partner to mapping out major career milestones, including headlining Glastonbury.
Now, she is turning her attention to literature, taking on the role of curator for this year's 19th London Literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, one of London's leading arts and cultural venues, and cementing her status as a literary goddess of our time.
The festival brings together established literary names and emerging writers for conversations, readings, and events that explore the stories and ideas shaping our lives.
Generously supported by Bukhman Philanthropies, this year’s edition also coincides with the Southbank Centre’s 75th anniversary.
Running until 1 November, the festival has already offered plenty to get stuck into. From conversations with literary icons to poetry confronting the realities of our time and powerful personal testimony, The New Arab looks at some of the standout moments and ideas that have stayed with us so far.
Literary icons, intimate conversations and the power of poetry
For one day only, Dua made an appearance at the festival, taking to the stage alongside some of the most celebrated names in literature.
First up was British novelist Zadie Smith, whose debut novel, White Teeth, was published when she was just 24 and went on to become one of the most celebrated novels of the new millennium.
The programme also featured American singer and writer Patti Smith, who discussed her memoir, Bread of Angels. She spoke about her family and early interest in art, recalling how seeing a Picasso painting at the age of 12 and leaving the church after being told there was no place for art helped shape the independent spirit that has remained a defining part of her life and work.
Dua also welcomed Mustafa Ahmed, known as Mustafa the Poet, to the stage to discuss Nour, a project created with WePresent that brings together poetry, photography, interviews and visual art. Made freely available in 2025, the project explores themes of faith, love, grief and everyday rituals.
During the conversation, Dua revealed that Mustafa officiated her wedding to Callum Turner and wrote a poem for the couple. She described the gesture as meaningful and dedicated Noor Hindi’s Ode to Friendship to him.
Their discussion also touched on friendship and the importance of allowing the people we love the freedom to change and grow.
Special guest readings from poets Victoria Chang and Safia Elhillo added to the programme’s celebration of poetry.
A celebration of British Somali poetry
The focus on poetry continued beyond Dua’s appearance with A Celebration of British Somali Poetry, which brought together five poets to explore identity, migration and belonging. Among them was Samatar Elmi, who shared The Genocide Will Not Be Televised, a poem that combines historical references with raw, contemporary outrage.
Samatar recited the poem, which includes the lines: “The genocide will not be televised. The genocide will not be brought to you by Newsnight, Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Piers Morgan will not ask if you condemn Hamas twice a day and thrice on Sundays. There will be no need to learn that if you place a gun to a parrot’s head, it squawks: ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ in [a hundred and sixteen] languages, because the genocide will not be televised.”
Nadia Murad on survival and reclaiming her life
From poetry confronting the reporting of violence, the festival moved to personal testimony.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nadia Murad sat down with BBC journalist Lyse Doucet to discuss surviving Islamic State group (IS) captivity in Iraq, becoming a leading voice for survivors of sexual violence and reclaiming her life beyond her past.
As Nadia put it, "Survival isn’t the same as finding peace. It’s an ongoing negotiation with memory." She also reflected on the expectations she faced early in her activism, when people pressured her to put her work before her own hopes of building a new life. "Are you supposed to suppress the part of myself that loved makeup and hair?" she asked.
Nadia also spoke about her mother, who was killed by IS, and the price women have to pay during violence and conflict.
Reflecting on how public conversations often focus on the numbers of soldiers and men killed, she said: "You know, the world focuses so much on how many soldiers are recovering or how many men were killed. It’s always about the numbers and the destruction.
"But there is always a specific price that women pay. My mother was killed because she was a woman, and they felt she was a threat to them. They thought that if she survived, she would rebuild that house or build a new one and bring the family together."
To end, Nadia reflected on how she met her now-husband, Abid Shamdeen, who was working as her translator at the time.
Describing him as the "love of her life, who gives me hope every day," she also shared a touching story from her latest book, I Choose My Beginning: A Story of Courage and Activism.
When Abid asked if there was one thing she wanted to do for herself, Nadia admitted that she felt self-conscious about her teeth. He never judged her for it. Instead, he eventually told her, "Nadia, I found you an orthodontist." Before she knew it, she had braces, "like a teenager."
Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi on Palestine and freedom
The festival also turned to questions of freedom and justice, as authors Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi joined journalist Nesrine Malik to discuss Palestine, decolonisation and their books, The Message and What Now: On Palestine, Freedom, and Our Global Future.
Tareq argued: "People who have and continue to colonise Palestine, there is no way in which the ‘us’ and the ‘them’, this colonial relationship, can coexist. Zionism means Palestinian extermination, so if we are committed to Palestinian life, we have to confront Zionism for what it is: this racist ideology that has no place in our world."
Ta-Nehisi, meanwhile, discussed how American slavery's need for expansion ultimately contributed to its own undoing, suggesting that oppressive systems can be driven by an insatiable appetite for more land and control.
He also pointed to Zionism's emphasis on maintaining a Jewish demographic majority as evidence of its exclusionary character, arguing that such a "project" cannot be separated from questions of racism.
Rama Duwaji brings the festival theme to the screen
Beyond the festival’s live events, a campaign film featuring words by Dua and animation by Syrian artist Rama Duwaji brings this year’s theme, Read the World Differently, to life on the Piccadilly Lights billboard and at the Southbank Centre.
One standout piece of writing on screen was an excerpt from Sufiyaan Salam’s Merky Books New Writers’ Prize-winning debut novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, which was also featured on Dua’s Service95 platform. The story follows three British-Pakistani friends on a chaotic night drive down Manchester’s Curry Mile.
A book swap for readers
For festivalgoers looking to take a little literary inspiration home, the festival’s book swap offers the chance to exchange books and leave recommendations for fellow readers.
It is a simple way to keep the conversation going beyond the stage, with each book offering the chance to discover a new favourite or see a familiar story in a new light.
And if there is one thing Dua’s own love life suggests, it is that a shared love of books can be a pretty good conversation starter.
The singer and Callum reportedly first bonded at a party in Los Angeles after discovering they were both reading Hernán Díaz’s Trust, having each just finished the first chapter when Callum joked, "So we’re on the same page."
The London Literature Festival runs until 1 November 2026, with events still to come
Zainab Mehdi is a British-Iraqi journalist and Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS

A group of former US government officials who resigned because of Washington’s policy in the Gaza Strip has urged candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination to pledge not to appoint officials they said enabled Israel's genocide in the enclave.
“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” Gaza Resignees said in a statement signed by 12 former officials.
“They violated U.S. and international law by providing U.S. weapons while Israel indiscriminately and disproportionately attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure, and as Israel arbitrarily blocked humanitarian assistance to Gaza,” it said.
The signatories include former State Department officials Josh Paul, Annelle Sheline and Stacy Gilbert, former diplomats Hala Rharrit and Mike Casey, former White House official Anna Del Castillo and former USAID senior adviser Alexander Smith. Also among them are former Army officer and Defense Intelligence Agency official Harrison Mann, former Air Force Maj. Riley Livermore, former Navy Lt. Cmdr. Hani Z. Nofal and former political appointees Tariq Habash of the Education Department and Lily Greenberg Call of the Interior Department.
“Not even two years since the end of their disastrous time in office, many of these same officials appear to be pursuing a path back into the halls of power,” they said.
“The most basic level of accountability, the most minimal level of consequences, is to ensure that those who have wreaked so much harm from within the highest levels of our Government cannot return to it,” according to the statement.
The group said that “Gaza has become a litmus test for the credibility of American politicians and the viability, in particular, of Democratic candidates.”
The pledge asks candidates to acknowledge US “complicity” in Israel's genocide in Gaza. It also asks them to exclude any past or present political appointee who was “an architect, leader, defender, or key enabler” of the policy.
In a video released with the statement, the former officials took turns reading the call over images of former Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who now sits on the board of directors of the Center for American Progress, a Washington think tank.
“We have watched as elite institutions have welcomed these officials,” said Mann, as the video showed former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, who is now with venture capital firm Lux Capital and a CNN commentator. It also showed former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power, who both joined Harvard Kennedy School after leaving office.
“We have watched as these officials have tried to launder their bloody reputations,” Paul said, with Rharrit adding, “and prepare to re-enter the halls of power.”
“And we say, enough,” the former officials said in the video. “Enough with the culture of impunity in Washington. Enough with policies that break our laws and defy our values.”
“They have blood on their hands,” they added.
Top Biden administration officials at that time acknowledged civilian suffering in Gaza but defended Israel’s right to defend itself following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
US-made weapons were photographed several times in Israeli strikes in Gaza, although US authorities have declined to confirm this.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 175,000, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. It has also caused widespread destruction affecting around 90% of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since an October 2025 ceasefire went into effect.

Elena Dudum's Palestinian memoir confronts identity and erasure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:57:55 UTC
00:57:55 KST

Breadcrumb
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful: Elena Dudum's memoir asks what it means to inherit a homeland
At its core, every coming-of-age memoir asks: How do I convince the world that I exist? However, Elena Dudum’s memoir They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful (Atria/One Signal) complicates this simple idea by asking: How do I prove my existence when the world is committed to destroying the evidence?
Unlike traditional coming-of-age memoir that simply deals with the trials of childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood, this memoir is dedicated to the process of coming into consciousness in the face of outright denial.
A Palestinian Christian raised in San Francisco, in some ways Elena’s upbringing follows the prototypical footprint for any diasporic Arab American — her grandparents came to America and built lives.
However, the particulars of her story stand out — her Palestinian-born grandparents married American-born Arabs, and contrary to post 9/11 American popular conception, she is not Muslim.
Instead, she was heavily involved in her Palestinian Christian community as a child. She moved through adolescence and young adulthood in proximity to privilege, privately educated and rubbing elbows with San Francisco's elite.
However, the truth is that although she was in the right rooms, people viewed her differently.
A third grader in 2001, she pulled her teacher aside: "I told Miss Crane that my cousin and I would not share where our family was from… We would tell people we were from Guatemala."
The fact of their origins, uttered in hushed tones. Disguised and distorted, for fear that true disclosure would mutate into misunderstood hatred.
Whether it was classmates' parents, a friend's boyfriend at the bar, or even the college administration, Elena Dudum constantly had to push against the idea of her identity rather than its reality.
A scene that stands out: Her own sense of self, punctured as an eight-year-old, when a friend's father driving her asks, "Where’s your family from again?" Which inspired a grown man to ask a child whether or not she supports Israel. The first of a lifetime of questions ended with the resolute thought, "You guys anti-Semitic or something?"
From a young age, she is forced to understand that her identity is immediately challenged. Her family, a threat.
But she didn't understand this alone. Her father, forever frenzied with the need to educate his children, through private education and lectures on the way to school, armed them with the phrase: "You would be attributing to me a prejudice to which I do not subscribe."
A legacy of proof
This memoir, of course, follows the coming-of-age canon by having a parent to push against, but what I admire most is that this father-daughter relationship is unsentimental and deeply unresolved.
Are family dynamics ever truly resolved? So many memoirs pretend they can be. But Elena does not stray from truth: the difficulty of her father, and the identity of being Palestinian.
From childhood to adulthood, her father's lecturing is consistent. But his command and ferocity deplete her (and him) over time, her willingness to listen as a child arms her for the revelations she finds on her own as an adult.
How do you not lose your mind when trying to prove something you know exists? Elena writes, "Now he scours the web for one-hundred-year-old magazines about Palestine: LIFE, National Geographic, even The Illustrated London News, the world’s first graphic weekly news magazine. For years, he would reference these mysterious documents but show them to nobody. ‘I have proof,’ he would say, ‘that Palestine exists.’"
He has the archive. The difficulty lies in his inability to trust, even when his own daughter tries to access what he has hoarded as precious truth.
The lack of sentimentality comes down to this fact: this book is about inheriting a mission, whether she wanted to or not.
Each chapter starts with an epigraph from her father's archive: A quote from a 1946 issue of Life Magazine, describing the beauty, bounty, and existence of Palestine.
As much as he tries to keep her from it — growing belligerent and paranoid at the request — the epigraphs nod to one simple fact: she has inherited his mission, his collection.
She doesn't want to inherit this mission; her very existence forces her to.
Refusing to be erased
Elena’s memoir looks hard at who gets cast as actor and who as victim in narratives of atrocity, and how American institutions and everyday language shape that framing.
Her writing is clear and cogent: it points to the syntax and grammar of oppression, as well as the deliberate silence it produces.
What I find most palpable in this text is the question of how language can erase, displacing blame and reframing crime as power.
But it's not simply syntax and grammar; it's a lifetime series of silences. She takes her reader through her experience as an undergraduate at Barnard and a graduate student at Columbia, both institutions I also attended.
However, I did not embody the very identity that those institutions deny, villainise, and deliberately silence. She takes us through her discussions with the president of Barnard after their banner was removed from Barnard Hall after one single day (which I witnessed firsthand).
Elena goes against her father's advice, fearing for her safety. She speaks up, but to no avail: "I resented him for instilling a fear in me just as much as he instilled a fire."
As a graduate student at Columbia, Elena audits a course called The Creation of Israel. After sitting in class, agitated by the rage she witnessed her father embody, she can’t help but push back on every claim backed by studied evidence and stats, and the professor ultimately asks her not to participate.
But Elena knows better. Her family’s orange grove, remembered by her grandfather, whom she calls Siddi. She imagines Siddi as a child, sitting in a tree with ripe fruit in his palm.
The gold jewellery on her wrist, all her Taita carried away with her during the Nakba. In her genome, through generational word of mouth: she remembers. Her family’s name, engraved above a doorway in Palestine. Now, no doubt: rubble. Her family’s history officially erased by acts of war.
When asking her father the very question she grapples with most: "When did I know I was Palestinian?" Her father replies, "‘It’s not because I’m Palestinian that I’m like this,’ he says. I can’t see him, but I know he’s shaking his head. ‘It’s just who I am."'
Ultimately, Elena’s personal narrative is the counter-archive: her life, testimony. She braids memoir with archival fragments; the form itself treats family memory as resistance. She knows the rage, the denial, the sheer fight, foisted upon her and her father: "Here I am, Palestinian in your wake."
Those who witness her and her memoir in entirety hold her rage and pick up the mantle. She is no longer alone in the fight for posterity, for truth. No one can ignore this memoir, or the power of rage-inducing truth.
Paulina Pinsky is a Los Angeles-based writer, author, writing coach, educator, podcaster and performer. She is the co-author of the teen guide to consent, It Doesn’t Have to Be Awkward: Dealing with Relationships, Consent, and Other Hard-to-Talk-About Stuff
Follow her on Instagram: @paulina_pinsky

UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:56:25 UTC
00:56:25 KST

Breadcrumb
UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030, plans to meet NATO targets by 2035
The UK will increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, Chancellor John Healey has announced in the Autumn budget on Wednesday.
The Chancellor said this was part of the UK's plan to meet NATO's defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
US President Donald Trump has pressured European members of NATO to spend least 3.5% of GDP on core defence requirements after several members of the military alliance failed to meet the previous defence spending target of 2% of GDP.
As well as spending on military forces, NATO counts spending on police forces who are trained in military tactics, and can be deployed abroad as part of military operations, as defence expenditure.
Healey said he will set out the details on how he will meet the defence targets next year.
He also announced an increase in private investment in defence.
Healey previously served as Defence Secretary in Kier Starmer's Cabinet, before resigning in June over the former Prime Minister's defence investment plan, which he said "falls well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time."
Healey's resignation is widely considered one of the key factors behind the end of Starmer's premiership earlier this year.
In 2025, while Defence Secretary, Healey said the UK is in "in a new era of threat," citing the previous US-Israeli war on Iran, and Russia's war on Ukraine.
"As the threat grows, Britain must step up," he said in the same speech in Parliament.
In his budget announcement on Wednesday, he repeatedly cited the war in the Middle East as a leading cause of the UK's high cost of living, especially due to rising energy costs.
"These are the global economic storms we face'" Healey said, "we must choose the course we steer through them."
Healey also announced a £100 winter energy payment for millions of households in the lowest council tax bands.
The Chancellor also announced an extension of the five pence cut to fuel duty until July 2027.
Duty for motor fuels was temporarily cut in 2022 after fuel costs spiked following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Healey announced that the measures to ease energy bills will be funded by a temporary 3% increase in taxes for banks. The rise will be on top of the 25% corporate tax rate they currently pay.
Healey also announced an end to gas standing charges from next year in a bid to help households with energy prices which rose after the US and Israel's February invasion of Iran.
Currently, households pay a fixed yearly fee on top of their household gas bill, regardless of their usage. Scrapping the standing charge will shift that payment onto the unit rates.
That means around 60% household that use less gas will save money, while those that use the most gas will see their bills increase.
The move will not cost the Government any money. Rather, it will shift some of the burden for energy bills from lower income households to those on higher incomes.

Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.

Russian Satellites Helped Houthis Guide Missiles Toward Saudi Arabia — AP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:54:23 UTC
00:54:23 KST

Russian reconnaissance satellites collected intelligence on a key Saudi oil pipeline ahead of attacks by Iran-backed armed groups.
The Associated Press reported this, citing data from analytical company AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence.
The company analyzed 40 missile and drone attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia carried out by Yemen’s Houthi rebels and armed groups in Iraq between July 1 and October 19.
According to the analysts, Russian satellites were over the target areas several days before and after each attack.
“What we found is a 100% match between the satellite activities and strikes,” AURORAH founder Nawaf Obaid reported.
According to Obaid, the pattern may indicate a link between Russian satellite activity and preparations for an attack.
In particular, Russian reconnaissance satellites passed over the East–West pipeline before drones attacked three of its pumping stations on September 10.
The strikes halted oil transportation through the 1,200-kilometer pipeline.
The East-West pipeline is strategically important to Saudi Arabia because it lets oil reach Red Sea ports, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipping through the strait has been threatened by Iranian attacks, making the alternative route important for maintaining Saudi oil exports.
According to AURORAH, Russian satellites also monitored King Fahd Air Base in Taif.
During a Houthi attack on the military facility, an Italian Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet inside a hangar was damaged.
Obaid said the strike’s accuracy indicated the use of high-quality intelligence. He emphasized that, in his assessment, neither the Houthis nor Iran could independently obtain intelligence at that level.
A Houthi representative told AP that Iranian advisers in Yemen had provided the rebels with information obtained from Russian satellites to help identify targets.
However, this statement alone does not establish all the circumstances surrounding Russia’s possible involvement in preparing the attacks.
A Saudi official also told the outlet that Russian satellite intelligence had helped Iran during March strikes on Prince Sultan Air Base.
The attack damaged a U.S. reconnaissance aircraft. According to the official, intelligence data may also have been used in a strike on a CIA unit located within the U.S. Embassy compound in Riyadh.
Moscow had previously publicly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure.

Zelensky expects trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi by Nov. 10, but no firm date set

Zelensky expects trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi by Nov. 10, but no firm date set
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 28 he expects the planned Abu Dhabi peace talks with Russia and the U.S. to take place in mid-November, adding that Washington is yet to confirm a date.
"We need to have this meeting till the end of (next) month, I hope... between Nov. 6 and 10," Zelensky said at a press conference with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten in The Hague, adding that the location of the talks could still change depending on the situation in the Middle East.
"We are waiting for the American side, I think that they'll be ready with all the answers after the elections." Zelensky expects the U.S. to confirm a date around Nov. 4, a day after the U.S. midterms.
The Kremlin is also yet to confirm a timeline for the talks.
The planned meeting follows a renewed push by the U.S. to revive negotiations, which had effectively stalled as the Kremlin continues to demand that Kyiv cede Donbas, a strategically vital region in eastern Ukraine that Russian forces have been unable to capture fully.
Moscow has also repeatedly turned down Western-backed proposals for a full and unconditional ceasefire, which Kyiv supported.
Ukrainian officials do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi, but hope the talks will help restart regular negotiations.
According to Zelensky, one or two rounds of technical talks could pave the way for a trilateral summit involving himself, U.S. President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The agenda of the technical negotiations would concern a potential energy and maritime ceasefire, exchanges of military and civilian captives, and the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
Moscow and Washington are also expected to prioritize territorial issues during the upcoming talks, but Zelensky stressed that any decisions on this topic can only be made at the leaders' level.

UN General Assembly backs resolution calling for end to US embargo on Cuba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:53:54 UTC
00:53:54 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the US against Cuba.
A total of 130 countries, including Türkiye, voted in favor of the draft resolution calling for the lifting of the embargo on Cuba. Seventeen countries, including the US, Israel, Ukraine, Argentina, and the United Arab Emirates, voted against it, while 25 countries abstained from voting.
Addressing the assembly before the vote, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla said the embargo was having a direct impact on the daily lives of Cubans, particularly through shortages of fuel, medicines, food and other essential goods.
“Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat,” Rodriguez said, arguing that the measures were being used as a form of economic pressure against the Cuban population.”
“We are not talking about numbers. We are talking about human lives,” Rodriguez said, adding that the effects of the embargo could be felt “at the dining table of Cuban families” and by patients in hospitals.
US Representative Mike Waltz rejected Havana's characterization of the sanctions, arguing that Cuba's economic difficulties were primarily the result of the policies of its own government.
Draft resolutions adopted by the UN General Assembly since 2012 have called on the US to end the embargo.
The UN General Assembly resolution is non-binding and serves as a recommendation, reflecting the position of the international community. The US embargo against Cuba was first introduced in 1960, and its scope was expanded further in subsequent years.

Netanyahu's Likud accuses Arab parties of election fraud, demands police probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:52:58 UTC
00:52:58 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party accused the Arab political parties Wednesday of stealing the country's parliamentary elections through alleged bribery, intimidation and ballot fraud, demanding an immediate investigation by police and domestic intelligence authorities.
The accusations came after a sharp increase in Arab voter turnout helped Arab parties make significant electoral gains, potentially giving them greater influence over the formation of the next government.
In a sharply worded post on X, Likud alleged that Arab parties had committed serious criminal offenses to manipulate the results of Tuesday's election, including distributing cash to voters, threatening election officials and using prohibited software to mobilize supporters.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters," the party said
The party said it had collected evidence of irregularities at numerous polling stations in Arab communities and would submit the material to law enforcement authorities.
Likud said it was transferring hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the Israel Police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
Among the alleged evidence, the party cited thousands of envelopes containing cash and ballot slips for Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, as well as reports of threats and violence against polling station officials.
It also alleged that multiple voters had entered voting booths together, that some people had voted under more than one identity and that discrepancies had been discovered between the number of ballot envelopes and the number of registered voters who cast ballots.
Likud further accused unnamed political operatives of using prohibited voter-mobilization software.
"We demand that the police and Shin Bet conduct a thorough investigation into the theft of the elections by the Arab parties and bring the perpetrators to justice," the statement said.
The party also demanded immediate action from the Central Elections Committee, arguing that the alleged offenses had severely compromised the integrity of the election and its results.
"This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens," Likud said. "Law enforcement agencies must act firmly and immediately."
Three arrested in suspected vote-buying scheme
The allegations followed the arrest Tuesday of three men from Bedouin communities in southern Israel on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters into supporting Ra'am.
Police said officers searched the suspects' homes in the Negev desert and seized envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials believed to be connected to the suspected offenses.
Investigators suspect the money was intended for distribution to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am. The investigation is ongoing. 
According to media reports, the suspects included a doctor, a transportation driver and another political activist. All three denied wrongdoing.
A court released the doctor despite police objections, while the detention of the other two suspects was extended by five days. The doctor's lawyer said his client had organized meetings to encourage support for Ra'am but had no involvement in bribery. The driver's attorney said the cash found at his home was intended to cover transportation expenses. 
Ra'am rejected the accusations and alleged that the arrests were politically motivated attempts to suppress Arab voter turnout.
The party said its activists had been arrested at their homes before polling stations opened, rather than while attempting to influence voters. It also accused authorities of unfairly targeting the party and reported missing or damaged Ra'am ballot slips in several Arab communities. 
The arrests establish that police are investigating suspected election bribery, but do not establish Likud's broader allegations of coordinated fraud across Arab polling stations.
Arab parties make electoral gains
The dispute comes amid a significant increase in Arab political participation, which has strengthened the representation of predominantly Arab parties in the Knesset and complicated coalition calculations.
In preliminary results Wednesday, the predominantly Arab Joint List was projected to win 12 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure seven, giving the two parties a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List brings together Arab political factions, while Ra'am, formally known as the United Arab List, is an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas and associated with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement.
Although both parties draw much of their support from Arab citizens of Israel, they differ in their political approaches. Abbas has pursued a more pragmatic strategy of negotiating with Jewish-led parties to secure funding and policy commitments for Arab communities.
Ra'am made history in 2021 when it joined the governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, becoming the first independent Arab party to formally participate in a governing coalition.
During the latest campaign, Abbas signaled his willingness to join another government if it committed to addressing violent crime, home demolitions, discrimination and other issues affecting Arab citizens.
The stronger showing by Arab parties has become particularly consequential because neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival pro-change bloc led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has secured a clear parliamentary majority.
The results have fueled debate over whether the opposition could form a government with support from Arab lawmakers, a prospect Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly rejected.

2026-10-28

President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, for talks on strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses and expanding defense and economic cooperation.
Announcing his arrival in a Telegram post, Zelensky said he and his team would meet Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten to discuss further support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We will discuss defense and economic cooperation, strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, and new steps in support of Ukraine,” he said.
The president also announced a meeting with representatives of Ukrainian and Dutch businesses and an audience with King Willem-Alexander.
According to a Dutch government statement, the visit begins with bilateral talks at the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence in The Hague.
Delegation-level discussions will follow, involving Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius and Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, before the business meeting.
The royal audience is scheduled for Wednesday evening at Huis ten Bosch Palace.
Air defense needs drive talks
The visit follows earlier discussions between Zelensky and Jetten about protecting Ukraine against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
During an Oct. 5 phone call, Zelensky said F-16 fighters supplied by the Netherlands were shooting down a significant share of those drones. The leaders discussed supporting the aircraft’s operation and protecting critical infrastructure, according to the Ukrainian readout.
Zelensky: Ukraine’s Data Center Strikes ‘Hurt Russia More’
Jetten subsequently pledged Dutch help with maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16 fleet.
Ukraine is simultaneously seeking additional missiles for its ground-based air defenses.
On Tuesday, Oct. 27, Zelensky urged Washington to authorize Patriot interceptor deliveries that he said had been delayed for nearly a month. He also raised delays involving NASAMS missiles.
The president said Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region in the two weeks since Oct. 14.
Kyiv is pursuing interceptor supplies through the US, European countries, and other partners holding PAC-2 and PAC-3 stocks. Transfers of American-made missiles can require US authorization.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has previously acknowledged that a batch of interceptors might not have arrived but denied that the delay was politically motivated.
Dutch government announces reconstruction support
The visit coincides with the Dutch government’s announcement of 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion) in non-military assistance for Ukraine over the next three years.
Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma announced the package during a separate visit to Kyiv on Wednesday.
The government’s announcement identifies energy, water infrastructure, and support for businesses as priorities.
The package aims to address urgent needs, contribute to recovery and reconstruction, and expand opportunities for Dutch companies working with Ukrainian partners.
Funding will support repairs to damaged infrastructure, emergency supplies, and cooperation with businesses able to provide equipment and expertise.
Sjoerdsma’s delegation includes representatives of Dutch employers, with discussions focused on investment opportunities and obstacles faced by companies operating in Ukraine.
Defense partnership includes joint production
Ukraine and the Netherlands have also sought to expand cooperation between their defense industries.
In July, Zelensky and Jetten signed a Drone Deal covering joint production, technology development, exchanges of expertise, and arms exports.
Their talks also addressed the need for Europe to develop its own anti-ballistic missile capabilities.
That agreement provides an existing framework for the defense and business cooperation on Wednesday’s agenda, as Kyiv seeks both immediate equipment deliveries and longer-term production partnerships.

Israel's high-turnout vote brushed aside in rest of the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:51:05 UTC
00:51:05 KST

Israel's high-turnout vote brushed aside in rest of the Middle East
CAIRO/BEIRUT/GAZA, Oct 28 - Israelis voted in record numbers in Tuesday's wartime election billed as a major turning point in the nation's history. Others across the Middle East were merely filled with more pessimism after a nationalist veteran prime minister and a former hawkish military chief competed for Israel's leadership.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, won the support of an unexpectedly clear majority of Israeli Jews in the contest, apparently ensuring he will survive at least in a caretaker role.
In Egypt, the first Arab country to make peace with Israel in 1979, 62-year-old lawyer Outhman Selim said his hopes that a Netanyahu defeat would steer the country away from the far right had been dashed.
With nearly 86% of votes tallied on Wednesday, Israeli media forecast Netanyahu's bloc of right-wing, hardline and ultra-Orthodox parties winning 53 seats in parliament, surpassing 48 for the opposition bloc of rival Gadi Eisenkot.
The election was the first since the Palestinian militant group Hamas shook Israel on October 7, 2023, killing 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage.
The ensuing war in Gaza, which flattened most of the territory and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to health authorities there, has left Israel increasingly isolated on the world stage, with a decisive shift in global public opinion against it, including in its closest ally the United States.
WIDESPREAD INDIFFERENCE
In Gaza, displaced Palestinian Majed Jundia made no distinction between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a former military chief.
"They want to eradicate the Palestinian people so they do what they want," said Jundia.
Netanyahu was heavily criticised over security failures leading up to the Hamas assault on Israel's deadliest day.
Portraying himself as the only leader who could protect the country, the consummate political survivor argued that his assassinations of the leaders of Hamas, Lebanon's Hezbollah and their ally Iran made Israel, and the world, safer.
Kamel Haddad, an 81-year-old Lebanese man who has witnessed Israel's conflicts with neighbouring states over decades, expected no changes.
"As for who wins? I couldn’t care less. Let them tear each other apart, what difference does it make to me?” he said. "They might get preoccupied with one another since there are issues between them now. Perhaps they would leave us be for a bit.”
While Netanyahu lost his bloc's majority in the 120-seat Knesset, as expected, his opponents were left with no hope of unseating him without an unlikely deal to accept broad backing from Arab parties, which many Jewish leaders reject.
Even then, he would remain as caretaker during any coalition negotiations, or until a new election next year.
Addressing his Likud party's faithful at its election headquarters in Jerusalem, Netanyahu called for the formation of "a strong, right-wing national government".
PROSPECT OF RENEWED WAR WITH IRAN
He also highlighted Israel's military successes and raised the prospect of renewed joint military action against Iran alongside his ally, US President Donald Trump.
"If one wins, he wants to strike you; if the other wins, he wants to kill you. That’s it, nothing else," said Jordanian Tarek al-Kaissy, reflecting on the competition between Netanyahu and his main rival Eisenkot.
Eisenkot emphasized his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his "Dahiyeh doctrine" of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel's 2006 war with Hezbollah in Lebanon.
His approach lowered any expectations of change, even before the election began.
In Tehran, banners with images of slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei reminded Iranians of the early days of US and Israeli strikes at the end of February, which kicked off the war. Just to the right was a poster of late Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, who was killed on Netanyahu's orders.
"I genuinely see the possibility of attack," said 50-year-old Iranian citizen Abdollah Karimi. REUTERS

Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli elections and news from across the region.

Syria's foreign ministry summoned Jordan's ambassador to Damascus and handed him a protest note over what it described as Jordanian strikes on civilian sites in Syria's Daraa province, state news agency SANA reported on Wednesday.
Likud claims election was 'stolen' by Palestinian parties
Netanyahu's Likud party has accused Arab-led parties of stealing Israel's election, making allegations of electoral fraud without publicly presenting evidence.
Likud repeatedly targeted Arab parties throughout the election campaign. On election day, prominent politicians from Arab-led lists accused Netanyahu of inciting hatred against Palestinian citizens of Israel as a "scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters" and boost his electoral prospects.

There was no immediate response from the Arab-led parties.

Israel must avoid another election, says president

Up to 480,000 ‘double envelope’ votes to be counted
The Central Elections Committee says the number of “double envelope ballots” that have yet to be counted is 430,000 to 480,000.
“Double envelope” votes are cast by citizens who are unable to leave their posts, such as nurses, diplomats or soldiers. They are tallied separately to ensure each voter has not already cast a ballot elsewhere.
The latest estimated figure is significantly lower than the 600,000 ballots previously reported.

With 85.6% of the votes in Israel's election counted, a bloc of parties led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats, as parties who seek to unseat him received 67 Knesset seats.
Netanyahu's Likud party is set at 26 seats compared to Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar at 21. The Arab parties have performed particularly well, projected at 18-19 seats.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," he said in comments to journalists on Wednesday, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea , where Allied powers redrew the world map in the wake of the Second World War.
Putin raised idea of three-way summit with Trump: What to know
The Kremlin has previously indicated that preparations were underway for a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit next month.
The Wall Street Journal first broke the news about the three-way summit earlier this month and said that Trump had not agreed to attend the summit at the time.
But the Journal said Trump was open to the proposal — that had been raised by Putin — since he wanted to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.
"What China, Russia and the United States might discuss has not yet been clearly defined," Zelenskyy said, adding that "Russia wants this meeting more than anyone," warning against handing Moscow "another major diplomatic advantage."
For years now, Russia has been seeking a new agreement with Washington on European security architecture, and in particular an end to what Putin considers NATO's aggressive expansion towards Russia.
Putin has falsely repeatedly said Ukraine war was an act of self-defense
Putin continues to cast the ongoing invasion of Ukraine as a response to such a NATO threat – a position widely rejected in Kyiv and the rest of Europe.
Zelenskyy's warning came ahead of planned talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US envoys in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) next month.
No specific date has been set for the Abu Dhabi meeting, but Kyiv is keen for it to take place before the potential Russia-China-US summit.
Before that, it was also confirmed on Wednesday that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the United States for a meeting with G20 counterparts in Atlanta on October 30-31.
Zelenskyy in Netherlands
Zelenskyy's remarks were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for meetings with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Dutch King Willem-Alexander in The Hague.
The Dutch government said on Wednesday it would provide Ukraine with €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) in non-military support over the next years.
Zelenskyy also held a phone call with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to thank him for an extra £10 billion ($13.29 billion/€11.94 billion) of support announced earlier on Wednesday.
"A truly strong very timely step coming right Russia needs to and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate," he wrote on social media.
But Ukraine's greatest assets in its defense against Russian aggression remain US Patriot air defense missiles, and Zelenskyy urged Washington to increase supplies.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been receiving 12 missiles a month this year but is being targeted with "150 ballistic missiles a month."
Oleshky truce holding for now, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile on the battlefield, officials said a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night.
The localized truce in the devastated town of Oleshky began on Tuesday and is due to last until Sunday, enabling a planned humanitarian operation to provide around 2,000 remaining residents with urgently needed food and medicine, and evacuate those who want to leave.
"We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people," said President Zelenskyy.
The plight of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region caught the attention of US first lady Melania Trump, who the White House said helped broker the humanitarian mission.
If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time in more than four-and-a-half years of fighting that both sides have observed a significant truce, with previous attempts quickly unraveling.
"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," said Ukraine's negotiator, Davyd Arakhamia, on Tuesday, adding every step brings peace closer.
Drone attacks in Kharkiv, Belgorod — and off Bulgaria
Elsewhere, however, the war raged on with five people, including a four-year-old child, injured in a Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight.
In Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses had downed 531 Ukrainian drones on Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, but local authorities in the Belgorod border region said one person was killed in a drone attack.
And in Sofia, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said three maritime drones struck a container ship in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria.
The crew evacuated the vessel and there were no immediate reports of casualties, according to Bulgarian state news agency BTA, but the incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia for trilateral talks focused on Black Sea security.
"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," said Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler.
"The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels."
A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria. Russia has not taken responsibility, but suspicion has increasingly fallen on Moscow.
"The logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month. "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

Global commodity prices projected to surge 23% in 2026 on Middle East conflict: World Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:48:35 UTC
00:48:35 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Global commodity prices are projected to surge 23% in 2026 to their second-highest level since 2013 due to the Middle East conflict, Black Sea shipping disruptions and weather shocks, the World Bank said on Wednesday.  
In its October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook report, the bank forecast that overall commodity prices will retreat by 7% in 2027 and 8.8% in 2028 as supply constraints gradually ease.
Energy prices are set to jump 32% this year before falling 11.5% in 2027, representing upward revisions of 7% for 2026 and 14% for 2027 compared to the bank's April projections.
Global oil supply is expected to drop by 5.5 million barrels per day, or 5.2%, in 2026, marking the largest decline in more than four decades outside the 2020 pandemic recession.
Brent crude oil prices are forecast to average $91 per barrel in 2026, up from $69 in 2025, before receding to $79 per barrel in 2027 and $70 in 2028.
Higher prices and supply shortages are projected to cut global oil consumption by 2.5%, or 2.6 million barrels per day, this year, the third-largest annual drop on record after 2020 and 1980.
European natural gas prices are forecast to surge 58.3% in 2026 to $19 per million British thermal units amid depleted liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, before easing 7.9% in 2027.
Food commodity prices are on track to climb 10.3% in 2026 and another 7.2% in 2027, driven by higher energy input costs, Black Sea shipping attacks and a strong El Nino weather pattern.
Grain prices are projected to rise 14.1% this year and 9.3% in 2027, led by a 28% jump in wheat prices in 2026 as global wheat output contracts by 3%.
Beverage prices are expected to drop 23.9% in 2026 as coffee and cocoa production recover, while fertilizer prices are forecast to rise 14.3% this year before falling 12.4% in 2027.
The World Bank's metals and minerals price index is projected to reach an all-time high in 2026, rising 24.5% on supply constraints and strong demand from renewable energy, electric vehicles and data centers.
Aluminum, copper and tin prices have all hit records since April, with copper projected to average $13,200 per metric ton in 2026, up 32.7% year-on-year, before edging down 1.5% in 2027.
Precious metal prices are forecast to surge 39.9% in 2026 on safe-haven demand amid geopolitical tensions, before declining 8.3% in 2027 as higher interest rates in advanced economies weigh on non-yielding assets.
Gold is projected to average a record $4,600 per troy ounce in 2026, up 33.6% from 2025, before easing to $4,250 in 2027, while silver is expected to jump 75.9% to $70 per ounce this year.
The report warned that in an adverse scenario involving an escalation in the Middle East conflict, prolonged Russian oil outages and severe El Nino crop losses, Brent crude could average $105 per barrel in 2027.
Under that adverse scenario, food commodity prices would exceed the 2027 baseline forecast by 12%, pushing global inflation higher and worsening food insecurity, which affected 779 million people worldwide in 2025.
To help countries cope with fiscal pressures and economic fallout from the Middle East conflict, the World Bank Group has made $50 billion to $60 billion available, with $8.7 billion already disbursed to 25 countries.

The term “meaning holism” is generally applied to views that treat the meanings of all of the words in a language as interdependent. Holism draws much of its appeal from the way in which the usage of all our words seems interconnected, and runs into many problems because the resultant view can seem to conflict with (among other things) the intuition that the meanings of individual words are by and large shared and stable….

The US and Russia are discussing a possible return of American oil companies to the Russian market as part of negotiations to end Moscow’s war against Ukraine, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Proposals include reviving joint production off Sakhalin and involving US oil companies in restoring Russian crude exports to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline, the newspaper reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Other ideas include resuming Russian titanium exports to the US and reopening Russian airspace to American airlines to reduce fuel costs.
No final decisions have been made.
Lukoil’s $22 billion assets already under discussion
The proposals would expand an economic dialogue that has continued alongside efforts to revive peace negotiations.
The Kremlin confirmed talks over Lukoil following Putin’s Oct. 21 meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said the two governments were reviewing numerous commercial projects, including the future of the sanctioned oil company’s overseas holdings.
The portfolio, initially valued at approximately $22 billion, includes oil production interests, refineries, and fuel distribution businesses across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia.
Lukoil put the assets up for sale after Washington imposed sanctions on the company in October 2025.
The US Treasury subsequently extended authorization for negotiations over their sale until Nov. 21. That permission allows due diligence and conditional purchase agreements – completing a transaction would require separate US approval.
‘Taken Off the Street’: Russia’s Forced Mobilization Spreads to Siberia
Treasury conditions require a sale to sever ties with the sanctioned company and prevent it from receiving immediate financial benefits. Proceeds owed to Lukoil must remain blocked until sanctions permit their release.
European energy proposals face separate obstacles
Reports of possible oil cooperation follow earlier proposals to revive Nord Stream and restore Russian gas supplies to Europe as an incentive for Moscow to accept a settlement.
The Economist described those ideas as part of a broader package involving sanctions relief, American commercial agreements, and normalized political relations.
Some proposed benefits, however, depend on decisions by European governments and institutions.
EU countries adopted a legally binding phaseout of Russian gas imports in January. The timetable ends remaining long-term Russian liquefied natural gas supplies from January 2027 and long-term pipeline imports later that year.
Germany also opposes reopening Nord Stream, which faces US and EU sanctions.
Nord Stream 1 stopped operating in 2022, while Nord Stream 2 never entered commercial service. Explosions damaged three of the system’s four lines in September 2022.
A revival would therefore require regulatory decisions as well as arrangements for damaged infrastructure. Washington and Moscow cannot independently guarantee access to Europe’s energy market.
Zelensky warns of an ‘economic marriage’
Ukraine has warned that expanding commercial ties could give Russia benefits before it ends its invasion.
In remarks published on Wednesday, Oct. 28, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Moscow could offer Washington an “economic marriage” built around its natural resources and centralized control over major industries.
“I believe the ‘diesel deal’ opens the door for the Russians to take further similar steps,” he said.
Zelensky suggested that future arrangements could involve fertilizers, gas, frozen assets, and sanctions relief for individuals and companies.
He warned that agreements with Russia could contain longer-term costs that were not immediately apparent, even when they appeared commercially attractive at first.
The concern echoes Ukrainian negotiators’ earlier fears that profitable US-Russian transactions could advance before a settlement of the war.
The sequencing of economic concessions remains central to the diplomatic dispute: US officials describe potential projects as part of a postwar settlement, while Kyiv is warning against allowing commercial incentives to weaken pressure on Moscow before peace is secured.

Putin salutes Musk's genius as Russia plays catch-up with Starlink
Oct 28 - President Vladimir Putin hailed Elon Musk as a genius on Wednesday, acknowledging Russia is only beginning to roll out its answer to his Starlink satellite internet system.
The admission was all the more striking because a version of Starlink, developed by Musk's SpaceX, has been used by Ukraine's military throughout the war with Russia as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications.
Putin made the remark while listening to a presentation by Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev, who said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites as it builds its own Starlink equivalent.
"Just a second, I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he's just a real genius," said Putin, who was accompanied by a group of African leaders attending a summit in Moscow.
PUTIN SAYS RUSSIA IN CONTACT WITH US PARTNERS

Starlink uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower than traditional geostationary communications satellites, reducing signal travel time.
Ukraine has relied heavily on the system and its military version Starshield, but complained earlier this month of speed restrictions that hampered its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.

At the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again fully functional, but Musk accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX's terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, have taken responsibility for imposing the speed curbs.

Merchant ship attacked off the coast of Bulgaria was the ninth civilian vessel to be struck near NATO coasts this month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:46:03 UTC
00:46:03 KST

On Oct. 28, naval drones attacked a container ship in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, Reuters reported, citing the country’s Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov. Data from the Starboard Maritime Intelligence service examined by The Insider indicates that the vessel is the Contship Jet (IMO 9348625), which sails under the Liberian flag and is owned by the Greek company Sevilla Maritime Co. Since the beginning of October, at least nine civilian vessels have been attacked off the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
According to Stoyanov, “A container ship was hit...with three naval drones, approximately 21 miles southeast of Shabla.” As Reuters notes, the container ship was in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone at the time of the attack. A source in the maritime security sector told the outlet that the ship’s crew had been evacuated.
According to Starboard data examined by The Insider, the Contship Jet left the Israeli port of Haifa on Oct. 24 and was heading to the Romanian port of Constanta. The attack on the merchant ship took place on the day of an emergency meeting between the defense ministers and chiefs of the general staff of Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania in Sofia – a gathering focused precisely on the safety of civilian shipping in the Black Sea.
Against the backdrop of frequent attacks, Romania proposed that NATO’s Black Sea countries create a joint command to protect against drones. In addition, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance will strengthen its grouping of maritime patrol aircraft and drones in the region.
However, as military analyst David Sharp explained to The Insider, ordinary patrolling will not help protect civilian ships from drones. As Sharp noted:
“Patrolling is more of a demonstration of presence so that the adversary does not get too bold. Of course, you can detect drones without destroying them and report the sighting to all ships in the area, including civilian ones. But sounding the alarm will not help here: at most, there might be time to put everyone into lifeboats. To truly protect civilian shipping, it is necessary to create a large grouping of ships and aircraft that will closely scan this part of the sea and destroy emerging threats. So everyone considering creating such groupings needs to answer the question of how far they are willing to go. Protecting civilian ships will require political will and specific decisions.”
Sharp stressed that NATO countries have the technical capabilities to counter even advanced naval drones, but the absence of a political decision to take on the protection of civilian shipping is explained by the alliance members’ fear of escalation with Russia:
“Civilian ships cannot protect themselves; they are too slow. They are a defenseless target. However, a political decision to cover civilian shipping would already imply, to some extent, participation in the war. You would have to hunt for drones and shoot at them, and also risk a drone hitting you. NATO avoids this. In Romanian or Bulgarian waters, ships would have to be covered, and aggression countered, but such actions in international waters amount to participation in combat operations.”
Notably, an exclusive economic zone is not considered part of a country’s territory, meaning that a hypothetical operation to destroy a drone like the one that struck the Contship Jet could be interpreted by an adversary in a variety of ways. As Sharp explains:
“When a sea drone operated by an unknown actor is sailing about its own business in neutral waters and you destroy it, some doubt arises: if it is not threatening you and did not enter your waters, on what grounds are you destroying it? Reasons to take defensive action appear only if it is clearly attacking a civilian ship.”

By Maria Cheng and Andrew Gray
OTTAWA/BRUSSELS, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Canada and the European Union agreed to ever closer association but dropped the contentious idea of associate membership in a draft statement seen by Reuters ahead of a summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Montreal starting on Thursday.
The draft declaration said work to define the relationship would continue until next year’s EU-Canada summit.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s suggestion of “associate member,” six weeks ago had been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries on the summit declaration, with Germany leading a group that argued they could not sign up to a concept that had no legal status and had not yet been fleshed out, diplomats said.
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s overwhelming economic and security reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian imports. Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU also risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
There is no precedent or legal definition for an EU “associate member.”
Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act,” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things.”
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week is the launch of further formal negotiations that will take another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member,” including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.
EU diplomats are currently negotiating a final version of the statement, which needs to be finalized by 6 p.m. (1700 GMT) Central European time.

Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out war with Iran
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:45:28 CET
00:45:28 KST

By Lili Bayer
JERUSALEM, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to face more constraints as Israel’s caretaker prime minister after Tuesday’s election, but experts say his government could still retain significant powers including when it comes to waging war on Iran.
Neither Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is projected by Israeli media to win a majority in the country’s 120-seat legislature. Eisenkot has acknowledged the prime minister was still in office as a caretaker but issued a warning that Netanyahu might use security for political ends.
Netanyahu’s office has previously rejected accusations he is using the Iran conflict for political gain. His office did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday.
“If you look at the letter of the law, a caretaker government has the same authority, has the same powers as a regular government,” said Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, adding however that a caretaker government “has a duty of restraint” and more limited discretion to act in some areas.
A caretaker government faces limitations when it comes to issues such as appointments, but has leeway to act in matters where there is a public interest, analysts say.
“In general, security issues are the clearest exception to this duty of restraint,” said Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, noting that Israel’s supreme court has previously held that a caretaker government must avoid far-reaching decisions unless they are justified by a pressing necessity.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset convenes and before its committees are formed,” Asher said, adding that “a caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran”.
After the final tally is in, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult party leaders and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government, with the nominee then getting up to 42 days to establish a government.
(Reporting by Lili Bayer in Jerusalem; Additional reporting by Steven Scheer and Rami Ayyub; Editing by Sharon Singleton)

After three young girls were murdered in the northern town of Southport that July, Robinson repeatedly posted about the killings as riots spread across Britain.
The Daily Mail tracked Robinson down to Cyprus, where he was on holiday with his family, and published a story which accused him of “stoking race riots from his sunbed”.
Robinson repeatedly contacted two journalists involved in the story, posted several messages about them on X and said he had photos of their home address and family.
Robinson claimed he had only intended to put pressure on the journalists and the Daily Mail to remove a picture of his ex-wife from their website.
But he was found guilty by a 10-2 majority on Wednesday and released on bail ahead of his sentencing in December.
