Iran war leaves ‘forever cruise’ residents stranded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:41:39 UTC
00:41:39 KST

Iran war leaves ‘forever cruise’ residents stranded
A cruise ship selling “permanent homes at sea” has abruptly suspended operations, leaving around 200 residents stranded in Cambodia as its operator blamed soaring fuel costs caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The 200-meter (656-foot) Odyssey, with a capacity for 650 passengers, departed Belfast in October 2024 on a “continuous” round-the-world “forever cruise.” It offered cabins for rent, purchase, or lifetime ownership starting at $59,999 and reaching $440,000, plus monthly fees for meals, drinks, Wi-Fi and other services.
On Monday, Florida-based operator Villa Vie Residences (VVR) ordered passengers – some of whom reportedly sold their homes or spent their life savings on cabins – off the ship during a stop in Cambodia’s Sihanoukville. They had just seven hours to pack and leave, passenger Randy Cassingham reported on his cruise blog.
Cassingham shared a message from VVR CEO Kathy Villalba saying the company was “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations” and that the Odyssey would enter a “temporary layup,” with crew remaining aboard. Other residents, many of whom also run travel blogs, confirmed the account.
Sihanoukville deputy governor Long Dimanche confirmed Tuesday that the vessel, which arrived from Thailand on October 23 with 203 passengers and 156 crew, was due to sail to Vietnam later this week, but instead disembarked all passengers. Some have since flown out of Cambodia, while others remain in Sihanoukville, he said in a statement to local media.
Passengers voiced their anger online. Cassingham blamed a “cascade of problems,” including a flawed business model and management mistakes, and accused the company of doing “absolutely nothing to help.” Another resident, Holly Hennessy, told CNN that problems had been mounting for months.
“It’s been incredibly tough since the war,” she said, adding that residents had been asked to pay a fuel surcharge in May, while the ship had reduced air conditioning to save energy.
Fellow residents Lynette and Johan, who run the YouTube vlog Living Life on a Cruise, also described months of financial uncertainty. Johan said he felt “really drained” and worried about those who had invested their life savings in the cruise.
VVR denied abandoning passengers, saying it was arranging temporary accommodation and disembarkation assistance. Company founder Mikael Petterson told Bloomberg that VVR would cover local lodging and transportation costs, but not passengers’ travel out of Cambodia.
In a statement on Tuesday, the company blamed “extraordinary” fuel costs tied to the Iran war, saying monthly fuel expenses had surged from $1,800 to as much as $8,000 per cabin in parts of Asia since February. Slower sailing and longer port stays had failed to contain costs.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said, announcing plans to restructure and seek financing within 60 days.
The cost of war
The US-Israeli war on Iran has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and shipping have further strained supplies, threatening the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Despite Gulf exports reportedly recovering to 80% of pre-war levels, Brent crude recently approached $117 per barrel.
US President Donald Trump has rejected Tehran’s latest settlement proposal and last week threatened another offensive. He also blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, rather than the Iran war, for the latest spike in fuel prices. Trump subsequently lifted restrictions on Russian diesel exports to the US in an effort to ease shortages, and Moscow said on Tuesday that three diesel tankers were already heading to America.
The move offers little immediate relief to the Odyssey, however, which refuels at ports along its route. Cambodia, for instance, relies entirely on imported petroleum products, with gasoline prices up 33.7% and diesel 46.7% since the Middle East escalation, according to its Ministry of Commerce. Marine gasoil, which powers the ship, has nearly doubled to $1,321 per metric ton in Singapore, the world’s largest refueling hub, according to ClearLynx.

TIANJIN, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Some of the farm machinery produced at German manufacturer CLAAS's factory in east China's Shandong Province is shipped to Europe, making the plant part of the company's global manufacturing network.
The factory in Gaomi City has been operating for more than a decade, combining production with research and development and technical training. It manufactures machinery for both Chinese and overseas markets and provides manufacturing services to other CLAAS plants.
"Exporting helps us improve the products we manufacture for Chinese customers," said Thomas Spiering, executive vice president of CLAAS, adding that meeting international quality standards also helps the company refine its manufacturing processes.
Spiering was among the international executives attending the China International Agricultural Machinery Exhibition (CIAME) 2026, held in north China's Tianjin Municipality from Monday to Wednesday. The event brought together more than 3,000 exhibitors from China and abroad.
China is a major market for farm machinery. In 2025, the country's comprehensive mechanization rate for crop plowing, sowing and harvesting reached 76.82 percent, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs.
U.S. manufacturer John Deere, which has operated in China for 50 years, plans to introduce new models which are designed specifically for Chinese farms and manufactured locally, targeting precision farming, autonomous operations and greener agricultural production.
Tianjin has long been an important manufacturing and operational base for the company, said Sun Baolin, president of John Deere China. "We have built our presence here over the years and have grown together with many of our customers and partners," Sun added.
Changes in China's manufacturing capabilities are apparent to longtime overseas buyers, and Chinese-made farm machinery and components are also reaching more overseas customers.
In the first eight months of 2026, China's exports of agricultural machinery, equipment and parts rose 21.95 percent year on year to 15.11 billion U.S. dollars, the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products revealed.
Among the Chinese manufacturers moving into more powerful agricultural equipment is Zoomlion Agriculture Machinery Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Zoomlion Heavy Industry Science & Technology Co., Ltd., one of China's leading high-tech equipment manufacturers. At CIAME 2026, the company unveiled its 9DX hybrid tractor, designed for large-scale farming and with a peak output of 1,600 horsepower.
Zoomlion said it independently developed the tractor's digital chassis, core components and control systems. The company noted that the machine was designed to improve field efficiency and reduce fuel consumption.
Huo Xiaofeng, deputy general manager of Zoomlion Agriculture Machinery, said the company has also made advances in autonomous driving, adaptive tillage-depth control and other technologies, with some intelligent components already in mass production. Some of its products have reached markets including Russia, Australia and Kazakhstan.
Nicolas Meunier, director of global electronic and electrical engineering at U.S. agricultural machinery manufacturer AGCO Corporation, said he was struck by the technology on display in Tianjin and the speed at which new Chinese competitors were emerging.
"A few years ago, we mainly saw low-horsepower tractors from Chinese manufacturers. Today, we are seeing high-horsepower tractors, including some very large models," he said.
Meunier added that the pace of development had been impressive, and that advances in technology and closer market ties could create further opportunities for cooperation between Chinese and international manufacturers. ■

Across China: Love born of language exchange blossoms into children's reading room in Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:40:37 CST
00:40:37 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- In a downtown reading room in Urumqi, capital city of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, children sit in a circle around Steven Dahlke, a 45-year-old German teacher.
He holds up a picture book and imitates the sounds of its animal characters. Beside him, his wife Gulayim Akim offers gentle prompts. The room is filled with laughter, amid the rustle of pages and children's eager voices.
This is no ordinary reading room. Opened in 2024 by Dahlke and Akim, it is a bilingual picture-book space where local children are introduced to languages through stories, games and patient encouragement. It is the latest chapter in a cross-border love story that has begun with language itself.
Dahlke comes from Rostock, Germany, and has lived and worked in China for many years. Fifteen years ago, an international language exchange program connected him with Akim, a young woman from Xinjiang. Language built a bridge between them and affection later followed. The couple married in 2015 and have since formed a warm cross-cultural family.
Four years ago, the family settled in Urumqi. While raising their son Jacob, the couple noticed his remarkable ability to absorb languages. Using picture books, stories and everyday conversation, they taught him Chinese, English and German. The boy's language skills improved rapidly.
"I wanted to share this experience with other parents and children," Akim said.
That desire led to the opening of the reading room in 2024. Drawing on years of university teaching experience, the couple carefully selected picture books and designed interactive games to make language learning enjoyable. They emphasize encouragement and patient companionship, aiming to spark children's initiative rather than pressure them.
"We found that when children are having fun, they easily take the initiative to learn," Dahlke said. "In the reading room, children learn together, and that makes it more enjoyable."
Their approach has gradually won recognition among local families. Outside the reading room, the couple also volunteer in the community and organize public reading activities during holidays, encouraging young people to fall in love with reading and language learning.
Dahlke said the community has been kind to them, and they hope to give back in whatever way they can.
For Dahlke, Urumqi's growth is visible almost every year. "In the past, the airport was very small. Now there is a modern international airport with routes to many countries," he noted.
The neighborhood where the family lives was under construction a decade ago. Today, it is surrounded by large parks and a cultural center.
"You can truly feel how this city has grown from a small western city into a big one," Dahlke said. He especially likes the nearby parks and often takes his son to the newly opened cultural venues.
Dahlke has traveled to other Chinese cities such as Shanghai, Beijing, Xi'an and Chongqing, and likes both the modern energy of metropolises and the deep cultural roots of historic cities. But what makes him feel most at ease is the life his family has built here.
Looking ahead, they are full of hope. "Language is an important bond that connects the world, links people and builds friendship. We met, got to know each other, and committed to each other through cross-border language exchange, and we hope to pass on the beauty and warmth that transcends borders," they said. ■

Explainer: What happens next after Israel's inconclusive election?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:40:12 CST
00:40:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Counting of votes in Israel's parliamentary election continued on Wednesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, both claiming a mandate to lead the country, despite neither appearing to have secured the majority needed to form a government.
Israel now faces political uncertainty, with analysts pointing to several possible scenarios, including prolonged coalition negotiations, a unity government or another round of elections, while Arab parties could hold the key to breaking the deadlock.
WHAT DO THE RESULTS SHOW?
With about 85 percent of the votes counted, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition bloc. The Arab-majority parties -- the Joint List, a coalition alliance of three parties, and the Muslim Ra'am party -- were projected to win a combined 19 seats.
The figures could still change, with votes cast under special voting arrangements yet to be counted, including those cast by soldiers, diplomats abroad and hospital patients. Final official results are expected by Nov. 4, according to a timetable issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee.
Israel's proportional electoral system adds to the uncertainty. Parties must win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter parliament, meaning minor shifts in voting margins could significantly alter the distribution of seats.
WHO WILL FORM THE NEXT GOVERNMENT?
Securing the most seats does not automatically give a party leader the right to form a government.
Following the publication of official results, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of elected parties before assigning the mandate to the lawmaker he deems most likely to assemble a viable majority -- not necessarily the leader of the largest party or bloc.
The designated candidate will have 28 days to negotiate a coalition, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If he fails, the president can assign another lawmaker to try to assemble a government.
Should that secondary attempt also collapse, a parliamentary majority can request a final opportunity to put forward a third candidate.
If all coalition attempts prove unsuccessful, parliament will automatically dissolve, forcing Israel into another election and extending the political stalemate for months.
In the interim, Netanyahu and his outgoing cabinet would remain in office as a caretaker government until a new government is formed.
On Wednesday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said that every effort must be made to avoid another round of elections.
COULD ARAB PARTIES DECIDE WHO BECOMES PRIME MINISTER?
To avoid such a costly deadlock, attention has turned to whether Israel's Arab-majority parties, projected to control 19 seats, could hold the balance of power in the next parliament.
Both Ra'am and Joint List have expressed willingness to help Eisenkot's "change bloc" replace Netanyahu. Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas said Tuesday night that his party wanted to join a coalition led by the bloc. On Wednesday, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said the alliance was "ready and prepared to pave the way" for replacing Netanyahu's government through an unprecedented political partnership with Eisenkot's bloc.
"Change can only come through Jewish-Arab partnership, a genuine and equal partnership," Jabareen said in a post on social media platform X.
However, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected forming a government dependent on Arab parties. Eisenkot has repeatedly ruled out including them in his coalition or relying on their parliamentary support from outside it.
Despite this stance, divergent views remain within Eisenkot's alliance, as Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats within the "change bloc", on Wednesday urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.
One possible outcome could be a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers from outside the coalition, an arrangement that would require Eisenkot to reverse his election pledge against partnering with Arab parties.
Such reversals are not unprecedented in Israeli politics, where coalition negotiations have often forced party leaders to compromise on campaign promises. ■

Across China: Chinese scientists solve puzzle of identifying extinct group of hominins
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:39:57 CST
00:39:57 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have revealed the shared morphological features of Denisovans, a new branch of ancient hominins, according to a research article recently published in the journal Nature.
The researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences obtained ancient protein evidence from Xujiayao hominin fossils, confirming that they belonged to Denisovans.
Denisovans are an extinct group of hominins who were first identified through DNA extracted from a tiny finger bone found in a Siberian cave in 2010.
This branch of ancient hominins interbred with modern humans and has gradually become a hot topic in paleoanthropology. However, due to the scarcity of fossil records, the academic community had been unable to reveal the shared morphological features of Denisovans.
To solve this problem, an ideal site was needed -- one where human fossils could be confirmed through molecular evidence as belonging to Denisovans, and which also has abundant hominin fossils, a clear stratigraphic context and reliable dating.
The Xujiayao site, discovered in Yangyuan County of north China's Hebei Province, dating back 199,000 to 138,000 years, thus became an important lead.
The research team drilled small amounts of bone powder from damaged surfaces of Xujiayao hominin fossils and extracted endogenous proteins. Via paleoproteomic analyses, they confirmed that these Xujiayao hominins belonged to Denisovans.
On this basis, the researchers systematically summarized typical morphological features of Denisovans in terms of the cranium, mandible and teeth.
Denisovans retained some primitive features similar to those of Homo erectus, such as a low braincase and thick cranial bones, while also showing some advanced features similar to those of later Homo members, like simplified premolar occlusal surfaces.
The research team, additionally, compared the Xujiayao hominins with previously confirmed Denisovans, as well as with ancient hominins in East Asia, whose taxonomic status remains unclear.
The results suggest that other ancient hominins in East Asia during the Middle Pleistocene likely also belonged to Denisovans, extending the distribution range of Denisovans to nearly the entire East Asian continent.
The study has made the mysterious ancient human group known as Denisovans, previously identified mainly through molecular evidence, recognizable, comparable and classifiable in terms of morphology, said Fu Qiaomei, a researcher at the IVPP. ■

Presenting the proposals to parliament on Wednesday, Kitila Mkumbo, minister of state in the President's Office responsible for Planning and Investment, said the plan seeks to accelerate economic transformation, strengthen competitiveness and improve people's welfare under the country's Development Vision 2050.
The government estimates that implementing the plan will cost 89.3 trillion Tanzanian shillings (about 35.7 billion U.S. dollars), with 20.7 trillion shillings expected from the government budget, 6.3 trillion shillings from commercially operated public corporations and 62.3 trillion shillings from private investment.
Mkumbo said Tanzania's economy grew by 6 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 6.5 percent in the second quarter, adding that economic growth is projected at 6.3 percent in 2026 and 6.6 percent in 2027, up from 5.9 percent in 2025.
The plan prioritizes industrialization, agricultural productivity, human capital development, environmental conservation, infrastructure expansion and improved governance, he said.
Mkumbo said key interventions include investment in energy, railways, roads, ports, airports, irrigation, digital services and value addition in mineral and agricultural products.
The government also aims to increase electricity generation capacity to 4,804 megawatts (MW) by June 2028, from 4,606.14 MW in September 2026, while expanding health insurance coverage to 32.38 percent of the population in the 2027/2028 financial year, he told the House.
Mkumbo said five value chains will receive particular attention, including horticulture, aquaculture, mineral exploration and processing, edible oil production, and textiles and garments.
He added that the government will strengthen project monitoring and accountability through a national electronic development project management system to ensure public resources produce measurable results.
The proposed plan forms part of Tanzania's Fourth Five-Year National Development Plan, covering 2026/2027 to 2030/2031, which is the first medium-term framework for implementing Development Vision 2050. ■

MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente on Wednesday pointed to an "inexplicable" decision by a railway control center to authorize a train to resume its journey despite a red signal as a possible cause of a deadly high-speed train collision in the province of Toledo, central Spain.
Speaking at a press conference in Madrid, Puente said that a computer communication failure had disabled the LZB railway safety control system, automatically bringing trains along a 63-km section of the line to a halt.
However, the control center subsequently authorized a Renfe train to resume its journey despite a red signal prohibiting it from proceeding.
Puente described the decision to authorize the train's movement while another train remained stationary on the track as "inexplicable."
The collision occurred on Wednesday morning on the high-speed railway line connecting Madrid and Seville. A Renfe high-speed train struck a stationary Iryo train from behind near Urda station in Toledo province, causing several carriages to derail, with some falling down an embankment.
According to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, the death toll has risen to 68, while 58 people have been hospitalized, including 15 in critical condition. Around 50 others with minor injuries are receiving medical attention at temporary treatment centers. The exact cause of the accident remains under investigation. ■

US and Russia Discuss Bringing American Oil Giants Back to Russia in Talks With Putin, FT Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:35:55 UTC
00:35:55 KST

- Category
- World
US and Russia Discuss Bringing American Oil Giants Back to Russia in Talks With Putin, FT Reports
The US and Russia are discussing potential postwar business deals as part of Washington’s effort to bring the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, into negotiations over ending the war in Ukraine, the Financial Times reported on October 27.
The proposals involve American oil majors, Russian energy projects, aviation, titanium, sanctions relief, and other sectors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to FT sources, the White House and Kremlin have floated reviving a joint venture involving US and Russian oil companies off Sakhalin.
It would also bring American majors into a possible resumption of Russian oil sales to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline.
Trump had already moved toward renewed energy trade with Moscow earlier in October, announcing an agreement with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to US and global markets. UNITED24 Media reported that the arrangement included an initial shipment of more than 300,000 tons, followed by larger deliveries planned for November and beyond.
US officials have stressed that such ventures would not proceed until the war ends and would be tied to a broader peace framework.
“President Trump’s representatives have discussed economic proposals with both sides of the war — including a postwar economic framework to create long-term growth and investment opportunities for Ukraine, and potential opportunities for postwar economic collaboration with Russia,” a US official told the Financial Times.
“Economic agreements would be included in and subject to a comprehensive peace framework that stops the killing in this brutal war; nothing is finalised,” the official added.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff discussed potential business arrangements with Putin during a meeting in St. Petersburg in early September, according to the report. During another visit to Moscow last week, photographs published by the Kremlin press pool showed “Business Deals” written on Witkoff’s notepad.
The Financial Times reported that Moscow sees the proposed deals as possible incentives for the Trump administration to normalize economic ties with Russia, even as the war continues.
The proposals under discussion extend beyond oil. They include restoring US airline access to Russian airspace, reviving cooperation on titanium production and supply, and potentially involving US companies in Russian energy projects.
The US and Russia have also discussed the possible sale of Lukoil’s international assets to investors connected to the White House, a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska involving Russia’s Novatek, and a possible revival of gas supplies to Europe through the surviving Nord Stream infrastructure.
Another proposal would relax sanctions on potash fertilizers and allow exports through Baltic ports, a move that would require EU approval.
The Financial Times also reported that one idea under discussion would transfer management of the temporarily Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant to a US entity, which would then divide electricity generated there between Ukraine and Russia.
European officials have repeatedly opposed lifting sanctions or striking economic deals with Moscow before the war ends. They have also stressed that decisions affecting EU interests cannot be made without European participation.
Many of the proposals face significant obstacles. ExxonMobil, which previously held a 30% stake in the Sakhalin-1 project, has been negotiating compensation over the seizure of its stake and has not indicated plans to return to Russia.
Boeing also suspended its Russian titanium joint venture after the full-scale invasion and has since diversified its supply chains.
The discussions come ahead of planned trilateral talks involving Ukraine, the US, and Russia in Abu Dhabi next month. The talks are expected to focus on postwar security guarantees and possible steps toward ending the war.
The Financial Times noted that previous US attempts to use economic incentives to move Moscow toward a peace deal failed to change Putin’s negotiating position, while European officials remain skeptical that commercial opportunities alone would be enough to alter the Kremlin’s demands.
It was previously reported that three tankers carrying around 140,000 tonnes of Russian diesel were heading to US ports under a temporary US license, including one vessel sanctioned by the UK, EU, and Canada.

Russia Moves to Legalize Stolen Cars From Europe, Canada, and Ukraine
Russia is advancing legislation that would allow vehicles reported stolen in Europe, Canada, and Ukraine to be registered legally in Russia, even if they remain on Interpol’s international wanted list.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russian media Kommersant on October 28, the Russian State Duma’s Transport Committee recommended that lawmakers approve a bill drafted by the Interior Ministry in its first reading. The proposal would establish special registration procedures for vehicles wanted by law enforcement agencies in countries Moscow officially classifies as “unfriendly.”
Deputy Interior Minister Igor Zubov told lawmakers that the proposed changes were partly driven by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
He explained that Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories have encountered difficulties registering vehicles previously registered in Ukraine because Ukrainian law enforcement agencies had placed them on Interpol’s wanted list.
Under existing Russian regulations, vehicles subject to international search notices cannot be registered, even if they have already entered Russian territory. Zubov described the proposed legislation as a temporary solution intended to prevent such vehicles from remaining unused.
The Interior Ministry prepared the proposal in February 2026, and the Russian government subsequently submitted it to the State Duma in June. The initiative follows a separate ruling by Russia’s Supreme Court involving a St. Petersburg resident who purchased a vehicle stolen in Canada.
In October, the court sided with the buyer after Russian traffic police refused to register the vehicle because of its international wanted status. The ruling was presented as protecting buyers who had purchased imported vehicles in good faith.
According to The Moscow Times on October 28, Russia has become a major destination for vehicles stolen in Europe and North America since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the introduction of Western sanctions.
Between February 2024 and July 2026, Interpol recorded 4,798 reports involving vehicles stolen in Canada that were subsequently operated in Russia, the outlet reported.
Thousands of additional imported vehicles entering Russia through parallel import channels, including routes through the United Arab Emirates, have also reportedly appeared in international stolen-vehicle databases.
During the early months of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian troops seized civilian vehicles from occupied Ukrainian territories, with some later spotted in Belarus without license plates and bearing Russian military “V” markings.
The United Nations also documented Russian forces confiscating vehicles from private homes, businesses, and civilians at checkpoints for military and personal use.

KPF completes Texas' tallest skyscraper in Austin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:34:02 UTC
00:34:02 KST

KPF completes Texas’ tallest skyscraper in Austin
New York architecture studio KPF has completed Waterline in Austin, Texas, a supertall skyscraper with a mixed-use programme that slopes away from Lady Bird Lake as it rises. It has a form that resembles a “cowboy boot”, according to its designers.
KPF, which is known for its skyscrapers around the world, was not originally meant to design the structure.
The building’s original developer was the coworking real estate company WeWork, which selected a design by its collaborator, architecture studio BIG, through a competition.
However, after WeWork’s failed IPO in 2019 and governance scandals, KPF was brought back in to take up the mantle on the project, which had already begun its early construction.
KPF president James von Klemperer told Dezeen that the concept of a “we-building” or a mixed-use building with overlapping functions remained part of the DNA of the building as the project was awarded to KPF by its new development team.
“Space isn’t as proprietary,” said von Klemperer of the project and concept. “No, it weaves together with other things, and with the spaces that are shared at the rooftop of the base of the building.”
The 1,025-foot-tall (312-metre-tall) structure features hotel and office programmes at the bottom, with luxury residences at the top. Double-height exterior floorplates supported by massive columns mark changes in the programme from the exterior, and the whole building slopes up and away from Lady Bird Lake, a wide section of the Colorado River that flows through Austin.
Deference to the waterway was one of the main goals of the project, as were nods to the regional heritage, and a desire not to “strangle” the low-lying historic Rainey District to the southeast of the site.
It was originally supposed to be multiple towers, but the studio decided that shoring its density into a single tower allowed for these goals to be achieved.
“The project grew into the design, if you will, the way it inclines down like a cowboy boot at the base,” said von Klemperer
“It inflects towards Lady Bird Lake, and I think that was a powerful profile in everybody’s estimation, because it says something about a vertical structure becoming a piece of landscape or geology.”
Von Klemperer also contrasted the skyscraper, with its wide-grid facade and columns, with black-glass skyscrapers with wide bodies that block urban view corridors, referencing recent skyscraper construction in New York.
It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community.
“It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community,” he said, adding that Waterline’s facade, which features rust-coloured details to reference Texas geology, is “lacy” and full of moments “where your eye can see through or see some depth or see pattern”.
“We hoped to make a beautiful little piece of waterway facade.”
Working closely with landscape architecture studio TPG Partners, the structure steps up from the creek, with massive columns meeting the ground plane.
These columns form what von Klemperer compared to an amphitheatre of sorts, adding “urban drama”.
“Cities should have places that support urban drama, and I think already this has shown it really works,” he said.
At the centre of the structure’s stepped podium is a paseo from the city to the water that is lined with stone and makes the lower part of the structure, mostly retail and parking, more porous.
On top of the podium, amenity spaces serve the 1 Hotel, which is taking over the middle part of the programme.
The columns at the base and at the breaks were designed with oak trees in mind.
The studio included some V-shaped columns to add to this character, but also to structurally aid the building as the floorplates changed to accommodate the programme shifts.
“From an office grid to the residential grid, those misalignments along the perimeter were actually beneficial for getting a better column placement in the residential above,” said KPF design director Andrew Klare.
At the top of the building is a sky lounge, and the bulkhead has a slight angle that echoes the slope of the skyscraper.
Von Klemperer said both the shifts in the facade and the tilted top of the skyscraper were subtle nods to the city’s slogan – Keep Austin Weird.
“It’s not an exceedingly weird gesture that interrupts the skyline, but it’s a bit of whimsy, which is in character with the rest of the skyscraper’s geometries,” he said. “It destabilises the conventional grid of the world.”
The mixed-use programme also came to pass during the Covid-19 pandemic, which was a period of doubt in the feasibility of downtown cores.
This didn’t stop the project, but intensified the studio’s desire to create an open building with multiple uses and to “multiply” the uses of the podium.
“It restores your faith in the urban agenda of development – to make such a mixed-use project with levels of shared use throughout,” said von Klemperer.
Other recent skyscrapers by KPF include a “beaux-arts” supertall in New York that is nearing completion and a pair of skyscrapers in Istanbul.

Interior design: Michael Hsu (Office), Studio Mai (Hotel), Ink & Oro (Residential)

Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:32:00 UTC
00:32:00 KST

Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE
It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players
An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.
Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.
The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.
A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.
The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.
The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

Carney to host European Union officials as draft declaration avoids 'associate member' discussion

Canada, European Union officials drop 'associate member' from summit declaration
OTTAWA/BRUSSELS, Oct 28 - Canada and the European Union agreed to ever closer association but dropped the contentious idea of associate membership in a draft statement seen by Reuters ahead of a summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Montreal starting on Thursday.
The draft declaration said work to define the relationship would continue until next year’s EU-Canada summit.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's suggestion of “associate member,” six weeks ago had been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries on the summit declaration, with Germany leading a group that argued they could not sign up to a concept that had no legal status and had not yet been fleshed out, diplomats said.
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney's strategy to reduce Canada’s overwhelming economic and security reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian imports. Still, Canada's efforts to draw closer to the EU also risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
There is no precedent or legal definition for an EU “associate member."
Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act,” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things.”
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week is the launch of further formal negotiations that will take another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an "associate member," including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.
EU diplomats are currently negotiating a final version of the statement, which needs to be finalized by 6 p.m. (1700 GMT) Central European time. REUTERS

The Verkhovna Rada supported amendments regarding the conduct of urgent searches
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:29:52 EET
00:29:52 KST

The Verkhovna Rada supported amendments regarding the conduct of urgent searches
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada approved Bill No. 15488-3 on searches in urgent cases as a basis. A 72-hour deadline will be set for applying to the court.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a bill that changes the procedure for conducting searches without prior court authorization, returning seized property, and registering reports of criminal offenses. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Draft Law No. 15488-3 "On Amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine Concerning the Improvement of the Institutions Governing Searches in Urgent Cases, as well as the Registration of Statements and Reports of Committed Criminal Offenses" was supported at first reading in principle by 265 members of parliament.
Under the draft law, an investigator, inquiry officer, or prosecutor shall have the right, before a ruling by an investigating judge is issued, to enter a person’s home or other property only in urgent cases related to saving people’s lives and property or to the direct pursuit of persons suspected of committing a criminal offense.
In such a case, the prosecutor, investigator, or inquiry officer, with the prosecutor’s approval, shall be required to apply to the investigating judge without delay, but no later than 72 hours after carrying out such actions, with a motion to conduct a search.
Currently, Part Three of Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides that an investigator, inquiry officer, or prosecutor shall have the right, before a ruling by an investigating judge is issued, to enter a person’s home or other property only in urgent cases related to saving people’s lives and property or to the direct pursuit of persons suspected of committing a criminal offense.
The bill proposes that, in such a case, the prosecutor, investigator, or inquiry officer, with the prosecutor’s approval, shall be required to apply to the investigating judge without delay, but no later than 72 hours after carrying out such actions, with a motion to conduct a search. That is, a 72-hour limit is established for applying to a judge to "legalize" the search.
A motion by a prosecutor, investigator, or inquiry officer to conduct a search shall be considered by a judge no later than three days from the date it is received by the court, with the participation of the owner of the property temporarily seized during the search.
The judge will be required to notify in advance the owner of the property temporarily seized during such a search, the owner of the home or other property in which such a search was conducted, or their representatives, of the date, time, and place of consideration of the prosecutor’s, investigator’s, or inquiry officer’s motion to conduct a search. The failure of these persons to appear at the court hearing shall not prevent consideration of the motion.
If the prosecutor does not approve the motion to conduct a search or the investigating judge refuses to authorize it subsequently, the seized property shall acquire the status of temporarily seized property and shall be returned.
Why the amendments became necessary
As stated in the explanatory note to the document, Article 30 of the Constitution of Ukraine establishes a general rule under which entry into a person’s home or other property, and the conduct of an inspection or search therein, is permitted only on the basis of a reasoned court decision.
At the same time, Part Three of this article establishes an exception to this rule: in urgent cases related to saving people’s lives and property or to the direct pursuit of persons suspected of committing a crime, another procedure for entering a person’s home or other property and conducting an inspection or search therein, as established by law, is possible.
The Criminal Procedure Code elaborates on the constitutional provision. In particular, Part One of Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine states that no one has the right to enter a person’s home or other property other than with the voluntary consent of the person who owns it or on the basis of a ruling by an investigating judge.
In particular, Part Three of Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine provides that an investigator, inquiry officer, or prosecutor shall have the right, before a ruling by an investigating judge is issued, to enter a person’s home or other property only in urgent cases related to saving people’s lives and property or to the direct pursuit of persons suspected of committing a criminal offense.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets reported in October that about 10 cases had been recorded in Ukraine in which representatives of territorial recruitment and social support centers entered private homes, yards, or other private premises and forcibly removed men from them.
According to him, such cases are being recorded in various regions of the country. In Lubinets’s view, this is a kind of test of the legal response.
The ombudsman emphasized that Article 30 of the Constitution of Ukraine guarantees the inviolability of the home. Entry into it is generally permitted on the basis of a substantiated court decision, while exceptions are provided by law for certain urgent cases.
The serving of a summons in itself is not among the grounds permitting entry into a home without the owner’s consent. The presence of police officers nearby also does not override the requirements of the law.

Syria says French jihadist killed in shootout with govt forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:29:31 UTC
00:29:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria says French jihadist killed in shootout with government forces
Syria on Wednesday said a French jihadist was killed in a shootout with security forces in the country's northwest, the latest violence with foreign fighters since Syria's new authorities took power.
In October last year, government forces clashed with French jihadists from the so-called Firqat al-Ghuraba (the Foreigners' Brigade), before the sides agreed a ceasefire that also involved the withdrawal of heavy weapons from the Harem camp, where they are holed up in Idlib province.
In a statement carried by state television, security forces in Idlib said a patrol observed "an armed group leaving the French camp... in violation of the agreement that prohibits exiting (the site) with weapons."
Some from the group began shooting at the patrol which had begun taking up pursuit, "requiring a response to the source of fire", the statement said.
One of the members of the armed group was killed and a civilian wounded, it added.
Firqat al-Ghuraba is led by Franco-Senegalese criminal-turned-preacher Oumar Diaby, also called Omar Omsen, and is estimated to include a few dozen to a hundred fighters accompanied by women and children.
On messaging app Telegram, a channel affiliated with the group published a statement accusing the security forces of opening fire after "our brothers went to buy food in the city", killing a man it identified as Abu Ayman al-Faransi, meaning "Abu Ayman the Frenchman".
The statement said the man had lived in Syria for 13 years and had fought against the forces of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by an Islamist alliance in December 2024.
Accusing Syria's authorities of killing the man, the statement vowed that "we will not leave this land before taking revenge".
The issue of foreign fighters who flocked to Syria during its civil war is a thorny one, with many countries refusing to take them back.
Hundreds of French citizens joined jihadist ranks in Syria during the war.
In September 2016, the United States designated Diaby, suspected of helping French-speaking fighters travel to Syria, as an "international terrorist".
Diaby, in his 50s, is also wanted on a French arrest warrant.
While some foreign fighters have joined the ranks of Syria's new military or security forces, the French jihadists have remained in Idlib where they had fought for years alongside factions that went on to help topple Assad.

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel fuel head to the U.S. after Trump and Putin agree on sanctions relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:28:22 UTC
00:28:22 KST

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel fuel are heading to the U.S. under a sanctions relief agreement reached by Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. Two of the tankers are under Western sanctions, AFP reports, citing data from the analytics platform Kpler.
According to Kpler, the tankers are in question are the Talisman (IMO number 9292060), which is under U.S. and EU sanctions; Leruo (IMO number 9385831), which is on the U.K. and EU sanctions lists; and Agioi Fanendes (IMO number 9798375). Together, the three vessels are carrying 924,000 barrels of diesel fuel, roughly one-third of the U.S. transportation sector’s daily diesel consumption.
Only one of the three tankers, the Talisman, sails under the Russian flag. Leruo flies the flag of Sierra Leone, and Agioi Fanendes that of Malta. The latter two are going around the UK, avoiding the English Channel.
The ships left the Russian port of Primorsk between Oct. 16 and 22. They are expected to arrive on the U.S. East Coast on Nov. 7–11. Agioi Fanendes is heading to New York; for the other two vessels; the specific destination on the U.S. Atlantic coast is not listed.
On Oct. 27, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed that three tankers carrying Russian fuel are heading to the U.S., adding that a fourth tanker is due to depart on Oct. 28.
The shipments became possible after Trump and Putin reached an agreement earlier this month to ease U.S. sanctions in exchange for Russia increasing the supply of diesel fuel on the world market. As AFP notes, the decision — which will not deliver appreciable quantities of diesel to the United States, and which will not result in actual deliveries until mid-November — is widely seen as an attempt by Trump to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the U.S. congressional midterm elections scheduled for Nov. 3.
The agreement has drawn sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies. Volodymyr Zelensky called Washington’s decision “weak,” and relations between Kyiv and Washington have worsened since the deal was struck.

Turkish Airlines reaches 92% load factor on Vietnam routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:28:19 UTC
00:28:19 KST

Kenan Irtak
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Turkish Airlines has reached an average load factor of nearly 92% on its flights to Vietnam, a key manufacturing, trade and tourism hub in Southeast Asia, a company official said.
Speaking to reporters in Hanoi, Turkish Airlines Hanoi Manager Dincer Sayici said Vietnam serves as one of the flag carrier's strategic markets in Southeast Asia. 
Sayici said the airline increased its total passenger numbers on Vietnam routes by 30% year-on-year in 2025 and projects around 11% growth by the end of 2026.
"With the strong connections we offer via Istanbul Airport and our increasing flight frequencies, we expect to maintain this growth sustainably," Sayici said.
"Our average load factor on our Vietnam routes stands at around 92%, and 92% of our passengers are transit passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport," he added.
Highlighting that connections to Europe and North America bolster the carrier's position in the market, Sayici noted that Turkish Airlines currently operates 20 weekly flights to Vietnam, split equally between Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.
The carrier plans to raise weekly frequencies to 11 on the Hanoi route on Jan. 5, 2027, and to 11 on the Ho Chi Minh City route on Feb. 7, 2027, bringing total weekly flights to 22.
Under a memorandum signed between the two countries' civil aviation authorities on Aug. 6, 2026, capacity was approved for up to 42 weekly passenger frequencies on the Istanbul-Hanoi and Istanbul-Ho Chi Minh City routes.
Turkish Airlines, which flies to more countries than any other airline, launched scheduled flights to Ho Chi Minh City via Bangkok on Dec. 29, 2010, and added Hanoi to its network on June 27, 2016.
The carrier operates nonstop flights from Istanbul Airport to both cities primarily using wide-body Airbus A350-900 and Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft.
Sayici also pointed to growing interest among Turkish tourists in Vietnamese destinations such as Hanoi, Ha Long Bay and Ninh Binh, noting that passenger demand from Türkiye jumped 56% in the first nine months of 2026.
To attract more Vietnamese travelers to Türkiye, the airline works closely with travel agencies and tourism stakeholders to promote destinations including Istanbul, Cappadocia and Pamukkale.
He added that granting electronic visa eligibility to Vietnamese citizens as of Sept. 1, 2025, has positively impacted tourism figures and will continue to boost travel.
On air freight operations, Sayici said Turkish Cargo transported approximately 53,000 tons of cargo between Istanbul and Vietnam in 2025 and aims to reach 60,000 tons by the end of 2026.
Electronics, high value-added industrial goods, machinery, spare parts and textiles make up the primary cargo shipments supporting bilateral trade, he said.
"In the coming period, our goal is to meet rising passenger demand and contribute to the development of commercial and cultural ties between Türkiye and Vietnam," Sayici added.
Home to more than 100 million people, Vietnam has expanded its industrial production, foreign trade and foreign investment since launching its Doi Moi economic reforms in 1986, emerging as a global supply chain hub for electronics, textiles, apparel and footwear as well as rice, coffee and seafood exports.

====================================================================================================

Israeli president urges every effort to avoid another election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:26:57 UTC
00:26:57 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday urged political parties to make every effort to avoid another election after preliminary results left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.
“Everything must be done, especially after yesterday, to avoid repeating another election,” Herzog told reporters in remarks carried by Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
He said he would begin consultations with parliamentary factions next week after receiving the official election results from the Central Elections Committee.
“I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind,” Herzog said.
He said he would listen to each faction, ask questions and hold discussions before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming a government.
Under Israel's basic law governing government formation, the president must consult parliamentary factions and assign a Knesset member the task of forming a government within seven days of the official publication of election results.
The selected lawmaker receives 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of extensions totaling up to 14 additional days.
If the first candidate fails, the president may appoint another lawmaker. At a later stage, at least 61 lawmakers can nominate a candidate to form a government.
Failure to establish a government could ultimately trigger another election.
Although coalitions generally seek support from at least 61 lawmakers, Israeli law allows minority governments to take office if more lawmakers vote in favor than against in a parliamentary confidence vote.
Until a new government wins the Knesset's confidence and takes office, Netanyahu's outgoing government will continue performing its duties.
According to Israeli Channel 12, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset after all regular ballots were counted Wednesday.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win 19 seats, the broadcaster reported.
More than 500,000 special ballots remained to be counted.
Neither main bloc has been projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

Kyivstar acquires Ukrainian cloud provider GigaCloud for nearly $50 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:26:30 UTC
00:26:30 KST

Kyivstar, the parent company of Ukraine's largest mobile operator, has signed an agreement to acquire GigaCloud, one of Ukraine's leading cloud infrastructure providers, for up to $50 million, Kyivstar announced.
The acquisition reflects Kyivstar's ambition to build a broader digital ecosystem beyond its core telecommunications business. In March 2025, the company acquired ride-hailing platform Uklon for $155 million. Kyivstar also owns a majority stake in health-tech platform Helsi and has pursued other digital-sector acquisitions.
"GigaCloud brings to Kyivstar a well-established cloud business, cloud engineering expertise, R&D capabilities and an experienced team," said Oleksandr Komarov, CEO of Kyivstar, said in a press release.
Founded in 2016, GigaCloud serves more than 1,800 corporate customers, including agricultural holding Kernel and state-owned energy company Naftogaz. The company provides cloud infrastructure and related services to businesses and public-sector organizations.
"By combining these capabilities with our connectivity, customer reach and investment capacity, we can help more businesses modernize their operations and build a larger enterprise technology business," Komarov said.
"This acquisition advances our digital strategy while supporting Ukraine’s long-term infrastructure need."
According to unaudited management accounts cited in Kyivstar's announcement, GigaCloud generated approximately $14 million in revenue and $4.7 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) in 2025.
The deal includes a $41 million acquisition price, up to $4 million in deferred debt obligations, around $3 million in performance-related payments and up to $2 million in capital expenditure reimbursements, subject to the agreement's terms.
In June 2025, Kyivstar also launched Kyivstar Cloud, its own cloud service for businesses and public-sector organizations.
In July 2026, Ukraine's Antimonopoly Committee approved Kyivstar's acquisition of control over GigaCloud, subject to commitments designed to preserve competition. These include ensuring customers can use GigaCloud's services independently of their internet provider and without being required to purchase other Kyivstar services.

====================================================================================================

Landmark study finds three in four NFL players die with CTE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:25:30 UTC
00:25:30 KST

American football can be brutal. Scientists have long known that the hits, tackles and other collisions that are central to the sport come with health risks, but what these impacts do to the brain has been less clear. What we do know is that many footballers have died with brains that have shown evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease associated with symptoms such as mood swings and dementia. But because a diagnosis requires that investigators look for damage in a person’s brain after they die, it’s unclear just how common CTE is among current or former athletes.
But now, in a study published in JAMA Network Open, an analysis of medical records from thousands of deceased former NFL players—including hundreds who donated their brains to science—estimates that about 75 percent of these players likely died with CTE.
“No other environmental or occupational exposure ever studied is known to have increased dementia risk at death by that amount,” says Yorghos Tripodis, senior author of the paper and a professor of biostatistics at Boston University.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The study is based on records of 2,362 former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 and played in the league for an average of five years. Among those who donated their brains—almost 400 players—a stunning 93.5 percent had CTE. Signs of CTE in the brain can include atrophy, or tissue wasting, as well as clusters of tau protein—a symptom that is also linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
The high incidence of CTE in those donors may reflect the sample itself: people who donate their brains to science tend to have more severe behavioral symptoms, Tripodis says. That could skew the dataset, potentially making CTE rates appear artificially high.
To better estimate how common CTE might have been across all 2,362 former players in the study, Tripodis and his colleagues analyzed the medical records of donors and nondonors. The team found that people with cognitive symptoms were about five times more likely to donate their brain. Given that, the researchers recalculated their incidence estimate to find that some three in four football players in the study likely had CTE.
For comparison, among the general population, fewer than 1 percent of brains in community-based brain banks show signs of CTE, Tripodis says.
The study only includes NFL players who had died, and it remains difficult, if not impossible, to diagnose CTE in living players. It is hard to say what the risk to NFL players today is, Tripodis says. The NFL has also taken steps to mitigate the risk of head injuries.
The records may also be incomplete or imprecise. For instance, symptoms of CTE such as dementia may not be listed on death records, Tripodis says. And even if dementia is listed, it can have other—even multiple—causes.
This study is “the best attempt so far to correct for selection bias in CTE brain bank data,” says Russell Lonser, a professor in neurological surgery at the Ohio State University, who was not involved in the study. But “it is an estimate from a model and should be read that way.”
"Without similar men who never played contact sports, we can’t tell how much of the pathology or dementia comes from football,” Lonser says. “The 75 percent includes any CTE pathology, even early changes that may never have caused symptoms.”
To better understand how football increases the risks of CTE, Lonser says, you’d need to study players, with and without symptoms, over time, along with conducting brain analyses and including a comparison group of people who had no exposure to head impacts. “Until that work is done, we won’t know how common CTE really is or what, specifically, it means for players.”
Still, Tripodis hopes the findings will prove useful for families who have been affected by CTE and will inform current and future players of the risks involved in the sport.
“CTE is a preventable disease. We find, in study after study, that the more blows to the head over your lifetime, the higher the risk of CTE,” Tripodis says. “If you reduce exposure to repetitive head impacts, then you reduce the risk of CTE.”

EU to boost refining capacity as energy crisis drives up fuel prices, commissioner says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:21:16 UTC
00:21:16 KST

Aysu Biçer
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The EU will work to increase domestic refining capacity and boost fuel production as geopolitical tensions drive up energy prices, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said Wednesday.
“Once again, due to geopolitical turbulence, Europe faces another energy crisis,” Jorgensen told a press conference in Brussels.
He said crude oil and petroleum product prices had increased significantly worldwide, putting pressure on European households and businesses.
“Fuel bills in the EU are skyrocketing,” he said, adding that the global diesel market is expected to remain tight well into 2027, keeping prices high.
Jorgensen said European refineries had played a vital role in ensuring security of supply, including jet fuel, despite challenging market conditions.
He noted that around a quarter of EU refineries had shut down over the past two decades, reducing domestic refining capacity by around 10%, while divestments had accelerated across Europe.
“But this crisis is a wake-up call: We need to counter this trend and ensure that we have adequate and flexible refining capacity in Europe. Today and for the future,” he said.
Jorgensen stressed that refining capacity was not only a matter of economic competitiveness but also of security, highlighting the need for reliable and affordable fuel supplies for citizens, businesses and defense.
The Commission will continue technical discussions with the sector and reconvene early next year to assess progress, he said.
“We will work to increase outputs from refining assets in Europe. The industry has made some suggestions that we need to assess,” he added.
Jorgensen said the EU would also examine the long-term future of the refining sector as the bloc pursues decarbonization, with a focus on expanding the production of biofuels and e-fuels.
“The production of renewable liquid fuels has already compensated some of the reduction in Europe’s refinery capacity. The potential is significant,” he said.

The law on the safety of employees at work needs improvement: the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine explained why it is asking the president to veto it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:19:16 EET
00:19:16 KST

The law on the safety of employees at work needs improvement: the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine explained why it is asking the president to veto it
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada adopted Draft Law No. 10147, but trade unions warned of risks to early retirement pensions and labor guarantees. They are asking the president to veto it.
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada voted in favor of the bill on the safety and health of employees at work as a whole. The document is intended to regulate occupational safety issues in line with European approaches. At the same time, the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine emphasizes the need to further refine the adopted version so that the new rules do not result in the narrowing of labor rights and guarantees.
The FPU explained that, during the preparation of the document in 2024–2025, a tripartite working group involving representatives of trade unions, employers, and the state worked on it. However, the law was ultimately adopted in the 2023 version, without taking into account the proposals developed during subsequent discussions. In the view of the trade union side, this creates risks for workers’ rights, particularly for those working in difficult, harmful, and dangerous conditions.
That is why the trade unions, as part of the Joint Representative Body, which brings together all representative associations of trade unions in Ukraine, appealed to the President of Ukraine, calling on him to veto the law and return it for further refinement. At the same time, the FPU emphasizes the importance of high-quality modernization of legislation in the field of occupational safety and stresses its readiness to participate in further work on amendments that will make it possible to take European approaches into account while preserving an adequate level of worker protection.
UNN spoke with Vasyl Andreiev, Deputy Chairman of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, about the trade unions’ concerns, the necessary amendments to the document, and the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine’s next steps.
What are the main risks that trade unions see in the adopted version of draft law No. 10147?
First and foremost, it is the threat of abolishing the right to early retirement for workers who have spent decades working in difficult, harmful, and dangerous conditions. This includes, in particular, people who work near metallurgical furnaces, underground, in electricity generation, and at chemical and oil and gas enterprises.
The so-called Lists No. 1 and No. 2 of industries, occupations, and types of work that grant the right to a preferential pension are critically important for workers who have suffered damage to their health as a result of prolonged employment in harmful and dangerous jobs. They earned the right to a preferential pension by giving years of their lives to their employer under poor working conditions. Now the employer must compensate the Pension Fund for the additional costs of early pensions.
This is highly significant for millions of people who, according to official statistics, work in conditions that do not meet state sanitary and hygienic standards.
What other labor guarantees could be at risk if the law enters into force?
In addition to early pensions, to which a clearly defined category of workers whose workplaces have been certified by the relevant commissions is entitled, legislation provides people working in harmful conditions with other measures to reduce the negative impact on their health. These include shorter working days and weeks, additional hygienic breaks, and therapeutic and preventive nutrition, which helps reduce the negative effects of harmful substances on workers’ bodies.
Such guarantees are provided by the employer, but their inclusion in the law is critically necessary for practical implementation. Workers also have the right to additional leave for longer rest after working in harmful conditions and to additional remuneration paid on top of the basic rate or official salary.
Why is preserving independent trade union oversight important for worker safety?
A major challenge for trade unions in protecting their members’ rights to safe and healthy working conditions is the erosion, under the adopted law, of the right to public oversight and to trade unions’ representation of their members before the employer.
Thousands of inspections at the enterprise level make it possible to identify problems in the organization of occupational safety before an accident occurs. Such commissions, committees, or individual occupational safety representatives should have rights and duties defined by law. Without proper powers, eliminating hazards will be very difficult, since one of the most effective ways to identify them is risk assessment independent of the employer. Trade unions, in particular, can ensure such independence.
What actions do trade unions expect from the president, and what will they do if the law is signed?
The range of problems with the new law is not limited to the challenges outlined above. Uncertainty about the future regulation of occupational safety and employees’ health in the workplace has caused great concern among trade unions. It has reached such a level that some sectoral trade unions decided to hold an information picket calling on the president to veto Law No. 10147. The action is scheduled for October 29.
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine has also sent the Office of the President of Ukraine a proposal to meet with representatives of trade unions at the national level. The purpose of the meeting is to explain the trade union side’s position on the law, its content, and the rights and guarantees that it eliminates or may dilute during practical application in workplaces.
We expect the Office of the President of Ukraine to receive a representative group of leaders of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine in the coming days.
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is already working on developing amendments and additions to the adopted law, even if the president of Ukraine ultimately signs it. The law genuinely requires changes that will strengthen the system for eliminating risks in workplaces, give employees a clear understanding of their rights and guarantees, and protect people who work in arduous, harmful, and hazardous conditions and have spent decades accumulating the service record required for early retirement.

British far-right activist Tommy Robinson has been found guilty of harassing two journalists following a trial at a London court, according to media reports Wednesday.
Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, 43, faced two charges of harassment causing fear of violence against two men over incidents in 2024.
He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence against Andrew Young, an investigative reporter, and Jacob Dirnhuber, an editor at the Daily Mail and MailOnline.
He was convicted by a jury majority of 10 to two following a trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, the BBC reported.
Robinson pleaded not guilty to the charges at a hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in 2025.  
Posts, messages
The charges related to two counts of harassment causing fear of violence against the journalists through US social media company X between Aug. 5-7, 2024.
They also involved an alleged phone call on Aug. 5, 2024. He was accused of telling Young in the call that he would go to his house, adding: “I’m coming to get you.”
In one of the direct messages he was accused of sending Dirnhuber on X on the same day, he allegedly said: “I’ll be knocking at your door.”
On Aug. 6, Yaxley-Lennon allegedly posted: “Got ya @Jdirnhuber this is Jacob, he likes to locate and endanger families.”
“Jacob and the rest of the Daily Mail journalists who were involved in endangering my children have today been located.”
He continued: “I look forward to hearing on camera your justification for doxxing my children’s location. I got all three of you tagged and bagged in one day.”
Later that day, he was also accused of messaging Dirnhuber to say: “I’ll bring my questions to all your doors.”
Robinson has a long criminal record, with convictions for multiple assaults, mortgage fraud, faking a passport, stalking, contempt of court and various public order offenses. He served five prison terms between 2005 and 2025.

Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out war with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:16:31 UTC
00:16:31 KST

Caretaker role could limit Israel’s Netanyahu, but not when it comes to waging war on Iran
- Benjamin Netanyahu is likely to face more limits as caretaker prime minister after Israel’s Oct 27 election, as no bloc is projected to win a majority.
- Experts say a caretaker government still has broad powers, and security issues are a key exception to restraint.
- Analysts warn Netanyahu could legally choose war with Iran, while President Isaac Herzog will later consult leaders and name a government candidate.
AI generated
JERUSALEM - Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to face more constraints as Israel’s caretaker prime minister after the Oct 27 election, but experts say his government could still retain significant powers including when it comes to waging war on Iran.
Neither Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is projected by Israeli media to win a majority in the country’s 120-seat legislature.
Eisenkot has acknowledged the prime minister was still in office as a caretaker, but issued a warning that Netanyahu might use security for political ends.
Netanyahu’s office has previously rejected accusations he is using the Iran conflict for political gain. His office did not immediately return a request for comment on Oct 28.
“If you look at the letter of the law, a caretaker government has the same authority, has the same powers as a regular government,” said Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, adding however that a caretaker government “has a duty of restraint” and more limited discretion to act in some areas.
A caretaker government faces limitations when it comes to issues such as appointments, but has leeway to act in matters where there is a public interest, analysts say.
“In general, security issues are the clearest exception to this duty of restraint,” said Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, noting that Israel’s supreme court has previously held that a caretaker government must avoid far-reaching decisions unless they are justified by a pressing necessity.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset convenes and before its committees are formed,” Asher said, adding that “a caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran”.
After the final tally is in, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult party leaders and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government, with the nominee then getting up to 42 days to establish a government. REUTERS
