14:30:54 GMT
23:30:54 KST

Sweden has begun a year-long maritime surveillance mission using four Saildrone Voyager uncrewed surface vessels to support Swedish Navy maritime domain awareness in the Baltic Sea, according to the company.
The Voyager is a ten metre wind and solar powered vessel that carries radar, cameras and acoustic sensors and can stay at sea for months without refuelling or a crew, which makes it suited to the persistent watch over shipping lanes and seabed infrastructure that Baltic states have been trying to establish.
The deployment follows a run of damage to cables and pipelines on the Baltic seabed, which has drawn NATO’s Baltic Sentry activity and a series of national responses. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration announced the programme alongside the company.
Saildrone vessels have been used by the United States Navy in the Gulf and the Caribbean and by NATO in European waters, and the Royal Navy has run its own trials of uncrewed surface vessels for maritime surveillance.
Ministers told Parliament last week that up to £330 million is going into improving Britain’s ability to deter, detect and respond to threats against critical undersea infrastructure.

What do young Europeans think about democracy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:30:25 UTC
23:30:25 KST

What matters to young people in Europe? How do they see democracy, and how would they like their voices to be heard?
The latest Eurobarometer on Youth and Democracy explores the views, concerns and expectations of young Europeans in 2026. The findings offer insights into how young people see democracy and their role in shaping Europe's future.
What are the main takeaways?
- Youth policies: Young people most often want youth policies to address real issues they face (40%). They also emphasise having a stronger say in decisions and greater financial support for youth programmes (32% each).
- Intergenerational fairness: Around one third consider that policymakers take long-term consequences into account. Similarly, 33% think young people have the same chances as 30 years ago or will have the same chances in 30 years' time.
- Civic engagement and societal change: Over half young Europeans have already participated in societal change actions (e.g. signing a petition, joining a rally, contacting a politician). Voting and social media are seen as the top levers to make young people's voice heard.
- Impact of EU actions and priorities for the future: Three in four young Europeans feel the EU has an impact on their daily lives. Young Europeans expect the EU to preserve peace, fight poverty and create jobs.
- Digital education: Young Europeans overall feel very confident in their ability to use AI safely but less confident when it comes to using it to deliver intended results.
Young people's perspectives matter. As the European Commission works to strengthen youth participation in policymaking and prepares for the next EU Youth Strategy beyond 2027, these findings can help inform efforts to ensure young people's voices are heard.

Why Arab parties may not be the ‘kingmakers’ in this Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:30:17 UTC
23:30:17 KST

Why Arab parties may not be the ‘kingmakers’ in this Israeli election
Exit poll projections show that if Eisenkot’s bloc teamed up with Arab parties, they could unseat Netanyahu. But observers don’t believe that will happen.
Israel’s Arab-led parties are projected to win a record number of seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, making them increasingly hard to ignore by the leading blocs.
“Probably the most important phenomenon of this election is the rise and the revival of the Arab vote,” Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador, said. “The statement is clear: You cannot disregard such a large portion of the electorate in the calculations for Israeli politics.”
The latest projections from Tuesday’s voting showed that the Arab parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – could hold a record combined 17 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
So far, no clear winner has emerged as partial results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 54 seats and the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot 49.
While Arab parties might theoretically wield influence as the two main blocs fail to win majorities in the Knesset, they are not “kingmakers”, observers said, pointing to what amounts to a political veto that limits Arab parties’ ability to turn electoral gains into influence.
“This veto is rooted in a racist structure that regards the Arab citizen as illegitimate and as an unwanted partner,” Honaida Ghanam, director general of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, told Al Jazeera, alluding to the resistance by the majority of Israeli parties to form any government with Arab-led lists.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected the idea of partnering with them, citing a lack of shared values.
What do the numbers say?
The numbers from exit poll projections thus far are looking clear: If Eisenkot’s bloc teams up with Arab parties, they could secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament and depose Netanyahu.
According to The Times of Israel, the latest partial results would give a partnership between Eisenkot’s opposition alliance and Arab-led parties 66 seats.
According to Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, the unwillingness by the opposition bloc to join forces is purely “ideological”.
“Eisenkot has imposed loyalty tests on Arab parties and ruled out relying on them even as the electoral arithmetic makes their support indispensable,” Najar told Al Jazeera.
How politically feasible is such a partnership?
Observers are divided on this.
According to Najar, a partnership with the Arab parties is not only feasible, it may be the only “realistic” route for Eisenkot to remove Netanyahu.
Omar Shaban, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, pointed to the fact that Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has already shown a willingness to join Eisenkot’s government if the Israeli candidate is elected, based on the condition that internal security matters will be handled by the Arab party.
Abbas has even appointed Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz to the number two spot on Ra’am’s electoral slate for the elections, Shaban explained.
Such a collaboration, if it came to fruition, could help foster better relations between Palestinian citizens and Jewish Israelis, he said.
Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his party is prepared to take responsibility for bringing Netanyahu’s far-right coalition down.
“The government has made the lives of every Arab citizen miserable,” Jabareen was quoted by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper as saying.
His movement “will know how to leverage” its political strength to advance its values, he added.
Ahmad Tibi, also a Joint List leader, on Wednesday said the bloc was extending its hand to the opposition alliance to oust Netanyahu, according to Israeli media reports. It was far from clear, however, that the bloc would formally join a governing coalition.
A roadblock to such a partnership is the more “radical” elements in Israeli society that Eisenkot would have to face who “don’t want the Israeli government to be supported or dependent on Arab votes”, Shabaan said.
Najar said Eisenkot would also have to persuade his prospective partners, including Naftali Bennett from the Together alliance and Avigdor Liberman, who heads the Yisrael Beytenu party.
“Politically, however, it would require him and his prospective partners, particularly Bennett and Lieberman, to abandon the longstanding Zionist consensus that Palestinian citizens of Israel may vote but that the parties representing them are not legitimate partners in governing the country,” he said.
Ghanam outlined four possible outcomes: another election, an opposition minority government supported from outside by Arab parties, defections from the opposition to Netanyahu’s bloc or a national unity government.
“Beyond the arithmetic, the most telling result of this election is the resilience of Netanyahu’s camp, which has proven deeply entrenched and cohesive,” she added.
What are the terms Eisenkot has laid out for a partnership with Arab parties?
According to The Times of Israel, Eisenkot has said he would consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.
He hasn’t, however, expressed whether Ra’am, with or without Jewish lawmaker Segalovitz, would meet those criteria, the outlet also reported.
Have Jewish and Arab parties teamed up before?
Yes, there is precedent for such a move.
Most recently, after the 2021 elections, Ra’am emerged as a possible kingmaker, and its support was vital for the formation of the short-lived Bennett-Yair Lapid government at the time.
“Ra’am participated in the 2021-2022 coalition while Arab parties have previously supported governments from outside, most notably during the Rabin period,” Najar said, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who served in the country’s top post in the 1970s and 1990s.
“The obstacle is, therefore, neither constitutional nor practical but ideological.”
What have other party leaders said about partnering?
Netanyahu said on Tuesday that a coalition with Arab-led parties to form a government would be “a shame and a disgrace”.
“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.
Bennett, meanwhile, who is currently in third place, has reversed course from the past: He has made clear that he now only wants “Zionist” parties in government and wants to exclude Arab parties.
By contrast, Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats party, which is part of the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, has urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.
What does the reluctance to partner say about Israeli democracy?
The reluctance of Jewish-led opposition parties to work with Arab parties “reveals the fundamentally racist structure of the Israeli political system”, Najar said.
“Jewish opposition leaders describe Netanyahu and the far right as an existential danger to democracy, yet many would apparently prefer Netanyahu to remain in power rather than share political power with Palestinian citizens of Israel,” he said.
Their objection is not only to a particular Arab party or programme but to the very idea that Palestinian representatives could possess genuine governing power, Najar added.
“A state cannot credibly call itself democratic when more than one-fifth of its citizens are permitted to vote but the representatives they elect are treated as inherently illegitimate,” he said.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, he pointed out, are accepted as voters when their participation serves the system but rejected as political actors when they seek the power to shape it, Najar added.
“This is not an accidental failure of Israeli democracy; it is the consequence of a system built to preserve Jewish political supremacy,” Najar said.
“If Eisenkot is serious about replacing Netanyahu, he must decide whether he is prepared to challenge that racist political order or remain confined by the same exclusionary logic that Netanyahu has spent years exploiting.”

France planning new riot crackdown law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:28:38 UTC
23:28:38 KST

France planning new riot crackdown law
France’s Senate has backed a sweeping “vandals pay” bill that could force people involved in violent gatherings to cover up to €10,000 ($11,100) in damage caused not only by them, but also by other members of the group. The vote follows weeks of nationwide protests which spiraled into looting, arson attacks, and clashes with police.
The bill was initially drafted by the government over the summer after violence following Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory, but it gained urgency after a new wave of mass public disorder. Demonstrations against soaring living costs and worsening quality of education turned violent in several cities this month, with rioters looting shops, torching vehicles, and destroying the 19th-century city hall in Limoges. Thousands of people were arrested during the unrest, with hundreds injured.
Senators passed the measure by 229 votes to 105 on Wednesday, backed by conservatives, centrists, and Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally despite fierce objections from the left.
While presenting the legislation, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez argued that it seeks “to deter vandals and looters who burden taxpayers and demonstrators with their misdeeds, and… to better compensate the victims of this damage.”
He added that the bill is also “firmly based on fault; fault exists when one participates in a group formed with the intention of committing violence.” Meanwhile, centrist Senator Olivier Bitz reassured that “it should not be assumed that this text would allow for the prosecution of passersby or peaceful demonstrators.”
The bill – which included around 20 additional provisions compared to its original version – establishes joint civil liability for people who knowingly join a group formed to commit violence or vandalism, or remain in a crowd after police dispersal warnings while aware of ongoing attacks. Those found liable could owe up to €10,000 for destruction committed by others, although the final sum is to be determined in court, and peaceful participation alone would not trigger the measure.
To recover court-ordered compensation, the legislation would also allow deductions from social benefits, including family allowances, housing assistance, and minimum-income payments. The bill would also exempt people who remain in a gathering for legitimate reasons, potentially including journalists and medical volunteers.
While centrists and right-wing supporters portrayed the bill as a more just measure to extract damages from those involved in vandalism and protect law-abiding taxpayers, socialist Senator Marie-Pierre de La Gontrie warned that the welfare measures risk penalizing entire families.
Nathalie Godard, Director of the Action Department at Amnesty International France, also argued that the bill “threatens to further deter people from taking to the streets to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” adding that it comes on the heels of the government’s push to crack down on protests.
The Senate passed the bill ahead of the 2027 presidential race, with two key contenders taking contrasting positions over the unrest. Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in recent polls, has championed the “vandals pay” principle, accusing President Emmanuel Macron’s government of failing to control the violence.
Her left-wing rival Jean-Luc Melenchon has backed the protests while condemning looting and vandalism and accusing the authorities of inflaming tensions through police brutality.
While the bill sailed through the right-dominated Senate, it now faces a much tougher test in the fractured National Assembly, where centrist and right-wing lawmakers together hold enough seats to outvote the left but remain divided over the proposed crackdown.

‘Night of Iran’ highlights need for better global understanding of Iranian civilization
TEHRAN - Iran has yet to properly present its rich history and civilization to younger generations and the international community, the cultural heritage minister Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri underlined at an event titled “Night of Iran,” calling for a more comprehensive and historically grounded account of the country’s cultural, scientific and artistic achievements.
“We have not yet succeeded in telling the story of Iran as it deserves, given the history, culture and civilization of this land,” the minister said on Tuesday evening. “We must address this shortcoming and present a comprehensive account of Iran based on historical evidence and facts.”
The event was held at the Museum of the National Bank of Iran in downtown Tehran and brought together cultural officials, archaeologists, researchers, lawmakers and other figures involved in the country’s cultural heritage sector.
The gathering also featured the unveiling of “Thousands of Years, Iran”, a collection of photographs by Herbert Karim-Masihi documenting aspects of Iran’s historical and cultural heritage.
Salehi-Amiri described Iran as a country with deep-rooted identity, an unbroken historical continuity and a living culture that has endured through thousands of years of upheaval and foreign invasions.
He said successive invasions and political upheavals, from the Mongol and Afghan incursions to more recent threats, had inflicted damage on the country but failed to destroy its cultural and civilizational foundations.
“Iran is like a tree whose branches may bend in a storm, but whose roots remain firm,” he said, arguing that the survival of Iranian civilization demonstrates its resilience across generations.
The minister said cultural heritage was among Iran’s most important national assets because it strengthens social cohesion, reinforces national identity and creates a shared sense of belonging among Iranians.
He described Iran as a unifying force for people across the world, bringing together those with different ethnic, cultural, social and intellectual backgrounds through their historical ties to the country.
Salehi-Amiri said Iran’s history and civilization should play a greater role in shaping the country’s international image, questioning why the country is often viewed primarily through the lens of war, missiles and political disputes.
“Iran has a history spanning thousands of years, an extensive heritage and an influential culture,” he said, adding that greater attention to these achievements could help international audiences develop a deeper understanding of Iranian identity.
He called for stronger efforts to introduce the country’s historical legacy through education, research and public cultural programs.
The minister underlined that schools should incorporate appropriate material on Iranian history and civilization into their curricula, helping students understand the historical and cultural background to which they belong.
Universities, he added, should expand teaching and research on Iran’s history, intellectual traditions, arts and national identity. Such efforts would encourage historical awareness, cultural responsibility and informed participation in shaping the country’s future.
Salehi-Amiri also emphasized that much of Iran’s historical heritage remains undiscovered or insufficiently documented. Continued archaeological excavations and historical research, he said, could reveal further aspects of the country’s past and bring lesser-known stories to public attention.
He referred to the views of scholar Zhaleh Amuzegar on the endurance of Iranian civilization, noting that political leaders and governments come and go while cultural achievements can survive across centuries.
The minister also said he had held discussions with managers of banking and economic institutions about their participation in the restoration and completion of historical projects, highlighting the potential role of the private and financial sectors in preserving the country’s heritage.
Addressing the country’s difficult circumstances, Salehi-Amiri called for national solidarity and said the government was working to support the public and ease their difficulties. He apologized for shortcomings and expressed confidence that Iran would overcome its current challenges.
Amuzegar, an Iranian scholar of ancient cultures and languages, mythology, and literature, also spoke at the event, emphasizing the importance of hope and confidence in younger generations.
“Iran will not die with the young people and artists it has, and we must not lose hope,” she said.
She argued that Iran’s cultural vitality rests on a broad base of creative talent rather than a handful of prominent figures. Across generations, she said, the country has continued to produce people capable of sustaining its artistic and cultural life.
“People come and go, but Iran remains,” Amuzegar said, expressing confidence in the country’s ability to preserve its cultural identity and continue developing its creative potential.
Mohsen Seyfi-Kafashgari, chief executive of Bank Melli Iran, said the bank’s century-long history was closely connected to the country’s economic and social development and deserved to be documented for future generations.
He said the institution had experienced numerous changes and challenges throughout its first 100 years and that preserving records of its activities and major events could help illuminate aspects of Iran’s contemporary history.
The documentation project, he added, would offer an opportunity to examine the relationship between the economy, society and national identity, while preserving the experiences of an institution that has played a significant role in the country’s financial history.
The ceremony was attended by Abdolhossein Khosropanah, secretary of Iran’s Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution; Gholamreza Amirkhani, head of the National Library and Archives of Iran; Kim Jun-pyo, South Korea’s ambassador to Iran; archaeologists, cultural heritage specialists, representatives of parliament and officials from cultural institutions.
Among those present were researchers and archaeologists Fakhri Daneshparvar, Jalil Golshan and Mehrdad Malekzadeh, as well as Jebrael Nokandeh, head of the National Museum of Iran, and Mohammad Mehdi Asgarpour, head of the board of directors of the Iranian House of Cinema.

The Israeli election hurt Netanyahu, but the country is still stuck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:26:17 UTC
23:26:17 KST

The Israeli election hurt Netanyahu, but the country is still stuck
The parliamentary elections in Israel were a major test of public confidence in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israelis went to the polls in the aftermath of the events of October 7, 2023, the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, the confrontation with Iran, and increasingly strained relations with several international partners. The composition of the next government will decide the direction of Israel’s political and strategic development.
Turnout was exceptionally high – the Central Elections Committee put it at 77.7%, the highest since 1999. The main contest unfolded between Netanyahu’s Likud party and an opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the centrist Yashar party. His potential allies include the parties of Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid (who had shared a rotating premiership in 2021-22), and other parties opposed to the incumbent coalition.
According to updated exit polls conducted by three major TV networks, the opposition bloc is projected to secure 47 seats, Netanyahu’s allies 54, and Arab parties outside either camp 19. Likud nevertheless remains the largest individual party, while other projections are more favorable to the right-wing bloc. The official results are expected to be published on November 4. For now, one thing is evident: Neither side has secured a clear parliamentary majority.
Political mobilization
The turnout reflects a profound political mobilization within Israeli society. Over the past several years, decisions made by the leadership have become increasingly intertwined with questions of personal security, economic well-being, and the future of individual families. As a result, even citizens who previously remained relatively disengaged from politics have become more actively involved.
The events of October 7, 2023 were the decisive catalyst for this transformation. The failure of the national security system severely undermined confidence in the political leadership, and the subsequent wars failed to produce lasting national unity around the government. Instead, they intensified questions of political accountability, the human and economic costs of military decisions, and the absence of a convincing strategy for ending the conflicts. Even supporters of a hardline security approach have grown disillusioned with its effectiveness.
Socioeconomic pressures have also played an important role. Rising military expenditure, the high cost of living, housing difficulties, and prolonged reserve military service have shown the people the price of continuing instability. Particularly contentious has been the exemption of sections of the ultra-Orthodox community from military service, while other segments of society bear the burden.
Israel’s deteriorating international standing has further compounded these challenges. Disagreements with traditional European partners over the war in Gaza, developments in the West Bank, and the policies pursued by far-right members of the government are leaving the country with less and less room for diplomatic maneuvers. Some voters increasingly blame the government for growing diplomatic isolation and economic risks.
The high turnout was not just against Netanyahu. Right-wing voters were also highly mobilized, as was the Arab electorate, whose parties achieved a notable result. Nevertheless, the elections suggest that the existing political situation is no longer widely seen as sustainable.
The coalition struggle
In Israeli politics, electoral success does not necessarily translate into political power. In the 120-seat Knesset, a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 members, a threshold that neither of the two main political camps is so far projected to reach. The decisive struggle will now move to negotiations between parties.
After the official results are released, President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions and entrust the task of forming a government to the candidate considered most capable of securing a majority. The initial period for coalition negotiations is 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If these efforts fail, another member of the Knesset may be given 28 days to form a government. Subsequently, members of parliament would have 21 days to nominate an alternative candidate with the support of at least 61 legislators, who would then receive a further 14 days to complete the process. Should this final attempt also fail, the Knesset would be dissolved and new elections called.
Under these circumstances, smaller parties have far more power than their number of seats would suggest. In exchange for supporting a coalition, they may demand ministerial appointments, budgetary commitments, and significant policy concessions. Netanyahu’s camp will have to seek additional support beyond its traditional allies, while the opposition faces the difficult task of reconciling the positions of centrists, right-wing opponents of Netanyahu, and more liberal parties.
Arab parties, which are projected to hold 19 seats, could become particularly important. Eisenkot and some of his potential coalition partners, however, have ruled out including them in the government. External parliamentary support or abstention during a confidence vote could theoretically alter the balance, but this would require politically sensitive compromises from the centrist camp.
Netanyahu’s extensive experience in coalition-building gives him considerable opportunities to negotiate with smaller parties and persuade individual political actors to abandon competing alliances. Even if he fails to assemble a majority, he will remain in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. His political position has undoubtedly weakened, but this does not yet amount to his removal from power.
The Netanyahu factor
Netanyahu entered these elections with a loyal electoral base intact, but with substantially weakened support beyond the right-wing camp. National security has always been his central political argument. Yet the consequences of October 7 and the prolonged military campaigns have seriously damaged his reputation, raising questions about the effectiveness of his leadership.
With this in mind, reports of preparations for a new military operation against Iran shortly before the elections deserve particular attention. Axios reported on discussions between Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump, the Financial Times described preparations for a large-scale strike in early October, and CNN reported on Israeli efforts to secure American support. According to these accounts, the Trump administration prefers to avoid another major escalation ahead of the US elections scheduled for November 3. Netanyahu denied reports that Trump prevented a planned Israeli attack, and some of the reported details have also been disputed by Israeli media.
A swift and successful military operation against Iran could have unified a substantial part of society around Likud, restored Netanyahu’s image as a decisive defender of national security, and pushed criticism of his domestic policies into the background. While this does not prove that a strike was being planned for electoral purposes, the potential political benefits are obvious.
On the other hand, a short war against Iran would have been an extremely risky gamble. Iranian retaliation, the involvement of Tehran’s regional allies, additional pressure on Israel’s missile defense systems, and potential disruption of global energy markets could have produced another crisis of public confidence. The combination of American constraints and unpredictable military consequences appears to have prevented this from happening before the election.
Ultimately, the election took place without a major military development capable of fundamentally shifting votes. Should Netanyahu remain in power, the most likely outcome would be the continuation of his hardline approach towards Iran and aligned armed groups. Continued dependence on far-right coalition partners could push this policy in an even more confrontational direction. Even so, Israel would still have to take Washington’s position into account, given the importance of American support for major military operations.
The Eisenkot alternative
Gadi Eisenkot, who served as chief of the General Staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019, has emerged as Netanyahu’s principal political alternative. His main advantage lies in offering a change of leadership without abandoning the centrality of national security. For voters dissatisfied with the incumbent prime minister but unwilling to embrace a fundamental ideological shift, this is an appealing compromise. Eisenkot presents himself as a centrist, institutionally minded political figure with extensive experience in military leadership.
Particular emphasis in his political program is placed on soldiers, reservists, and their families. His party has proposed expanding housing, tax, and education benefits, increasing social assistance, and raising the remuneration of conscripts by 15%, with a 50% increase for combat soldiers in their third year of service. These proposals have the potential to attract military families that have long demanded more equitable social protection. It would, however, be an exaggeration to suggest that Israel’s entire security establishment supports a single candidate.
Another important part of Eisenkot’s electoral base consists of citizens disillusioned with the governing coalition’s style of leadership, its disputes with state institutions, and its dependence on far-right parties. Eisenkot promises to restore confidence in government, broaden the principle of compulsory military or national service, and reduce divisions within society. His political appeal is centered on effective governance rather than ideological transformation.
On the Palestinian question, however, fundamental changes are unlikely. Eisenkot opposes the establishment of a fully independent Palestinian state under present conditions and insists on maintaining Israeli control over essential security matters. Although some Jewish parties support the two-state solution, the core of a new coalition would most likely consist of nationally oriented parties. Nevertheless, Eisenkot’s criticism of illegal settlement outposts and settler violence suggests that a change in political methods is possible.
There is much more room for change in foreign policy. A departure from a government of far-right politicians whose rhetoric has complicated Israel’s relations with European partners and Arab states could, in itself, help reduce diplomatic tensions. A more pragmatic cabinet would have the opportunity to restore working relationships, ease Israel’s international isolation, and pursue a gradual normalization of relations across the region.
However, a more restrained diplomatic approach should not be mistaken for the abandonment of military deterrence. Eisenkot regards Iran’s nuclear program, its missile capabilities, and its network of regional allies as serious threats to national security. Under his leadership, Israel would likely maintain a firm policy of containment while seeking closer coordination with Washington and a more balanced combination of military and diplomatic instruments. This approach could reduce certain risks, but it would not eliminate the underlying confrontation.
The main dilemma emerging from the election is that many Israelis who voted against Netanyahu expect greater stability and a reduction in regional tensions, yet the country’s security environment and the positions of opposition leaders themselves impose significant constraints on any rapid political compromise. Eisenkot could change the style of governance and improve the atmosphere of Israel’s relations with the outside world, but he cannot guarantee peace. Netanyahu, by contrast, would be more likely to continue along the current path.
Until the official results are published and coalition negotiations concluded, it is impossible to predict with confidence who will become the next prime minister. The elections have nevertheless exposed profound public fatigue with a prolonged period of crisis and the absence of a clear political mandate for overcoming it.
The ultimate outcome will determine far more than the composition of the next government. It may also shape the future trajectory of the entire Middle East, influencing whether the region moves towards a period of cautious stabilization or enters another phase of escalating confrontation.

FACTBOX - Spain’s latest collision recalls Europe’s deadliest rail crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:26:01 UTC
23:26:01 KST

A collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain killed at least 64 people on Wednesday, according to regional authorities, bringing another major disaster to a country still dealing with the aftermath of January’s deadly Adamuz crash.
Renfe AVE train struck the rear of a stationary Iryo service on the Madrid-Seville line on Oct. 28, derailing two carriages that fell down an embankment. The trains carried 397 and 147 passengers, respectively, regional spokeswoman Esther Padilla said.
Emergency crews rushed to the scene as authorities worked to reach trapped passengers. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez canceled scheduled engagements to monitor the response. The cause remained unknown, and officials warned the death toll could rise.
It came nine months after an Iryo train derailed into the path of an oncoming Renfe service near Adamuz in southern Spain, killing 46 people.
Here is a look at some of Europe’s deadliest passenger train, metro and funicular crashes in recent years, and the investigations and legal proceedings that followed.
An Iryo train traveling from Malaga to Madrid derailed near Adamuz in Cordoba province on Jan. 18, 2026. Its rear carriages entered the adjacent track and collided with a Renfe Alvia train traveling from Madrid to Huelva.
The death toll eventually reached 46 after a 42-year-old passenger died in hospital on Jan. 30. The disaster was Spain’s deadliest rail crash since the 2013 derailment near Santiago de Compostela.
Investigators focused on a broken rail and a possible failure at a welded joint.
RTVE reported in September that a Guardia Civil inspection document identified a fracture where rail segments manufactured in 1989 and 2023 had been joined.
The findings strengthened an existing hypothesis but did not establish a final cause.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said laboratory examinations were needed before conclusions could be drawn, underscoring the distinction between evidence of a fracture and proof of how the crash began.
The Gloria funicular derailed on a steep central Lisbon street on Sept. 3, 2025, and crashed into a building, killing 16 people. Portuguese news agency Lusa later reported 24 injured, including nine seriously.
Inaugurated in 1885, the service connects Restauradores Square with the Bairro Alto neighborhood. Its two cabins are linked by a cable, with the descending cabin helping counterbalance the one climbing the hill.
The cable broke at its attachment to one cabin.
An October 2025 preliminary investigation found that it failed to meet specifications and was not certified for passenger transport, while also identifying maintenance and oversight shortcomings.
Investigators cautioned that its noncompliance had not yet been established as the reason it broke.
Portugal declared a day of national mourning, and other Lisbon funicular services were halted for inspections.
By the first anniversary, investigators had postponed publication of their final report until the first quarter of 2027 because of the complexity of technical examinations.
A passenger train carrying more than 350 people collided head-on with a freight train near Tempi, close to Larissa, on Feb. 28, 2023. The impact derailed carriages and triggered a fire, killing 57 people in Greece’s deadliest rail disaster.
Many victims were university students returning to Thessaloniki, while nine railway crew members were also among the dead. The trains had been traveling in opposite directions on the same track.
An investigation report released on Feb. 27, 2025, described a combination of human error, inadequate training, outdated infrastructure and systemic failures.
It examined how an undertrained stationmaster at an understaffed Larissa station routed the passenger service onto the track used by the oncoming freight train.
The aftermath extended beyond the crash investigation.
On its second anniversary, a general strike and mass demonstrations brought much of Greece to a halt, with victims’ families and supporters demanding accountability and safer railways.
Two trains operated by Ferrotramviaria collided head-on between Andria and Corato in southern Italy on July 12, 2016, killing 23 people and injuring dozens.
The crash occurred on a single-track section of the Bari-Barletta railway, near a bend bordered by olive groves that restricted the drivers’ view of one another.
The front carriages were destroyed, while the absence of a direct access road complicated rescue efforts in the summer heat.
Train movements on the section were controlled through a telephone system: stationmasters had to obtain clearance from the next station before authorizing departure. The investigation examined failures in those safety procedures.
On Oct. 7, 2026, Italy’s Court of Cassation upheld the convictions of two railway workers and the acquittals of Ferrotramviaria and two managers.
According to ANSA, the final ruling attributed the collision to human error rather than a failure to invest in safety.
An Alvia train traveling from Madrid to Ferrol derailed on the A Grandeira curve near Santiago de Compostela on July 24, 2013, and struck a concrete wall.
Black box data showed that the train was traveling at 179 kilometers per hour when it derailed on a section limited to 80 kilometers per hour. The driver had been distracted by a work-related telephone call and failed to slow down sufficiently before the curve.
The widely reported death toll was 80, although a 2024 court ruling attributed 79 deaths directly to the crash, finding that one passenger’s later death resulted from a serious pre-existing illness.
In January 2026, an appeals court upheld the driver’s sentence of two-and-a-half years for negligent homicide and injuries. It acquitted a former Adif safety director who had also been convicted at the initial trial, a decision opposed by one of the three judges.
Two passenger trains collided almost head-on near Buizingen, southwest of Brussels, on Feb. 15, 2010, killing 19 people and injuring 171.
A local train traveling from Leuven to Braine-le-Comte collided with an InterCity service from Quievrain to Liege during the morning rush hour. The official investigation reconstructed the accident as following the local train’s passage beyond a red signal at about 60 kilometers per hour.
The driver applied the emergency brake after seeing the other train crossing its path, but could not prevent the collision. A third train approaching the scene stopped in time.
Investigators concluded that relying on drivers’ compliance with signals was insufficient and called for automatic speed and braking protection. Rail operator SNCB and infrastructure manager Infrabel were subsequently found partly responsible and fined following legal proceedings.

Rail Baltic construction focused on Tallinn-Pärnu section
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

Rail Baltic construction focused on Tallinn-Pärnu section
Rail Baltic Estonia is currently focusing primarily on the construction of the Tallinn-Pärnu section, which should reach its final stages by the end of 2030.
According to the new schedule, the main construction work on the Tallinn-Pärnu section will reach its final stages by the end of 2030, while construction will begin from Pärnu to the Estonian-Latvian border. The Tallinn-Pärnu section is scheduled to enter service by the end of 2032. The entire Estonian section will be completed by the end of 2034.
Currently, attention is focused on the Tallinn-Pärnu section. The first test runs should also begin at the end of 2030.
"Testing, to put it simply, means making sure that all these different components work together and that they do so safely. We are currently planning to use the Ülemiste-Tootsi section as the first test section. Whether it will be shorter or longer will become clear as work progresses, but at least the initial goal is to begin testing the Ülemiste-Tootsi section at the end of 2030," said Rail Baltic Estonia CEO Anvar Salomets.
Almost half of the project's funding is taken up by so-called preparatory work.
"Building one kilometer of embankment costs approximately €7 million to €8 million per kilometer. If we now consider that the entire construction budget is €3.5 billion and we are building 200 kilometers, that comes to around €17 million per kilometer, meaning that embankment construction accounts for slightly less than half of that. The rest is the track superstructure, technical equipment, traffic management and electrification," said Rail Baltic Estonia board member Lauri Ulm.
A large share of the funding is expected to come from the European Union's Connecting Europe Facility, but agreements on the European Union's new budget are still being negotiated. Both Salomets and Ulm believe that the funding will be secured and that construction of Rail Baltica will not be canceled.
"Of course, this is still based on assumptions at present, as the relevant agreements on the new European Union budget are still being negotiated. In setting Rail Baltic Estonia's schedule, we are proceeding on the assumption that the state will ensure funding. As for what gives the state this confidence, I think perhaps the most important argument is that CEF funding has been applied for so far and has also been received. So what is expected from the next financial period is comparable in terms of the amounts involved," Salomets said.
"I do not see a scenario in which Rail Baltica is not built as a realistic possibility. It is a strategic project. It has also survived several governments, including those that are currently in opposition. I do not believe the Rail Baltica project could be halted. The state may, under any government, review priorities, deadlines and funding, which could have an impact primarily on the final completion date. But I think the question of whether Rail Baltica will be built or not was settled long ago. It will be built; the question is when," Lauri Ulm added.
The government has said that postponing the completion of Rail Baltica will make it possible to use approximately €660 million more from the European Union's new budget period.

Cassis to visit North Korea as Swiss mission reopens
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis is due to begin a three-day trip to North and South Korea. On Thursday and Friday, he will be in Pyongyang, where he will attend the offiical reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office.
On Saturday, the foreign minister will continue his trip to South Korea. The last – and indeed the only – member of the Federal Council to visit North Korea was Foreign Minister Micheline Calmy-Rey in 2003.
The diplomatic office in the North Korean capital resumed operations on October 19, 2026. The permanent diplomatic mission aims to “strengthen direct contacts with the North Korean authorities and promote political dialogue”, the Swiss foreign ministry said on Wednesday.
The office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, China, which remains responsible for diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. It was closed in March 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
“After several years of isolation”, North Korea is gradually resuming diplomatic contacts with other countries, Nicolas Bideau, head of communications at the foreign ministry, told the Keystone-ATS news agency. Switzerland is therefore seizing this opportunity to re-establish its diplomatic presence in the country.
Meeting with Kim Jong-un?
To mark the reopening of the office, Cassis will also hold political talks, the ministry has announced. But it is not known whether there will be an official meeting with leader Kim Jong-un.
Instead, the minister from canton Ticino will meet North Korea’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Choe Son-hui, as well as a representative of the Central Committee of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea (WPK), the Swiss ministry said. Discussions will also focus on the resumption of bilateral consultations between the Swiss foreign ministry and the North Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

‘Long-standing’ commitment and sanctions
Bideau described Switzerland’s diplomatic engagement with North Korea as “long-standing and concrete”, adding that, at the same time, Switzerland enforces UN Security Council sanctions, particularly those relating to North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.
“Our aim remains to contribute to peace and stability in the region, whilst upholding our principles and values,” added Bideau.
Since 1953, Switzerland has been involved in monitoring the armistice concluded that same year on the Korean Peninsula. This armistice effectively still functions as a ceasefire, with the creation of a Demilitarised Zone along the 38th parallel.
In this context, five Swiss officers are stationed at Panmunjom as part of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC), alongside five Swedish officers.

The commission accompanies inspections, observes certain military activities and reports independently on compliance with the agreement.
Regular dialogue since 2003
Switzerland has maintained diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and has engaged in regular political dialogue since 2003. Micheline Calmy-Rey has so far been the only member of the Swiss government to pay a diplomatic visit to North Korea. “It was a different era,” she told Keystone-ATS.

Surgical oncologist Polina Marinova teaches at leading centre in Strasbourg

Surgical oncologist Polina Marinova teaches at leading centre in Strasbourg
“When people are sad and under stress, it gives cancer a chance to develop,” says the specialist in an interview with Radio Bulgaria
Wednesday 28 October 2026 15:04
Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 15:04
PHOTO Medical University–Pleven
Font size
Assoc. Prof. Dr Polina Marinova is the first Bulgarian surgeon invited to teach on an international course at IRCAD in Strasbourg, one of the world’s most prestigious centres for training and innovation in minimally invasive and robotic surgery. At the Institut de recherche contre les cancers de l’appareil digestif, they value not only her surgical expertise in oncology but also her ability to pass on knowledge and experience. She takes a patient approach to training, repeating particular steps as often as necessary until the surgeon being trained has mastered the stages of the operation.
“I had the opportunity to train younger surgeons at Medical University–Pleven,” says Dr Polina Marinova. “Apparently, they could tell straight away that I had experience training younger surgeons, and that helped IRCAD decide to keep me on. This opened the way for Bulgarian surgery in the West.”
Dr Marinova learns something from every training course and encounter with leading specialists, adding to the experience she draws on in her work. “In an international setting, you can learn both from your students and from professors and mentors, including about different cultures and traditions,” she adds.
PHOTO Medical University–Pleven
“Surgical oncology chose me,” says Dr Marinova.
She is the first doctor in her family, although her mother used to work as a nurse. From an early age, she dreamed of being part of an operating team. She initially practised surgery of the liver, pancreas and bile ducts. Three years ago, Prof. Dobromir Dimitrov, head of the Clinic of Surgical Oncology, brought her into his team.
“Surgical oncology is a branch of surgery that is advancing rapidly as it adopts robotic technology,” says Dr Marinova. “We have achieved a great deal in introducing these technologies in Eastern Europe. Academician Grigor Gorchev is the pioneer, and Prof. Dimitrov is continuing his work. As surgeons he has trained, we are embracing innovations in the treatment of cancer patients. With robotic systems, we see not only technical progress but also faster recovery, less scarring and bleeding, and greater psychological and physical comfort for patients.”
PHOTO Medical University–Pleven
Despite scientific advances and their application in clinical practice, we are still a long way from being able to cure all cancers. Can a doctor leave behind at the hospital the emotional impact of what happens in the operating theatre and the weight of the words they sometimes have to say to their patients?
“A day in surgery is certainly exhausting, but we also carry an emotional burden that is difficult to cope with,” says Dr Marinova. “We cannot be morally and emotionally indifferent and tell ourselves: ‘Everything stays at work, and once the working day is over, I am a different person.’ Every surgeon is emotionally affected by what their patients go through, especially in more difficult cases. Our profession is about helping, showing compassion, understanding people’s needs and supporting them through this critical period.”
The doctor draws strength from her family to keep going. “I can see that my child sees me as a kind of superhero, helping people and saving lives,” she says. She also sees being a woman as an asset in her work: it makes her more attentive and sensitive, able to recognise her patients’ emotions, take a motherly approach to their care and even bring balance to a male world. Alongside surgery, she teaches at Medical University–Pleven and works as part of an ambulance crew, providing first aid to local residents.
PHOTO Exacta medica medical centre
“Pleven means a great deal to me,” says Dr Marinova. “What keeps me here is my family, followed by the Medical University. This is the only place where I ever wanted to study medicine. I am proud to be a graduate, and now, as a lecturer, I find fulfilment in passing on my knowledge and experience to future generations. There must be people who stay, keep traditions alive and, at the same time, encourage young people to be innovative and creative and to advance medical science.”
Dr Marinova is optimistic about the future of cancer treatment.
“Looking at the latest scientific advances, I think surgery will increasingly be replaced by treatment at the molecular and genetic level,” she says. “Why shouldn’t cancer become curable with a pill or a vaccine, just as treatments once thought unimaginable have become possible for other diseases? I think we are already moving in that direction. Perhaps in 20 to 30 years, our children will see a time when surgery is no longer the main method of treatment.”
PHOTO Medical University–Pleven
But how can we protect ourselves against cancer, and what role does our state of mind play in its development?
“Of course, our state of mind plays a crucial role in the development of cancer,” says Dr Marinova. “When people are constantly under stress, feel sad or have problems, it affects the way the whole body functions, weakens its defences and gives the disease a chance to develop. That is why I say Bulgarians should smile, feel good and make room for positive emotions. Perhaps what is missing from our busy daily lives is a smile, a kind word and a sense of ease both at home and at work.”
There is a simple message that can have a positive ripple effect: “Be kind!” Perhaps it can help us feel healthier, too. Dr Marinova says it to her child, but her message is for all of us: “Let kindness be the virus that spreads through our society!”
Editor: E. Karkalanova

Liverpool’s lessons for Burgas: What hosting Eurovision brings to a city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:22:57 UTC
23:22:57 KST

News
Liverpool’s lessons for Burgas: What hosting Eurovision brings to a city
“Eurovision is a gift that comes once... It is up to the city itself to make the most of this opportunity,” says Claire McColgan, Director of Culture at Liverpool City Council.
Wednesday 28 October 2026 15:29
Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 15:29
PHOTO artav.co.uk
Font size
As Burgas prepares to host Europe’s biggest song contest in 2027, Liverpool is sharing its experience with Bulgarians.
The topic of Eurovision took centre stage at the Sofia Hotel Investment Forum (HTIF 2026). Delegates heard that the direct economic impact for Liverpool reached £55 million, with over 300,000 tourists visiting the city. Claire McColgan*, Director of Culture at Liverpool City Council, spoke to Radio Bulgaria about hosting Eurovision in 2023. Liverpool took on the hosting duties on behalf of Ukraine due to the war, just as the world was emerging from the COVID-19 pandemic.
How did Liverpool manage the challenge of combining the glamour of the stage with the reality of war?
“The concept for Liverpool wasn’t just that the city was hosting Eurovision, but that it was hosting on behalf of Ukraine,” McColgan replies. “And that idea guided every decision we made. We created an entire programme: 12 national and international creative projects brought Ukrainian and local artists together to build connections and create art that was both dedicated to Eurovision and spoke to the situation in Ukraine. It felt as though the entire city was wrapped in a giant Ukrainian flag. And yet, it was a glorious, joyful celebration of life.”
PHOTO Elizabeth Radkova
McColgan says the city turned the cause into a personal mission for every resident. The extensive programme reached even schools. She recalls a heartfelt moment during a visit by Oleksandr Tkachenko, then Ukraine’s Minister of Culture. The children at one of the schools the minister visited performed the Ukrainian anthem in sign language as a gesture of solidarity.
When it comes to practical lessons and advice for future hosts in Burgas, Claire McColgan is clear that the key lies in how visitors are treated:
“Eurovision is a gift that comes once... It is up to the city itself to make the most of this opportunity. Most visitors will be coming to Burgas for the first time, and it matters how you welcome them and make them feel comfortable, so that their overall experience – from museums and galleries to beaches and bars – is positive.
PHOTO BTA
She also pays special attention to local businesses, advising hotels and restaurants not to give in to the temptation of price-gouging. A price increase of 20 to 30 per cent is understandable, but anything more is not. The owners who kept prices most reasonable in Liverpool during Eurovision reaped the greatest long-term benefits, McColgan explains.
According to her, the music contest has a loyal, well-travelled audience whose members are quick to find alternatives. The businesses that win are those that adapt what they offer and commit to the true spirit of Eurovision.
What attracts more tourists to Liverpool – music or sport?
“That’s a great question, the best anyone has ever asked me,” says Claire McColgan. “I would say music, although sport has its place too. But if you look at major music events, people stay much longer and the city comes alive in a completely different way, because culture is always unique.
PHOTO Elizabeth Radkova
Beyond the intensive organisation and the millions recorded in the economic reports, it is the emotional moments that have stayed with McColgan. One of the most emotional came on the night of the final, when fans of the city’s two rival football clubs sang together in the fan village:
“In Liverpool, we have two rival football teams – Everton and Liverpool. And Everton fans wouldn’t sing Liverpool’s anthem, ‘You’ll Never Walk Alone’, for the world. But back then, in the fan village on the night of the Eurovision final, fans of both clubs, alongside European partners and people carrying flags from all nations, were singing that song on Liverpool’s famous waterfront. That was a huge moment for me; I cried. I cried quite a bit during the event, but that was the moment I cried the most.”
*Claire McColgan is Director of Culture and Major Events at Liverpool City Council and was one of the leading organisers of Eurovision 2023 in Liverpool. She has over 30 years of experience in culture, urban regeneration and tourism, and played a leading role in Liverpool’s European Capital of Culture programme in 2008. For her services to culture and the promotion of the city as a tourist destination, she was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE).

English editing: E. Radkova

Bulgarians made 1,031,700 trips abroad in September 2026, up 2.7% from the same month last year, according to preliminary data from the National Statistical Institute. Travel increased across all categories.
Meanwhile, visits by foreign nationals to Bulgaria fell by 4.1% to 1,251,900. Visits for purposes other than holidays or business declined by 6.3%, while holiday and leisure visits were down 3.1%. The most popular destinations for Bulgarian travellers were Türkiye, Greece, Serbia, Romania and Germany. Most foreign visitors to Bulgaria came from Türkiye, Romania, Ukraine, Greece and Germany.

UK raises bank taxes to fund energy relief for households
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:22:09 UTC
23:22:09 KST

Britain’s Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, holds up the red ministerial box outside No 11 Downing Street before departing to the House of Commons to deliver the first budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government on Oct. 28.
Britain announced a temporary increase in bank taxes on Oct. 28 to help fund household energy relief as Finance Minister John Healey presented his first budget.
The surcharge on bank profits, paid on top of corporation tax, will rise from 3 to 6 percent from January 2027 for 15 months.
“I am looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families,” Healey told parliament.
The package includes a £100 energy payment this winter for 20 million households in the four lowest council tax bands, A to D.
He also extended the five-pence-per-liter fuel duty cut and a VAT reduction on electricity bills until July 2027.
The government plans to remove fixed daily charges from household gas bills in 2027 or as soon as possible afterward, moving the costs into the price per unit of gas.
Higher borrowing costs constrain the government’s efforts to support households and businesses while meeting its fiscal rules. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecast economic growth of 1.2 percent this year, 1 percent in 2027 and 1.6 percent in 2028.
Healey said he retained a £15 billion buffer against the rule requiring day-to-day spending to be covered by tax revenues in 2029-30, while using some fiscal room to cushion the Iran war’s impact.
For retail, hospitality and leisure firms, the threshold for full relief from business rates, a tax on commercial premises, will rise from £12,000 to £18,000.
The change will exempt another 70,000 businesses, while others in those sectors will face no above-inflation increases for two years.
The national minimum wage and national living wage will rise by 3.9 percent, benefiting 2.3 million workers.
He scrapped plans to cut the annual allowance for cash individual savings accounts (ISAs), keeping the tax-free contribution limit at £20,000.
Healey also announced an additional £20.4 billion for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank over the coming years to support investment in British companies.
Next year’s spending review would set out how Britain aims to raise defense spending to 3 percent of gross domestic product in 2030 and meet its NATO commitment of 3.5 percent by 2035, he said.

Israel's final election results expected Thursday evening: Election official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:20:51 UTC
23:20:51 KST

Şahin Demir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Israel’s final parliamentary election results are expected Thursday evening, Israeli news website Ynet reported Wednesday, citing an election official. 
Elad Naveh, director of the Central Elections Committee’s control center, said the counting of special double-envelope ballots would begin Wednesday evening and was expected to be completed Thursday evening, although the process could continue until Friday. 
The committee said the estimated number of double-envelope ballots had been revised to between 430,000 and 480,000, according to Ynet. 
Processing was still underway, and not all special envelopes had been processed, the committee noted, stressing that the estimate was preliminary and could change as the work progressed. 
The special ballots were cast by voters outside their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers, and displaced residents. 
Under the system, voters place their ballot inside an envelope, which is then placed in a second envelope containing their identification details to prevent duplicate voting. 
As of the latest count, 85.6% of votes had been counted. 
Partial results showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to win 53 seats, the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48 seats, and predominantly Arab parties 19 seats. 
Neither major bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority in the 120-member Knesset. 
Naveh cautioned that the distribution of seats could change once the remaining ballots were counted. 
More than 7.3 million Israelis were eligible to vote in Tuesday’s elections. 
The elections were Israel’s first since the start of its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

COP17 is being held in Yerevan from October 19 to 30, bringing together countries to assess progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and discuss ways to accelerate conservation efforts, mobilize financial resources, and strengthen international cooperation.

Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
October 28, 2026
Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm election on November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.
Saudi Arabia said the trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.
A senior Pakistani official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.
Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.
Tehran presents the meeting as a success
Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."
Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.
A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."
Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.
These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.
Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?
The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants.
Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.
"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.
Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.
At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And having a defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.
Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: It can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.
Ryad pushing for a 'diplomatic solution'
Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks have damaged its infrastructure and economy, but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.
"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."
Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran, and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.
Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki said direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.
Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting
Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejected the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.
He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.
"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.
He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.
"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said, adding that an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.
Diplomatic game continues
Dorbeiki argued that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.
The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.
Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.
The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

French Frigate Intercepts Ballistic Missile in Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:19:47 UTC
23:19:47 KST

A French Navy frigate intercepted a ballistic missile near the Belgian minehunter Primula while escorting the vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area.
Baird Maritime reported the incident, citing confirmation from the French Armed Forces General Staff on October 27.
According to the French military command, the incident occurred on October 13, 2026, while the French frigate was escorting a Belgian Tripartite-class minehunter.
The French General Staff emphasized that the crew’s actions were purely defensive. No one was injured, and neither vessel sustained damage.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen first reported the interception on October 26. Belgium’s Ministry of Defense subsequently confirmed the information to VRT NWS journalists.
Initial assessments suggest that the missile may have been launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who have attacked vessels in the Red Sea. However, their involvement has not been officially confirmed.
The French military command has not disclosed the name of the frigate that carried out the interception or the type of surface-to-air missile used.
A French Ministry of the Armed Forces operational update for October 8-15 reported that a FREMM-class multipurpose frigate was operating in the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden as part of the European Union’s EUNAVFOR ASPIDES operation.
One of the French ships operating in the area was the frigate Languedoc. In early October, it shot down a drone while escorting the CMA CGM Champs Elysées container ship through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
However, no confirmation currently indicates that Languedoc intercepted the ballistic missile on October 13.
The Belgian Primula (M924) belongs to the Tripartite class of mine countermeasures vessels, jointly developed by Belgium, the Netherlands, and France.
The ship is designed to search for, identify, and neutralize naval mines. However, it lacks the missile-defense systems needed to independently counter ballistic threats.
According to Belgium’s Ministry of Defense, on May 28, Primula and the Dutch minehunter Willemstad departed Zeebrugge for the Mediterranean to join NATO’s Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2).
The deployment was also intended to enable the Belgian vessel to participate in potential mine-clearing operations in the Strait of Hormuz, should the relevant political decision be made.

Ukraine May Return to Light Masking Over Russian Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:19:07 UTC
23:19:07 KST

Ukraine may have to return to light masking because of Russian drones, said Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, the president’s adviser on defense technology development.
In a Telegram post, Beskrestnov said such a step could be needed if Russia begins using the “Susanin” optical navigation module at night on a mass scale. He named the Geran-5 drone, along with other drones and missiles, as carriers of the module.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This especially applies to lighting of roads and highway sections,” he wrote.
What is ‘Susanin’?
“Susanin” is a flight controller that lets a drone navigate using visual cues.
Beskrestnov explained that the drone loads satellite images of the terrain into its memory beforehand, and the onboard computer compares the camera feed with them in flight. A drone flying using terrain imagery does not rely on GPS or radio-control links, and thus is not affected by electronic warfare jamming or spoofing.
The idea is not new, as it is similar to the Terrain Contour Matching System (TERCOM) used in US Tomahawk missiles.
Russia already uses similar technology on smaller drones such as the Molniya, V2U, and Lancet, and it was recently found on the jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Ukrainian air defense has been shooting down jet-powered Geran-5 missiles near Kyiv, launched from about 400 km (249 miles) away.
Beskrestnov also compared the situation with the initial days of Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Poland, UK Sign 3-Year Defense Cooperation Plan
By his account, light masking was introduced then out of fear and a lack of understanding. This time, he suggested, the question may need to be approached consciously.
Light masking is a wartime tactic that dims or switches off lights after dark so aircraft and drones cannot spot targets, and it was implemented at the onset of the 2022 invasion.
Under a Cabinet resolution, Ukrainian authorities introduced a curfew and a special light-masking rule, and patrols enforce them. In Kyiv, a curfew from 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. began on Feb. 28, 2022, and shops, pharmacies, and public transport had to stop operating by 7 p.m.
Curfew hours in Kyiv were later reduced to midnight to 5 a.m., then to 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. as of publication.
More accidents were also reported on roads after blackouts.
Later in 2022, when Kyiv cut street lighting to save energy after Russian strikes on power infrastructure, Kyiv patrol police reported a 25% rise in pedestrian deaths in road accidents, though no direct link was established.

India looks to private players to boost space economy fivefold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:18:43 UTC
23:18:43 KST

India looks to private players to boost space economy fivefold
India is building additional launch pads, deploying new technologies, and boosting private players and startups in an ambitious program to grow its space industry fivefold to $44 billion by 2033.
New Delhi introduced reforms to its space industry – where the publicly-owned Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) was the sole player – to promote private sector participation in 2020.
“Earlier, only ISRO could do end-to-end activities, while other companies were working as vendors to ISRO,” Vinod Kumar, director at the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe), told ANI recently. IN-SPACe is the regulatory and promotional agency for non-government entities in India’s space sector.
India’s space ecosystem has expanded rapidly since, with 50 large firms, 450 space startups, and 300 small and micro-medium enterprises currently active in the $8.4 billion market.
The growth comes even as the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV) program, launched in 2023 with an outlay of $1 billion, is expected to triple India’s launch pad capacity. This additional launch capacity is critical for realizing missions including manned flights to the Bharatiya Antariksh Station and lunar exploration, as well as meeting launch demands from domestic industries.
“We have SSLV, and we have augmented launch capacity with a new launch pad at Kulasekarapattinam in (the southern state of) Tamil Nadu,” Kumar said. The SSLV is a launch vehicle for small satellites, crucial to meeting the rising demand from low-earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations for internet connectivity and earth observation satellites.
“That business will (now) stay in India,” Kumar was reported as saying. Two Indian companies – billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb – have sought licenses for providing satellite internet services in the country, alongside Elon Musk’s Starlink.
The federal government also wants the private players to expand their role in technological development, satellite manufacturing, and space-based applications.
NewSpace India Limited, the commercial arm of ISRO, has signed 118 technology transfer agreements to enable the domestic industry to access and utilize technologies that its parent has developed. A rejigging of the space policy in 2023 and changes to foreign direct investment norms have also contributed to growth in the sector.
India launched a $102 million venture capital fund and $52 million technology adoption fund for space startups. The cumulative funding in Indian space start-ups touched $618.5 million as of March 31. The funding pattern has also shifted from early-stage seed support to larger, growth-stage rounds, according to the government.
