MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- At least 64 were killed in a train accident that occurred on Wednesday in the Spanish province of Toledo, south of Madrid, local authorities confirmed.
Emergency services continue to search for bodies of the victims with the help of trained dogs, and "even more" victims could still be found among the passengers of the two trains involved in the accident, said Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha which includes the province of Toledo.

In pics: agricultural science and technology industrial park in Jinhua City, China's Zhejiang
China
Unknown Publisher

An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 27, 2026 shows a night view of a smart greenhouse at an agricultural science and technology industrial park in Jindong District of Jinhua City, east China's Zhejiang Province. The agricultural science and technology industrial park was established in September 2023 as a designated benchmark project for modern agriculture in Jindong District of Jinhua City.
The park covers an area of 198.2 mu (about 13.2 hectares), including modern agricultural smart greenhouses, outdoor standardized planting areas, as well as supporting facilities such as water sources and parking lots. It aims to create an intelligent agricultural comprehensive industrial park integrating seedling research and development, ecological planting, deep processing, brand sales, tourism, and agricultural technology demonstration.
The park has introduced specialty fruit and vegetable varieties of pineapples, dragon fruits, and blueberries to build a demonstration model for high-end tropical fruit and vegetable planting. It has revitalized the idle land resources in the area, optimized the regional agricultural industrial structure. (Xinhua/Xu Yu)

====================================================================================================

Feature: South Sudanese farmers turn floodwater into rice harvests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:06 CST
22:58:06 KST

JUBA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For years, seasonal flooding has threatened the livelihoods of farmers in South Sudan's Northern Bahr el Ghazal, destroying sorghum crops and undermining household food supplies.
But in Aweil, the capital of Northern Bahr el Ghazal, some farmers are learning to capitalize on the waterlogged land by cultivating rice.
Santino Akech, a 45-year-old farmer, said rice cultivation had offered his community an alternative to traditional crops that struggle to survive in flooded lowlands.
"When flooding came, it affected sorghum, but the rice succeeded," Akech said during a recent interview in Aweil.
Haileselassie Berhanu, head of program at the World Food Program (WFP) Aweil Field Office, said, "We have tried to consider the flood as a potential opportunity, not as a threat," explaining that the WFP and local communities began exploring rice cultivation in waterlogged areas several years ago.
This year, more than 2,100 households were participating in rice cultivation, with approximately 1,000 hectares under cultivation across the wider initiative, according to Berhanu.
Farmers previously cultivated individually but had limited capacity to expand production, said Akech. Through group farming, they pooled resources, expanded their cultivated land and received training in rice-growing techniques from a local partner. In 2025, Akech said that farmers harvested 42 bags of rice weighing 90 kg each from about 1.68 hectares of land.
However, he also identified weeding and harvesting as major challenges, noting that rice cultivation was still a relatively new practice for many community members. Farmers need machinery to prepare waterlogged land, training in improved cultivation methods and access to rice varieties suited to local conditions as well.
In a recent field trip to Aweil, Mutinta Chimuka, WFP country representative for South Sudan, said helping communities produce their own food was an important part of the agency's work to improve food security, alongside the distribution of food assistance.
She described the crop observed as promising, saying the location had retained water despite a dry spell that had affected agricultural production elsewhere.
The crop was flowering and expected to be ready for harvesting soon, Chimuka said.
Chimuka urged closer cooperation with state and national authorities to identify the most suitable locations for rice cultivation and varieties that could perform well under local conditions.
Chinese Ambassador to South Sudan Ma Qiang, who also joined the field visit, said the rice initiative demonstrated the potential to leverage natural conditions, strengthen agricultural production and improve resilience to climate-related shocks.
Ma said that China's experience and agricultural technologies could provide opportunities for further cooperation with South Sudan, including through engagement with national and local governments and other partners.
China has previously donated agricultural machinery to local communities, he added.
Martha Abuk, a 40-year-old farmer who also cultivates rice in Aweil, said that farming and participation in group savings activities had helped her household meet some of its needs, including school fees for the children.
As the WFP and its partners explore ways to expand rice cultivation, the experiences of farmers in Aweil illustrate both the opportunities and the constraints involved in adapting agriculture to climate-related challenges.
Sustaining that progress, however, will depend on farmers' access to suitable equipment, technical knowledge and resources to increase production. ■

KAMPALA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Mbale City in eastern Uganda and Guiyang City in southwest China have signed a letter of intent to establish friendly exchange and cooperation relations, laying the groundwork for a future sister-city partnership, Uganda's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Wednesday.
The agreement, signed on Monday in Guiyang by Mbale City Mayor Joyce Matuka Kidulu and Wang Hong, mayor of Guiyang, outlines five priority areas for cooperation: smart city development and digital governance, industrial development and investment, agriculture and value addition, tourism and cultural exchange, and environmental sustainability, according to a ministry statement issued in Kampala.
The two cities agreed to establish a joint working group within two months and arrange a technical visit to Mbale to explore investment opportunities in industrial development, coffee processing and tourism, the statement said.
The proposed partnership aims to link Mbale's strengths in Arabica coffee production with Guiyang's expanding coffee industry and expertise in digital technology and green development.
Located near Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda, Mbale is a major coffee-producing area and an important industrial hub. Guiyang, the capital of China's Guizhou Province, has developed a strong presence in big data and digital industries.
The signing took place during a working visit to Guiyang by a Ugandan delegation, which also participated in a coffee trade promotion and business-matching session with the Guiyang Coffee Industry Association.
Uganda's coffee exports to China increased by 224 percent in the 2025/2026 financial year, the statement said, pointing to opportunities to expand market access and promote value addition through the cooperation framework. ■

Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
The deployment marks the first time in years that three Vanguard-class vessels have been at sea at the same time.
The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea for the first time in five years, The Times reported on Wednesday.
At least one of the vessels – known as Vanguard-class submarines – was said to be armed with ballistic missiles which carry nuclear warheads.
The report named the three submarines at sea as HMS Vanguard, HMS Vigilant and HMS Vengeance, with the fourth, HMS Victorious, currently undergoing maintenance.
A navy source quoted by The Times described the deployment as “unusual”, without elaborating.
The UK continuously deploys at least one of the four submarines as a security guarantee.
The deployment has raised questions over whether the UK has changed its defence posture after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned last week that Britain should be prepared for war.
Here’s what we know:
Has this happened before?
The last time three submarines were at sea was more than five years ago, according to The Times.
Navy Lookout, the UK’s leading independent publication on the Royal Navy, says one submarine carrying ballistic missiles has been at sea without interruption since 1969.
It said the second vessel was believed to be preparing to relieve a patrol boat, while the third was likely conducting sea trials or work-up activity.
Last year HMS Vanguard patrolled the seas for 200 days, just a week shy of the longest known submarine deployment of 207 days, carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.
What has the UK government said?
According to Sky News, a spokesperson for the defence ministry said the country’s nuclear deterrent is the “cornerstone of our national security, protecting the UK and our NATO allies every moment of every day”.
“We remain the only European ally to commit its nuclear deterrent to the defence of NATO. This means that all NATO allies already benefit from the protection of our nuclear deterrent,” the spokesperson added.
Last week, British and French fighter jets flew together in their first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capability.
The French armed forces ministry said British RAF Typhoon fighters escorted the French jets, simulating a nuclear strike.
France’s Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said that having “independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination”.
“Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom continues to deepen,” she added.
The UK’s Streeting said that in an “increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt”.
“The United Kingdom and France stand together in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” he added.
What are the UK’s ‘war readiness’ plans?
On Saturday, Streeting wrote in the Telegraph newspaper that Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days.
“Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030, their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack,” Streeting wrote.
“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win. This Government will make sure it is mission accomplished,” he said.
His message followed last week’s launch of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign, which called on households to store three days’ supply of tinned food and water bottles, cash and a wind-up radio in case of a cyberattack or a weather event which disrupts infrastructure.
The warning also followed reports that Russia has been using fishing trawlers to track and spy on the UK’s undersea cables.

Zelensky reveals what to expect as Ukraine, Russia head back to peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:55:47 UTC
22:55:47 KST

As Ukraine, Russia head back to peace talks, here's what Zelensky expects
President Volodymyr Zelensky, following an interview in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 18, 2026. (Olga Ivashchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
A planned meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi will focus on de-escalating Russia's war, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 27, as Moscow seemingly agreed to resume talks with Kyiv after a pause of more than eight months.
Although Ukrainian officials do not expect the first round to produce a major breakthrough, Kyiv hopes the meeting will restart regular negotiations and deliver limited results.
"They had the impression the Russians are serious about the meeting in Abu Dhabi," Zelensky told reporters, referring to a call Norwegian and Finnish leaders held with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 27.
The planned meeting follows renewed U.S. efforts to bring the sides together, including visits by President Donald Trump's envoy to Kyiv and Moscow.
But even if the talks resume, major disagreements over territory and security guarantees are likely to remain obstacles to any potential settlement.
What to expect?
The latest push for a trilateral meeting began in early September, when Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Kyiv and Moscow to seek progress toward ending Russia's war before the U.S. midterm elections.
The visits produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a meeting involving Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
Putin initially declined to meet with the Ukrainian side after the September trip, but the Kremlin signaled readiness to resume talks after Witkoff visited Moscow on Oct. 21.
Zelensky said the planned meeting should focus on immediate steps toward de-escalation.
"The agenda should cover the following issues: initial steps toward de-escalation, the main priorities for the Ukrainian side — particularly security priorities — and, more broadly, ending this war," Zelensky told reporters.
"We hope for a result regarding energy and at sea, an exchange of prisoners, and a discussion of the possible format for a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."
The Ukrainian president added that Kyiv hopes the technical groups will agree on practical measures or make progress.
One senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first meeting is unlikely to produce any results, arguing that the sides need to reestablish a shared understanding after such a long pause in negotiations.
Still, Kyiv hopes subsequent meetings will become regular and deliver at least limited gains each time. The official said that prisoner exchanges and sector-specific ceasefires, including one focused on energy infrastructure, are priorities.
A recent example of a limited ceasefire was the temporary truce in Oleshky, a city in Kherson Oblast that has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces. The truce was intended to address the humanitarian situation in the city.
A meeting between Putin and Zelensky remains a much more uncertain prospect. The two leaders have not met since 2019, and Moscow continues to insist that Zelensky travel to Russia for direct talks — a proposal Kyiv rejects.
During a phone call with Finland's president and Norway's prime minister on Oct. 27, Putin said Zelensky could come to Moscow. Ukraine views the proposal as a sign that the Russian leader is unwilling to meet Zelensky on mutually acceptable terms.
Trump, however, told reporters on Oct. 27 that a meeting between the two leaders could happen "soon."
Security guarantees, Donbas
Even if the planned talks resume, the sides will face the same disagreements that stalled previous negotiations, particularly over Donbas and the security arrangements that would accompany an end to the war.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the parts of Donbas that Russia has failed to capture militarily. The strategically important region in eastern Ukraine remains a central point of talks.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
In earlier negotiations, U.S. representatives proposed establishing a demilitarized zone in Donbas, an idea both sides initially supported. However, Putin insisted that Moscow should effectively control the territory, a position Kyiv rejected.
Zelensky said U.S. envoys have again raised the issue of Donbas in discussions with Ukrainian and Russian teams. Moscow continues to link the territorial question to the broader terms for ending the war, including security guarantees.
"Russia links the issue of territories to ending the war, security guarantees, and the possible forms those guarantees could take," Zelensky said.
He added that Ukraine's partners had avoided an in-depth discussion of territorial concessions because they understood Kyiv considers the issue a red line.
"Our partners couldn't go into the territorial issue in depth because they know it's a red line for us," Zelensky said. "This is an issue that can only be discussed by the leaders of the countries at war, and only at their level."
Zelensky said Ukraine had been prepared to discuss a buffer zone or demilitarized zone on both sides of the line of contact as a possible compromise.
But the dispute over control of the territory remains unresolved, leaving the planned meeting focused primarily on whether the sides can agree on immediate steps toward de-escalation rather than a settlement. At least for now.

Ukraine Finds Way to Strike Back at Data Center Attacks. “More Painful for Russia,” Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine has developed a way to counter Russian attacks targeting its data centers and digital infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with The Sun.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s retaliatory strikes have a greater impact on Russia due to its centralized infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a statement shared on his official X account on October 28, Zelenskyy said Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure since September 2026 had prompted Kyiv to develop countermeasures.
“Many people didn't see that Russia was attacking our data and cyberspace over a long period of time. Then we found a way to weaken Russia's strategy, to respond to their attacks on data,” Zelenskyy said.
He emphasized that Ukraine’s technological development and decentralized digital infrastructure had helped maintain essential communications despite repeated Russian strikes.
“Ukraine is more technologically advanced. The Russians attacked our data centers so many times, and still we had cell service and an Internet connection. Because we are digitally decentralized and advanced,” Zelenskyy noted.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s retaliatory strikes were more “painful for Russia because they are more centralized.” He explained that Moscow relied on extensive air defense systems to protect its facilities, while Ukraine, facing a shortage of such capabilities, had decentralized its infrastructure, including data systems.
“But we always try to respond and do so only after Russian attacks against us,” the president added.
Zelenskyy’s remarks come amid continued Russian attacks on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure, including a recent strikes that damaged major Ukrainian data centers.
The first large-scale Russian attack on Kyiv’s data centers occurred on September 23, 2026, damaging at least four facilities, including Parkovy, NewTelco, and United DC, as well as infrastructure operated by UTELS and Pavutyna.
The strikes disrupted internet connectivity for approximately 100,000 households and subscribers in Kyiv and other regions, temporarily affecting the operations of several internet providers and online services.
Further attacks followed in October, causing additional damage to the country’s data infrastructure.
An overnight Russian ballistic missile attack on October 19 destroyed the Datagroup data center’s equipment and infrastructure, rendering the facility inoperable and beyond repair.
The company confirmed the damage in a Facebook statement, saying that restoring the data center and resuming its operations would not be possible.
Additionally, on October 20, a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital damaged the GigaCenter data center, raising concerns about potential disruptions to servers and IT equipment hosted at the facility.
In a Facebook statement, GigaCenter confirmed the damage and said its technical teams were working to mitigate the consequences of the strike and maintain stable operations.
The company also warned customers that equipment hosted at the facility could experience temporary service interruptions as recovery efforts continued.

Ukraine Unmasks Who’s Behind Russia’s Starlink Rival Built for War
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has identified 49 Russian and Belarusian companies involved in developing Rassvet, Moscow’s planned alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network, which Ukrainian intelligence says is being designed primarily for military operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, with the findings released on October 28, 23 of the 49 identified organizations, including Russia’s space agency Roscosmos, remain outside international sanctions.
The project brings together technology companies, microelectronics manufacturers, research institutions, aerospace enterprises, and organizations affiliated with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Its main developer is Bureau 1440, part of the Russian technology conglomerate ICS Holding. Companies within the group manufacture solar panels, satellite terminals, printed circuit boards, electronic modules, and other components required for the system.
Roscosmos and other aerospace enterprises are responsible for developing launch vehicles, propulsion systems, and satellite components, as well as deploying spacecraft into orbit.
Russia’s state-owned VTB Bank has also provided financial backing for the project, while Roscosmos chief Dmitry Bakanov oversees its implementation within the space agency.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Rassvet is intended to provide strategic communications for Russian military units, command centers, strike platforms, and unmanned systems.
Russian plans also include integrating the constellation into space-based missile targeting infrastructure and installing satellite terminals on command vehicles associated with the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system.
HUR reports that the system’s priority coverage area will include Ukraine and European Union countries. Once sufficient satellite coverage is established, Russia could also use the network to support hybrid operations against other states.
The project has also faced technical challenges. According to orbital tracking data reported on October 13, two Rassvet satellites launched in July were losing altitude and were projected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere by late October or early November. While most satellites from the same batch reached approximately 500 kilometers, the two remained near 250 kilometers.

Finland buys German RGW110 anti-tank weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:47:07 UTC
22:47:07 KST

- Finland will buy the RGW110 heavy disposable anti-tank weapon from Dynamit Nobel Defence for about $94 million, excluding value-added tax.
- The weapon will replace the APILAS launcher bought in the 1980s, with deliveries and training starting in 2027.
Finland will buy the RGW110 heavy disposable anti-tank weapon from Germany’s Dynamit Nobel Defence to replace the APILAS launcher its soldiers have carried since the 1980s, the Finnish Army said on Oct. 28.
The purchase is worth about €84.5 million (about $94 million) excluding value-added tax, and deliveries of the weapons, training equipment and instruction will begin in 2027, Finland’s government said after Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen authorized the deal. The Finnish Defence Forces did not say how many launchers it is ordering.
“The main battle tank will remain a threat on the battlefield in the future as well. The new disposable launcher system is intended for destroying tanks at close range and will replace the APILAS system acquired in the 1980s as the troops’ heavy close-range anti-tank weapon,” said Col. Ari Mure, inspector of infantry at Finnish Army Command.
The RGW110 is a shoulder-fired, single-use weapon that a soldier fires once and throws away, so units can carry it like ammunition and spread it across many fighting positions without the support crews that guided missile systems need. The Finnish Army said this lets several soldiers fire at the same tank from different positions at once, while keeping the logistics burden and the load on each soldier lighter. The rocket is unguided, so it cannot be jammed, and the army said it works in any light or weather, from towns to forest and in both attack and defense.
The trade-off is range. The army acknowledged that the unguided round has a relatively short reach, but said Finland’s broken, heavily wooded terrain makes up for it by letting soldiers get close to enemy armor unseen. Dynamit Nobel Defence lists an effective range of up to 800 m (2,600 feet), roughly twice that of the Panzerfaust 3 it was designed to succeed, European Security & Defence reported.
Penetration drove the choice. The Finnish Army said a modern anti-tank weapon must first clear a tank’s explosive reactive armor, the boxes of explosive bolted to the outside of the hull to disrupt incoming warheads, and then carry a large enough caliber to punch through the main armor behind it. The RGW110 uses a 110 mm tandem warhead, in which a small lead charge sets off the reactive armor before the main charge strikes, and its maker says it can penetrate about 1,000 mm of armor steel behind reactive armor. Finland compared the systems on the market, tested the one that met its criteria against a target with realistic armor protection, and then worked with the manufacturer to further improve the warhead. The army said observations from the war in Ukraine confirmed its earlier assessments of how well an adversary’s tanks are protected.
The RGW110 is the larger, 110 mm member of Dynamit Nobel Defence’s RGW family, whose 90 mm RGW90, known as MATADOR, has been used in combat in Ukraine since Germany cleared exports and Ukraine received more of the German-made anti-armor weapons from the company’s stocks in 2022. Hungary became the first customer for the RGW110 in 2022 and has set up a joint venture with Dynamit Nobel Defence to build parts of the weapon locally, while the warheads are still made at the company’s plant in Burbach, Germany.

Supreme Court says legality of EC's 'logical discrepancy' checks in SIR remains undecided
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:47:04 UTC
22:47:04 KST

The clarification came during a hearing on a petition alleging a lack of transparency in notices.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday clarified that it has not yet delivered a final ruling on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) use of the “logical discrepancy” category to flag voters’ details during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said its earlier decision allowing the Election Commission to use the category in West Bengal was only an interim measure. It also clarified that the court’s ruling on the SIR exercise in Bihar had not settled every legal question surrounding the revision process.The clarification came during a hearing on a petition alleging a lack of transparency in notices issued to voters during the ongoing SIR exercise in Delhi. Senior advocate D S Naidu, appearing for the Election Commission, had argued that the court had examined all stages of the SIR process and upheld its validity.Justice Bagchi rejected the suggestion that the earlier proceedings had conclusively settled the legality of the logical discrepancy category.“Bihar is not a final determination of every question arising in these proceedings. In Bihar, the Election Commission had not initially undertaken logical discrepancy as a category.
We permitted it as an interim arrangement in West Bengal. We have not finally adjudicated upon the legality of the logical discrepancy exercise,” Justice Bagchi was quoted as saying by the news agency PTI.The judge also cautioned against treating oral observations made during hearings as final judicial decisions, particularly in sensitive cases.
"We do not wish to make further comments because observations in sensitive matters are sometimes taken out of context. These observations are not conclusive. There is a difficulty when judicial observations are repeatedly cited out of context as if every issue has already been decided," he said.
What is the ‘logical discrepancy’ category
During the SIR exercise, the Election Commission uses the “logical discrepancy” category to flag inconsistencies in voters’ records. These discrepancies are identified through ERONet, the poll panel’s centralised technology platform, which uses automated checks to examine electoral data.Such flags can arise when information in a voter’s profile or details linking family members appear inconsistent with mathematical, biological or clerical records. The category is intended to identify entries that require scrutiny.

Meloni furious as Italian judge frees man accused of inciting violent protests
MILAN, Oct 28 - An Italian judge has ordered the release of a university researcher accused by police of helping orchestrate violent protests this month, infuriating Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who denounced the decision as "shameful".
Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian freelance journalist and geopolitics graduate of Moroccan origin, was detained by Milan prosecutors on October 24 on charges of incitement to commit crimes, aggravated by alleged terrorist purposes.
But in a sharp rebuke to prosecutors who had portrayed him as a dangerous militant, Milan judge Tiziana Landoni said the investigation appeared deeply flawed.
"There are no serious grounds for believing that (Siher) committed the offences with which he has been charged, nor is there a risk of flight," Landoni wrote in her ruling.
Siher himself always denied any wrongdoing. Prosecutors did not immediately comment, but Meloni was swift to denounce the decision.
"I think this is an unbearable humiliation of the work of the police and investigators," she said in a video posted on social media.
"I really don't know how a normal state can defend decent people in the face of these decisions by certain sections of the judiciary," she added.
Italian police had identified Siher as the administrator of the Telegram group "October 17 Movement", which was created following violent protests in Milan.
According to the detention order, Siher published what investigators described as "subversive content" and messages calling on protesters to gather on October 24 with the aim of carrying out offences against public order.
However, Landoni said such comments were posted by other group members, not Siher himself. "Siher was not found to have encouraged or in any way supported the violent actions advocated by those users," she wrote.
The case is notable because prosecutors cited a new offence introduced under a security decree enacted by Meloni's government this month as part of its latest law-and-order crackdown.
The newly defined crime carries prison terms of between four and 12 years for organisers of groups that, while taking part in public demonstrations, endanger public safety or cause damage.
Siher's arrest has sparked concern among legal observers and members of the Italian Bar Association.
Critics also questioned the extensive media coverage of the case, with some Italian newspapers portraying him as guilty and revealing detailed descriptions of his life and family. REUTERS

Russia imports five times more prosthetic arms and legs from Germany than before the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia imports five times more prosthetic arms and legs from Germany than before the war
Germany supplied Russia with prosthetic arms and legs, as well as artificial joints, worth 79 million euros in the first half of 2026, almost a third more than a year earlier, according to Eurostat data reviewed by Forbes Russia.
Prosthetic arms and legs and related components accounted for 41.2 million euros of that total, while endoprostheses — artificial hip, knee, and other joint replacements — accounted for 37.8 million euros.
Supplies of prosthetic arms and legs grew 5.4 times compared with 2021, while shipments of endoprostheses grew 6.1 times.
Russia received prostheses and endoprostheses worth a total of 144.9 million euros from European Union countries in the first half of 2026, compared with 66.5 million euros during the same period in 2021.
Russia’s prosthetics market is growing, but domestic production capacity is not keeping pace with demand, Forbes writes. People with disabilities received 152,661 prosthetic arms and legs from the state in 2024, more than in any of the previous 10 years, according to the Labor Ministry.
Market participants say prosthetics are now being issued significantly faster and recipients have become significantly younger. Young people accounted for about 8% of those needing prosthetics before 2022, but their share had grown to 15–20% by 2025, according to Rostec, the Russian state defense conglomerate. Most are people who fought in the war with Ukraine and were wounded there.
Younger patients need more complex, technologically advanced devices, but production of these prostheses in Russia has “historically developed somewhat more slowly,” experts say. As a result, Russian-made products account for about 80% of the prosthetics market by unit but only 30% by value, and imports account for up to 70% of the market for expensive, high-tech components.

Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?
October 28, 2026
As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.
"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.
CDU: 'We must prevent scenes like those in France at all costs'
In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.
Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.
Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."
Concerns over internationally coordinated far-left extremists
In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.
Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.
But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.
Koos: 'Not driven by anger as in France'
Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."
At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."
Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.
"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."
Greens express understanding for the protests
For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.
"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.
"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."
Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."
He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.
By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.
This article was translated from German.

Swiss government introduces measures to limit heatwave risks
The Federal Council on Wednesday adopted a climate adaptation strategy and action plan for 2026–2031, outlining measures to better prepare Switzerland for the impacts of climate change.
This strategy sets out objectives for adapting to climate change and identifies measures in 30 areas, bringing the total number in the action plan to 56.
The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) has been asked to establish a centre of expertise to coordinate between the relevant stakeholders and to monitor health to assess the effectiveness of the adaptation measures.
More
Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Funding for research projects to strengthen animal health and food security is also on the agenda.
This strategy is based on the Federal Office for the Environment’s 2025 climate risk analysis, as well as on the 2025 climate scenarios from the federal technology institute ETH Zurich and the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology MeteoSwiss.

Signal boosters for Russian drones still active in Belarus, but no troop build-up observed, say Ukrainian border guards
Signal repeaters in Belarus that boost the signal for Russian drones attacking Ukraine continue to be detected as operating. However, no build-up of Russian forces near Belarus' border with Ukraine has been observed.
Source: Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, in a comment to Ukrinform
Quote: "Everyone is particularly concerned about the possibility of a build-up of forces in Belarus towards our border, but fortunately that is not happening."
Details: Demchenko said Ukrainian intelligence services continue to monitor the situation in Belarus, a close ally of Russia.
The operation of signal repeaters on Belarusian territory remains a threat to Ukraine. Demchenko explained that the equipment boosts the signal for Russian drones.
Quote: "Unfortunately, their operation continues to be detected. This does not necessarily mean that a repeater there is switched on around the clock, but we are seeing them periodically changing the locations where they are activated."
Details: Demchenko added that Belarus continues to help Russia carry out attacks on Ukraine in this way.

Ohio man convicted in US of lying about role in Rwandan genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:40:57 UTC
22:40:57 KST

Ohio man convicted in US of lying about role in Rwandan genocide
BOSTON, Oct 28 - A Rwandan-born Ohio man has been convicted of US charges that he lied during a 2019 criminal trial as part of a decades-long scheme to conceal his involvement in the African nation's 1994 genocide.
A federal jury in Boston on Tuesday found Eric Nshimiye guilty of perjury and obstruction of justice charges stemming from testimony he gave during the earlier immigration fraud trial of a former classmate who was also accused of participating in the atrocities.
Nshimiye, 54, is scheduled to be sentenced on January 26, according to a spokesperson for US Attorney Leah Foley, whose office prosecuted the case.
"We are obviously very disappointed with the verdict, but we will continue to pursue all avenues of relief on Eric's behalf," Kurt Kerns, Nshimiye's lawyer, said in a statement.
Nshimiye has lived in the United States since 1995, when he gained admission as a refugee. He became a US citizen in 2003. At the time of his arrest in 2024, he was working as an engineer for Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co while living in Uniontown, Ohio.
Prosecutors said Nshimiye falsified and concealed information about himself to hide that he participated in the massacre by the hard-line Hutu regime of an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus during three months of slaughter in his native Rwanda.
Citing witnesses, prosecutors alleged that when the violence broke out, Nshimiye was in Butare, where he had been attending university as a medical student along with his classmate Jean Leonard Teganya.
Prosecutors said both men belonged to the political party that helped perpetrate the genocide, and that Nshimiye during the violence attacked Tutsis and handed Tutsis over to be raped or killed.
Yet when called as a defense witness in Teganya's 2019 trial, Nshimiye denied participating in the genocide or being a member of the ruling Hutu-dominated party, the National Revolutionary Movement for Development.
Teganya was convicted of perjury and visa fraud charges and was sentenced later in 2019 to more than eight years in prison.
Kerns, Nshimiye's lawyer, told jurors in his opening statement on October 13 that the charges against Nshimiye were based on "fabricated accusations" and that he was not even in Butare when the violence began. Kerns argued that prosecutors charged Nshimiye only after he stepped up to help a friend by testifying as a character witness in Teganya's case. REUTERS

Putin says only Russia has low-capacity NPPs already in operation

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia is the only country that has not only developed but also operates low-capacity floating nuclear power plants (NPPs), President Vladimir Putin said while viewing an exhibition on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit, adding that no other nation in the world, including those in the West, has managed to achieve anything of the kind.
"This is not just a development project. This plant is in operation. It is located in the Arctic zone in northern Russia, and since 2020 it has been working and generating energy," he said referring to the Akademik Lomonosov low-capacity floating nuclear power plant. "It is quite efficient: they are in demand in certain conditions," the Russian leader added.
"And our competitors, French, Japanese, American companies, all claim they are ready to develop small power plants. However, no one has practically done anything yet. In Russia, there is [the plant] that has been built and is operational. Nothing like it exists anywhere else in the world yet," he stated.

Fines of up to 170,000 hryvnias and imprisonment: how fraud involving bank cards will be punished in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:40:47 EET
22:40:47 KST

Fines of up to 170,000 hryvnias and imprisonment: how fraud involving bank cards will be punished in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada adopted a law against illegal transactions involving cards, accounts, and wallets. Drop schemes are punishable by a fine of up to 170,000 hryvnias or up to 6 years in prison.
The Verkhovna Rada has adopted a law that strengthens criminal liability for illegal transactions involving bank cards, accounts, and electronic wallets. The document provides for fines of up to UAH 170,000 and imprisonment for up to six years for organizing and using so-called drop schemes. This was reported by UNN, citing the parliament's press service.
Details
On October 28, parliament adopted draft law No. 16013 in its entirety, aimed at strengthening the protection of citizens' funds from financial and cyber fraud. The relevant decision was supported by 270 members of parliament.
The draft law was initiated at one point by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy. It provides for amendments to the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine. In particular, it establishes separate criminal liability for transferring, acquiring, storing, and using payment instruments and access to bank accounts for the purpose of committing fraud or other criminal offenses.
What changes the law provides for
One of its key tasks is to counter the activities of so-called drops (individuals through whose bank accounts criminals conduct illegal financial transactions — ed.). The adopted document updates Article 200 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, which regulates liability for illegal actions involving payment instruments, documents for the transfer of funds, and means of access to bank accounts.
In particular, criminal liability is established for misappropriating or stealing payment instruments, obtaining them through deception or abuse of trust, as well as for other methods of illegally obtaining them.
In addition, the Criminal Code has been supplemented with a new Article 200-1, which establishes liability for transferring, receiving, acquiring, storing, or selling payment instruments, personal data used to access accounts, and electronic wallets for the purpose of conducting criminal transactions.
At the same time, the law distinguishes between the liability of persons who knowingly transfer their own payment instruments for illegal transactions and that of participants in schemes involving the acquisition and distribution of other people's bank cards.
Fines and imprisonment: what punishment violators will face
The transfer of one's own bank card or other payment instrument for the purpose of enabling fraud by other persons is punishable by a fine of 300 to 1,000 non-taxable minimum incomes of citizens. In monetary terms, this amounts to UAH 5,100 to 17,000.
A more severe punishment is established for receiving, acquiring, storing, selling, or transferring other people's payment instruments for carrying out fraudulent transactions.
The following penalties are provided for such actions:
-  a fine of UAH 51,000 to 85,000; 
-  restriction of liberty for a term of up to three years; 
-  imprisonment for a term of two to four
 years. 
For repeated commission of the relevant offenses or their commission by an organized group, a fine of UAH 85,000 to 170,000 or imprisonment for a term of four to six years is established.
However, the law provides for the possibility of exempting from criminal liability a person who committed an offense related to transferring their own payment instrument for the first time, voluntarily reported it to law enforcement authorities, and actively assisted in uncovering and stopping the crime.
Separate amendments concern the application of criminal-law measures to legal entities if their activities are connected with the relevant offenses.
What are drop accounts and how do fraudsters use them?
Drops are people whose bank cards or accounts are used to receive, transfer, or withdraw funds, including funds obtained through criminal means. Usually, the organizers of fraudulent schemes offer citizens a monetary reward for handing over a bank card, account details, or access to mobile banking. After that, financial transactions are conducted through such accounts, making it possible to conceal the movement of funds and complicate the identification of their ultimate recipients.
In some cases, people are recruited into such schemes under the guise of legal employment, being offered jobs involving the transfer of money between accounts.
As noted during the preparation of the draft law, networks of nominee payment accounts have become systemic in nature and have become part of the infrastructure of economic, drug-related and cybercrime. Therefore, the new provisions are intended to create legal mechanisms for holding participants in such schemes accountable as early as the stage of transferring or acquiring means of access to funds.
Does the punishment threaten ordinary bank card holders
An important aspect of the new legislation is the issue of liability for citizens who transfer their payment instruments to other people. The mere fact that a bank card is used by a relative or acquaintance does not automatically entail criminal liability.
Under the provisions of the adopted law, this concerns the transfer of a payment instrument or access to an account specifically for the purpose of committing fraud or another criminal offense.
At the same time, experts from the Centre for Political and Legal Reform warned that the new law could result in criminal liability even for people who became involved in fraudulent schemes without knowing it because they had been deceived. In particular, human rights advocates noted that citizens might agree to transfer funds or provide access to accounts without understanding their true purpose. In addition, experts expressed reservations about the broad wording concerning the use of payment instruments to commit other criminal offenses, which, in their view, could create risks of ambiguous interpretation of the provisions.
How much Ukrainians lose to bank fraudsters
The need to strengthen the fight against financial fraud is confirmed by statistics from the National Bank of Ukraine. According to the regulator, in 2025, the number of illegal actions and fraudulent payment card transactions that resulted in losses fell by 5% compared with the previous year, to 256,000 cases. However, the total amount lost by citizens and other payment card users increased by 24%, reaching UAH 1.4 billion. The average amount of a single fraudulent transaction was UAH 5,536.
One of the most common tools used by criminals remains social engineering, in which fraudsters, under various pretexts, persuade citizens to disclose their card details, passwords and verification codes themselves or to provide access to banking applications. However, it is drop accounts that allow criminals to move the funds obtained through third-party accounts, making them more difficult to trace.
European standards for combating financial fraud
The adoption of Law No. 16013 is also related to the fulfillment of Ukraine's European integration obligations. The document is aimed at implementing the provisions of European Union Directive 2019/713 on combating fraud and counterfeiting involving non-cash means of payment.
European legislation provides for the criminalization of a number of illegal actions involving payment instruments, including their theft, counterfeiting, illegal acquisition and use. The relevant changes are also envisaged by the Roadmap on the Rule of Law, which covers measures to combat organized crime and cybercrime.
The new criminal law mechanisms are expected to enable law enforcement agencies to investigate financial crimes more effectively and hold accountable participants in schemes involving the use of other people's bank accounts.
Reminder
Earlier, we reported that lawmakers proposed creating a "drop registry".

80% of Ukrainians back strikes on Russian refineries even if US cuts support, poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:39:32 UTC
22:39:32 KST

80% of Ukrainians back strikes on Russian refineries even if US cuts support, poll shows
The vast majority of Ukrainians want Kyiv to continue striking Russian refineries, even if the U.S. threatens to end or curb its support, according to a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) published on Oct. 28.
Some 80% of respondents back the continued strikes, even if Washington restricts intelligence sharing or Starlink operations. Only 11% said Ukraine should pause the attacks, despite Russia's ongoing attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid and other civilian facilities.
U.S. President Donald Trump has urged Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries, a key source of revenue for Moscow's federal budget that helps fund its war against Ukraine.
As Washington ramped up pressure, Ukraine said it had faced a temporary pause in U.S. intelligence sharing on incoming Russian ballistic missiles, restrictions on Starlink operations, and delays in Patriot air defense missile shipments.
The U.S. administration has denied ordering any restrictions to pressure Kyiv.
Trump unilaterally declared an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11. Kyiv then largely suspended strikes against Russian refineries for three days, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
In the meantime, Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy facilities, driving fears about energy and heating outages as winter approaches.
According to the KIIS poll, 63% of Ukrainians are ready to endure the war as long as necessary, a rate that has remained largely stable since summer.
Some 76% of respondents supported continued armed resistance against Russia, even if Moscow's attacks in winter result in outages in electricity, heat, and sewage.
The survey was conducted between Oct. 16 and 25 through telephone interviews with 828 respondents living in the government-controlled territories.

Zelenskyy's autumn: inside the President's Office ahead of Ukraine's toughest winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:39:00 EET
22:39:00 KST

Zelenskyy's autumn: inside the President's Office ahead of Ukraine's toughest winter
It's been clear since his presidency began that sharing power is not something Volodymyr Zelenskyy likes to do. He hasn't resorted to excessive micromanagement as his predecessor Petro Poroshenko did, or built complex systems of checks and balances in the style of Leonid Kuchma (who was president in 1994-2005). But he has never let anyone who might outshine him into his inner circle.
For years, those close to President Zelenskyy have been people who made no claim to an independent political identity, but knew how to ensure unconditional loyalty and maintain control over everything happening around them.
Andrii Yermak, the former head of the President's Office, was the perfect embodiment of this. His dismissal seemed to mark the end of a major political era. But at the President's Office, reshuffles don't always mean a change in the rules of the game.
The new head of the Office, Kyrylo Budanov, had no desire to become "another Yermak", but neither did he change the team working there.
But politics in Ukraine has not stood still. The ousting of defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, the latest "cardboard protest", and further special operations by the anti-corruption agencies, dubbed Carthage and Forrest Gump – which led to the dismissal of Iryna Mudra, a deputy head of the President's Office, and the flight of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – were bound to trigger another restructuring of the architecture of power.
One thing never changes: throughout the political turbulence, Zelenskyy remains the central figure in every configuration of power, and access to him is still one of the key factors that determines how influential a person can be in Ukraine today.
Who has the greatest influence over Zelenskyy today? Has Yermak really lost his former all-powerful position for good? And whose status has risen since the recent series of scandals? Ukrainska Pravda takes a closer look.
New favourites vying for a place at Zelenskyy's side
Andrii Yermak has not been seen in the building on Bankova Street, where the President's Office is located in Kyiv, since he stepped down as its head. However, several people in the president's team who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said that "Yermak is still a contact in Zelenskyy's phone". Since being formally served with a notice of suspicion in the case involving the construction of the high-end Dynasty housing complex, Yermak has been communicating with the president by phone.
In July, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Yermak had been involved in arranging Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal as defence minister. Moreover, at the height of the conflict between Fedorov and former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi in the summer of 2026, Yermak travelled to a command post in a frontline area to meet Syrskyi.
Nevertheless, Yermak's absence from the President's Office on Bankova Street and his detachment from the daily flow of events have significantly limited his ability to influence developments in real time, depriving him of the near-omnipotence he once enjoyed.
"All of Andrii's power rested on his proximity to the president," a senior official at Bankova told UP off the record. "It's not possible to exert the kind of influence that he had from afar. I'd say he's lost 90% of his former power. He might still speak to the Big Man, but he certainly can't call people with his stupid ideas or assign them tasks."
Since Yermak's dismissal, one of the people most frequently seen in Zelenskyy's office has been his adviser, Dmytro Lytvyn, who oversees all of the president's media communications, co-writes speeches for his key public appearances, and advises him on how to respond to "attacks" by world leaders – which regularly brings him into conflict with Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the President's Office.
Lytvyn has taken over one of Yermak's functions: continually finding new enemies around the President's Office. He interprets other politicians' actions and statements as he sees fit, and Zelenskyy listens to him.
"Dima is no fool," one senior official says of Lytvyn. "He understands the president's personality and knows how to exploit it. Lytvyn's role goes beyond the media. His access to the president enables him to put forward his own perspective on all the challenges facing the authorities – from foreign policy and the war to personnel decisions and even the economy."
But Lytvyn isn't the only person whose position has been given a boost by the changes at the Office. Since Yermak's dismissal, the influence of Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, has grown considerably.
Just a year ago, Arakhamiia was on the verge of being formally notified that he was a suspect in a treason case. Now he is one of Zelenskyy's main pillars of support.
"It's true that Davyd has grown closer to the president and can get into his office without much difficulty. That's hardly surprising. Look at our team – Davyd is almost the only one who's been there from the very beginning. The others have been rendered toxic by either Yermak or NABU [the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine]," one member of Zelenskyy's team explains with a note of irony.
As leader of the Servant of the People faction, Arakhamiia marshals votes in parliament, both within the ruling parliamentary majority and beyond it, among other factions and groups. His control over Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, is his main asset, and it enables him to influence government appointments.
Arakhamiia was directly involved in last summer's Cabinet reshuffle and actively advocated for Fedorov's dismissal.
At least three ministers in the new Cabinet are close to him: Veterans Affairs Minister Vitalii Kim, Justice Minister Denys Maslov, and Communities Minister Vitalii Bezhin.
Maslov and Bezhin were Servant of the People MPs under Arakhamiia's leadership before joining the government, while Kim is a long-time friend of his.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal could also be considered an ally. During Shmyhal's long tenure as prime minister, he and Arakhamiia developed a working partnership.
Beyond parliamentary affairs, Arakhamiia is also actively involved in negotiations. He is officially a member of Ukraine's negotiating team in talks with the United States.
Arakhamiia also maintains friendly contact with Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, who is in direct contact with Vladimir Putin.
Arakhamiia first crossed paths with Abramovich at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, when the Russian oligarch presented himself as a "neutral party" during talks in Istanbul between the Ukrainian and Russian delegations.
In June 2026 Abramovich travelled to Kyiv, where he met with President Zelenskyy. It's hard to believe that Arakhamiia was not involved in arranging the meeting.
Another interesting contact of Arakhamiia's is self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko. In the early days of the full-scale invasion, Arakhamiia acted as an intermediary between Zelenskyy and Lukashenko after the Ukrainian president refused to communicate directly with Putin's ally. Ukrainska Pravda sources say Arakhamiia has maintained his contact with Lukashenko.
The head of the parliamentary majority is also actively thinking about creating new political actors (parties).
Over the past six months, Ukrainska Pravda has repeatedly heard from various sources that Arakhamiia is seriously considering launching a political project that could fill the space once occupied by the pro-Russian parties Opposition Platform – For Life and Opposition Bloc. Vitalii Kim and Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, both of whom enjoy a high level of public recognition, could become the public faces of that political force.
"Remember how Ostap Bender was portrayed by Ilf and Petrov? Such an energetic, charismatic person, so good at manoeuvring and scheming, right? Well, if you pitted Bender against Davyd, Davyd would have him for breakfast," one of the most senior members of Zelenskyy's team laughs.
The president's enforcers
Since Andrii Yermak's dismissal as head of the President's Office, Deputy Head Oleh Tatarov's position has only got stronger. Within the President's Office, Tatarov is responsible for the law enforcement and security agencies. Over the years, he has also acquired considerable practical political experience, developing a keen understanding of who's who in the power hierarchy and how to deal with people from very different backgrounds.
Tatarov retains considerable influence over the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI), the Ministry of Internal Affairs – including the National Police – and certain courts.
The recent high-profile NABU cases have worked in Tatarov's favour. For example, he had a long-standing feud with Iryna Mudra, who was responsible for liaising with the judiciary at the President's Office.
"Ira and Oleh had separate areas of responsibility, but they crossed paths at important meetings. Whenever legal issues came up, they would start arguing," says one source close to the President's Office.
"To give you an idea of the extent of their mutual dislike, Oleh would openly call Ira stupid in front of other people. He couldn't stand her, and she couldn't stand him either," adds another member of Zelenskyy's team.
After Mudra was served with a notice of suspicion, Tatarov was effectively rid of a rival within the President's Office.
His conflict with Ruslan Kravchenko, the former prosecutor general, was far more serious.
As Ukrainska Pravda reported earlier, Kravchenko had been conspicuously purging Tatarov's allies from the Office of the Prosecutor General, refusing to coordinate his work with Tatarov, and deliberately moving towards an open confrontation.
Operation Carthage knocked the prosecutor general out of the game altogether. Before fleeing to Vienna, Kravchenko had issued notices of suspicion against the heads of the anti-corruption agencies, SAPO and NABU. However, the notices were promptly revoked by his deputy, Maksym Krym. According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, Tatarov himself was involved in their annulment.
Following the scandals surrounding Kravchenko, Tatarov has generally strengthened his position within the Office of the Prosecutor General.
"To avoid unnecessary questions and problems, Oleh steers clear of direct contact with the acting prosecutor general and isn't installing his own people there," says one senior law enforcement official. "Instead, he discusses work-related matters with the deputies, primarily [Oleksandr] Khomenko. Overall, people in the prosecutor's office listen to Tatarov these days."
Another key figure in the law enforcement system for Zelenskyy is Oleksandr Poklad, the acting head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU).
Poklad demonstrated his effectiveness and conspicuous loyalty to the president and to Yermak when he headed the SSU's Counterintelligence Department. Yermak was among those who lobbied for Poklad's further promotion.
One indication of Zelenskyy's particular regard for Oleksandr Poklad is that when he was first deputy head of the SSU, the president gave him special assignments, bypassing Yevhen Khmara, then the service's acting head.
Ukrainska Pravda sources who have worked with Poklad describe him as a tough and at times even ruthless individual.
Sources within the governing team describe the SSU chief as the "guardian of Zelenskyy's political system", someone who employs a wide range of methods to achieve the president's objectives.
One example of what the acting SSU chief is capable of was the operation to bring Fedir Khrystenko, an MP wanted on suspicion of treason, back to Ukraine. According to the Dzerkalo Tyzhnia newspaper, Poklad personally travelled to the United Arab Emirates to detain him.
Poklad also has another, less obvious task on Zelenskyy's behalf: keeping Kyrylo Budanov's influence in check.
A public feud between the two men has been simmering since the days when Budanov was head of Ukraine's Defence Intelligence.
The animosity goes back years and stems from rivalry between the intelligence agencies. In March 2022, Denys Kirieiev, a banker who was a member of the Ukrainian delegation in negotiations with Russia, was shot dead in central Kyiv by SSU officers. The SSU claimed that Kirieiev had been a Russian spy.
However, according to sources within Defence Intelligence, Kirieiev had worked for Ukrainian military intelligence for years and was personally close to Budanov. People in Budanov's circle are convinced that Poklad was behind the killing.
The extremely strained relationship between Budanov and Poklad was further exposed by the events of early September 2026, when their rivalry escalated into an open armed confrontation between Defence Intelligence and Security Service units.
The immediate trigger was an SSU operation. Several days before the clashes, SSU operatives had effectively abducted Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RVC), a formation that operates under Defence Intelligence's direction. The SSU claimed that Kaplunov had been plotting to carry out a terrorist attack against a Russian opposition figure. According to law enforcement sources cited by Suspilne, the intended target was Akhmed Zakayev, head of the government of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria in exile. Kaplunov himself said that the purpose of his detention was to force him to give testimony specifically against Kyrylo Budanov.
The behind-the-scenes power struggle culminated in street clashes between Defence Intelligence and Security Service special forces in Kyiv's Berezniaky neighbourhood on 2 September.
The lonely general
The appointment of Kyrylo Budanov as head of the President's Office in January 2026 did not mean that Volodymyr Zelenskyy wanted a new Andrii Yermak. The president had entirely different objectives in mind.
First, reputation. After the corruption scandals and Yermak's departure, the president needed someone the public could trust. Budanov fitted the bill.
In a poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) in July 2026, 61% of the respondents said they trusted Budanov. For comparison, the figures were 56% for Zelenskyy, 63% for Mykhailo Fedorov and 66% for former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi.
Second, the president wanted to strip Budanov of his influence over Defence Intelligence. In the course of the full-scale war, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence has grown into an organisation with vast capabilities: combat units, international operations, and contact with foreign intelligence agencies as well as all the key military figures and politicians both in Ukraine and abroad. According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, Budanov now has relatively few levers of influence over the agency.
The new Defence Intelligence chief, Oleh Ivashchenko, actively coordinates his actions with SSU chief Oleksandr Poklad. A senior law enforcement officer told Ukrainska Pravda that Ivashchenko is doing everything he can to get rid of Budanov's influence within Defence Intelligence.
Third, politics. Political strategists and pollsters have long viewed Budanov as a potential independent political player. That means a possible rival to Zelenskyy is now working alongside him at the President's Office – a situation that brings to mind the saying "Keep your friends close and your enemies closer."
"Budanov knows what Zelenskyy wants, and Zelenskyy knows what Budanov wants. That's how they manage to coexist, pretending that everything's fine," one Ukrainska Pravda source says of their relationship.
Budanov has also shown an interest in several areas beyond the President's Office. In recent months, for instance, he has been working extensively with parliament.
According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in the Verkhovna Rada, he has been helping Davyd Arakhamiia secure votes and personally negotiating with parliamentary groups.
A senior member of the Servant of the People party says: "Budanov asks us for a weekly breakdown of how everyone is voting. And he isn't just interested in our faction, but the entire parliament. He looks into why some groups refuse to vote and what their demands are, and considers different ways to reach a compromise. He goes around meeting people, listening, making suggestions and negotiating where Davyd cannot."
Budanov's contacts are not limited to the president's parliamentary majority. He can also talk to Petro Poroshenko and Yuliia Tymoshenko – politicians with whom relationships have long been difficult for the current government.
Another area of his work is engagement with the business community. Budanov chairs the Council for Entrepreneurship Support and draws on contacts he established during his time at Defence Intelligence.
But his main task remains the negotiations on ending the war with Russia.
Officially Ukraine's negotiating delegation is led by Rustem Umierov, but according to Ukrainska Pravda sources, Budanov handles most of the political coordination of the negotiations.
The former intelligence chief has established informal communication channels to facilitate rapid information sharing and coordinate positions. He previously spoke extensively with Keith Kellogg, the former US special presidential envoy for Ukraine, and is now in contact with Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
***
One year on from Yermak's departure from Bankova, the system of influence over the president is no longer monolithic. The days when a single key person controlled access to the head of state are over.
The Yermak era has given way to a more complex arrangement in which various players, with differing ambitions and methods, seek to gain the president's ear.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy remains the sun around which this system revolves, and an official's influence is still determined by their access to him. Yet his new inner circle – from media adviser Dmytro Lytvyn and indispensable political intermediary Davyd Arakhamiia to hard-line security officials Oleh Tatarov and Oleksandr Poklad – lacks the unity that once characterised the team.
Will this new system prove robust enough to maintain control of the country through domestic turbulence and a gruelling war?
This autumn has shown that the president continues to set the rules of the game. Yet his new inner circle, like the one before it, is becoming not only his main source of support, but also one of his greatest challenges.
Volodymyr Fomichov, Roman Kravets, Ukrainska Pravda

Rosatom Says It’s in Advanced Talks to Supply Floating Nuclear Power Plants to African Countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom could supply floating nuclear power plants to coastal African countries and is in advanced discussions with at least four nations, senior company executives said Wednesday at the Russia-Africa Summit.
Vladimir Aptekarev, deputy head of Rosatom's machine-building division, said that 38 of Africa's more than 50 countries have sufficient coastline to host a Russian-made floating power unit.
At present, only one floating nuclear power plant is in operation globally, in Russia's remote Chukotka region, dating from 2020. Floating plants use smaller reactors, are contained within a vessel which can be towed to a destination and require less infrastructure on land. They also make it possible to secure a new source of energy quickly and at a lower cost.
"As a first step, a floating nuclear power unit can serve as a good entry point, enabling a country both to address its energy needs and to join the nuclear club," said Aptekarev.
Rosatom is proposing implementing such projects under a power purchase agreement (PPA) model, with servicing and refuelling cycles carried out in Russia, allowing the unit to operate for up to 60 years.
"With this source of electricity, we are effectively addressing all the key issues and challenges facing the African continent," he said.
Rosatom is currently building Egypt's first nuclear power plant, El Dabaa, which will become the second nuclear power station on the African continent after South Africa's Koeberg plant, built using French technology in the mid-1980s. The project comprises four 1,200-MW power units with Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors.
Rosatom Chief Executive Alexei Likhachev told reporters the company is in advanced discussions on potential floating nuclear power plant projects with Egypt, Togo, Namibia and Tanzania.
The prospect of deploying floating nuclear power plants in Egypt could also gain momentum following a meeting between the presidents of Russia and Egypt scheduled for Wednesday, he said.
For international markets, Rosatom is offering floating power units with a capacity of 100 megawatts with RITM-200M reactors adapted for warm climates.
Rosatom has already reached an agreement with Indonesia on what it describes as the world's first export supplies of electricity generated by two floating nuclear power units with a combined capacity of 200 megawatts.

Japanese football association vice president resigns over actions surrounding FIFA World Cup
Unknown

2026-10-28

Saadet Gökce
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Japan Football Association Vice President Takeshi Okada resigned Wednesday, citing a "significant gap" between his principles and how the organization is handling issues surrounding the upcoming FIFA World Cup.
"Throughout my career, I have valued the social significance of sports guided by my conviction that sports must be conducted with integrity," he said in a statement. "However, the series of responses to the issues surrounding the upcoming FIFA World Cup has revealed a significant gap between those responses and my own convictions. As a sportsman, I cannot accept them.”
The resignation comes one week after Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa pledged the AFC’s support for Gianni Infantino’s bid for another term as FIFA president.
Okada said he understood that aligning with the AFC was a practical option, given Japan's relationship with the body and the potential effect on Japanese soccer.
Infantino faced mounting calls to stand down two months ago following the controversy surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.
The proposal would have involved transferring a portion of FIFA's commercial rights to a private investment firm through a new commercial entity, including rights linked to FIFA competitions such as the World Cup.
It was abandoned within days of details emerging, prompting criticism from several confederation presidents and major European leagues.
Infantino has led FIFA since 2016 and is seeking another term in the March 2027 election.

The British leadership intends to continue fighting by proxy on foreign soil, as evidenced by military medical drills conducted by the country’s Defense Ministry in October, Yulia Zhdanova, head of the Russian delegation to the Vienna talks on military security and arms control, said.
She recalled that in mid-October, the ministry organized a three-day command-post exercise for its medical command involving more than 100 representatives of the armed forces, the National Health Service and other agencies, as well as military personnel from the United States and Canada. "Apparently, just as before, Britain intends to fight by proxy, and certainly not on its own territory," the diplomat concluded.
