Font size
A container ship was struck by three drones in the Black Sea, approximately 21 nautical miles southeast of cape Shabla, Minister of Defence Dimitar Stoyanov announced at a press conference following a trilateral meeting between the defence ministers and chiefs of defence of Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye, dedicated to security and defence in the Black Sea region.
The Liberia-flagged container ship CONTSHIP JET (IMO: 9348625), which departed from Haifa, Israel, was struck while sailing past Cape Kaliakra en route to the Romanian city of Constanța, BNR correspondent in Varna Daniela Stoynova reported.
A tanker was dispatched to assist the vessel. Some of the crew members evacuated onto a life raft near the ship. Meanwhile, a drone was heading towards them by sea, posing a threat to the sailors’ lives.
“Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye unequivocally condemn drone attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea. These tragic incidents constitute a dangerous escalation of tensions and pose serious risks to the safety of maritime navigation”, Dimitar Stoyanov added.
Representatives of the three countries called for an immediate halt to the attacks, which endanger commercial shipping, maritime infrastructure and the safety of maritime activities.
The Bulgarian Navy is currently carrying out an operation to rescue the 18 crew members of the container ship attacked in the Black Sea. Three naval vessels are at the scene. Further details are expected once the rescue operation is complete.
The CONTSHIP JET is the fifth ship to be targeted by drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.

Kravchenko remains on the run, despite not being officially charged.
The former prosecutor general broke a month-long silence after fleeing Ukraine to Austria amid a corruption scandal involving senior officials from the Prosecutor General's Office.
His statement came after two Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) officers were detained in Austria in early October, Austrian newspaper Der Standard reported.

Kravchenko didn't elaborate on his sources, saying he "lacked reliable information on who had issued" the alleged order.
"The statement regarding NABU and SAPO's involvement in any of the events mentioned is untrue," the bureau told the Kyiv Independent, describing Kravchenko's statement as an attempt to "secure protection for himself in his country of residence."
Austria rarely extradites Ukrainian nationals to Ukraine, making it a potential refuge for former Ukrainian officials facing corruption charges at home. Several have sought shelter there, complicating Kyiv’s efforts to bring them back to face prosecution.

"Such exhibitions are crucial for expanding the reach of domestic exporters, both within the Chinese market and into third countries."
A Chinese delegation - led by Ma Yuxian, a member of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and former Vice Minister of Agriculture, alongside Sun Haiwen, Deputy Director of the Fisheries Bureau under the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs - visited the Russian pavilion. The delegation was welcomed by Kirill Kolonchin, Director of the Russian Federal Research Institute of Fisheries and Oceanography (VNIRO); Sergey Mikheyev, Federal Agency for Fishery’s representative in China; and Ivan Fetisov, CEO of Expo Solutions Group, the pavilion's organizer. The parties reviewed products from Russian enterprises and exchanged views on the prospects for future cooperation.
The Russian pavilion has been a fixture at the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo for 10 years, becoming an essential component of Russia’s presence in the Chinese market and a key tool for promoting domestic fishery products.
The China Fisheries & Seafood Expo is China's largest international exhibition for the fisheries, seafood, and related technology sectors, held annually in Qingdao. In 2025, the event hosted over 1,500 companies and welcomed 45,000 visitors from 139 countries. The Russian national pavilion has participated in the exhibition since 2016.

Pakistan bars Taiwanese airlines from its airspace in support of One-China policy: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:35:56 UTC
22:35:56 KST

Pakistan restored overflight rights to Taiwanese airlines after banning them from using its airspace in line with its One-China policy, local newspaper Dawn has reported.
The Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority authorised China Airlines Ltd. and EVA Airways Corp. to use the country's airspace from Oct. 28 to March 27, 2027, according to documents seen by Dawn on Wednesday.
Bloomberg earlier reported that Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told Bloomberg News that aviation authorities had followed "the One China policy — only mainland China is allowed."
He had said that Islamabad only allowed airlines from the People’s Republic of China to fly over Pakistan, excluding Taiwan.
Taiwanese carriers reroute flights
According to flight-tracking data, Taiwanese carriers began rerouting flights over the weekend, with China Airlines Ltd. and EVA Airways Corp. no longer flying over Pakistan since Sunday.
The two carriers declined to comment to Bloomberg, while Taiwan’s Civil Aviation Administration did not address the rerouting.
Islamabad's restrictions were even stricter than those imposed by China, which allows Taiwanese airlines to fly over its territory.
Beijing considers Taiwan a breakaway province, while Taipei insists on its independence.
Pakistan severed official relations with Taiwan in 1951 in support of the One-China policy.
Islamabad and Beijing have bolstered ties under Beijing's ambitious Belt and Road Initiative, through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, which has channelled billions of dollars into Pakistan.
China is also Pakistan’s largest supplier of weapons and launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor on Tuesday.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hsinchu Mayor Kao Hung-an (高虹安), who is seeking reelection, signed a pledge addressing eight education policy demands at a forum on Wednesday.
The forum was jointly organized by Hsinchu City Teachers Association and Hsinchu City Teachers’ Union, with representatives of teachers’ and parents’ groups invited to discuss education policy, per CNA.
The eight demands cover smaller classes and adequate staffing, lighter administrative workloads, special education, school safety, teachers’ professional dignity, a friendly school environment, teachers' well-being and labor rights, and stable education funding.
The mayor said the city’s education budget had risen from NT$9.67 billion (US$298.33 million) in 2023 to NT$14.1 billion this year, and is projected to reach NT$15.68 billion in 2027, per UDN. She said the city plans to spend NT$60 billion on education over the next four years, with annual spending of at least NT$15 billion.
The city had introduced full-academic-year contracts for substitute teachers and invested nearly NT$60 million in salary improvements, Kao explained. Previous work experience now counts toward salary placement, allowing eligible teachers to advance on the seniority-based pay scale.
The city will allocate NT$24 million in the 2026-27 school year to hire 30 additional elementary school substitute teachers, according to Kao. It also plans to reduce elementary school class sizes in three phases, targeting 28 students per class by 2028-29, and cut weekly teaching loads for junior high school teachers in certain subjects from 20 to 18 periods.

Replacing summer tires with winter tires: when it should be done, and whether there are penalties
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:31:41 EET
22:31:41 KST

Replacing summer tires with winter tires: when it should be done, and whether there are penalties
Kyiv • UNN
Winter tires are recommended when the average daily temperature falls below +7°C. There are currently no fines, while a bill providing for a 340-hryvnia fine is still under consideration.
"Changing tires" ahead of the winter season is a routine and familiar procedure for every driver. This is especially relevant for those who drive to work or run errands in their cars every morning. UNN explains when it is worth changing tires, whether fines are предусмотрены for this, and how much it costs to change tires.
When to change to winter tires
According to the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center, the first snow may fall in Kyiv as early as next week—on November 6. The probability of snowfall will reach 85%, which raises the question of "changing tires."
The first snow in Kyiv - forecasters have issued a forecast28.10.26, 10:24 • 4236 views
In recent years, drivers have often failed to comply with the requirement to replace summer tires with winter ones. This is explained by the fact that in recent years, winters in Ukraine have not been very cold or snowy. Nevertheless, one should be cautious, as sudden snowfalls do occur and can catch even the most experienced drivers off guard. When sudden frosts arrive, many road accidents occur because drivers ignore the requirement to change tires.
Summer tires are designed for driving on dry or wet roads, but they are effective only at high temperatures. In cold weather, they lose their properties, so grip on the road deteriorates when driving on them. The risk of road accidents also increases due to the longer braking distance. When used at low temperatures, summer tires wear out faster.
The time when it is necessary to change to winter tires depends on the average daily air temperature. If it drops below +7 degrees, this means it is time to replace the tires. Some drivers do not wait for a sharp cold spell and visit a tire service center at the beginning of October, when it is still relatively warm, so as not to waste time waiting in queues at the tire service center.
Fines for changing tires late
Ukrainian legislation does not regulate when summer tires must be replaced with winter ones, so each driver decides for themselves when to do it. According to the traffic rules, it is prohibited to operate vehicles whose remaining tread depth is less than 1.6 mm. For vehicles weighing more than 3.5 tonnes, the limit is 1.0 mm; for buses, 2.0 mm; and for motorcycles and mopeds, 0.8 mm.
In 2023, lawmakers submitted to the Verkhovna Rada a bill that would introduce fines for driving a car not equipped with winter and/or all-season tires between November 1 and March 31.
The fine for such a violation was proposed at 340 hryvnias. For now, the bill remains under consideration in the Rada.
Cost of "changing tires"
The cost of replacing tires depends on the type of vehicle and the size of the tires themselves. For example, the cost of replacing one tire with a radius of R13–14 starts at 140 hryvnias per wheel.
The cost of replacing one tire with a radius of R19 starts at 250 hryvnias per wheel for passenger cars.
For minibuses and SUVs, the price will differ. For example, the cost of replacing one R15 tire for this category of vehicle starts at 225 hryvnias.

Turkey warns against further attacks by Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Turkey warns against further attacks by Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea vessels
ANKARA, Oct 28 - Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler on Wednesday warned Russia and Ukraine against further attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, saying Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes, in Turkey's most direct intervention to date.
NATO member Turkey, which has maintained good ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly called on both sides to halt attacks in the Black Sea that have also struck Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned commercial vessels.
Ankara says it is waiting for responses to a proposal it conveyed to Russia and Ukraine aimed at stopping the intensifying attacks and ensuring the safe shipment of grain from the region.
Speaking in Sofia after a security meeting between defence ministers and military chiefs of Black Sea littoral states Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria, Guler said commercial vessels sailing and operating in the Black Sea had been affected by drone attacks, stray mines and missiles during the conflict.
"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," he said, adding that another commercial vessel had been struck by three drones inside Bulgaria's maritime jurisdiction on Wednesday.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on a Greek container ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
"We also reserve every legal right regarding attacks on Turkish-flagged or Turkish-owned vessels and follow developments very closely... The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels," Guler added.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on ships and infrastructure facilitating Russian oil and grain exports since July, when Russia intensified its missile and drone strikes on the main Ukrainian grain export hubs of Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.
In a late September meeting, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskiy that attacks by Russia and Ukraine on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were inexplicable and steps must be taken to stop them.
Guler also said Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria — which operate a de-mining operation in the Black Sea — agreed it was important to also focus on protecting critical subsea infrastructure. REUTERS

UK defence spending target of 3 percent by 2030
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:31:23 GMT
22:31:23 KST

The Chancellor has set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, and will set out at next year’s spending review how Britain meets its NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035, according to the Budget statement.
John Healey, who held the defence portfolio before moving to the Treasury, told the Commons: “At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.”
On how it will be paid for, he said: “Today, I am getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way, that will include looking hard at public spending, as I have done today, to fund the defence investment plan. But I am also determined to use more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies.”
A new innovative defence finance task force will lead the work ahead of the spending review, the first of four measures announced. Treaty negotiations will begin on a multilateral defence mechanism, which Healey also called a bank, with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands, intended to boost defence investment and joint procurement across NATO allies. The government will seek the maximum private investment into the defence industrial base, including through public-private partnerships. And the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank will launch a new focus on defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability, deploying up to £5 billion of investment and lending over the next four years.
Healey said: “I will ensure this record defence investment works twice: once for our national security, and once for British jobs and British business. Places across all four nations: Barrow, Rosyth, Aldershot, Plymouth, Glascoed, and Belfast, reindustrialised and transformed.”
On Ukraine, the Chancellor said he and the Prime Minister had called President Zelensky that morning to tell him what the Budget contained, and that the response was “you’ve made my day”. The package is £10 billion of additional economic and military support based on loans and export finance guarantees, together with urgent military funding for this winter.
Healey said: “The whole house, the whole country, is united for Ukraine, and today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.”
The Chancellor made the case personally, drawing on his own family: “I say this as Chancellor. I say this as former Defence Secretary. And I say this as a dad whose son is an army reservist, a reservist that came back four years ago from early training to say they had no kit and they had no bullets to fire. That’s the truth.”
He said that for fourteen years Conservative governments had hollowed out and underfunded the armed forces, and that the defence budget this year is £14 billion higher than in the final year of the last government, which he described as the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the Cold War.
Britain signed up at the NATO summit in The Hague to three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent. Ministers had previously described three per cent as an ambition for the next Parliament, and attaching a target date of 2030 to it is firmer than the language used before.
Industry witnesses told the Defence Committee this month that the Defence Investment Plan is not investable as it stands, that most defence technology firms report a declining market, and that the department’s small business office has four staff. The finance task force and the £5 billion through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank are the Treasury’s answer to that.

MOD appoints its first Director General Innovation

MOD appoints its first Director General Innovation
The UK’s commitment to be a leader in innovative defence technologies will be strengthened as Anthony Reeves takes up DG Innovation role.
- Anthony Reeves appointed as the first Director General Innovation, bringing extensive military, government and industry experience.
- Role oversees 4,800 innovation experts and scientists and a £3.7 billion science, technology and innovation budget over the next four years to ensure the UK remains at the cutting edge of warfighting.
- National Armaments Innovation harnesses UK ingenuity and boosts military technology, as part of a drive to turbocharge innovation.
After an external competition, Anthony will become the newest 3* senior civil servant within National Armaments, part of the organisation’s Executive Committee, and the Ministry of Defence’s first Director General (DG) Innovation.
Taking up the role this Autumn, Anthony will lead the newly designed National Armaments Innovation area, which includes some 4,800 experts and scientists working in the Defence Investment Unit (DIU), the Defence Science & Technology Laboratory (Dstl), the Defence Uncrewed Systems Centre (DUSC) and UK Defence Innovation (UKDI).
Anthony will oversee a ringfenced £1.6 billion defence innovation budget over the next four years, as well as supporting £2.1 billion investment in core science and technology.
He will play a pivotal role in accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge technologies, fostering collaboration with industry, academia and government departments, and embedding innovation as a core military capability.
Rupert Pearce, the National Armaments Director, said:
  Anthony’s appointment marks a gear shift for UK Defence as we place innovation at the heart of the way we maintain war-fighting readiness, become an engine for economic growth and learn from the lessons of Ukraine to deter our adversaries.
As a leader, Tony brings a rare combination of frontline military experience, deep technical expertise and a proven track record of delivering transformation across Defence, government and industry.
His leadership will be instrumental as we strengthen Defence’s innovation ecosystem, accelerate the adoption of emerging technologies and deliver the capabilities our Armed Forces need, now and in the future.
Anthony joins National Armaments from Deloitte, where he led the UK and NATO Digital Defence section and was National Armaments Practice Head and Global AI Leader for Defence and Security.
He has worked extensively across UK Defence, NATO, AUKUS partners and defence industry organisations and his experience spans operational military service, national security, emerging technologies, AI and large-scale transformation programmes.
Commenting on his appointment, Tony said:
  Innovation in Defence must be about mindset before toolset. I look forward to working with brilliant colleagues across Defence, industry, academia and our international partners to make innovation everyone’s business, bring new technologies into military service at pace, and deliver tangible growth for the UK.
Under Anthony’s leadership, National Armaments Innovation will identify, mature and exploit emerging capabilities, strengthen collaboration with industry, academia and allies, and help ensure the Armed Forces can access the technologies and capabilities needed to maintain operational advantage.
Anthony’s earlier career included responsibility for delivering critical communications, networks and information capabilities for military operations and specialist users, alongside operational deployments as an infantry officer in the British Army, which included Northern Ireland, Bosnia, Kosovo and Sierra Leone.
Before joining Deloitte in 2020, Anthony advised defence organisations on digital transformation and technology adoption at Microsoft, and led major defence and national security programmes within PA Consulting and Detica.
He is a regular speaker on defence innovation, digital transformation and artificial intelligence, and serves as a Board member of the AI Institute UK, and mentor to future leaders through King’s College London and the Common Mission Project.

While Musk has warned of impending collapses and consolidation among the more than 200 dedicated graphics processing unit (GPU) rental ventures known as “neoclouds”, Huang remains bullish, insisting that robust market demand will unlock the capital needed to keep the sector afloat.
The dispute highlights the growing liquidity pressures facing AI infrastructure providers worldwide, including in China, where tech giants and specialised data-centre developers are committing tens of billions of dollars to build computing capacity before clear monetisation pathways emerge.

Construction of a new radar facility in Kaliningrad has been under way for some time and forms part of wider Russian investment in military capability that Britain and NATO allies are monitoring, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Gregory Campbell, the Democratic Unionist Party member for East Londonderry, asked whether the government would raise the construction of the radar at Gvardeysk, close to the Polish border, with NATO partners.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government remains in close consultation with NATO Allies on developments that may affect the security environment in the Euro-Atlantic area, including monitoring and assessing Russia’s investment in its military capabilities.
“Construction of the radar facility in Kaliningrad has been underway for some time and forms part of this wider investment. The UK and NATO Allies routinely monitor relevant Russian military developments and share information and assessments where appropriate.
“NATO continues to maintain an effective deterrence and defence posture, including on its Eastern Flank.”
Gvardeysk lies around thirty miles east of Kaliningrad city and has hosted Russian early warning radar infrastructure for years, including a Voronezh-DM site that watches across central and western Europe. The exclave has no land connection to the rest of Russia, hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet at Baltiysk, and carries air defence and missile systems whose reach extends well into allied airspace.
Kaliningrad borders Poland to the south and Lithuania to the north and east, and the stretch of frontier between them, the Suwalki gap, is the only land route between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Wednesday with his counterparts from Australia, Japan, and the Philippines to advance practical defense cooperation along the Pacific Ocean’s First Island Chain, stressing military readiness and deterrence.
“Deterrence is built on real capability and ready partnerships,” Hegseth said on US social media company X, calling the meeting “productive.”
“We are moving beyond words to practical cooperation along the First Island Chain—bolstering readiness to ensure peace through strength,” he added.

Russia building new drone launch site near Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast, HUR says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:28:49 UTC
22:28:49 KST

Russia building new drone launch site near Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast, HUR says
Russia is building a new site for operating attack drones near Millerovo airfield, close to the Ukrainian border, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 28, citing satellite imagery.
The airfield is located in the village of Dolotinka in Russia's Rostov Oblast, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) east of Ukraine's Luhansk Oblast.
According to HUR, the facility's design indicates it is intended for the preparation and launch of jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5 models and their variants.
"The construction of the facility in the Rostov Region may be part of Russia's preparations to intensify its attacks on Ukrainian territory, particularly during the winter," HUR said.
HUR estimated that once construction is complete, the site could accommodate up to 100 drone launches per day.
The site's actual operational tempo will depend on several factors, including supplies of ready-made drones, the availability of fuel and warheads, the number of trained drone crews, equipment readiness and the missions assigned by Russia, the statement read.
As of late August 2026, there were no significant signs of active construction at the site. Since then, launch positions and other infrastructure for drone operations have been established, HUR said.
The agency added that the rapid pace of construction may be attributed to the use of already-developed technical solutions.
Located just 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles) from Millerovo airfield, the new site could benefit from the air defense systems already deployed to protect the airfield. Its operation could also be supported by the airfield's existing road network, utilities, logistics infrastructure and technical support systems, HUR said.
As Russia expands the drone launch site, it is also upgrading its range of jet-powered drones. The updated Geran-4 features additional autonomous navigation systems and a new warhead designed to target bridges and power transmission towers, according to the agency.
The new facility would expand Russia's network of drone launch sites, which currently numbers at least 12.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can strike targets at distances of up to 770 kilometers (nearly 480 miles) and 950 kilometers (590 miles), respectively, posing a threat not only to Ukraine but also to neighboring countries, HUR added.

Metinvest plans four months ahead, reviews market and production capacity monthly amid strikes – CFO
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:28:27 EET
22:28:27 KST

Mining and metals group Metinvest plans four months ahead, reviewing market conditions and production capacity each month before drawing up cash flow forecasts and budgets, although circumstances can change dramatically even within that period, Chief Financial Officer Yulia Dankova said at the 24th Ukrainian CFO Forum in Kyiv.
Despite the uncertainty, Metinvest has retained annual business planning, preparing a plan for the following year each autumn. However, the process has changed to incorporate a baseline operating scenario, potential risks and contingency reserves for unexpected events.
Dankova said the situation could change significantly between planning cycles, with attacks, shutdowns of Black Sea ports, the introduction of EU steel import quotas and changes to national programs all affecting the business. The company selects the scenario it considers most likely and is prepared to defend, then identifies additional measures it could take even under an aggressive planning scenario. It subsequently tracks which contingency measures have been used, which risks have materialized and which unforeseen events, or "black swans," have emerged.
The company has also changed the assumptions underpinning its plans. Rather than forecasting when the war might end, it assesses practical operating conditions, including when Black Sea ports might reopen, the railway's capacity to transport cargo and whether its plants can operate.
Businesses must be prepared to revise plans continuously, Dankova said. The planning process helps management teams understand their objectives, assess different scenarios and choose economically and operationally sound decisions. For large corporations in particular, she said, the key is to quickly assess how a change in one factor affects the entire business.
Metinvest must therefore be able to reorganize operations quickly. If logistics are disrupted, cargo may need to be diverted from Black Sea ports to Poland and Romania. If raw material supplies are interrupted, the company must find alternative sources and recalculate production economics.
"Unfortunately, there was another strike on Oct 17. The plants are not operating. At the same time, we are already planning the next four-month cycle, which will include two months of next year, and preparing decisions within the selected scenario," Dankova said.
Metinvest reviews its scenarios whenever a significant event could affect operations, including a blockade of Black Sea ports or changes to EU export conditions under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
Dankova said the company approved its business plan in December last year, only to learn in early January that Ukraine had not received an exemption from CBAM. Since the decision affected the plan, Metinvest immediately reviewed its operating scenarios.
The group uses dedicated platforms for sales and production planning and for consolidating plant cost data, while continuing to use Excel. Decisions are made locally or centrally depending on the circumstances and the scale of the problem. For example, if raw materials must be allocated among several plants, management needs to determine where they will deliver the greatest benefit.
Regular revisions of plans and decisions have become an integral part of Metinvest's operating model. Whereas sales, production and margin targets were previously set during the planning process, they are now reviewed by budget committees and at weekly operational meetings.
"This is adaptive management, which we use in crisis situations. And we have been living in such conditions since 2014," Dankova said.
She also stressed the importance of rapid information sharing and cooperation between departments. Decisions depend on teams understanding one another's needs, with working capital management requiring coordination with the commercial director and inventory and procurement management involving the operations director.
Metinvest is a vertically integrated mining and metals group with operations primarily in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Its main shareholders are SCM Group, with a 71.24% stake, and Smart-Holding, with 23.76%. Metinvest Holding LLC is the group's managing company.

European parcel tax: Millions in revenue and far fewer cheap parcels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:27:01 UTC
22:27:01 KST

Over the past three months, 65 per cent fewer cheap parcels from countries including China have been declared than in the same period last year, according to Belgian customs authorities. This sharp decline is entirely due to the introduction of the European parcel tax of 3 euros per item. Moreover, in just a few months, the tax has generated tens of millions of euros.
European parcel tax: Millions in revenue and far fewer cheap parcels
The European Union – including Belgium – has for years been grappling with the massive influx of cheap parcels, the vast majority of which come from China. Think of the Sheins, Temus and AliExpresses of this world. Last year, 1.3 billion such parcels arrived via Liège Airport (Belgium).
It is not uncommon for these to contain counterfeit goods or products that do not meet European safety standards, but the customs service simply cannot manage to check them all.
More revenue
To bring this under better control, the EU introduced a temporary parcel tax of 3 euros per item from 1 July this year. This applies to parcels worth less than 150 euros that do not originate from the EU. On top of that, from 1 November – this coming Sunday – a fixed European handling fee of 2 euros per item will also apply.
The parcel tax is already proving to be a great success, as customs figures show. In total, it has raised 364 million euros in European taxes since July – or around 28 million euros per week. Belgium is entitled to keep a quarter of that sum.
Kristian Vanderwaeren from the Belgian customs service does, however, warn of an increase in attempts at fraud. “For example, people are now trying to declare the value of parcels as over 150 euros in order to pay less tax. Sometimes they also declare fewer items than are actually in the parcel, just to pay the parcel tax only once. But my team is working on ways to detect this.”
The business organisation Unizo is pleased with the results. “This is a victory for us, but above all for our businesses and the economy, as the measures are clearly delivering results,” says CEO Bart Buysse.
He believes the government should reinvest the millions generated by the tax. “For us, it is essential that this revenue is actually invested in additional customs officers, better technology and stricter checks. Because as long as foreign online shops can sell products that aren’t even allowed on shop shelves here, competition remains unfair.”
And the government must go even further, Buysse adds. “We must also close the loopholes. Anyone who repeatedly sells unsafe products must be dealt with much more strictly. And if a single dangerous product is found during an inspection, the rest of the consignment must not simply be allowed to pass through unchecked.”

Swiss to vote on nuclear power, foie gras and naturalisation in February 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:26:49 UTC
22:26:49 KST

Swiss to vote on nuclear power, foie gras and naturalisation in February 2027
Swiss citizens will vote on February 28, 2027, whether new nuclear power stations can be built in Switzerland, ten years after their construction was banned. Four other issues are on the agenda.
The Federal Council wants to lift the ban on the construction of new nuclear power plants and has presented an indirect counter-proposal to the “Stop the Blackout” popular initiative. The initiative committee, comprising the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party and representatives from the business community, says it is happy with the counter-proposal.
The Greens, the Social Democratic Party, the Liberal Green Party and members of the Centre Party are against it. Swiss voters had approved a phase-out of nuclear power in 2017, banning the construction of new power stations.
More
Why climate change and wars are reviving interest in nuclear energy
Foie gras and naturalisation
Four other issues are on the ballot list next February. Voters will be asked to decide on an initiative that seeks to ban the importation of foie gras.
This ban would also apply to private individuals, who would no longer be able to import these products for personal consumption. The initiative currently enjoys broad support, especially in German-speaking Switzerland.
More
Foie gras initiative: indirect counter-proposal tabled
The Swiss will also vote on the “Democracy Initiative”, which seeks to standardise the naturalisation process in Switzerland. Launched by the group Action Quatre Quarts and supported by left-wing circles, the proposal calls for naturalisation to be possible after five years’ legal residence in Switzerland, regardless of the type of residence permit held.
Currently, the law requires at least ten years’ residence in Switzerland, including three of the five years preceding the submission of the application, for holders of a C permit (settled foreign nationals). The centre-right camp is opposed to the proposal.
More
What an eased path to Swiss citizenship could mean for the Swiss Abroad
Warm-up
The free trade agreement between the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and Malaysia is also on the vote agenda. Parliament supports the deal, which is set to reduce customs duties on 12,500 tonnes of palm oil.
However, a coalition of left-wing parties and organisations has tabled a referendum. They are concerned about the devastating consequences for tropical forests.
The vote will send an interesting signal regarding another highly anticipated referendum: the free trade agreement with Mercosur. A referendum has been tabled for similar reasons.
More
Beyond tariffs: how Switzerland turned trade talks into climate action with Mercosur
Vote on minimum wages
Finally, the public will vote on a Federal Council proposal aimed at giving collective labour agreements precedence over cantonal minimum wages. Trade unions and the left oppose the idea.
At present, a collective agreement can only be extended if it contains nothing contrary to federal or cantonal law. Consequently, cantonal minimum wages take precedence over those set out in agreements between the social partners. The proposal aims to reverse this practice.

Russian gas supplies to the European Union and operation of the Nord Stream pipeline will not resume after the end of Russia's war against Ukraine, the European Commission said on Wednesday, responding to media reports that the United States and Russia are discussing a possible restoration of supplies.

Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers

Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers
A blind Ukrainian man was allegedly held for days at a conscription center despite being clearly unfit for military service, according to court papers.
The case, reported by Ukrainian media on Wednesday, stems from a complaint filed by the unidentified man with a district court in Odessa seeking an official investigation. A judge ruled in his favor last week, ordering the authorities to look into the allegations, a decision that was made public shortly afterward.
According to the complaint, the man has been visually impaired since childhood and was exempted from military service as early as 1994, with his status reaffirmed in 2020 and 2023. Despite this, he says draft officials refused to recognize his condition and held him for almost five days.
He was allegedly seized on a street in Odessa in March, held incommunicado without being formally booked, and released only after intervention by his lawyer.
The regional branch of the State Bureau of Investigation, which had earlier refused to register his complaint, was ordered by the court to reverse that decision. The man had separately secured a court ruling ordering his removal from a list of people wanted for draft evasion.
Kiev relies on compulsory mobilization of fighting-age men to sustain its war effort against Russia, but the campaign has been marred by widespread corruption among draft officials and public perceptions that the system is deeply unfair. The government has responded to draft evasion with heavy-handed enforcement that has repeatedly involved the illegal use of force by military officials.
Illegal detention at recruitment centers has become a recurring problem, according to the office of Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmitry Lubinets.
In one high-profile case reported by Lubinets in June, 21 men were found to have been illegally held in poor conditions at a conscription center in Uzhgorod, some for more than 50 days.
In another case, the three-day detention of 39-year-old Aleksey Ivanko at a Kharkov recruitment center in May 2025 ended with him jumping from a third-floor window to his death. Lubinets said in his annual report that his office found no evidence Ivanko had been physically abused by draft officials, but concluded there had been no legal grounds to restrict his freedom and that the prolonged confinement had contributed to the circumstances of his death.

Türkiye is ready to sign an agreement with Egypt on maritime boundary delimitation based on mutual interests, the Turkish National Defence Ministry has said.
"We once again emphasise that we are ready to sign an Agreement on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas with Egypt in line with mutual interests," it said in a statement on Wednesday.
The potential deal could grant Cairo a larger maritime jurisdiction than a potential agreement with Greece, it added.
"It is assessed that if Egypt signs such an agreement with our country, it would gain more than 15,000 square kilometres (5,792 square miles) of additional maritime jurisdiction compared to a potential agreement it could conclude with Greece."
The ministry stressed that Türkiye would continue protecting its legitimate rights and interests in the Eastern Mediterranean within the framework of international law while contributing to regional peace, security and stability.
The ministry also hailed Libya's approval last week of the memorandum of understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction signed with Türkiye in 2019.
"The approval by the Libyan House of Representatives on October 20 of the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas, signed between our country and Libya in 2019, is an important development supporting our country's approach based on international law and the principles of equity, which takes into account the legitimate rights and interests of the relevant coastal states," the spokesperson said.
Türkiye welcomes efforts to strengthen security in Sinjar
During the weekly press briefing at the ministry, the ministry’s spokesperson Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk welcomed efforts by the Iraqi central government to strengthen state authority and normalise conditions in the Sinjar region.
"Ending the presence of terrorist organisations in the region and ensuring security through Iraq's official security forces is an important development for establishing lasting peace and stability in Sinjar and achieving the goal of a terror-free region," the ministry said.
It added that the process is being closely monitored in coordination with relevant Turkish state institutions.
Defence cooperation and Kosovo mission
The spokesman stressed that the Turkish army continues contributing to regional and global peace, security and stability through cooperation with friendly and allied countries, training and advisory activities, and participation in multinational missions.

"Under the Türkiye-Greece Confidence-Building Measures Implementation Plan, the commander of the Greek Tactical Air Force and an accompanying delegation will visit our Combat Air Force commander on November 3-5," he said.
He added that Türkiye assumed the deputy command of the NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR) for a one-year term during a ceremony held on Tuesday.
"As during our country's command of KFOR, we will carry out the deputy command with an understanding of impartiality, transparency and professionalism, continuing to contribute to Kosovo's security and the preservation of regional peace and stability," he said.
Joint naval exercise planned with Egypt
Akturk said national and international training and exercise activities continue uninterrupted to enhance the Turkish Armed Forces' effectiveness and deterrence across land, sea, air, space and cyberspace.
He said the National Anatolian Phoenix Exercise, named after martyred Air Force pilot Major Ibrahim Bolat, is under way in Konya and will conclude on November 6.
The Crossed Swords Exercise, to be conducted remotely in Estonia, will begin on November 2.
He also announced that the Sea of Friendship-2026 Exercise will take place in Alexandria, Egypt, from November 4 to 9, with the participation of Turkish and Egyptian naval units and personnel.
The exercise will include surface and anti-submarine warfare, air defence operations and underwater offensive training.
He said the Turkish frigates TCG Gokceada and TCG Yildirim will begin their deployment to Somalia on October 30 to transport supplies by sea and conduct personnel rotations.
On the same day, a Turkish airborne early warning and control aircraft will conduct a mission flight in NATO airspace over Romania as part of assurance measures.
Turkish fighter jets will also participate in the Nexus Ace training in the Mediterranean alongside a NATO AWACS aircraft.
New defence systems enter service
The spokesperson said Türkiye's domestic defence industry continues strengthening the Turkish Armed Forces' deterrence and operational capabilities through critical systems developed for land, naval, air and cyber operations.
He announced that the Land Forces Command completed inspection and acceptance procedures for various quantities of Karayel Hull Boats and Kablolu Kamikaze-2 uncrewed ground vehicles over the past week.
Turkish defence manufacturer Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation (MKE) also delivered various quantities of MAM-15 sniper rifles to defence industry stakeholders.
He added that MKE will participate in Euronaval 2026, one of the world's leading international naval defence and maritime technology exhibitions, scheduled for November 3 to 6 in Paris, France.

A bilateral meeting between Poland’s deputy prime minister and defense minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and the UK’s defense secretary Wes Streeting took place in Warsaw on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at which they signed a three-year defense plan.

According to Kosiniak-Kamysz, the main areas of cooperation will include new technologies, artificial intelligence, drones, anti-drone systems, modern deterrence measures, as well as traditional exercises to build capabilities, and cooperation under different scenarios.

Streeting said: “We hear very clearly what Poland experiences every day in the form of what some describe as hybrid threats from Russia – I prefer to describe it directly as state-sponsored terrorism – the daily mobilization of your forces and air defense in the face of drone intrusions.”

It also will build on the jont construction of modern warships including the Polish “Miecznik” (Swordfish) and the British Type 31 frigate programs, which are said to be on schedule. This will go hand-in-hand with increased naval activity in the Baltic Sea which, through exercises and regional coordination, will allow the two countries to protect vital lines of communication in the waterway
The agreement also sees cooperation on cyber security and resilience to help both countries protect defense-related and civilian networks from hostile threats.
The two men say there will also be closer links between their defense industries that will include closer defense procurement coordination with companies including MBDA UK, in the area of missiles with BAE Systems,and Poland’s PGZ working together in the production of large-caliber ammunition.
The plan sees continued UK and Polish participation in large-scale exercises such as Steadfast Defender, Polish Dragon, and Joint Warrior, which will ensure their forces retain the capability to fight future conflicts, including the use of counter-drone warfare, electronic warfare, and missile defense.
The ministers said both nations are fully committed to supporting Kyiv in the war against Russia. They will both provide contingents for November’s major “Coalition of the Wiling” exercise in Poland, which will see the deployment thousands of personnel earmarked for the Multinational Force Ukraine, intended to support the military training and post-war rebuilding of the war torn country.
The exercise was announced in August by French President Emmanuel Macron, the UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Euro News reported that the meeting also saw discussions on Europe’s relations with the US, which Kosiniak-Kamysz said reached agreement on the need to strengthen and build up Europe’s defense capabilities without disengaging with Washington.
He said “Poland and the United Kingdom support strengthening this alliance [with the United States - ed.], the transatlantic alliance, because the United Kingdom is the best example – everything connected with the transatlantic alliance grew out of Britain. We are in favor of reinforcing it and building our own capabilities, of greater independence for Europe, but not independence from the United States.”

Booking can compel staff to spend two days in the office: court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:21:04 UTC
22:21:04 KST

Booking can compel staff to spend two days in the office: court
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A court has ruled that travel website Booking.com can compel its staff to spend at least two days a week in the office, settling a dispute with the company’s works council.
The decision was widely expected after the judge remarked at an earlier hearing that requiring employees to spend 40% of their contracted hours on site was “very normal”.
Just over a quarter of Booking.com’s 7,000 staff currently travel to its head office in Amsterdam twice a week. The company had advised its workers to spend two days in the office to promote better workplace relations, training and efficient working practices.
But when bosses tried to make the two-day guideline a mandatory requirement, the works council objected. It said the impact on people’s work-life balance, commuting times and travel costs was too great and questioned whether it would lead to improved performance.
The judge said the company had taken employees’ concerns into account and responded by introducing a six-month transition period and deciding to set the minimum office time at 40% rather than 50% or 60%.
Booking said it welcomed the judgment, pointing out that the two-day rule was not a new measure but a “strengthening of our current policy”.
“We value the relationship with our works council and will continue to hold constructive dialogue with them and our employees as we roll this policy out further,” a spokesman said.
Employment lawyer Pascal Besselink told RTL Nieuws other companies that wanted staff to spend more time in the office would be studying the judgment closely.
“They will always strive to maintain a good relationship with their employees and works council and consult thoroughly on arrangements about home working,” he said.

Hebron under siege: Is Israel testing a new West Bank strategy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Hebron under siege: Is Israel testing a new West Bank strategy?
Hebron - Mayar Imriash, 24, was busy preparing for her wedding when the Israeli army demolished her family's home in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron.
What should have been a time of joyful anticipation has instead been marred by displacement, with Mayar now sharing a single room with seven relatives in her uncle’s home.
Among the possessions buried beneath the rubble was the handwoven tatreez dress that Mayar had planned to wear for her henna night, a traditional Palestinian celebration for female guests held the night before the wedding.
A litter of newborn kittens was also trapped inside the home when it was demolished, according to her younger brother, Ahmed Imriash.
“Their mother keeps coming back, day after day, meowing and looking for them,” he told The New Arab.
Following a shooting attack by Palestinian gunmen at an army checkpoint on 23 October, the Israeli army launched a major military operation in Hebron, placing the West Bank’s largest city under lockdown.
Entrances and exits to the city have been sealed, and large swaths of the city have been deserted. Civilian vehicles, reportedly stolen by the army, are being used as roadblocks into residential neighbourhoods.
In the five days since the attack, the Israeli military has forcibly displaced nearly 5,000 people from al-Jilda and Deir Baha, the neighbourhoods where the gunmen reportedly hailed from.
The military subsequently demolished at least four structures, including the Imriash family home.
The military operation has uprooted thousands of Palestinians who had nothing to do with the shooting, including the Imriash family.
“The Israeli occupation is using collective punishment against Hebron and its residents,” Yousef Jabari, head of Hebron’s municipality, told The New Arab.
“It is very clear that Netanyahu has used what happened in Hebron for his election campaign to get as many votes as possible from the extreme right, settler movement,” he said.
Family given 'two minutes' before demolition
Just a few hours after the shooting, Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich stood watch as the army demolished the Imriash family home.
In a video posted on his X account, he poses in protective gear as a hydraulic jackhammer tears into the stone house, and a dusty trampoline tumbles through the yard.
"We're already here with the equipment on the ground, sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: If you mess with us, we will exact a very, very painful price from you,” the far-right minister says.
The family had two minutes’ notice to grab what they could before their three-story home was levelled, Ahmed told The New Arab. The army shot tear gas at the family as they fled to a nearby building, where they watched the demolition unfold.
In a video of the demolition, Mayar stands motionless, hands clasped behind her back, in what many have compared to Handala - the Palestinian cartoon symbolising resilience and stoicism.
Three days later, Mayar walked hand in hand with her fiancé through the ruins of her home, finding bits of their belongings strewn across the ground.
“Look, my shoes are everywhere… Just like any other girl, I was supposed to be preparing for my happiest moment," she said. "They didn't leave us any happiness, but we will still create joy, and we will continue, God willing.”
“What’s left here is only memories,” said 23-year-old Ahmed, sitting on a dusty chair in what was once his courtyard. “At least they left us with this,” he said, while motioning towards the concrete patio.
The humiliation is especially pronounced for Ahmed and Mayar’s father, Riyad Imriash, who spent 25 years saving and working in Saudi Arabia to afford the construction of their home, which the family had moved into three years earlier.
The army had targeted the home long before the shooting attack, with Riyad first receiving an order to cease construction in 2021.
After a lengthy and expensive legal battle, the family secured a court ruling overturning the order and legalising their property, Riyad said. But it was ignored.
“We showed the court order prohibiting the demolition, and a soldier told us to shove the paper up our ass,” said Ahmed. “We can’t even defend ourselves.”
“We applied for all the legalisations, procedures, and protocols, and applied for everything that would protect this house. But on Friday, this shooting happened in Hebron, and I was the first to be targeted. I don’t know why,” Riyad told The New Arab.
A future precedent?
Residents of Hebron fear the Israeli army’s operations could mark a new phase, where the military increasingly occupies the West Bank’s cities.
Others believe it was an isolated political stunt to shore up support for Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud ahead of the Israeli elections.
“We will apply in the cities the successful offensive model we implemented in the refugee camps,” announced Netanyahu, referring to the Israeli army’s forced eviction of 33,000 Palestinians, who have been barred from returning to their homes in the refugee camps since early 2025.
“What’s happening here is just for propaganda, to make some Israelis happy, specifically the right-wing extremists. These people are very happy to see what is happening to us, and the goal [of this operation] is to secure their vote,” Reem Ahmad Alsharif, a city councillor in Hebron, told The New Arab.
For now, some of the city’s displaced have moved in with relatives, while others are staying at shelters established by the Hebron municipality.
Palestinian volunteers gather at the municipality each day to collect food, clothing, and hygiene products for the displaced, with plastic mattresses ready for distribution lining the halls.
“We don’t have nearly enough resources to meet the need,” said Alsharif, rummaging through a box of children’s toys stocked with stuffed animals and a hula hoop.
She hopes the families will be allowed to return soon, but there is no clear timeline for when the Israeli army will withdraw, or what the future holds for the city.
“We have never been displaced like this,” she says. “It’s the first time they’re doing this in Hebron, and inshallah it’s the last time.”

Scale AI rejects claims it illegally surveils AI-training workers
Scale AI on Oct 28 rejected the privacy complaints filed against it in four European countries as unfounded, saying its platform’s practices were disclosed to workers and required their consent.
Privacy group noyb filed the complaints on Oct 27 in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria, alleging Scale’s Outlier platform illegally monitors more than 900,000 freelancers who produce training data for AI models, and asked regulators to fine the company.
“The report’s claims are unfounded and inaccurate,” Scale said in an emailed statement to Reuters.
Scale said it uses standard tools to verify identities, prevent fraud, protect confidential project information and ensure accurate payments.
Contributors know their pay rates before accepting tasks and those rates reflect skills, project details and location, it added.
A company spokesperson said certain projects use a separate tool that records time spent and screen activity, which contributors opt into and manually activate before starting work.
Scale does not sell workers’ personal data to third parties or use it to train customers’ AI models, the spokesperson said. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Why NASA's Artemis III Mission Will Be One of its Most Complex Flights Ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:14:52 UTC
22:14:52 KST

The last time the folks at NASA tested a crewed lunar lander in low-Earth orbit, here’s how they did it. First, a Saturn 5 rocket lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida carrying three astronauts, an Apollo spacecraft, and a lunar module. Then they got to orbit and the astronauts flew both ships. Then they came home. That straightforward mission was accomplished 57 years ago, during the flight of Apollo 9.
The next time NASA attempts something of the kind—during the planned flight of Artemis III in the summer of 2027—things will be a lot more complicated. First an uncrewed Blue Origin New Glenn rocket will launch from KSC carrying the company’s Blue Moon lander into orbit. Then NASA will launch its prosaically named Space Launch System (SLS) moon rocket, carrying the four Artemis III astronauts aboard an Orion spacecraft. Then the crew will rendezvous with the Blue Moon, dock with it and enter it, checking out its systems before returning to the Orion. Then SpaceX will launch a Starship rocket carrying its own Starship lander, which will also be uncrewed. The astronauts will rendezvous and dock with that ship too, but not enter it since it will not yet be equipped with a life support system. Then they will separate and the crew will spend a few more days running tests on the Orion. All of that work will take up to 17 days from first liftoff to splashdown. And only if everything goes just right with that mission can NASA achieve its goal of landing astronauts on the lunar surface during the 2028 flight of Artemis IV—and in the process, win a new space race with China.
On Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman—along with Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya and Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons—conducted a marathon two-hour press conference at KSC, detailing plans for Artemis III and IV, conceding that the hurdles are considerable, but insisting the goals are within reach. The current NASA, with its tight funding and long timelines, may not be the old NASA that used its generous budgets and garage full of rockets to pop off nine crewed Apollo lunar missions just from 1968 to 1972, but it will be no less successful.
“In that remarkably short span of time, the ambitions of generations once confined to the pages of science fiction became humanity's greatest achievement, and for the first time in billions of years, life born on Earth would set foot on another world,” said Isaacman. “Now, in this incredibly demanding and dangerous business of putting astronauts [back] on the moon, NASA must own the near impossible…That is how we give Artemis IV the greatest possible chance of safely and successfully returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.”
The extreme complexity of Artemis III is owing in part to a pair of decisions NASA made in 2021 and 2023 and in part to the simple limits of known rocket technology. If the engineering physics were perfect—and engineering physics are never perfect—a lunar crew could use just one spacecraft to get to the moon, land, blast back off, and return home. But a spacecraft that could do all of those jobs and remain robust enough to reenter the Earth’s atmosphere would simply be too heavy for a lunar landing and subsequent liftoff. Instead, as in the Apollo days, the job will be divided between two ships—one lightweight one to perform the landing and liftoff and one orbiting mothership to bring the crew home when the lunar exploration is done. During Apollo, the space agency selected Grumman Aircraft Engineering to build its squat, four-legged 23-ft. tall, lunar module (LM). It was a simple ship with a low center of gravity, ensuring a stable foothold on the lunar surface. Grumman inked the contract in 1962 and delivered the goods in time for Apollo 9 and the missions that followed. In 2021, NASA similarly awarded a contract for a crewed lunar spacecraft—this time to SpaceX and its Starship lander. The decision was a headscratcher.
Starship is a silo-like cylinder with a tapered nose cone, measuring 165 ft. tall, calling to mind less an actual spacecraft than the 1953 illustrated book about Tintin’s adventures on the moon. Apollo astronauts used a nine-rung ladder to get down to the lunar surface. Artemis astronauts aboard Starship will use an elevator. Critics and competitors pounced on the plan—not least because of the risk that the giant machine could tip over on the moon—and in 2023, NASA issued a second contract, this time to Blue Origin, which promised to build a lander more in keeping with the low-slung Apollo lunar module. Both companies have continued to produce their landers and both will get a shot to fly on the historic Artemis IV mission—with the winner to be determined by the performance of the ships during Artemis III.
But neither company has had an easy go of things. SpaceX has launched 14 Starships since 2023, only achieving Earth orbit for the first time in September 2026. Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, meanwhile, launched three times from January 2025 to April 2026, before a massive explosion on the launch pad during a test of its first stage engines occurred in May 2026. The disaster marked a major setback for Blue Origin, not least because the pad infrastructure itself was partially destroyed in the blast. The company has been working feverishly since to rebound, and at the Oct. 23 press conference, the NASA brass praised its efforts.
“Blue Origin's New Glenn team has amazed the world with their progress for return to flight after the incident in May,” said Parsons. “We're working closely with them. We have over 100 NASA team [members] engaged throughout return to flight…and I have seen Blue Origin mobilize an absolute army working around the clock.”
Assuming the company can maintain that pace, it stands a good chance of being the winner in the Artemis III sweepstakes. That’s partly because its rival, SpaceX, will not fly a full-up version of its Starship lander during the mission, but rather what amounts to a boilerplate ship equipped with a docking port that will test only whether the Orion and the Starship can meet and link up in orbit. Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander won’t be a fully operational vehicle either, but it will have a functioning crew compartment that will allow the Artemis III astronauts to enter and run tests.
“They're going to open up the hatch. They're going to enter the lander. They're going to evaluate the environmental controls, the life support systems,” says Parsons. “We'll confirm that the spacecraft can maintain the right atmospheric pressure, and we're also going to test emergency scenarios, dual vehicle control, and we're going to put our Mission Control teams through their paces."
For all of the confidence expressed at the press conference, no one at NASA pretends that the Artemis III mission doesn’t have a lot of moving parts and a lot of things that could go badly wrong before the space agency can tee up the 2028 Artemis IV landing. And even if the mission does completely succeed, NASA will still require both competing spacecraft to execute an uncrewed lunar landing and liftoff to prove their mettle further. Only then will the landers be certified to carry crew.
Whether the two companies can perfect the engineering and fly the uncrewed missions in the maximum 18 months that will elapse between the launch of Artemis III and the flight of Artemis IV at the end of 2028 is uncertain. Isaacman, for one, expresses confidence that the target date can be met without slipping into 2029 or later. But he acknowledges that NASA’s years of uncertainty since the Apollo program—with priorities shifting from Skylab to the shuttle to the International Space Station, and with start-stop programs to return to the moon that burned through money but never got anywhere—have set the agency back, especially as it concerns the ongoing competition with China.
“Here we are today, very much in a new space race, and despite decades of accumulated knowledge and extraordinary advancements in technology, this race will be much closer than it ever needed to be,” he says. “That brings us to the moment we find ourselves in today, because the appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion. We are here for the mission, and to deliver the outcomes the world expects of the most accomplished space agency in history.”
