- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a majority; a unity coalition may prevent another election - analysis
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a majority; a unity coalition may prevent another election - analysis
A deal could see Eisenkot serve as prime minister in the second half of the term, with Netanyahu positioned as the government’s candidate to succeed Herzog as president in July 2028
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot both delivered victory speeches to their constituents early Wednesday morning.
In Eisenkot's speech, he prematurely eulogized Netanyahu and declared that the public had voted to end his tenure. Had he waited half an hour to start his speech when more results were in, perhaps he would have been more careful.
Netanyahu defiantly defended all his current coalition partners, mercilessly mocked the rival camp, and called for a right-wing nationalist government. Had he waited, perhaps it would have become clearer that he lost his 64-MK majority in this election.
The truth is that neither side won. Simple math: Neither of them have the 61 MKs out of 120 needed for a stable government.
So what happens now? Is Israel doomed to go to perpetual elections?
The answer is it depends on the success of the president. Which president? Three of them, actually.
President Isaac Herzog can try to condition granting Netanyahu a mandate on him making a serious effort to draft a national unity government with Eizenkot as defense minister, Naftali Bennett as foreign minister, and Itamar Ben-Gvir and Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties as spectators in the opposition.
President Donald Trump can do the same, knowing that a unity government in Israel can help him advance his foreign policy at a time when his domestic agenda could be handcuffed by Congress.
And Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian can continue to reject compromises and bring about another round of war with Israel and the United States.
Wars are good excuses to break campaign promises, which Eizenkot must do to prevent an election in which he would likely no longer be his bloc's candidate for prime minister. He could be prime minister in the second half of the term, without taking the risk of another race.
It is, of course, a risk to trust Netanyahu to hand over power after he did not honor an agreement with Benny Gantz. But Netanyahu could be made the government’s candidate to replace Herzog as president in July 2028, shortly before Trump's term ends, perhaps replaced by a president less friendly to Israel.
Netanyahu’s criminal trial, which was the initial reason for boycotting him, has been petering out anyway.
Such a government would enable Eizenkot to keep his promise about forming g a coalition without the haredim that could pass a tougher draft law.
And what about the Arabs, whose impressive showing in the election cannot be ignored? Banishing Ben-Gvir would be a victory for them. They would not join the government or the coalition, but vast initiatives to fight inter-Arab crime and poverty could be initiated and well-funded, overseen by the Knesset Interior and Public Security committees, led by Arab MKs.
This scenario is not what Netanyahu or Eizenkot called for in their victory speeches. But it could bring the stability and reconciliation needed at a time of war.

Zelensky said he spoke with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb on Tuesday night, following a meeting in Oslo, shortly before their conversation with Putin.
“We discussed the topic. In principle, we had a briefing in Oslo on the topic of the upcoming planned trilateral meeting of the negotiating groups in November in Abu Dhabi,” he said.

Russian Commander Organized Widescale Fraud Based on Fake ‘Action’ Videos
Zelensky also pointed to their clarification that they were speaking on behalf of their own countries, rather than representing Europe as a whole. As Russia’s neighbors, he said, Norway and Finland have a particular interest in the discussions.
Zelensky said Norway and Finland should share the information with other Europeans and discuss the agenda with Ukraine, Europe, and the US.
“They want to play a bigger role,” he said, adding that while Norway is not an EU member, it is part of Europe more broadly.

“When there are security guarantees that Ukraine wants to discuss and security guarantees that Russia wants to discuss, they believe that this is also a serious challenge for them – both for Russia’s neighbors, for European countries, and for our serious partners,” Zelensky said.

Zelensky also recalled the meeting between Putin and US President Donald Trump in Alaska, saying it had effectively ended Russia’s diplomatic isolation.
“It’s a fact: The ‘Russians’ were diplomatically isolated by a significant part of the world, and Alaska lifted this isolation,” he said.
Zelensky added that European contacts with Russia had taken place even before the Alaska meeting, although they were less public. He also pointed to communications involving national security advisers and intelligence services, as well as contacts with Turkey and countries in the Middle East.
“In addition to Europe, Turkey and the countries of the Middle East communicated. That is, this is happening,” he said, adding that Kyiv had learned about some other contacts only after they had taken place.
In contrast, Zelensky described the Norwegian and Finnish initiative as an open process involving advance discussions, a full briefing, and clear objectives.
“Finland and Norway show that they want to open another channel of communication so that Europe can receive information not only through the US and so that Russia can hear certain things directly,” Zelensky added.
Putin focused on medieval slavic history during talks
Meanwhile, the Financial Times (FT) reported that Putin’s conversation with Støre and Stubb did not go as the Nordic leaders had expected.
According to the report cited by RBC-Ukraine, Putin devoted a substantial part of the discussion to his interpretation of medieval Slavic history.
The conversation was the Russian leader’s first contact with any of Ukraine’s European allies since he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron in July.
However, Putin showed little urgency to address current issues, the FT reported, highlighting the challenges Europe faces in trying to influence future peace negotiations with Russia.
Stubb told Finnish media that the conversation had initially been scheduled to last less than 30 minutes but ultimately continued for an hour and a half.
Three sources familiar with the discussions told the FT that, rather than engaging in substantive debate about how to end the war, Putin spent considerable time discussing what the Kremlin calls the “root causes of the conflict.”
The sources also said the issue of an immediate ceasefire – which Ukraine has insisted upon – was barely raised. The Nordic leaders deliberately refrained from interrupting Putin’s historical digressions, seeking to assess how willing he was to engage in dialogue with Europe.
Previously, Putin also cited “the latest genetic research” to support his claim that Russians and Ukrainians are one people. He presented the argument through his own interpretation of Russia’s historical development and contemporary realities.

Israel’s election: The battle between change and anti-Palestinian sentiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:22:20 UTC
21:22:20 KST

Israel’s election: The battle between change and anti-Palestinian sentiment
With both blocs short of a majority, parties face a choice: to break the taboo on Arab allies or return to the polls.
With Israel’s governing and opposition blocs failing to secure a majority in Israel’s election, and neither appearing ready to ally with Arab parties that could allow them to form a coalition, speculation is growing over the future shape of the government.
The vote on Tuesday, billed as one of the most important in Israel’s history, saw turnout reach 77.7 percent of eligible voters – the highest level since 1999.
With nearly 80 percent of votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, the outgoing coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, centred around his Likud party, had secured 54 seats, short of the 61 needed to establish a governing coalition.
Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist opposition, drawing from parties as diverse as Yair Golan’s relatively left-wing Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s hard-right Yisrael Beiteinu, had 49 seats, also short of a governing majority in the 120-strong Knesset.
Holding the balance of power, in theory at least, are the Arab-dominated Ra’am and Joint List, with 17 seats, more than enough to give either bloc a majority with which to appoint a speaker, pass legislation and form a working government.
Those figures are not final, however, with the final tally expected by Friday and official results formally published on November 4 .
What happens next is a matter of procedure as much as politics.
President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on who they want as prime minister, before tasking the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government. That candidate has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. If they fail, the mandate can pass to another member of parliament, and if that also fails, the Knesset is dissolved and Israelis return to the polls, with the current cabinet staying on as caretaker.
Turnout
Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, who account for one-fifth of the total population, reached about 80 percent, according to some estimates, also above the 1999 figures.
Analysts said the surge was propelled by the harsh treatment of the Israeli-Palestinian minority by the Likud-led government, which increased significantly following the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. Netanyahu’s outgoing government is the most right-wing in Israeli history, featuring far-right figures such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose policies and rhetoric against Palestinians have essentially made him a recruiting sergeant for the pro-Arab parties.
Analysts also attributed the strong performance to a well-organised campaign that targeted the demands of Israel’s Palestinian community and the opportunity for a greater voice in the Knesset.
“Having just two well-organised lists significantly improved their vote-collecting efficiency and ground-level mobilisation – particularly for Ra’am, the Islamist party, which ran a much more efficient campaign than usual,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera.
“The broader shift, however, comes down to how voters view their place in Israeli politics,” he added, “especially following October 7 and the subsequent war,” Zur added.
“On one hand, many voters feel more integrated into Israeli society, driven by shifts in how the public processed both the October 7 attacks and the government’s subsequent policies, making them feel more invested in the political system.”
Polarised puzzle
However, both blocs ran campaigns that critics have described as profoundly racist. Likud spent much of the election race making unsubstantiated claims that the opposition was planning to form a government reliant on Arab parties after the vote, while petitioning to bar the Joint List from running.
On the opposition side, Lieberman ruled out a coalition with either Arab or ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties, while Together’s Naftali Bennett, whose 2021-22 coalition included Ra’am, told an activists’ conference there was “no mandate” to form a government with Arab parties after the October 7 attack.
“The ‘opposition’ bloc continues to think you beat Bibi by being Bibi-lite, offering no substantive alternative or hope,” said former government adviser Daniel Levy, using a common nickname for the Israeli prime minister. “Really, the opposition got what they deserved,” he added, arguing it would have won the election if its members’ commitment to removing Netanyahu had outweighed their “commitment to a racist ethno-centric version of Zionism”.
Levy sees four possible scenarios ahead for either bloc, listed in no particular order: the possibility of a new election; Likud drawing enough defectors from the right of the opposition to form a government; a so-called “unity government” led by Netanyahu that draws on the right across the Knesset; and “Eisenkot and company biting the bullet and using the anti-Netanyahu majority to form a minority government with Arab support,” he said.
“Even if they announce it’s time-limited before another election, the Arab parties’ asking price will not be particularly high,” he said, with the caveat that he considered such a coalition unlikely.
Wheeling and dealing
The chance of defection amidst what is seen as a highly polarised society remains unclear.
Much of the Eisenkot bloc’s campaign, and by extension its vote, rested upon opposition to the de facto exemption from military service offered by the Likud-led government to the Haredi parties in return for their support in the Knesset. Rivalling the pressure to extend the draft to Israel’s ultra-Orthodox youth were the calls for an independent inquiry into the government’s alleged security failings before the October 7 attack, calls rendered more pressing in light of the reports of the alleged advance warnings given by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt.
“I think it would be very hard to see Eisenkot working with anyone in Netanyahu’s camp because of the ultra-Orthodox draft issue and because of October 7,” said Mairav Zonszein, an analyst with the Crisis Group. “His main demands are a state commission of inquiry and a universal draft for everyone, so he couldn’t work with a lot of the partners there, including Netanyahu,” she added.
“However, Bennett and Lieberman are different stories. Bennett has swerved once before,” she said, referring to him reneging on election promises and working with Ra’am in 2021.
“Lieberman, as much as he hates Netanyahu, is also a very hard-right politician,” she said of the likelihood of Yisrael Beiteinu allying with Likud to prevent any liberal-leaning politics.
For now, though, speculation continues. For some, including Levy, that includes the possibility of the Netanyahu government seeking a military escalation, potentially against Iran, as a pretext to establish an emergency government.
For others, such as Israeli political psychologist Daniel Bar Tal of Tel Aviv University, the future rests upon the more prosaic mathematics of a government coalition.
“It is a very challenging moment in the history of Israel,” he said, reflecting on the many opportunities to gain power missed by the opposition.
“It is hard to know [what will happen] because the majority of Israelis are rightists, racists, religious and nationalists,” he said, before cutting to the heart of the dilemma faced by many in Israel on the day after the election: “They want change but do not want to cooperate with Arab parties.”

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Kiev is preparing at least 11 Ukrainian cities for 360-degree defense, including Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Kharkov, and Kherson, a pro-Russian underground source told TASS.

And the impasse in which the country now finds itself seems to many to be unsolvable due to the categorical stance of either Zelensky himself or his handlers," they said.

Iranians cut essentials and put dreams on hold as war-hit economy bites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:21:19 UTC
21:21:19 KST

Iranians cut essentials and put dreams on hold as war-hit economy bites
DUBAI, Oct 28 - Iranian families are cutting back on food, housing and education as the eight-month-old war with the United States fuels one of the country's worst inflation surges in decades, eroding incomes and pushing households to the brink.
The strain is being felt far beyond the country's major cities. Workers say wages no longer cover basic expenses, while businesses face rising costs and weakening demand as families spend most of their budgets on food, rent and other necessities.
The conflict, triggered by US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and followed by Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf, has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
Reuters spoke to more than two dozen people across Iran from different social and economic backgrounds who said worsening conditions had left them struggling to afford food, housing, healthcare and education.
"We have no money, no future and no hope. We're tired of living in fear, fear of another US attack and fear of not being able to make ends meet at the end of every month," said Mohammadali, a 47-year-old shopkeeper and father of two in the northeastern city of Mashhad.
Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh on Tuesday apologised for the mounting cost-of-living pressures facing Iranians, state media reported, saying pensioners, workers and civil servants were bearing the brunt of soaring prices and high inflation.
Iran's inflation surge has shown little sign of easing. Consumer prices in September were nearly 90% higher than a year earlier, while annual inflation accelerated to 73.6%, according to official data and figures reported by state media.
Food prices have risen even faster. The cost of food and beverages was 121.8% higher than a year ago, forcing many families to cut spending elsewhere.
PRICES OUTPACE PAYCHECKS, JOBS DRY UP
For Mahmoud, a 44-year-old government employee in the central city of Isfahan, the gap between wages and living costs widens every month.
"With my salary of less than $100, you can survive only for 10 days ... My wife and I lie to our daughters all the time when they ask for a toy or new clothes," he said.
Official estimates put the minimum monthly cost of living for a three-person working-class family at around $336, more than three times the average monthly wage of roughly $92 at the free-market exchange rate.
As wages fail to keep pace with inflation, many families have exhausted savings, cut consumption or borrowed money to cover daily expenses. Government-mandated pay increases have been swiftly overtaken by rising prices.
For many Iranians, the challenge is no longer preserving their standard of living but avoiding financial collapse.
"We had to move to my parents' house last month because my husband got laid off from a small tile factory in May. We spent all our savings. But my husband is still jobless and we could no longer afford rent," said Hamideh, a 39-year-old mother of two in the northern city of Rasht.
Rising housing costs have added to the squeeze on family budgets. Rents in September were 32.8% higher than a year earlier, while housing, utilities and fuel costs were up nearly 38%, according to official data.
The pressure extends to the labour market. The official unemployment rate climbed to 9.1% in the spring, up 1.8 percentage points from a year earlier. The economic participation rate fell to 40.7%, indicating fewer working-age Iranians were employed or actively seeking work. Nearly a quarter of young people aged 15 to 24 are unemployed.
"I have been looking for work since graduating in advertising, but after months of searching I've started to lose hope. Companies are cutting budgets, not hiring. Most of my classmates are either unemployed or working in fields unrelated to what they studied," said 23-year-old Firouzeh, who lives with her parents in the northwestern city of Urmia.
STUDYING ABROAD A DISTANT DREAM
The weakening rial is also closing off opportunities once seen as pathways to upward mobility. Iran's currency has lost more than half its value over the past year, putting overseas education beyond the reach of many families.
"Both my parents are government employees. Their dream was to send me abroad to become a medical doctor. But after two years studying in Turkey, I could not pay the tuition for this year and I am returning home," said Shahriyar, 25, in Istanbul. He said several of his friends were in the same situation.
Washington's expanded sanctions, announced on August 24 as part of "Operation Economic Outcast" and aimed at cutting Tehran's funding for the war, have added to the economic strain on ordinary Iranians, analysts said.
Businesses are under pressure. Sanctions and war-related disruptions have increased the cost of imports and restricted access to foreign currency and raw materials, while retailers and small businesses face higher operating costs just as demand weakens, threatening revenues and jobs.
For Iran's rulers, the challenge is maintaining essential imports and public services while financing a costly conflict. Central Bank Governor Abdolnasser Hemmati said in mid-October that US claims Iran's economy was collapsing were "an illusion".
The deterioration in living standards also presents a growing political challenge for the authorities, who remain wary that worsening economic conditions could reignite nationwide unrest.
Economic grievances have fuelled repeated waves of protests in recent years, leaving officials sensitive to signs that war, inflation and rising unemployment are further eroding public patience.
The clerical establishment responded to previous outbreaks of unrest with a sweeping crackdown that, according to Iranian officials and rights groups, killed thousands in January. REUTERS

The Army will procure a Heavy Wheeled Recovery Vehicle to recover Boxer in the field, the order remains at 623 vehicles with more than five hundred being built in Britain, and seventy two Boxer RCH artillery vehicles are being bought, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked how Boxer will be repaired in the field given that no repair and recovery variant has been ordered.
Luke Pollard MP said: “Boxer is a world-class vehicle that will boost our soldiers in a variety of military missions and scenarios across the globe. As I said in Parliament on 19 October 2026, the programme is hugely successful, delivering important capability and national benefit.

He also set out that Boxers currently recover one another peer to peer, backed where needed by the Support Vehicle (Recovery) and the Challenger Armoured Repair and Recovery Vehicle.
The RCH 155 is the wheeled self-propelled gun built on the Boxer drive module, pairing the artillery turret developed by Krauss-Maffei Wegmann with the vehicle already in British service. Seventy two of them will replace the AS90 in the close support artillery role.
All 623 Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard, and ministers confirmed last week that a planned third batch is no longer being pursued through the Boxer programme, a decision that cannot be tied to a single date because it was taken as part of the work on the Defence Investment Plan.

South Korea and the US have delayed a key bilateral security dialogue to next year amid Seoul’s demand that the Pentagon return wartime operational control of South Korean forces.
The decision to postpone the annual Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) came during a maiden meeting between US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul, who met in Cebu City of the Philippines.
They are attending the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, which also brings together the defense chiefs of China, Japan, Australia, and India, although Beijing this year did not send its defense minister.

Kang and Hegseth will, however, meet again in Washington, DC, in December, the statement added.
The annual SCM is usually held in late October or early November.
"Seoul seeks to regain wartime OPCON (operational control) before the Lee Jae Myung administration's five-year term ends in 2030, pushing to announce a target year for the OPCON transfer at the upcoming SCM," Yonhap News reported.
South Korea hosts around 39,000 American soldiers under a mutual defense treaty, and the administration of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has committed to restoring command over the forces by the end of his term in 2030.
Hegseth “reaffirmed the United States' commitment to the wartime operational control transition, and both ministers agreed to closely cooperate to ensure the transition proceeds smoothly at the right time,” said the statement.

Russian satellites have consistently appeared in the skies above facilities in Saudi Arabia that Iranian-backed Houthis and Iraqi militia groups have struck with missiles and drones over the past several months, the Associated Press reported Tuesday.
Nawaf Obaid, founder of the Geneva-based firm AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence, told the news agency that he and his colleagues tracked 72 Russian military and government satellites between July and October, finding them orbiting above Saudi sites before and after they were attacked.
“What we found is a 100% match,” Obaid said.
The targeted facilities include Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, which was forced to shut down immediately after it was attacked in September.
Another example is the Kind Fahd Air Base. When the base was attacked last month, an Italian fighter jet was struck while a nearby Saudi aircraft was left unscathed.
Obaid said the apparent precision of the strike on Kind Fahd suggests vital intelligence is being collected and transferred for Houthi and Iraqi militia targeting, given that the groups lack sophisticated reconnaissance capabilities on their own.
An official briefed on Saudi investigations into the recent attacks told AP that evidence showed Russian satellites were being used for targeting. A senior Houthi official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Iranian military advisers are directly providing the Russian reconnaissance information.
Moscow is one of Tehran’s closest partners and has repeatedly condemned the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. In 2025, the two countries signed a strategic partnership agreement that includes provisions for countering shared threats.
American officials, including President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have sought to minimize a growing number of reports that Russia is actively helping Iran target U.S. forces in the Middle East.
Trump claimed last week that Russia is “doing very little, if anything” to help Iran in the war. That came as President Vladimir Putin reiterated that Russia is ready to play a mediating role in ending the conflict.

Hegseth and Koizumi agree on new Japanese missile production line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:18:24 UTC
21:18:24 KST

- Japan and the United States agreed on Oct. 28 to build an AMRAAM air-to-air missile final assembly plant in Japan.
- Defense chiefs Shinjiro Koizumi and Pete Hegseth also agreed to share technical data to expand SM-3 Block IIA interceptor production.
Japan will host a final assembly plant for the AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile after Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth agreed on Oct. 28 to build the facility as part of joint U.S.-Japanese missile production, Nikkei reported.
The two met for about 30 minutes in Cebu, the Philippines, on the sidelines of an expanded meeting of Southeast Asian defense ministers. The facility, known as a final assembly and check-out plant, or FACO, is where completed components are put together into finished missiles and tested before delivery, Financial News reported, citing the Asahi Shimbun and NHK. Hegseth welcomed Japan’s work to strengthen its defense production base, and the two sides also agreed to expand joint exercises, including live-fire drills.
The ministers also agreed to share technical information to expand production of the SM-3 Block IIA, a ship-launched interceptor that destroys ballistic missiles in space, Nikkei reported. The Japanese side said Hegseth did not press for a specific increase in Japan’s defense budget, and the Defense Ministry said the talks were not held with any particular amount or outcome in mind.
The AMRAAM is a radar-guided missile that fighters fire at enemy aircraft beyond visual range, and it guides itself to the target after launch, so the pilot can turn away or engage another threat. It arms U.S. and allied F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 fighters, including the F-35s that Japan is buying, and it also serves as the main interceptor for the ground-based NASAMS air defense system. Raytheon builds the missile in the United States and in February agreed with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual AMRAAM production to at least 1,900.
The plant would take a years-long effort a step further. The United States and Japan first agreed in July 2024 to explore joint production of the AMRAAM and the PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptor, and Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency then ran a feasibility study with Mitsubishi Electric and Raytheon. In April, the two governments identified circuit card assembly, the production of the missile’s electronic boards, as part of Japan’s share, with a final assembly plant in Japan raised as a possibility, Mitsubishi Electric said. Japan is also a major AMRAAM customer: in January 2025, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of up to 1,200 AIM-120D-3 and AIM-120C-8 missiles to Japan, valued at an estimated $3.64 billion.
The SM-3 Block IIA has a longer history as a shared program. Raytheon and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries developed it jointly, and it entered full-rate production in 2024. In March, the two governments agreed to quadruple production of the interceptor in Japan, and Japan now pays for a large share of new orders, covering nearly half the immediate funding in a $745 million contract for SM-3 Block IIA missiles awarded this summer.
During the meeting, Koizumi briefed Hegseth on Japan’s plan to revise its three main national security documents by the end of 2026. He said Japan would strengthen what it calls denial defense, the ability to stop an invading force from succeeding, along with deterrence intended to discourage an attack in the first place. The ministers also agreed to step up cooperation against cyberattacks, The Japan Times reported.

The prospect of seeing the architect of Israel’s genocide of the Palestinian people, Benjamin Netanyahu, ousted from political office would be a small, albeit completely pyrrhic, ‘victory’. This is a politician who has spent the past three years justifying industrial-scale levels of civilian slaughter, the enforced starvation of an entire civilian population and the complete levelling of the Gaza Strip. He has been the public face of Israel on the global stage for the best part of 20 years, rubbing shoulders with world leaders and garnering support for the expansion of Israel’s settler colonial mission in historic Palestine.
As something of a political cockroach, he has managed to survive various high-profile scandals. These include criminal proceedings brought against him on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, and a (largely symbolic) arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court, one that he and leaders in the West have completely ignored. Nevertheless, it seems that Netanyahu has become increasingly awakened to the fact that his time may well be running out. He turned to his X account to post an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb hitting downtown Tel Aviv in an ever so subtle effort to stir up feelings of existential dread amongst an Israeli public who have fully drunk the anti-Iranian Kool-Aid.
Waiting in the wings to take over could be former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. He is a man said to be fervently against Palestinian statehood and fully committed to the destruction of Hamas. His ‘achievements’ include the creation of the ‘Dahiya Doctrine’, a policy born of the 2006 Lebanon war that promotes the use of extraordinary and excessive military force against civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Whilst there can be no doubt that the Zionist project of expansion and the associated erasure of Palestinians have been moving at warp speed since 2023, those who are watching the Israeli elections from afar (including many in the activist community) and hoping for change would do well to adopt a longer gaze.
It has never really mattered who is in charge in Israel. The policies that undergird decades of relentless genocide and ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians have, over the years, largely remained the same. Political commentators euphemistically throw around terms like ‘hawk’ and ‘dove’ to provide the illusion that there is even the slightest possibility an Israeli leader is remotely interested in ‘peace’. But the terms are meaningless, and as with everything in the region, Israeli leaders’ actions speak louder than hollow words.
READ: Trump claims his endorsement helped Netanyahu perform better than expected in Israeli election
Take, for example, the tenure of Yitzhak Rabin: winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, architect of the ‘break their bones’ policy (sounds peaceful, right?) and the person responsible for signing the Oslo Accords. Under his watch, Palestine continued to be subjected to the scourge of relentless settlement expansion and the house demolitions that went with it. ‘Peace’ for Rabin was far removed from ending the occupation. Instead, it meant managing and containing the Palestinian population and their legitimate demands for self-determination, whilst subscribing to a ‘peace’ plan that outsourced responsibility for the occupation to a subservient Palestinian Authority and willing accomplices in the West.
Then there is the chameleonic Shimon Peres, a man who enjoyed adulation amongst many in the West. They would do well to google the Qana massacre in southern Lebanon, an abhorrent act of barbarity that he once famously said he was at ‘peace’ with (no pun intended). See also Ehud Olmert, who, whilst being relatively outspoken against the ongoing genocide in Gaza (not using that language, of course), oversaw the targeted assassination of Palestinian leaders, the 2006 war in Lebanon and the continued expansion of illegal Israeli settlements. Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak was threatened with arrest whilst visiting the UK in 2009 over allegations of war crimes committed in Gaza while he was defence minister. Others, including Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, have made it very clear that they have little to no interest in making ‘peace’ with Palestinians, nor even in countenancing the notion that there would ever be a Palestinian state.
What should be abundantly clear, therefore, is that for Palestinians, as Elaine Bradley and I have previously argued, the passing of time can be mapped on to a series of failed ‘peace’ processes, from Madrid to Oslo to Wye River to Camp David. The consistent theme has been the creeping erasure of Palestine and a doubling down of the West’s support for Israel’s expansive settler colonial aims.
I don’t say any of this whimsically, but those who are advocating for Palestine must be far more critical in their analysis than simply hoping for change based on the possible downfall of Netanyahu.
If you are committed to Palestinian liberation, you must shun any false ‘hope’ that comes with the appointment of a new political leader in Israel. It is a mirage and an unhelpful distraction. No matter who is in charge, without a fundamental reckoning with the racist ideology that undergirds the Zionist state-building project and a full dismantling of the architectures of militarisation and apartheid, things will continue along the same path. Our role, therefore, is not to place any false hope in a change of leadership inside Israel, but to double down on our efforts to ensure we do all at our disposal to support inevitable Palestinian liberation.

Factbox-Spain’s deadliest train disasters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:16:23 CET
21:16:23 KST

Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 30 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided south of Toledo in Spain on Wednesday, regional authorities said.
It is the second deadly accident in less than a year on the line and will likely raise further questions over the country’s train infrastructure ahead of November’s snap election.
Here are some of Spain’s deadliest train disasters, starting from the most recent:
ADAMUZ (2026)
Forty six people died and more than 120 were injured in southern Spain after a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming one on January 18 near Adamuz, in the province of Cordoba.
The accident is still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
SANTIAGO DE COMPOSTELA (2013)
A railway accident in the summer of 2013 left 80 people dead and 145 injured when an eight-carriage high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend near the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela, slamming into a concrete wall and bursting into flames.
A Transport Ministry commission concluded that the accident was caused by speeding and the driver being distracted by a call from a superior, but a victims’ association blamed the accident not only on human error but also on the railway’s security systems.
MADRID COMMUTER TRAIN BOMBINGS (2004)
On March 11, 2004, 10 backpack bombs detonated on four Cercanias commuter trains, killing 193 people and injuring thousands of others during Madrid’s rush hour. The attacks were carried out by Islamists opposing Spain’s participation in the Iraq war.
EL CUERVO (1972)
An accident caused by a head-on collision between two trains on the Cadiz-Seville route left 86 people dead and more than 150 injured near the southern town of El Cuervo in 1972. The accident was caused by a driver’s failure to stop at a red light at El Cuervo station, according to an investigation by state-owned rail operator Renfe.
URDULIZ (1970)
A head-on collision of two trains killed 33 people in the town of Urduliz, near the northern city of Bilbao, in the summer of 1970. A stationmaster was initially blamed for the accident, but it later emerged that he had been working 16-hour shifts for the previous four days.
GRISEN (1965)
A train on the Madrid-Barcelona route caught fire in 1965 in the town of Grisen, near northeastern Zaragoza, killing dozens of passengers. Though the train operator said at the time that 30 people died, later reports have said the real death toll was up to 80 and that the Francoist leadership tried to play it down.
TORRE DEL BIERZO (1944)
The 1944 crash of three trains in the El Bierzo region of León province is considered one of the deadliest railway disasters in Spain, with the estimated death toll of 78 still being debated due to censorship under Francisco Franco.
A train travelling from Madrid to A Coruña suffered a brake failure and collided with a locomotive inside a tunnel, just before a third train entered the same gallery and crashed into the wreckage.
(Compiled by Mirko Miorelli and Javi West Larrañaga in Gdansk; Editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak and Alison Williams)

Reuters, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Sea drones struck a container ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on Wednesday, the ship’s owner and the government said, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised concerns about the growing scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on the Greek ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ), or what the vessel’s 421 containers were carrying.
“A container ship was hit…with three naval drones, approximately 21 miles southeast of Shabla,” Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters on the sidelines of a regional security meeting.

The ship’s owner, Contships Management, confirmed the attack and a company official said all the crew of 14 Filippinos and 4 Ukrainians, were safe and ashore.
A maritime security source with knowledge of the matter said the ship had been badly damaged and was listing.
INTERNATIONAL CONCERN
Drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria have likely killed some two dozen international seafarers in recent weeks, according to government statements on missing crew members. At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
The strikes have been in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, an area that stretches beyond Bulgaria’s waters but where the country holds sole rights to explore and manage resources.
The attacks have prompted international condemnation and concern about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Ukraine has blamed the attacks on Russia and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appear to benefit Russia, but Moscow has denied involvement.
In a sign of the international concern, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler warned Russia and Ukraine on Wednesday against carrying out attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. He said Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes.

Japanese navy shadows Russian Vishnya-class spy ship near Tsushima
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:12:05 UTC
21:12:05 KST

- A Russian Vishnya-class intelligence ship, hull number 535, sailed southwest through the Tsushima Strait toward the East China Sea on Oct. 27 and 28.
- Japan tracked the ship with the minesweeper Hirashima and a P-1 maritime patrol aircraft, the Joint Staff Office said.
A Russian Navy intelligence-gathering ship sailed southwest through the Tsushima Strait between Japan and South Korea on Oct. 27 and 28 and headed into the East China Sea, Japan’s Joint Staff Office said.
The Joint Staff identified the vessel as a Vishnya-class intelligence collection ship and released a map showing its hull number, 535. That number belongs to the Kareliya, a signals intelligence ship of Russia’s Pacific Fleet based in Vladivostok. Japan’s Maritime Self-Defense Force tracked it with the minesweeper Hirashima of the 3rd Mine Warfare Squadron, based in Sasebo, and a P-1 maritime patrol aircraft of Fleet Air Wing 4 flying from Atsugi.
The map shows the Kareliya passing east of Tsushima Island, which sits in the middle of the strait, before continuing southwest past the Goto Islands off Kyushu toward the open waters of the East China Sea. The Joint Staff did not say whether the ship entered Japan’s territorial waters or contiguous zone, the band of sea up to 24 nautical miles (44 km) from the coast, during the transit.
Vishnya-class ships, known in Russia as Project 864, are built to collect radio, radar and other electronic signals, letting the Russian Navy listen in on military communications and map the sensors of foreign forces. Poland’s Stocznia Północna shipyard in Gdańsk built seven of them for the Soviet Navy in the 1980s, and all remain in Russian service. The 91.5 m (300-foot) ships have a top speed of about 16 knots.
The Kareliya is a familiar sight to the Japanese military. In January, Japan tracked it as it passed through the contiguous zones around Yonaguni and Miyako Islands before heading into the Pacific, and in February 2025 Japan reported that it spent more than a week operating near Okinawa and Kyushu. The ship has also operated far from Japan, including off Hawaii, where it was spotted in 2021 13 nautical miles west of Kauai, home to the U.S. Navy’s Pacific Missile Range Facility.
The Tsushima Strait is one of the main routes Russian Pacific Fleet ships use to sail between the Sea of Japan and the East China Sea, and Japan publishes a release each time it detects a Russian or Chinese warship passing through the waterways around its islands. The ship was commissioned in 1986 and returned to the fleet in 2017 after a three-year repair and upgrade.

- Summary:
- Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released.
- Share:
Fire salamanders are among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black and yellow coloring and the poisonous substances they release to deter predators. Despite their familiar appearance, scientists are still uncovering surprising details about their biology. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as "vulnerable" on its Red List of Threatened Species. Fire salamanders typically inhabit damp forests, streams, and mountainous regions, where habitat destruction and fragmentation increasingly threaten their survival.
New research has revealed that fire salamanders possess an unexpected ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The glow is most pronounced on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. Researchers traced the fluorescence primarily to glands in the animals' skin and the substances those glands release. Remarkably, these secretions can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after leaving the salamander's body.
"It is fascinating that such a well-studied species still harbors unknown phenomena like this. It reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools," says Bernat Burriel, a researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona and the study's first author.
The phenomenon occurs when compounds in the salamander's skin absorb ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see, and reemit that energy as visible light. This process produces vivid green and cyan colors. Known as biofluorescence, it requires an outside source of illumination and should not be confused with bioluminescence. Animals such as fireflies produce their own light through chemical reactions, while fluorescent organisms must first absorb light from their surroundings.
Scientists once believed that biofluorescence occurred almost exclusively in marine organisms, with scorpions standing out as an unusual example on land. More recent studies have challenged that assumption, identifying fluorescent properties in a growing variety of terrestrial animals, including reptiles, birds, and amphibians.
Why Do Fire Salamanders Glow?
Although researchers have confirmed that fire salamanders fluoresce, the biological purpose of this ability remains uncertain. One possibility is that the glow serves as a form of communication, helping individuals recognize one another or assess potential mates. Another is that it makes their warning coloration more noticeable to predators.
"Fluorescence meets several criteria that suggest a communicative function. It could help salamanders detect each other in nocturnal or particularly dense environments, or act as an additional defense signal," says Martin Kaltenpoth, director of the Department of Insect Symbiosis at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-author of the study.
The discovery that toxic skin secretions are also fluorescent raises additional questions about how salamanders interact with predators and other animals in their environment.
For now, these proposed functions remain hypotheses. Animals with particularly sensitive vision may be able to detect the green and cyan fluorescence even when it is extremely faint. Humans, however, need a UV lamp to observe the effect.
In the forests where fire salamanders live, nighttime illumination comes primarily from moonlight and starlight. Researchers note that full moonlight contains a greater proportion of ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight, which has a more evenly distributed spectrum. Under these conditions, fluorescence could create small green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings, potentially making them easier for other salamanders to spot.
Could the Fluorescent Glow Warn Predators?
Another possible explanation involves aposematism, a defensive strategy in which animals display conspicuous colors to advertise that they are poisonous or otherwise dangerous. Fire salamanders already use their distinctive yellow and black patterns as warning signals, and fluorescence might provide an additional visual cue.
Scientists established a connection between salamander warning colors and chemical defenses more than a century ago when they identified samandarines. These highly toxic steroidal alkaloids are produced from cholesterol precursors and contribute to the animals' chemical protection.
Despite decades of research into salamander toxins and skin chemistry, the newly observed fluorescence came as a surprise.
"The presence of this fluorescent compound was surprising because salamander skin secretions have been studied chemically for decades, and we were unaware of any published reports on fluorescence," says Andrés Brunetti, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-first author of the study.
The Mysterious Chemical Behind the Glow
One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns the substance responsible for the fluorescence. Researchers have not yet determined its chemical identity, although the evidence suggests it may be a molecule not previously recognized in fire salamanders.
"We still don't know what the compound responsible for this fluorescence is, but everything indicates that it is a molecule unknown until now in this species. Identifying it will be key to understanding its origin and function," adds Salvador Carranza, a researcher at the IBE (CSIC-UPF) and another co-author of the study.
The team is now working to identify and chemically characterize potential compounds responsible for the effect. Determining which molecule produces the glow could help explain how the fluorescence develops and whether it plays a meaningful role in salamander behavior or survival.
A New Discovery With Implications for Amphibian Conservation
Beyond revealing an unexpected feature of a familiar species, the findings demonstrate how new research techniques can uncover biological traits that have escaped scientific attention for decades.
Understanding whether fluorescence influences communication, mating, or predator avoidance could also contribute to conservation efforts. Such information may help researchers better understand the behavior and ecological needs of fire salamanders, which already face significant threats from habitat loss and fragmentation.
The research also involved scientists from the Institute of Subtropical Biology and the Catalan Society of Herpetology. It forms part of a pioneering amphibian conservation project in Catalonia supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.

Glandular biofluorescence in fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra): first evidence and ecological implications. Royal Society Open Science, 2026; 13 (5) DOI: 10.1098/rsos.251991

Drones Set Fire to One of Russia’s Largest Chemical Plants Linked to Military Explosives

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Drones Set Fire to One of Russia’s Largest Chemical Plants Linked to Military Explosives
A drone attack sparked a fire at the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, Russia’s Tula region, overnight on October 28. The facility is one of Russia’s largest producers of nitrogen fertilizers and has supplied chemicals to a manufacturer of military explosives.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage published by the monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 28 showed flames at the industrial complex following the attack. Analysis of the available images suggested that the AM-70 ammonia production unit may have been struck.
Tula region Governor Dmitry Milyaev confirmed a drone attack on the region and reported damage to infrastructure in Novomoskovsk’s industrial zone. However, he did not specify which facilities were affected.
The Azot plant belongs to the EuroChem group and produces ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, methanol, and other industrial chemicals. Its products are used in agriculture and chemical manufacturing, while some also serve as raw materials for explosives production.
According to OSINT Varta, the facility produces nitric acid and ammonium nitrate, chemicals used in both civilian industries and the manufacture of explosives and ammunition.
Between February 2022 and September 2024, the Novomoskovsk plant supplied nearly 5,000 metric tons of nitric acid to the Sverdlov Plant in Dzerzhinsk, Nizhny Novgorod region, according to Ukrainian intelligence data.
The Sverdlov facility produces RDX and HMX, two high explosives widely used in military ammunition and other weapons systems.
The attack followed a series of Ukrainian strikes against Russian military infrastructure. On October 27, Ukraine’s General Staff reported that its forces had targeted ammunition depots, military equipment, supply facilities, and troop concentrations across the Luhansk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions on October 26–27. The extent of the damage was not disclosed.

No decision on Palantir role in targeting network
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:10:50 GMT
21:10:50 KST

Palantir products are used across the defence digital and data ecosystem and that is expected to continue in some form, but no decisions have been taken on which parts of the Digital Targeting Web the company will provide, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked which element of the Digital Targeting Web will be provided by Palantir, referring to the strategic partnership announced in September last year.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “Palantir products are currently used in the defence digital and data ecosystem, and this is expected to continue in some form. However, no decisions have been made on future consumption of Palantir products and services for the Digital Targeting Web. The process for industry to engage with the Digital Targeting Web is via the Challenge Book which runs a fully open and transparent assessment and selection process for potential candidate products.”
The Digital Targeting Web is the programme intended to connect sensors, decision making and weapons across the services so that a target found by one platform can be engaged by another. Pollard told Parliament last week that the department intends to invest up to £1.8 billion in it over four years, with £266 million allocated for the current financial year, £352 million for 2027-28 and £1,213 million for the two years after, and that the profile is being refined in the planning round now under way.
In a separate answer, Pollard said no assessment has yet been made of British integration with NATO’s Maven Smart System, which reached full technical operating capability in June, because work in the integration space is continuing. Maven Smart System is the alliance’s artificial intelligence targeting and decision support tool, built on technology from Palantir.

Two Convicted Russian Killers Caught Trying to Hide in Ukraine’s Capital
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detained two Russian soldiers previously convicted of murder after they deserted their positions on the front lines, changed into civilian clothing, and attempted to reach Kyiv, where they reportedly planned to hide with relatives.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the SBU on October 28, the two men served under contract with Russia’s 291st Motorized Rifle Regiment of the Southern Military District. Ukrainian counterintelligence officers intercepted them at a checkpoint near the border between the Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
Both soldiers were traveling in civilian clothes in a vehicle they had stopped while hitchhiking. During the inspection, security officers discovered a Russian military identification tag around the neck of one of the detainees.
Investigators established that one of the men was a resident of temporary occupied Dovzhansk in Ukraine’s Luhansk region who had been convicted of murder twice.
He had reportedly fought against Ukrainian forces since 2016 and later participated in battles near Bakhmut following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, serving as an assistant gunner for an anti-tank missile system.
The second detainee was a Russian citizen who signed a military contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry while serving a prison sentence for murder.
According to the SBU, both men had recently been deployed to assault Ukrainian positions in the Kramatorsk sector of the front. However, they abandoned their positions and entered a settlement in the contested gray zone between Russian and Ukrainian forces.
There, the soldiers reportedly found civilian clothing inside an abandoned house, buried their Russian military uniforms and issued weapons, and continued on foot toward a nearby town.
During their journey, they persuaded a passing driver to take them to Dnipro, from where they intended to travel onward to Kyiv. Their journey ended when Ukrainian security officers detained them at a checkpoint before they could reach Dnipro.
In a separate case, Ukraine’s Security Service reported on October 15 that a Russian soldier who fled his positions and changed into civilian clothes was charged with killing five unarmed Ukrainian servicemen and a civilian in the Kharkiv region. He faces life imprisonment if convicted.

Spain High-Speed Train Collision Kills 64, Injures Over 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:10:28 UTC
21:10:28 KST

A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 64 people and injured scores more on Wednesday, with the toll likely to rise, authorities said in one of Europe’s deadliest such disasters this century.
AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another after the second such accident to strike Spain this year.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Some carriages were lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment, while dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site.
“We are speaking of approximately 64 (dead), but this is probably going to grow even more,” Castilla-La Mancha’s leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene, raising a previous toll of 31.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.
Helicopters hovered above the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.
State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
Iryo said in a statement that its train, which was carrying 147 passengers and five staff including the driver, “was hit from behind” by the Renfe service.
Cyberattack Hits Spanish Train Operator User Data
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, 49, who lives in the nearby village of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz added that the passengers of the Iryo told him their train was stationary when the collision happened, describing a “horrific, horrible” scene that “smelled of an accident, of metal”.
- Rail safety under scrutiny -
The accident comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year’s first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.
Sanchez’s office said he was heading to the scene. The premier had said on X that he was “shocked” by the accident and sent “my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families”.
Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was “shocked and concerned” by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
An EU spokeswoman said the bloc was “ready to help Spain if needed”, while European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” with the victims after the “devastating news”.
The Spanish football federation postponed 24 matches in the first round of the Copa del Rey “as a mark of respect and solidarity”.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world’s second-largest after China and a source of national pride.
But Wednesday’s accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country’s railways.
That crash was Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year’s accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.
The cause of the latest disaster, which happened on a straight stretch of track in sunny, dry conditions, was unknown. Five people wearing white overalls were examining the tracks and taking photographs, AFP saw.
One of the country’s busiest routes, it was Spain’s first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition.

JERUSALEM, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Senior Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi confirmed Wednesday that the Joint List, an alliance of Arab-led parties, is in talks with the bloc opposing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the formation of an alternative government following Tuesday's parliamentary election.
The Joint List is a political alliance of Arab-majority parties in Israel, comprising Ta'al, Balad, and Hadash.
In an interview with Israel's state-owned Kan Reshet Bet Radio, Tibi, chairman of the Ta'al party, said the Joint List was ready to help the so-called "change bloc" replace Netanyahu, although it was unlikely to formally join a governing coalition.
"We have blocked the possibility of Netanyahu forming a government," Tibi said, referring to the election results. "Our public wants us to go further and influence the shape of the political system after the elections."
Tibi said the alliance was open to discussing parliamentary arrangements, including how and when its lawmakers would vote, in exchange for progress on issues affecting Israel's Arab minority, including crime, house demolitions, infrastructure and incitement.
"We will probably not be an organic part of this government," he said, adding that other arrangements were possible.
Yair Golan, leader of the center-left Democrats party, which is part of the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Golan wrote on social media platform X.
Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List, also expressed willingness to help Eisenkot replace Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a real alternative to Netanyahu's bloodstained government will have to talk to us," Jabareen said in a statement. "We are ready to pave the way for Netanyahu's removal."
These remarks came as vote counting continued after an election that appeared to leave neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the rival bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
With about 77 percent of the votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 54 seats in the 120-seat parliament, compared with 49 for Eisenkot's bloc, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee, which oversees the election. The Joint List and the Muslim Ra'am party were projected to win a combined 17 seats, with 11 going to the Joint List.
The Joint List could play a decisive role in efforts to form a government, potentially by providing parliamentary support from outside the coalition. However, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have previously ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, complicating efforts to assemble a majority. ■

Meet Kolibri Advance—Ukraine’s FPV Drone That Uses AI to Find and Follow Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:10:18 UTC
21:10:18 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Meet Kolibri Advance—Ukraine’s FPV Drone That Uses AI to Find and Follow Targets
Ukrainian defense manufacturer TAF Industries has launched a new version of its Kolibri 10” FPV drone equipped with AURA AI, an artificial-intelligence targeting system.
This system is capable of detecting, identifying, locking onto, and tracking targets even when GPS or communications are disrupted, RBC-Ukraine reported on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new Kolibri 10” Advance uses an AURA AI module developed by DOD Solution. The system can identify both moving and stationary targets and assist the operator throughout the attack.
Once the AI detects and locks onto a target, the pilot confirms the engagement. AURA AI can then continue tracking the target and handle the terminal guidance itself.
That reduces the pilot’s workload and allows the drone to continue its mission in environments where GPS is unavailable, electronic warfare is active, or the communications link becomes weak or disappears entirely.
“The automatic terminal-guidance module from DOD Solution recognizes targets, increasing the drone’s level of autonomy using AI. This function primarily helps pilots see all potential threats and targets by outlining them with a rectangle. Essentially, the AI module highlights targets the pilot might have missed,” said Andrii Atamanenko, Product Owner for FPV drones at TAF Industries.
According to Atamanenko, the system can also distinguish between different classes of vehicles, further reducing the cognitive burden on the drone operator.
The Kolibri 10” Advance with AURA AI has already been used by Ukraine’s 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade and the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
AURA AI runs on a custom single-board computer developed by DOD Solution specifically for artificial-intelligence algorithms aboard FPV drones. Physically, the computer is installed as an additional board within the drone’s electronics stack.
TAF Industries said integrating AURA AI into a new drone platform typically takes about one to two weeks. Integration with the Kolibri Advance took longer because the collaboration involved additional preparation and testing beyond simply installing the module.
Previously, reports emerged that the number of successful strikes on Russian targets using AI-powered auto-homing drone technology has increased tenfold since the start of the year.

====================================================================================================

The 82nd anniversary of the expulsion of the Nazi occupiers from Ukraine: history, cost, and the present day
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:09:59 EET
21:09:59 KST

The 82nd anniversary of the expulsion of the Nazi occupiers from Ukraine: history, cost, and the present day
Kyiv • UNN
On October 28, Ukraine commemorates the expulsion of the Nazis, although the fighting continued until November. The war claimed approximately 8 million lives.
On October 28, Ukraine marks the 82nd anniversary of the expulsion of the Nazi occupiers. In 1944, the Red Army’s offensive was coming to an end along the western borders of present-day Ukraine. However, the historical trials for our people did not end there. Fighting continued in November, millions of Ukrainians did not survive World War II, and the return of Soviet rule not only postponed the achievement of independence.
UNN explains today how the Nazis were expelled, why historians have doubts about October 28 as the date, and what price Ukraine paid.
The commemorative date was established by a 2009 decree of President Viktor Yushchenko under the official name "Day of Liberation of Ukraine from Fascist Invaders." However, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINM) recommends a different wording — "the expulsion of the Nazi occupiers from Ukraine." They explain that this more accurately describes the events, since the disappearance of the Nazi occupation administration did not bring political freedom to Ukrainians.
How the Nazi troops were expelled from Ukraine
World War II began on September 1, 1939, with Germany’s attack on Poland. Part of the Ukrainian lands was already in the combat zone at that time. In June 1941, Nazi Germany attacked the USSR. Over the following year, German troops and their allies occupied the entire territory of present-day Ukraine. The establishment of the occupation regime was accompanied by mass executions, forced labor, looting, and the destruction of entire settlements.
The Red Army’s first attempts to launch a counteroffensive ended in failure. After the defeats of Soviet troops near Kharkiv and in Crimea in 1942, the situation remained critical. The turning point came in 1943. Following the Battles of Stalingrad and Kursk, Soviet forces launched a large-scale offensive. On August 23, 1943, Nazi troops were finally driven out of Kharkiv; in the autumn, the Battle of the Dnipro began, and on November 6, the Red Army captured Kyiv.
In 1944, the fighting moved to Right-Bank Ukraine, the south, and the west of the country. The Dnipro–Carpathian offensive opened the way to the western regions; on April 10, the Nazis were expelled from Odesa, and in May, the fighting for Crimea ended. On July 27, Soviet troops entered Lviv. In the autumn, the offensive continued in Zakarpattia: on October 27, they occupied Uzhhorod, and the following day reached Chop.
Millions of Ukrainians took part in the defeat of Nazi Germany. They served in the Red Army and the armies of other states of the anti-Hitler coalition, and operated in underground and partisan units. A separate chapter was the struggle of members of the Ukrainian liberation movement, including the UPA, who opposed the Nazi occupation while also seeking to establish an independent state.
Why October 28 is considered the day of liberation
October 28 is often presented as the day the Nazis were finally expelled. However, according to the UINM, on that day in 1944 Soviet troops merely reached Chop and began fighting for the city. In some parts of Zakarpattia, hostilities continued until November 25–26. Therefore, the date has commemorative significance but does not coincide with the actual completion of the expulsion of the occupiers from the territory of Ukraine within its present-day borders. The confusion is also connected with changes in borders. In 1944, Zakarpattia was not yet part of the Ukrainian SSR: the region was annexed to Soviet Ukraine in 1945 under an agreement with Czechoslovakia. Therefore, October 8 initially appeared in the Soviet tradition, and later the commemoration was linked to the October battles in Zakarpattia.
Despite historians’ debates, Presidential Decree No. 836/2009, which established October 28 as a commemorative day, remains in force.
The price of victory: millions of Ukrainians killed and a devastated country
According to estimates cited by the UINM, Ukraine’s direct human losses in World War II amounted to approximately eight million people: about three million military personnel and five million civilians. It should be noted that this refers to people connected with Ukraine, of various nationalities, not only ethnic Ukrainians. The exact figures remain the subject of historical and demographic research.
The overall demographic losses were even greater. According to estimates published by the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, they amounted to approximately 10.4 million people, including about 2.4 million children who were never born because of the war.
Among the most horrific crimes of the Nazi regime was the Holocaust. In the occupied territory of Ukraine, hundreds of Jewish communities were destroyed, and historians estimate that the number of Jews killed reached approximately 1.5 million. Babyn Yar in Kyiv became one of the symbols of this crime. Roma, prisoners of war and other population groups were also subjected to mass persecution and murder. More than two million people from Ukraine were deported for forced labor in the Third Reich.
The war also destroyed the country’s economic foundation. According to the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, approximately 700 cities, 28,000 villages and 16,000 enterprises were damaged or destroyed as a result of hostilities and punitive operations.
Did the expulsion of the Nazis bring freedom to Ukraine
The removal of the Nazi regime meant the end of its policy of terror in Ukrainian lands. However, Ukraine did not gain state independence. Its territory once again came under the control of the USSR, where one-party dictatorship, censorship and a punitive system remained in place. The return of Soviet rule was accompanied by repression against real and alleged opponents of the regime, as well as checks on former prisoners of war and forced laborers. In May 1944, the Soviet authorities deported the Crimean Tatar people from Crimea. In the western regions, the confrontation with the Ukrainian underground continued, with mass arrests and the expulsion of families. The postwar famine of 1946–1947 brought new human losses.
That is why historians now distinguish between the expulsion of a specific occupier and the liberation of a state. As the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory emphasizes, Ukraine gained the ability to determine its political future independently only after declaring independence on August 24, 1991.
The Second World War and the Russo-Ukrainian War: parallels and differences
After the start of Russian aggression, the history of the Second World War took on new meaning. The occupation of Ukrainian cities, the killing of civilians, the forced displacement of populations and attempts to impose a controlled government recall the danger posed by the violent deprivation of people’s right to their own state.
Russian propaganda actively exploits the memory of victory over Nazism, portraying the current aggression as a fight against alleged "Nazism" in Ukraine. Historians warn against this approach: the memory of the victims of the Second World War cannot serve as a justification for a new invasion.
How Ukraine commemorates those who fell and suffered 82 years later
October 28 remains an official day of remembrance, but its contemporary interpretation is increasingly linked to the stories of specific people.
In Ukraine, military graves and memorials are preserved, archives are studied, family testimonies are collected, and history remembrance lessons and thematic exhibitions are held. The commemoration honors both frontline soldiers who survived and the civilians who were killed, Holocaust victims, "Ostarbeiters" and those who lived through the occupation.
An important part of this work has been the rethinking of Soviet symbols and formulations. The Ukrainian Institute of National Memory emphasizes that the contribution of Ukrainians to the victory over Nazism can be remembered without reproducing the myth of a single "victor people" and without concealing the crimes of the Stalinist regime.
In 2026, the anniversary falls during a new war for Ukrainian independence. It reminds us that behind every date on the calendar are people’s lives, and that victory over one occupying regime does not guarantee freedom forever.

Timeline: Major Chinese cultural relics returned from overseas in recent years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:40 CST
21:09:40 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The National Gallery of Australia (NGA) handed over two Chinese cultural relics to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration in Canberra on Wednesday.
The two relics are the head of a military official statue and the head of a civil official statue, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127). According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province.
The following is a timeline of major cultural relics returned to China from overseas in recent years:
Sept. 17, 2026:
-- The United States returned 64 Chinese cultural relics and paleontological fossils to China.
May 16, 2025:
-- The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art officially returned the Zidanku Silk Manuscript volumes II and III: Wuxing Ling and Gongshou Zhan from the Warring States period to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration.
Nov. 9, 2024:
-- A total of 56 lost Chinese cultural relics were returned from Italy.
June 27, 2024:
-- The Chinese Embassy in Argentina received 14 pieces of cultural relics returned to China from the South American country.
April 18, 2024:
-- China's relentless quest to retrieve lost cultural relics from overseas received a significant boost, as 38 artifacts were returned by the Manhattan District Attorney's Office. The prized haul comprises mainly Tibetan Buddhist objects spanning from the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368) to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911).
Feb. 7, 2024:
-- An ancient bronze ritual vessel that had been lost overseas after being stolen 40 years ago finally made its way home.
Unearthed in 1978 at an archaeological site dating back to the late Western Zhou Dynasty (1046-771 BC) in Famen Township of Baoji City, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, the bronze vessel, named "Feng Xingshu Gui" was classified as the top-grade cultural relic of the state.
May 10, 2023:
-- The Consulate General of China in New York received two illegally transported Chinese cultural relics from the Manhattan District Attorney's Office.
The returned cultural relics are two stone-carved tomb beds dating back about 1,100 to 1,600 years, according to the National Cultural Heritage Administration.
Dec. 1, 2020:
-- A bronze horse head sculpture, a treasure of China's Old Summer Palace that went missing after Anglo-French allied forces' looting 160 years ago, returned to its original palace home. ■
