Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:41:24 UTC
20:41:24 KST

At an event held at the Antwerp Stock Exchange, where the price of imported cocoa beans used to be set, Italian Tommaso Grollero won the World Chocolate Masters. This prestigious competition was held in Antwerp for the first time in 20 years. “I think the jury appreciated the personal touch in my creations and the way I’ve made my best desserts ever,” beamed the winning chocolatier.
Becoming a World Chocolate Master is one of the most coveted titles in the world of chocolate. For the past 20 years, the competition has taken place in Paris; this time, organiser and chocolate manufacturer Barry Callebaut chose Antwerp and the historic Antwerp Stock Exchange for the first time.
“If you look at the chocolatiers and pâtissiers here in Antwerp, the city really is one of the hotspots for chocolate. Not just in Belgium, but actually all over the world,” says organiser Dries Roekaerts.
‘Throughout the four challenges, Tommaso Grollero demonstrated just how exceptionally well he combines flavour, technical precision and a distinctively creative vision. He epitomises a chef’s consistent and clear vision of flavour,’ says Amaury Guichon, chair of the World Chocolate Masters judging panel.
The Italian beat 14 other international competitors. Lyu Haoran from China and Keita Koshimizu from Japan completed the top 3.
The port also plays a major role in the development of the chocolate industry in Antwerp. “It is the port in Europe where the largest quantity of cocoa beans is stored,” says Piet De Lombaerde of Antwerpen Koekenstad, the non-profit organisation that promotes the historical heritage of chocolate and biscuits.
“Only the port of Amsterdam handles a greater volume of cocoa beans. The reason for this is that the Dutch company Van Houten invented the process for effectively separating cocoa from the oil – the butter – contained within it. That is why most roasting takes place in the Netherlands.”
Thanks to cocoa imports through the port of Antwerp, the industry soon began to focus on chocolate production. The Felix Archive contains an application from 1852 by an entrepreneur who wished to install a machine for roasting cocoa beans in Antwerp’s Kasteelpleinstraat.
“Antwerp has been a pioneer in many areas. For example, the very first chocolate bar was launched here with the ‘Perrette’,” says De Lombaerde. “Chocolaterie Meurisse, Belgium’s first major chocolate factory, which opened in 1845, launched the bar at the Liège World’s Fair in 1905. The idea arose during a crisis. Chocolate in larger forms had become too expensive, so a smaller bar was developed.”

Bolsonaro touches down in US as legal pressure mounts in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:38:59 UTC
20:38:59 KST

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami with his family on Wednesday after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, escalating tensions between Brasilia and Washington following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The U.S. government has said it will grant entry visas to Bolsonaro and his family, despite the Brazilian investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
Reuters TV footage showed Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 private jet at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Their journey to the United States unfolded across several countries under a cloud of secrecy. Argentina's migration department said the family entered northern Argentina late Tuesday before traveling by private jet to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and then continuing to Miami.
Argentina's presidency, Ecuadorian government ministries and Baires Fly, the private jet operator, did not respond to requests for comment.
The arrival followed conflicting reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts. CNN and The Washington Post reported Tuesday that he had reached the United States, citing anonymous sources, while a Brazilian police source told AFP there was no formal record of his departure.
The source also said Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled. However, the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document reviewed by AFP.
Bolsonaro's departure threatens to further strain relations between the two largest countries in the Americas, as Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of helping the Bolsonaro family regain power.
Reuters reported before Sunday's election on a U.S. State Department campaign aimed at restoring the family to office.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Bolsonaro's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, said Wednesday he supported Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States. The State Department had announced a day earlier that it would issue visas to the senator and his family.
Trump has repeatedly portrayed Jair Bolsonaro as a victim of political and judicial persecution in Brazil. He also claimed Monday that Brazil's election was rigged following Flavio Bolsonaro's defeat, without providing evidence.
Jair Bolsonaro traveled to the United States in December 2022 after losing that year's presidential election to Lula and refusing to concede. He returned to Brazil three months later and was eventually sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his supporters' storming of government buildings in Brasilia.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on a pledge to secure his father's release. He was widely expected to win Sunday's election after finishing ahead of Lula in the first round, but the incumbent secured 51.8% of the vote in the final round.
The senator rejected the result and said he would seek to have it annulled, citing an extension of polling hours intended to address transportation difficulties that prevented some voters from reaching polling stations. Both campaigns had requested an extension, with Bolsonaro's team citing bad weather in parts of the country.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came days after a Supreme Court justice ordered him to surrender his passports. The senator had said Monday he intended to comply and defend himself against what he described as an attempt to intimidate him.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
His defeat also puts his legal position at greater risk. Bolsonaro is expected to lose parliamentary immunity when his Senate term ends in February, potentially exposing him to further legal action.
His campaign manager, Rogerio Marinho, said Tuesday he had been unable to establish the senator's whereabouts.
Marinho told reporters in Brasilia that Bolsonaro had sent him a text message that morning, saying he would wait before speaking to the campaign team. He said he had received no further communication and expressed shock at reports that the senator had left the country.
Lula condemned the reported departure, calling it shameful and suggesting it raised questions about Bolsonaro's intentions.
Separately, Brazil's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered police to investigate alleged foreign financing of Bolsonaro's campaign and possible overseas interference, including the manipulation of social media.
Lula's campaign had accused Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, of algorithmic manipulation that affected the election. Meta denied favoring either candidate, although it acknowledged that some of Lula's campaign advertisements had been mistakenly deactivated because of technical errors.

Families brace for a fourth winter of wind, rain and floods in Gaza’s camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:36:04 UTC
20:36:04 KST

Families brace for a fourth winter of wind, rain and floods in Gaza’s camps
Gaza’s impending winter is likely to lead to further devastation for Palestinians.
Gaza City — Mohammed al-Jamal, 60, tries to secure the nylon sheets of his family’s worn-out tent as a storm approaches his displacement camp on a beach in western Gaza City.
He and his sons pull at the tarpaulin, trying to fasten it firmly to the ground for protection from rain and wind coming in from the sea.
This will be the fourth winter that displaced Palestinians in Gaza have faced without adequate shelter. Many still live in tents and makeshift structures that offer little protection against the impending winter weather when temperatures can drop to 7C (below 45F) but can feel much colder due to strong coastal winds and rain.
The family cannot afford to fix their damaged tent with a replacement tarpaulin costing between 120 and 150 shekels ($37-$47) in local markets.
All al-Jamal can do is patch up the damaged shelter and hope it holds through the coming storm.
“We are trying to prepare as much as we can to protect ourselves from the water and the wind,” he said. “We follow the weather reports, and whenever there is a warning of a storm, we start preparing. But once the storm comes, everything gets torn apart, and we have to start all over again. It is continuous suffering throughout the winter.”
Mass displacement
Al-Jamal, originally from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood, has been displaced several times since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
About 30 members of his extended family live in these difficult living conditions.
“We are just trying to adapt to what we have. This is what is available to us. We need everything,” he said.
When it rains, water enters the tent and floods their living space, risking damage to their meagre belongings.
When temperatures drop, tents offer little protection for the displaced, with al-Jamal and his family having no choice but to put on more layers of clothing.
“We are out in the open. We are living in the street, not in houses that protect us,” he said.
Al-Jamal said he had repeatedly heard promises that shelter materials and caravans would be allowed into Gaza, but none had arrived for his family, and he had not seen any of them enter.
He described these announcements as “false promises and lies” that had left displaced families waiting for help that never came.
“Our demand is to have our lives back the way they were before,” he said.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians and destroyed or damaged more than 80 percent of buildings. With homes and infrastructure in Gaza destroyed, about 1.5 million of Gaza’s 2.3 million people are living in tents or makeshift shelters.
Many of the displaced have been forced to move from city to city when Israeli assaults begin on their homes or camps.
At least 294,250 families in Gaza need winter shelter assistance, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), but with current supplies, only 52,000 families, roughly 18 percent of those in need, have access to partial humanitarian assistance.
More than 65 percent of displaced households were living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to a Shelter Cluster survey, with more than half of those shelters in poor or very poor condition.
Israel’s siege on Gaza has also affected supplies reaching the enclave, with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) saying on October 5 that at least 500 truckloads of shelter materials were awaiting entry or procurement.
At the current pace, NRC said, it could take more than seven months for those supplies to enter Gaza. The materials include tents, tarpaulins, ropes and other items needed to repair shelters.
Winter around the corner
For families already living in torn tents, the shortage leaves few options beyond repeatedly repairing the same shelters.
Khitam Salman, 39, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, has been displaced multiple times over the past two years.
Now living near the beach, she is trying to prepare for winter with tents that have already suffered repeated damage.
“Every time there is a storm, we put up the tarpaulins and tie them down, only to have to do it all over again,” she said. “With every low-pressure system, it is the same.”
Khitam said one of the family’s tents had collapsed four times while they were sleeping inside and was torn, allowing sand to enter and offering little protection from rain and wind.
She is trying to cover the family’s tents and the space where they store their belongings, but the costs are beyond their means.
“We need a tarpaulin for this tent, another for the other one, and one for the room where we keep our belongings,” she said. “But we don’t have the means. We have done what we can.”
Her husband works in the health sector, but she said he receives his salary only once every three months, and it is not enough to cover the family’s needs.
“The tents are not suitable for living in any more,” she said. “They are torn, and sand gets inside. It is exhausting.”
Last winter, after their tent collapsed and their belongings were soaked, Salman said she became so overwhelmed that she walked away and sat by the sea for hours.
“I was so frustrated,” she recalled. “The tent had fallen, everything was flooded, and all our belongings were wet.”
“I’m worried about this winter … that the whole nightmare will repeat itself all over again.”
Damaged roads, drainage and sewage systems also increase the risk that rainwater will mix with wastewater and swamp the camps.
Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for Gaza Municipality, said more than 85 percent of the city’s infrastructure had been damaged and its rainwater drainage system was operating at about 20 percent of its previous capacity.
Rubble, damaged drainage networks and shortages of heavy machinery, fuel and maintenance materials are hampering preparations for winter, Muhanna said.
The municipality has begun emergency cleaning and maintenance work, but its efforts remain constrained by a lack of resources.
Flood risks beyond tents
Yosra Mesleh, 45, was displaced from her home in Gaza City’s Nassr neighbourhood when her home was destroyed and is preparing for her second winter living in a tent.
Preparing for winter means thinking about what to do when water enters their tents and soaks bedding and belongings. When this happens, they often have nowhere dry to sit, cook or eat.
“When it rained last winter, the water came inside and reached the bedding. Everything got wet,” she said. “It was difficult to find somewhere to sit while we waited for everything to dry.”
In summer, the heat and humidity inside the tent were unbearable, she said, with water shortages compounding their dire living situation.
“The place where we are living is not healthy or safe. It is not suitable for summer or winter,” she said.
Her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war, while her son is struggling to cover his own expenses.
“We need tents and tarpaulins. We need cooking utensils and a proper place to prepare food. We also need a regular supply of gas,” she said.
Without cooking gas, she worries about how the family will prepare meals when rain keeps them inside.
She remembers life before the war, when life was hard but they had an apartment and her husband ran a tea and coffee shop. They have since lost their home and their only source of income.
“We are not asking for towers or anything extravagant,” she said. “We are asking for tarpaulins and tents, for a dignified life.”

Moscow aims to strengthen economic and security ties with African leaders during the two-day gathering.
Trade and security are expected to be on the agenda as delegations and leaders from dozens of African countries gather in Moscow for a two-day summit with Russia.
The third instalment of the Russia-Africa Summit will run through October 28–29 and will be chaired by Russian President Vladimir Putin and the current African Union chair, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye.
Russia has boosted security and trade cooperation with African nations as it grapples with Western sanctions imposed in response to its war against Ukraine.
So who will be attending and what is at stake?
Here’s what we know.
What is the Russia-Africa Summit?
The Russia-Africa Summit is a two-day diplomatic and economic meeting being held in Moscow on Wednesday and Thursday.
Leaders and delegations from 48 African countries are meeting to discuss bilateral cooperation spanning politics, defence and technology.
This high-profile forum is the third of its kind. The first summit took place in October 2019 in Sochi, marking an unprecedented turn in Russian-African relations.
What’s on the agenda for the summit?
The event’s official theme is Developing Mutually Beneficial Cooperation and “unlocking the potential of every African country”.
More than 40 sessions and about 100 speakers will cover trade, investment, technology transfer, food and energy security, healthcare, education and youth exchange.
There will also be a business programme, culminating in a plenary session.
Who is attending?
Representatives from 48 African countries will participate, as well as 22 heads of state, according to Kremlin presidential aide Yury Ushakov. Heads of state from 17 countries attended the last summit in 2023.
Fewer leaders came to the last two summits, compared with the first gathering in 2019, when 43 took part, a decline which Moscow blamed on Western pressure.
Russian President Putin is scheduled to meet with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The guest list includes leaders closely tied to Russia’s growing security role in Africa, including Burkina Faso’s Ibrahim Traore and Niger’s Abdourahamane Tchiani.
Kenya’s William Ruto, Uganda’s Yoweri Museveni and Namibia’s Netumbo Nandi-Ndatiwah are also expected, as well as Sudan’s Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed al-Menfi, the chairman of the Presidential Council of Libya.
What is the relationship between Russia and Africa like?
Russia has gained far more influence in Africa through security than trade, according to a report by the African Security Analysis group (ASA), a security consultancy.
Russia’s security presence has risen significantly in the region. In 2023, Russian forces, mostly from the Wagner Group, operated in only a few African countries, but the ASA now counts Russian missions or troops in at least nine countries.
Trade between African countries and Russia has exceeded $28bn. It was estimated to be about $16.8bn in 2019, when the first summit was held. But trade is mainly concentrated in a few countries and overshadowed by that of China and the European Union.
Russia’s strongest ties to the continent are in energy, fertilisers, defence and nuclear power, where the state-owned firm Rosatom has signed a string of agreements.
Russia has been an essential supplier of fertilisers and wheat to many countries in the region.
In 2023, Russia exported 200,000 tonnes of grain to Mali, Somalia, the Central African Republic, Burkina Faso, Eritrea and Zimbabwe.
Why does this summit matter?
This is the first summit since 2023, so it will be an indicator of how far the relationship has developed and where it is heading, analysts say.
A final declaration and a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum plan should be adopted by the end of the Summit to cover 2027-2029.
Analysts have said that meetings on the sidelines could be more important than the main event, as talks between African delegations and Russian defence officials can illustrate where Moscow plans to expand its military ties.
The recruitment of Africans to fight in Ukraine could also be a growing problem for Moscow, as it has already caused diplomatic concern in countries such as Kenya.
Amnesty International has used the run-up to the summit to raise the issue of Africans being recruited to fight with Russia.
In an open letter, the directors of Amnesty’s African section urged leaders attending the summit to demand that Moscow end what the group describes as deceptive and coercive recruitment of Africans to fight in its war in Ukraine.

High voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel threatens Netanyahu

High voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel threatens Netanyahu
A historic voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel could unseat Benjamin Netanyahu and position Arab parties as decisive political kingmakers.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have turned out in unprecedented numbers for Israel’s parliamentary elections, with some towns reporting participation rates exceeding 70 percent.
Historically, however, Arab towns have witnessed lower participation rates in Israeli elections, ranging between 45 and 65 percent in recent years.
This electoral surge from Palestinian citizens of Israel now threatens to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing coalition.
For many from this contingent, who might normally have abstained from voting, this election was perceived as a chance to defeat a government that was totally hostile to Palestinians and Arabs at large.
There have been a number of measures enacted by Israel’s current right-wing government that encouraged high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel in this election. These include attempts by Jewish settlers to establish an outpost on Palestinian land in Majd al-Krum in the Upper Galilee.
“The people who were indifferent to the elections, and who did not want to participate or vote, the matter provoked them,” Hussein Manna, a resident of Majd al-Krum, told Al Jazeera. “They know very well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”
Path to power
Netanyahu and his far-right allies, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have heavily targeted Arabs in their campaigning. But this appears to have backfired and instead encouraged Palestinian citizens of Israel to go out and vote for Arab parties, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am).
Preliminary reports suggest that these parties could secure up to 17 seats combined, enough to prevent Netanyahu from reaching the required 61-seat majority.
“It is fateful for Netanyahu and for his political future, and it is also fateful for the State of Israel because it will determine its identity later on,” Walid al-Omari, Al Jazeera’s bureau chief in Palestine, said.
He added that if Netanyahu’s coalition remains in power, Israel “will move more towards racism and towards extremism”.
Ahmad Tibi, head of the Arab Movement for Renewal, told Al Jazeera: “The first goal: bringing down the government of Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben-Gvir, the government of crimes, the government of failure, and the government of racism and incitement against us.”
But he warned that the leaders of almost all parties opposed to Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties.
“What is the excuse? It is post-October 7, and this is a racist position,” Tibi stated. “We are ready to extend our hands to cooperate with the opposition to bring down the speaker of the Knesset [Amir Ohana] and also to prevent Netanyahu from becoming the head of a transitional government.”
In exchange for this tacit support, the Arab parties have strict demands. “The next alternative government is not our knight in shining armour and will not be a government of peace, but it will not have Ben-Gvir and Smotrich and the racist ministers,” Tibi said.
“Accordingly, we will make room for the establishment of another less bad alternative government that dialogues with us on issues that concern our society as a safety net for our society, such as issues of crime, violence, personal security, home demolitions and racism, as well as an important political horizon on our part because we have a clear political position on the occupation and on the crimes of the occupation and war crimes.”
Al-Omari said if Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, Netanyahu’s main opponent in the election, gets 53 seats, and Ra’am, headed by Mansour Abbas and most acceptable to the Eisenkot-led alliance, wins eight, then a coalition of 61 members could be formed.
‘Voter intimidation’
When the prospect of high Palestinian voter turnout emerged, Netanyahu and the far right launched a frantic campaign, warning supporters about this.
Netanyahu posted AI-generated images of Arab voters to incite his base, a move the Joint List condemned as an attempt to create a “misleading scene”.
Mohannad Mustafa, an academic and expert in Israeli affairs, believes that Netanyahu considers the Arab vote illegitimate. He said racist fearmongering and a hostile environment during the campaigning set a dangerous precedent.
“This is also what led to the assassination of Rabin in 1995 when Netanyahu said Rabin’s government in approving the Oslo Accords relies on the Arab lists in the Knesset,” Mustafa added, referring to former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
There were also reports of right-wing parties deploying activists to polling stations, which was widely interpreted as a form of intimidation against Palestinian citizens of Israel who were voting.
“I toured the ballot boxes here in Taibe, Tira and Qalansawe; in every box there is [someone] obstructing the electoral process and slowing it down specifically so that long queues form at the boxes,” Tibi stated.
He believes the right hoped such tactics would make Palestinian citizens of Israel tired of waiting in line at the polls and leave without voting. Instead, he saw the community’s “determination to stay until the voting is done”.
The outcome of the election carries significance for the broader Middle East, with Netanyahu launching the genocide in Gaza, killing more than 74,500 Palestinians, and assaults on Syria, Lebanon and Iran during his term.
Tariq Hamoud, a political analyst, noted that an Israeli government without Netanyahu might have implications for these ongoing military engagements.
What could determine the election, though, is that Netanyahu “bears responsibility for the security failure on October 7, which opened the doors” to these wars.

Ice patrol ship will miss a second Antarctic season
United Kingdom

11:30:38 GMT
20:30:38 KST

HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season, leaving Britain without an ice patrol ship in the South Atlantic for a second consecutive year while the government looks at how to cover the gap, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what steps are being taken to ensure an ice patrol vessel is available for the coming season.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Due to unforeseen circumstances, HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season. The Ministry of Defence is working apace with partners across Government to develop options to support the UK’s Antarctic requirements in the absence of an ice patrol ship in 2026/27 and restore an ice patrol capability as soon as possible.
“The Defence Investment Plan announced plans to replace HMS Protector with a more modern variant to maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory. Decisions on the method of procurement and the exact replacement timeline will be taken in due course.”
Answering a separate question, Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, confirmed that the ship last went south during the 2024-25 season. Pollard told Parliament last week that Protector could not sail from Teesside to Devonport under her own power this month because of propulsion defects and had to be towed, and that she missed the 2025-26 season because of prolonged essential and mandatory maintenance.
The ship is the Royal Navy’s only ice patrol vessel and carries out Britain’s survey and inspection commitments under the Antarctic Treaty, alongside supporting the British Antarctic Survey and maintaining a presence around the British Antarctic Territory. She was bought in 2011, originally built as the Norwegian vessel Polarbjørn, and was taken on initially as a short-term replacement for HMS Endurance, which was crippled by flooding in 2008 and never returned to service.

Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh
Scottish architecture studio Page\Park has completed The Allardice Centre, a health and wellbeing hub for Fettes College in Edinburgh, which is topped with a lantern-like roof.
Named after the independent day and boarding school’s alumnus David Allardice, the 469-square-metre centre brings together medical and pastoral care services in a fully accessible building nestled into a wooded plot.
According to Page\Park, the centre’s design was informed by the late Allardice’s interest in Eastern philosophy, in particular the elemental philosophy of Wuxing, which led to a palette of timber, stone and metal.
The building’s structure is made from Scots-grown timber, while Darney stone quarried nearby forms the external load-bearing cladding, which is contrasted by a bronze roof.
“Allardice spent much of his working life in East Asia, and was drawn to ancient Chinese philosophy and the five essential elements, fire, water, wood, metal and earth,” the studio told Dezeen.
“This narrative directly influenced the design, materiality and construction approach, which can be seen through the strata-like stone cladding, burnt bronze metal roof, and connection to the outside,” it added.
The Allardice Centre is organised across a single storey, with an open wellbeing hub at its centre, wrapped by a series of individual treatment and counselling rooms overlooking the surrounding woodland.
Illuminating the central hub is a mono-pitched, lantern-like roof. This creates a ring of clerestory windows, framed by the exposed glued-laminated timber (glulam) structure designed in collaboration with Scottish engineering firm Will Rudd.
“Fitting the full brief for both medical and pastoral functions into this constrained site, while avoiding level changes to maximise accessibility, forced the plan to be quite deep,” explained the studio.
“Bringing natural light into this deep plan therefore became a challenge. To resolve this, the glulam structure extends and branches out at high level to reveal a triple-glazed clerestory lantern formed of timber curtain walling,” it added.
Inside The Allardice Centre, white walls allow the timber structure to come to the fore. In the treatment rooms, leaf-print and green fabrics create a visual connection to the surrounding site, which was developed by landscape architects Harrison Stevens.
“We were interested in the didactic implications of exposing the glulam timber frame, offering an insight into how the building was crafted, celebrating its sustainability principles and the elemental philosophy underpinning the design,” said the studio.
“The Darney stone chosen for the project was quarried only 75 kilometres away, and had fantastic mineral veins through it which paired neatly with the varying course sizes, leaning into the earth element theme, and giving a sense of permanence,” it added.
Other projects in Edinburgh recently featured on Dezeen include the extension of a Georgian townhouse by Pend, which complemented the existing stone structure with skinny red brickwork.
Elsewhere, Page\Park recently completed a teaching building for the University of Stirling, which was shortlisted for the 2025 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award.

BeeX shows ALPHA mine-killing drone in UK after U.S. Navy win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:29:57 UTC
20:29:57 KST

- BeeX’s ALPHA underwater drone placed and fired charges against a moored mine and a floating steel plate during a UK demonstration on Sept. 17.
- The U.S. Navy named BeeX a winner of its Mine Countermeasure Modernization Prize Challenge, with winning systems set for fleet integration.
Singapore-based BeeX used its ALPHA underwater drone to place explosive charges on a moored sea mine and a swinging steel target and then destroy both during a closed-door mine countermeasures demonstration in the United Kingdom, the company said on Oct. 27.
The one-day event, held on Sept. 17 and hosted by British defense consultancy Copper Turtle, brought together representatives of the UK Ministry of Defence, the Royal Navy, industry and academia. BeeX worked alongside three other firms: Alford Technologies, which supplied the charges, Blueprint Subsea, which supplied the acoustic firing system, and ELWAVE, which supplied an electric sensor for finding mine-like objects.
ALPHA is a hovering autonomous underwater vehicle, a drone that can stop and hold its position in the water instead of cruising past a target like a torpedo-shaped survey vehicle. That ability to hover is what let it do the hands-on part of mine clearance during the demonstration. Operating semi-autonomously from a laptop, ALPHA approached each target, held station close to it, and used its sonar and cameras to inspect and identify it.
It then attached Alford’s Remote EOD Delivery System neutralizers, confirmed the charge was ready, backed away and fired. The first target was a moored mine, the kind anchored to the seabed and floating at a set depth below the surface. The second was a steel plate hung from a buoy, chosen to make the job harder because it rotated unpredictably in the water. BeeX said ALPHA still placed the charge accurately on the moving plate. After each detonation, the drone used its sonar and cameras to check the damage and confirm the targets had been neutralized.
Blueprint Subsea’s through-water fire set sent the detonation command acoustically, through the water, so no cable had to run to the charge. The event also included the successful detonation of an Alford magnetic charge. Alford says its system is operational to a depth of 950 m (3,117 feet) and can produce either a full explosion or a smaller, controlled effect against underwater explosive ordnance.
ELWAVE’s EPULSE sensor demonstrated the search end of the process. It uses electric sensing to detect objects regardless of water visibility or murkiness and can find objects that are exposed, buried or partly buried in the seabed.
BeeX also showed how the drone can be reprogrammed from far away. Its engineers in Singapore accessed ALPHA over Starlink during the event and changed its mission settings remotely. The company says the same connection could eventually let navies send firing commands from anywhere, keeping personnel out of the danger area.
The UK demonstration follows a U.S. win for BeeX. On Oct. 1, the U.S. Navy and the Defense Innovation Unit named BeeX one of three winners of the Mine Countermeasure Modernization Prize Challenge, alongside BlackSea Technologies and Vatn Systems. The challenge drew 80 submissions, and 11 companies were chosen to compete across near-surface mine neutralization, bottom mine detection and bottom mine neutralization. The U.S. Navy said the winning systems will be integrated into the fleet’s autonomous mine countermeasure kits.
Mine clearance has moved up the agenda for both navies this year. The U.S. Navy used underwater drones to help clear Iranian mines from the Strait of Hormuz, while the Royal Navy fitted the support ship RFA Lyme Bay in Gibraltar to act as a mothership for uncrewed mine-hunting systems. Other companies are also bringing new drones to the field, including French firm SEABER, which launched its RAVEN mine-hunting drone this week.
BeeX was spun out of the National University of Singapore in 2018, and in October 2025 Singapore’s Defence Science and Technology Agency awarded it a contract to supply its hovering drones to the Singapore Ministry of Defence. The company says ALPHA can operate untethered, so several units can be deployed at once, and can be launched from autonomous surface vessels.

China’s disarmament union calls on IAEA to boost supervision of Japan's plutonium stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:29:52 UTC
20:29:52 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) needs to strengthen surveillance measures over Japan in a situation where the country is building up its plutonium reserves, Chairman of China Arms Control and Disarmament Association Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He said that Japan's plutonium reserves now stand at 44.4 tons. "The IAEA should proactively strengthen the scale and frequency of comprehensive control measures for Japan. And all countries should approach nuclear cooperation with Japan with caution to ensure that such cooperation is used exclusively for peaceful purposes," he said.
Dai Huaicheng added that Japan had long justified the plutonium reserves growth by developing a nuclear cycle and intending to produce MOX fuel (Mixed-Oxide fuel - mixed uranium-plutonium oxide fuel). However, in light of the facts, this justification does not stand up to criticism. Firstly, there is a serious imbalance between supply and demand," said the head of the association.
"After the 2011 accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, many of Japan’s nuclear reactors were shut down for a long time, and the number of reactors in which plutonium is actually loaded and consumed is very limited, which is why significant amounts of plutonium only enter [reserves], but are not consumed."
Secondly, the expert pointed out, this runs counter to Japan's obligations to the international community.
"In 1997, Japan gave the IAEA a written commitment to ensure the ‘absence of excess plutonium.’ That is, that all the separated plutonium will be used in reactors [as fuel], but today it has accumulated dozens of tons of excess plutonium, which means we see a difference in what they say and what they do. Thirdly, plutonium stored abroad can also be used for military purposes. As soon as Japan makes a political decision, more than 30 tons of plutonium stored outside the country can theoretically be quickly delivered [to Japanese territory]," Dai Huaicheng said.
The MOX technology uses secondary nuclear production materials for the production of fresh fuel - depleted uranium and plutonium extracted from irradiated nuclear fuel.

National call launched to advance Persian medicine, herbal research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:29:33 UTC
20:29:33 KST

National call launched to advance Persian medicine, herbal research
TEHRAN - Iran has launched a national call for scientific, research, and technology-based proposals in Persian medicine, medicinal plants, traditional pharmacy, and natural products, focusing on technological development, artificial intelligence (AI), international cooperation, and commercialization.
The initiative aims to identify and support the country's scientific and technological capacities, facilitate innovation and help translate research findings into marketable products. Projects involving multiple national committees and research centers will receive particular priority.
The call covers education, research, AI applications, international partnerships, pharmaceutical development and industrial production. It seeks to strengthen links among universities, research institutions and industry, supporting projects from initial scientific investigation to the development and commercialization of new products.
Advancing research in Persian medicine
Persian medicine, one of the world's oldest traditional medical systems, has a long history of scholarship associated with prominent physicians such as Rhazes and Avicenna. Its traditional framework places considerable emphasis on maintaining health, preventing disease, and adopting appropriate lifestyles.
According to figures previously reported by the health ministry, the country ranks third globally in traditional medicine clinical trials registered on the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), following China and India. Traditional and complementary medicine trials account for approximately three percent of all clinical trials registered in Iran, while specialists in the field represent around 0.3 percent of the country's healthcare workforce.
The national call seeks to build on this research capacity by supporting clinical trials, cohort studies, molecular research, microbiology, bioinformatics, and other scientific approaches. It also emphasizes preclinical investigations and the evaluation of the safety and effectiveness of traditional medical interventions.
These priorities reflect a broader effort to connect Iran's traditional medical heritage with contemporary research methods and evidence-based healthcare.
Medicinal plant resources
Iran's rich plant diversity offers considerable potential for herbal medicine research and the development of natural products. Around 8,000 plant species are found in the country, according to figures previously cited in reports on Iran's medicinal-plant resources.
A scientific review published in Medicina in 2020 documented 245 plants used in Iranian traditional medical practices and identified scientific studies involving 89 plants collected in Iran. The review highlighted the potential of traditional knowledge to inspire pharmaceutical research, while noting that many herbal remedies still require further scientific investigation and validation.
The national call aims to help researchers and manufacturers explore this potential through the development of herbal medicines, natural pharmaceutical ingredients, functional foods and nutraceuticals. It also supports product standardization, quality assessment, technology transfer and the establishment of pilot production facilities.
The proposed initiative identifies Iranian products such as saffron, Damask rose, rosewater, pomegranate, barberry, pistachio, black seed, licorice, cumin and Shirazi thyme as potential areas for research, product development and branding.
Plans also include strengthening distribution networks, developing domestic and international brands, and helping small-scale manufacturers and knowledge-based companies bring research-based products to market.
Artificial intelligence and health research
Artificial intelligence and digital technologies are central to the initiative. Proposed projects include AI-based healthcare tools, research databases, digital patient records and improved health information systems.
Research priorities include nutrition, sleep, stress management, reproductive health, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver disease and digestive disorders. Other areas include cardiovascular disease prevention, respiratory and musculoskeletal conditions, neurological diseases, mental health, addiction treatment and healthy aging.
The program encourages researchers to investigate potential applications of Persian medicine in these areas through appropriate scientific methods. AI and digital infrastructure could also support data analysis and collaboration among research centers.
Education and international cooperation
The call also prioritizes professional education, research networks, reference books, clinical guidelines, and digital learning platforms. These measures are intended to strengthen the skills of healthcare professionals and improve the documentation and scientific assessment of traditional medical knowledge.
International cooperation is another key component, with proposed activities including joint research and development, clinical trials, drug discovery and partnerships with BRICS member states, neighboring countries and Indian Ocean nations. The initiative also encourages technology transfer, international co-branding and cooperation in the production and marketing of traditional medicines and natural products.
By bringing together scientific research, digital innovation and industrial development, the call seeks to strengthen the evidence base of Persian medicine and expand opportunities for Iran's medicinal-plant and natural-product industries.

The Yemeni forces said the attack on the airport caused injuries among civilians and material damage.
Air traffic was halted after the strike, two transport ministry officials told Reuters. An aid source said some UN staff left the airport shortly before the attack and no one was hurt.
A flight with aid workers on-board departed from Aden airport safely on Wednesday morning to Amman before the incident at the airport, two aid sources told Reuters.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the evacuation warning was prompted by what he said was the presence of a Saudi military cargo aircraft delivering weapons.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and most of northwestern Yemen, have repeatedly targeted Aden airport in the past. Residents said explosions had also been heard elsewhere in the city before the warning was issued.
The International Organization for Migration said that its personnel travelling through Aden were safe and accounted for after reports of an attack.
FIGHTING ESCALATES
The attack comes as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s government has intensified in recent weeks, opening a volatile new front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
Last month, Houthi forces advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most strategically important shipping routes, which lies opposite the Strait of Hormuz across the Arabian Peninsula.
Government forces have since pushed to retake territory on the Red Sea coast in a move that could loosen the Houthis’ grip on the chokepoint, while the coalition has stepped up strikes against Houthi positions in response to the group’s escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia.
On Tuesday, medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said that one of its aircraft was about to take off from Aden airport a few days ago when humanitarian workers were told to seek shelter as a missile struck nearby.
“Aden airport is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies and medical equipment to the southern parts of Yemen, and safe access to it is crucial,” the organisation said in a statement.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that 14 people were killed and 15 others were injured in what it described as a Saudi attack on the northern Yemeni Jawf region.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted major attacks in the conflict, which began after the Houthis drove the government from Sanaa in 2014.
Aid agencies warn the latest violence is rapidly worsening conditions in a country already suffering from one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Oct 28 (Reuters) - Hundreds of people permanently living aboard a touring cruise ship were forced to disembark in Cambodia this week after the vessel’s operator said fuel price increases from the Iran war had made operations prohibitively expensive.
The Villa Vie Odyssey had been cruising the world for at least 755 days as one of only a handful of ships that offered passengers the opportunity to rent or buy long-term or even permanent residences on board.
On Tuesday the ship’s owner, Villa Vie Residences, announced it was suspending operations and disembarking those passengers in Cambodia while working to find them temporary accommodation.
Monthly fuel expenses that historically averaged approximately $1,800 per cabin have recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement.
“The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure.”
Villa Vie Residences did not immediately respond to questions. The Odyssey can house 650 people but its rooms, including “villa suites” that cost $440,000, were still being filled. An inside villa on the vessel costs $120,000.
There were 203 passengers and 156 crew members on the ship, said Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province.
Some passengers had already departed on flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, he told media.
The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving Cambodia on Saturday, he added.
Social media videos by residents showed uncertainty and disappointment as they heard the news. Others said they would relish the extra time to explore Southeast Asia.
Randy Cassingham, who lived on the Odyssey with his wife and who writes about his lifestyle on ResidentialCruising.com, said that Florida-based CEO Kathy Villaba posted a message shortly after 7 a.m. in Cambodia telling residents they had until 2 p.m. to disembark and to coordinate with staff if they were unable to remove all their belongings in time.
It was not entirely surprising, he wrote in a post on his website.
“It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more,” he said.
Since the Iran war began in late February, the company had taken steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but those measures were not enough to offset the “extraordinary” increase in fuel costs, Villa Vie’s statement said.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it added. The company would seek to restructure and recapitalize over the next 60 days, though no financing has been finalized.

====================================================================================================

Analysis-Mbappe’s Mao remarks expose costs of crossing China’s red lines
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:28:45 CET
20:28:45 KST

By Casey Hall
SHANGHAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe’s rapid fall from favour in China after remarks about Mao Zedong followed a familiar pattern: online outrage, corporate distancing, platform restrictions and official intervention.
Within 24 hours of a podcast clip surfacing in which the France captain referred to Mao as “some guy - I think he’s a Chinese dictator”, sponsors including Mengniu Dairy, Shanghai Milkground and energy drink-maker Eastroc ended cooperation with the footballer.
State broadcaster CCTV removed Mbappe-related advertising and Chinese social media platforms restricted access to his accounts. Mbappe apologised on Tuesday, describing his remarks as “ill-judged”.
The speed of the fallout will be familiar to companies, brands and celebrities with exposure to China. Analysts say the episode is the latest reminder of a business risk that remains difficult to manage despite years of similar controversies.
Foreign brands have repeatedly faced public backlash in China, from Dolce & Gabbana’s cancelled Shanghai fashion show in 2018 and apologies by Versace, LVMH-owned Dior and Tapestry’s Coach in 2019, to boycotts of H&M, Nike and Adidas over Xinjiang cotton and the NBA’s fallout with CCTV after a Houston Rockets executive expressed support for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
The details differ, but the pattern is similar: a remark, image or statement gains traction online, commercial partners come under pressure to respond, and reputational damage quickly outgrows the original offence.
“You don’t need to think like a Chinese person to succeed in China, but you do need to understand how Chinese audiences will react and the cultural implications of not self-policing,” said Michael MacRitchie, founder of MGI Group, which connects global celebrities with Chinese brands.
A MATTER OF RESPECT
A central question in such episodes is how much of the backlash reflects genuine public anger and how much is amplified by state media, online platforms and official actors.
The Mbappe case illustrates how difficult that distinction can be to draw. As the controversy unfolded, the original comments about Mao were largely inaccessible on China’s heavily censored internet. Many consumers were therefore exposed less to what Mbappe said than to reports that sponsors had dropped him and official media were condemning him.
“What we’ve had in this situation is to a certain extent a manufactured outrage,” said Mark Dreyer, a sports analyst and author of “Sporting Superpower”, a book about China’s sporting ambitions.
Even so, Dreyer said it would be unwise for leagues, clubs and athletes to underestimate the reaction such incidents can provoke.
“They can’t be seen to be giving a stated directive to their players not to say anything that could offend China,” he said. “Of course, behind the scenes, I’m sure people are being told, just be careful, be sensible, be aware that these sorts of reactions can happen.”
Zak Dychtwald, founder of BridgeWorks Global, which advises multinational organisations, said that although these controversies remain relatively common, they are preventable.
“If you are participating in this market, the expectation is that you respect China’s self-narrative and you have a basic understanding of what it is. Red line education should come at the foundation of it,” he said.
Another challenge for brands, leagues and celebrities, however, is that while China’s political and cultural red lines are broadly understood, they are rarely clearly defined. That uncertainty can encourage companies and commercial partners to distance themselves from controversial figures before the scale of any offence has been fully established.
“There is no rule in black and white for what crosses a line,” said Wei Kan, founder of consultancy Conduit Asia. The line shifts depending on “how consumers feel, the wider mood in society, and how platforms and media amplify a story,” he said.
For foreign businesses, China’s sensitivities should no longer come as a surprise. Yet analysts say political and cultural risks are still often treated as secondary considerations rather than routine commercial hazards.
MacRitchie said his firm includes behavioural and reputational clauses in endorsement contracts; others point to market-specific briefings, media training and crisis-response planning as increasingly necessary safeguards rather than optional precautions.
“When it goes well, everybody celebrates,” Dychtwald said. “But when you get (China) wrong, it can be extraordinarily painful and swift in its retribution.”
(Reporting by Casey Hall in Shanghai, additional reporting by Josh Arslan in Beijing, editing by Ed Osmond)

The United Nations has marked earlier efforts to resolve the Cyprus issue with a symbolic gift to the island’s two leaders: Olive oil produced from trees planted during negotiations 17 years ago.
Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman and Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides each received a bottle of olive oil made from olives harvested from the trees.
The trees were planted on Oct. 15, 2009, by then- Greek Cypriot President Demetris Christofias and then-Turkish Cypriot leader Mehmet Ali Talat as a gesture of their shared commitment to peace.
The gifts were presented as Christodoulides and Erhürman arrived for their latest meeting at the United Nations office at the buffer zone on Oct. 27.

The latest meeting between Christodoulides and Erhürman came two days before the scheduled arrival U.N. envoy Maria Angela Holguin on Oct. 29.
The initiative dates back to a period of intensive direct negotiations between Christofias and Talat under U.N. auspices.
Before another round of talks on Oct. 15, 2009, the two leaders planted the olive trees at the entrance to the negotiating venue. Civil society representatives and U.N. officials attended the ceremony.
Representatives of more than 40 Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot organizations also took part. The groups had launched an initiative to support the negotiations and presented the leaders with a resolution backing efforts toward reconciliation and the reunification of Cyprus, according to UN records.
A decade later, on Sept. 21, 2019, Elizabeth Spehar, then the U.N. secretary-general’s special representative in Cyprus, unveiled a commemorative plaque between the trees. The ceremony, held on the International Day of Peace, recalled the significance of the original initiative.

Canadian volunteer who rescued hundreds of animals is killed in Russian drone strike in Donetsk Oblast
Canadian volunteer Jesse Adams, who rescued animals and helped people in Ukraine, has been killed by a Russian drone strike while evacuating animals in Donetsk Oblast.
Source: the Animal Rescue Kharkiv community
Details: Jesse's vehicle was struck by a Russian FPV drone.
In Canada, Jesse had founded the RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, which is dedicated to rescuing and rehoming animals. In Ukraine, he helped evacuate animals and assist residents of frontline settlements.
"When someone travels halfway across the world to work alongside you in some of the most challenging conditions, it means more than words can express. Thanks to Jesse, hundreds of animals are alive today," Ukrainian volunteers said.
A few days before his death, Jesse reported that his group of volunteers had rescued 80 dogs and cats in Kramatorsk in a single day. He urged people not to forget the people and animals in Ukraine who need help.
Jesse wrote: "These poor animals do not understand war and are simply innocent victims of another country invading Ukraine. Each day more and more innocent civilians and animals are injured or killed by drones, bombs, and missile attacks.
Some of these animals' owners were killed, some are being evacuated to be reunited with their families to a safer region of Ukraine, some have been asked to be rehomed, and others are strays struggling to survive in a place that causes a lot of damage and suffering.
It breaks my heart that we even have to do this type of work, but it is my privilege and honour to be a small part of helping these animals reach a better life for themselves and their families, or to be adopted into new families."
On 25 October, Jesse was getting another group of animals ready for evacuation. No sooner had the animals been loaded into the vehicle than it was attacked by a Russian drone. The strike hit the windscreen, leaving Jesse with severe injuries.
He was taken to the local hospital straight away. Doctors tried to resuscitate him and performed emergency surgery, but they were unable to save him.
The Animal Rescue Kharkiv community said: "Jesse, it's been an honour for us to work alongside you. We will always remember you as a kind, compassionate and truly extraordinary person. We will miss you dearly.
Our heartfelt condolences go out to everyone who knew and loved Jesse. We are so grateful for the time we spent with him, for his courage, and for every life he helped us save."
Background: In July, animal rescue volunteer Olha Kuzmenko was killed in Druzhkivka, Donetsk Oblast, when a guided aerial bomb struck the city.

Tunisia sentences former Ennahda leader to nine years in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:24:21 UTC
20:24:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisia sentences former Ennahda leader to nine years in prison
A Tunisian court has sentenced the former acting leader of the moderate Islamist opposition Ennahda movement Mondher Ounissi to nine years in prison in a case involving leaked audio recordings, as authorities continue their crackdown on political opponents and journalists.
The ruling was issued late on Tuesday by the criminal chamber specialising in terrorism cases at the Tunis Court of First Instance,
Journalist Zied El Heni was also sentenced to four years in prison in the same case, while several defendants tried in absentia received 25-year prison terms.
Those sentenced in absentia include former minister and senior Ennahda official Rafik Abdessalem, journalist Maher Zid and media personality Shahrazad Akacha. The sentences were issued with immediate enforcement orders.
The case dates back to September 2023, when an audio recording allegedly featuring Ounissi in a telephone conversation with Akacha was leaked.
In the recording, Ounissi reportedly discussed internal disputes within Ennahda, allegations of corruption and claims that the party had received foreign funding.
According to Tunisia's official news agency TAP, citing a judicial source, the defendants were convicted of offences including failing to report information concerning the commission or possible commission of "terrorist crimes".
The charges also included establishing contacts with agents of a foreign state with the intention of harming Tunisia's diplomatic interests in connection with terrorism-related offences.
Ounissi's wife, Rahma Laabidi, expressed shock at the verdict in a Facebook post and called for her husband's release.
The Tunisian Journalists' Syndicate separately condemned the four-year sentence handed to El Heni, describing it as another escalation in the targeting of journalists and press freedom.
The syndicate said El Heni had initially been summoned as a witness in the investigation into Ounissi's leaked recordings and questioned about his relationship with sources who had provided information about the case.
However, his legal status was subsequently changed from witness to defendant, and he was charged under Tunisia's anti-terrorism and money laundering legislation.
The charges included forming a terrorist organisation, disclosing secrets for the benefit of a terrorist organisation, failing to report a terrorist offence and contacting foreign state agents to encourage actions harmful to Tunisia's interests.
The syndicate described the prosecution as politically motivated and raised serious concerns about whether the defendants had received a fair trial.
Ounissi previously served as acting president of Ennahda, one of Tunisia's main opposition parties, which has faced mounting legal and political pressure since President Kais Saied consolidated power in July 2021.
Saied suspended parliament that year and subsequently dissolved it, before introducing a new constitution that significantly expanded presidential powers.
Opposition groups have accused his administration of dismantling democratic institutions and using the judiciary to silence critics, allegations Saied has rejected.
Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi has been imprisoned since April 2023 and has received several prison sentences in separate cases.
The movement was a major force in Tunisian politics following the 2011 revolution that overthrew longtime ruler Zine El Abidine Ben Ali.
Since Saied's power grab, numerous opposition politicians, activists and journalists have faced prosecution on charges ranging from conspiracy against state security to terrorism-related offences.

Preparations for Ukraine talks, protests in Europe: senior Russian diplomat’s statements

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia is now preparing for the upcoming talks on Ukraine, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov told reporters at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
He noted that France should focus on resolving the issues within its own country instead of criticizing Russia’s cooperation with Africa.
TASS has compiled the senior diplomat’s key statements.
Relations with US
Moscow is skeptical that the results of the US midterm elections will change the White House’s approach to Russia: "Let’s wait for the results. We don't pin our hopes on the election results drastically improving our relations. Unfortunately, a bipartisan anti-Russian consensus has formed in the US, and it seems like reasonable forces are forming outside the current Congress."
There are forces in the US who want peace and cooperation and view Russia as a potentially important partner: "Elections in any country are an important tool for gauging public opinion. In the case of the US, we can clearly see a big gap in the approach to international affairs between elites, including the Congress component, and people who are removed from politics. They want peace, they want cooperation and they want a prosperous life and they regard Russia as a potentially significant partner, despite all propaganda."
Ukrainian settlement
Russia hopes that its close dialogue with the Trump administration will allow Moscow to launch settlement talks and tackle the root causes of the Ukrainian conflict: "We are currently engaged in close, intensive dialogue with the Trump administration. We expect the US president’s and his team’s efforts on the Ukrainian track, in particular, to reach a point where we can really speak about ensuring a sustainable and reliable settlement that guarantees our fundamental interests and corresponds to the provisions of our Constitution. This will allow us to solve the problems stemming from the conflict’s root causes, ranging from security to the rights of the Russian-speaking population and the Russian Orthodox Church, which we constantly mention."
Russia is now preparing for the upcoming talks on Ukraine: "It is premature to talk about the Abu Dhabi negotiations. Of course, there is a preliminary understanding that soon there will be talks that take place at this very venue, Abu Dhabi, that's true. But in general, we are only preparing for it now."
Russia will counter the efforts of the "war party" residing in European capitals to interfere in the Ukrainian settlement: "The experience of the past meetings in general have demonstrated the rather vigorous opposition of the so-called war party, which is first and foremost represented by European capitals, to the rational approaches of the [US President Donald] Trump administration. This creates false hopes in Kiev and essentially prolongs the conflict. We have seen this before. We don't want this story to repeat itself now that the upcoming meeting in Abu Dhabi is being discussed seriously. We will counter it."
Arms trafficking from Ukraine
Ukrainian militants penetrating into Africa is a dangerous phenomenon: "We have seen it and we continue to see it in several states and in many directions. The events in North Africa and the Mediterranean Sea, particularly the attack on the Arctic Metagaz LNG carrier (which was attacked by drones launched from the territory of Libya - TASS) remind us of the troubling nature of Ukrainian militant incursions in Africa."
"Kiev is now boasting its capability to develop drone technologies."
"And now, against the backdrop of arms trafficking, including of Western weapons, in many countries, against the background of the rising risks in the terrorist sphere, including as a result of this know-how, we must work with the corresponding countries to double our efforts to put an end to this."
Cooperation with other countries
Western sanctions will not force Russia to abandon cooperation with African countries, BRICS partners, and other partners in the Eurasian space: "No sanctions and no attempts to invoke this trite rhetoric about Russia's so-called isolation will move us off this path. We will continue to cooperate with everyone: Africans, BRICS participants, and our neighbors in the vast Eurasian region."
Recently, Russia "has not only spoken out, but also worked actively on this path": "So there is a lot to do, and former colonial powers aren’t the only fish in the sea."
"Of course, we welcome the big interest to the Moscow event seen in the African continent and beyond. The Russia-Africa forum is a world-scale event, no cap."
European countries "have cut themselves off from cooperating with Russia of their own volition."
Western colonial instincts and protests in Europe
Instead of criticizing the cooperation between Russia and Africa, France should focus on resolving its domestic situation: "I recommend that our French colleagues find a way to quickly remove all trash from the streets of Paris and other cities, wash away graffiti from monuments, and compensate businesses of all sizes for the damage they suffered as a result of protests."
Western countries cannot get over the loss of territories, which "they once considered subordinate to them out of colonial domination, nor can they accept the sovereign decision of African states and people to seek partners around the world who are willing to cooperate equally."
"This is where the events in London and Paris come from; these are their colonial instincts speaking."
"It is high time to think about what has led to these events and what domestic tensions in these countries are provoking their populations to take such drastic measures to express their protest. This is what people should be doing."

Russia is building drone launch site near Millerovo to launch up to 100 Geran UAVs a day, Ukrainian intelligence says – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:23:00 EET
20:23:00 KST

Russia is building drone launch site near Millerovo to launch up to 100 Geran UAVs a day, Ukrainian intelligence says – photos
Russia is building a new launch site for attack drones near the Millerovo military airfield in Rostov Oblast, which borders temporarily occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) on Telegram
Details: DIU said satellite images confirm that the new site is under construction.
Quote: "The configuration of the facility indicates that it is intended for preparing and launching jet-powered attack drones, likely the Geran-4 and Geran-5, as well as their modifications. Early estimates suggest that, once construction is complete, the site will be capable of supporting up to 100 launches per day."
Details: According to DIU, the actual intensity of operations at the site will depend on the supply of ready-made drones, the availability of fuel and warheads, the number of trained crews, the serviceability of equipment, and assigned tasks.
DIU noted that in late August, there were no visible signs of active construction at the site. However, by mid-October, Russian forces had already established launch positions and other infrastructure.
The intelligence agency said the rapid pace of construction could be explained by the use of previously tested technical solutions and by concentrating resources on building relatively simple launch infrastructure.
"The construction of a new drone launch facility just 3.5 km from Millerovo airfield indicates that Russia intends to use the same air defence systems protecting the airfield to defend the new site," DIU added.
It also noted that the new site could benefit from access to the airfield's existing road, communications and logistics infrastructure, as well as its technical support systems.
Russia is also upgrading its jet-powered attack drones. A new version of the Geran-4 has been equipped with additional autonomous navigation capabilities, including an optical terrain-matching system. A similar system is being integrated into the K5 version of the Geran-5 drone.
"In addition, the Russians have equipped the Geran-4 with a domestically produced jet engine and a new warhead designed to strike bridges and electricity transmission towers," DIU said.
The Geran-4 has a range of up to 770 km, while the Geran-5 can fly up to 950 km.
The new facility will expand Russia's network of attack drone launch sites, which, according to DIU, already includes at least 12 permanent facilities. DIU believes the new facility may be part of Russia's preparations to intensify attacks on Ukraine, particularly over the winter.

Background: Ukrainka Pravda previously reported, citing Ukrainian OSINT community Absolutely Reliable Source, that Russia was building the Millerovo drone launch facility. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Wednesday defended his and Finnish President Alexander Stubb's phone call the day before with Russia's Vladimir Putin, saying it was meant to ensure the Kremlin heard the views of European leaders about ending the war against Ukraine.
Tuesday's phone conversation marks the first time a leader from one of Ukraine's European allies spoke to Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's phone call with the Russian president in July 2025.
Both Finland and Norway said their leaders were speaking as representatives of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole. Still, the phone call with Putin was met with criticism from some European leaders.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” of the initiative and did not believe Russia wants peace with Ukraine or Europe.
Støre told the public broadcaster NRK he and Stubb were "focused on looking forward, what must happen for this war to not continue endlessly for months, with people dying ... and it is even more difficult to find a solution."
"I don't think [Putin] will change his mind, but he gets to hear our position very clearly," Støre added. "I am worried that some of these messages do not reach him when the Americans talk to him."
Norway, the prime minister said, is looking for ways to de-escalate the conflict, including ending attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine, as well as putting a stop to strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain.
But Støre also emphasized that Ukraine was unlikely to ever sign a peace agreement that would recognize its occupied regions as Russian territory.
"Whether they can take the current frontline as a reality and as a starting point, that is a different question," he told NRK.
"And the big question is what kind of security guarantees can there be for [Ukraine] after a peace deal? Putin recognizes that this is the big question," Støre added.
Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday's call offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict and that European countries were simply seeking to insert themselves in negotiations being led by the United States.

Houthis strike Yemen's Aden airport after evacuation warning
ADEN/DUBAI, Oct 28 - Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden airport on Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said, after the Iran-aligned group warned people to evacuate the facility as fighting escalated in the impoverished country caught in the wider Middle East conflict.
Residents in the southern port city, where the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government is based, said they heard an explosion near the airport, a humanitarian lifeline and the main gateway to southern Yemen.
The Yemeni forces said the attack on the airport caused injuries among civilians and material damage.
Air traffic was halted after the strike, two transport ministry officials told Reuters. An aid source said some UN staff left the airport shortly before the attack and no one was hurt.
A flight with aid workers on-board departed from Aden airport safely on Wednesday morning to Amman before the incident at the airport, two aid sources told Reuters.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the evacuation warning was prompted by what he said was the presence of a Saudi military cargo aircraft delivering weapons.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and most of northwestern Yemen, have repeatedly targeted Aden airport in the past. Residents said explosions had also been heard elsewhere in the city before the warning was issued.
The International Organization for Migration said that its personnel travelling through Aden were safe and accounted for after reports of an attack.
FIGHTING ESCALATES
The attack comes as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has intensified in recent weeks, opening a volatile new front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
Last month, Houthi forces advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most strategically important shipping routes, which lies opposite the Strait of Hormuz across the Arabian Peninsula.
Government forces have since pushed to retake territory on the Red Sea coast in a move that could loosen the Houthis' grip on the chokepoint, while the coalition has stepped up strikes against Houthi positions in response to the group's escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia.
On Tuesday, medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said that one of its aircraft was about to take off from Aden airport a few days ago when humanitarian workers were told to seek shelter as a missile struck nearby.
"Aden airport is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies and medical equipment to the southern parts of Yemen, and safe access to it is crucial," the organisation said in a statement.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that 14 people were killed and 15 others were injured in what it described as a Saudi attack on the northern Yemeni Jawf region.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted major attacks in the conflict, which began after the Houthis drove the government from Sanaa in 2014.
Aid agencies warn the latest violence is rapidly worsening conditions in a country already suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. REUTERS
