Fugitive prosecutor general Kravchenko accuses Ukraine of plotting "violent acts" against him, stays silent on why he has not returned
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:40:00 EET
19:40:00 KST

Fugitive prosecutor general Kravchenko accuses Ukraine of plotting "violent acts" against him, stays silent on why he has not returned
Former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko has claimed that the heads of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) asked for a group to be sent to Austria to carry out "violent acts" against him, supposedly on the orders of the President's Office. However, he did not explain why he had not returned to Ukraine after his official trip.
Source: Kravchenko on social media
Quote: "Back in September, I received information that a group of individuals had been sent after me to carry out unlawful acts of violence against me. I was told directly at the time that the heads of NABU and SAPO had requested that this group be sent."
Details: Kravchenko claimed that two military personnel from Defence Intelligence of Ukraine's (DIU) Artan unit were detained in Austria. He said that one of them had previously worked in NABU's surveillance unit, while the unit's commander, Viktor Torkotiuk, was also in Austria when his subordinates were detained.
Kravchenko also asserted that the group had received orders from the Office of the President.
Quote: "I also know that the orders to this group came from the Office of the President. However, to pre-empt possible speculation, I do not yet have reliable information about who exactly issued the criminal order. According to my information, Torkotiuk was promised a promotion in exchange for this.
I also see parallels with similar events that took place in Monaco this summer. Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General are among those handling that criminal case. I have information about the circumstances of those events."
Details: Kravchenko also singled out journalists from Ukrainska Pravda who had been looking for him in Vienna. He claimed that Austrian authorities are investigating four people, including two UP representatives.
He pointed out that Mykhailo Tkach had been in Monaco shortly before the incident involving DIU personnel and in Vienna during their detention.
"The legal assessment of these circumstances, the links between the individuals involved and the nature of their activities in both cases fall within the remit of European law enforcement authorities," he said.
However, Kravchenko still did not explain why he had not returned to Ukraine after his official trip and remained abroad.
Update: In comments to Interfax-Ukraine and Ukrainska Pravda, NABU rejected Kravchenko's claims, describing them as an attempt to obtain protection abroad.
Previously: The former prosecutor general left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September. According to an order he signed himself, he was due to spend five days in Paris to attend hearings under the auspices of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) on Ukrainian children. However, his name did not appear on the list of participants in the discussion.
His official trip ended on 18 September. Ukrainska Pravda was told by Mariana Haiovska, spokesperson for the Office of the Prosecutor General, that Kravchenko had not returned to work by 21 September.
Background:
- Vienna prosecutors said the detention of Ukrainska Pravda journalists Mykhailo Tkach and Yaroslav Bondarenko was prompted by "eyewitness testimony". UP believes the law enforcement authorities exceeded their powers. The prosecutors did not answer a number of questions, including how they had verified the reliability of the testimony.
- Tkach and Bondarenko were detained on 8 October while carrying out an editorial assignment related to locating Kravchenko. According to Austria's Interior Ministry, Tkach was suspected of espionage, but the suspicion was subsequently not substantiated.
- On 9 October, UP editor-in-chief Sevgil Musaieva reported that Tkach had been released, although the newsroom had not yet been able to contact him. She also said that Bondarenko had been injured during the detention.
- Tkach said that, following their detention, he and his cameraman were accused of three offences: espionage on behalf of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organisation and causing harm to Austria. Tkach described how armed masked men smashed the windows of his car and dragged him and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko out onto the road as they were arrested in Vienna. One of the men then knelt on Tkach's neck as he repeatedly insisted he was a journalist.
- On 14 October, Tkach said that testimony from people linked to Kravchenko might have led to the Ukrainian journalists' detention in Vienna. He said UP had requested materials from the Austrian law enforcement authorities to establish who had provided testimony that may have led to the film crew's detention. He also noted that, by the time of questioning, investigators already knew that the detainees were Ukrainian journalists.
Earlier developments:
- On 29 June, an explosion in Monaco injured sanctioned Ukrainian businessman Vadym Yermolaiev and people close to him. Three people were injured in total, two of them very seriously. Yermolaiev later accused DIU personnel of involvement in the attempted assassination in a letter published by Nice-Matin. He claimed that the attackers had seen his wife and child beside him and suggested that their intention had been to kill all three of them. The businessman called for an independent investigation and asked the authorities in Monaco, Ukraine and France to guarantee his family's protection.
	
Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

Ukrainian MP Poturayev heads OSCE Parliamentary Assembly
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:39:02 EET
19:39:02 KST

Chairman of the Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy Mykyta Poturayev has become President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, reported the press service of the Verkhovna Rada.
"This came as the result of long and coordinated work by the entire Ukrainian delegation in the international arena," Poturayev emphasized during a speech from the rostrum of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.
According to him, this international success would have been impossible without the daily feat and courage of the Defense Forces of Ukraine. He stressed that he perceives his new mandate primarily as an assignment from Ukrainian defenders and commits to not letting them down.
Mykyta Poturayev is a People's Deputy of the Verkhovna Rada of the 9th convocation from the Servant of the People party. He has served as Chairman of the Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy since June 17, 2020.
On July 16, 2026, Poturayev submitted a resignation statement to surrender his parliamentary mandate due to the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Later, following the appointment of Mykhailo Drapaty as Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and Yevhen Khmara as Minister of Defense, he reconsidered surrendering his deputy mandate.
The OSCE PA brings together parliamentarians from the organization's participating states and serves as a platform for discussing issues of security, democracy, human rights, and international cooperation.

Lockheed breaks ground on Alabama factory for ARRW hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:37:25 UTC
19:37:25 KST

Lockheed Martin has broken ground on a factory expansion in Troy, Alabama, that will triple the space it uses to build the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, the U.S. Air Force’s first hypersonic missile to enter production.
The company held the groundbreaking for the expansion of its Building P-20 on Oct. 27, the day after the U.S. Air Force disclosed that it had awarded Lockheed a $694 million contract to produce and field the missile. The project adds 4,366 m² (47,000 square feet) of production space and, according to Lockheed Martin’s announcement, will equip the building for ARRW production with advanced manufacturing processes, robotics and digital technologies, while adding jobs over the next four years to the company’s workforce of almost 4,000 in Alabama.
Lockheed said it spent $67 million of its own money on the facility expansion and production equipment before receiving government funding, as part of an $8 billion to $9 billion investment the company plans through 2030 to meet demand for munitions. It also said it funded the work, materials and equipment needed to start ARRW production ahead of the contract award.
“The ARRW production contract award showcases Lockheed Martin’s ability to develop and begin production on cutting-edge systems at unprecedented speed and scale,” said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control.
The U.S. Air Force signed the contract on Sept. 29 and announced it on Oct. 26, moving its first hypersonic missile from flight testing into production. The service did not disclose how many missiles it ordered or when they are due, citing operational security. ARRW is too large for most fighter aircraft and will first be carried by the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, the platform Lockheed says it is integrated on, and it has also been tested on the B-1.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon. A solid-fuel rocket booster carries it to more than five times the speed of sound, or Mach 5, before the booster drops away and releases a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward its target. That combination of speed and maneuvering makes it harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Lockheed says the weapon uses advanced materials to withstand the extreme heat of hypersonic flight and is designed to strike targets from long standoff ranges.
The production order follows a long development path. Lockheed began work on ARRW under an August 2018 Air Force contract, and in June 2019 a B-52 flew the first captive-carry test of the missile out of Edwards Air Force Base, California. In March 2023, the Air Force said it would not pursue follow-on procurement once prototyping ended, but it continued test flights, including a final end-to-end launch from a B-52 flying out of Guam in March 2024, and in 2025 told Congress it intended to buy the weapon. The fiscal 2026 budget provided $362 million to begin procurement, and the fiscal 2027 request seeks $452 million more, along with funding for an Increment 2 version with a terminal seeker and a data link.
Troy is one of Lockheed Martin’s main munitions sites. Earlier this year the company broke ground on a new Munitions Production Center, Building 47, in Troy to support THAAD interceptor production and future work on the Next-Generation Interceptor, and in 2021 it opened a hypersonic missile assembly facility in nearby Courtland, Alabama.

A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo)
A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage has suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it said. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port on Oct. 28.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew’s status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey’s voyage did not address the second ship.

Ireland High Court overturns Gaza student visa refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:36:20 UTC
19:36:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Ireland High Court overturns Gaza student visa refusal
As dozens of Gazan students wait for their chance to study in Ireland, the country's High Court offered a glimmer of hope on Tuesday by overturning the refusal of a study visa to a Palestinian student in Gaza, citing "significant and demonstrable errors".
Student Shaymaa Abudalu was offered a place at University College Cork to study engineering, but her visa was refused in July, on the grounds that she submitted insufficient documents to support her application.
The case is part of a series of similar lawsuits brought by Palestinian students denied visas by the Minister for Justice, Jim O'Callaghan.
The students took the Irish government to court, with their lawyers arguing that the decision to refuse the study visa was unlawful.
"No student trapped in Gaza should have to take the Minister for Justice to the High Court simply to have documents she already submitted properly considered," Sinead Marmion, lawyer at Phoenix Law, told The New Arab.
Abudalu, who has lived in the Gaza Strip amid Israel's ongoing genocide, has lost several family members, including her mother and siblings.
"Today's judgment exposes a serious failure in the way our client's application was handled. While the ruling turns on the particular circumstances of her case, Jim O'Callaghan should not dismiss this as an isolated mistake," Marmion added.
"We have seen strikingly similar refusals affecting other Palestinian students. The Minister should urgently review those cases rather than force students trapped in Gaza to fight his Department one by one through the courts."
While Monday's ruling does not grant Abudalu a visa, it has quashed the refusal and now requires a new, lawful decision.
The court has ordered the Minister of Justice to reconsider Abudalu's application and issue a fresh decision within 10 working days of receiving it.
The judgement also noted that the next assisted evacuation flight from Gaza is scheduled for 23 November, and that a quick visa decision could allow the student to begin her studies this academic year.
The decision comes amid growing public and legal pressure on the Irish government to grant visas to Gazan students.
The Irish government faced intense scrutiny after it was discovered they had rejected visas for Palestinian students over what lawyers describe as "unrealistic" requirements not being met, such as failure to provide documents, insufficient financial evidence or gaps in education and employment.
According to figures cited in Irish reporting, the Department of Justice refused 114 of 138 Palestinian long-stay study-visa applications this year, an 83 percent refusal rate, including 55 students from Gaza, compared to the 13 percent rate in 2025.
Over 40 prominent Irish artists and public figures, including Nicola Coughlan, Hozier, and Kneecap, signed an open letter calling on the Taoiseach and Government to intervene for the 55 students.

Türkiye is ready to sign an agreement with Egypt on maritime boundary delimitation based on mutual interests, the Turkish National Defense Ministry said Wednesday.
"We once again emphasize that we are ready to sign an Agreement on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas with Egypt in line with mutual interests," it said in a statement.
The potential deal could grant Cairo a larger maritime jurisdiction than a potential agreement with Greece, it added.
"It is assessed that if Egypt signs such an agreement with our country, it would gain more than 15,000 square kilometers (5,792 square miles) of additional maritime jurisdiction compared to a potential agreement it could conclude with Greece."
The ministry stressed that Türkiye would continue protecting its legitimate rights and interests in the Eastern Mediterranean within the framework of international law while contributing to regional peace, security and stability.
The ministry also hailed Libya's approval last week of the memorandum of understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction signed with Türkiye in 2019.
"The approval by the Libyan House of Representatives on Oct. 20 of the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas, signed between our country and Libya in 2019, is an important development supporting our country's approach based on international law and the principles of equity, which takes into account the legitimate rights and interests of the relevant coastal states," the spokesman said.
Developments in Iraq's Sinjar region
During the weekly press briefing at the ministry, spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk welcomed efforts by the Iraqi central government to strengthen state authority and normalize conditions in the Sinjar region.
"Ending the presence of terrorist organizations in the region and ensuring security through Iraq's official security forces is an important development for establishing lasting peace and stability in Sinjar and achieving the goal of a terror-free region," the ministry said.
It added that the process is being closely monitored in coordination with relevant Turkish state institutions.
Bilateral defense cooperation, Kosovo mission
The spokesman stressed the Turkish army continues contributing to regional and global peace, security and stability through cooperation with friendly and allied countries, training and advisory activities, and participation in multinational missions.
He said the Türkiye-Albania Naval Forces Cooperation Meeting is scheduled to take place in Türkiye on Nov. 2-5.
"Under the Türkiye-Greece Confidence-Building Measures Implementation Plan, the commander of the Greek Tactical Air Force and an accompanying delegation will visit our Combat Air Force commander on Nov. 3-5," he said.
He further said that Türkiye assumed the deputy command of the NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR) for a one-year term during a ceremony held Tuesday.
"As during our country's command of KFOR, we will carry out the deputy command with an understanding of impartiality, transparency and professionalism, continuing to contribute to Kosovo's security and the preservation of regional peace and stability," he said.
Military training, exercises
He said national and international training and exercise activities continue uninterrupted to enhance the Turkish Armed Forces' effectiveness and deterrence across land, sea, air, space and cyberspace.
He said the National Anatolian Phoenix Exercise, named after fallen Air Force pilot Major Ibrahim Bolat, is underway in Konya and will conclude on Nov. 6.
The Crossed Swords Exercise, to be conducted in Estonia remotely, will begin on Nov. 2.
He also announced that the Sea of Friendship-2026 Exercise will take place in Alexandria, Egypt, on Nov. 4-9, with the participation of Turkish and Egyptian naval units and personnel.
The exercise will include surface and anti-submarine warfare, air defense operations and underwater offensive training.
He said the Turkish frigates TCG Gokceada and TCG Yildirim will begin their deployment to Somalia on Oct. 30 to transport supplies by sea and conduct personnel rotations.
On the same day, a Turkish airborne early warning and control aircraft will conduct a mission flight in NATO airspace over Romania as part of assurance measures.
Turkish fighter jets will also participate in the Nexus Ace training in the Mediterranean alongside a NATO Awacs aircraft.
New defense systems enter inventory
The spokesperson said Türkiye's domestic defense industry continues strengthening the Turkish Armed Forces' deterrence and operational capabilities through critical systems developed for land, naval, air and cyber operations.
He announced that the Land Forces Command completed inspection and acceptance procedures for various quantities of Karayel Hull Boats and Kablolu Kamikaze-2 uncrewed ground vehicles over the past week.
Turkish defense manufacturer Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation also delivered various quantities of MAM-15 sniper rifles to defense industry stakeholders.
He added that MKE will participate in Euronaval 2026, one of the world's leading international naval defense and maritime technology exhibitions, scheduled for Nov. 3-6 in Paris, France.

Tokyo can create means of delivering nuclear weapons, China says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:15 UTC
19:35:15 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan has the industrial and technical potential to develop delivery systems for nuclear weapons, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
According to him, Japan has been actively expanding its military capabilities in recent years by acquiring advanced US weapons. Besides, it has its own technologies that can be used for military purposes, Dai Huaicheng said.
"Japan has long held a leading position in the world in the field of large launch vehicles, has mastered the key technologies necessary for the development of medium-and long-range ballistic missiles, such as guidance and reentry systems, and also has the technical base for the development of ships with a nuclear power plant," he said.
"This means that if it makes the relevant political decision, Japan will face no insurmountable industrial and technical obstacles either in the field of nuclear warheads or in their delivery systems.
"Japan is the only non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons that possesses nuclear fuel reprocessing technologies, is capable of extracting weapons-grade plutonium and has operating fuel reprocessing facilities, as well as the only country outside the nuclear club that has a full-fledged nuclear fuel cycle. In addition, Japan has a powerful industrial base and economic potential, which theoretically enable it to produce and obtain nuclear materials using existing reactors and reprocessing technologies to manufacture nuclear explosive devices."
According to Dai Huaicheng, Japan has been building up its military potential in recent years with support from the US military industry.
"As for the means of delivery, the F-35A, F-15 and F-2 fighters in service with the Japan Air Self-Defense Forces are potentially capable of carrying nuclear bombs. Japan has also decided to purchase several hundred Tomahawk cruise missiles, modify the launchers on ships equipped with the Aegis combat information management system, and deploy US Typhon medium-range ground-based missiles," he said.

Defence official flagged plans for social media ban request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:33:20 UTC
19:33:20 KST

Defence official who sought to block social media clips claimed she flagged plans with minister
In short:
A senior defence official who sought to block the use of clips from parliamentary hearings on social media claimed in emails she had support from a government minister.
In an email obtained under FOI, Celia Perkins wrote that Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil was "fully supportive" of the plan.
Another government official has since raised concerns that the editing and sharing of social media clips from hearings invited "ridicule and hostility" towards public servants.
A senior Department of Defence official said she had approval from a government minister to try to block the public release of her evidence to a parliamentary hearing due to concerns about "vile" social media commentary.
Deputy secretary Celia Perkins said she had approval from Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil when she told a parliamentary committee hearing last month that she did not "consent" to her evidence appearing on social media.
The request was swiftly rejected by committee chair senator Jess Collins, on advice from parliamentary officials.
"It is our right as senators and members of the public to disseminate the evidence that is provided by the witnesses today in the manner in which we see fit," Senator Collins said.
Emails between Defence officials ahead of the hearing, obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, reveal Ms Perkins told colleagues she raised her plans to make the statement with Mr Khalil and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles's office two days before the hearing.
"(Department secretary Meghan Quinn) is fully supportive, as is AMINDEF. I discussed today in a meeting with AMINDEF and staff from DPMO and his office," she wrote in the email.
"I'll pass the opening statement to them tomorrow."
AMINDEF refers to Mr Khalil, and DPMO is the Deputy Prime Minister's office.
The ABC understands Mr Marles's office provided no input to Ms Perkins's statement before she made it. Comment has been sought from both Mr Khalil and Mr Marles.
During a Senate estimates hearing this week, Senate Clerk Richard Pye was asked about the advice he provided the committee after Ms Perkins request.
"It's absolutely not something that a witness can do," he said.
"It was profoundly unhelpful, I thought on the day, for the matter to be raised in that way without any notice to anybody, not through the secretariat, not to the chair and not to other members of the committee."
But he added that there were genuine concerns about the effect of footage from committee hearings on social media.
"This is not to minimise the fact that there are some people who have been very bruised by their experiences before Senate and House committees and the treatment of footage that has come out of those," he said.
Concerns over 'vile' commentary
The emails reveal some of the reasoning Ms Perkins put forward before her request.
In an email to Ms Quinn a week before the hearing, she raised her plans.
"You may recall after the last hearing we had some unpleasant social media posts and reactions," she wrote.
"I also want to test with you this idea: I'd like to add an explicit statement that the Defence witnesses appearing do not consent to our evidence being reproduced in edited format on social media platforms."
She said the main argument was that she had to maintain a "safe workplace" for Defence staff, and that online commentary could be "distressing".
"Social media posts using footage from previous hearings in edited and embellished formats had generated significant vile, personal commentary that was distressing for staff and invited online bullying," she said.
Ms Perkins also suggested the posts could raise security concerns, including assisting foreign espionage.
"As senior leaders in Defence — we actively discourage security clearance holders from a social media presence that identifies us and our roles — and these post (sic), designed to invite outraged responses, increase the personal risk from malign online actors, including cyber and foreign intelligence threats."
While Ms Perkins's request was immediately shut down, the Secretaries Board, made up of all federal government departmental secretaries, soon after took up the issue, suggesting new standards were needed to guide the use of evidence given to parliamentary hearings online.
This week Steven Kennedy, head of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, told estimates he did not support censoring footage, but did have concerns.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.

French Senate adopts bill requiring protesters to pay for damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:32:20 UTC
19:32:20 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The French Senate adopted a bill, known as the "rioters-pay," which seeks to hold protesters participating in violent gatherings responsible for damage caused, broadcaster Public Senat reported Wednesday.
The Senate adopted the bill overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday by 229 votes to 105. It seeks "compensation for damage resulting from violence or damage committed in public spaces and the recovery of damages.”
The bill was initially presented as a response to the violence that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory in May and later evolved due to scenes of vandalism and looting during demonstrations that took place on Oct. 17.
The bill reportedly won broad support from the Senate’s right-wing majority but drew criticism from the left, which argued that it undermined several constitutionally protected principles, including freedom of assembly, freedom of expression, and the individualization of penalties.
The bill allows individuals who participated in violent gatherings to be held jointly liable for damages, even if they were not directly responsible for the destruction. The state could seek up to €10,000 ($11,000) in compensation per person.
It also permits the seizure of part of family allowances, housing assistance and France’s minimum-income benefit to recover damages owed.
The Senate also approved an amendment allowing authorities to request the removal of online content likely to cause serious public disorder, particularly material inciting violence, vandalism, or insurrection.
Under the measure, social media platforms would have 24 hours to remove such content or face blocking or delisting.
The Senate further approved tougher security measures, including new administrative bans on demonstrations, additional penalties barring foreign nationals from French territory, harsher sentences, expanded use of judicial drones and algorithmic video surveillance, and evictions from social housing for troublemakers.
The bill will now be examined by the National Assembly, where political divisions could complicate its legislative passage.

The European Commission estimates that non-EU allies have pledged only €4 billion ($4.3 billion) in aid for Kyiv next year, a sharp drop from €19 billion ($20.5 billion) in 2026, while G7 members the US, UK, Canada, and Japan are set to contribute just €1 billion ($1.1 billion) combined, according to a Financial Times analysis.
Kyiv states it faces a €70 billion ($75.5 billion) financing gap next year, a figure confirmed by the European Commission that includes military funding following the final delivery of Biden-era weaponry, while US President Donald Trump has ended all direct US financial support for Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Additionally, NATO’s 32 members remain €13 billion ($14 billion) short of their commitment to provide €70 billion ($75.5 billion) in military assistance to Ukraine, with the EU and its member states currently accounting for 80 percent of all pledged support for 2027.
In response to the expected drop in financial aid from non-EU nations, Brussels is applying diplomatic pressure on G7 partners including Ottawa, Tokyo, and London to increase their funding commitments.
European Commission officials are developing emergency plans to secure alternative funding sources to maintain Ukraine’s financial stability next year, including options such as issuing joint debt, which will be discussed at a summit in late November, as reported by the Financial Times.
EU leaders previously agreed at an October summit to seek additional support for Ukraine’s 2027 needs and urged international partners to rapidly increase their aid.
A Commission spokesperson stated that “Europe cannot meet Ukraine’s financing needs alone. International partners must also step up, including NATO allies.”
Meanwhile, UK Chancellor John Healey remarked that it was time to “step up support for Ukraine” and noted that he was “very acutely aware of that bigger picture and the pressures on Ukraine,” adding that “the future of Ukraine is the future of European security.”
On July 15, the European Union released a new installment of military assistance worth €1 billion ($1.14 billion) to Ukraine for the purchase of drones under the Support for Ukraine Loan for 2026–2027.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed during a joint press conference in Kyiv that the EU’s broader €90 billion ($102.91 billion) loan program had become fully operational, with more than a third designated for Ukrainian defense production.

US midterms: Six days left – who leads in the polls as Trump, Obama rally
Democrats lead national polls as Trump and Obama campaign in key states six days before the US midterm elections.
With six days to go before the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, Democrats are leading Republicans in national polls, but several key Senate races seem too close to call.
President Donald Trump has stepped up his campaigning, holding two Republican rallies in Texas on Tuesday before heading to Ohio on Wednesday. Ex-President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris are also hitting the campaign trail in Georgia for the Democratic Party.
Here is what the latest polls say, what happened on the campaign trail and what to expect on Wednesday.
What do the latest polls suggest?
With less than a week to go before the midterms, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests the Democrats are ahead of the Republicans by nine points.
According to the October 22-26 survey, 47 percent of voters support the Democrats, compared with 36 percent who support the Republicans. When undecided voters’ leanings were taken into account, Democrats lead with 50 percent compared with Republicans’ 41 percent.
Trump’s approval rating improved by a percentage point to 32 percent, with 73 percent of US adults saying the cost of living was going in the wrong direction.
In Texas, where Democrats have not won a Senate election since 1988, James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are virtually tied in the polls.
Trump has made several trips to the state ahead of the midterms, but the polls indicate a much tighter race than the president has suggested.
“The good people of Texas have probably never seen so much of President Trump. Four visits in seven weeks, which, to put that into context, is twice as many as we saw at the comparable period leading up to the 2024 election, which perhaps shows just how concerned Republicans are,” Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle said, reporting from the Texas coastal city of Corpus Christi.
Lavelle said local analysis suggested more Republicans have voted early than Democrats, but Talarico has also been courting Republicans dissatisfied with Trump.
“That doesn’t mean Republicans are voting for Republican candidates,” Lavelle said.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are also competing in a closely contested Senate race.
“I was a Republican forever, but I became an independent in the last two elections,” Michael Alexander, a Native American backing El-Sayed, told Al Jazeera.
“I don’t really vote for a party any more. I vote for who I think will do the best job.”
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but Republican incumbent Roger Marshall now faces a close contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton.
The race has brought Trump and his deputy, JD Vance, to the state.
“There’s a reason why we’re seeing not only US President Donald Trump but also Vice President JD Vance heading to Kansas because it’s actually in play,” Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said.
According to The Associated Press news agency, both parties and their allied groups have committed about $71m to campaign advertising in the Kansas race, making it the most expensive Senate contest in the state’s history.
What happened in the US midterm campaigns over the past 24 hours?
Trump addressed two campaign rallies in Texas on Tuesday in support of Paxton.
In Corpus Christi, Trump pointed to a tanker that he said was carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan oil and called it a win for his administration. He also suggested the idea of making Venezuela the 51st US state. The Trump administration has signed an oil deal with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez, after abducting socialist President Nicolas Maduro in a military operation in January.
Trump also announced plans to roll back the Biden-era restrictions on methane emissions from oil and gas production, stating that it would help bring down energy prices.
Fuel prices have become a huge election issue as the US-Israel war on Iran continues. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also joined Trump for a rare campaign-trail appearance in Texas.
In Alaska, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski has backed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor rather than Bernadette Wilson, the Trump-endorsed candidate.
What’s next for Democrats and Republicans on Wednesday?
Trump heads to Ohio on Wednesday for his third rally in the state this month, as Republicans try to defend a Senate seat being challenged by former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.
The US president is scheduled to speak in Chillicothe at 23:00 GMT. Republican Senator Jon Husted, who took over Vance’s seat when he became vice president, is facing Brown, who is seeking a return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024.
The two are in a closely contested race, with more than $400m spent or reserved for campaign advertising as of October 8, according to an Axios report.
Republicans are particularly concerned in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa, where even a few percentage points for a third party could swing the outcome.
Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Ohio on Wednesday and Iowa on Sunday.
Vance will be in Kinston, North Carolina, campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper. The vice president is expected to speak at 16:30 GMT.
In Georgia, former President Obama will campaign in Atlanta alongside Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms at 20:00 GMT.
Ossoff is running against Republican Mike Collins, while Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in the governor’s race. Trump won Georgia in the 2024 presidential election.
Former Vice President Harris also begins a three-day visit to Georgia on Wednesday, with early in-person voting due to end on Friday, October 30.
In Wisconsin, Marquette Law School will publish its latest statewide poll at 18:15 GMT.
Wednesday’s poll will also examine voters’ views on inflation, tariffs, the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s presidency.

Norway and Finland hold rare phone call with Putin: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:31:22 UTC
19:31:22 KST

Norway and Finland hold rare phone call with Putin: What that means
The two Nordic leaders are attempting to influence US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi to end the war in Ukraine.
The leaders of Norway and Finland have held a rare call with Russian President Vladimir Putin to push for an end to the war in Ukraine, ahead of a planned round of United States-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi next month.
The call on Tuesday marked a break from a longstanding policy among Western European heads of state to avoid direct talks with the Russian leader.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere spoke with Putin for 90 minutes.
Here’s what we know.
What was behind the call?
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday that direct talks between the Russian and Ukrainian presidents would happen “very soon”. But with Trump increasingly siding with Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Western leaders have been largely sidelined from US-led negotiations to end the Ukraine war.
Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had “manoeuvred themselves into a dead end” when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday’s call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue.
The Nordic leaders are hoping to influence the diplomatic process, following a policy shift by US President Donald Trump in favour of Russia. US ties with Ukraine have sunk to their lowest point in 18 months since Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities for the rise in the cost of diesel, which has doubled in the US this year.
Trump struck a deal with Putin to release Russian diesel stocks to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil. He also waived newly approved US sanctions on Russia, causing anger in Europe and within his Republican Party, which had largely supported them.
Ukraine also accused the US of restricting its access to Starshield, the military-grade Starlink satellite system that provides missile guidance intelligence.
What happened during the conversation?
Stubb described the discussion with Putin as “frank and substantive”.
“We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” the Finnish president said.
Stoere said he and Stubb had “stressed the importance of de-escalation” to Putin.
In a post on X, Stubb said the call “was a follow-up to the meeting in Oslo on 20 October”, referring to talks between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelenskyy, held amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv. Stubb said the conversation with Putin was prepared “in consultation with Ukraine and the United States .
Stubb stressed that the joint call was held in individual capacities as leaders of Norway and Finland, not as representatives of Europe.
“We emphasised that our support for Ukraine remains unwavering,” Stubb said.
Stubb said all Western allies were consulted on the initiative, and that Ukraine had sought the opening of a new channel of communication, arguing that Europe could not contribute to peace efforts by giving Russia “the silent treatment”.
Norway’s Prime Minister Stoere added: “Talking to the other side does in no way mean that we take off the pressure. So I believe that that is something Europe also should do with voices that can be understood on that side.”
The conversation with Putin was followed up with a call to Zelenskyy.
How did Putin respond to the call?
The Kremlin’s summary of the conversation suggests the Russian president maintained a hard line.
“It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” it said.
The Kremlin also made reference to “the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the call was “constructive and substantive” adding that “Putin’s position is well known. It’s consistent, and he has spoken about the need to address the root causes.”
But Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the Nordic leaders’ call with Putin offered “nothing new” to end the Ukraine conflict, saying that European countries were simply seeking a role in negotiations.
Meanwhile, responding to proposals for direct talks between Putin and Zelenskyy, Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov said: “The current leader in Kyiv is not legitimate.”
“If Zelenskyy truly wants to hold direct talks, he should come to Moscow, where all necessary conditions will be provided for him, including security,” Ushakov added.
How have European countries reacted?
The Norwegian and Finnish leaders’ call with Putin was greeted with scepticism by some European leaders.
“My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation,” Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson told local media.
He said some European leaders had not been informed.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warned against individual diplomatic approaches to Moscow, saying European countries must maintain a united position. “I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” she said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he told Stubb and Stoere that “absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts”.
In a post on X, Lithuania’s Foreign Affairs Minister Kestutis Budrys said Europe must be at the table when peace in Ukraine is negotiated, “but not as a collection of fragmented voices”.
“Any contact with Russia must be backed by a united position, real leverage and a list of European demands,” Budrys said.

Ukraine’s Drone Hunters Take Down Russia’s Rare $100,000 “Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg” UAV Over Sumy Region
Ukrainian forces have shot down a Russian “Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg” drone valued at approximately $100,000, alongside a significant number of other Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 21st Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on October 26 that its interceptor drone units destroy dozens of Russian UAVs daily, targeting aircraft used by Russian forces to carry out repeated attacks against civilians in the region.
The brigade also reported intercepting numerous Russian Molniya drones, noting that although these UAVs are relatively inexpensive to produce, they can inflict significant damage.
“Our brigade’s interceptor drone crews shoot down dozens of enemy drones every day, which Russian forces continuously use to terrorize residents of the Sumy region,” the brigade added.
The Russian-developed “Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg” drone has a maximum speed of 130 km/h, an operating altitude of up to 100 meters, and a flight range of 45 kilometers.
According to Russian sources, one of the drone’s key advantages is its reported survivability, partly attributed to its resemblance to Ukrainian UAVs, which can make it difficult for Ukrainian troops to identify.
The drone is designed to conduct reconnaissance, adjust artillery fire, and assess the results of strikes carried out by other UAVs.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone units have continued targeting Russian military logistics, including a recent strike on a convoy carrying vehicles and fuel supplies.
On October 27, Ukraine’s 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems reported that operators from its Signum Battalion had destroyed three Russian Ural military trucks and two fuel tankers, forcing accompanying mobile fire teams to seek cover.
The strike came despite Russian efforts to disperse logistics operations following repeated Ukrainian middle-strike attacks. Russian troops reportedly assembled the convoy under the protection of pickup trucks carrying mobile fire teams, leaving the vehicles vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The party's letter is classified in the ministry's document register as being for internal use only, under a provision covering information containing personal data whose disclosure could significantly harm the data subject's privacy.
The replacement is not in itself unexpected: the foundation's board traditionally includes representatives of the relevant ministries, parties represented at the Riigikogu, and experts in the field, and Jašin had been from the second of these categories.

SDE was in office with Reform and Eesti 200 until spring last year and has a representative on the XXX board in Henri Kaselo, formerly Kohtla-Järve's mayor.
Jašin was a member of Eesti 200 from November 19, 2018 until October 2, 2026, and joined SDE on October 14. Before the switch he had been discussed as a possible new leader of Eesti 200, and is a former Tallinn deputy mayor.
The Integration Foundation (Integratsiooni Sihtasutus) supports the development of an integrated and cohesive society as a competence center in the field, with both foreign residents of Estonia and Estonians living outside the country being in its target groups, the organization says on its website.

Kowloon leads as 70% of Hong Kong’s subdivided flats registered for grace period

About 70 per cent of subdivided flats in Hong Kong have been registered for a grace period under a new law aimed at eradicating substandard homes, with most submissions coming from landlords in Kowloon’s Yau Tsim Mong district, according to the Housing Bureau.
The bureau told the Legislative Council on Wednesday that 75,070 subdivided homes across about 21,000 whole flats had been registered for the three-year grace period since applications opened in March under the new Basic Housing Units Ordinance.

Turkic world integration among Kazakhstan’s foreign policy priorities, foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:30:17 UTC
19:30:17 KST

Kazakhstan attaches importance to developing comprehensive cooperation with Türkiye and strengthening ties within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), with the integration of the Turkic world among the country’s key foreign policy priorities, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said.
Tileuberdi spoke to Anadolu ahead of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Ankara on Wednesday and the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, to be hosted by Türkiye.
Noting that the current international environment is shaped by profound geopolitical changes, transformations in the global economy, and intensifying technological competition, Tileuberdi stressed the growing importance of relations based on mutual trust, respect for national interests, and a willingness to act jointly.
“Kazakhstan and Türkiye are united by centuries-old historical ties, spiritual affinity, shared cultural traditions, and the rich linguistic heritage of the Turkic world,” he said.
“Today, bilateral relations have acquired the character of an expanded strategic partnership covering political dialogue, trade, investment, energy, transport, industry, education, digital technologies, and other areas. At the current stage, the most important task is to resolutely continue transforming the accumulated political capital into tangible economic results, new production facilities, employment opportunities, and long-term projects,” he added.
Tileuberdi described Tokayev’s visit to Ankara as a natural continuation of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s state visit to Astana in May.
He recalled that the two leaders signed a Declaration on Eternal Friendship and Expanded Strategic Partnership during Erdogan’s visit to the Kazakh capital.
Emphasizing Kazakhstan’s commitment to expanding cooperation with Türkiye on the basis of shared historical and cultural values, Tileuberdi said relations between the two countries were developing steadily across all areas of cooperation.
“Consistent political dialogue" between Tokayev and Erdogan "determines the strategic direction of bilateral cooperation and creates favorable conditions for implementing comprehensive joint projects,” he said.
“The priority is therefore not only to preserve the level of relations achieved so far, but also to adapt the bilateral partnership in a timely manner to new international conditions,” he added.
Describing Türkiye as one of Kazakhstan’s main trade, economic, and investment partners, Tileuberdi said bilateral trade volume rose 66.5% in the first eight months of 2026 from the same period last year, reaching $5.66 billion.
Kazakhstan’s exports to Türkiye nearly doubled during the period to $4.75 billion, he said, adding that the figures demonstrated significant potential for further expanding economic ties.
Tileuberdi stressed the importance of diversifying products, removing non-tariff barriers, and facilitating trade procedures to increase bilateral trade volume. He also said investment cooperation between the two countries is developing actively.
Turkish investments in Kazakhstan have exceeded $6 billion, while Kazakh investments in Türkiye have surpassed $2.5 billion, he said.
More than 100 joint projects have been implemented in Kazakhstan, while over 50 projects are being implemented and negotiations are ongoing for another 70, he added.
Over 4,000 companies with Turkish capital operate in Kazakhstan, which Tileuberdi described as an important indicator of Turkish investors’ confidence in the country.
He said Kazakhstan will continue developing mechanisms to support investors, protect their rights, and establish a predictable, long-term business environment. The country provides support throughout the investment process, from identifying suitable locations for production facilities to implementing projects, he added.
Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan had played a leading role in establishing the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States, which later evolved into the Organization of Turkic States.
He said Kazakhstan had consistently supported the development of the organization’s institutional structure and efforts to raise its international profile.
“Kazakhstan has regularly hosted various events within the framework of the OTS. In this regard, I would like to recall that the first summit of the Organization of Turkic States was held in Almaty in 2011, while its most recent informal summit was successfully held in May this year in Turkistan, the spiritual capital of the Turkic world,” he said.
Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan had taken a leading role in initiatives including the establishment of the Coordination Committee of Turkic Cooperation Organizations, the preparation of the Turkic World Vision 2040 document, and the creation of a mechanism for permanent representatives to the OTS.
Kazakhstan had also initiated the establishment of the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY), the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), the Turkic Academy, and the Turkic Investment Fund, he said.
“These institutions have contributed to the development of scientific research, the promotion of cultural exchange, and the expansion of practical cooperation among countries,” he added.
Tileuberdi said the OTS reached a new level of institutional development during the 2018-2022 tenure of Kazakh representative Baghdad Amreyev as its secretary-general.
He recalled that Uzbekistan was admitted as a full member, while Hungary and Turkmenistan received observer status. An OTS representation office opened in Budapest, and the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry was established in Istanbul, he added.
Assessing Kazakhstan’s policy toward the Turkic world, Tileuberdi said the country was the successor to the Golden Horde and the ancestral homeland of Turkic peoples connected by shared culture, language, and traditions.
“This important factor underlies the natural rapprochement between Turkic countries and peoples. Since gaining independence, our country has attached great importance to Turkic integration,” he said.
“The integration of the Turkic world is one of the important priorities of Kazakhstan’s foreign policy. The Organization of Turkic States holds an important place among regional cooperation platforms, alongside the United Nations and other multilateral organizations,” he added.
Referring to Tokayev’s statement that the OTS “is not a geopolitical project or a military alliance and should not be used as a tool against other states,” Tileuberdi said Turkic integration should contribute to strengthening regional stability, expanding economic opportunities, and developing constructive dialogue with external partners.
He described economic cooperation as one of the organization’s main areas of activity and said Kazakhstan’s trade with OTS member states had been growing steadily.
Trade between Kazakhstan and OTS members increased 42% in the first eight months of this year to $10 billion, he said.
Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan had established the Turan Special Economic Zone in Turkistan as an initiative to attract investment, develop industry and strengthen infrastructure.
“Mutual recognition of electronic documents, harmonization of customs systems, digitization of certificates of origin, and the simplification of border-crossing procedures will reduce time and cost losses in trade transactions,” he said.
“In the long term, we aim to create a more closely interconnected economic environment in which companies from OTS member states can find business partners more quickly, obtain market information, and implement joint projects,” he added.
Tileuberdi said the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, was particularly important both for Kazakhstan and the wider Turkic world.
As demand grows for the Middle Corridor, an alternative transport route between Asia and Europe, its strategic importance is increasing, he said, adding that Kazakhstan is working to expand the capacity of its railways, ports, and border-crossing points.
Tileuberdi stressed that the corridor’s efficiency depended not only on the capacity of individual sections within each country but also on coordination among all countries involved in the transport process.
He said joint steps were needed to digitize logistics procedures and reduce administrative costs.
Cargo volumes transported through the Middle Corridor have increased more than fivefold over the past five years, while delivery times have fallen to one-third of their previous duration, Tileuberdi said.
“These figures demonstrate growing demand for the corridor and the need to further expand its capacity. Kazakhstan aims to increase annual cargo volumes transported through the Middle Corridor to 10 million tons by 2030,” he said.
Tileuberdi said Turkic integration should be developed on the basis of pragmatism, mutual respect, and equal consideration of the interests of all participating states.
He also shared Kazakhstan’s expectations for the upcoming OTS summit in Ankara.
“We view the Ankara summit from a broad perspective. We hope that the summit will not only reaffirm the determination of the states to deepen cooperation, but also provide an opportunity to set concrete goals for joint work in the future,” he said.

British submarine command course has not run for a year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:30:15 GMT
19:30:15 KST

No Submarine Command Course has taken place since November 2025, and the Royal Navy schedules the course to maintain sufficient suitably qualified personnel to meet defence requirements, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the reason no course had run since then, following up an answer given on 16 October.
Calvin Bailey, the Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Royal Navy schedules the Submarine Command Course to maintain sufficient suitably qualified personnel to meet Defence requirements.”
The Submarine Command Course, known throughout the service as Perisher, is the qualifying course for command of a British submarine. Candidates who pass take command appointments; those who fail leave the submarine service and, by tradition, leave the boat immediately. It is run by the Submarine Command Course Teacher, a serving officer who holds that post, and combines attack training in simulators with sea phases against surface ships.
Royal Navy submarine availability has been under scrutiny for some time, with the Defence Committee reporting this month that it is not clear the attack submarine force is putting to sea as often as it should, and ministers declining to put availability figures on the public record.

Pro-European Union campaigners hold flags near parliament as Britain's Prime Minister attends the weekly session of Prime Ministers Questions in London on May 20, 2026. (AP File Photo)
For a decade, British governments have observed a cardinal rule: Don’t mention Brexit. In particular, don’t suggest that voters’ 2016 decision to leave the European Union should be reversed.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who marked his 100th day in office on Oct. 27, has broken that code of silence and reignited a debate that bitterly divided the country. He says Brexit has been a failure and the U.K. should seek a much closer relationship with the EU, with options up to and including rejoining the 27-nation bloc.
“I am positive about closer ties with Europe and I’m not hiding that,” Burnham told the Sunday Times. “I think it will add to British GDP. I think it will give us stronger control of migration. I want to make those arguments.”
In recent interviews, Burnham has said the country should have an “evidence-based debate” about the consequences of Brexit. He gave the example of immigration. Supporters of Brexit argued that it would give the country control over its borders by ending the right of EU citizens to live and work in the U.K., and of British nationals to settle across the bloc.
While Britain now sets its own immigration policy, Burnham said leaving the bloc had made it harder to control unauthorized migration because Britain has lost access to EU databases and agreements.
“The truth of the matter is we’ve lost immigration control in the way that we once had,” Burnham told broadcaster ITV on Oct. 26.
Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy, but few politicians have wanted to reopen the painful debate.
The decision of British voters, by 52 percent to 48 percent, to leave the bloc after four decades of membership was followed by years of U.K.-EU wrangling over divorce terms. Britain finally left the EU in 2020 with a bare-bones trade deal that erected new barriers to doing business with the bloc of 450 million people on the U.K.’s doorstep.
In seeking closer ties, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Burnham says that could change after the next national election, which must be held by 2029.
He told the Labour Party’s annual conference last month that “Brexit has done more harm than good” and he will seek political consensus on a new relationship, with future options including rejoining the bloc.

Luminous viewpoint by Ryue Nishizawa rises within Japanese landfill site
A giant orange cone designed by Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa acts as an observation deck at this large recycling complex on Shikoku island in Japan.
Nishizawa, co-founder of Japanese studio SANAA, positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin at Oono Associates, a recycling complex in the city of Toon, and open up this closed-off industrial space to the public.
Named Observatory, it was created for the inaugural edition of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, an art and architecture festival held across industrial sites in Japan.
Specifically, it forms part of the Landscapes of Waste – A landscape shaped by nature, industry, and people exhibition, curated by Nishizawa’s studio partner Kazuyo Sejima, with whom he founded SANAA in 1995.
Nishizawa positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin within the vast recycling complex in Toon, Ehime, revealing the closed-off industrial setting to the public.
The bright orange cone measures 33 metres in diameter and four metres in height. Its size was intended to emulate an artificial hill.
Its luminous orange finish was chosen to deliberately contrast the blue-green hues of the surrounding landfill lining and landscape beyond it.
The platform encourages visitors to observe how the landscape is shaped by nature and human activity, and experience the processes of material circulation at the recycling plant.
Alongside Nishizawa’s observation platform, the Landscapes of Waste exhibition includes bus stops by architectural studio Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa Otsubo, as well as buses and visitor workwear by Suzuko Yamada Architects.
Visitors are required to take these buses to the site and put on the workwear, as seen in the photos. The festival team said this brings “visitors themselves into the composition of the landscape”.
“Together, these interventions invite a closer encounter with the relationship between nature, industrial infrastructure and human activity,” it added.
Setouchi Art and Industry 2026 was organised by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation. Artists and architects were invited to work with industrial sites across Okayama and the Ehime prefecture on Shikoku to create a “decentralised museum” that opens these settings to the public.
Its inaugural edition runs until 31 October across seven venues, which also include a salt production site, a textile factory, a shipbuilder and a battery manufacturer.
“Developed through collaboration between artists and participating companies, the exhibitions offer access to industrial spaces usually closed to the public, revealing the technologies, materials and people behind everyday life,” said Setouchi Art and Industry.
“We hope that many people, including the younger generation, will re-examine Japan’s industries from a fresh perspective and discover the charm and potential hidden within them,” added Japan Industrial Art Foundation director Masahiro Ito.
Other recent projects by SANAA include the Taichung Green Museumbrary in Taiwan and a proposal for the National Museum of Ecuador.

NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:29:36 UTC
19:29:36 KST

NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- The Henryk Niewodniczanski Institute of Nuclear Physics Polish Academy of Sciences
- Summary:
- NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration.
- Share:
NASA's Artemis I mission has provided new insights into how much cosmic radiation astronauts may encounter near the Moon compared with low Earth orbit. Using experimental detectors made from lithium fluoride crystals aboard the Orion spacecraft, researchers have obtained preliminary measurements that reveal unexpected differences in radiation exposure between the two environments.
During the uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022, Orion traveled around the Moon carrying more than 10,000 tiny crystals embedded inside two human-shaped mannequins. These devices recorded radiation exposure throughout the journey. Among them were several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors created by scientists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. The researchers have now described a new method for analyzing the information stored in these crystals, offering insights into both cosmic radiation levels and the performance of the detectors. Their findings were published in the journal Radiation Measurements.
"The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope," explains Prof. Pawel Bilski (IFJ PAN), one of the co-authors of the paper.
How Tiny Crystals Detect Cosmic Radiation
The lithium fluoride detectors work by capturing microscopic changes caused by radiation. When electrically charged particles pass through a crystal, they disrupt its internal atomic structure, creating defects known as color centers. Scientists can later illuminate the crystal with blue light, causing these altered regions to glow red. By examining that fluorescence under a microscope, researchers can identify the paths taken by individual radiation particles.
The detectors were part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study conducted during Artemis I. Several dozen experimental lithium fluoride detectors were placed inside both mannequins, including some containing high concentrations of the lithium-7 isotope. The contribution from IFJ PAN extended beyond these experimental devices. Its scientists also supplied nearly 600 thermoluminescent crystal detectors, which use a different technique to measure radiation exposure.
One major advantage of the new lithium fluoride detectors is that they simplify the process of examining radiation tracks. Traditional passive detectors made from plastic require chemical etching before scientists can study the marks left by incoming particles. Lithium fluoride crystals eliminate that step, allowing researchers to inspect the tracks directly with a standard fluorescence microscope.
As a result, observing the radiation tracks collected near the Moon was relatively straightforward. The more difficult task was determining exactly what those tracks revealed about radiation exposure. To obtain reliable numerical measurements, the team had to develop sophisticated calibration and analysis techniques.
Why Measuring Deep Space Radiation Is So Difficult
Unlike the controlled conditions of a laboratory, cosmic radiation is highly unpredictable. In a typical physics experiment, researchers can expose a detector to a beam containing a known type of particle with a specific energy and direction. In space, radiation arrives from every direction and includes many different particles and atomic nuclei traveling across an enormous range of energies.
This complexity makes the microscopic tracks difficult to interpret. Because incoming particles strike the crystals at different angles, their tracks extend in multiple directions. A microscope captures the section of each track within its focal plane (approximately one micrometer in size), but it also records a blurry glow from portions outside that narrow region. This additional light influences the measured fluorescence intensity, which scientists use to estimate how densely a particle ionizes the material.
Different particles also produce very different track patterns. Those that cause strong ionization leave continuous, sharply defined lines, while particles that produce weaker ionization may appear as scattered, disconnected dots. These differences further complicate the task of translating fluorescence measurements into meaningful radiation data.
To overcome these challenges, the researchers introduced several corrections and developed software capable of removing unwanted background signals. The improved analysis brought their measurements into close agreement with results from established detector technologies while also revealing radiation events that older devices could not detect.
"After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date," Prof. Bilski emphasizes.
Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Difference in Moon Radiation
The Artemis I measurements also allowed researchers to compare radiation exposure near the Moon with findings from an earlier experiment aboard the International Space Station.
More than a decade before Artemis I, the MATROSHKA experiment investigated radiation exposure using human-shaped mannequins on the space station. Some of the radiation recorded during that mission came from low-energy protons trapped within Earth's Van Allen radiation belts. As these particles traveled into the mannequins, they deposited energy at different depths, producing an uneven distribution of radiation doses.
Conditions near the Moon are substantially different. The Van Allen belts do not extend into the lunar environment, so the radiation encountered there contains a greater contribution from high-energy particles originating elsewhere in the galaxy.
These galactic particles carry enough energy to travel through the entire human body, releasing only a portion of their energy as they pass. Consequently, the Artemis I detectors recorded radiation doses that were distributed almost uniformly throughout the mannequins, unlike the uneven patterns observed in the earlier space station experiment.
The researchers also identified a finding that may seem counterintuitive. Although astronauts near the Moon are exposed to more radiation than those in low Earth orbit, the difference is not necessarily as dramatic as might be assumed.
"Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet's magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect," Prof. Bilski notes.
New Radiation Detectors Could Help Protect Future Astronauts
The fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors aboard Artemis I were manufactured using the Czochralski method, a technique for growing crystals. Scientists at IFJ PAN first developed the technology about a decade ago and have continued refining it ever since.
Their compact size is one of their most useful features. Measuring just a few millimeters rather than several centimeters (on the order of millimeters rather than centimeters), the detectors are small enough to be worn comfortably by people, making them practical for monitoring radiation exposure during space missions.
They also provide sharper images of particle tracks than conventional plastic detectors that require chemical etching. This improved resolution allows scientists to distinguish individual tracks even when radiation doses are relatively high. In addition, the crystals can register a broad variety of particle types and energies, potentially providing a more complete picture of the radiation environment.
Another advantage is their ability to detect neutrons, particularly when the crystals are enriched with the lithium-6 isotope. When neutrons interact with lithium nuclei, they can trigger nuclear reactions that generate secondary charged particles. These particles leave detectable changes in the crystal, much like other forms of ionizing radiation.
Together, these capabilities make lithium fluoride detectors a promising tool for studying the complex radiation environment beyond Earth. The measurements from Artemis I offer a clearer picture of how cosmic radiation behaves near the Moon and demonstrate how compact detectors could help scientists evaluate radiation exposure during future missions.
The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

“There was a proposal to create a buffer zone or a demilitarized zone on both sides of the line of contact,” Zelensky said.
He traced the discussions back to the American 28-point peace plan, saying the ideas had subsequently evolved across different documents.
For Donbas, the proposal envisaged a zone extending in both directions from the front line. Zelensky described Ukraine’s willingness to discuss it as a potential compromise.
A separate proposal concerned demilitarizing part of the Kinburn Spit, in Ukraine’s southern Mykolaiv region, which could remain under Ukrainian control.
Other American suggestions addressed the future of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant and possible territorial exchanges, described during negotiations as land swaps.
Zelensky said Washington had raised demilitarized zones again during subsequent discussions, but there was currently no further progress on the territorial question.
Territorial decisions require leaders’ talks
The president said territorial questions could not be settled through draft documents or preliminary contacts alone. They required meetings at the appropriate political level.
Zelensky Warns of Russia’s ‘Economic Marriage’ With US as Ukraine Feels ‘Home Alone’ Without Patriots
He added that Ukraine remained prepared to discuss the issue because Russia repeatedly raised it and made it part of the negotiating agenda.
The distinction is central to Kyiv’s position: Willingness to examine a negotiating proposal has not amounted to acceptance of Russian sovereignty over occupied Ukrainian territory.
Reported US framework includes Donbas zone
The remarks follow reports that Washington is developing a broader package combining security arrangements, economic incentives, and proposals for disputed territorial questions.
A reported American framework included a demilitarized zone in Donbas, alongside an investment package and the prospect of EU membership for Ukraine in exchange for abandoning its NATO bid.
The Economist’s account also described potential benefits for Moscow, including commercial agreements with American companies, sanctions relief, and restored political relations with Washington.
Neither Ukraine nor the US announced that Kyiv had accepted those terms.
The reported package followed consultations in Oslo on Oct. 20 involving Zelensky, US envoy Steve Witkoff, and European partners. Witkoff then met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Kyiv seeks a ceasefire and lasting security
Zelensky has separately said Ukraine is prepared to freeze the front line to halt the fighting while refusing to recognize occupied territory as Russian.
In an interview reported on Saturday, Oct. 24, he rejected the suggestion that Russia already controlled 25% of Ukraine, putting the figure at 19.3%. Reaching the higher figure, he said, would require Ukraine to surrender the rest of Donbas.
That position distinguishes stopping combat along existing military positions from legally ceding Ukrainian land.
Kyiv is also pressing for enforceable security guarantees and sustained support for its armed forces to prevent another Russian invasion.
Addressing Washington’s Hudson Institute on Friday, Oct. 23, Zelensky called for at least 10 years of international military financing. He said Ukraine still needed clear answers about how American and European partners would respond to renewed Russian attacks.
He has argued that a ceasefire must be backed by a strong Ukrainian army and concrete allied commitments, including potential US guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5 and approved by Congress.
