Three brothers, including two prominent luxury real estate agents, were each sentenced to 30 years in prison for operating a yearslong sex trafficking and sexual abuse scheme that targeted women and minors, the US Justice Department said Tuesday.
US District Judge Valerie Caproni sentenced Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, in Manhattan federal court following their convictions on multiple federal sex offenses.
Each brother was also sentenced to 10 years of supervised release following his prison term.
The three were convicted on all counts on March 9 following a six-week trial, including on charges of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking.
According to evidence presented at trial, the brothers worked together and with others from at least 2008 until 2021 to drug, sexually assault and rape numerous women.
Oren and Tal Alexander used their prominence in the luxury real estate industry and their social and financial connections in New York and Miami to create opportunities to target women, prosecutors said.
The brothers and their associates recruited women through social media, dating applications, personal encounters and party promoters. Victims were offered luxury travel, accommodations and access to exclusive parties before being taken to private locations.
Prosecutors said the brothers secretly placed sedative drugs in some women’s drinks, leaving them with impaired movement, speech and memory and preventing them from resisting or escaping.
In several cases, the victims were physically restrained while one or more of the brothers assaulted them, despite their cries and explicit demands that they stop.
The scheme also involved women the brothers encountered at bars, nightclubs and social events, according to the Justice Department.
“Alon, Oren, and Tal Alexander are convicted sex traffickers and serial rapists,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement.
McDonald said they had used “their careers and social status to conceal the danger they posed” and praised the victims who came forward.
Alon Alexander was sentenced for crimes including sex trafficking a minor and aggravated sexual abuse. Oren Alexander’s convictions included the sexual exploitation of a minor, while Tal Alexander was sentenced for offenses involving several victims, including a minor.
The three continued to deny drugging, raping or trafficking women during the sentencing hearing.

State Budget for 2027 passed its first reading in Verkhovna Rada - what is included and what comes next
Kyiv • UNN
On October 28, the Verkhovna Rada approved the 2027 budget with 239 votes. Priorities include defense, social benefits, and pay increases for military personnel.
The State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 was adopted by the Verkhovna Rada in the first reading on October 28. This was reported by Parliament, UNN writes.
Security and defense, as well as social payments, are the main areas of expenditure provided for in the draft State Budget for 2027. The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine adopted the document in the first reading (No. 16000). It was supported by 239 members of Parliament
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi has already responded to this, announcing preparations for the second reading.
"I thank the members of Parliament for their joint work and support for the draft Budget for 2027 in the first reading. This is a Budget that takes into account the realities of the full-scale war and the state's key needs for next year. First and foremost, this includes the necessary funding for security and defense, maintaining financial stability, and fulfilling important social obligations to the people. The Government will process Parliament's Budget conclusions and prepare the draft for the second reading," Koretskyi wrote on social media on October 28.
As reported by MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak, a member of the Finance Committee, the first-reading version of the 2027 Budget includes and confirms, among other things, amendment No. 1279 on raising military personnel's salaries. According to him, an amendment banning the financing of "Cashback" with budget funds was also adopted.
According to Zhelezniak and his colleague Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk, amendment No. 1003 on capping officials' salaries at UAH 80,000 was among those rejected. It proposed setting an upper limit for salaries in state bodies, local self-government bodies, and budgetary institutions at UAH 80,000 per month for 2027. The restrictions were also proposed for members of Parliament, judges, including Constitutional Court judges, members of the High Council of Justice and the High Qualification Commission of Judges, prosecutors, and National Bank employees. An exception was provided for those involved in ensuring defense and repelling Russian aggression. The list of relevant positions was to be determined by the Cabinet of Ministers.
Key indicators of the draft State Budget-2027 for the first reading
According to the Ministry of Finance, the following is envisaged:
-  UAH 5 trillion 648 billion — budget revenues (+UAH 452.1 billion, or 8.7% compared with 2026); 
-  UAH 7 trillion 272 billion — budget expenditures (+UAH 864.9 billion, or 13.5% compared with 2026); 
-  UAH 4 trillion 885 billion — for security and defense. This amounts to 43.8% of projected GDP and is UAH 517.9 billion more than the amended plan for 2026; 
-  UAH 540.3 billion — for social payments and measures of the Ministry of Social Policy, which is UAH 72.6 billion more than the amended plan for 2026. 
"The Government continues active negotiations with international partners regarding sources of budget financing. External assistance is critically important for ensuring social and humanitarian expenditures, and its receipt directly depends on the adoption of laws and the implementation of reforms," the Ministry of Finance stated.
The day before, on October 27, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the draft resolution on the Budget conclusions (No. 16000/П) as a basis. This was the first stage in adopting the draft State Budget in the first reading.
The document contains 90 proposals, which the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget Issues formulated on the basis of 5,236 amendments submitted by members of Parliament, committee chair Roksolana Pidlasa said while presenting the document in the session hall.
After being adopted by the Verkhovna Rada, the Budget conclusions become a list of changes that the Government must take into account or consider when refining the draft budget for the second reading.
The Verkhovna Rada reported that the committee's main proposals included:
-  increasing military personnel's financial support and doubling state guarantees for defense industry enterprises, to UAH 60 billion; 
-  additional funds for medicines for patients with rare diseases, on top of the UAH 21 billion already allocated; 
-  allocating 4% of personal income tax to community budgets; 
-  increasing funding for housing for internally displaced persons; 
-  expanding the war-risk insurance and agricultural support programs, as well as banning the payment of the «National Cashback» from the UAH 9.4 billion program supporting production and entrepreneurship. 
According to the Ministry of Finance, Parliament adopted the Budget Conclusions, which set out the directions for finalizing the document.
"The Government will process them, coordinate the updated draft with international partners, and submit it to the Verkhovna Rada for consideration at the second reading," the Ministry of Finance noted.
What’s next
As Yaroslav Zhelezniak, a lawmaker from the Finance Committee, explained, after the Verkhovna Rada votes on the 2027 State Budget draft, it will be forwarded to the Government, and "the second reading and the final vote are planned for November 23–26."
Reminder
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP.

Everything you need to know about bats but were too afraid to ask
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:26:28 UTC
19:26:28 KST

Bats are not the world’s most beloved creatures. Mostly night animals, they’ve become a symbol of Halloween—associated with vampires, death and general ghoulishness. Sure, a few bat species do, in fact, feed on animal blood. Some bats have a face only a biologist could love. And yes, bats can be reservoirs of disease. But in their more than 50 million years on Earth, these maligned creatures have developed some admirable qualities, too.
For one, they’re everywhere: bats live on every continent except Antarctica. They echolocate, using sound to navigate their world—and they are the only mammal to evolve true flight. They also eat insects such as mosquitoes—contributing billions of dollars in value annually for the world’s farmers—and are critical pollinators of tropical plants.
“We need them,” says Emma Teeling, a professor and founding director of the Center for Irish Bat Research at University College Dublin.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
So, in honor of spooky season, here are seven bat facts you may not know:
Bats are “super agers.”
In nature, larger animals, such as elephants and whales, tend to live longer than smaller animals, such as mice and shrews, Teeling says. Bats are an exception.
“Bats are some of the smallest mammals in the entire world and can live for this extraordinary long time,” she says. Some of the oldest bats have been known to live for decades.
Teeling and other bat researchers are studying aspects of the animals’ longevity, including bats’ ability to repair their DNA and harbor viruses without getting sick, for clues in order to enhance our own lives.
Vampire bats could help us treat stroke victims.
When vampire bats such as Desmodus rotundus, also known as the common vampire bat, feed on birds and other mammals, they bite their prey and lick the wounds, Teeling says. An anticoagulant in their saliva prevents the blood from clotting up.
Researchers have studied this protein in the hope that it may offer a way to treat blood clots in stroke victims—while lowering the risk of causing brain bleeds. Although drug development stalled a decade ago after lackluster results, the treatment may still have potential, according to a recent review.
There are about 1,500 bat species—and counting.
Bats are incredibly diverse—across all mammals, bats include more species than all but one other group, rodents, says Rachel Page, a scientist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. In fact, there are about 1,500 known bat species worldwide.
Some, such as the vampire bats, drink blood. Others eat nectar, while others still eat insects, fish and even frogs.
Some bats “eavesdrop” on their prey’s mating calls.
For the frog-eating bats, meals can be treacherous. Some frogs are poisonous. Others are so big they could pose a danger. To meet this challenge, the fringe-lipped bat, Trachops cirrhosus, “eavesdrops:” the bats listen for the loud, “conspicuous” nighttime mating calls of their prey and then attack, Page says.
“They exploit those calls. They use them to detect, to locate, and then also to assess those prey” for size and toxicity, she says.
Bats likely evolved in Europe.
In September, Teeling and more than 130 other scientists across the world published a paper in Nature in which they sequenced genomes across all 21 bat families.
By pairing these genetic data with fossil records, they made a breakthrough—bats likely evolved in Europe and then spread to Africa and around the world, they found. Until then, it was thought bats might’ve emerged somewhere in North America, among other theories. “We rewrote evolutionary history,” Teeling says.
Many bats have a signature scent.
Across bat species, 9 percent are known so far to have odor-producing glands and other structures, but research on this is sparse, according to a 2021 paper in Mammal Review co-authored by Page. T. cirrhosus males employ a “pungent” golden crust with a “musky” scent on their forearms, likely to attract females, Page says.
Vampire bats will throw up to feed a friend.
If a vampire bat doesn’t feed for about two nights in a row, it will die, Page explains. “It doesn’t have the energetic reserves to make it beyond that,” she says. But research shows that if a vampire bat comes back to its colony hungry, other bats will step in and regurgitate blood to share—a costly but lifesaving sacrifice.

MADRID, October 28. /TASS/. At least 50 people have died and 179 more have been injured in a collision between two high-speed passenger trains in Spain’s central province of Toledo (in the Castilla La Mancha region), local television channel Antena 3 reported.
TASS has compiled the key details about the tragic accident.
Details of the accident
- The accident took place at around 9:00 a.m. local time.
- According to Europa Press, two passenger trains collided near the town of Urda in the Castilla La Mancha region.
- El Pais daily reported later that the accident took place between two residential settlements in the Province of Toledo.
- Two cars of one of the trains derailed, according to reports.
- EFE news agency specified that the two trains involved in the collision were passenger trains.
- Medics and fire and rescue teams are working at the scene of the accident.
- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez confirmed that the emergency relief services are working at the scene of the tragedy.
- According to him, they are providing assistance to the victims and ensuring their safety in coordination with all relevant authorities.
Casualties
- According to the latest figures provided by Antena 3 TV channel, at least 50 people have died and 179 more have been injured in a collision between two high-speed passenger trains.
Possible causes of the accident
- The Spanish government considers human error to be one of the possible causes of the collision between two passenger trains, El Pais daily reported, citing its sources.
- According to the daily, the possible cause of the accident was human error by an Adif company operator (the operator of the railway network) due to a failure in the security system.
- The daily pointed out that the system is fully automated and train movements were initially halted due to a malfunction; however, switching to manual control could have led to the malfunction, ultimately causing the disaster.
- ABC claimed in turn, citing its sources, that an employee responsible for overseeing the safety system failed to issue an earlier warning about the dangerous proximity of the approaching trains.
Reaction
- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was shocked by the news of the passenger train collision in the Province of Toledo.
- Sanchez pointed out that he was in permanent contact with Transport Minister Oscar Puente and the regional authorities.
- The Russian Embassy in Madrid told TASS that it had received no inquiries from Russian nationals regarding the railway disaster in the Spanish Province of Toledo.

U.S. President Donald Trump met with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Türkiye, Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (AP Photo)
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 28 that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, would be set up “very soon.”
The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters.
Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that a trilateral meeting between Kiev, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Meanwhile, a local truce aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct. 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents told AFP last month that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
“The possibility of evacuation from Oleshky is very good news for me and for the people who are trapped there,” Olga, a former resident, told AFP on Oct. 27.
“My acquaintances are ready to leave,” she said.
Announcing the truce last week, U.S. first lady Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require.”
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
AFP was not able to immediately verify details about the humanitarian mission or whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
The Russian military does not routinely grant international media, including AFP, access to areas under Russian occupation.
Right-leaning U.S. cable network Newsmax said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city.

Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers to meet in Ankara on Thursday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:24:25 UTC
19:24:25 KST

Muhammet Tarhan and Busra Nur Cakmak
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Participants expected to approve administrative and financial documents related to the organization’s operations
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) on Thursday as part of the organization’s 13th summit.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, foreign ministers of the member states will convene for the fifth time this year, with one regular and four informal council meetings, at the gathering in Ankara on Oct. 29-30.
The meeting is expected to include consultations on areas of cooperation within the organization and efforts to strengthen its institutional structure.
Participants are also expected to approve several administrative and financial documents concerning the organization’s operations at the end of the meeting.
Fidan is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the gathering.
In his address, Fidan is expected to emphasize that political dialogue and the capacity for joint action among Turkic states have been strengthened under the organization's umbrella, while shared historical, linguistic and cultural ties and bonds of brotherhood have been translated into concrete cooperation.
During Türkiye’s chairmanship of the organization, Fidan is expected to underline that priorities will include enhancing the organization’s institutional capacity, improving the human and financial resources and capabilities of its secretariat, and strengthening coordination among Turkic cooperation organizations.
He is also expected to stress the importance of translating economic and strategic cooperation into tangible results, particularly in energy, trade, investment, digital transformation and the defense industry.
Fidan is expected to highlight the importance of strengthening the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor to improve connectivity between Asia and Europe and reinforce economic resilience.
He is also expected to draw attention to developments in Afghanistan and their implications for regional security, stability and connectivity, emphasizing the need to increase consultations and coordination on the issue among member and observer states.
Organization of Turkic States
The organization was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States under the Nakhchivan Agreement signed on Oct. 3, 2009, by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its name was changed to the Organization of Turkic States at the Istanbul Summit in 2021.
Its main objectives include strengthening mutual trust and political solidarity among Turkic states, developing and deepening economic and technical cooperation, and documenting and promoting the historical and cultural heritage of the Turkic world.
Headquartered in Istanbul, the OTS has five members -- Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan -- and four observers: Hungary, Turkmenistan, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) and the Economic Cooperation Organization.
13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States
The OTS’s 13th summit will be held in Ankara on Oct. 29-30, hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Inspired by Erdogan’s vision of the Century of the Turkic World and the motto of Ismail Gasprinski, the summit will be held under the theme Turkish Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action.

EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:24:00 UTC
19:24:00 KST

EU's 'Made in Europe' plan unnerves global auto suppliers
October 28, 2026
It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.
Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.
After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.
Close to Europe, but not close enough
Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.
While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.
"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."
Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.
Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.
Protecting auto parts made in Europe
The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.
However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.
Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.
"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.
Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.
These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.
China seeks a side entrance
Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.
They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.
BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.
Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.
For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.
Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.
South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.
Carmakers fight to keep cheap imports
Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.
"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.
EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.
Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.
Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."
'Stop the bleeding' say auto parts suppliers
European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.
"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.
Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."
With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.
"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.
Additional reporting by Aram Ekin Duran.

Two Russian contract soldiers fled the front and wanted to make their way to Kyiv - SBU detained them
Kyiv • UNN
In Donetsk region, two Russian contract soldiers were detained after fleeing the front, changing into civilian clothes, and hitchhiking to Kyiv. One of them was charged with high treason and collaborationism.
In Ukraine, two Russian militants who fled the front and tried to reach Kyiv disguised as civilians were detained. The SBU reported this on October 28, UNN writes.
The counterintelligence unit of the Security Service detained two contract soldiers of the 291st Motorized Rifle Regiment of Russia’s Southern Military District in the frontline area of Donetsk region. Both were dressed in civilian clothes and were traveling toward Kyiv in a car they had stopped by hitchhiking. SBU officers detained them at a checkpoint upon entry into Dnipropetrovsk region
According to the intelligence service, "an identification tag belonging to a Russian army serviceman was found around the neck of one of the suspects." "According to available information, the racists hoped to reach the capital of our country, where one of them has relatives, and "lie low,"" the statement said.
The investigation established that "one of the detainees was a two-time convicted murderer from the temporarily occupied city of Dovzhansk in Luhansk region, who has been fighting on the enemy’s side against the Defense Forces since 2016." "After the outbreak of the full-scale war, the repeat offender took part in battles near Bakhmut as an assistant operator of an anti-tank missile system," the intelligence service stated.
"Another suspect is a Russian citizen who signed a contract with the defense ministry of the aggressor state while serving a prison sentence for murder," the SBU noted.
According to the case materials, "recently both militants were sent to assault the positions of Ukrainian troops in the Kramatorsk sector, where they subsequently fled the line of contact and entered a settlement in the "gray" zone." "There, they changed into civilian clothes found in an abandoned house, buried their uniforms and the Russian army’s issued firearms in the house, and set off on foot toward the district center. On the way to the city, they stopped a car whose owner agreed to give the suspects a ride to Dnipro, from where they planned to travel to Kyiv," the SBU explained.
But their plan failed—the two perpetrators were detained in the area of the administrative border of the frontline region.
Investigators from the Security Service notified the enemy accomplice from Luhansk region that he was suspected of two offenses under the Criminal Code of Ukraine: Parts 1 and 2 of Article 111 (high treason committed under martial law); Part 7 of Article 111-1 (collaboration activities).
The investigation is ongoing to establish all the circumstances of the crime. The perpetrator is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property. His accomplice—a Russian citizen—is currently being held as a prisoner of war, the SBU reported.

Australia returns 2 cultural relics to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:21:53 CST
19:21:53 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows two Chinese cultural relics, the head of a military official statue (L) and the head of a civil official statue, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127), returned from Australia, in Canberra, Australia. The National Gallery of Australia (NGA) handed over two Chinese cultural relics to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration in Canberra at 2:52 p.m. local time on Wednesday. According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province. (Photo by Chu Chen/Xinhua)
CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia returned two Chinese cultural relics to China at a handover ceremony held at the National Gallery of Australia (NGA) in Canberra on Wednesday.
Tang Wei, deputy director of China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA), Liu Jinsong, Chinese Ambassador to Australia, and Nick Mitzevich, director of the NGA, attended the ceremony and delivered remarks.
The two relics are the head of a military official statue from the Yongyu Mausoleum and the head of a civil official statue from the Yongchang Mausoleum, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127). According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province.
The Chinese side said that returning displaced cultural relics to their countries of origin is an important step towards safeguarding cultural heritage, respecting the cultural rights and national sentiments of peoples around the world, and protecting the achievements of human civilization.
Noting the handover as a significant outcome of China-Australia cooperation in implementing international conventions and protecting cultural heritage, the Chinese side said it would further promote people-to-people exchanges and empathy between the two peoples.
The Australian side said that the return represented more than the physical transfer of cultural objects, reflecting respect for cultural heritage, a sense of responsibility and the importance of international partnerships. It added that the handover would help strengthen Australia-China relations and encourage continued cooperation in cultural heritage protection.
In 2025, the NCHA, working with China's Ministry of Public Security and cultural heritage and public security authorities in Henan Province, submitted a memorandum and supporting evidence to the NGA, formally requesting the return of the two relics.
The successful return was achieved through close coordination between the NCHA and the Chinese Embassy in Australia, within the framework of the UNESCO 1970 Convention on the means of prohibiting and preventing the illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property, a bilateral memorandum of understanding on cultural heritage protection signed by China and Australia in 2009, and the NGA's 2021 policy on due diligence and provenance research. ■

Norway's premier says call with Putin was effort to present European views
OSLO, Oct 28 - Norway's prime minister defended on Wednesday a three-way call with Vladimir Putin and Finland's president, saying it was intended to ensure the Russian leader heard European as well as US views.
Tuesday's call between Russia's Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian premier Jonas Gahr Stoere broke a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin, and was criticised by allies including Denmark's Mette Frederiksen.
The 90-minute call came ahead of what are expected to be the first face-to-face talks since February between Ukrainian and Russian officials, in Abu Dhabi next month.
"We (Stubb and I) were focused on looking forward, what must happen for this war to not continue endlessly for months, with people dying ... and it is even more difficult to find a solution," Stoere told public broadcaster NRK.
"I don't think (Putin) will change his mind, but he gets to hear our position very clearly. I am worried that some of these messages do not reach him when the Americans talk to him," he said.
Norway, said Stoere, was keen to introduce de-escalation steps such as stopping attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine, halting strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain and conducting prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Asked whether there could be peace without Ukraine ceding territory, Stoere said: "Today Russia controls nearly 20% (of Ukrainian territory). Ukraine will never sign a deal that recognises that they have lost territory, but whether they can take the current frontline as a reality and as a starting point, that is a different question."
"And the big question is what kind of security guarantees can there be for the country (Ukraine) after a peace deal? Putin recognises that this is the big question."
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said Tuesday's call offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process. REUTERS

Poland and UK sign Warsaw Defence Plan to “deter Russian threats”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:21:10 UTC
19:21:10 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”.
The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea.
The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership.
Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L
— Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026
“Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw.
“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added.
His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine.
Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies.
Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones.
The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”.
The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems.
Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty.
The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026
This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.
Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.
In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.
In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal.

Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over "interference"
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.

Iran, Russia near agreement on joint development of small modular nuclear reactors
Iran is finalizing a protocol with Russia to accelerate joint development of small modular nuclear reactors, Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman and deputy for international, legal and parliamentary affairs at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, has announced.
Speaking to Iran's Shabakeh Khabar television network, Kamalvandi said the agreement would facilitate closer cooperation on the construction of small modular reactors, a technology attracting growing international interest as countries seek reliable, low-carbon electricity sources. SMRs are far smaller than traditional large-scale reactors.
Kamalvandi also highlighted rising global electricity demand, driven in part by artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. He said nuclear power could provide stable baseload electricity while helping reduce emissions.
He claimed Iran's nuclear industry had reached a mature stage and said the country had developed substantial domestic capabilities in nuclear plant construction, fuel-cycle technology and nuclear safety. The public prosecution service (OM) is demanding prison sentences of 10 and 6.5 years for two suspects accused of involvement in a counterfeit medicine webshop, whose products appear to have led to the deaths of three people.

People bought the pills online without knowing what was actually in them. Some contained powerful synthetic opioids like nitazenes, which can be far more deadly than fentanyl.

Both suspects say they had no idea they were helping distribute contaminated pills. A lawyer for one of the defendants described his client as a “glorified assembly-line worker”.

EU prosecutors still await von der Leyen’s statement in Pfizer vaccine probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:20:07 UTC
19:20:07 KST

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has yet to receive an in-person statement from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as part of its investigation into the bloc’s COVID-19 vaccine procurement, news outlet Politico reported Wednesday, citing a source familiar with the matter.
The investigation, known as “Pfizergate,” concerns alleged criminal wrongdoing linked to vaccine negotiations between von der Leyen and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla.
EPPO took over the Belgian-led investigation in 2024.
Legal documents cited by Politico indicate that prosecutors have been examining allegations of “interference in public functions, destruction of SMS, corruption and conflict of interest.”
Von der Leyen has yet to give an in-person statement to EPPO as part of its investigation, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Asked about reports that von der Leyen had not provided an in-person statement, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the institution had cooperated extensively with EPPO.
He added that the cooperation had taken place with the full support of von der Leyen, who remained willing to address outstanding questions within the limits of her duties and availability as commission president.
Meanwhile, EPPO Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruta Kovesi said some EU officials had refused to respond to summonses issued by her office.
“Some politicians think that they are above the law,” Kovesi told Politico in an interview. “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.”
She said her office faced difficulties exercising its investigative powers, particularly when cases involved high-profile politicians or wealthy individuals with political connections.
However, Kovesi declined to comment on whether von der Leyen was among the officials she was referring to.
Established in 2017 and operational since 2021, EPPO is responsible for investigating and prosecuting crimes affecting the financial interests of the European Union.

Berlin man who drugged and raped women jailed for 12 years
A Berlin court has sentenced a 69-year-old man to 12 years in prison for drugging, raping and filming women he met through online dating platforms.
The defendant had "deliberately sought out victims," presiding judge Jakob Weber said. Judges also ordered preventive detention after his sentence, finding that he remained a danger to the public.
The electrician, who sometimes posed as a police officer or military pilot, was convicted of 22 counts of rape involving 14 women between 2016 and 2022.
At his Berlin apartment, he spiked their drinks with sedatives before attacking them. The women only discovered what had happened during the police investigation.
Investigators found a camera aimed at his bed that ran "24/7," alongside meticulously kept records of recordings, a police officer told the court.
An investigator described "extreme dehumanization" in online groups the man used, saying women were "traded as commodities."
The defendant admitted the rapes at the start of his trial. A psychiatric expert found no evidence that his ability to control his actions was diminished.
Investigations into suspected offenses involving another 44 women are continuing. The ruling can still be appealed.
BASF presses case for Evonik takeover
German chemicals giant BASF has stepped up its push to acquire rival Evonik, arguing that a combination would create a more competitive and resilient global business.
BASF CEO Markus Kamieth said the companies' strengths complemented each other and a deal would make sense as consolidation gathers pace across Europe's chemical industry.
But he stressed that any takeover must benefit BASF shareholders. "We will not pay an excessive price," he said, declining to discuss the status of talks or a timetable.
BASF has raised its offer for Essen-based Evonik to €24 per share, valuing the company at just over €11 billion, the German dpa news agency reported.
The proposal has drawn criticism from Dennis Radtke, who heads the workers' wing of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). He warned that thousands of jobs could be lost and called for the takeover attempt to be abandoned.
Evonik's largest shareholder, the RAG Foundation, holds around 43% of its shares, giving it a key role in any deal.
Girl seriously injured in animal attack at German wildlife park
An eight-year-old girl was seriously injured in an animal attack at a wildlife park south of Berlin, police said.
The girl was inside an enclosure with two other children and a staff member when at least one animal attacked her. The others suffered no visible injuries.
The girl, who was visiting Wildpark Johannismühle near Baruth/Mark in Brandenburg, was airlifted to hospital. Police are investigating whether negligence was involved.
Authorities have not identified the animal involved.
The privately run park said it was cooperating fully with investigators and supporting the girl's family. It declined to provide further details while proceedings were ongoing.
German tourist found dead on Seychelles island
A 30-year-old German tourist has been found dead on the Seychelles island of La Digue after leaving his hotel at night to look for swimming goggles, police said.
The man went out at around 9 p.m. local time (1700 GMT) on Monday to retrieve goggles he had left on a beach. His wife alerted authorities when he failed to return.
A search team found his body in a rocky area away from a hiking trail leading to Anse Coco beach.
Police said the circumstances remained unclear and an investigation was underway to establish the cause of death.
Mercedes cuts profit outlook as China sales slump
German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has lowered its annual profit forecast as falling sales in China and rising costs overshadow a sharp increase in quarterly earnings.
The Stuttgart-based company now expects earnings before interest and taxes to remain at last year's level, having previously forecast a substantial increase.
Market conditions had become more challenging, particularly in China, CEO Ola Källenius said. Mercedes also expects higher costs in the fourth quarter, including for raw materials.
Third-quarter net profit rose 28% to €1.52 billion, although the comparison reflects restructuring costs that weighed on earnings a year earlier. Revenue fell 4.5% to €30.7 billion.
Car sales in China plunged 31%, pushing overall sales down 8% to 407,200 vehicles. Outside China, sales rose 1%.
Fully electric car sales provided a brighter spot, climbing 61%. Källenius also pointed to continued sales growth in Europe and the US.
Merz: Trade allies could 'own the restaurant' together
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has proposed a global alliance to defend international trade rules and coordinate responses to economic pressure.
Speaking in Tokyo, Merz called for like-minded countries to strengthen and reform the World Trade Organization (WTO), according to his speech manuscript.
Members could commit to rejecting unlawful tariffs and economic coercion, he said, in an apparent reference to the US and China.
They could also agree to accept trade dispute rulings as binding despite the current paralysis of the WTO's appeals body, and respond jointly when other countries break the rules.
Merz urged Germany, Japan and other partners to work more closely together, echoing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's call for an alliance of middle powers.
Acting together would mean countries no longer had to ask whether they were "on the menu" or "at the table," Merz said: "Because then we would jointly own the restaurant."
Who is in the running to succeed Steinmeier?
We've already mentioned some potential successors to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in this blog. Here's a broader look at the names being discussed.
Much of the debate has focused on choosing a woman, as Germany has never had a female head of state. Potential candidates include:
- Ilse Aigner: Bavaria's state parliament president, from the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). She has backing from CSU leader Markus Söder and senior Social Democrats and Greens.
- Julia Klöckner: Bundestag president, from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
- Karin Prien: Federal education and family minister, also from the CDU.
- Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer: Former CDU leader and defense minister.

- Juli Zeh: Author and constitutional court judge in Brandenburg, and a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).
- Ursula von der Leyen: European Commission president and CDU member.
However, a woman is not certain to get the job. The state premier of Hesse, Boris Rhein, has also been mentioned, while comedian and author Hape Kerkeling is the subject of a public petition rather than a party nomination.
Merz eyes fighter jet cooperation with Japan
Geman Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany and Japan would explore jointly developing a fighter jet as they seek closer industrial ties.
"We also want to explore whether cooperation in fighter aircraft construction is possible," Merz said after meeting Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo. Takaichi also backed closer defense cooperation.
Britain invited Germany earlier this month to join the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), following the collapse of the rival German-French-Spanish Future Combat Air System project.
Britain, Japan and Italy are developing a sixth-generation fighter jet under GCAP, aiming to have it operational by 2035.
Ines Claus: a possible Steinmeier successor
Could the name of the next German president be Ines Claus? The discussions around Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s successor, whose term ends next year, have reached the German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on his trip across the Indo Pacific.
Steinmeier will have spent two terms in office when he retires next year. And while the president’s role is largely a ceremonial one in Germany, the process of picking a suitable candidate is a highly political affair, happening largely behind closed doors, unlike in many other countries.
That process is now in full swing. There’s largely bipartisan agreement that the next president should be a woman, which would be a first for the country. Chancellor Merz was one of those early on saying he was in favour of a woman taking the job, but had otherwise stayed out of the discussion so far.
That has now changed. The strong positioning by the Bavarian conservatives from the CSU in favor of Ilse Aigner, a former state agriculture minister, taking the job, seems to have pushed its bigger sister party, the CDU, to find a candidate from their own ranks.
Ines Claus, a lawyer and legal expert, was named by some within the CDU during Merz's Asia trip. It’s unusual for the chancellor to comment on party political discussions while travelling, but his team has now stressed that they are awaiting "an orderly process." In other words, choosing Steinmeier's successor is far from a done deal.
The CDU is reportedly preparing to discuss who they should put forward at their next board meeting on November 9. They will also take into account the wishes of the CSU, the Social Democrats (SPD), and even the Greens, wanting the future head of state to have broad public support.
How is Germany's president elected?
Instead, a special Federal Convention brings together Bundestag lawmakers and an equal number of delegates chosen by Germany's 16 state parliaments.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and their coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), together hold a majority.
That means they could elect a candidate without support from other parties, provided their delegates agree.
Initial talks will involve CDU state leaders and the CSU, with November 9 seen as an important milestone. Discussions will then widen to include the SPD and environmentalist Greens.
German parties weigh candidates to succeed Steinmeier
German political parties are weighing who should succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, with Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner attracting support across party lines.
The presidency is Germany's largely ceremonial head-of-state role, separate from the chancellor, who leads the government. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term, and his successor will be elected on January 30.
Germany has never before had a woman as federal president.
Aigner belongs to the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). The CSU leader and Bavarian premier Markus Söder has endorsed her.
She has also drawn backing from politicians outside the conservative bloc, including senior Greens politician and Bundestag deputy speaker Omid Nouripour.
"We need someone in these times who holds the country together," Nouripour said during Steinmeier's state visit to China, arguing that Aigner had the experience and authority required.
Center-left Social Democratic Party politicians have also voiced support.
But Merz's CDU says it should nominate the candidate. Sources close to the chancellor denied reports that he favored Ines Claus, who leads the CDU parliamentary group in the state of Hesse, saying he had "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal."
Most Germans plan to sit out Halloween, poll finds
Nearly three-quarters of Germans are unlikely to celebrate Halloween, despite its popularity among younger adults, according to a YouGov poll.
Some 74% said they were very or fairly unlikely to take part, whether by dressing up, attending a party, decorating or handing out sweets to children.
By contrast, 23% said they would probably celebrate in some way. That figure rose to 50% among 18- to 24-year-olds, compared with just 11% among those aged 55 and over.
The survey found no difference between respondents in eastern and western Germany.
YouGov surveyed 2,666 adults in Germany on October 27. The poll was described as representative.

Ukraine lacks unified vision for postwar reconstruction – IMF Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:18:59 EET
19:18:59 KST

Funding for Ukraine's recovery following Russian aggression, which the World Bank currently estimates at $588 billion, should be viewed as part of a broader model and institutional architecture for reconstruction, with a vision for the postwar country being a key element, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), believes.
"This vision must be shared and supported by the majority of Ukrainians. Frankly speaking, we do not yet have such a vision," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan said that the IMF does not develop such a vision because the Fund's task is to ensure current macrofinancial stability: preventing high inflation, sharp currency depreciation, and crises in the banking sector, the budget and the balance of payments.
"Structural reforms are being implemented for this purpose, but overall, this is merely a foundation for further development. Some criticize Ukraine's IMF program for lacking ambition. But its purpose is to sustain our resilience," Ukraine's representative at the Fund explained.
According to him, the Future Economy initiative, launched by the Ukrainian government and the Ministry of Economy, is intended to help shape a broader vision. The IMF participates in the initiative as an analyst rather than a strategist. "The World Bank provides more active assistance, but the key role belongs to the Ukrainian authorities and society," said Rashkovan, who has been working on issues related to Ukraine's reconstruction for many years.
He added that an interesting discussion is also underway around the Prosperity Plan: what Ukraine should become after the war and how much funding and investment will be needed for it to become a new European tiger.
"However, neither this plan nor the Future Economy initiative is a Marshall Plan at this stage. They are more like ideas that need to be developed. Money does not solve everything: an institutional architecture is needed that can sustain reconstruction over several political cycles in Ukraine and partner countries," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
He added that Ukrainian ownership of the process is one of the key principles on which reconstruction should be built. "No one will take better care of us than we do ourselves, and no one will shape a vision for Ukraine's future on our behalf," Rashkovan explained.
The expert said that this vision must be translated into strategies. "We already have many regional and sectoral strategies, perhaps even too many. They need to be aligned. And again, it is important not merely to have strategies but to live by them. All of them must contribute to realizing a shared vision," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
In his view, reconstruction is not a task that can be completed in a day or a few months; it will take decades, if not generations. Therefore, it must be planned, and the necessary institutions must be established in advance.
In addition to the IMF program focused on macrofinancial stability, without which long-term investment planning is impossible, he also cited security guarantees as a prerequisite for reconstruction.
At the same time, Ukraine's representative at the IMF believes that the end of the war is not a mandatory condition for beginning reconstruction.
"We are already rebuilding a great deal despite the war. Not on the scale we would like, but billions of dollars have already been spent on recovery," he said.
Among the other elements of the reconstruction model, he also cited European integration, noting that if Ukraine is moving toward the European Union, reconstruction should be planned in accordance with EU standards.
As for financing, Rashkovan noted that a considerable number of instruments are already available. These include the Pillar 2 investment component under the Ukraine Facility; the EUR 1 billion European Flagship Fund for the Reconstruction of Ukraine, managed by Dragon Capital and Amber Infrastructure; projects supported by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), resources from the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD); and the Co-Investment Platform, which brings together 19 development finance institutions from different countries.
"All of these are working for Ukraine's benefit, but we are still far from the scale required. We need to understand that the probability of all $588 billion coming from public funds provided by international partners is zero. Historical experience shows that 75–85% will come from private sources," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said.
He clarified that private investment typically arrives significantly later than donor funding, which is why Ukraine is currently relying more heavily on donor resources.
Finally, Rashkovan said the importance of structural reforms to attract private capital, including protection of property rights and the continuation of land and anti-corruption reforms. He recalled that the Czech Republic and Poland attracted most of their private investment before joining NATO and the European Union, driven by strong investor expectations.
"If the world expects Ukraine to join the EU and we maintain the pace of reforms, the same could happen here, especially amid friendshoring – the relocation of production and procurement to geopolitically friendly countries," the expert believes.

Kazakhstan sees 5.6-fold increase in cargo transit over decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:16:44 UTC
19:16:44 KST

Kazakhstan sees 5.6-fold increase in cargo transit over decade
Cargo transit through Kazakhstan increased 5.6-fold over the past decade, rising from 6.5 million tons in 2015 to 36.3 million tons in 2025. The strongest annual growth came in 2025, when transit volumes jumped 70.8%, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Energyprom.kz.
According to Kazakhstan's Bureau of National Statistics, which cited data from the Ministry of Finance's State Revenue Committee, cargo transit volumes grew steadily over the decade, reaching 11.6 million tons in 2020, 15.6 million tons in 2022, and 21.3 million tons in 2024.
The upward trend continued in 2026, with government figures showing that 32.6 million tons of cargo transited through Kazakhstan between January and September, a 13.1% increase from the same period last year.
Kazakhstan aims to raise annual cargo transit volumes to 100 million tons by 2035 through the construction of new railway lines and the modernization of existing infrastructure.
Rail transport accounted for the largest share of transit cargo in 2025, with volumes rising from 13.3 million tons in 2024 to 18.7 million tons. Meanwhile, cargo transported by road vehicles, including trucks and trailers, nearly tripled to 16.8 million tons, up from 5.7 million tons a year earlier.
China remained a major source of transit cargo, with shipments to Uzbekistan reaching 6.5 million tons in 2025. Another 4 million tons consisted of consolidated cargo from China destined for Kazakhstan and other countries.
The China–Russia route handled 3 million tons of cargo, while other major routes included Uzbekistan–Russia (2.2 million tons), China–Iran (2.1 million tons), and China–Poland (1.6 million tons).
Cold-rolled iron and steel products accounted for the largest share of transit cargo by commodity, totaling 5.6 million tons. They were followed by motorcycles, mopeds, and similar vehicles at 2.2 million tons, passenger cars at 619,200 tons, certain polymers at 482,400 tons, and automotive parts at 478,200 tons.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan transported 712.1 million tons of cargo across all modes of transport in the first nine months of 2026.
However, year-on-year comparisons were affected by a change in statistical methodology, which excluded empty railcars from railway freight calculations. When both periods are measured using the same methodology, total freight volumes show a 0.9% increase.
Between January and September, road and urban electric transport carried 270.4 million tons of cargo, followed by railways at 248.5 million tons and pipelines at 189.8 million tons.
Transport companies generated 4.5 trillion tenge in revenue from freight, baggage, and cargo-baggage services during the nine-month period, up 5.3% from a year earlier.
Rail transport accounted for the largest share of revenue at 1.8 trillion tenge, followed by pipeline transportation at 1.4 trillion tenge and road and urban electric transport at 1.2 trillion tenge.
The expansion of transit routes is opening up new opportunities for Kazakhstan's transport sector, with logistics services, warehousing, and vehicle maintenance and repair playing an increasingly important role alongside growing cargo volumes.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan had announced plans to expand its international route network to 160, with Europe, China, India, the U.S., Türkiye, and Russia identified as priority destinations.

King sees challenges and successes on visit to asylum centre
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
King Willem-Alexander has visited one of the Netherlands’ longest running accommodation centres for asylum seekers to talk to refugees and local residents.
The king received an enthusiastic reception from the 530 people living in the centre in Leersum, Utrecht province, which has been operational for 35 years.
He said he wanted to see how a refugee centre “can be integrated into a local community”, but also gain an insight into the challenges for people living in the area.
During his visit he was shown the facilities in the centre such as a women’s café with yoga and cooking workshops, a bicycle repair shop and support for refugees looking for work or training.
“We all know what the problems are and we see them a lot,” the king said. “But it is also good to be able to show, by being here and bringing lots of journalists along, that things can go very well.”
He was handed a bundle of letters from primary school children, in which they told their personal stories and described how they missed their parents.
The head of the school, Bea, who has been teaching refugee children for 16 years, told AD.nl that the outlook was bleaker than at any time she could remember because of the length of time it is taking for asylum claims to be processed.
“A large group of children are still waiting for their parents, whom they haven’t seen for two or three years in some cases, to be given residency permits,” she said. “We have to deal with that as well as teaching classes.”

Russia ready to play part in ‘second awakening’ of Africa – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:15:09 UTC
19:15:09 KST

Russia ready to play part in ‘second awakening’ of Africa – Lavrov
Russia is ready to expand cooperation with African countries and regional organizations through new partnerships in business and other sectors, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Speaking at a meeting with the heads of leading African media outlets on Tuesday, Lavrov said Moscow was open to developing additional forms of engagement with the African Union, individual countries and regional blocs.
“Our partnership is already quite extensive, and there is certainly room to enrich and refine it; we are fully open to that,” Lavrov said.
The minister also stressed that Russia seeks to strengthen ties with Africa on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, helping countries develop domestic industries and become more independent in global finance and technology. He said Moscow’s approach follows UN principles of mutual respect and non-interference.
Lavrov argued that Africa’s next major transformation will be economic, noting that many countries remain dependent on former colonial powers despite having gained political independence.
“The second awakening [of African countries] will, of course, be economic, including achieving a situation where the richest resources of the African continent are not simply extracted and exported as raw materials, but are used in Africa itself so that added value is created there, rather than in the former colonial powers,” he said.
Turning to UN reform, Lavrov opposed increasing Western representation on the Security Council, arguing that Western countries already occupy six of its 15 seats despite their declining share of global economic output.
“Like China and many other countries, we [Russia] maintain that only nations from the Global South should be granted new seats—whether permanent, non-permanent, or a mix of both,” Lavrov said.
The 15-member UN Security Council has five veto-wielding permanent members and ten elected members serving two-year terms. Africa currently holds three seats, occupied by DR Congo, Liberia and Somalia, with Zimbabwe set to replace Somalia in January 2027.
The remarks came at the four-day Russia-Africa Media Forum, which opened in Moscow on Monday. The gathering comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum, taking place on Wednesday and Thursday in Moscow.
