Press review: Europe seeks restoration of Russia ties as aid operation starts in Alyoshki
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Europe seeks to restore channels of communication with Russia; a humanitarian operation begins in Alyoshki; and Russia highlights the need to safeguard the global gas market. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia
Media: Europe seeks to restore channels of communication with Russia
The leaders of Russia, Norway and Finland agreed to maintain direct contact during a telephone conversation on October 27. However, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, denied they were speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole, Izvestia reports.
The joint call by Finland’s president and Norway’s premier signals that Europe is getting ready for the next round of peace negotiations, Tigran Meloyan, an analyst at the Higher School of Economics’ Institute for Global Military Economics and Strategy, said. Such steps by leaders of NATO and European Union countries are always preceded by diplomatic consultations with allies, so it is safe to assume that the idea had been coordinated with Kiev and Brussels, the expert added.
Western media reports say the European Union is discussing the appointment of a special envoy for talks with Russia. Ultimately, the bloc could select several representatives, European Parliament member Fernand Kartheiser of Luxembourg said. EU member states hold widely differing positions, as some remain skeptical about the very principle of talks, while others, such as Slovakia, seek to normalize bilateral relations with Russia as much as possible. That said, appointing multiple negotiators could better represent the range of opinions within the EU, Kartheiser added.
Yegor Sergeyev, senior researcher with the Institute for International Studies at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, pointed out that it was still too early to speak of European countries becoming fully involved in the negotiation process. The analyst pointed to the lack of constructive proposals as one of the reasons.
The initiative by Stubb and Store is not part of EU diplomacy but reflects the national interests of Russia’s European neighbors, Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at the Russian State University for the Humanities, told Vedomosti. According to him, the Norwegian premier and the Finnish president did not call Putin as European envoys but as national leaders. "This does not indicate a change in attitude toward Russia or a decline in support for Kiev. This can also be viewed as an effort to avoid being left out of discussions of future European security," the expert noted.
Izvestia: Humanitarian operation begins in Alyoshki
The humanitarian operation in Alyoshki will continue until 10:59 p.m. on November 1, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said. Its main goals are to provide civilians with medicine, food and essential supplies and evacuate those wishing to leave the town. A successful outcome could pave the way for the resumption of trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, Izvestia notes.
The Russian army suspended fire in the Alyoshki area at 4:00 a.m. on October 27 to prepare for the humanitarian mission, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Meanwhile, provocations by the Ukrainian armed forces during the ceasefire in Alyoshki cannot be ruled out, military expert Alexey Leonkov told the newspaper. In this regard, he cited 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone attacks carried out by Kiev’s forces against Alyoshki and the main roads leading to the town during the week of October 19.
"Numerous ceasefires have been announced since the start of the special military operation. Humanitarian ceasefires were also declared before that, particularly during the period when the Minsk Accords were in effect. Still, Ukraine failed to honor these agreements each time," Leonkov noted. According to him, Kiev could use the pause in fighting to deploy additional troops to this part of the front and replenish its ammunition stocks.
"Ukrainian forces are not currently staging provocations as they have to honor a promise presumably made to Melania Trump. But once the humanitarian ceasefire ends, they could resume attacks on Alyoshki and once again lay mines along roads leading to the town," military expert Viktor Litovkin pointed out. Nevertheless, the ceasefire should be used to the fullest to address humanitarian needs.
However, although humanitarian and political efforts continue in parallel, with the two processes not directly connected, a successful operation in Alyoshki could create favorable conditions for the resumption of trilateral negotiations between Moscow, Kiev and Washington. A new round of negotiations could take place after November 4.
Media: Russia highlights need to safeguard global gas market
Discussions at the Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow on October 27 focused on volatility in energy markets, driven by tensions in the Middle East, and sanctions on Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin and speakers from other GECF member states discussed these issues in their remarks, Vedomosti reports.
The main issue today is disruptions to gas supplies, which highlight the need to develop ways to optimize transportation routes, taking into account the geographic locations of GECF member states, the Russian leader said. Most GECF members and observer nations called for peace and security to be maintained to ensure stable gas supplies. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has demonstrated how geopolitical changes could affect the energy sector, GECF Secretary General Philip Mshelbila pointed out.
Moscow has never refused to engage in dialogue with European countries, but the European Union has made a series of short-sighted political decisions, digging a hole for itself rather than for Russia, Izvestia notes, citing Putin.
The 2026 Middle East crisis has worsened the fragmentation of gas markets, Kept expert Nikita Illeritsky said. In his opinion, US liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports are now seeking to strengthen their positions in Europe and Northeast Asia to recoup billions of dollars invested in their facilities.
Still, many European countries continue to prioritize political decisions over their economic interests. In a bid to cut Moscow’s revenues, the European Union has undermined its own economy. Abandoning stable pipeline gas supplies from Russia and shifting to the spot market, where prices are much higher, has dealt a direct blow to European industry. Nevertheless, neither restrictions nor market disruptions can halt the global trend toward a growing role for natural gas as a pillar of the global energy sector, industry and international trade.
Vedomosti: BRICS boosts its economic influence in Africa as Western presence wanes
The shares of Europe and the United States in financial and economic influence across African countries have fallen to 29% and 10%, respectively. Meanwhile, BRICS countries have broadened their presence, raising their share to 16%, according to Vedomosti estimates.
When it comes to Africa, it’s more accurate to speak of "a fragmented international security market" rather than "zones of influence," as African governments decide which external actors to work with, while global powers compete for access, influence, mineral resources and trade routes.
"This is not a division but ‘a competitive coexistence’ of numerous external forces in one space," said Mikhail Margelov, acting head of the UNESCO Department at Moscow State University’s Institute of Asian and African Studies and vice president of the Russian International Affairs Council. Formal zones of influence no longer exist in Africa, as the colonial-era division of the continent has been replaced by competition among external powers. These changes are especially evident in the Sahel region, where Russia has consolidated its position following the withdrawal of French and US troops.
African nations are increasingly seeking to balance their ties with foreign partners while reinforcing their sovereignty. The West describes this approach as multi-alignment, with countries maintaining relations with several centers of power at once, Denis Degterev, senior researcher with the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, and professor with the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and the Higher School of Economics, explained.
Economic influence in Africa depends not only on trade and investment but also on defense and political cooperation, as well as debt burdens, Degterev noted. Creditors such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have particularly strong leverage. Even Sahel countries, which have rejected military cooperation with the West, remain reliant on these institutions. As for the European Union, it should not be viewed as a single player, because France, Germany and Italy often vie for influence.
Deeper African integration has become a crucial trend, including efforts to develop a continental free trade area, a regional payment system and financial institutions. "The only way for African nations to implement major industrial and infrastructure projects and reduce their reliance on foreign countries is to pool resources. Africa needs industrialization," Andrey Fyodorov, leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, emphasized.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Resumed diesel exports could help increase Russian oil production
Russian oil refineries are ramping up diesel production after the government partially lifted its export ban. The resumption of diesel exports and higher output could help sustain domestic oil production, Rossiyskaya Gazeta notes.
Valery Andrianov, associate professor at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation, pointed out that the return to operation of refineries following scheduled maintenance was supporting Russian oil production. However, growth remains limited by Russia’s quota under the OPEC+ agreement. Earlier, domestic output fell short of the quota because demand from processing facilities had declined and logistics issues had hampered efforts to increase crude oil exports.
According to energy expert Kirill Rodionov, the current level of oil production in Russia is shaped by three factors: oil exports, domestic refining and various fuel export bans. Crude exports are currently hindered by shipping difficulties in the Black Sea. Meanwhile, domestic oil processing depends on the completion of maintenance work at Russian refineries and the regulator’s export restrictions, which are now being partially lifted.
The expert stressed that the Russia-US diesel deal would have little impact on the oil production situation because the export volumes agreed by the two countries were too small. However, a full lifting of the diesel export ban, at least for oil refineries, could pave the way to higher petroleum product exports and oil production.
In Andrianov’s view, Russia could raise oil output by 1.3 mln barrels per day. However, achieving this target will depend on the pace of refinery maintenance and the intensity of attacks on the facilities.
Rodionov identified shipping issues in the Black Sea as another risk. He does not expect Russia to achieve sustained oil production growth before 2027.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

Paris braces for more unrest as riots reshape the city's streets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Riots across France have left more than 3,000 businesses attacked or looted. Paris shopkeepers have boarded up windows and bought pepper spray and tear gas.
- The unrest has left Paris a city of contrasts: Daily life continues alongside shattered windows, police helicopters and residents’ fear of renewed violence.
- Many residents of Paris, Marseille and other major cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
PARIS — Business is up tenfold at a weapons store near Place de l’Opéra in Paris: Shopkeepers from all over the city have been stocking up on pepper spray and tear gas.
In the nine days since riots erupted in cities across France, thousands of merchants have also boarded up their storefronts, radically altering the Paris streetscape. The screech of electric saws and pounding of nails into plywood are now background noise in the French capital.
“They’re afraid their stores will be attacked and looted,” Yves Gollety, owner of the weapons store, explained.
Adding to the dark mood are police helicopters hovering, with searchlights blazing, to enforce a late-night curfew in the Les Halles and République sections of Paris.
And the city has removed many of the huge street-corner bins where Parisians are accustomed to dropping their empty wine and beer bottles. Rioters had been knocking them over to get glass ammunition against police.
Yet daily life has barely changed in much of Paris, where it can seem like normal times amid the chaos. Friends chat in cafés with shattered windows. Customers ignore plywood covering the front doors of shops.
But the social and economic grievances that boiled over so violently have not gone away, and nobody can escape the dreaded question: What’s next?
More demonstrations, for sure, and a strike planned for Nov. 5, which has left many resigned to toggling, for now, between upheaval and ordinary life.
The contrasts can be jarring.
At Cycles Laurent, a bike store on Boulevard Voltaire, a makeshift wooden window doubles as a spray-painted sign urging people to come on in.
“We remain open,” it says.
The bike shop is one of more than 3,000 businesses attacked or pillaged in France in the aftermath of giant protests against the government of President Emmanuel Macron the weekend of Oct. 17.
Although a tense urban peace has taken hold since then, many residents of Paris, Toulouse, Marseille and other cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
“This whole climate is horrible,” said Yolande Montagnac, a retiree who has lived for 45 years near the Gare de Lyon in Paris and was heartbroken by the damage to the city.
Scattered curfews and a police surge to keep nationwide protests under control have helped to stop the looting. More than 400,000 protesters returned to the streets on Saturday, by the police count; closer to double that number, according to unions. Apart from a few tear-gas skirmishes, the demonstrations ended peacefully.
The unrest began after high school students took to the streets last month to denounce poor conditions and resources at their campuses. On Monday, Macron said the government would take “concrete measures” to address those concerns.
As the turmoil has grown, Paris has been the setting of odd contrasts.
As boulevard barricades were burning Oct. 17 in Les Halles, the lilting harmonies of a roving choir singing a peace ballad were soothing passersby shopping for cheese and wine a few blocks away.
Hours later, vandals smashed scores of windows around the corner and ransacked stores as neighbors watched in horror from apartments above. Unchecked by police, looters returned the next night.
Not a week had gone by before a gaggle of fashionistas, testing the limits of decency and humor, gathered on the same stretch of the Rue Étienne Marcel for a riot-porn glamour shot in a wrecked ad-poster frame.
In the distance was a bronze statue of Louis XIV on a rearing horse in the majestic Place des Victoires, its stone pedestal stained by protesters’ splashes of red paint.
On Place de la République, the scene of violent clashes between police and protesters on Oct. 17, the usual skateboarders were back on Sunday morning. By then, graffiti had been scrubbed from the central monument that pays tribute to the French Republic, including its tradition of insurrection.
At Gollety’s weapons store, Armurerie de la Bourse, dozens of guns are on display, but firearm restrictions are so tight in France that merchants were not trying to buy any.
“In France, nobody shoots a robber,” he said. “You go to prison.”
Arnaud, 24, a pastry chef who works at a bakery and declined to share his last name, bought tear gas Friday “to neutralize someone if need be.”
“It’s incredible that it’s come to this,” he said as he left Gollety’s shop. “I think we’ve reached that limit where the French are saying, ‘OK, the state isn’t protecting me, I’m going to try to protect myself until the state protects me.’”
Arnaud supports France’s far right. “There’s no center anymore, no core that can bring everyone together. It’s a loss of bearings, and it’s a mess,” he said.
In the run-up to the protests on Saturday, the Paris police commissioner, Patrice Faure, heightened anxieties by advising merchants to hire security guards, saying police alone could not “guarantee the protection of every business.”
Florence Portelli, the mayor of Taverny, a Paris suburb, was mortified by the call for self-defense.
“The day we start opening the door to that, we end up with what sometimes happens in the United States, in countries where things go absolutely, completely crazy,” she told BFM television.
Since the protests started, they have expanded to cover the high cost of living, aggressive police tactics and other grievances. French police have arrested about 12,000 people.
At the Paris protest on Saturday, a row of police in riot gear led the crowd along the authorized route down boulevards on the city’s outskirts. Just behind them was a group of “black bloc” militants yelling ACAB, the international slogan for “all cops are bastards.”
The sea of 100,000 people marching behind them was a wide mix of union members, students, leftists and others unhappy with Macron.
Chloé Brani, a 21-year-old student from the suburbs, carried a sign that summed it up: “We’re all fed up.”
She blamed inequalities in France on “elites who don’t care.”
If military and police money “were simply put back into the causes we’re asking for — a normal salary, normal living conditions for workers in every possible profession, and high schools in good condition — there actually wouldn’t be a problem,” she said as she marched. “It’s the distribution of wealth that’s unjust.”
Montagnac, a retired executive assistant, sees France’s political leadership in a state of collapse, most evident in its loss of control during the riots. But she also thinks the turmoil is rooted in the decline of human contact in the digital age.
“Everyone is on their phone all the time,” she lamented Sunday morning at the bustling Aligre outdoor produce market, where neighbors were, just like before the riots, buying fruit, vegetables, meat and fish. “There’s no more friendliness. People don’t take the time to stop and chat. It’s always a rush.”
For Montagnac, 69, it was especially painful to see the owner of a furniture store on Boulevard Diderot hauling his sofas and chairs into the back of the shop to deter looters.
“He can’t sleep at night, he’s so scared,” she said.

Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.
Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.
“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.
Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.
But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.
In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.
The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.
“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”
Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.
A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.
While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.
If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.
The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

Please Let the Internet Die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The internet must be put out of its misery.
Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web—and the social fabric woven there—is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself.
Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements.
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.
In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.
It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”
With this anxiety hammering at my prefrontal cortex day in and out, I was more than intrigued by the absolutist title of technologist and Pulitzer-winning journalist John West’s new book, The Internet Will Die, and So Will You: On Learning to Live in Our Digital Age. In his discerning treatise, West confirms what many have suspected for a good while now: The platforms once seen as enduring archives of knowledge and communication are being cannibalized by ideological warfare and basic greed.
But that’s not the whole story. For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.
If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in a losing arms race for attention with low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.
West draws a sharp contrast between this holographic environment of monetization and a passionate, personalized internet that spanned from the primordial GeoCities to Tumblr, describing how these innovative communities have been gradually erased. While some endure in half-dead and highly corrupted form, others are lost. In middle school, West maintained a web page devoted to his love of anime; later, he kept a blog documenting his college years. Looking back as an adult, he’s vexed by the fates that have befallen each.
“I really wanted to delete my anime site,” West tells WIRED. “I don't have access to the AOL account anymore, and I couldn't do it.” Instead, it lives on as a zombie page, cluttered with spam ads and dead-end links. As for the college blog, he had neglected to pay domain fees toward the end of his time writing it, and so the final year of posts disappeared. “I kind of got obsessed with this idea that the things we want to last really don't, and then oftentimes the things that we kind of wish would go away hang on for way too long,” West says.
These shifting sands are a far cry from the flawless, collective, permanent memory that internet users originally believed they were building. “‘Forever’ is such a strong word, and it's the wrong word,” West says. Online spaces are memento mori, the same as individuals who self-promote across them (and that includes certain longevity-obsessed biohackers). Sure, there was a time when a celebrity could be “canceled” for tasteless posts unearthed years later, but in 2026, it’s not so easy to surface specific messages when you go hunting for them in your AI-powered Gmail account. Zeitgeist-defining platforms like Vine can be vaporized in an instant, a fact reinforced in January 2025, when Americans posted farewell TikTok videos ahead of an expected US ban on the app.
This random ephemerality, West points out, has eroded any confidence in claims previously backed up by hypertext cross-references, and thus any kind of consensus truth. An analysis of hyperlinks in articles on The New York Times website between 1996 and mid-2019 found that 25 percent of all links were inaccessible. According to a 2016 study, “three out of four citations in scholarly articles have drifted—the websites they purport to cite no longer say what they once did,” he writes. “Over half of Wikipedia’s entries contain at least one link in its references section that goes nowhere, a Pew report found.”
The impulse to drive engagement spreads to users themselves: West noticed, for instance, that when he recently reread a favorite book, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, he had the nagging thought that while he loved returning to the novel for the fourth or fifth time, he wouldn’t be able to count it toward his annual Goodreads stats. West says this fixation on the internet’s hollow validations creates “the exact conditions for a space to be filled by something that isn't human.”
Wouldn’t it be liberating, then, to actually deny our attention to astroturfed outrage, engineered virality, and influencer sponcon? To let the mainstream digital economies propped up by AI-enabled surveillance finally fall to ruin? If what the titans of the industry have to offer us these days are “pervert glasses” and the suppression of ads for a probably unflattering documentary, why are we helping them stay in business? Leaving their platforms for dead might be the last lever of power available to the masses.
Doing so could free people to explore dormant corners. West notes that some of the most interesting parts of the internet are the ones that nobody sees, like web portals to streams of YouTube videos that have almost no views. “Some of it’s fucking weird and creepy, but a lot of it’s just people singing a song and having a blast,” he says. West also cites the bustling, zero-revenue, circulation of poetry in web journals as proof that “you can find meaning and make meaning online all the time,” provided there is no financial motivation.
When you eliminate what the platforms want you to fixate on, it’s clear what you’ve been missing, and how you were steered away from it. Your opinions are shaped in a bubble by avatars you’ve never met, weaponized against equally hermetic rival camps. The internet doesn’t really have winners, unless you count the few without the sense to stop chasing relevance at any cost. That’s why the main characters are so malleable in their beliefs; never afraid to pivot, betray, and discard what they once held to be the core of their identity. And that’s when they stood for anything to begin with.
Absent a sudden, lasting outage due to a fresh and severe catastrophe, the internet as it exists won’t perish anytime soon. There are, however, splintering cracks in its facade, which may create room for emergent and strangely evolved life-forms. There’s no reason to assume that the present tech empire will rule the century to come; the organic and anarchic web stands to mount a triumphant renaissance if (or when) it falls.
“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.
Then again, as West’s book sought to remind me, I am destined to die as well. Maybe I’ll be mixed in with the soil.

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Despite missile strikes that killed people, disrupted air travel and postponed major events, Riyadh Season opened with thousands attending concerts, comedy and attractions in the Saudi capital.
- Residents say daily life feels largely normal, but renewed Houthi attacks and the Iran war are weighing on the kingdom.
- Government messaging which once touted economic and cultural development, promotes patriotic themes.
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — The lineup was announced months ago, with top-flight stars in tennis, DJing, comedy and more set to descend on the Saudi capital for a 10-week run of events known as Riyadh Season.
But after successive missile strikes hit Riyadh’s airport this month, killing more than a dozen people, shuttering parts of the country’s airspace and setting off a flurry of cancellations, many wondered if audiences would show up, or if there would be anything to show up for at all.
The answer to both questions came this past weekend, when crowds gathered for Riyadh Season’s opener at Boulevard City, a car-free district in the capital that’s part open-air mall, part amusement park and part entertainment venue.
By the time sunset had turned to dusk, families were milling about a replica of Times Square. Patrons assembled for a sold-out comedy play at one of two theaters, while others went to a 7,000-seat arena, where a famous Lebanese pop star was debuting his comeback tour. It too was sold out.
This is a twilight moment for the Saudi capital. In normal times, October is when the convection-bake temperatures of Riyadh’s ferocious summer give way to a bearable, even pleasant heat, and the city hosts dozens of large-scale events aimed at showcasing Vision 2030, the kingdom’s all-out drive to transform itself into a sporting and entertainment powerhouse.
But between the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Riyadh’s escalating grudge match with the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, these are hardly normal times.
For years, the war with the Houthis — whose official name is Ansar Allah, or Partisans of God — had ebbed and flowed between campaign and ceasefire, but for most Saudis, it had remained background noise. That changed in recent months, with a truce breaking down, and the Houthis lobbing drones, ballistic and cruise missiles across Saudi Arabia.
All of a sudden, the war took on a more present form, unsettling a kingdom unused to conflicts playing out on home turf. Almost every night in Riyadh brings the bass-drum booms and thuds of interceptors launching to destroy incoming projectiles.
Government messaging has turned pugilistic, replacing paeans to Vision 2030 and the country’s leadership with images of Saudi F-15s en route to do battle over Yemen, or commercial billboards declaring “Our bravery brings us together” or “Stable home, reassured hearts.”
In October alone, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi airports have killed at least 21 people and wounded hundreds, forcing authorities to shut down operations in the country’s main international airport in Riyadh and curtailing travel in others. (On Sunday, officials announced some flights at the Riyadh airport had resumed.)
Schools shifted to online-only learning, while many businesses — including Saudi Aramco, the country’s state-owned oil company — were ordered to evacuate headquarters and have all staff work remotely. The U.S. Embassy ordered “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” in Saudi Arabia to leave.
The attacks come at an inopportune juncture. Many of the kingdom’s marquee, international-facing gatherings have been affected, including the World Petroleum Congress, a summit between the European Union and Persian Gulf nations, and the government’s flagship investment conference, the Future Investment Initiative.
Though the congress went ahead — with many top oil executives attending virtually — the summit and investment conference were shelved till next year. Also postponed were some of Riyadh Season’s major sporting events, such as the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament.
But other events — including boxing and UFC championships and the WWE Crown Jewel event — remain stubbornly on the calendar. The first few days of Riyadh Season have gone ahead with little incident, even if participants were forced to divert to other cities or even neighboring Bahrain or Kuwait before being ferried back to the Saudi capital.
That shrugging off of the war was a common attitude among visitors to Boulevard City, organizers say.
In the replica Times Square, building-sized screens cast windows of light as people grabbed elaborate drinks made with iced tea, coffee or hibiscus. Trackless trains, their carriages mocked up as reindeer, ferried kids around a giant illuminated orb.
“Between foot traffic in Boulevard City, audiences for the plays and the concerts, we had something like 27,000 people coming in,” said Hassan Albar, Boulevard City’s director, a note of pride — and some relief — creeping into his voice.
“And we’re still at the beginning of the season.”
Despite the daily cellphone alerts that warn residents to remain indoors until danger passes, people interviewed emphasized a show-must-go-on disposition.
“We like to keep it positive, so we’re not going to be staying inside. It’s human nature to feel afraid if you don’t have control, but the situation is fine,” said Neetika Malotra, 33, who was taking pictures of Ankid Abishaikh, 34, before a Boulevard City sign.
Abishaikh said conditions in Saudi Arabia are different from how they’re portrayed online.
“Our parents are outside in India, so when they see news channels or social media, it looks very scary. But we tell them that what they see there is not always right,” he said.
“When you’re here, everything feels normal and we’re doing well.”
Both the U.S.-Israel war on Iran and the Houthis’ campaign have harmed Saudi Arabia’s oil production, with closures of the Strait of Hormuz denying the kingdom its main energy export corridor. In addition to missiles at Riyadh‘s airport, the Houthis over the weekend targeted crude oil pumping stations, an oil refinery, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the East-West Pipeline, which transports oil to terminals on the Red Sea coast.
The Saudi military has struggled to defend against Houthi missiles, hampered by the sheer size of the country — Saudi Arabia’s territory is more than five times the size of California — and a fast-depleting supply of interceptors.
The fighting with the Houthis is compounding the economic headwinds forced on the kingdom by the Iran war and a general economic slowdown; Saudi officials already have had to reassess some of the grander ambitions underpinning Vision 2030.
Contractors, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to jeopardize future professional prospects, say that staff working on so-called gigaprojects have been drawn down, reassigned or let go. Ancillary businesses — catering and events organizers — have endured losses of up to two thirds of revenues amid a cost-cutting pullback.
Yet despite those complaints, the consensus among many residents is that the war hasn’t had a drastic impact on their lives, at least in terms of their sense of safety.
“It’s very secure here. I don’t feel anything like what’s said on the news,” said Abdul Rahman Al-Hassan, 38, a dentist who moved to Riyadh nine months ago from Moscow.
He compared the situation here to the Russian capital, which has been the frequent target of a Ukrainian drone campaign.
“Journalists say the same sort of thing about Moscow: That it’s very dangerous and that people are hiding in their basements from the drones,” he said.
“But it’s not true there, and it’s not true here. You can have an attack in one area, but people are still going out normally.”
That may hint at a head-in-the-sand mentality, and it’s hard to gauge public sentiment in a country where openly expressing dissatisfaction with government policies can land you in jail or have you deported. But among Saudis, the conflict with the Houthis appears to have spurred a rally-round-the-flag moment.
“We fully trust the government and the leadership in charge,” said Awatef Mohammad, a 31-year-old English teacher strolling with her partner through Boulevard City.
Similar sentiments emerge even in places more directly in the line of fire. Over the weekend, spectators gathered at Riyadh’s King Abdulaziz Racecourse for an evening of horse racing, despite the fact that the track is barely three miles from the airport.
Jamil Mohammad, a 42-year-old occupational therapist, had his children Jad and Joury in tow. He propped up Joury on a railing to watch the horses saunter past as they prepared for the race. His eyes on his daughter, he expressed a belief in God’s protection that, to many outsiders, can sound like fatalism.
“Look, whether I’m here near the airport, or anywhere else in the world, if God says it’s my time to die, then it’s my time to die. It won’t matter,” he said.
“Death only comes once. I’m not going to let it stop me living my life.”

Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
Unknown

18:57:56 KST

Belgian industry is in the doldrums. Nearly 30% of all the machines in Belgian factories currently stand idle, according to financial dailies De Tijd and L’Echo. The metal and technology federation Agoria describes the industrial slump as “unprecedented”. Sector federations are therefore calling for measures to tackle high costs and are warning of further job losses.
Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
‘In our sector, we have been struggling with a capacity utilisation rate below 80 per cent for four years now. That is unprecedented,’ Patrick Slaets, chief economist at the metal and technology federation Agoria, told VRT NEWS.
“The cause lies in a lack of demand. There is too little investment, due to the high interest rates brought about by inflation and excessively high energy costs resulting from the geopolitical situation.” This is why energy-intensive companies are suffering the most.
A fall in capacity utilisation also means a greater risk of job losses, warns Slaets. “If the machines aren’t running, there’s no need for people to work there. In the technology sector, 20,000 jobs have already been lost over the past three years. That represents a 6 to 7 per cent reduction in capacity compared with pre-crisis levels.”
Chemical sector also reeling from high energy costs
The chemical sector is also facing tough times. According to a study by consultancy firm Roland Berger, European capacity fell by 9 per cent between 2022 and 2025. On top of that, only 69 to 70 per cent of that (reduced) capacity is being utilised.
It’s been announced that chemical company Vynova in Tessenderlo-Ham is temporarily halting production due to high energy prices. 600 employees are at risk of temporary unemployment.
“It is gradually becoming clear that this crisis is more severe than the previous one,” says Gert Verreth, spokesperson for the chemicals’ federation Essenscia.
It is being argued that urgent action is needed to address issues such as high energy costs and bureaucracy. This applies not only to Belgium, as the rest of Europe is also grappling with similar problems.
‘There is political awareness, but progress at European political level is too slow,’ says Verreth. On the one hand, the high costs must be tackled, but on the other, Europe must also send a strong signal on the geopolitical stage.
There is the context of increasingly aggressive industrial policies, with Trump’s tariff war and the mass production being encouraged by the Chinese government. “Europe must act more swiftly and urgently show its teeth.”
It’s being argued that in Belgium, in particular, labour costs must be kept under control. They are already higher than in neighbouring countries and are threatening to rise even further. “If they are not kept in line with our neighbours, we could end up in an industrial recession next year,” Slaets also fears.

While the leaders of the Baltic states and Poland have repeatedly reaffirmed their commitment to completing the project at the European level, public debate in Latvia has once again turned to whether the country can afford it, Kivila noted.
He stressed that European Union (EU) support for Rail Baltica is not merely a political declaration. This is demonstrated by the 4.5 billion euros in funding already allocated, reflecting the project's strategic importance at the European level.
"Therefore, at this stage of the project, the most important question is not whether Latvia can afford Rail Baltica, but how Latvia will continue construction, fulfil its commitments and make full use of this substantial EU support," Kivila said.
He recalled that on 16 October, the leaders of four countries reaffirmed their commitment to completing Rail Baltica during the next EU multiannual budget period in a joint letter to EU leaders, calling for predictable European funding for the project.
Project implementers take such commitments seriously because construction planning and contractual obligations are based on them.
They also take seriously public statements that raise doubts about the project's financing prospects.
Kivila pointed out that such signals reach other EU member states and Brussels, making it difficult to demand predictable European funding when Latvia's own decision-making remains unpredictable.
"The financing challenges facing Rail Baltica are well known. Simply repeating them will not build a single kilometre of railway. Latvia did not arrive at its current situation overnight. It has also been shaped by postponed decisions, including those concerning the project implementation schedule, financing plan and infrastructure manager, as well as inadequate financial planning and the inability to agree on priorities in time," Kivila said.
In his view, it would be paradoxical to use these same problems as arguments for further delaying the project.
Kivila explained that several financing scenarios are available, combining EU co-financing, national contributions and other financial instruments while spreading investments over a longer period.
He believes Latvia needs a concrete decision that reflects the country's fiscal capacity.
According to Kivila, Estonia has recently demonstrated how such challenges can be addressed in practice.
Its revised schedule envisages completing the Tallinn–Pärnu connection by 2032 and the cross-border section by 2034.
At the same time, planned investments for 2027 have been reduced from 919 million euros to 541 million euros, while investments for 2028 have been cut from approximately 1.06 billion euros to 453 million euros.
Kivila emphasised that Estonia's plan also depends on future EU funding and that the country has not resolved all its financing challenges.
However, Estonia has made decisions on how to address them. He believes Latvia needs an equally concrete approach.
Rail Baltica construction is already underway in all three Baltic states, Kivila noted.
More than 40% of the first phase of the main railway line is either under construction or ready for construction to begin.
In Latvia, construction contracts cover more than 200 kilometres, but the actual pace of work is significantly slower than in neighbouring countries, Kivila acknowledged.
Meanwhile, the implementation deadlines for several Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) funding agreements expire in 2028, with some extending into 2029.
Kivila stressed that EU funding deadlines will not wait for Latvia to finish discussing why making decisions is difficult.
"Moreover, Latvia is not alone in this project. Estonia and Lithuania are investing millions to establish a connection with the rest of Europe, and its full operation also depends on the Latvian section. Our neighbours can make their own decisions and build their own railways, but they cannot build Latvia's section for it. Latvia's delays also postpone the return on their investments. This is a responsibility that extends beyond Latvia's national budget," Kivila said.
He explained that slowing construction is not a cost-free solution.
It creates risks associated with renegotiating contracts, price indexation and additional expenses.
Kivila stressed that unused EU funding means the same construction work will cost more in the future.
At the same time, delays postpone the benefits of the new railway connection with Europe, including opportunities for freight and passenger transport, business development and military mobility.
Kivila also highlighted that construction investments generate fiscal returns.
According to project estimates, approximately 19–21% of invested funds return to the national budget through tax revenues.
As previously reported, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis of New Unity (JV) said on Monday, 26 October, during TV3's programme 900 Seconds that the new government would have to assess whether and how Latvia could afford to continue implementing Rail Baltica while preparing the next national budget.
Kozlovskis explained that Russia's war in Ukraine and other geopolitical developments require serious consideration and decisions, as it is clear that Latvia can no longer continue with the approach used so far.
Furthermore, there is currently no clarity regarding funding from the EU in future planning periods or financing from the European Commission.
LETA previously reported that the first phase of Rail Baltica's main railway line in Latvia is planned within the existing scope.
This includes establishing a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from the Lithuanian border to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station to enable connections between Rail Baltica and the existing railway network.
Consequently, the first phase does not include the so-called Riga loop.
It has also been reported that the first phase of Rail Baltica could cost 14.3 billion euros across the Baltic states, including 5.5 billion euros in Latvia.
However, after accounting for price indexation, Latvia's costs could reach six billion euros.
According to the project's cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros.
The previous cost-benefit analysis, conducted in 2017, estimated the project's total cost at 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica aims to establish a European standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian–Polish border, connecting the Baltic states with the wider European railway network.
The project envisages constructing 870 kilometres of new European standard-gauge railway tracks, with a gauge of 1,435 millimetres, across the Baltic states.
Trains on the new railway are expected to reach maximum speeds of 240 kilometres per hour.

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds, Anadolu reports.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.

Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine’s trains keep on rolling
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:54:06 CET
18:54:06 KST

By Yurii Kovalenko
ON A TRAIN BETWEEN DNIPRO AND ODESA, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Ukrainian beauty salon owner Antonina Viter is getting used to having her travel plans disrupted by the threat of Russian drone attacks, as she criss-crosses the country by rail to keep her business going.
“Every third trip, we end up evacuating once, twice or even three times,” she explained on board a train from the southeastern city of Dnipro to Odesa on the Black Sea.
“What can you do? How else do you get to your client?”
Kyiv has set new rules for rail passengers during air-raid alerts and, sure enough, soon after she spoke, the 36-year-old was standing outside under a pitch-black October sky, wrapped in a blanket, waiting for the “all-clear”.
In a country long reliant on its vast rail network, hours-long delays and repeat evacuations when air-raid sirens sound are another way in which Russia’s escalating missile and drone attacks are wrecking everyday life for civilians.
New Russian jet-powered drones that are hard to shoot down have attacked everything from shopping centres and filling stations to power plants and other critical infrastructure. And the railways are no exception.
UKRAINIAN RAILWAYS ATTACKED 1,700 TIMES THIS YEAR
The state operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, says Russia has attacked more than 1,700 rail facilities this year, including stations, locomotives and passenger wagons. Russia says its targets are objects used by Kyiv’s military.
A trip on the line from Dnipro to Odesa, some 400 km (250 miles) to the southwest, showed how Ukrainians are coping with those disruptions.
The outward journey featured eight evacuations of roughly 30 minutes each, the return journey - one more.
Direct attacks, like the drone strike that killed two train drivers on the Dnipro-Odesa line on August 13, are an ever-present threat.
But air-raid alerts can unexpectedly double the travel time on any route, and some stations in the east and south have been shut indefinitely as fighting creeps closer.
The prospect of being hit is one that 41-year-old IT worker Larysa Konstantynova - who was travelling from Dnipro to Odesa with her teenage son at the start of a holiday trip to Europe - prefers not to think about.
Like Viter, who travels at least six times a month to manage two salons in Kyiv and Dnipro, she says she is adapting.
“It’s how your mind works: you just try to be positive and survive with the way things are.”
Other attacks have included a strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in September.
For some, overnight rail journeys - once opportunities to unwind with few distractions - are now spent in anxious anticipation.
During air raid alerts, passengers can be jolted awake and forced to scramble into fields or up and down embankments, sometimes with children or pets in tow. In the winter, temperatures are often below freezing.
RAILWAY JOURNEYS HAUNTED BY RISK OF RANDOM DEATH
Huddled outside her train with a colleague, Viter tracked a nearby drone on a cell-phone app after hearing its distinctive ‘whoosh’ overhead.
It was the third evacuation in two hours.
“Better to stand in a field for an hour than to risk never getting to see the next hour,” she said, knowing she had to teach a beauty workshop in Odesa the next day.
In fact, although delays of 5 to 12 hours are not unusual on the Dnipro-Odesa route, this train arrived just an hour and 20 minutes late.
Nevertheless, the risk of random death has soared as Russia has broadened its drone and ballistic-missile campaign, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of air defence missiles.
More than 50 railway workers have died on duty this year alone, according to Ukraine’s infrastructure minister, and dedicated staff have had to adapt their routines to maintain a network that appears to be close to their hearts.
At the beginning of each journey, conductors sweep through the carriages closing curtains to block out light that might alert a Russian drone.
“They can see us, so we have to hide a bit,” said train attendant Olha Boniuk, 49, with the air of a mother soothing her child.
After each evacuation, chief conductor Mykola Zakharchenko, 47, sits in his cramped booth diligently recording the interruption.
All the same, he smiles recalling conversations with passengers, and still enjoys watching dawn break through the carriage window: “Train work, as they say, is romance.”
Locomotive driver Mykola Kovalenko put it another way.
“If I quit,” he said, “who will drive the trains?”
(Additional reporting by Thomas Peter; Writing by Dan Peleschuk; Editing by Mike Collett-White and Kevin Liffey)

By Liz Lee and Fernando Kallas
MADRID/BEIJING, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Real Madrid issued an apology on Wednesday after their French forward Kylian Mbappe sparked a fierce backlash over his comments referring to the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator.
After apologies from Mbappe and LaLiga did not quell the response in China, LaLiga President Javier Tebas set up a crisis unit and met with Chinese ambassador Yao Jing.
The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative Chinese market, where satire about Mao, modern China’s founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.
“Real Madrid CF wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappe,” Real said in a statement.
“Our club maintains a deep respect for China, its history, its culture and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid.”
China’s state-owned broadcasting platform Migu is not showing Real Madrid’s LaLiga game against Racing Santander on Sunday, and Chinese brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage ceased all cooperation with Mbappe.
REAL MADRID GAME NOT ON TV
Migu is scheduled to show nine of LaLiga’s 10 games this weekend, with Real Madrid’s match the only one not covered. Migu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
LaLiga moved quickly to set up a crisis unit and reached out to Real Madrid, a significant move following years of strained relations between Tebas and the club due to a power struggle within Spanish football. Real Madrid recently called for Tebas’ resignation.
Both parties put aside their differences, however, acknowledging the potential immediate and long-term financial repercussions of Mbappe’s comments. Following Real’s statement, people at LaLiga said Tebas was considering travelling to China to neutralise the threat of a massive financial loss for Spanish football.
LaLiga will also consider strengthening its institutional engagement with Beijing amid serious concerns about a sharp drop in revenue, as Chinese state television awaits further gestures of reconciliation.
In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a humorous meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.
Fans have previously created memes superimposing Mbappe’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for. Mbappe has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press.
On Wednesday, when asked what China thought of Mbappe’s apology, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: “We take seriously the apology that the person has made.”

Isamaa lawyer: No ruling in criminal case to come before Riigikogu election

Isamaa lawyer: No ruling in criminal case to come before Riigikogu election
A criminal case against opposition party Isamaa will not reach a court ruling before the March 2027 Riigikogu elections, the party's lawyer has said.
Jaanus Tehver, Isamaa's lawyer, said prosecutors are yet to decide whether to bring charges, but will do so soon.
The suspicions date to last November, when prosecutors notified Isamaa of a prohibited donation totaling €110,234 allegedly accepted between November 2020 and April 2024.
Tehver said he will file no further requests with the Prosecutor's Office and is waiting for the formal charges, which he expects given the prosecution's stated position since spring.
The Prosecutor's Office for its part said the defense has been given until next Monday to examine the evidence materials, after which prosecutors will decide how to proceed.
According to the suspicions, prohibited donations — mainly advertising services — totaling approximately €330,000 were made to Isamaa, of which the party allegedly accepted €110,234. Isamaa and all other suspects deny the allegations.
Tehver said that, purely in terms of timing, no ruling can now be issued ahead of the elections — at best, a preliminary hearing could be held, he added.
"This means that, until the Riigikogu elections, the best that can be said is that charges have been brought before the court and that the Isamaa party is accused of this or that crime," he said. "Unfortunately, we will not know the court's position on what it thinks of these charges before the elections. Regrettable, but what can you do."
"For me, the Prosecutor's Office's position is clear, and in a situation where they have made the decision that I believe they have made, there is no point in my submitting any further requests," Tehver added.
Isamaa's hairman Urmas Reinsalu said it was in the party's interest for clarity to come quickly, but said that the proceedings had not been an issue when recruiting candidates or preparing the election campaign. "Perhaps Isamaa's opponents are more interested in that. But in my opinion, this stirring up of dust already received a public verdict at the end of last year, when we presented our expert analyses and assessments," Reinsalu said.
Reinsalu added cases like this can work the other way too and exert a sort of rallying-round-the-flag effect, as supporters come to see the charges as unfounded – while charges would attract attention, this would not be enough to distract from offering a political alternative to the Reform Party-led government, he said.
Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Kauri Sinkevicius said that if charges are brought and the case goes to court, the court will take over responsibility for the proceedings, and can take circumstances such as the upcoming elections into account when scheduling hearings.
Background:
Last November the Prosecutor's Office notified Isamaa that it was suspected of accepting a large-scale prohibited donation totaling €110,234 between November 2020 and April 2024. Tehver has previously stated the party is suspected of having benefited from coordinated activity by major donor Parvel Pruunsild, Tõnis Palts and the nonprofit MTÜ Isamaalised, who provided advertising and analysis services, with the costs covered by MTÜ Isamaalised. Under the Political Parties Act, companies and nonprofits are prohibited from financing party activities or providing free benefits with monetary value.

By Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Sunday and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented only “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”, and that Tehran’s policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme to be part of negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions — which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports — must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.
ATTACK ON SAUDI OIL REFINERY
In late September, Iran presented another seven-day proposal under which Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.
Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on February 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia — a key US ally and the world’s largest crude exporter — opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.
Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than $115 per barrel on Wednesday after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over supply risks.
Fighting with the Houthis intensified last month as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.
CONCERNS ABOUT RISK OF NEW STRIKES
The official briefed on the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of Sunday’s meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
On Monday, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of de-escalation efforts. Qatar said on Tuesday that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.
Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.
The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has eroded Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress.

Klitschko accuses central government of trying to oust him

Speaking to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty on Oct. 20, he alleged that officials were behind a protest demanding his resignation. He named no officials and provided no direct evidence linking the government to the demonstration.
“Everything is being done to establish a military administration, implement centralized control, create a hierarchical structure, and destroy local self-government,” Klitschko said.
Several hundred people gathered outside Kyiv’s city administration building on Oct. 17, demanding his resignation over winter preparations, shelter shortages and spending priorities. Protesters also criticized urban improvement projects during wartime.
Klitschko pushed back against criticism of the city’s shelter network, saying Kyiv had more than 4,000 shelters. He also said funds allocated for mobile shelters remained unused because district administrations had not submitted requests.

The conversation between Stubb, Støre, and Putin took place at the initiative of Western leaders. The Kremlin reported the day before that the Russian president had “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine, recalling the “root causes of the conflict,” and had also drawn attention to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting.” A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of seizing the entire territory of Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary.
During conversations with Western politicians and journalists, Putin has repeatedly spent a long time recounting his version of the history of Russia and Ukraine. He did so, for example, in an interview with American journalist Tucker Carlson in 2024, and during a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in Alaska.

NEW DELHI: Explaining his decision to vacate his Nandigram stronghold and retain Bhabanipur, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Wednesday that vacating the Bhabanipur seat would have given his predecessor, Mamata Banerjee, another opportunity to contest the subsequent bypoll and return to the state assembly.Adhikari, who won both seats in the West Bengal assembly elections in April, defeated Mamata Banerjee in Bhabanipur. Dozens killed in Spanish high-speed train collision (VIDEOS)
At least 64 people have been killed after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo, Spain, Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page has said, according to Spanish newspaper ABC. More than 179 people have reportedly been injured.
The crash occurred at 8:54 AM local time on Wednesday between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, around 120 km south of Madrid, on the high-speed line linking the Spanish capital with Andalusia. A Renfe AVE train reportedly struck an Iryo train from behind, sending two carriages off the tracks and down an embankment, according to rail infrastructure operator Adif.

The two trains were carrying a combined total of more than 500 passengers, according to Spanish media reports.
Spain’s Transport Ministry has identified human error by an operator at rail infrastructure manager Adif as the leading preliminary explanation for the crash, according to ABC. An operator reportedly authorized the Renfe train to pass a red signal despite the Iryo service remaining stationary on the same track.

Wednesday’s disaster is the latest in a series of serious railway accidents in Spain this year, raising concerns over the safety of the country’s rail network. On January 18, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz in the southern province of Cordoba, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150. Investigators have identified a broken section of track as the likely cause, although the investigation is ongoing.

Just two days later, a commuter train struck a collapsed retaining wall near Barcelona, killing the driver and injuring dozens. Another passenger train collided with a crane near Cartagena on January 22, injuring six, and a collision at a level crossing in February reportedly left one person dead.
The incidents have fueled concerns over railway infrastructure and maintenance standards, prompting demands for stronger safety measures. Japan flags 3 reasons for ‘deteriorating’ security environment in Southeast Asia, vows support to regional bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:48:08 UTC
18:48:08 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Japan on Wednesday flagged “three reasons” for the “rapidly deteriorating” security environment in Southeast Asia, pledging support to the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
“Disasters are growing more severe, striking communications, medical care, and transport at once. Conflicts worldwide are reaching our supply chains and energy supplies, and the military balance is shifting fast, raising the risk of collision against a vulnerable and of dangerous miscalculations,” Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, told a joint meeting of ASEAN defense chiefs in Cebu City, the Philippines, current chair of the Southeast Asian bloc.
“These crises do not merely adapt; they overlap and amplify one another,” said Koizumi, stressing ASEAN’s “unity, centrality, and resilience.”
“Japan values all three” as they “are international public goods, safeguarding peace, prosperity, and every nation's freedom to choose,” he said.
Koizumi said the ASEAN members “are strengthening their own ability to respond and deter.”
“ASEAN as a whole is tackling shared challenges from disaster response to maritime security. These efforts complement each other, and Japan … will support both,” he said.
“Our aim is simple: to widen the options for ASEAN and for each member to understand, decide, and act on its own,” said the Japanese defense chief, urging ASEAN and Japan to “update our areas of cooperation.”
He pledged that Japan “will do everything it can” to turn ASEAN “choices into real strength.”
The meetings in Cebu City mark the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, which also brings together the defense chiefs of US, China, South Korea, Japan, Australia, and India, although China this year did not send its defense minister.
