US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

US and China share a love of “new things and innovation” says Ma Yansong
Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.
Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.
“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.
The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.
“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.
Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.
“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”
His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.
At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.
Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.
The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.
Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.
The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.
Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.
He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.
The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.
“You create a dream. That’s important.”
The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.
Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.
“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.
“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”
Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.
“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”
“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”
For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.
“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”
“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”
At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.
The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.
“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”
“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”
“I like the future, but not the cold future”
The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.
Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.
And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.
“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”
Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.
“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.

He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.
The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.
“You create a dream. That’s important.”
The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.
Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.
“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.
“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”
Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.
“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”
“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”
For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.
“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”
“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”
At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.
The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.
“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”
“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”
“I like the future, but not the cold future”
The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.
Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.
And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.
“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”
Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.
“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.
Dezeen In Depth

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry considers limiting foreign internet traffic for Russian users
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is discussing a plan to route all traffic from foreign domains through the country’s internet traffic filtering system (TSPU) and limit its volume, Forbes Russia reported. Several sources — including officials at the ministry and people in the IT industry — told the outlet that the measures could be included in a bill overhauling the telecommunications sector.
The ministry is expected to gain the authority to restrict foreign traffic for Russian users once it exceeds a limit that has yet to be set. From an operator’s standpoint, VPN use looks like foreign traffic.
Industry representatives polled by Forbes Russia said determining which traffic is foreign will be difficult. “A Russian website hosted abroad would be classified as foreign, while a server rented in Russia would be classified as domestic,” said a technical expert at RKS Global.
The Digital Development Ministry announced that “these issues are currently being worked out, but it would be premature to say which of them, and in what form, will be included in the final version of the amendments.”
There have been repeated reports that the Digital Development Ministry wants to charge higher fees for foreign traffic.
Demand for VPNs in Russia has surged as authorities block popular social networks, services, and messaging apps. In response, Russian authorities have intensified their fight against means of circumventing the blocks. The budget for the next three years allocates a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering.

Two high-speed trains collide in Spain, at least 10 dead
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:58:10 CET
17:58:10 KST

By David Latona, Guillermo Martinez and Michael Francis Gore
URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain’s second fatal rail crash this year and Europe’s deadliest since 2013.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a televised address from near the accident site south of Madrid that “all of Spain” was in mourning, while the opposition People’s Party said it had cancelled all campaign events for the day ahead of an election next month.
Sanchez said the “terrible tragedy” would be investigated and vowed to address any failures that came to light, adding that the causes of the two crashes appeared to be unrelated.
“If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sanchez said.
RED SIGNAL
Spain’s transport minister said the crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue its journey despite an active red signal due to a stationary train ahead.
Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, and an erroneous decision had been made to restart the Renfe train.
At the scene, ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters had parked next to one of the trains on an elevated track section, while twisted metal and wreckage were strewn across an embankment down which at least three carriages had plunged.
The head of Castilla-La Mancha’s regional government said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescue workers were still going carriage by carriage looking for other crash victims.
Passengers, some splattered with blood or bandaged, were evacuated along a nearby road in the aftermath of the accident, which Spain’s health minister Monica Garcia said on social media had injured 80 people, 15 of them very seriously.
Salvador Arriza described the chaos in his carriage.
“I was very close to the door, but (other passengers) were breaking the windows to be able to get out. Some people practically couldn’t move because they were trapped amongst the seats,” said the 62-year-old.
INVESTIGATION UNDER WAY
The accident, the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela in which 80 people died, follows another in January between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people.
In that crash, a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, prompting a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance.
Renfe said in a statement on Wednesday that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know”.
“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
Iryo and Adif did not respond to requests for comment.
PASSENGERS SENT FLYING
A Castilla-La Mancha regional spokesperson said 147 people were on board the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe service, which crashed at around 9 a.m., causing two Iryo carriages to derail.
Passenger Rafael Barcelo said he felt lucky as he had stepped away from his seat for a coffee, adding there had been at least eight victims from his carriage.
“We were having breakfast, drinking a coffee when we felt a very strong impact and we were sent flying,” he said.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols.
At a school in Urda where relatives of those missing were being sent, a woman who gave her name as Ana fought back tears as she said there was no news of her husband Pepe and his name was not on the list of those identified, but police had found their dog, Trece.
MAINTENANCE SPENDING
The causes of the January accident are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period last year, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain’s competition authority.
Meanwhile, accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year, according to Spain’s railway safety authority.
European Commission data shows Spain’s maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000 km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged other large European countries.
Although Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any other country, most of this was to build new infrastructure with only around 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.
(Reporting by David Latona, Emma Pinedo, Mireia Merino, Corina Pons, Victoria Waldersee, Benjamin Mejias, Joan Faus and Pietro Lombardi; Writing by Charlie Devereux and Alexander Smith; Editing by Toby Chopra and Alison Williams)

The banker, the basketball star, the cardiologist and the chemist: meet Serbia’s potential new leaders
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:57:40 CET
17:57:40 KST

BELGRADE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - After a leaderless student-led protest movement swept Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vucic from power in a historic snap election on Sunday, the country is waiting to hear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key ministerial positions as it forms a government.
Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students’ list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution’s independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic’s government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, pointing to Serbia’s standing and declining scores on international transparency metrics, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions.
Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policy amendments of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement’s lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement’s “Guardians of the Constitution” bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system “at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients”. In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building “a better Serbia, nothing else is important”.
He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Tuesday wrote on X that he had held a “good” telephone conversation with Srdanovic, saying that the priority is to establish a new government without delay.
Some of Srdanovic’s policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of those of the previous government. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. During the campaign he also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national “existential survival”.
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement’s most prominent public speakers.
He described Sunday’s election as a fight “for the return of a country that has been hijacked”.
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan “We have our God, his name is Bodiroga.”
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students’ election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a “citizens’ victory”.
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic’s resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was “occupied from within” and said he was ready to put “even his life” at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a “temporarily occupied territory” and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic’s recent resignation from the post.
(Writing by Aleksandar Vasovic, editing by Kirsten Donovan and Edward McAllister)

Ebola disease: Providing mental health support to patients and their loved ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:57:30 UTC
17:57:30 KST

In Butembo, in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Kasoki Zawadi spends her days with her husband, who is being treated for Ebola disease. A plexiglass window separates them, but they can talk to each other. In Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) treatment centres, psychological support is available to both patients and their loved ones.
In the corridor of Kitatumba's Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, North Kivu province, Kasoki Zawadi sits on a plastic chair facing the window that separates her from her husband, Victoire. He has been in hospital for 13 days. On the other side of the plastic screen, he smiles from time to time.
The hospital where Victoire is being treated is one of the facilities where MSF supports treatment for patients with Ebola disease. In Butembo, 1,472 cases were confirmed and 735 deaths recorded between May and 22 October 2026.
The outbreak is hitting people already facing insecurity and economic hardship. Many families are sheltering relatives displaced by fighting in neighbouring areas, while movement restrictions and reduced trade have made daily life even harder.
At the treatment centre, teams provide support not only to patients but also their loved ones, as they cope with fear, uncertainty, and the wait for test results. From the moment of admission, psychologists are there to listen to concerns, explain the care being provided, and help families manage the mental strain of hospitalisation.
Every morning, Kasoki arrives at around 6.30 am and stays until 6.30 pm. Her brother-in-law takes over at night.
“We manage to communicate despite the window,” she says. “We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.”
We manage to communicate despite the window. We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.
Kasoki Zawadi, whose husband is receiving treatment for Ebola disease
Since her husband was admitted, she has stopped working as a teacher. Their family is supporting them during this time. She also worries about her own health. And when she leaves the centre, the separation weighs heavily on her.
“In the evening, when I go home and can’t see my husband, I find it hard to sleep,” says Kasoki.
A few days later, Kasoki explains that a negative test result had given them hope that they would soon be able to go home. But a second test came back positive.
“When he tested positive again, we were exhausted, mentally and physically,” she says. “Fortunately, the psychologists’ support helped us feel calmer, and we managed to wait.”
Staying in touch during hospitalisation
The disease and hospitalisation can be distressing for both patients and their loved ones. In Butembo, Patrice Muyisa Kokotz, mental health activity supervisor, provides psychological support. He describes people who arrive not only fearing the disease, but also worried about what awaits them at the centre. Some fear that isolation means they will be abandoned.
“We give them time to express themselves, talk about their past and their emotions,” explains Patrice. His team introduces people to how the centre works, explains the care provided, and organises visits. He says seeing other patients and their caregivers helps reassure families.
Some suggest that psychological support can have an impact on patient outcomes.
“Ebola disease is traumatic and sudden; it is a viral illness. So you are under stress, always expecting death at any moment,” says Rachel Kashimoto, a clinical psychologist working with MSF in Beni, also in North Kivu. 
“If you are not mentally stable and not well cared for, even physically, things may not go well,” says Rachel. “But if you are mentally stable, well supported, and well monitored, there will also be physical improvement. Because when you have hope of recovering, you follow all the instructions the medical staff give you, and then there can be rapid improvement.”
Supporting the return home
Psychological support does not end when patients leave the centre. In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, it continues through the survivors’ clinic.
“We organise individual consultations as well as group discussions,” explains Phoebe Zueya Yonkeu, who manages mental health activities at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Mongbwalu. 
“Many tell us they faced stigma when they returned home, lost their jobs or were rejected by their communities, who believed they were still contagious,” says Phoebe. “Others feel guilty towards loved ones who did not survive the disease, and they even wonder whether they were the ones who infected them.”
While some patients face stigma and the trauma of having come close to death after leaving the treatment centre, returning home can also bring immense relief to them and their loved ones.
In Butembo, on the twenty-third day of Victoire’s hospitalisation, the couple learns that he is due to leave that same day. The positive result, following the first negative result, prolonged their wait: now that he has finally tested negative twice.
Kasoki and Victoire say they are very happy to finally be going home.
“Kasoki’s presence really is part of my care,” says Victoire. “I feel comforted. When I see her, it reduces my stress.”

Turkish defense giant ASELSAN adds $7.5 billion in orders in one quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:56:16 UTC
17:56:16 KST

- ASELSAN’s order backlog reached a record $30.7 billion after the third quarter of 2026, rising $7.5 billion from the previous quarter.
- Nine-month revenue rose 28% in real terms to 151.5 billion lira, while new export contracts grew 34% to $1.9 billion.
ASELSAN, Türkiye’s largest defense electronics company, ended the third quarter of 2026 with a record order backlog of $30.7 billion, after adding $7.5 billion in a single quarter and passing the $30 billion mark for the first time in its history.
The Ankara-based company reported its results for the first nine months of the year on Oct. 27 in a disclosure to Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform. Revenue reached 151.5 billion Turkish lira, up 28% in real terms from the same period of 2025, and new export contracts rose 34% to $1.9 billion. ASELSAN reports in inflation-adjusted lira, a requirement for Turkish listed companies, so the growth figures are measured after accounting for the country’s high inflation.
The backlog figure is the headline number because it shows how much work the company already has under contract and has yet to deliver. ASELSAN said its book-to-bill ratio, which compares the value of new orders signed to the revenue recorded in the same period, rose to 4.4, meaning it booked more than four times as much new business as it billed. The company reached the $30 billion level ahead of its own forecast: in August, when it reported a first-half backlog of $23.2 billion, chief executive Ahmet Akyol said ASELSAN expected to see levels of $30 billion from next year onward. At the end of the first quarter, the backlog stood at $20.7 billion, when the company also posted its strongest quarterly export performance in years.
“2026 is not just a year in which ASELSAN has grown, it is the year we redefined the very scale of our growth,” said ASELSAN CEO Ahmet Akyol.
Air defense, radar and electronic warfare systems led revenue in the period, alongside underwater systems, AI-powered urban security systems, guided munitions, electro-optics and communications equipment. ASELSAN’s recent product launches span much of that portfolio, from a trailer-mounted version of its 35 mm counter-drone turret to the KILIÇ underwater strike system and TUFAN unmanned surface vessel unveiled at SAHA 2026 in Istanbul in May.
Profitability rose with sales. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a common measure of operating profit, climbed 38% to 40.6 billion lira, and the margin improved by 1.9 percentage points to 26.8%. Akyol attributed the gain to the use of artificial intelligence in company processes, digital transformation and a growing share of higher-value products, and said revenue per employee rose 4% in dollar terms.
ASELSAN is spending heavily to turn that backlog into deliveries. Capital investment at its new Oğulbey Technology Base and existing campuses rose 228% to $684 million in nine months, which Akyol said is nearly twice the company’s total capital spending for all of 2025. The first phase of Oğulbey, whose foundation was laid in 2025 and which the company describes as the largest single defense industry investment in the history of the Turkish Republic, came into operation during the period, along with a new Guided Ammunition Systems Production Center and expanded robotics and automation for air, naval and land systems production.
Research and development spending increased 36% to $1.3 billion. ASELSAN said it is directing that money toward low Earth orbit satellites, quantum computing, underwater technologies, high-power microwave systems, microelectronics, and smart munitions and propulsion. The satellite effort, called ASTRALINK, was presented for the first time at the International Space Congress in Antalya.
“ASELSAN which has provided Turkish Armed Forces’ communications on land, at sea and in the air since its founding, will now also provide satellite communication services,” said Akyol.
Operating cash flow reached 23 billion lira, financial liabilities stood at 14% of total assets, and financing expenses fell 10.3% from a year earlier. ASELSAN’s equity ratio was 55%, its return on equity rose 4 percentage points to 16.6%, and its return on assets reached 9%.
ASELSAN has also climbed in international rankings this year. In August it rose three places to 40th in Defense News’ Top 100 list of defense companies and became the first Turkish defense firm included in the Forbes Global 2000.
“Our primary responsibility moving forward is to convert this portfolio into timely deliveries, expanded production capacity, and sustained technological superiority,” said Akyol.

Switzerland seeks direct defence contracts with US manufacturers
The Federal Office for Defence Procurement (Armasuisse) plans to purchase defence equipment directly from American manufacturers in future, rather than through the US government.
“That is one of the key lessons learnt from the F-35 purchase,” said Armasuisse chief Urs Loher in an interview on Wednesday.
But it remains to be seen whether such direct purchases are possible. This would require the go-ahead from the US authorities, Loher told the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).
More
Swiss government accepts it could have handled F-35 procurement better
He believes this might be possible for the Patriot air defence system.
“As this is a system that has been tried and tested for years, selected components are certainly available directly from the manufacturer,” said Loher. A direct purchase of state-of-the-art fighter aircraft such as the F-35 is, however, out of the question, he said.
‘Significant pitfalls’ of US scheme
Armasuisse typically handles procurements from the US via the US government’s “Foreign Military Sales” (FMS) programme. This allows the US government to retain control over which countries gain access to cutting-edge military technology, said Loher. The government also benefits from economies of scale, enabling it to purchase at lower costs itself.
More
Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
At first glance, the government programme appears to be an “all-inclusive, worry-free package”. It spares one “lengthy negotiations with defence giants”, said Loher.
But he says Switzerland’s procurement of the F-35 fighter jets from the US has revealed “significant pitfalls”. For instance, there is no jurisdiction in the event of disputes, such as over a supposed fixed price. Also, buyers are dependent on US priorities, and in the event of delayed deliveries, contractual penalties are generally not possible.
Partial refund of Patriot advance payments
Armasuisse has experienced delivery delays and revised priorities in the delivery of the US-made Patriot system. Delivery is currently delayed by five to seven years. The federal office has therefore evaluated a second system, and a final decision is with the Federal Council, said Loher.
More
Swiss procurement of second missile defence system faces delays
Switzerland has also slipped down Washington’s list of priorities. The US intends to supply Germany with Patriot systems that were originally planned for Switzerland.
“We’ll come away empty-handed for the time being, but at least we’ll get some – if not all – of the advance payments back,” said Loher. To date, these have amounted to just over CHF1 billion. However, it is also unclear when this partial repayment will take place.

Syria reopens Jordan border crossing after mending ties
- Syria reopened the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 after both sides tried to calm tensions caused by a deadly Jordanian strike.
- Jordan said its raid targeted “Daesh sites” after a church attack killed nine people in Karak, while Syria called the strike an “unacceptable violation” of sovereignty.
- Civilian deaths in southern Syria deepened anger, and a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet soon to discuss action against IS.
AI generated
Damascus – Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces.
Jordan’s strike – a reprisal against a gun attack on a church – sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Syria condemned the strikes on the country’s south as an “unacceptable violation”, while Jordan said it killed more than 20 jihadist fighters in its raid.
Jordan sought to ease tensions on Oct 27, saying it had “great respect” for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.
The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of the morning of Oct 28, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA.
Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan’s Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 – prompting a military response from Amman.
While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria’s civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children.
On Oct 27, Jordan’s Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan’s “full respect for Syria’s sovereignty... and security”, while also expressing “sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims”, according to a joint statement.
The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as “Daesh sites”, using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group.
Earlier, Jordan’s government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that “the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh’s ranks – estimated at more than 20 fighters”.
He also said “a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation” had been destroyed.
‘Blatant violation’
Earlier, Syria’s foreign ministry issued a “condemnation and rejection” of the strikes, calling them “an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination”.
It also said the raid was “a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty”.
In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.
“We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children – two boys and a girl – were killed,” said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag.
An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family’s destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble.
Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Oct 27 that both sides were handling the dispute through “diplomatic and legal channels” with the aim of securing justice for the victims.
‘Dark ideologies’
On Oct 26, Amman said the authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage.
The authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” King Abdullah II said.
IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country’s more than 13-year civil war.
But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces.
The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province. AFP

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:50:55 UTC
17:50:55 KST

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
The agreement aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Canada and the United Arab Emirates have signed a comprehensive trade deal to lower barriers between the economies and boost investment, the governments have said.
The deal comes as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties amid tension with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) on Tuesday, which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has pledged to double Ottawa’s non-US trade over the next decade as US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have rippled through Canada’s economy.
Subsequent attempts to reach a deal with Washington have broken down, which has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
“Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE,” the Prime Minister’s Office said in a statement.
“That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators.”
“The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors,” it said, adding that CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
Multiple deals
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing – all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” the UAE’s Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart, Maninder Sidhu.
The UAE is the largest Middle East market for Canadian exports and a major buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery.
Two-way trade between the countries was worth 3.5 billion Canadian dollars ($2.48bn) last year. It has been growing at 10 percent annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE also committed up to $50bn in investment in Canada last year.

The Verkhovna Rada considered rejected amendments by MPs to the draft state budget for 2027 until 3:00 AM on Wednesday, and during the session on Wednesday, October 28, will vote separately on two of them, reported MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak (Holos faction) on his Telegram channel.
According to him, the first of these (No. 611) concerns the allocation of funds from plea bargain agreements: they must be credited exclusively to the state budget or for compensation under a civil lawsuit, and funds exceeding the damage caused—to a special fund for the monetary allowance of Ukrainian Armed Forces servicemen. The amendment also instructs the government to verify the legality of agreements for 2022–2026 and submit a report to parliament by September 1, 2027.
The second amendment (No. 1003) provides for a restriction in 2027 on the maximum monthly salary of 80,000 UAH for employees of government authorities, local self-government, budgetary institutions, as well as MPs, judges, members of the High Council of Justice, the High Qualification Commission of Judges of Ukraine, prosecutors, and NBU employees (excluding positions involved in defense).
In addition, during Wednesday's session in the assembly hall, all amendments incorporated by the Budget Committee will be put to a confirmation vote, in particular proposal No. 1279 regarding an increase in servicemen's monetary allowances.
According to information on the Rada's Telegram channel, the document will be considered in the first reading as a basis. As Zheleznyak specified, the Rada will consider it in the second reading in November.
As reported, on October 27, the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee approved Budget Conclusions for the draft state budget for 2027, which contain 90 summary proposals formed from 5,236 deputy amendments, and recommended that parliament adopt them as a basis and send the budget draft to the government for preparation for the second reading.
The government's draft state budget for 2027 provides for general fund revenues at the level of 5.65 trillion UAH (8.7% more compared to 2026) and expenditures amounting to 7.27 trillion UAH (an increase of 13.5%).

Dadgar elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation
TEHRAN – Ali Dadgar has been elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation after securing a majority of votes in the federation’s electoral assembly.
The election was held under the chairmanship of Mohammadshervin Asbaghian, Deputy Minister of Sports and Youth for Championship and Professional Sports Development.
Dadgar was elected as the federation’s new president after receiving 26 votes from the 51 members of the assembly.
Six candidates had initially been approved to contest the election: Ebrahim Barkhordari, Ali Dadgar, Hossein Zakizadeh, Salar Mohammadnia, Abbas Mohammadipour, and Masoud Nosrati Qazvininejad.
However, Barkhordari, Mohammadnia, and Nosrati Qazvininejad withdrew their candidacies before the voting began, leaving Dadgar, Zakizadeh, and Mohammadipour to compete for the presidency.
In the first round of voting, Dadgar received 25 votes, followed by Zakizadeh with 19 and Mohammadipour with five. One ballot was declared invalid.
As no candidate secured an absolute majority in the first round, the election proceeded to a runoff between Dadgar and Zakizadeh.
In the second round, Dadgar narrowly defeated Zakizadeh by 26 votes to 25, securing the presidency of Iran’s Shooting Federation for the next four years.
Dadgar has previously served as president of the federation.

Collingwood has announced a review of its struggling AFLW program, saying it remains committed to ensuring the club is ready for success.
The Magpies have won just one game this season, and coach Sam Wright and captain Ruby Schleicher will leave after the final match of the year.
What's next?
Collingwood will finish its season against Essendon on Sunday.
Collingwood has pledged to thoroughly review the wreckage of its AFLW program, admitting "we haven't got it right".
The day after announcing that women's coach, Sam Wright, is about to leave, the Magpies said they would bring in a consultant to help with the strategic review.
Collingwood is a perennial AFLW under-achiever, winning only one game so far this season to be second-last.
Including the last two seasons, their record is five wins and 29 losses.
With Wright about to leave and captain Ruby Schleicher about to return home to WA, there are also reports of a mass player exodus once the season ends.
"Our AFLW program is an integral part of Collingwood, and we are committed to ensuring it is positioned for sustained success," president Barry Carp said in a club statement.
"The board, together with the executive team, acknowledges that we haven't got it right — we take responsibility for that and are committed to getting better, both on and off the field.
"Engaging an expert outside Collingwood is important for us to provide a broader perspective, challenge our existing approaches and identify what needs to improve or change."
He added the expert would work with their AFLW sub-committee to ensure the women are set up for long-term success.
"We have a responsibility to our players, coaches, staff, members, supporters and the wider game to listen to feedback and be prepared to make meaningful, considered changes across the club to build a stronger AFLW program for everyone at Collingwood," Carp said.
Wright will coach Collingwood for the last time on Sunday against Essendon at Windy Hill. It will also be Bombers coach Natalie Wood's last game.
St Kilda are also looking for a new AFLW coach after Nick Dal Santo's departure, and expansion team Tasmania are the fourth team in the market.

What else we know about the Belgrade attack?

"This means tighter security checks and an increased police presence at sensitive sites, including infrastructure facilities and places where large crowds gather," he said.

Deadly cyclone smashes into India’s east coast (VIDEOS)
A “very severe” cyclone slammed into India’s east coast on Wednesday, killing at least five people as winds of up to 150 kph uprooted trees and knocked out power. More than 180,000 people were evacuated before the storm hit.
Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast of Andhra Pradesh state near Yanam between 2 and 8 AM, with sustained winds of 125-135 kph. It weakened to a “severe” cyclone after moving inland, the India Meteorological Department said.
Satellite images show Arnab’s broad cloud bands stretching across large parts of eastern and southern India. Although its winds weakened after landfall, the authorities warned that heavy rainfall could continue through Thursday, raising the risk of further flooding.
The six-hour landfall battered coastal districts, including Kakinada, Konaseema, and West Godavari. Strong winds brought down trees and electricity poles, blocked roads, and disrupted power supplies. The coastal road near Uppada in Kakinada district was washed away, while flooding affected low-lying areas.

Russia conducts tests of SOVA autonomous navigation system for UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:47:50 UTC
17:47:50 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia’s SOVA (Comparative Optical Visual Authentication) autonomous navigation system, designed to ensure precise positioning of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) when GPS/GNSS signals and external communications are unavailable or jammed, has been successfully tested in the field, the Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (CUST) told TASS.
"The developer of the solution, VA Technologies, is a finalist in the third cohort of the CUST Special-and Dual-Use Projects Accelerator. The SOVA system is based on computer vision technology. During flight, the system compares images from an onboard camera with a satellite map of the terrain and determines the UAV’s location in real time. During testing, a drone equipped with the SOVA system completed a route that had no clear landmarks and included substantial differences between the satellite map and the actual terrain," the company said.
The CUST specified that the flight path was star-shaped. "The UAV, equipped with the autonomous navigation system, sequentially visited four waypoints and returned to its launch site. To make the task more challenging, satellite images from the spring of 2025 were used instead of an up-to-date map. Thus, the tests were conducted with a known discrepancy between the actual terrain and the map data used by the drone," the center noted.
According to the CUST, the most challenging section for the system was the stretch between the second and third waypoints. "The second waypoint on the satellite map was located over dark plowed land, while the actual terrain featured a light-colored field covered with stubble. With no landmarks to guide it, the UAV deviated from its course. However, upon reaching a tree line, the SOVA system promptly corrected its course and successfully reached the third waypoint," the company said.
VA Technologies, commenting on the situation, emphasized that such a scenario is not a failure but a standard operating condition for which the system was designed. "According to the developer, in the absence of GPS, SOVA is capable of increasing the UAV mission reliability rate to 99%," the CUST noted.

The antiwar organization reported that relatives of affected residents have been posting complaints on 2GIS, a Russian digital mapping platform, about the Sirius-55 military recruitment center. Reviewers claim that men are being detained without warning and pressured into signing contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense. The allegations have not been independently verified.
In a review published on October 26, a woman reported that her father-in-law was seized from the street on the evening of October 25. She claimed he was taken to Sirius-55 and beaten, subsequently requiring medical treatment at a hospital.
In another review published on October 23, a woman reported that her 60-year-old father disappeared after leaving for a store. She claimed that he was forced into military service, issued a new passport the following day, and transferred to Yurga in Russia’s Kemerovo region. According to her, his family has received no further information about his whereabouts. She accused those responsible of treating men as expendable and sending them to war against their will.
Another woman reported that her brother had traveled from Russia’s Kemerovo region to Omsk in search of employment. On October 18, he left to visit a store and disappeared. The following day, relatives were informed that he had signed a military contract at the recruitment center on Maryanovskaya Street.
According to his sister, the man was taken without identification documents or a mobile phone. She emphasized that he had previously categorically refused to participate in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The latest complaints follow earlier allegations of coercive military recruitment in Omsk. In a September 9 review, another user claimed that two acquaintances had been seized from the streets and forced to sign contracts. One had traveled to Omsk to care for his bedridden mother. The reviewer alleged that the absence of identification documents did not prevent the authorities from sending both men to war.
The pressure on recruitment centers reflects mounting demands on regional authorities, who face penalties for failing to meet the Kremlin’s contract-soldier quotas.
Courts in at least 51 regions have prosecuted local officials over recruitment shortfalls, with fines of up to $357 under an October 2022 presidential decree. In August 2026, the Russian government submitted a bill to the State Duma imposing fines of up to $595 or suspensions of up to three years on officials.
Contract enlistments have dropped 10 percent this year despite sign-on bonuses of up to $40,400, while monthly battlefield casualties outpace new recruits by roughly 6,000 personnel.

Ukrainians back retaliatory strikes on Russian refineries even if US halts aid, 80% say – KMIS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:46:30 EET
17:46:30 KST

More than three-quarters of Ukrainians support continuing the armed resistance against the Russian Federation despite Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the winter, and an even larger majority favors retaliatory strikes on Russian oil refineries even if the U.S cuts off military aid to Ukraine as a result, according to a survey conducted between October 16 and 25 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KMIS).
Specifically, 76% of Ukrainians maintain that even if Russia attempts to target the energy sector in winter to leave people without electricity, heat, or sewage, Ukraine must still continue its armed resistance. Meanwhile, 15% believe that under such conditions, Ukraine should agree to any Russian demands, even if they look like capitulation. Another 9% were undecided.
KMIS notes that macroeconomic breakdowns show no significant regional differences, and figures remain virtually unchanged from August-September within the margin of error.
An even greater share of respondents—80%—expressed the view that strikes on Russian oil refineries should still be carried out even if the U.S stops or limits its assistance to Ukraine. Only 11% answered that such strikes should be halted, while 8% were undecided.
During the poll, 63% of Ukrainians stated they are ready to endure the war for as long as necessary, while 5% mentioned a timeframe of 1 year. Shorter periods (several months to half a year) were cited by 21%, with the remaining 11% undecided. KMIS noted no significant changes compared to results obtained on October 8–16.
Additionally, 62% of respondents expressed trust in current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while 35% do not trust him (a balance of +27%). The institute noted that trust in the president stood at 43% (with 52% distrust) on October 8–9, but rose to 57% trust (and 39% distrust) by October 10–16.
"Following October 9—that is, after the 'diesel deal'—Ukraine and Ukrainians found themselves under triple pressure: from the Russian enemy and its terror campaign of jet drones and ballistic missiles (accompanied by information warfare), from certain domestic actors (some of whom insist on de facto peace at any price, while others prioritize an uncompromising struggle against the government), and from our strategic partner, the U.S... Despite these pressures, Ukrainians maintain resilience in repelling the enemy: the majority are ready to endure the war as long as needed, insist that despite a potentially difficult winter Ukraine must not yield to Russian peace terms, and believe that even with the risk of losing US support, strikes on Russian oil refineries must continue," commented KMIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetskyi on the survey results.
He also noted that despite calls from certain public figures for Zelenskyy to step down, trust in him continues to grow.
"Ukrainian society has wisely mobilized for unity during this difficult period, but the Ukrainian authorities must also learn the right lessons and avoid euphoria from success, otherwise we will quickly return to a downward trend in trust... In any case, our data demonstrate that Ukrainians, despite everything, have the will to continue resistance until an acceptable outcome in the war is achieved," Hrushetskyi concluded.
The survey was conducted via telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all government-controlled regions of Ukraine among 828 adult respondents. Under normal conditions, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a 0.95 probability and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) does not exceed 4.4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.9% for indicators close to 5%. Under wartime conditions, certain systematic deviations are added alongside the formal margin of error, but the results retain high representativeness.

[FEATURED]
WAYFINDING system FOR Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
Located in Medora, North Dakota, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library is embedded directly within the terrain of the Badlands. Designed by Snøhetta with architect of record JLG Architects, the library campus connects three institutions across expansive indoor and outdoor environments. Studio Loutsis was commissioned to develop the comprehensive signage, wayfinding, and donor recognition system spanning the site, treating graphic wayfinding as an architectural and landscape-driven extension of the campus.
graphic maps, architecture, and landscape into a unified system
To unify varied scales, from monumental exterior markers to pedestrian trail placards, Studio Loutsis collaborated with Commercial Type to engineer a bespoke typeface, paired with a custom iconography system. Exterior wayfinding incorporates heavy timber pylons, directional panels, campus maps, and dark metal dimensional lettering engineered to withstand North Dakota’s extreme climate while weathering alongside the building envelope.
Fabricated under stringent Living Building Challenge sustainability parameters, all materials, non-toxic coatings, and mechanical assemblies adhere to strict ecological standards. Indoors, signage mounts directly to vertically articulated timber partitions using custom-milled infill blocks, while the central lobby’s ‘Wall of Gratitude’ integrates flush donor wood panels into the primary architectural cladding.

Kazakhstan to develop new Civil Code

Russian online marketplace Ozon lost billions of rubles to Ukrainian drone strikes on its warehouses

The loss figure includes the cost of goods destroyed in the warehouses, damaged equipment, and what the report describes as “other losses and expenses.”
The report says some of the company’s own risks were insured, and Ozon is continuing negotiations with insurance companies over possible compensation.
Despite the losses from the strikes, Ozon’s net profit grew 25% in the third quarter, reaching 3.7 billion rubles. Revenue increased 1.6-fold to 421.2 billion rubles, and Ozon delivered 1.2 billion orders to customers over the same period, 76% more than a year earlier.
Ukraine expanded its target list for strikes on Russian infrastructure in the summer of 2026, moving beyond oil refineries and defense plants to marketplace warehouses. Ukrainian drones attacked a warehouse belonging to Wildberries for the first time on July 18, and 36 of the company’s warehouse facilities came under attack over the next three months. Attacks on Ozon’s warehouses began on August 22.
Ukraine’s armed forces shifted to digital infrastructure in October. From October 8–11, Ukraine carried out a series of strikes on three data centers belonging to Yandex. Ukrainian drones attacked a data processing center belonging to Sberbank on October 14, and a data center belonging to the Federal Tax Service on October 23. The strikes caused widespread disruptions to services at Yandex, Mail.ru, Ozon, MegaFon, VKontakte, and other companies.

Details

India has invited all 10 member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), including Pakistan, to participate in its inaugural Civilisational Dialogue Forum, scheduled to be held in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, Indian media reported on Wednesday.
The invitation marks the first time since the four-day war between India and Pakistan last year that India has invited a senior Pakistani minister to the country.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh announced the initiative at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20, confirming that all member states had been invited to participate.
“At the end of this year, India will host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum. We invite all SCO countries to participate in it,” Singh had said.
Pakistan Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar was present at the meeting.
Pakistan’s Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurangzeb Khan Khichi has been invited to the forum, according to diplomatic sources cited by India Today. The forum aims to strengthen cultural ties and foster mutual understanding among SCO member states.
The invitation comes against the backdrop of strained relations between India and Pakistan following their four-day war, launched by India in May 2025 in what it described as a response to an attack in India-administered Kashmir’s Pahalgam, for which India blamed Pakistan. Pakistan firmly denied the accusations, for which India has provided no evidence.
If Khichi attends the event, it would mark the first visit by a senior Pakistani minister to India since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari participated in the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Goa in May 2023.
The proposed forum is aimed at deepening cultural engagement and promoting greater mutual understanding among the countries in the grouping.
Pakistan has yet to issue any official statement regarding its possible attendance.
Pakistan assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term on September 1. It took over the position from Kyrgyzstan following the SCO summit held in Bishkek.
The SCO has 10 member states: Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India became a full member of the organisation in 2017.

Zelensky pushes back against Musk, says Ukraine uses Starshield to defend itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:43:56 UTC
17:43:56 KST

Zelensky pushes back against Musk, says Ukraine uses Starshield to defend itself
Ukraine has used SpaceX's Starshield satellite systems only to defend itself against Russian forces on its own territory, not for attacks on Russian soil, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 27.
The comments come as a rebuff of SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who claimed Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service" by using the systems for offensive drone attacks.
Ukraine widely uses both commercial Starlink terminals and their militarized version, Starshield.
Starshield was temporarily speed-restricted to 160 kilometers per hour in Ukraine earlier this month, hampering Ukrainian drone interceptors' ability to down Russian jet-powered drones and disrupting other military operations.
"When Elon Musk said that we use Starshield against the Russians — yes, against the Russians, but on our own territory. This is not offensive; it's defensive," Zelensky told journalists at a press briefing.
"But the point is that we use it against Russian troops on our territory, not on Russian territory. They came here to kill," he said.
Musk alleged that Kyiv used commercial Starlink terminals for "offensive drone strikes to kill people," adding that the "loophole" has now been closed. However, he rejected responsibility for Starshield restrictions, saying the militarized terminals are controlled by the U.S. government.
Ukrainian officials have previously rejected Musk's claims about Kyiv violating Starlink's service terms. Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the commercial Starlink has a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers per hour and does not work on Russian territory.
Zelensky confirmed on Oct. 24 that both Starlink and Starshield are again working at full speed. Nobody has publicly claimed responsibility for the throttling of Starshield, though Trump administration officials have pointed fingers at Musk.
"Of course, civilians died while Starlink/Starshield were switched off," Zelensky said. "We're now shooting down about 90% of (Shahed-type drones). When the (latest wave of) attacks began, we were shooting down between 50% and 75–78%. Then that rate dropped back again."
The president revealed that Ukraine was just successfully testing its jet-powered Bars drone interceptors — 2,000 units of which were paid for by a European country — when the restrictions hit.
"So I really don't know who told SpaceX to do that," Zelensky said, suggesting it could either be Musk's personal decision or an instruction by a U.S. official. "I only know that, technically, SpaceX turns these systems on and off."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered the SpaceX CEO to lift the restrictions, while the U.S. president publicly claimed he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
The restrictions came amid deteriorating ties between the U.S. and Ukraine, with Trump easing sanctions pressure on Moscow while accusing Zelensky of not being interested in peace — despite Kyiv repeatedly backing various U.S.-backed ceasefire proposals, which were turned down by Russia.

Two high-speed trains rear-end in Spain, rail operator says

Two high-speed trains collide in Spain, at least 64 dead
MADRID – At least 64 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided in Spain on Oct 28, the second deadly accident in less than a year on the line connecting Madrid to the southern Andalusia region, the regional authorities said.
Footage from regional Castilla-La Mancha Television showed a derailed train with several carriages remaining on an elevated section of the track, while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.
Miguel, a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train.”
A person briefed on the disaster said an express operated by Spanish train operator Iryo stopped near Toledo due to a signal fault, on orders from infrastructure manager ADIF. A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.
There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Renfe.
Passenger describes seeing fatalities
The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the death toll had risen to 64 from 30, after earlier warning that it could rise.
Jesus Perez Martin, mayor of the nearby town of Los Yebenes, said the situation was “horrific” and pointed to a severe tragedy.
“They are telling me about mutilations and very serious injuries,” he told RTVE.
Health Minister Monica Garcia urged people in a post on social media platform X to donate blood.
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she felt a strong impact that threw her forward, initially making her think the train had made an emergency stop.
She realised the seriousness of the accident only after seeing injured people, and being told to evacuate.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage.
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said. “I saw dead people,” she added.
Second fatal accident on line in a year
Castilla-La Mancha region spokesperson Esther Padilla said 147 people had been travelling on the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe train.
The collision comes nine months after an accident between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators on the same line that killed 46 people.
That crash in January, which occurred after a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz in Cordoba province, triggered a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Election due next month
The Renfe and Iryo trains crashed just after 9am, causing two Iryo wagons to derail, a spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha region said, adding that the cause was not yet clear.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols.
The latest accident comes as Spain gears up for an election on Nov 29.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s agenda, published on the Spanish government’s website, was cleared for the day.
The opposition People’s Party also cancelled all campaign events, a spokesperson said.
“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo. My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families,” Sanchez said on social media platform X.
Rail operator Adif said the incident occurred on the line from Madrid to Seville.
Manuel Galan, mayor of the nearby town of Urda, told Cadena SER that emergency services had asked the town council to prepare emergency facilities, including a sports hall, to accommodate passengers and the injured.
Rail safety record
Accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 in 2025, according to Spain’s railway safety authority.
In the same period, problems such as deterioration and breaks in the rails went from 494 and 667, a level below the 716 registered in 2024.
Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period in 2025, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain’s competition authority.
European Commission data shows Spain’s maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000km of high-speed lines has lagged large European peers, despite an unmatched drive to expand the network.
Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion (S$2.14 billion) a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any other country.
However, the vast majority went to new infrastructure, with only some 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.
Spain had registered among the lowest fatality rates in the EU from train incidents before the 2026 accidents, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand km of railway tracks, according to the latest available Eurostat data from 2024.
More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the European Union, according to the EU railway agency.
Alongside Belgium and Switzerland, its networks have the largest amount of rail equipped with a Europe-wide signalling standard. REUTERS

Elron plans to modernize trains and rent them to Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

Elron plans to modernize trains and rent them to Latvia
Estonia's state-owned passenger rail operator Elron wants to modernize the trains running between Tartu and Riga to attract more passengers to the route. It would also like to rent the trains to Latvians for use on local routes.
Elron wants to make the trains operating between Tartu and Riga more comfortable and use funds allocated for operating the route to do so, according to a letter the company sent to the Ministry of Climate.
The funds are available because the initially planned second daily departure has not yet been launched due to a shortage of trains.
The state allocates Elron €2 million annually to operate the route with two departures per day in both directions, with an additional €300,000 allocated this year for preparatory costs.
According to Elron's calculations, this year's funding would cover the operation of the route with one daily departure as well as the modernization of three trains.
Citing passenger feedback, Elron said more comfortable trains would help increase passenger numbers on the Tartu-Riga route and provide an opportunity to generate revenue by renting out the trains while they are in Latvia.
All this should help better cover the costs of the Tartu-Riga route, Elron CEO Lauri Betlem noted.
The plan to rent out trains in Latvia is linked to a procurement by Latvian passenger rail operator Vivi, which wants to rent diesel trains for three routes: Lithuanian border–Daugavpils–Riga–Daugavpils–Lithuanian border; Riga–Valga–Riga; and Riga–Daugavpils–Riga. The procurement procedure is still ongoing.
"We submitted a bid for the last route because the current direct Tallinn-Riga service arrives in Riga at around 9 p.m. and begins its return journey at 7.30 a.m. The time in between is free, during which it would make sense to put the train to work. This would also expand connections for Estonian passengers to central and southeastern Latvia," Elron's head of customer experience Kristi Unt told ERR.
New seats, carpets, footrests
Elron plans to modernize the seats in three trains, equip every seat with a power socket, replace the tables with longer ones, add footrests to standard-class seats, replace the carpet in first class and redecorate one train. There are also discussions about adding luggage areas and vending machines.
Unt said that there are no plans to completely rebuild the trains. "We are primarily talking about limited interior work," she explained.
In total, the modernization of the three trains would cost €756,000, including a small reserve, or €252,000 per train. Together with the costs of operating the route, this would amount to slightly less than €2.2 million, which is less than the state allocated to Elron this year.
Betlem said Elron can start modernizing the trains in early November when a four-car diesel train that was sent for repairs following a traffic accident in 2025 returns to service.
The ministry has given Elron preliminary approval, but final confirmation is now needed from the Ministry of Climate.
Elron currently has three two-car trains and one three-car train authorized to operate on Latvia's railway network. The European Union Agency for Railways is expected to authorize another three three-car trains soon.
