TEL AVIV, October 28. /TASS/. Israel’s Likud party, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is holding on to its lead in the October 27 parliamentary elections, with 57.3% of the vote counted, according to data released by the Central Elections Committee.
The Yashar party of Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is in second place.
The Central Elections Committee is expected to announce preliminary results on October 29, with the final election outcome to be officially published no later than November 4.
TASS has compiled key details available so far.
Exit polls and seat distribution
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is holding on to its lead in the elections, with 57.3% of the vote counted, according to data released by the Central Elections Committee.
- According to this data, Netanyahu’s party is projected to win 28 seats in the 120-seat parliament.
- His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar opposition party, is in second place with 21 seats.
- Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s bloc of parties is currently projected to win a total of 55 seats, while the opposition is expected to secure 49.
- Arab parties are projected to win 16 seats, although neither Likud nor the opposition is prepared to form a coalition with them.
- According to exit polls, the Beyachad (Together) bloc, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, ranks third with 14 seats.
- The center-left Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, are expected to win ten seats each.
- Avigdor Lieberman’s party, Our Home Israel, which focuses on the interests of Israel's Russian-speaking community, is projected to win eight seats.
- The United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, and the far-right party Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, are projected to receive seven seats each.
- The ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, along with the far-right bloc comprising the Religious Zionist Party and Zehut, are each expected to win six seats.
- Other political forces are not expected to surpass the 3.25% electoral threshold.
- A total of 36 parties and alliances participated in the elections.
- A governing majority requires 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but, according to exit polls, no political force is expected to reach that number.
Voter turnout
- Parliamentary elections in Israel are held under a party-list system.
- A total of 7.3 mln Israeli citizens are eligible to vote.
- Voter turnout in the elections to the 26th Knesset was 77.7%, the highest level since 1999, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.
- United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas said that turnout in Arab-populated areas had reached 80%.
- He stressed that Arab voters had been more active than other voters.
Election results
- The Central Elections Committee is expected to announce preliminary results on October 29, with the final election outcome to be officially published no later than November 4.
- Once the final results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties that have won seats in the Knesset before asking one of them to form a new government coalition.
Prime minister’s post
- According to Amjad Shbeita, coordinator of the Joint List coalition of Arab parties, left-wing and democratic forces have a strong chance of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
- Netanyahu previously claimed that opposition parties were trying "to steal the elections" from his bloc.
- Posts urging supporters to turn out in greater numbers appeared on Netanyahu’s X account approximately three times an hour, along with allegations that Arab parties were transporting thousands of their supporters to polling stations to secure more votes.
- As a rule, the leader of the party that wins the most seats in parliament becomes a candidate for the post of prime minister.
- However, the president may also task a politician whose party did not win the most seats with forming a cabinet, provided the party has a chance of forming a coalition.
- The first candidate for prime minister will have 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of a two-week extension.
- If the candidate fails, the president will assign the task to another lawmaker, who will have two weeks to form a cabinet, with no option for an extension.
- If no government can be formed with the support of at least 61 members of parliament, a new election will be called within 90 days.

Netanyahu likely to win most seats in Israeli polls: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track to win the most seats in Israel's parliament after an election this week, though neither he nor his main competitor, Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a majority.
Votes are now being tallied, followed by potentially long negotiations as parties try to assemble a governing coalition. If those talks fail, Israel could head to another round of elections.
Israel's Central Election Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday, and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election are known.
The committee will also tally hundreds of thousands of ballots by Israeli soldiers, as well as diplomats, who voted from outside the country.
The committee's tallying followed exit polls from major Israeli TV channels. Those polls can help give a general sense of each party’s relative strength but are not considered a reliable barometer of precise results, particularly in Israel’s fragmented political system.
The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov. 4.
Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.

“I really don’t want this to be ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4,’ when influence is being redistributed,” Zelensky said, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, United States and United Kingdom discussed the postwar order in Europe.
He argued that today’s fragmented, technologically advanced world was fundamentally different from the one that emerged after World War II, making a similar redistribution of power impossible.

Russia may seek NATO concessions in peace talks
Zelensky also warned NATO against accepting Russian demands to roll back the alliance’s military presence to its 1997 configuration while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
His remarks follow an Oct. 25 report by The Telegraph, which cited diplomatic sources as saying Moscow could use renewed peace talks to secure concessions on NATO enlargement and military deployments near Russia’s borders.
According to the report, a potential Russian demand could involve withdrawing NATO forces from Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland, all of which border Russia.
The reported demand has not been confirmed as an official Russian negotiating position, and there is no indication that a NATO rollback has formally been added to the talks’ agenda.
The Kremlin has nevertheless signaled that it wants a broader discussion of European security. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 22 that future negotiations should address security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, as well as the “architecture of European security as a whole.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has also argued that European countries should be involved in negotiations to end the war.
Zelensky said on Monday, Oct. 27, that Moscow’s security demands went beyond preventing Ukrainian attacks and amounted to an attempt to secure a separate agreement with NATO or the United States.
“They say: ‘If you want security guarantees for Ukraine, then we want them for Russia.’ We need to understand what Russia means by this. It is not simply about Ukraine refraining from striking Russia. For them, this is a much broader and more specific issue,” he said.
The president said discussions about broad security guarantees for Russia should wait until the terms for ending the war and Ukraine’s own security arrangements were clear.
“First, we need to resolve the issues related to this war, and only then seek answers to the questions Russia raises based on its own perceptions and expectations of security,” Zelensky said.
Moscow’s 1997 demands date back to before the invasion
Russia’s push to change NATO’s military posture in Europe predates its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In December 2021, Moscow presented the United States and NATO with draft security agreements that sought to halt further alliance enlargement, including Ukraine’s potential accession, and restrict military deployments in countries that joined NATO after May 1997.
NATO rejected Russia’s attempt to restrict its open-door policy, while saying it remained willing to discuss arms control and other security issues.
A return to NATO’s 1997 military configuration could have significant implications for the alliance’s eastern flank. Poland joined NATO in 1999, the Baltic states joined in 2004, and Finland became a member in 2023 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia’s renewed demands could reshape the wider European security architecture. He suggested Moscow had raised similar issues in talks with then-US President Joe Biden before launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He argued that NATO members should determine the alliance’s military posture themselves, without negotiating those arrangements with Russia, which is not a member.
“Any retreat, any rollback of security, is a weakness for the alliance,” he said.
Trilateral talks could resume in November
The diplomatic maneuvering comes as Ukraine, Russia and the United States prepare to resume technical-level negotiations after a lengthy pause.
On Oct. 23, Zelensky said the next round of talks was expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi among the possible venues.
On Oct. 25, Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations after Russia’s Nov. 4 National Unity Day holiday, describing the next meeting as preliminary and exploratory.
The format and participants remain unsettled, including whether European representatives will take part in a broader discussion of continental security.
Kyiv has insisted that any settlement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine and prevent Russia from using a pause in hostilities to prepare for another attack.

Most of Britan’s nuclear missile submarine fleet now at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:37:38 GMT
17:37:38 KST

Three of the Royal Navy’s four Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines are at sea at the same time, an arrangement naval sources described as unusual, according to reporting in The Times.
One of the boats is understood to be conducting the deterrent patrol, carrying Trident II D5 missiles, which is the task the Royal Navy has maintained without a break since 1969. The other two are believed to have been on sea trials and preparing to take over the patrol. HMS Victorious, the fourth boat, is at Devonport undergoing maintenance and was not among those at sea.
The Ministry of Defence declined to comment.
Having three boats out at once is not a sign of extra capacity, though, as the Vanguard class was designed around a four boat cycle in which one submarine is on patrol, one is working up or recovering, one is in training or trials, and one is in deep maintenance, and the fourth hull is what keeps continuous at sea deterrence going as the submarines age. Running three at sea at the same time means the cycle has been compressed, and it is as consistent with pressure on availability as it is with a deliberate signal.
The Times was told by a former senior naval source that the service had been operating in what submariners call 2BA, or two boat availability, for a prolonged period. In that condition only two of the four boats are available for operational tasking at any time, which leaves no margin, because a defect on the boat at sea has to be covered by a single relief.
The strain is visible in how long the boats are staying out, Navy Lookout reported in March 2025 that a Vanguard class submarine had returned to the Clyde after 204 days, breaking a record set in 2023, and patrols of more than two hundred days have since been reported again. Deterrent patrols were historically planned around three months. Crews now routinely spend five months or more submerged with no contact with their families.
Forces News reported last week, in an account of life aboard the boats, that Commander Roger Ireland, a retired submariner who served on the earlier Resolution class, described the length of modern Vanguard patrols as horrendous. Resolution boats carrying Polaris went out for around eight weeks at a time.
Maintenance has been the other great difficulty, and HMS Vanguard emerged from a refit at Devonport in 2023 that took around seven and a half years against a planned three and a half, after an unscheduled nuclear refuelling pushed the cost from roughly £200 million towards £500 million, as this publication reported when she sailed.
The four Vanguards entered service between 1993 and 1999 and were designed for around twenty five years each. All four are now beyond that, and they must hold the deterrent until the Dreadnought class arrives from the early 2030s. The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, covering Dreadnought, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure behind them.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition since March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
In a separate statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Abdelatty and his Emirati counterpart discussed the latest regional developments, particularly growing indications of possible escalation in the coming period.
Abdelatty stressed the need for regional countries to “unite their efforts to reach peaceful solutions and return all parties to a peaceful political track to prevent the region from sliding into a more dangerous phase of the current crisis.”
The call came as mediation efforts continue to contain tensions between Washington and Tehran amid ongoing disagreements over the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
On Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.
On June 18, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding and began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements, including maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global energy and goods supplies.

Japan seeks to develop nuclear capability — China Arms Control and Disarmament Association
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:36:44 UTC
17:36:44 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan is seeking to develop a nuclear capability, according to Dai Huaicheng, Secretary-General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA).
"Since the current Japanese government took office, the country's right-wing forces have clearly demonstrated their ambitions to revive militarism, violate the 'three non-nuclear principles,' and pursue the creation of an indigenous nuclear arsenal - rapidly accelerating their progress along this misguided path. These statements are by no means isolated incidents; rather, they represent long-conceived, dangerous 'probing' steps that are part of a pre-planned strategy to 'gradually loosen restrictions in the nuclear sphere'," he stated.
Dai also noted that Japan’s current cabinet denies the country’s history of aggression during World War II, seeks to "whitewash the war crimes that were committed," and is actively pursuing remilitarization - all of which, he warned, "poses a serious threat to peace and stability in the region."
"As a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, Japan is bound under international law not to acquire, develop, possess, or proliferate nuclear weapons. There is no room for negotiation on this matter," Dai concluded.
Japan adheres to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles: not to possess, produce, or permit the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. Although these principles are not legally binding, successive Japanese prime ministers have reaffirmed their commitment to them. For decades, even discussing a possible revision was considered taboo. Some politicians have referred to an unwritten "fourth principle" - the prohibition on discussing the issue - and called for at least this constraint to be lifted.
Following Sanae Takaichi’s appointment as prime minister, media reports indicated that a review of Japan’s national security strategy would include discussions of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. In particular, Takaichi was reported to be prepared to advocate lifting the ban on the introduction of US nuclear weapons into Japan.
Amid the reports, however, Takaichi stated that she had not instructed officials to revise the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as part of the deliberations on the updated national security strategy.

Villa Ginori, Versilia home of marquis Puccini dedicated La Bohème to, goes on market
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:34:42 CET
17:34:42 KST

Villa Ginori, a historic residence in the coastal Versilia area of Tuscany, in the province of Lucca, has gone onto the market with Lionard Luxury Real Estate (https://www.lionard.com/exclusive-historic-villa-on-lake-versil ia-hinterland.html). 
The home once belonged to Marquis Carlo Ginori Lisci, heir to the celebrated Ginori porcelain factory at Doccia and a close friend of Giacomo Puccini, who dedicated La Bohème to him. 
Overlooking Lake Massaciuccoli in Massarosa, the villa remains in the hands of descendants of the Ginori Lisci family. 
It preserves rooms once frequented by the composer, who lived across the lake in Torre del Lago, as well as Liberty-style decorations by Francesco Fanelli, a painter who studied under Giovanni Fattori. 
The estate owes its present appearance to Carlo Ginori Lisci. In 1887, the marquis acquired Lake Massaciuccoli and the surrounding land from the Minutoli family, transforming an existing building into a residence in the Tuscan neo-Gothic style. 
The villa's architectural character is defined by its direct relationship with the water. The lake extends beneath the building's great arches to a private covered boathouse, making it possible to reach the residence directly by boat. 
The same relationship continues inside, where the large windows of the loggia and winter garden open onto the lake. Irises, botanical motifs and Oriental-inspired lines by Fanelli, who was asked in 1900 by the marquis to decorate several rooms, echo the surrounding landscape across the walls. 
The estate comprises approximately 4,000 square metres of built space across eight buildings and 10 hectares of private land. 
Alongside the main villa, which measures about 1,200 square metres, stand an 800-square-metre 19th-century residence and a clubhouse created from a former boat shelter, as well as a chapel, a limonaia and other service buildings. 
The park, dotted with historic palm trees and exotic botanical species, is crossed by navigable canals. 
"The most authentic expression of Made in Italy is not only what we produce, but also what we have been able to build, preserve and pass on," said Dimitri Corti, Founder and CEO of Lionard Luxury Real Estate. 
"Villa Ginori represents a dimension of luxury that goes beyond the material value of a property. A building can be restored, transformed and adapted to new needs. What cannot be recreated is its history, its relationship with the people who lived there, and with the land to which it belongs. That is what makes certain places truly irreplaceable."

Chinese team reveals how brain neurons support flexible decision-making
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:56 CST
17:33:56 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese research team has revealed how brain neurons support flexible decision-making. According to a study recently published in Science, rule-related information and sensory information are compared within the same neuron, which itself takes part in cognitive computation.
Traditional theory holds that neurons are the basic structural and functional units of the nervous system. For a long time, most studies treated each neuron as a simple point-like unit that performs summation.
However, researches in brain science and artificial neural networks have found that higher cognitive functions such as flexible decision-making require the integration of massive contextual information and abstract rules, as well as dynamic adjustment of output. Such complexity is difficult to explain with the simple structure of point-like neurons.
Xu Ninglong, a researcher at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and his team designed a series of experiments in which mice heard different sounds and had to infer hidden rules. Once the mice had learned the current rules, the team changed the rules to see how quickly the mice adapted to the new logic. The team used two-photon microscopy to observe neurons in the mice's auditory cortex.
A neuron is like a tree with many branches. The cell body is the main part of the neuron, while dendrites are branch-like extensions. The distant branches are called apical dendrites.
The experiments found a clear division of labor within the same neuron. Apical dendrites mainly encode the abstract rule inferred by the mouse, while the cell body more strongly represents external auditory sensory input. The two types of signals undergo nonlinear integration within the neuron, producing a decision output that drives behavioral choice.
The experiments demonstrated that a single neuron is itself a microcomputer and that the interactions between a neuron's dendrites and cell body can perform decision-related cognitive computation. Only after a hypothesis has been verified multiple times and confirmed to be reliable does the brain slowly strengthen neuronal synapses and store the rule permanently.
The team found that although AI can also use context and existing information to adjust its answers, its mechanisms differ greatly from those of the brain. Large models mainly develop capabilities through training on data, whereas the brain combines experiential learning, internal states, and real-time information processing. Even a single neuron has a rich internal computational structure.
The team also found that the brain can support flexible behavior while using limited energy. Its biological mechanisms are worth studying for insights that could help make AI systems more flexible and more efficient. ■

Swiss village remains on alert over unstable Weisshorn Glacier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:33:45 UTC
17:33:45 KST

Swiss village remains on alert over unstable Weisshorn Glacier
The hanging glacier on the eastern side of the Weisshorn mountain above Randa, in southern Switzerland, will continue to be closely monitored and safety measures will remain in place due to the potential dangers, the authorities said on Tuesday.
Access to a local danger zone is still forbidden and access points for pedestrians and cyclists remain closed. The residential area is not affected by the current situation. Local authorities and experts are in close contact and are monitoring developments.
In mid-August, several rockfalls were recorded on the Weisshorn East hanging glacier. Due to a significant increase in movement, the authorities raised the monitoring to level 3 (on a scale of 1-5). Additional rockfalls have not been ruled out.
More
Swiss municipality raises alert level following glacier break-offs
Due to increased activity, movements on the glacier have been monitored since the end of June. A danger zone has been defined and marked out.
The first heavy snowfalls could significantly increase the risk of a glacier collapse, the Walliser Bote newspaper reported in mid-October. A block of ice measuring around 300,000 cubic metres remains suspended on the hanging glacier, moving downhill at a rate of up to 20 centimetres per day.
If a large amount of fresh snow were to fall on the Bis Glacier plateau below, a calving event could trigger a dangerous ice-and-snow avalanche. This would have a significantly greater reach than a pure ice calving event in summer.
More
Why do Swiss mountains collapse? It’s complicated
Repeated glacier break-offs on the Weisshorn
In the past, there have been repeated glacier break-offs on the Weisshorn. The largest historically documented event dates back to 1819. The avalanche triggered at that time is said to have caused extensive damage in the village of Randa. Further events in 1972 and 1973 were less severe and came to a halt on a glacier field.
The municipality of Randa has also historically been affected by other natural hazards. In 1991, a triple rockslide occurred on the Längenfluhberg. Within a few weeks, almost 50 million cubic metres of rock tumbled into the valley.
The rock masses buried the railway line and the main road. They also dammed up the River Vispa. No one was injured in the rockfalls, but livestock were killed and 33 buildings were destroyed.

Seven Chinese golfers set for Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:42 CST
17:33:42 KST

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven Chinese golfers, including four debutants, will compete at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship (AAC), which begins Thursday at Te Arai Links in New Zealand.
The 17th edition of the championship runs from October 29 to November 1 on Te Arai Links' South Course, with 120 players from 39 countries and regions competing in the 72-hole stroke-play event.
The winner will earn invitations to the 2027 Masters Tournament, the 155th Open Championship and the 131st Amateur Championship.
China's seven-player contingent comprises Zhou Ziqin, Wu Qiyou, Li Zhi, Hou Zenghao, Wang Yixiang, Liu Yiming and Cui Jingguo. Li, Wang, Liu and Cui will make their tournament debuts, while Zhou will be competing for the fifth time.
Zhou, 20, is ranked No. 55 in the World Amateur Golf Ranking and finished runner-up in 2024, one stroke behind compatriot Ding Wenyi.
"That was really close, just one shot back. But honestly, that was two years ago, and I believe my game has improved this season," Zhou said Wednesday.
"I wasn't playing my best for a period, but I played really well last season, and my game is starting to come back now."
Zhou said he was confident in his preparations but expected putting to play a decisive role on the links-style course.
"I think I did a good job preparing for this week, and I'm really ready. We have beautiful courses, and I feel like it's going to be a putting contest this week," he said.
Li, making his championship debut, said he was eager to test himself against the region's leading amateur golfers.
"I'm very happy to have the opportunity to play in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship. Receiving the invitation is a recognition of my ability at this stage," Li said. "I believe I'll learn a lot and benefit from the experience."
Li added that the fairways, undulating greens and coastal winds would present a stern challenge.
"The fairways and greens are very firm, and the greens have considerable slopes. Combined with the wind, these factors will make the course challenging," he said.
Thailand's Fifa Laopakdee returns to defend his title in a tournament that has helped launch the careers of several leading golfers from the region.
Chinese players have won the championship five times, with Guan Tianlang claiming the title in 2012, Jin Cheng in 2015, Lin Yuxin in 2017 and 2019, and Ding Wenyi in 2024.
The championship was established by the Asia-Pacific Golf Confederation, The R&A and the Masters Tournament. ■

California governor signs orders to prepare for El Nino storms
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:31 CST
17:33:31 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed two executive orders, easing environmental requirements for flood-prevention work and requiring a risk review of Highway 1 ahead of potential El Nino storms.
The orders were signed at Crystal Cove State Park in Newport Beach, Southern California, following a statewide emergency declaration issued on Sept. 21, according to the governor's office.
One order allows the suspension of state requirements for eligible public-agency work to limit flooding, landslides, debris flows and erosion, while requiring advance eligibility approval and safeguards for fish, protected species and waterways.
The second order establishes a Highway 1 Task Force, convened by state transportation and natural resources agencies, to prepare the corridor for El Nino storms and address longer-term climate threats.
Highway 1 runs about 1,056 km along California's Pacific coast and has suffered repeated landslides and closures in the Big Sur area in recent years.
On Tuesday, the U.S. National Weather Service warned of significant coastal flooding in Orange and San Diego counties in Southern California until Thursday.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center said on Oct. 8 that there was a more than 83-percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Nino through January to March 2027. ■

Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:27 CST
17:33:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families and before children turn 10, according to an Australian study.
The study analyzed Australian Child Maltreatment Study data from 8,503 Australians aged 16 and older, focusing on 2,623 individuals who reported experiencing physical abuse during childhood, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Curtin University.
One in four Australians aged 16 to 24 reported experiencing physical abuse by a family member. Family members were responsible for 85 percent of reported perpetration, while 4 percent occurred in institutional settings and 5 percent involved both family and institutional settings, the study found.
Among children abused before age 10, both parents were identified as perpetrators in one in three cases. Abuse involving both parents was also associated with the earliest onset and longest duration, according to the findings published in the journal Child Maltreatment.
Childhood physical abuse remains a major public health concern globally and is associated with substantial adverse mental, physical and social outcomes across the lifespan, said the researchers, noting that prevention efforts must extend beyond institutions and place greater emphasis on the home. ■

AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.
The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.
“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”
Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.
The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.
“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”
Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.
As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.
In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.
Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust, said Sutton. “They're losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”
In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.
“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there's a chemical plume coming my way, the phone's ringing, the radio's blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.
Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.
Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.
Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.
The original alert read, “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.
The new alert read: “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.
EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.
“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They're using their own personal accounts, or they're using free ones.”
It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.
“We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue.
As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.
Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.
“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.
The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 12:30 p.m. local time, just over 84.5% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues

- As of 12:30 p.m. local time, just over 84.5% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.

GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

EU: Frontex reform compounds risk of EU complicity in rights violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:28:27 UTC
17:28:27 KST

Responding to the European Commission’s proposed reform of the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation (the Frontex Regulation) that vastly expands the agency’s budget, powers, staff and mandate, without commensurately expanding its human rights safeguards and transparency obligations, Eve Geddie the Director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office said:
“The European Commission’s proposed changes to the Frontex mandate once again prioritize expanding the agency’s powers to deport, enforce border control, and operate beyond the EU without expanding the agency’s human rights obligations in turn.
“This includes giving Frontex new powers to carry out forced returns between non-EU countries, paving the way for a broader role in ‘return hubs’ in third countries. This reform compounds the risk of EU complicity in human rights violations and raises further hurdles to transparency and accountability. It should be rejected outright.
“Time and again we see the European Commission doubling down on Fortress Europe – increasing border security, surveillance and deportations without ever questioning the growing powers of an agency that has facilitated the trapping of people in human rights abuses.
“Frontex’s mandate explicitly requires respect, protection and promotion of human rights. Yet instead of addressing structural deficiencies and flawed approaches that fuel violations and abuses against people at Europe’s borders, today’s decision will turbocharge this flawed approach in countries outside the EU.
“As people across Europe protest over access to housing, and underfunding of education and public services, the European Commission continues to present migration control as the continent’s existential challenge, and to disproportionately pour resources into deportations and border enforcement. A fundamental reassessment of its priorities is long overdue.”
Background
On 27 October, the European Commission presented two proposals: an amendment to the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation increasing the number of Frontex officers to 30,000, giving the agency a greater role in returns and ‘crisis response’, as well as a regulation to digitalize return, readmission and reintegration procedures.
Amnesty International has long followed the work of Frontex, acting as a member of its Consultative Forum on Fundamental Rights from its inception in 2012 until the end of 2022. A series of reforms of Frontex have rapidly expanded its powers, budget, and operational capacity since its creation in 2004, with its budget ballooning to over €1 billion annually for 2026.
Amnesty International has raised concerns over the role of Frontex’s maritime aerial surveillance activities in the Mediterranean in illegal interceptions of refugees and migrants by the Libyan Coast Guard.
Amnesty International has also consistently questioned Frontex’s continuation of operations in EU countries adopting practices that are incompatible with EU law on asylum and migration, urging it to take swift action in cases of reported or alleged fundamental rights violations, and to initiate proceedings in line with the requirements in Article 46 of the existing Frontex Regulation to suspend or terminate its operations in such cases.

German drone maker unveils armed version of its Reliant spy drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:28:02 UTC
17:28:02 KST

- Quantum-Systems showed its Reliant long-range drone carrying a mixed load of 82 mm mortar rounds and 40 mm grenades.
- U.S. chief executive Dave Sharpin shared images of the armed configuration on social media and thanked partners from Orbital.
Quantum-Systems has unveiled an armed version of its Reliant long-range drone, showing the aircraft fitted with a mixed load of 82 mm mortar rounds and 40 mm grenades.
Dave Sharpin, chief executive of Quantum-Systems Inc., the U.S. arm of the German drone maker, shared images of the configuration on social media on Oct. 28, thanking partners from Orbital for their work on the project. The photos show the munitions carried on the drone’s wing hardpoints, combining two calibers on a single aircraft.
Each caliber gives the drone a different kind of strike: the 82 mm round, the standard size for medium mortars in many armies, carries a heavier explosive charge suited to larger targets, while the 40 mm grenade, the size fired by infantry grenade launchers, is smaller and lighter, so several can be carried and released one at a time against individual targets. Mixing the two lets an operator choose the right weapon for each target found during the same flight.
Reliant is a fixed-wing drone that takes off and lands vertically, so it can launch from a small clearing or a ship deck and then cruise like an airplane without a runway. Quantum-Systems introduced it at SOF Week in Tampa in May 2024 as a Group 2 aircraft with a 3.9 m (12.8-foot) wingspan and more than 10 hours of endurance from a hybrid-electric power system, and in July 2026 it announced an upgraded version with greater payload capacity, a maximum takeoff weight of 45 kg (99 pounds) and integration into the company’s MOSAIC UXS software, which lets operators control several types of unmanned systems together.
The armed configuration grows out of a version Quantum-Systems developed for U.S. customers, with hardpoints on each wing that can carry additional modules and release munitions or smaller drones. The company has also presented Reliant as a carrier for the Archer first-person-view attack drone built by U.S. manufacturer Neros, whose Archer the Pentagon has ordered in large numbers and which the U.S. Marine Corps recently flew with live warheads in Japan.
Reliant sits at the top of Quantum-Systems’ family of aircraft, above the short-range Twister and the mid-range Vector, the reconnaissance drone that made the company’s name in Ukraine. Sharpin has said Vector has flown more than 20,000 combat hours in Ukraine, and the company has fed that experience back into its designs, including after a Vector returned from a mission despite being hit 11 times by small arms fire. Quantum-Systems has also expanded production inside Ukraine, where it now builds Vector fuselages locally.
Quantum-Systems has offered Reliant to the German military as well as to U.S. buyers, and the armed version adds a strike option to an aircraft the company has so far marketed for long-range reconnaissance, surveillance and target acquisition.

Ukrainian mobile operator Kyivstar acquires cloud provider GigaCloud for nearly $50 mln
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:27:22 EET
17:27:22 KST

Kyivstar Group Ltd. (Nasdaq: KYIV), the parent company of Ukraine's largest telecommunications operator, Kyivstar, has announced the acquisition of GigaCloud, one of Ukraine's leading cloud infrastructure providers, for nearly UAH 2.28 billion (almost $50 million) to expand its cloud solutions capabilities for businesses.
"By combining these strengths with our telecommunications infrastructure, customer reach and investment capabilities, we will be able to help even more companies modernize their operations and develop a stronger technology business for the enterprise segment," Kyivstar Group Ltd. President Oleksandr Komarov was quoted as saying in a press release.
He added that the acquisition would help develop infrastructure that Ukraine will need over the long term.
The transaction is expected to close after the standard closing conditions for deals of this kind have been met. GigaCloud will continue operating as a separate business unit within Kyivstar Group Ltd., retaining its own brand and management team.
In particular, the company's founders are expected to continue running the business.
The agreement also provides for no changes to existing customer contracts, service levels or commercial terms.
"Together with Kyivstar Group Ltd., we will be able to accelerate infrastructure investment, expand our market presence and continue providing services at the level of quality our customers expect," GigaCloud CEO and co-founder Nazarii Kurochko said in the press release.
GigaCloud co-founder Anton Khvastunov, in turn, emphasized that the partnership would strengthen the company's ability to scale secure cloud services and enable it to continue contributing to Ukraine's digital development.
Kyivstar added that the investment would expand the operator's technological capabilities for the corporate sector, further strengthen its capabilities in sovereign cloud infrastructure and enable the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based services tailored to the needs of Ukrainian businesses and government institutions.
Founded in 2016, GigaCloud currently serves more than 1,800 corporate customers. The company specializes in providing relevant services to businesses. Its clients include agricultural holding company Kernel, Naftogaz and others.
The mobile operator's press release specifies that, according to unaudited management accounts, GigaCloud generated approximately $14 million in revenue and $4.7 million in EBITDA in 2025, corresponding to an EBITDA margin of approximately 34%.
"The agreement is expected to have a positive impact on the development of Kyivstar Group Ltd. The transaction valuation takes into account GigaCloud's growth rate, expertise in cloud technologies, leading market position and the expected benefits of combining the businesses," Kyivstar said.
The transaction structure includes $41 million in acquisition consideration, up to $4 million in deferred debt obligations, approximately $3 million in payments tied to the achievement of agreed performance targets, and up to $2 million in compensation for capital expenditures (CAPEX), in accordance with the terms of the deal.
As reported in the summer of this year, the Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine authorized Kyivstar Private Joint Stock Company to acquire control of GigaCloud LLC, the cloud provider operating under the GigaCloud brand.
In June 2025, the mobile operator launched its own cloud service for Ukrainian users, Kyivstar Cloud, which is available to small, medium-sized and large businesses, as well as public-sector organizations.
Kyivstar increased its revenue by 29.1% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, reaching UAH 28.9 billion, while revenue in U.S. dollar terms rose by 22.8% to $662 million. Kyivstar's net profit for the period increased by 36.1% compared with the first half of 2025, reaching UAH 7.1 billion, while net profit in U.S. dollar terms rose by 28.8% to $162 million.

Breadcrumb
US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
The US military has spent over $47 billion so far for the war on Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the 3 November midterm election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war's impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon's latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called "platform losses," which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump's initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran's defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military's Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.
