- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 531 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 27 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 28, the Defense Ministry reported.

Consequences
- One person required medical attention in the Lipetsk Region, Governor Igor Artamonov said on his Max channel.
- Falling UAV debris damaged apartment buildings, private houses and infrastructure in the nearby industrial zone in the city of Novomoskovsk in the Tula Region, Governor Dmitry Milyayev reported on his Max channel.
- According to the governor, emergency services have been sent to the scene.

Shabab Al Ahli more clinical in decisive moments: Bakhtiarizadeh
TEHRAN - Esteghlal head coach Sohrab Bakhtiarizadeh said that the difference between his team and Shabab Al Ahli came down to two decisive goal-scoring moments, in which the Emirati side showed greater professionalism and managed to score.
Speaking at the post-match press conference following Esteghlal’s 2–0 defeat to Shabab Al Ahli of the United Arab Emirates, Bakhtiarizadeh said: “My players gave everything they had today. We could have performed well and earned points, as we did in previous matches, although we knew we were facing a difficult challenge.
“We have played several demanding matches over the past two months. I apologize to our supporters, and we will do everything we can to make up for this defeat,” he added.
“The way we played in the second half did not suggest that we were heading for a defeat,” Bakhtiarizadeh stated.
“The difference between us and Shabab Al Ahli was in two goal-scoring situations. Their players acted more professionally in those moments and managed to find the back of the net.”
“We also created scoring opportunities, but we lacked precision in front of goal. It was natural for us to play deeper because we were playing away from home,” he went on to say.
“Our aim was to deny the opposition space. If Shabab Al Ahli had traveled to Tehran to play at Azadi Stadium, they probably would have spent much of the match defending deeper as well.”
“The only negative aspect of the match was the refereeing. I have never seen officiating like this at this level of football,” Bakhtiarizadeh concluded.

Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone fleet gets radar warning software fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:55:22 UTC
16:55:22 KST

- Lockheed Martin received a $9.8 million contract to update AN/ALQ-230 radar warning software and a mission data tool for Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone helicopters.
- Canada is funding the work through Foreign Military Sales, with Naval Air Systems Command contracting and completion expected in October 2030.
Lockheed Martin will update the radar warning and electronic support software on Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone maritime helicopters under a $9.8 million contract awarded through the U.S. Navy, with work running until October 2030.
Naval Air Systems Command placed the contract with Lockheed’s Owego, New York, operation on behalf of the Canadian government, which is paying the full amount through Foreign Military Sales. It covers a new version of the operational flight program software for the helicopter’s AN/ALQ-230 electronic support measures and radar warning receiver, along with new Canadian Mission Data Load Tool software, and includes development, documentation, testing, installation and training aimed at fixing software and system trouble reports already logged against the equipment. Owego accounts for 97% of the work, with the remaining share split evenly between Ottawa, Halifax and Patuxent River, Maryland, and the contract was not competed.
The AN/ALQ-230 is the Cyclone’s passive electronic warfare sensor, a Lockheed system developed for Canada’s Maritime Helicopter Program that listens for radar emissions from ships, aircraft and air defense sites, identifies them and warns the crew when the helicopter is being tracked. The operational flight program is the software that runs the receiver itself, while the mission data load is the library of emitter signatures the system uses to recognize what it detects. A Canadian tool for building those mission data files lets the Royal Canadian Air Force prepare and update its own threat libraries, which have to change as new radars appear and as crews deploy to different regions.
The contract announcement does not describe the trouble reports or say how many have been recorded, and neither Lockheed nor the Canadian Department of National Defence has said whether the work will add capability or only correct existing faults.
The Cyclone is a militarized, fly-by-wire version of the Sikorsky S-92 built by Sikorsky, which Lockheed Martin owns, and it shares its basic airframe with the U.S. Marine Corps’ VH-92A presidential helicopter, which is also built on the S-92. Canada ordered 28 Cyclones in 2004 to replace the CH-124 Sea King, but development problems delayed deliveries until June 2015, and the helicopter did not reach initial operational capability until June 2018, the same year the last Sea Kings retired. The aircraft flies from Royal Canadian Navy Halifax-class frigates for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, search and rescue and utility missions, carrying a multi-mode radar, a HELRAS dipping sonar, two torpedoes and a mission system developed by General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada in addition to the ESM suite.
National Defence puts the cost of acquiring the Cyclone, including project management, infrastructure and contingency, at C$3.75 billion, and the cost of major in-service support at C$11.17 billion. Its 2025 briefing notes set full operational capability for the fleet in September 2026 and the aircraft’s estimated life expectancy at 2043. One Cyclone was lost on April 29, 2020, while operating from HMCS Fredericton in the Ionian Sea, killing six Canadian Armed Forces members, which leaves 27 airframes from the original order.
The electronic support suite has been linked to an earlier fleet problem. Cracks found on almost all Cyclones in 2021 were caused by structural loads from the ESM and satellite communications antenna mounts in flight, according to National Defence, and Sikorsky repaired the aircraft. In April 2025, the fleet was briefly paused again after questions arose over whether some spare parts were in use beyond their service life.
Keeping the Cyclone’s mission systems current has been a recurring concern in Ottawa. Internal documents reported by CBC News in January 2024 showed the air force was worried about sustaining the helicopter’s weapon system over the medium and long term, partly because Canada is the only country flying the CH-148 and therefore bears the full cost of software and hardware updates unique to the type.
Lockheed’s Owego site also builds the AN/ALQ-210 electronic support system for the U.S. Navy’s MH-60R, and NAVAIR, which manages that work, is buying the Canadian update on Ottawa’s behalf, with part of the testing planned at Patuxent River.

Norway Allocates $45.5 Million to Strengthen Ukraine’s Energy Grid Before Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category

Norway Allocates $45.5 Million to Strengthen Ukraine’s Energy Grid Before Winter
Norway announced the allocation of 500 million kroner ($45.5 million) to bolster Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of the upcoming winter season.
The funding will arrive through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund in November and December to enable quick repair work, equipment purchasing, and investments in critical infrastructure damaged during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian officials highlighted a specific need for new power cables to maintain stable electricity distribution across the country.
“Ukraine will soon enter another winter under war conditions. To ensure the most stable energy supply possible and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is crucial that Ukraine receives funds to purchase equipment for strengthening and restoring critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombings,” stated Energy Minister Terje Aasland.
The minister noted that companies such as Nexans, based in Halden, could manufacture and supply the required subsea cables.
“Ukrainian authorities indicated that the supply of subsea cables is one of Ukraine’s top priorities. Such cables, for example, can be manufactured and delivered by Nexans from Halden,” Aasland added.
The funds form part of the 85 billion kroner ($7.73 billion) Nansen Support Programme for 2026, which designates 70 billion kroner ($6.37 billion) for military needs and 15 billion kroner ($1.36 billion) for civilian and humanitarian support.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Norway has directed over 16 billion kroner ($1.45 billion) toward gas purchases, energy infrastructure restoration, and new technological solutions.
As a harsh winter looms, Ukraine's air defenses are dangerously depleted as the country prepares for an expected surge in Russian energy strikes.
International supplies of Patriot interceptors are severely constrained, leaving Kyiv scrambling alongside European allies to secure hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles before the cold sets in.
With Ukrainian air defense intercepting only a fraction of incoming ballistic missiles, experts and officials warn that the upcoming winter threatens to bring severe energy disruptions and critical infrastructure challenges across the country.

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:53:28 UTC
16:53:28 KST

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.

Hemus Magazine will continue to build bridges between Bulgarians and Hungarians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:52:59 UTC
16:52:59 KST

Author
Joan Kolev
Interview
Hemus editor-in-chief Svetla Kyoseva for Radio Bulgaria:
Hemus Magazine will continue to build bridges between Bulgarians and Hungarians
Interview with Svetla Kyoseva
Wednesday 28 October 2026 09:02
Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 09:02
PHOTO Facebook /Bolgár Országos Önkormányzat
Font size
Hemus, a bilingual Bulgarian-Hungarian magazine covering culture and public life, is celebrating the 35th anniversary of its first issue, published in 1991.
Its editor-in-chief is Svetla Kyoseva, whose life has been closely connected with Hungary since 1984. That year, she arrived in Budapest and began working at the Hristo Botev Bulgarian School, where she spent 13 years. In 2004, former pupils invited her to head the Bulgarian School for the Mother Tongue, where she remained director for 15 years. Alongside her educational work, she has pursued an active career as a translator, with more than 200 published contributions and 40 books to her name.
In recognition of her contribution to presenting and promoting Hungarian literature in Bulgaria, Svetla Kyoseva has been awarded the prestigious Baumgarten Honorary Prize for 2026. In a special interview with Radio Bulgaria, she discusses the significance of the distinction, as well as the history and future of Hemus, a magazine popular with both Bulgarian and Hungarian readers.
Svetla Kyoseva
PHOTO BTA
“This is a very interesting award that enjoyed considerable prestige between the two world wars, after which it was discontinued. It has now been revived at the initiative of citizens, with funds raised through donations. A special jury made up of writers and translators decides who should receive it. The recipients are mainly Hungarian writers, but the work of translators of Hungarian literature is also recognised,” Ms Kyoseva explained, referring to the award named after the Hungarian patron of the arts Ferenc Baumgarten.
As in previous years, Hemus publishes two issues annually, each devoted to a particular theme. This approach also defines the magazine’s character in 2026.
First issue of Hemus Magazine for 2026
PHOTO bolgarok.hu
“We call the first issue the Danube issue because we have brought together works by Bulgarian authors devoted to the River Danube. The idea was prompted by an invitation to contribute Bulgarian works to an anthology entitled The River: A Different Anthology of the Danube. It was first published in German and Hungarian, followed by translations into Romanian, Slovak and Serbian. We now feel that the time has come for a Bulgarian edition, with each country able to add works on the subject that it considers important. For this issue, we selected a range of texts, including works by the writer Yordan Yovkov and contemporary pieces, some written especially for the magazine. I hope we will soon find a suitable publisher willing to take on this exceptionally interesting anthology.”
Speaking about the second Hemus issue of the year, the editor-in-chief of the bilingual magazine says:
Second issue of Hemus Magazine for 2026
PHOTO bolgarok.hu
“It brings together Bulgarian communities in the countries neighbouring Hungary, as their histories, origins and present-day circumstances are quite similar. One common thread is Bulgarian gardening, which began spreading across Europe in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, giving rise to communities that have survived to varying degrees to this day. The issue includes an excerpt from Georgi Gospodinov’s book The Gardener and Death, as well as a text explaining to children what market gardening is.”
This issue of the magazine was officially presented during the World Meeting of Bulgarian Media in Budapest. Svetla Kyoseva chaired one of the discussion panels, entitled “Media and Enlighteners”:
Svetla Kyoseva at the World Meeting of Bulgarian Media in Budapest (20 October 2026)
PHOTO BTA
“The discussion brought together representatives of Bulgarian communities in neighbouring countries, including Diana Glasnova from Zagreb, Desislav Payakov from Vienna, and the media outlet Bulgarski Vesti, represented by its editor-in-chief, Gabriela Hadjikostova. She received an award from the 13 Centuries of Bulgaria National Endowment Fund in recognition of the contribution made by a Bulgarian-language media outlet abroad to the promotion of Bulgarian culture.”
Gabriela Hadjikostova
PHOTO BTA
As a magazine that continues to maintain a print edition, Hemus inevitably faces challenges. Unlike most Bulgarian media outlets abroad, however, which rely on targeted funding from Bulgaria to continue their work, the publication serving the Bulgarian community in Hungary does not depend on such support.
“We do not need this kind of assistance because the Bulgarian community in Hungary receives funding from the Hungarian state,” Svetla Kyoseva said. At the same time, she acknowledged that “funding is a serious problem for many Bulgarian publications abroad. Those that do not receive support from the countries where they are based face considerable difficulties in producing their publications.”
The future plans for Hemus reflect its ambition to remain a bridge between the Bulgarian community and Hungarian society by covering subjects of interest to both readerships. The magazine also aims to reach out to other communities and countries.
PHOTO Facebook /Bolgár Országos Önkormányzat
“Some colleagues and I were invited to contribute to Slovak publications on the subject of Bulgarian gardening being recognised as part of Hungary’s cultural heritage. Bulgarians in Slovakia are currently taking similar steps, which is why they showed great interest in our experience. I have also invited authors from other countries to write for the magazine.”
In 2027, one of the magazine’s issues will mark the centenary of Miklós Mázárov, a Hungarian artist of Bulgarian descent, Svetla Kyoseva announced. She added that, from this year, the gallery at the Bulgarian Cultural and Educational Centre in the Hungarian capital has also borne his name.
“After his death, his widow established an award in his name, presented to Hungarian artists. Receiving this award is a great honour. Every year, it provides an opportunity to talk not only about the artist himself, but also about Bulgaria and Bulgarian artists in Hungary, who form a very close-knit and strong community.”

Tokayev proposes three-year moratorium on small business inspections from 2027

Tokayev proposes three-year moratorium on small business inspections from 2027
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed introducing a new three-year moratorium on inspections of micro- and small businesses from January 1, 2027. He announced it while delivering his annual State-of-the-Nation Address in еру Qurultay today, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The Head of State called on Qurultay deputies and the Government to discuss the expediency of the measure, taking into account both the positive and negative outcomes of the previous moratorium, which was in effect from 2020 to 2023.
“In this regard, the experience of the 2020-2023 moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses will be valuable. It proved to be effective. I propose that Qurultay deputies and the Government discuss the expediency of introducing another three-year moratorium from January 1, 2027, taking into account all the positive and negative aspects of the previous one,” Tokayev said.
The President also highlighted changes in business inspection figures. According to him, the number of violations by individual entrepreneurs fell by 34% in the first half of the year, while the total amount of fines increased by nearly 11% and the number of unscheduled inspections rose tenfold.
Tokayev also called for improving the conditions for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to participate in procurement by government agencies and quasi-public sector companies. In particular, he proposed reserving a share of procurements for SMEs and easing requirements for suppliers.
The President said the proposed moratorium should serve as a strategic pause to overhaul the inspection and supervision system and transition to a digital regulatory model.
Earlier, the President ordered a new large-scale system of long-term financing for farmers.

Tokayev outlines historic mission to build a new Kazakhstan for future generations

Tokayev outlines historic mission to build a new Kazakhstan for future generations
Around 70 healthcare facilities and nearly 50 education, sports and cultural facilities are planned for construction across Kazakhstan’s regions. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev made the announcement in his Address to the People of Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the President, the National Fund’s main goal and mission is to preserve the country’s wealth, increase it, and use it for the benefit of current and future generations.
“For many years, the National Fund has fulfilled this core task, making a significant contribution to financial stability. To ensure the well-being of younger generations, we must take concrete and bold steps now. We cannot postpone addressing pressing problems. Every issue must be resolved. This is the main requirement. We must pass on to future generations a civilized, advanced and renewed state. This is our duty and responsibility to future generations,” Tokayev said.
The Head of State noted that the country’s historic responsibility to future generations involves more than leaving them financial savings in bank accounts. It also means building and passing on a fundamentally new country, one that is technologically advanced, has a strong and competitive economy, modern infrastructure and high living standards, and offers every citizen opportunities for self-realization.
“This is our main task, a mission of historic significance. It means long-term investment in human capital, improving citizens’ quality of life and, therefore, investing in the country’s future,” the President stressed.
At the same time, he said Kazakhstan must maintain a balance between accumulating funds in the National Fund and spending them.

Ukraine's intelligence names nearly 50 companies involved in developing Russia's Starlink rival
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:51:00 EET
16:51:00 KST

Ukraine's intelligence names nearly 50 companies involved in developing Russia's Starlink rival
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released information on 49 Russian and Belarusian companies involved in developing Rassvet, a satellite communications system that Russia is developing as an alternative to Starlink.
Source: War&Sanctions
Quote: "The system comprises a constellation of low-Earth orbit satellites, ground-based control infrastructure, gateway stations and user terminals for fixed and mobile facilities."
Details: DIU said the project involves IT companies, microelectronics manufacturers, research centres, and entities affiliated with Russia's state space corporation Roscosmos and the Russian Defence Ministry.
According to DIU, the project's main contractor is Russia's Bureau 1440, a limited liability company that is part of the ICS Holding IT group. Other companies within the group supply components and manufacture solar panels, user terminals, printed circuit boards, electronic modules and other system components.
"Roscosmos and other companies in Russia's aerospace industry are responsible for developing and manufacturing launch vehicles and upper stages, electric propulsion engines and other satellite components, as well as adapting the satellites, preparing them for launch and placing them into orbit," DIU said.
DIU said Roscosmos head Dmitry Bakanov directly oversees the Rassvet project. He previously headed the Gonets Satellite System, which partnered with the UK's OneWeb and established a joint venture to develop low-Earth-orbit satellite communications services for the Russian market.
Entities affiliated with the Russian Defence Ministry are responsible for operating the spaceport, coordinating project participants, and eventually integrating the system into the military communications infrastructure. Russian bank VTB is among the investors in Rassvet.
According to DIU, 23 of the 49 companies and institutions involved in the project have not been sanctioned by any country in the sanctions coalition. These include Roscosmos.
The intelligence agency notes that Rassvet is primarily intended for military communications.
"Russia plans to make extensive use of the system to support its armed forces, including for strategic communications and command and control, controlling strike platforms, equipping command posts and military equipment with user terminals, supporting the combat use of unmanned systems and ensuring the operation of Russian Defence Ministry facilities," DIU said.
According to DIU, Russia plans to integrate Rassvet satellites into a space-based system that provides targeting data for missile systems and equip the command vehicles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system with user terminals.
"The planned coverage is primarily intended to include the territory of Ukraine and the EU. Once sufficient coverage has been achieved, Russia could use the system in hybrid acts of aggression against other countries," it warned.
The intelligence agency has called for sanctions to be imposed on companies involved in the project and for restrictions on the supply of components, equipment and software to them.
Background: According to DIU, Russia is deploying the Rassvet satellite system ahead of schedule. In March 2026, 16 satellites were placed into orbit. Russia plans to expand the constellation to 292 satellites by 2027 and 924 by 2035.

Armed Zaporizhzhia police officers walk along a street during a humanitarian mission to evacuate a family with an elderly woman with low mobility from the front-line settlement of Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, October 19, 2026. (Dmtro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
Russia has lost 1,583,350 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 28.
The number includes 1,510 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to thereport, Russia has also lost 12,448 tanks, 25,609 armored combat vehicles, 167,738 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,674 artillery systems, 2,241 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,727 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,032 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky toldFrance TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

U.S. Navy finalizes Lockheed order for F-35 power and cooling upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:47:21 UTC
16:47:21 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order for F135 Engine Core Upgrade integration and power and cooling work.
- The modification definitizes an earlier undefinitized order, moves the F-35’s power and thermal management upgrade into preliminary design, and runs through April 2027.
The U.S. Navy has added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order covering integration of the F-35’s upgraded F135 engine core and the move of a new power and cooling system for the fighter into preliminary design.
Naval Air Systems Command announced the cost-plus-fixed-fee, level-of-effort modification on Oct. 27, definitizing an undefinitized contract action, which means the government and Lockheed have now agreed on final terms for work that began before the price was settled, and extending the effort to April 2027. No money was obligated at award, and the work, which supports the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and the F-35 cooperative program partners, was not competed.
The modification sits on a delivery order NAVAIR first issued in fiscal 2025 as a not-to-exceed $107 million undefinitized order, which paid Lockheed to run trade studies and an alternatives assessment of every potential power and thermal management solution for the F-35, along with the integration work needed to fit Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade into Block 4 aircraft. That order was due to finish in December 2026, so the new action pushes completion back four months while shifting part of the effort from study to design as the power and thermal management upgrade enters its preliminary design phase.
Fort Worth, Texas, where Lockheed builds the F-35, accounts for 47% of the work, while Torrance and El Segundo, California, take 19% between them and two sites in Britain, Blackburn and Cheltenham, take 6% each, with the remainder spread across Haltom City, Texas; South Bend, Indiana; Windsor Locks and West Hartford, Connecticut; Rockford, Illinois; and Orlando, Florida.
The engine and cooling work both stem from the amount of heat the F-35’s electronics generate. The F-35 Joint Program Office has said Block 3 jets produce about 30 kilowatts of waste heat, a figure expected to reach 47 kilowatts in Block 4, while the current engine is optimized to absorb about 14 kilowatts. That heat is removed by the Power and Thermal Management System, or PTMS, a Honeywell unit that draws bleed air from the engine and also provides auxiliary and emergency power, engine starting and cabin environmental control, and because the PTMS takes more air from the F135 than its designers planned, the engine runs hotter and wears out faster, raising sustainment costs across the fleet.
Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade, or ECU, redesigns the F135’s core to produce more thrust, supply more bleed air and electrical power, and restore the engine life lost to heat, while the separate Power Thermal Management Upgrade, or PTMU, will replace or enlarge the cooling system that uses that air. In October 2024, the Joint Program Office named Lockheed the lead systems integrator for the PTMU after concluding that no other company could manage the integration, and the order modified this week is the contract vehicle for that role.
Honeywell, which builds the current PTMS, unveiled a near-term cooling option called P40 in September that would raise capacity from about 32 kilowatts to 40 kilowatts through software changes and liquid-cooling modifications, with no airframe changes and fielding planned for 2029 or 2030, and the company says the architecture could later grow to 62 kilowatts or more. Collins Aerospace, a sister company of Pratt & Whitney within RTX, is competing with a new design called the Enhanced Power and Cooling System, and the two companies have said that pairing it with the ECU would yield about a 7% gain in range and thrust along with double the cooling capacity, figures that come from the manufacturers. The modification does not say which approach Lockheed’s trade studies favored or whether preliminary design will cover one solution or several, and the government has not announced a PTMU selection.
The Pentagon chose in March 2023 to upgrade the F135 instead of re-engining the F-35 with an adaptive-cycle design from the Adaptive Engine Transition Program, citing cost and the difficulty of integrating a new engine into the short-takeoff F-35B and carrier-based F-35C. Pratt & Whitney then completed the ECU’s preliminary design review in July 2024 and later that year received a contract worth up to $1.3 billion for design maturation, rig testing and aircraft integration through March 2028.
In late August, the Navy added a modification worth up to $240.8 million to move the ECU into engineering and manufacturing development and buy long-lead hardware for a spare test engine, and Pratt & Whitney completed the upgrade’s risk reduction design review on Sept. 15. The company describes the ECU as a drop-in replacement core that can be installed on new engines or retrofitted at F135 depots, and John Sneden, the U.S. Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for propulsion, said in July that ground testing is planned for late 2027 and flight testing for around 2030, later than the 2029 fielding date Pratt had cited in 2024.
Lockheed’s share of the integration covers the aircraft side of the engine change, since a new core alters bleed-air flow, electrical power extraction, engine controls and heat loads, each of which affects the airframe’s fuel, cooling and mission systems. The engine and cooling upgrades also have to be timed together, because the extra cooling capacity Block 4 needs depends on both programs delivering.
The Government Accountability Office has warned of integration risks to the ECU timeline, and the Block 4 upgrade, which carries the new sensors and weapons responsible for much of the added heat, has slipped repeatedly. The fiscal 2027 budget request seeks $317.5 million for F-35 propulsion work, up from about $121 million in 2026, with much of the increase meant to accelerate the ECU and PTMU.

The attack occurred shortly after midnight when a suspect believed to be a minor approached the Gendarmerie officer guarding the embassy and attacked him with two knives, Dacic said in a statement.

Following the incident, Serbian authorities raised the country's security threat alert to its highest level and ordered increased police presence and security checks at key locations, including critical infrastructure and crowded public areas.
Authorities are investigating the circumstances of the attack and working to identify the assailant, who is believed to be from the western Serbian city of Sabac.
According to Israeli news outlet Ynet, the incident was the second attack targeting security personnel guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade, following a June 2024 crossbow attack that left a police officer wounded in the neck.

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with half of votes counted

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 12:30 p.m. local time, just over 84.5% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."

Minister: Economic recovery does not happen overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:45:00 UTC
16:45:00 KST

Minister: Economic recovery does not happen overnight
Economic recovery will take a little longer for people to feel its effects, Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Liina Vahtras (Reform) said on Tuesday, commenting on the latest consumer confidence survey.
Businesses believe the economy has improved this month, but consumers were more pessimistic, data from Statistics Estonia published on Tuesday shows.
Companies have held this view for some time, so the survey results were no surprise to the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications. The industrial sector is in its strongest position in four years.
"Of course, major negative events also took place four years ago, and confidence then plummeted. By now, we have climbed out of that hole. However, according to surveys, consumer economic confidence has fallen to its lowest level in six months," said Mario Lambing, chief analyst at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
Since May, Statistics Estonia has conducted economic confidence surveys instead of the Estonian Institute of Economic Research, and the ministry comments on the results once a quarter.
Vahtras also commented on the results.
"Economic recovery and improvement simply take a little more time; they do not happen overnight. People will feel that things have actually improved for them. And the effects of the income tax reform implemented at the beginning of the year will simply be felt a little later," she said.
High motor fuel prices and the winter heating season have made people more cautious about the future. "If this winter is colder and heating bills rise, the government will discuss how to compensate both private consumers and businesses," the minister added.
Lambing said the change in survey provider has made consumers' opinions more pessimistic.
"One factor is indeed the change in survey provider, but a bigger change may have come from the fact that consumers were now surveyed online instead of by telephone, and these methods can produce different results, even if you ask exactly the same person exactly the same question," he said.

Q3: UBS posts $2.7 billion profit
UBS recorded a net profit of $2.7 billion (CHF2.2 billion) between July and September. The bank is on track to meet its annual targets and complete the integration of Credit Suisse this year, it said on Wednesday.
Profit before tax reached $3.6 billion in the third quarter, and $4.1 billion on a like-for-like basis, representing year-on-year increases of 27% and 14%, respectively.
The bank benefited from strong client momentum across its various market segments. Operating income rose by 5% to $13.35 billion. On a like-for-like basis, the increase was 10% to $13.39 billion, UBS said.
More
‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
In wealth management, new money inflows reached $55.1 billion in the third quarter. Growth was driven by the Asia-Pacific region and the Americas.
Shareholders already have reason to be pleased, as the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio and the CET1 leverage ratio stand at 14.7% and 4.6%, respectively, paving the way for a dividend increase of around 15% and the implementation of the $3 billion share buyback programme by the time the results for the final interim period of 2026 are published.
The annual targets are within reach. Following a return on Common Equity Tier 1 (RoCET1) of 16.7% on an underlying nine-month basis (or 14.8% unadjusted), UBS believes it is on track to exceed its 2026 target, which stood at around 15% . Meanwhile, the cost-to-income ratio, which stood at 69.6% between January and September, is expected to be in line with expectations (below 70 per cent) for the full year.
More
What the too-big-to-fail Swiss parliament vote means for UBS
The results are in line with expectations, with both adjusted and unadjusted operating income, as well as adjusted pre-tax profit, even exceeding the AWP consensus estimates.
Furthermore, UBS is on track to finalise the integration of its former rival Credit Suisse by the end of the year. Additional cost savings of $0.6 billion were realised in the third-quarter results, bringing total gross savings to $13.2 billion. By the end of 2026, UBS expects to have achieved savings of $13.7 billion, compared with the $13.5 billion previously forecast.
A number of macroeconomic, political and geopolitical factors will weigh on investor confidence in the final quarterly results.

Zelenskyy: temporary Starshield restriction stops operation of 2,000 'Bars' drone interceptors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:43:23 EET
16:43:23 KST

Ukraine received 2,000 Bars drone interceptors funded by a European country, and during testing, one of them destroyed a Russian Shahed, but Starshield restrictions halted the operation of these interceptors, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
"We found a European country. They paid for 2,000 units. I knew we had 2,000. I said: 'Let's test it. Maybe it can destroy targets.' They tested it, and it destroyed a Shahed. We were very happy. And then Starshield stopped working," Zelenskyy said at a meeting with journalists on Tuesday, an Interfax-Ukraine agency correspondent reports.
He noted that he does not know who exactly made the decision to turn off the system, which is technically turned on and off by SpaceX. Zelenskyy also explained that Ukraine uses Starshield against the Russian military on its own territory, rather than on the territory of the Russian Federation. In addition, the system is used primarily for logistics, in particular providing the military with food and water, as well as to counter "Shaheds" and jet-powered drones.
According to the President, Ukraine currently destroys about 90% of Russian Shaheds, whereas at the beginning of the attacks this figure was 50–75%, sometimes reaching 78%. Zelenskyy also stated that during the Starlink/Starshield disconnection, civilians died, although he emphasized that this happened for various reasons.
As reported, on the night of October 14, the Ukrainian military recorded restrictions on the operation of Starshield terminals – the military version of Starlink satellite communications. According to Interfax-Ukraine sources in the Ministry of Defense, terminals lost connection while moving at speeds exceeding a set threshold, which on various equipment was approximately 72–161 km/h. This complicated the tasks performed by drone interceptors and strike UAVs, as well as logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay. The Ministry of Defense held consultations with the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners and checked backup communication channels.
On October 24, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported that Ministry of Defense monitoring systems were recording the restoration of Starlink/Starshield speed capabilities.
"We are recording speeds of more than 400 km/h, the connection is stable. This is another example of how direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yield results. And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, drone operations, logistics, and communications," Khmara commented in response to journalists' questions on Saturday.

Aussie Diamonds avoid Constellation Cup clean sweep to Silver Ferns
The Diamonds have defeated the Silver Ferns 68-58 in front of a sold-out crowd of 9,471 at John Cain Arena to avoid a Constellation Cup clean sweep.
Despite falling to an overall 3-1 series defeat, the victory gives Australian fans hope ahead of the team's title defence at the 2027 Netball World Cup.
Both sides were only separated by a single goal at the half-time break, 32-31, before the hosts outscored the Commonwealth Games gold medallists in the second half, 37-26.
The result extends the Diamond's 11-year undefeated record against New Zealand in Melbourne.
New Zealand head coach Noeline Taurua made 19 changes to her team throughout the game to try and slow down the Diamonds in attack.
Australia, meanwhile, were unchanged for the entire 60 minutes.
A new shooting combination between Sophie Garbin and Georgie Horjus looked promising for the Diamonds. Together, the pair finished with an overall accuracy of 91 per cent.
It was the first time Horjus has got a proper chance at goal attack. She was named in that position on Sunday for game three but quickly had to slot back into wing attack following a finger injury to Kate Moloney on the first centre pass.
Horjus was named Player of the Match for her efforts inside the circle on Wednesday night.
Despite being 12cm shorter than her direct opponent Karin Burger, and 20cm shorter than goal keeper Kelly Jackson, she was not spooked by their wingspan or height.
There were points where Garbin was sandwiched between the Silver Ferns defenders and Horjus had to step up, sharing the shooting load and scoring a total 26 goals.
Speaking with the media after the match, Horjus conceded she was nervous to start the game but grew in confidence as the minutes wore on.
"There was a lot of talk about Kelly's long arms and the defence over the shot, but after the first quarter I got a little more relaxed," Horjus said.
"Having the support from Liz and Sophie around me just to shoot it.
"I train against the best in the world every week [in Super Netball] so I think my mindset just changed a little bit and I was more confident to go to post."
Liz Watson had a much improved game at her preferred position.
Taking back the wing attack bib, the Australian captain shrugged off criticism that has followed her performances this series to finish the match with a huge tally of 50 feeds.
Jackson topped the gain stat, but newcomer Jessie Grenvold wasn't far behind. The goal keeper has been a star in her first appearances for the Diamonds at 23 years old.
Her stats sheet read: one intercept, seven deflections and one rebound.
Grenvold was the only Australian defender to consistently ruffle Kiwi powerhouse Grace Nweke's feathers throughout the Constellation Cup.
Grenvold and Amy Parmenter (three gains) helped to turn the screws in the back half of the match. They hunted ball with a sense of urgency and disrupted the flow of the Silver Ferns.
Head coach Taurua said her team looked tired and weary, and the Diamonds were simply too good on the night.
They may yet take out the number one ranking when World Netball does its calculations and updates its list on December 1st.
"It was a bittersweet feeling," New Zealand captain Karin Burger said.
"We still won the Cup and according to statistics we're actually equal first [in the rankings], so we'll take that for what it is and then we'll work really hard for next year."
"As I understand when we came in, we needed to win 4-0 to be number one outright, three [wins] we'd be drawn and anything less, we'd be in the same position," Taurua added.
"We've been looking at that for six weeks which is why this series has been massive for us, to try and get that ranking."

What's on the line tonight
New Zealand could do something they haven’t done in 16 years.

Fourth-tier Fleetwood stun Premier League champions Arsenal in League Cup shootout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:41:52 UTC
16:41:52 KST

Dilara Hamit
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Fourth-tier Fleetwood Town produced one of the biggest upsets in English League Cup history by eliminating Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties Tuesday.
Fleetwood won the shootout 5-3 at Highbury Stadium after the fourth-round tie ended 1-1 in normal time, reaching the competition’s quarterfinals for the first time.
The English Football League said the hosts entered the match 84 places below Arsenal in the English football pyramid.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood a surprise lead in the 21st minute, overpowering Arsenal teenager Marli Salmon before finishing past debutant goalkeeper Illan Meslier.
Arsenal controlled possession after falling behind but struggled to convert their chances against Fleetwood’s disciplined defense.
Mikel Arteta introduced captain Martin Odegaard at halftime, and Viktor Gyokeres equalized five minutes after the restart. The Swedish striker converted from close range following an attack involving 18-year-old Ceadach O’Neill, who was making his first senior start for Arsenal.
The visitors increased the pressure as the second half progressed, but goalkeeper Jay Lynch repeatedly denied them. He made important late saves against Ben White and Odegaard to send the match to penalties.
Arsenal finished the game with 10 players after 16-year-old Max Dowman was shown a red card for kicking out following a challenge by Fleetwood midfielder Harrison Neal in the 85th minute.
Fleetwood converted all five of their penalties through Ronan Coughlan, Neal, Will Davies, Andy Cannon and Conor Haughey.
Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Gyokeres scored Arsenal’s first three attempts, but Lynch saved substitute Bruno Guimaraes’ fourth penalty. Haughey then converted the decisive kick, sparking a pitch invasion and celebrations among the home supporters.
The match had also been interrupted shortly after kickoff when an unauthorized drone flew above the stadium, causing play to be suspended for several minutes.
Arteta fielded a much-changed side ahead of Arsenal’s Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday, although the starting lineup still included Gyokeres, Havertz, Martin Zubimendi, Jurrien Timber and Piero Hincapie.
Fleetwood had never previously reached the League Cup’s fourth round. Before Tuesday, they were also winless in five matches against top-flight opposition.
Arsenal’s elimination echoed their 2012 League Cup defeat to fourth-tier Bradford City, who also knocked the London club out on penalties following a 1-1 draw.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine wants Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting before potential U.S-China-Russia summit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:41:30 EET
16:41:30 KST

Ukraine would like the tripartite meeting of the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the U.S, and Russia in Abu Dhabi to take place prior to a potential meeting between the US, China, and Russia, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
"We will see what kind of meeting this will be. We would very much like our meeting in Abu Dhabi to happen before that," Zelenskyy said at a meeting with journalists on Tuesday, an Interfax-Ukraine agency correspondent reports.
Commenting on the possible meeting of the leaders of the U.S, China, and Russia, the President noted that it will likely discuss the situation in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine.
At the same time, Zelenskyy expressed concern over the possibility of a redistribution of spheres of influence by analogy with the Yalta Conference.
"I really don't want this to be a 'Yalta – 2, 3, 4,' when there is a redistribution of influence. I would even say not influence, but opinions – that things can be redistributed this way. Today we have a different world, a fragmented world that is very different from the world of World War II, both before and after. A completely different technological world. Therefore, I think it is impossible to simply make such a redistribution between the three. Although Russia really wants to," the President emphasized.
In his opinion, such a meeting would be more beneficial to Russia than to China.
"I believe that after Alaska, this will be the second such diplomatic, serious advantage for Russia, if everything happens exactly as the Russians are now 'leaking' regarding their desires for a new 'Yalta,'" he said.
The President added that currently, holding the tripartite meeting in Abu Dhabi depends on the American side.
"The Russians have confirmed, we have confirmed. In my opinion, today this no longer depends on the Russians and not on us. Today Abu Dhabi depends on the American side," he noted.
According to him, all parties view the possibility of holding such a meeting positively, but the development of the situation in the Middle East is affecting U.S plans.
"There may be escalation there, and many are talking about it. I think there will be," the President believes.

Brussels cyclist loses sight in his left eye following serious road rage incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:40:32 UTC
16:40:32 KST

Cyclist Laurent Nyssen was the victim of a serious road rage incident in the Brussels borough of Schaarbeek. As a result of which he has probably lost sight in one eye. It all began with an argument over a blocked cycle path. “The guy got out of his car at the traffic lights; after that, I don’t remember what happened” Laurent told Brussels media outlet Bruzz.
Brussels cyclist loses sight in his left eye following serious road rage incident
On Wednesday 14 October, Laurent Nyssen was out on his bike to collect a parcel in Schaarbeek. At around 6.45 pm, he got into an altercation with a motorist on Koninklijke Sinte-Mariastraat.
“There was a traffic jam. I rang my bell at the many cars blocking the cycle path – something that happens every day in Brussels.” The street has wide cycle paths, but they are not separated from the road and the cars.
A van driver travelling behind him must have been annoyed by the ringing. “He was really worked up and gave me a proper telling-off at the traffic lights. I gave him a piece of my mind, as I often do, but at the second set of traffic lights he got out of his van. I have no memory of what happened next.”
Two witnesses did see what happened, and a CCTV camera also recorded everything. “He completely lost it,” Laurent recounts. “I was hit on the head about ten times. He hit me so hard that I fell to the ground.”
Eye surgery
Laurent was taken to hospital, but he cannot remember anything about that either. The blows left him with a broken jaw and damaged his left eye.
“I’ve had two operations on my eye, but the doctors fear I’ll never be able to see out of it again. There’s still a very small chance that some of my sight might recover over time, but it won’t ever be the same as it was before.”
At home with an ankle monitor
The man, aged around 30, who had carried out the attack was arrested that very evening. “The police came to my hospital bed in the middle of the night to tell me he’d been arrested. He spent six days in a cell and is now at home with an ankle monitor. Other than that, I know nothing about him,” says the cyclist. According to Laurent, his story is not an isolated incident. “There’s a culture of hatred towards cyclists in Brussels. It’s the law of the jungle on the streets. And the aggression towards cyclists is getting worse every year. Motorists feel like they own the roads in Brussels; they pay absolutely no attention to cyclists. And if you say anything about it, you get a proper telling-off.”
“Virtually all my friends who cycle have experienced aggression. One of them even ended up in hospital after a ‘discussion’ with a driver. Fortunately, his injuries weren’t too serious at the time.”
Food delivery riders
Laurent feels that cyclists are viewed with suspicion, particularly in the boroughs of Schaarbeek and Anderlecht. “I’m well aware that there are cyclists who don’t follow the rules. A lot of food delivery riders race through the city to get through as many orders as possible. But that’s completely out of proportion to the danger cyclists face.”
The attacker will have to answer in court in November; Laurent will be bringing a civil claim. “The police told me I was lucky to have survived. I think he should be tried for attempted manslaughter.”
Living with one eye
Laurent is recovering and trying to get his life back on track. He is at home on sick leave, preparing for a life with vision in only one eye. “The doctors have told me that the brain adapts quickly to seeing with just one eye. At first, I was worried about my job; I work as a graphic designer. I’ve realised I can manage. It’ll take a bit of getting used to it. Especially when I’m walking down the street, I find I can’t judge distances very well.”
“I’m getting a lot of support from my girlfriend and daughter, from my family and friends,” he says gratefully. “And I’m determined to start cycling again. Not straight away, but as soon as winter’s over. I won’t let anything keep me off the streets.”

Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE discuss regional de-escalation, with Türkiye-led mediation mechanism in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:39:36 UTC
16:39:36 KST

Amer Solyman and Ikram Kouachi
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Egypt discussed regional de-escalation efforts with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, emphasizing coordination through a four-way ministerial mechanism involving Türkiye and Pakistan, according to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held separate phone calls Tuesday with his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, and UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed, the ministry said in two separate statements Wednesday.
During his call with bin Farhan, Abdelatty discussed regional developments and “efforts to contain the current crisis amid growing risks of escalation,” stressing the need to “advance political and peaceful solutions through dialogue.”
The two foreign ministers agreed to “continue close consultations and coordination bilaterally and through a four-way ministerial mechanism that also includes Türkiye and Pakistan.”
The mechanism brings together Egypt, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia to strengthen consultation and coordination on de-escalation and support political solutions to regional crises.
The call came a day after Egypt’s parliament approved, by a two-thirds majority, a mandate for President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take necessary measures to support Saudi Arabia and defend its territory, sovereignty and holy sites, in coordination with the kingdom.
It also comes amid ongoing military escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group since July, including Houthi attacks on civil aviation facilities and energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition since March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
In a separate statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Abdelatty and his Emirati counterpart discussed the latest regional developments, particularly growing indications of possible escalation in the coming period.
Abdelatty stressed the need for regional countries to “unite their efforts to reach peaceful solutions and return all parties to a peaceful political track to prevent the region from sliding into a more dangerous phase of the current crisis.”
The call came as mediation efforts continue to contain tensions between Washington and Tehran amid ongoing disagreements over the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
On Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.
On June 18, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding and began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements, including maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global energy and goods supplies.

At the same time, he noted that Kyiv's resilience plans were not fully implemented, and the capital's critical infrastructure facilities are not fully protected.
"It would be wonderful if Kyiv could protect itself or at least prepare for dangers. But this did not work in any of the aspects. Now we can only go through these challenges together with all institutions," the president added.
According to him, daily work by various institutions is currently underway regarding the electricity and water supply situation in the capital, as well as the functioning of bridges. He emphasized that the protection of critical infrastructure must be ensured regardless of who formally owns a particular facility.
"Critical infrastructure facilities must be protected. They did not protect them to the end. Resilience plans were not fully completed," the president noted.
At the same time, Zelenskyy emphasized that he does not consider the situation in Kyiv to be a matter of political confrontation, but acknowledged the difficulty of interacting with the city authorities. According to him, when he discusses the possibility of strengthening the capital with managers, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko perceives it as an attempt to replace him.
"I would very much like the mayor to do everything himself. But he cannot do it alone. And working together is difficult," Zelenskyy said.
The president cited Kharkiv as an example, where, according to him, the head of the regional state administration and the mayor work together despite different political plans for the future. He noted that such interaction helps solve problems and maintain the situation in the city.
Zelenskyy also reported that he spoke with various managers about the possibility of heading the Kyiv administration or joining the work to strengthen the capital. According to him, he discussed this issue in particular with Vasyl Maliuk, Oleksandr Kubrakov, and Volodymyr Hroysman, as well as representatives of business and public administration, but no volunteers were found to join.
"I wanted to involve Maliuk in this group in the context of security issues. I also spoke with Kubrakov, Hroysman. Sukhomlyn refused – as soon as he heard about Kyiv," the head of state explained.
He emphasized that he has no personal claims against Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, but the capital must be prepared for a difficult winter. According to Zelenskyy, despite the fact that massive Russian attacks started earlier than expected, this should not be a reason just to look for those to blame.
"He (Klitschko) should have called all these people himself and met with them, rather than me. During such a war, it doesn't matter whose bridge it is on paper. The main thing is that it stands and functions as one of the capital's most important logistical arteries," Zelenskyy said.

War with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion - NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:38:10 EET
16:38:10 KST

War with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. spending on the war with Iran has reached $47.1 billion, with more than 60% going toward munitions. The Pentagon is requesting up to another $70 billion.
For the United States, the cost of the war with Iran had risen to $47.1 billion as of October 16, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60 percent of the expenditures. The Pentagon reported this to Congress last week, UNN writes, citing The New York Times.
Details
Even though U.S. President Donald Trump has so far refrained from resuming major hostilities, the Pentagon still incurred additional costs of about $3.5 billion over roughly six weeks since the estimates were presented to lawmakers last month.
These figures were the latest look at the unclassified breakdown of costs incurred by each branch of the armed forces, as well as by specific categories, such as damaged or destroyed weapons.
In the latest cost estimates, for example, the U.S. Air Force spent $7.6 billion to cover the operation of dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons. The U.S. Navy spent $1.5 billion deploying more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers. And maintaining troops in the region cost the Army $2.1 billion. Overall, according to U.S. Central Command, more than 50,000 service members are involved in this military mission.
Members of Congress shared these cost estimates with The New York Times after they were provided to national security committees on Capitol Hill.
Since the war began on February 28, the U.S. military has spent $29 billion on munitions, depleting global stocks of certain critical weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, and redirecting supplies from U.S. military commands in Asia and Europe.
The Pentagon spent $6.1 billion replacing dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft and other weapons and equipment. It spent $645 million deploying and supporting several thousand special forces personnel in the region.
The information also revealed spending on other important items. According to one member of Congress, the military spent $24.5 million on "internal medical support" for U.S. service members. The Pentagon reports that 18 service members have been killed in the war and more than 860 have been wounded.
According to an official, U.S. Transportation Command spent $92.2 million moving cargo and equipment, while U.S. Cyber Command spent $14 million on "cyber support operations."
According to members of Congress on Tuesday, the department's figures are almost certainly understated, as the Pentagon acknowledged that its estimate does not include $1.5 billion for fuel and other expenses that the Trump administration requested in a supplemental request to fund the war.
The information provided to Congress also did not include the costs of repairing or replacing U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, such as the U.S. Navy base in Manama, Bahrain. The Pentagon indicated that it may close them or not rebuild them. If the military or host countries restore the facilities, the costs could amount to tens of billions of dollars, according to members of Congress.
Meanwhile, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration are seeking up to $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war with Iran, as well as to purchase new weapons and personnel.
