Australia moves to tighten sunscreen rules amid concerns over SPF claims
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:37:20 CST
16:37:20 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) is developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen regulation and improve consumer confidence and the reliability of sun protection factor (SPF) claims.
The proposed reforms include strengthening sunscreen testing requirements, setting quality requirements for specific ingredients and limiting the SPF claims that cosmetic sunscreens can make, according to a TGA statement released Tuesday.
The agency said it will also review good manufacturing practice guidance to clarify expectations and responsibilities and support continued confidence in the quality and performance of sunscreen products in Australia.
The reforms follow a public consultation held from March to May that received almost 120 responses from industry, testing laboratories, health professionals, consumer groups, academia and other stakeholders.
Australia has the highest incidence of skin cancer in the world, the TGA said, adding that the primary objective of sunscreen regulation was to ensure product quality, safety and efficacy in protecting consumers from harmful ultraviolet radiation, and to reduce the incidence and impact of skin cancer.
David Whiteman, a distinguished scientist at Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, backed reforms to improve the rigor and transparency of sunscreen testing and review manufacturing practices, following reports that some sunscreens failed to meet their labelled SPF in independent tests, shaking public confidence.
The TGA said further consultation on SPF labeling would take place before progressing with any proposed changes. ■

China confirms identities of 8 more volunteer soldiers killed in Korean War
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:37:08 CST
16:37:08 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China has confirmed the identities of eight more Chinese People's Volunteers (CPV) martyrs who lost their lives during the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-1953), the Ministry of Veterans Affairs said on Wednesday.
This marks further progress in efforts to identify the remains of CPV martyrs repatriated from the Republic of Korea (ROK), the ministry said.
More than 70 years ago, the CPV crossed the Yalu River and fought alongside the army and civilians of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) against the ROK army and U.S.-led UN forces. China sent 2.9 million CPV soldiers to assist the DPRK during the war, of whom more than 360,000 were killed or injured. Most of the fallen CPV soldiers were buried on the Korean Peninsula.
According to an agreement between China and the ROK signed in late 2013, the two sides consult every year on the handover of remains of Chinese soldiers found in the ROK.
Since 2014, China and the ROK have completed 13 consecutive handovers involving the remains of 1,023 CPV martyrs.
In recent years, China has intensified efforts to identify the remains of CPV martyrs, including the creation of a DNA database for martyrs and their relatives, offering solid technical and data support to help more families find their missing loved ones.
To date, the identities of 44 of the martyrs have been confirmed and their relatives have been located. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For biotechnology graduate Ng Boon Ful, choosing the right educational institution can lay the foundation for high-quality learning and a successful career, especially amid rapid technological development.
With a thirst for multidisciplinary knowledge combining biology, chemistry, physics and even oceanography, Ng chose Xiamen University Malaysia, a renowned and highly regarded name in the sciences. He shared these thoughts with Xinhua on the sidelines of his recent graduation ceremony.
"Marine biotechnology is different and unique compared with programs related to marine science at other universities," he said, explaining that the field usually focuses on marine science in general or marine agriculture.
"This marine biotechnology course also allowed me to learn a greater variety of knowledge... This is quite a unique program that is very hard to find at other universities in Malaysia," he said, adding that he would recommend it to others interested in the field.
Ng noted that the university also gave him access to a valuable exchange program with China, providing him with access to a variety of specialized equipment and broadening the scope of his education to include marine chemistry, environmental science and other aspects of the field. "When I participated in the study exchange programs at Xiamen University and in China, I was very impressed," he said.
The university held the first ceremony of its eighth convocation on Oct. 10, with a total of 1,677 students from 23 undergraduate and seven postgraduate programs graduating at this convocation, including 978 local Malaysian students and 699 international students.
Among those in attendance were the Chief Executive Officer of the Malaysian Qualifications Agency, Mohammad Shatar Sabran, and Xiamen University President Prof. Hu Wenping.
In his remarks to the graduates, Hu reminded them of the importance not only of academic qualifications but also of growing as human beings with a broad global outlook to better prepare them for the rapidly changing world they will be entering as employees.
"What Xiamen provides is precisely a multicultural environment, where students from more than 50 countries and regions learn and interact... Years of multicultural immersion have taught you to understand differences, respect diversity, and collaborate responsibly across cultures. What this experience has given you is not just a broad perspective, but also the ability to live, work, and create with people from different cultural backgrounds," he said.
For his part, Mohammad Shatar urged the graduates to adopt a view that will help them build bridges as they continue their careers, whether locally or abroad, and to use what they have learned to build lasting bonds: "You are graduating from a university that represents something bigger: a bridge. A bridge between Malaysia and China. A bridge between East and West. A bridge between cultures. A bridge between knowledge and opportunity. And increasingly, a bridge between education and the future," he said.
The university welcomed its first batch of students in 2016, and over the past decade it has made remarkable progress, with the campus hosting more than 10,800 students from 53 countries and regions. The strength of the university has made its graduates favored not only by Chinese companies and their overseas branches but also by international companies seeking to expand into the Asian market. ■

16:35:14 KST

Drones attacked the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, Tula region, Russia, which supplies components for the production of explosives. A fire broke out at the facility.
The monitoring resource Exilenova+ reported on this.
According to an analysis of publicly released footage conducted by Militarnyi, the ammonia production unit AM-70 may have been hit.
According to OSINT Varta, Novomoskovsk Azot is one of Russia’s largest chemical enterprises and is part of the EuroChem Group. The plant specializes in producing ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, methanol, and other chemical products.
The facility also produces nitric acid and ammonium nitrate, which are used not only in civilian industry but also to manufacture explosives and ammunition.
Between February 2022 and September 2024, Novomoskovsk Azot supplied nearly 5,000 tonnes of nitric acid to the Sverdlov Plant in Dzerzhinsk, Nizhny Novgorod region.
The facility produces RDX and HMX, explosives used in military munitions.
Drone attacks have repeatedly targeted Novomoskovsk Azot. In particular, on June 14, 2026, a strike destroyed one of its production workshops and damaged ammonia production units. A second attack took place on June 26.

“If the new member states follow our rules, they will not even feel them,” she said. “But if they will go against them, then those safeguards will bite hard. So this is the main philosophy of these new safeguards.”

In addition to problems with democratic fundamentals such as an independent judiciary, Serbia has been held back in its bid to join the EU by shortcomings in its “strategic alignment in the field of foreign and security policy,” Kos said.

Netanyahu bloc leads partial count but lacks majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:31:13 UTC
16:31:13 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to his supporters at Likud party headquarters in Jerusalem after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo)
The camp of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ahead of his rival’s opposition bloc but still short of a majority on Oct. 28, as Arab parties secured historic gains in the key elections.
After turnout reached nearly 78 percent, its highest level since 1999, voters delivered their verdict on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who has steered the country sharply to the right and launched a series of wars in response to Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Polls estimated voter turnout among Arab citizens of Israel at around 80 percent.
Following the vote, both Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot vowed to form a government despite neither being projected to win a majority.
With 84.5 percent of ballots counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was shown to have 54 of the 120 seats in the parliament.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc had 49 seats and the country’s non-aligned Arab parties had 17.
The partial results are likely to change as more votes are counted.
Exit polls had shown that Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc were neck-and-neck with Netanyahu’s hard-right camp, with both winning about 51 seats, well away from the threshold for a majority.
The strongest gains went to Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.
The partial results suggest that Eisenkot’s bloc would have enough seats for a majority if it entered into a coalition agreement with the Arab parties, something most of its members expressed reluctance to do on the campaign trail.
But Yair Golan, the head of Israel’s main left-wing party, which is part of Eisenkot’s camp, called for precisely that on Oct. 28.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said on X. “We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens.”
Eisenkot had said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers, echoing the position of Netanyahu, who has suggested a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.
Arab lawmakers could also give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes on an ad hoc basis, enabling him to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition.
A lack of clear majority for either camp could mean weeks spent trying to cobble together coalitions, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.
A stalemate could in the immediate term benefit Netanyahu, who would remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
Full results are expected by Oct. 29 evening or Oct. 30 morning.
Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention center called for a “strong government of the right” and said the “Jewish and Zionist majority must unite.”
The 77-year-old prime minister, who has governed Israel on and off for nearly two decades, was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on Oct. 28 that his endorsement of Netanyahu had helped “a lot.”

The Swedish banking group Swedbank plans to cut about 500 jobs across its operations, including around 100 in the Baltic states, as part of a broader restructuring that could lead to further layoffs as artificial intelligence advances, the bank’s Estonian chief executive said.
Olavi Lepp, chairman of the management board and CEO of Swedbank Estonia, told Estonian public broadcaster ERR that the group was reducing its workforce while reorganising operations and investing in business development.
Swedbank employs more than 6,000 people across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and the planned cuts will affect about 100 of them, Lepp said. Nearly 500 positions will be eliminated across the group as a whole.
The bank said it was offering existing employees opportunities to move into different roles during the restructuring, although not everyone would be able to make the transition.
“Naturally, in the process, we are also offering existing employees the opportunity to retrain for other roles, but this does not suit everyone and, unfortunately, layoffs are also needed,” Lepp said.
He explained that the restructuring followed a period of exceptionally high profitability several years ago, when the bank decided to increase investment in information technology development and projects involving data modelling.
With profitability now back at more normal levels, the bank no longer needs as many employees, he said.
“Today, when profitability is at normal levels, we do not need as many people,” Lepp said, adding that maintaining the same workforce made little sense when the bank was no longer carrying out large-scale development projects.

Live: Australia begins day two at crease after Starc blitz flattens South Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:30:17 UTC
16:30:17 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 11:00 pm, Final score, IAW 117, AAW 4/121
Josh Inglis and Alex Carey's unbeaten stand helps Australia take control of Cape Town Test against South Africa
An unbeaten 145-run partnership between Josh Inglis and Alex Carey has put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town.
Inglis finished day two unbeaten on 85 while Carey finished 51 not out as Australia took a first innings lead into stumps, finishing the day's play on 4-330, one run ahead of South Africa's first innings total.
Carey and Inglis counterattacked sensationally in the final session, keeping South Africa wicketless after tea while also successfully negotiating 10 overs of the second new ball before stumps.
It was a stark contrast to South Africa's efforts against the second new ball late on day one.
The day's play began with Australia's inexperienced batting line-up needing to prove itself after the bowlers' terrific response to end day one.
Australia's new opening pair of Travis Head and Matt Renshaw looked assured against the new ball, putting together 58 for the first wicket before Head was bowled for 41 after an inside edge onto his stumps off the bowling of Simon Harmer.
Head's dismissal brought the under-fire Marnus Labuschagne to the crease and his torturous innings lasted just five deliveries before he nicked Harmer to slip for a duck.
Harmer's double-strike brought about fears that South Africa might once again run through the Australian batting line-up, but the opposite ensued.
Cam Green, batting at number four in Steve Smith's absence, showed just what his absence had denied Australia in a crucial stand alongside Renshaw.
The pair each survived scares en-route to a 126-run partnership that spanned the majority of the middle session.
Gerald Coetzee thought he had Green caught at slip on 22 but the third umpire deemed that the ball had not carried to Harmer, much to South Africa's dismay.
Six overs later, Harmer had a massive LBW shout against Renshaw, which was given not out on the field when Renshaw was on 49.
South Africa reviewed and the on-field decision was upheld with ball tracking showing the ball would've only clipped the bails.
Renshaw looked nailed on for a century before he tried to uppercut Marco Jansen and was caught behind for 74, with that decision also bizarrely given not out on the field before being overturned following a successful South African review.
Jansen then doubled up by removing Green for 65 as a part of a devilish five-over spell before tea that saw him register figures of 2-3.
Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day two as it happened.

Jansen rises to number one in ICC all rounder rankings
Marco Jansen has had some series.
With the bat he got scores of 26 and 35 in Durban, taking match figures of 4-113.
Then, in Gqeberha he added 85 runs and a brilliant 5-33.
His second consecutive half ton yesterday was full of quality and helped dig the South Africans out of a hole that was threatening to collapse in on themselves.
That was his fifth Test half century and, although he averages just 25.66 with the bat, he is fast becoming one of the best all rounders in world cricket - and that's not counting some of his fielding.
In fact, he is officially the number one all rounder, according to the latest ICC rankings (and slightly less objectively, by Dale Steyn).
Jansen has taken over top spot from Ravindra Jadeja, knocking the Indian star off the top for the first time in four years.
He has also climbed to the top of the Test bowling rankings, just ahead of Mitch Starc.
In the 23 Tests that he has played, Jansen's bowling average is 20.80.
He has taken 99 Test wickets.
Given the series he is having, don't count him out bringing up his century in the next few hours...

Starc speaks ahead of action on day two
Mitchell Starc is speaking to Mark Howard on Fox Cricket before the beginning of play on day two.
Starc explains how Australia was able to get itself back into the contest after a nightmare opening session yesterday.
"We put the first two hours out of our mind, I think," he said.
"The wicket didn't do what we expected, I suppose. In Cape Town you expect a bit more pace in the wicket, it had a bit of that tennis ball bounce.
"We had to reassess at lunch. That [short ball tactic] is a ploy we can go to, we've got three tall men, four when Greeny is bowling.
"After lunch we were what we expected of ourselves.
"It wasn't a lot [of discussions at lunch time], to be fair. A few little individual discussions. I saw one or two little conversations with Ronnie and James Franklin.
"We've played a lot of cricket, so it doesn't take much to reassess, which I think is a feature of our group, being able to problem solve on the go."

I've seen this come up as well, and it it is an interesting talking point.

16:30:00 KST

When the Ostrogoths besieged Rome in 537 AD, their first military act was to cut the aqueducts. Eleven gravity-fed channels supplied the city with up to a million cubic meters of water per day, more than enough to sustain a population of over a million, fill the public baths, and scour the sewers. Without the aqueducts, Rome became a fortified enclosure around a contaminated river, proving that water was essential to the city's existence.
Unlike land, which can be fenced off, or oil, which can be stored, water is a resource that nobody can fully own, yet everyone depends on. It moves through aquifers, across borders, and down rivers. The Romans were cognizant of this fact; as the aqueducts constituted public infrastructure, the water flowing into fountains was accessible to all. Frontinus, the administrator who oversaw Rome's water system in the first century AD, documented every allocation, every illegal connection, and every abuse of the system with the rigor of someone who understood that water management was a civic act. Architecture, in this sense, has always had the capacity to make water a common good, and equally, by the same means, a privilege.
Upstream and downstream are positions in a watershed that determine, with the precision of topography, who absorbs the consequences of decisions made. Architecture has always known how to work with gravity; what it has been slower to acknowledge is that gravity is, also, political.
Related Article
Unearthing the Ground: Architecture and the Politics of Waste
The Dam
In 1997, Jiang Zemin, the fourth paramount leader of China, presided over the ceremony marking the completion of the Yangtze River diversion. Jiang is reported to have said that "man must conquer nature," a motto that came to stand for the project. The main wall was completed in 2006, is 2.3 kilometers long and about 181 meters tall, and the reservoir took years to fill. By the time it reached its final height in 2010, it had submerged 13 cities, 140 towns, and 1,350 villages, along with more than 1,300 known archaeological sites.
The Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric project ever built, and also the largest resettlement project in history. The dam generates enough electricity to supply a significant portion of China's eastern seaboard. But at the cost of that generation, 1.3 million people were resettled along the reservoir's edge, among farming communities in Chongqing and Hubei whose land disappeared underwater, whose replacement plots on the steep hillsides above the waterline were too eroded to cultivate, and whose promised compensation was frequently absorbed. The project protected some 15 million people downstream from catastrophic flooding while displacing over a million upstream.
This is the architecture of the dam, not the engineering of its face or the spectacle of its spillways, but the territorial logic it enacts. Every impoundment creates a geography of beneficiaries and a geography of renunciation. The dam does not distribute its consequences according to need or merit but according to position in the landscape, which is to say according to existing power. Architecture is not an aesthetic vessel but an apparatus that organizes and hierarchizes bodies in space, and the dam is among the most explicit examples of that hierarchy. The history of modern architecture is full of admiration for large hydraulic infrastructure, the precision of its engineering, the scale of its ambition, and the image of civilization imposed on natural systems. But what is consistently omitted is the other side of the reservoir, the disappearing towns, the arable land, the displaced communities. Architecture, like any discipline, produces its objects through the questions it chooses to ask; when it asks how a dam stands, how its spillways perform, how its mass meets the landscape, it is also choosing not to ask what the landscape was before, and whose it was. Hydrology has models for sediment displacement; ecology has frameworks for habitat loss; displacement studies have methodologies for tracking resettled populations. Architecture, which claims the organization of space as its core competence, has so far known what it erases without learning how to work with what remains.
The Aswan High Dam, completed in Egypt in 1970, displaced an estimated 100,000 Nubians from their ancestral territory along the Nile; something described as epistemic, erasing a culture that had already survived one previous displacement by the Aswan Low Dam, built by British colonialists in 1902. The dam was Egypt's symbol of postcolonial modernity and industrialization; the Nubians who lost their villages to its reservoir were, in this sense, the cost of someone else's progress.
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile reopens that history from the other side. When Ethiopia began construction in 2011, it broke a water allocation framework that had stood since the colonial era, a 1929 treaty (renegotiated in 1959) that guaranteed Egypt an annual supply of 55.5 billion cubic meters of Nile water and gave Cairo effective veto power over any upstream infrastructure project. The treaty was signed without Ethiopia's participation and allocated, between Egypt and Sudan, the entirety of a river whose largest tributary (the Blue Nile, contributing roughly 85 percent of the Nile's total flow) originates in the Ethiopian highlands. Despite supplying most of the water, Ethiopia was entitled to use less than one percent of it. The colonial framework had, in effect, built a legal structure that controlled the river's benefits as surely as any physical impoundment.
The GERD, now the largest dam in Africa, represents Ethiopia's assertion that this arrangement was a colonial artifact. Egypt responds that the dam constitutes an existential threat to its water security, as 98 percent of its renewable water resources come from the Nile. Without a guaranteed minimum annual flow, agriculture and electricity generation would both fail. Two irreconcilable claims about the same river, both grounded in genuine need. Unlike the communities displaced by the Three Gorges, who were at least nominally subjects of the state that displaced them, eligible for compensation however poorly administered, Egypt has no legal mechanism to compel a sovereign upstream neighbor.
Day Zero
In January 2018, the city of Cape Town announced that it was approaching a point when dam levels would fall below 13.5 percent of capacity, and the municipality would be forced to shut off taps to most of the city's 3.7 million residents. The Day Zero announcement made international headlines as evidence of a new kind of urban catastrophe: a major city in the modern era on the verge of running out of water. By July, strong winter rains had pushed dam levels back above 50 percent, and the crisis was declared over.
Across cities in the Global South, water infrastructure was designed for populations smaller, less dense, and distributed according to colonial planning logics that reserved formal services for some neighborhoods and withheld them from others. When those cities grew informally, they absorbed millions of residents into settlements that accumulated on the periphery. The infrastructure did not expand to meet this new condition; without water pressure, without metered connections, without the redundancy that makes a system resilient. By 2018, the informal settlements of Khayelitsha and Mitchell's Plain were receiving water through communal standpipes delivering less than 25 liters per person per day (the Day Zero ration the city was proposing as an emergency measure for the formal city).
During apartheid, water and sanitation services were divided across 25 separate municipalities, each serving a racially designated population; the townships received what remained after white residential areas had been supplied, and the pipes that reached them were poorly maintained by design. When apartheid ended in 1994, the physical infrastructure did not disappear. By 2018, formal households consumed 66 percent of the city's water supply. The informal settlements, where 14 percent of Cape Town's households lived, used 4 percent. The restrictions that arrived with the drought fell equally on a household using 300 liters a day and a household already using 30.
The anthropologist Nikhil Anand, studying Mumbai's water infrastructure, called this condition hydraulic citizenship, the capacity of residents to be recognized by city agencies through legitimate water connections. Those who are not connected are not simply underserved; they are, in the administrative logic of the municipality, not yet fully urban. The geographer Erik Swyngedouw, working across Guayaquil and other cities in the Global South, argues that water does not flow according to need but through networks of power, technology, and meaning, making scarcity a socially produced condition. In Guayaquil, where 600,000 people lacked easy access to potable water while the city sat on abundant resources, poor neighborhoods relied on private tanker trucks charging prices that consumed a disproportionate share of household income. The struggle for water in cities like Guayaquil or Cape Town is, in Swyngedouw's terms, not just for the right to water but for the right to the city itself.
The Border
The political theorist Stuart Elden argues that we have been thinking about territory in the wrong dimension; as area rather than volume, as a flat surface to be divided rather than a three-dimensional space that extends above and below the ground, into the sub-soil and the sub-marine. China is doing exactly that in the South China Sea, as it is not claiming a line on a map but constructing a volume; dredging material from the seabed, raising it above the surface, and then asserting that the column of space above it, and the water around it, now belongs to a different political jurisdiction. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) was written for a world of surfaces. The artificial island operates in depth. Modern territorial law, including the legal architecture of the sea, was built on the assumption of surface (the line on the map, the continental shelf). But what is missing is depth; the political control over what lies above and below simultaneously.
Between December 2013 and October 2015, China dredged sand and coral from the seabed of the Spratly Islands and deposited it on seven submerged reefs, creating close to 3,000 acres of new land. What China built was not, in Elden's terms, a surface but a volume. It extracted material from the seabed, raised it above the waterline, and then asserted that the column of water and airspace surrounding it now fell within a different political jurisdiction. The legal frameworks governing the sea were written for a world of surfaces; the artificial island operates in depth, manufacturing the ground on which its claims would stand from the ground that was beneath the water. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs described the construction as aimed at optimizing functions and improving living and working conditions.
Under UNCLOS, artificial islands generate no territorial sea of their own. The 2016 arbitral tribunal ruling, brought by the Philippines, found that China's nine-dash line claim had no legal basis, and that China had violated the Philippines' sovereign rights. But the pattern is consistent: build first, dispute later, and rely on the fact that no enforcement mechanism exists capable of removing what has already been constructed. Water, across all the cases in this article, has been directed, contained, rationed, and manufactured into territory by infrastructure. The architecture is irreversible in a way that the legal argument is not, which is precisely the point.

Source: Zelenskyy in a comment to the press, as reported by Ukrinform
Quote: "We buy a lot [of weapons] from the US. Europe paid for them, everything arrived, and everything was fine. But some things are a real challenge, especially Patriot missiles. In 2026, we've been receiving an average of 12 missiles a month."

He said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has signed off on a package of 12 missiles, but approval is still needed for a further 23 missiles that Ukraine has sourced from other countries.
Quote: "The US has a package of 12 missiles, and he's signed off on it. That's great. But we've used 35 just this month. The issue now is getting approval for another 23 that I've secured from other sources."
Details: Zelenskyy also said he had asked US President Donald Trump during a meeting in New York to approve a "winter package" of missiles. He said he had specified how many missiles Ukraine needed and told Trump that if the request were approved, Ukraine would not strike oil refineries.
When Trump asked where the missiles would come from, Zelenskyy named the countries that have them. According to Zelenskyy, Trump replied that the US would do everything it could to help, but it also needs missiles itself and has limited supplies.
Background: On 26 October, Zelenskyy announced that Kyiv has been waiting for nearly a month for Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems. He said he had instructed his team to discuss the matter with the US again.

Malaysia foils $12M AI chip smuggling attempt at Kuala Lumpur airport

07:28:14 UTC
16:28:14 KST

Malaysia has foiled an attempt to smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips through Kuala Lumpur airport in a case worth more than $12 million, customs officials said on Wednesday.
The bust was the fifth case this year involving a syndicate smuggling advanced AI chips, with the total estimated value exceeding $24 million, officials said.
The Southeast Asian nation, an emerging data-centre hub, is seeking to prevent itself from being used as a transit point for restricted chips destined for other countries.
A team inspecting Kuala Lumpur airport’s free trade zone this month seized 30 server units containing advanced AI chips worth 49.5 million ringgit ($12.1 million), airport customs director Aspalila Ag Tuah said.
Malaysia tightened export and transshipment controls on US chips last year, requiring strategic trade permits and advance notification when there is suspicion of misuse or diversion.
“The servers were declared as ‘electronic components’ to avoid detection by the authorities,” Aspalila told a news conference.
“Initial investigations found that the servers were to be re-exported to another country in Asia,” she added.
The syndicate used Malaysia as a transit point to avoid restrictions during the export of the servers to their next destination, she said.
Aspalila said the servers came from “an Asian country”, declining to specify their exact origin, where the chips were manufactured or where they were headed.
“The case is still under further investigation and the company that facilitated the shipment has been called in to assist investigations,” she said.
The United States has tightened restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports through Malaysia and Thailand in an effort to curb their diversion to China.
Malaysia has also launched several investigations, including one into how servers containing US-made Nvidia chips destined for Singapore ended up in Malaysia.
Authorities said at the time they had found no evidence of illicit trade in advanced semiconductors.

‘The Story of the Panda Bears’ to be staged in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:26:56 UTC
16:26:56 KST

‘The Story of the Panda Bears’ to be staged in Tehran
TEHRAN- Iranian director Maryam Amini is set to stage “The Story of the Panda Bears Told by a Saxophonist Who Has a Girlfriend in Frankfurt,” a play by Romanian-French playwright Matei Vișniec, at the Medea Hall of Tehran Theater.
The production, translated into Persian by Hanieh Rajabi and produced by Vahid Salekfard, will begin performances on Thursday.
Iranian actors Khayyam Vaqar Kashani and Ghazaleh Akrami will perform in the two-character play, which explores an unusual encounter between a man and a woman, unfolding over nine nights and blurring the boundaries between reality, memory and imagination.
The story begins when a man wakes up to find a woman beside him whom he does not recognize. Despite the uncertainty surrounding their encounter, he asks her to stay with him for nine nights. The woman eventually agrees, and the two embark on a strange and intimate journey that gradually raises questions about their identities, their relationship and the nature of their shared experience.
Rather than following a conventional dramatic structure, the play develops through a series of encounters between its two central characters. Their conversations and interactions gradually reveal fragments of their inner worlds, leaving audiences to interpret the events and the meaning of their connection.
The play’s surreal atmosphere and poetic dialogue are characteristic of Vișniec’s theatrical writing, which frequently combines elements of the absurd with reflections on human relationships, loneliness and the instability of reality. In “The Story of the Panda Bears,” the seemingly simple premise of a man asking a stranger to remain with him becomes a framework for exploring the need for companionship and the uncertainties that shape human encounters.
The nine-night structure also provides the drama with a sense of anticipation, as each meeting adds another layer to the relationship between the man and the woman. The audience is invited to piece together the significance of their exchanges while confronting the ambiguity at the heart of the narrative.
Born in Romania in 1956, Vișniec is a playwright, poet and journalist who has established an international reputation for his works exploring the absurdities of modern life, political realities and the human condition. He moved to France in 1987 and has since written extensively for the stage, with his plays translated and performed in numerous countries.
His dramatic works often employ fragmented narratives, symbolic imagery and unconventional situations to examine questions of identity, communication and existence. His writing combines philosophical concerns with theatrical experimentation, allowing directors to approach his texts through a range of interpretations.
“The Story of the Panda Bears Told by a Saxophonist Who Has a Girlfriend in Frankfurt” will remain on stage at the Medea Hall of Tehran Theater for a month.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Japan will impose definitive anti-dumping duties on nickel-added cold-rolled stainless steel products from Taiwan and China for five years starting Oct. 31, the Japanese government said Tuesday.
The relevant ordinance is set to be published Friday, with the duties taking effect the following day and remaining in force through Oct. 30, 2031, per CNA.
According to the Japan Iron and Steel Federation, duties on Taiwanese products range from 3.6% to 20.1%, while those on Chinese products range from 27.7% to 42.1%. The rates are unchanged from the provisional duties imposed in July.
The products, which contain nickel and are cold-rolled, are valued for their corrosion resistance and durability, per CNA. They are used in automotive exterior components and exhaust systems, railway carriages, and household items such as cutlery.
Japan’s Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry launched the anti-dumping investigation on July 22, 2025, following an application from Japanese steelmakers. Provisional duties took effect on July 9, 2026, after the investigation found evidence of dumped imports and material injury to Japan’s domestic industry.
After reviewing the investigation’s findings, the Council on Customs, Tariff, Foreign Exchange, and Other Transactions recommended definitive duties on Oct. 19. The government approved the five-year measure to protect Japan’s domestic steel industry.

Tehran exhibition explores Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra’s legacy through art

Tehran exhibition explores Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra’s legacy through art
TEHRAN – An exhibition bringing together calligraphy, traditional crafts, visual arts and religious performances to celebrate the legacy of Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA), the daughter of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), opened at Tehran’s Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex on Monday.
Titled “The Wisdom of Zahra Was Imprinted on the World,” the event showcases works inspired by the spiritual teachings and cultural heritage associated with Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA), a revered figure in Islam whose life is widely associated with piety, compassion, modesty and devotion to her family.
The opening ceremony was attended by the CEO of the Rudaki Foundation Mohammad Allahyari Foumani, Director General of the Visual Arts Office Aydin Mahdizadeh, Rudaki Foundation Deputy for Artistic Creation Amirabbas Setayeshgar, Deputy for Coordination of Halls and Centers Reza Mardani, and Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex Director Seyyed Mohsen Hosseini, along with artists and cultural figures.
Organized by the Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex, the program brought together 110 artists from different disciplines. Visitors have the opportunity to view exhibitions, attend artistic workshops and speak with participating artists about their creative approaches and the religious concepts behind their works, the Rudaki Foundation reported.
One of the main sections is an exhibition dedicated to Hadith al-Kisa, a narration describing an occasion when Prophet Muhammad gathered his close family members under a cloak. In Islamic tradition, the narration is associated with the special status of the Prophet’s household, known as the Ahl al-Bayt. Seventy calligraphers participated in the exhibition by writing the Arabic text of the narration and its Persian translation.
Another 20 calligraphers contributed works featuring Ziyarat Ashura, a devotional text associated with Imam Hussein (AS), the third Shia Imam and the grandson of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
The opening ceremony also included the unveiling of a book of Ziyarat Ashura featuring the contributions of the participating calligraphers.
A separate workshop, held under the event’s title, brought together 15 artists working in engraving, qalamkari (traditional Persian textile printing), painting, miniature painting and calligraphy. The artists created works drawing on Fatemi teachings and the artistic traditions through which religious ideas have been expressed and preserved across generations.
The exhibition also features a section on modesty and hijab, supervised by artist Zohreh Abdollahi, exploring women’s identity and dress through an artistic lens. A performance by the Daughters of the Revolution choir added a ceremonial element to the program.
Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA) holds a central place in Islamic history and devotion. As the daughter of Prophet Muhammad and Khadija, she is revered by Muslims, particularly in the Shia tradition, as a model of faith, dignity and moral integrity. She was the wife of Imam Ali (AS) and the mother of Imam Hassan (AS) and Imam Hussein (AS). Her life and legacy have inspired centuries of religious literature, poetry, calligraphy and other art forms.
Events celebrating Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA) are often held in connection with Fatemiyeh, a period of mourning and commemoration observed by many Shia Muslims in remembrance of her death. The occasion provides an opportunity to reflect on her place in Islamic tradition and the values associated with her life.
The exhibition’s combination of sacred texts, traditional crafts and contemporary artistic expression offers a setting for exploring these themes through Iran’s cultural heritage.
The exhibition will remain open to visitors for four days, through Friday, October 30.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nearly three-quarters of Taiwanese view the Chinese Communist Party unfavorably, including more than half of KMT supporters, according to a survey released Tuesday by pollster Tai Li-an (戴立安).
The Taiwan Public Sentiment Survey found that 73.5% of respondents held an unfavorable view of the CCP, while 8.9% expressed a favorable opinion and 17.5% gave no clear answer, per Liberty Times. The unfavorable rating was unchanged from September, while the favorable rating rose 1.4 percentage points.
Among respondents who leaned toward the opposition pan-blue camp, 53.7% viewed the CCP unfavorably and 30.2% favorably. KMT supporters were similarly negative, with 50.3% viewing the CCP unfavorably and 34% favorably.

Unfavorable ratings exceeded 75% among women, respondents aged 20 to 49, people with university-level education or higher, residents of Taichung, Changhua, Nantou, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and pan-green supporters.
The survey also found that 66.1% of respondents who considered Taiwan's economic situation poor viewed the CCP unfavorably, according to Liberty Times. Among those dissatisfied with President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德) performance, 60.4% viewed the CCP unfavorably, while 19.4% viewed it favorably.
Tai designed and analyzed the survey, which Beacon Market Research conducted from Oct. 20 to 22, interviewing 1,075 adults aged 20 and older across Taiwan's 22 cities and counties. The poll included 696 landline and 379 mobile telephone interviews, with a maximum sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) warned Wednesday that legislation covering health insurance premiums for many seniors could leave some of the poorest elderly people worse off.
Speaking before a legislative hearing, Shih raised two concerns about the changes, CNA reported. He said they could deprive vulnerable seniors of medical subsidies and undermine the National Health Insurance, per Knews.
The legislature passed amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act on Oct. 16, backed by the opposition KMT and TPP. The changes would require the central government to cover health insurance premiums for people aged 65 and older whose income falls below the tax filing threshold or whose income tax rate is below 20%, subject to an income cap, per Rti.
Shih's first concern was that the amendments remove provisions requiring local governments to help seniors who cannot afford medical expenses. These include patient copayments and treatments not covered by health insurance, per Knews.
Under the previous rules, assistance could also reach seniors whose average household income was between 1.5 and 2.5 times the government's minimum living standard. Shih said these people could lose financial support even if the government pays their insurance premiums, per TVBS News.
The health ministry warned that the changes could affect subsidies for dentures, artificial lenses used in cataract surgery, and heart stents.
Shih's second concern was that the amendments conflict with the principle that people should contribute to health insurance according to their ability to pay. He said the government should focus assistance on those in financial need rather than exempt people based largely on age, per CNA.
The ministry estimates that about 83% of seniors aged 65 and older would qualify for the premium subsidy. Shih has warned that such broad coverage could place additional pressure on government finances and threaten the insurance system's long-term sustainability, per ETtoday.

Antalya agenda: COP31 can turn zero waste from a theme into a delivery discipline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:25:47 UTC
16:25:47 KST

Every climate summit is measured by what it leaves behind.
When governments gather in Antalya from November 9 to 20 for COP31, the annual UN climate conference, the real measure of success will be whether commitments begin to show up in cities, markets, landfills and household bins.
Waste is one of the places where that test is most visible, and where Türkiye has something concrete to offer.
Alongside COP31, governments will meet as the governing body of the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol, while the climate process’s two subsidiary bodies, which provide scientific advice and oversee implementation, hold their 65th sessions during the first week.
Türkiye will host the conference and lead its Action Agenda, the track that brings governments together with cities, businesses and civil society.
Under a Türkiye-Australia partnership model, Australia’s Chris Bowen has been appointed President of Negotiations, leading the talks in consultation with Türkiye.
The negotiating agenda is long.
Under the Paris Agreement, governments are due to address several programmes, including the Global Stocktake, the United Arab Emirates Just Transition Work Programme, the Sharm el-Sheikh mitigation work programme and further guidance on countries’ national climate plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
The list also includes support for transparency reporting under Article 13, the Global Goal on Adaptation, loss and damage, climate finance, and international cooperation under Article 6.
Several of these issues arrive in Antalya unresolved.
Work on making the Just Transition Work Programme operational was carried over from the previous technical session, the mitigation work programme faces a decision on whether it continues, and guidance on NDCs is back on the table.
The success of COP31 will therefore depend less on the breadth of its agenda than on whether it links negotiation to implementation.
Waste to action
The Presidency has framed the conference around dialogue, consensus and action, and has said it wants COP31 to turn commitments into measurable results. That is the right yardstick.
Zero waste belongs at the heart of that implementation effort, though precision matters.
Waste, circular economy and methane reduction are not standalone items on the formal negotiating agendas.
They are, however, explicitly part of the official COP31 Presidency Action Agenda, where zero waste is described as unlocking the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular-economy solutions.
The Presidency’s thematic calendar also designates November 11 as Zero Waste Day, coinciding with the first day of the Leaders Summit.
This is more than a technicality. Negotiations produce collective decisions, rules and guidance.
The Action Agenda is where governments, cities, businesses and civil society turn those frameworks into projects and partnerships on the ground.
Rather than competing with mitigation, adaptation or finance for attention, zero waste can help make all three tangible.
The numbers support this. According to the Global Methane Assessment of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), landfills and wastewater account for about 20 per cent of human-caused methane emissions.
In 2026, UNEP also reported that food loss and waste generate 8-10 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, and that food waste alone accounts for up to 14 per cent of global methane emissions.
Preventing waste, separating it at source, managing organic waste properly and keeping resources in use are near-term climate measures, not only matters of cleanliness or recycling.
Waste also offers a bridge to national climate plans. The UN climate secretariat's NDC synthesis report, published in October 2025, covered 64 new plans, representing about 30 per cent of global emissions in 2019.
The UNFCCC itself cautioned that such a limited sample could not support wide-ranging global conclusions.
That caution is worth heeding: implementation claims at COP31 will need to hold up to scrutiny, with figures that are clear about their coverage and method.
The same rigour should apply to transparency.
Waste and methane initiatives presented at COP31 should be designed so that their emissions impact can be measured, reported and connected to national implementation systems, so that they add up to more than a series of isolated showcases.
This is where the Zero Waste Foundation has a clear and meaningful role.
Its president, Samed Agirbas, has been appointed COP31 Climate High-Level Champion, with a mandate to work with business, financial institutions, cities and regions, and civil society.
The role sits outside the formal negotiations, in which the Foundation itself holds no mandate, but it links the Foundation’s experience directly to the actors who must deliver COP31’s commitments.
UNEP has acknowledged the foundation’s role in global climate action.
At home, the foundation follows a local-to-national model. Its Istanbul Zero Waste Week programme drew participation from all 39 districts of the city and more than 1,500 project applications from public institutions, local administrations, universities, NGOs, and the private sector.
In Antalya, a foundation workshop brought together roughly 400 participants from public institutions, local governments, universities, civil society, professional chambers and business.
They worked across 16 thematic tables on issues such as food waste, plastics, circular industry, finance and data. These figures come from the foundation’s own reporting, and they show the kind of stakeholder network that turns a summit theme into local action.
Antalya agenda
The opportunity for COP31 is practical.
Governments can connect waste and methane measures to their national climate plans. Cities can build credible project pipelines to prevent food waste, separate organic waste, and cut methane from landfills.
Businesses can redesign material flows, financiers can ask for measurable climate outcomes, and civil society can help programmes earn local legitimacy.
None of this replaces progress in the negotiations on finance, adaptation, loss and damage, a just transition or mitigation. It makes those goals easier to achieve.
Delegations should leave Antalya with a simple standard for zero waste climate action: measure what is avoided, finance what can scale, disclose what is delivered and link local projects to national commitments.
The Zero Waste Foundation and other non-state actors can contribute most by convening the institutions that run waste systems, direct investment, hold data and shape public participation, and by turning visibility into verifiable results.
The official Action Agenda provides a platform to build projects that cut methane, prevent waste, and strengthen circularity, and to hold each one to that standard.
COP31 can make zero waste a delivery discipline, not just a theme.

Russia is selling Africa dependence disguised as partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:25:41 UTC
16:25:41 KST

Russia is selling Africa dependence disguised as partnership
As African leaders gather in Moscow, the Kremlin is securing resources and protecting allied rulers while failing their people.
This week, Moscow will host the third Russia-Africa summit, bringing together African leaders as President Vladimir Putin seeks to expand Russia’s economic, military and political reach across the continent. Yet Russia’s growing influence has done far more to advance Moscow’s interests and protect allied rulers than to deliver the prosperity and security promised to ordinary Africans.
Putin is scheduled to cochair Thursday’s plenary session with Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, current chair of the African Union. Alongside the summit, a two-day economic and humanitarian forum will discuss investment, industrial production, food security, energy, technology and payment systems. Organisers have placed trade and investment at the centre of the programme with a new plan for 2027-2029 expected to advance what they call “mutually beneficial cooperation”.
On August 20, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova outlined plans for another substantial round of intergovernmental agreements and commercial contracts at the Moscow summit. The Sochi gathering in October 2019 produced 92 agreements, and Putin pledged to double annual trade to $40bn. Four years later, the July 2023 summit in St Petersburg yielded 161 more accords and a 2023-2026 action plan.
The economic results have not matched Moscow’s promises. As the 2023-2026 plan nears its conclusion, Russia’s own trade statistics expose the shortfall: Merchandise trade with Africa reached just $27.1bn in 2025 against Putin’s $40bn target.
The trade imbalance persisted into 2026 with Russia exporting $14bn in goods to Africa during the first eight months of the year while importing just $3.2bn.
Agricultural exports help explain Africa’s significant trade deficit with Russia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Russia shipped 10.2 million tonnes of wheat to Africa, with Egypt its largest agricultural customer. These supplies meet genuine food security needs, but exports of wheat and fertiliser benefit Russian producers more than they contribute to African industrial development.
Russia’s investment record exposes a substantial gap between agreements signed and projects completed. At the 2019 summit, fertiliser producer Uralchem and Angola’s Grupo Opaia agreed to build a $1.2bn ammonia and urea complex, scheduled to begin production in 2023, but Uralchem abandoned the venture that year.
Egypt offers clearer evidence of progress: Rosatom is building four nuclear reactors at El Dabaa, where more than 18,000 Egyptians are employed in their construction. But the project is being financed largely through a $25bn Russian loan that Egypt must repay with interest.
Even when Russian-backed projects advance, the contract terms determine who stands to benefit, who bears the financial risks and how public revenues will ultimately be shared. In the Republic of Congo, a proposed petroleum-products pipeline between Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville would give Russian interests 90 percent of the joint venture and Congo’s state oil company 10 percent with a 25-year concession and guaranteed transport tariffs.
In April, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said design work would begin this year with operations planned for 2029. Russian officials have also described the pipeline as a means of protecting petroleum exports from Western sanctions imposed following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s commercial ambitions are matched by a widening military footprint. On October 8, Sweden’s Defence Research Agency identified at least 57 Russian military and security agreements involving 39 African countries, although many remain limited in practice. Others facilitate training and access to military infrastructure.
Russia initially relied on the Wagner Group, a Kremlin-linked mercenary network, before transferring many operations to the Ministry of Defence-controlled Africa Corps with Wagner remaining active in the Central African Republic. Russian personnel provide direct combat assistance, training and protection to allied governments, particularly in Mali and the Central African Republic.
Nonetheless, Mali exposes the limits of Russia’s military assistance. Wagner fighters and Malian troops captured Kidal, a strategic northern city, in November 2023, only to lose it to separatist rebels in April 2026. On October 6, Russian-backed forces regained the city after an air campaign prompted the rebels to withdraw. Moscow has helped Mali win territory, but it has failed to deliver lasting security for Malians.
According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, Malian forces and Russia’s Africa Corps carried out 49 air strikes from April to August, killing 89 civilians. Human Rights Watch reported that on July 10, Africa Corps fighters killed nine people, including four children, and burned homes in Bombori, a village in central Mali’s Mopti region.
Other abuses include beatings, electric shocks and waterboarding of noncombatants detained by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps personnel at a military base in Sevare from May to August.
For civilians caught between insurgents and forces sent to defeat them, Moscow’s military assistance has brought more violence and no dependable protection.
At the same time, Russia has proved its value to allied rulers in the region.
On August 29, Russia’s Africa Corps helped General Abdourahamane Tiani crush a mutiny in Niger. Russian troops provided ground and aerial support, and Moscow’s ambassador confirmed their role. While Tiani’s government survived, Nigeriens remain without political parties or an election timetable, and civil liberties are severely restricted. The junta also stripped five more exiled critics of their nationality on September 17.
In the Central African Republic, Moscow has helped President Faustin-Archange Touadera, in power for 10 years, tighten his grip on the country. On March 5, Touadera personally thanked Putin, acknowledging that Russian security forces had made possible December’s presidential election, which secured his third term despite an opposition boycott.
Wagner mercenaries continue to protect Touadera’s government while political opponents face repression and journalists risk arrest. Russian fighters have carried out killings, torture and attacks against civilians.
For continued protection of Touadera’s government, Moscow reportedly demanded close to 14 million euros ($15.7m) a month to deploy Africa Corps in place of Wagner while Russian-linked companies continued profiting from the Central African Republic’s gold resources.
Moscow is also helping friendly rulers shape the information their citizens receive. In July, Russia’s state broadcaster RT signed a content-sharing agreement with Tafouk TV, the new channel run by the military governments of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.
Broadcasting from Bamako since September, the station promotes official military successes, often overlooking insurgent attacks, while local journalists face arrests, disappearances and censorship. Moscow’s campaign to shape African public opinion extends beyond state broadcasters. An April 3 investigation by France 24 uncovered nearly 650 pro-Russian articles placed in 35 West African media outlets from June to October 2024. Leaked documents listed payments of $250 to $700 per article with some outlets unaware that Russian operatives had arranged the placements.
Russian-linked efforts to shape African politics are not confined to news media. In July, an Angolan court convicted two Russians associated with Africa Politology, a political influence network with ties to the Kremlin, of terrorism and espionage. Prosecutors accused them of exploiting protests over fuel prices to incite antigovernment unrest and attempting to sway Angola’s 2027 election. Igor Ratchin received an 11-year prison sentence and Lev Lakshtanov eight years, but both denied the charges and appealed.
Russia’s expanding presence is entrenching a deeply unequal and destabilising relationship in which Moscow gains preferential access to African mineral resources, strengthens its military foothold and protects illiberal rulers.
Meanwhile, ordinary Africans are forced to endure insecurity, political repression and unfulfilled development commitments. Far from delivering shared prosperity, the Kremlin is exploiting Africa’s wealth and political vulnerabilities to advance its own economic and geopolitical interests.
No power, regardless of history, deserves exemptions.
In Moscow, Africa must demand of Russia the same standards it expects of the United States, Europe and China: fair trade, productive investment, respect for sovereignty and accountability for civilian abuses.
African lives matter, too.

Europe struggles to top up gas storage at four-year high prices ahead of winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:21:22 UTC
16:21:22 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. In late October, European countries continue to inject small volumes of gas into underground storage facilities (UGS) ahead of the cold season, despite prices hitting a four-year high, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Meanwhile, several countries have been net-withdrawing gas from European UGS facilities for the second consecutive week - with withdrawal volumes outstripping injections--signaling the gradual start of the heating season in the region.
To date, Europe has managed to inject only 75.5% of the gas volumes required for the upcoming winter, which amounts to 51 billion cubic meters.
As of October 26, European UGS facilities were 74.93% full, down from 82.9% a year earlier and 14.65 percentage points below the five-year average for this date. This remains the lowest level recorded for this date since monitoring began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold approximately 82.1 billion cubic meters of gas, which is 9.4 billion cubic meters less than last year and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that European gas inventories might fail to reach even the 75% mark, warning of a challenging autumn-winter season for the region.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas reserves. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU nations may only manage to fill their storage capacities to 70-75%, an all-time low for the start of a heating season.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is permitted under difficult filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must reach at least 68 billion cubic meters to meet the requirement for the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season. However, hoping for a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% this year.

Thirty hours of a ceasefire regime in Oleshky without a single incident. This was made possible, among other things, by constant communication between me and the Commissioner for Human Rights in the Russian Federation, Yana Lantratova. We remain in contact and coordinate the implementation of the agreements reached
The ombudsman separately expressed his gratitude to U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, "who personally devotes her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky." "Her direct involvement and coordination of the parties' efforts are an important component of this process," he emphasized.
"I also thank her entire team for its consistent support, constant communication, and all its efforts. Our common goal is to provide assistance to the civilian population of Oleshky and create conditions for the safe departure of those who need it. We continue to work. The most important things are people's lives and safety," Lubinets stated.
What is known about the humanitarian mission in Oleshky
Ukraine announced that, starting at 03:00 Kyiv time on October 27, a ceasefire regime would be introduced in a designated area of temporarily occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region. This is necessary to conduct a humanitarian operation, deliver aid to the city's residents, and prepare for the safe evacuation of the civilian population.
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov announced the start of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky on the morning of October 27.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets went to the site and will be responsible for coordinating the process.
Lubinets stated overnight: "Oleshky: the ceasefire regime has begun; the Ukrainian side is fulfilling its agreements."
The ceasefire regime will last from October 27 until 22:59 on November 1, said one of Ukraine's negotiators at the peace talks, Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia.
Meanwhile, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine called on citizens to rely exclusively on official reports regarding the humanitarian operation.

Pentagon chief holds talks with counterparts from India, Australia, South Korea, Japan in Philippines

Ahmad Adil
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held talks with his counterparts from India, Australia, Japan and South Korea on the sidelines of a meeting in the Philippines, according to official statements.
In a bilateral meeting, Hegseth and Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh “took stock of progress on operational coordination, information sharing, and defense industrial cooperation,” the Pentagon said in a statement.
The meeting took place in Cebu City, which is hosting the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ meeting through Thursday. The defense chiefs of the 11-member bloc will also hold separate summits with partner nations including the US, India, South Korea, and Australia as well as Japan.
China's Defense Minister Dong Jun skipped the summit, with the defense attache of China’s Embassy in Manila attending in his stead.
Hegseth and Singh also “exchanged views on areas for further collaboration and committed to expanding the U.S.-India major defense partnership in support of shared interests across the region.”
During his meeting with Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, the two leaders discussed ongoing initiatives to strengthen defense cooperation and the US-Australia alliance.
They “agreed on the need to swiftly execute force posture collaboration, including investments at Australian air force bases and investments to enhance combined logistics capacity,” the statement said.
The two leaders also “discussed opportunities to better coordinate on U.S. and Australian approaches to regional deterrence and support common-sense strategies to preserve a favorable balance of power in the Pacific.”
In his meeting with Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, Hegseth “reaffirmed the indispensable role of the U.S.-Japan Alliance in preserving peace and stability in the Pacific,” the Pentagon said.
The two leaders also discussed “efforts to strengthen deterrence through enhanced bilateral access, presence, and realistic training and exercises across Japan, including live-fire exercises.”
The Pentagon chief also met South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul.
The US-South Korea alliance “is built on peace through strength-ready forces, decisive capability, and combined lethality that deters aggression,” Hegseth wrote on US-based social media platform X.
“America stands with allies that are serious about their own defense,” he said.

Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:08:00 UTC
16:08:00 KST

Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
The metal is generating billions, but mining communities say basic services have failed to keep pace.
Mimosa, Zimbabwe – Zimbabwe’s platinum industry is generating billions of dollars, but residents in mining communities say roads, schools, water and other basic services have failed to keep pace with the wealth extracted from beneath their land.
Platinum prices hit an all-time high of $2,923 an ounce on January 26 during a broader precious metals rally and continued concerns over the platinum supply, according to the World Platinum Investment Council.
For Zimbabwe, home to the world’s second largest known deposits of platinum group metals (PGMs) after South Africa, the price surge offers an opportunity to increase revenue from a sector central to the economy. Mining accounts for about 75 percent of the country’s exports and about 14.5 percent of its gross domestic product, according to the International Trade Administration in the United States.
The mining sector generated a record $8.5bn in export earnings in 2025, up from $5.9bn the previous year, according to John Musekiwa, then-president of the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe. He said the increase was driven by strong output and favourable prices, particularly for gold and PGMs.
But in communities surrounding some of the country’s biggest platinum operations, residents said the wealth extracted from beneath their land has not translated into adequate roads, schools, water supplies and other basic services.
In Mhondoro-Ngezi, one of Zimbabwe’s major platinum-producing areas, that tension is visible on the ground.
A rich mineral belt, struggling communities
The Great Dyke, a geological formation stretching across central Zimbabwe, contains extensive deposits of PGMs. Zimplats operates mines, concentrators and processing facilities in the Mhondoro-Ngezi district there.
Inside the mining complex, ore is processed in modern facilities, and heavy trucks move between mines and plants. Outside, residents of Turf, Mamina, Murambwa and nearby villages said infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with the area’s growth.
Ernest Denhere, headman of Denhere village in Ward 3, said mining companies should leave a lasting legacy in the communities where they operate.
“We call upon Zimplats and other mines to build a road from Kadoma/Kwekwe to Turf, Benhura, Mamina, Murambwa and Kadhani, linking to the Harare-Masvingo highways,” Denhere said.
Ward 3 Councillor Emmah Chikwai said some children travel long distances to reach secondary school.
“Children from Jompani, Majoki, Maleti and Makwavarara walk between 15km and 25km [9 to 15.5 miles] to reach Musinambi Secondary School,” she said. “My appeal is for the mines to assist in setting up a satellite secondary school in Makwavarara.”
Schools, water and livelihoods under pressure
During a September 7 visit, Al Jazeera saw pupils at Turf Primary School learning under trees as rising enrolment strained the school’s facilities.
Nearby, women and young men searched through piles of waste for plastic they could sell. Cattle and goats moved among the rubbish.
For Sakina Lice, collecting plastic is how she supports her family.
“I have 11 children and nine grandchildren. Picking up plastics is the only way I survive. When I resell them, I can make maybe $20 a month,” she said.
“I am the breadwinner. My husband is late, so it is just hand to mouth. My wish is for the mine to empower women, so we can start projects and support our families.”
Residents also raised concerns about the Ngwazani River, about 100 metres (330ft) from the dump site, alleging that sewage from the mining area has entered the waterway and affected its use for household needs and small gardens.
Edson Mabure, whose family was relocated as mining activities expanded, said the river has become a problem for residents in his new community.
“Our village was where the mine is today, so we were relocated. From our new village, I cross the Ngwazani River, which is now flooded with sewage coming from the mine,” he said.
“Since the mine started operating, there is nothing tangible that has been done to leave a lasting legacy for the community. I don’t know whether the responsibility lies with the council or Zimplats.”
Agnes Handidikundiona, whom Al Jazeera met crossing the river with her children, said residents once relied on it for household activities and gardens.
“We are facing a serious challenge because the water is no longer clean,” she said. “Before the sewage spill, we used to use this water for domestic purposes, such as washing clothes and watering our nutritional gardens.”
She said flooding also has prevented some children from reaching school.
“Children from many villages cross here to go to school. Sometimes when the river is flooded, they cannot go to school. We need a footbridge here,” she said.
Ward 11 Councillor Nhomboka Kurebwa Javangwe said the area’s population has increased as mine workers and their families have moved in.
He said Zimplats has built classrooms and houses but demand continues to outstrip available facilities. He called for the company to build and operate a primary school.
Javangwe also said local councillors have limited direct access to the company.
“We do not have direct access to the mine to raise the concerns of our people,” he said, adding that only the council chairperson was authorised to meet with Zimplats officials.
Mines point to community investment
The same concerns are being raised in other platinum-producing areas.
In Shurugwi, home to the Unki Platinum Mine, residents have called for more investment in local infrastructure.
“I call upon Unki to consider assisting with classroom blocks for schools, water and sanitation, and roads in Shurugwi town,” said Bulle Madzitire, chairman of the Shurugwi Residents Association.
In nearby Zvishavane, Kamino Simango, chairman of the Zvishavane Residents Association, said the Mimosa Platinum Mine should focus more on infrastructure benefitting the wider community.
Unki told Al Jazeera that it has invested an average of $1.5m a year in community development over the past five years, covering education, healthcare, water and sanitation, agriculture and infrastructure.
Its public relations manager, Evelyn Mawimba, said the mine has built 63 boreholes, supported 32 schools through its STEP-UP programme and contributed $2.75m towards land purchases and development of the Impali housing estate.
Unki also pays about $130,000 a year in municipal levies to the Shurugwi Town Council and contributes about $850,000 annually to the Tongogara Rural District Council, Mawimba said.
Mimosa did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions despite several attempts to contact the company.
Al Jazeera also contacted the chairperson of the Mhondoro-Ngezi Rural District Council, Alderman Ephraim Pepukai Chengeta, about Zimplats’s contributions and development plans. He promised to respond but did not return calls or messages. The council’s chief executive officer, Itai A Mawonde, asked for the questions in writing.
Zimplats’s head of corporate affairs, Hama Saburi, also said he would respond but did not do so by publication.
For residents of Zimbabwe’s platinum belt, the demands are straightforward: better roads, schools, water and other services in communities living alongside some of the country’s most valuable mines.
“What is beneath our land speaks volumes,” Denhere said. “We need to see a lasting legacy for our communities.”

KAPO requests access to bank data register after shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

KAPO requests access to bank data register after shutdown
Internal Security Service (KAPO) head Margo Palloson has requested restored access to the state Enforcement Register and e-arrest system.
KAPO has been blocked from accessing the register by the Justice Ministry for failing to implement a data tracker tool by the October 1 deadline, and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) has been hit by the same block.
Palloson says the legislation permits KAPO to continue accessing the register without installing the tracker, at least in the case of national security matters.
"It has now become clear that the Police and Border Guard Board and KAPO have not established the necessary interfaces, which means that these agencies' access to the Enforcement Register and the e-arrest system must be closed. I ask the Center of Registers and Information Systems (RIK) to arrange the immediate technical shutdown of the services," Justice Ministry Deputy Secretary General Mari-Liis Mikli wrote in a letter to the RIK.
However, KAPO Director General Palloson says that, under the Code of Enforcement Procedure, the requirement for a technical solution — in this case a data tracker — does not apply to security authorities when performing tasks stipulated in the Security Authorities Act or conducting security vetting specified in the State Secrets and Classified Information of Foreign States Act.
"Consequently, we request continued access to the Enforcement Register and the e-arrest system for the performance of tasks stipulated in Section 6 of the Security Authorities Act and for conducting security vetting under the State Secrets and Classified Information of Foreign States Act," he wrote.
Palloson also specified which data KAPO wants its right to query restored: the existence of a bank account, account balance, account statement, persons authorized to use the account, who the beneficial owner of the account holder is, and whether a safe deposit box exists.
The KAPO director general confirmed that since October 1 his authority has not made any queries via the Enforcement Register as part of criminal proceedings, and has now also technically disabled the corresponding type of query.
"We also confirm that KAPO has taken measures to ensure the lawfulness of data processing and exercises sufficient oversight over it," Palloson noted.
The Enforcement Register (Estonian: Täitmisregister) is a state channel allowing authorities to query bank account data and place attachments. In 2025 Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise found agencies had been accessing confidential bank data without the correct legal basis. The solution was the data tracker, which lets individuals see who has queried their data. Legislation putting this in place passed at the Riigikogu, with the installation deadline set at October 1. Other authorities initially blocked but now able to access the register, having installed the tracker, are the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) and the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), which combats money laundering.
