Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.

AD—WO to Renovate the Heinz Architectural Center at Pittsburgh’s Carnegie Museum of Art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum of Art has commissioned architecture and urban design practice AD—WO to reimagine the Heinz Architectural Center. The practice, led by Emanuel Admassu and Jen Wood and one of the winners of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards, was recognized for exploring relationships among people, place, history and material culture, bringing an interdisciplinary approach to the architecture experience. The Heinz Architectural Center is the museum's forum to present, explore and incubate architectural ideas, currently located in the institution's main building, which dates from 1907. The new design aims to transform the Center into a contemporary facility that brings together exhibitions, collections, research, learning and public engagement. AD—WO is working with R3A as architect of record, Buro Happold for engineering and sustainability, Tillotson Design Associates for lighting and VizzAcoustics for acoustics.
The Heinz Architectural Center's activities focus on examining architecture and the built environment across histories, geographies and perspectives. The Center hosts exhibitions organized by Carnegie Museum of Art curators and other institutions, with a program that "reexamines architectural history, investigates the present, and considers possible futures for architecture and the built environment." Its collection includes around 6,000 architecture-related objects available for research and public display. The museum also houses a Hall of Architecture, dating to 1907, which includes more than 140 plaster casts of architectural structures from the ancient cultures of the Near East, Egypt, Greece and Rome, as well as the European Renaissance. Opened in 1993, the Heinz Architectural Center brings a contemporary perspective to the museum's classical architecture collection.
The Center is currently situated in the 1907 historic building designed by Longfellow, Alden & Harlow, between the historic halls and the 1974 Scaife Galleries designed by Edward Larrabee Barnes. The new design aims to strengthen connections across the museum, making its work more accessible through new gallery spaces, a collection study center and infrastructure that gives curatorial research more visibility. The project increases access to natural light and uses a material palette that includes firebrick and aluminum. It will also reimagine the existing collection study center and create flexible gallery spaces supporting exhibitions, education, research and public programs. Over the coming years, AD—WO will continue to collaborate with Carnegie Museum of Art staff to shape the construction and evolution of the space.
Related Article
20 Practices Expanding Architecture’s Agency: Winners of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards
Also in the United States, RAMSA (Robert A.M. Stern Architects) has unveiled the design for a new Welcome Hall at the Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago. The proposal is part of a masterplan completed by the firm in 2024 that examines the use of the museum's existing exhibition and public areas. In Rotterdam, Mecanoo is advancing the renovation of the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, one of the oldest museums in the Netherlands, which houses works ranging from the early Middle Ages to contemporary art. In Belgium, Design Museum Gent recently opened a new wing designed by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA. The wing links the museum's existing buildings into a single visitor route, organized into six zones structured around three principles: welcoming, open and adaptable.

Experts outline conditions for Russian investment in African countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:25:56 UTC
14:25:56 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russian investment in Africa should be concentrated in countries and projects where established trade flows or anticipated long-term demand already exist, according to the authors of a report titled "Africa’s Investment Landscape: Conditions, Opportunities, and Models for Russian Business Presence," prepared by the Financial University, the Roscongress Foundation, and Vedomosti business newspaper.
The report noted that Russia’s offerings to Africa have a distinct sectoral focus. Investments are most frequently associated with energy, nuclear technologies, mineral fertilizers, geology, mining, metallurgy, mechanical engineering, transportation solutions, and education.
Meanwhile, Chinese companies primarily invest in large-scale infrastructure and production chains, companies from the Gulf states favor logistics, energy, and real estate, while Western companies focus on mining, finance, and services. "It would be more rational for Russia to focus its capital where technological expertise is combined with existing trade flows or guaranteed long-term demand," the report’s authors believe.
Russia holds strong positions in the agricultural sector, where Russian suppliers account for approximately 20% of the African fertilizer market, as well as in energy, particularly when it comes to large integrated projects, and mining, where Russian expertise can be applied not only through asset acquisitions but also through geological exploration, engineering services, equipment supplies, and energy provision.
Russia is also interested in exporting educational services to Africa. "This interest is linked to training specialists for projects, as shortages of qualified personnel often directly limit the extent to which operations can be localized," the report said.

Canada and UAE sign free trade agreement to strengthen economic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:14:47 UTC
14:14:47 KST

Canada and UAE sign free trade agreement to strengthen economic ties
The Canada-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement was signed in Ottawa on Tuesday during a meeting between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and visiting Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, according to a statement from the Canadian Prime Minister’s Office, Qazinform News Agency cites Xinhua.
Negotiations were completed in a record 47 days, marking the shortest time either country has taken to conclude a free trade agreement, the statement said.
Once fully implemented, the agreement will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE. It will also address non-tariff barriers, improve predictability for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services.
The agreement covers a broad range of sectors, including industrial products, agriculture, forestry, fish and seafood, environmental services and engineering. It is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The visit also marked the first time an Abu Dhabi crown prince had visited Canada, representing further progress toward the UAE’s commitment to invest 70 billion Canadian dollars (US$50 billion) in Canada. The investment pledge was announced during Carney’s visit to Abu Dhabi in November 2025.
In addition to the trade agreement, the two countries signed several commercial and energy cooperation arrangements, as well as memorandums of understanding on defense cooperation and diplomatic training.
Canada and the UAE also announced plans to begin negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty, according to the statement.

Despite these challenges, strong remittance inflows, adequate foreign reserves and banking system liquidity continue to provide economic buffers.
The report also highlighted risks from a widening trade deficit and potential El Nino impacts on agriculture and water resources, underscoring the need for prudent fiscal management to sustain growth and create jobs. ■

Chalmers lowers hopes for fuel discounts after high inflation result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:12:09 UTC
14:12:09 KST

Jim Chalmers resists blame for another high inflation result
In short:
Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is not the main driver of inflation, but acknowledges today's figures are still "too high".
The treasurer has downplayed the likelihood of further fuel tax discounts, citing budget pressures.
What's next?
The Reserve Bank is considered likely to hike interest rates when its monetary policy board meets on Tuesday.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is urging "perspective", with today's disappointing inflation result making another rate hike a near certainty.
Facing fresh accusations from the opposition that a government "spending addiction" is putting pressure on inflation, Mr Chalmers repeated his longstanding insistence that the government's budget was playing "a helpful role" and was not a "primary driver".
"There are other factors at play," he told reporters today, naming the Middle East war and a surprising burst of private investment in data centres and other areas.
"For every five dollars of demand in our economy, four dollars [are] private and one dollar is public. I think that's an important bit of perspective when it comes to some of the commentary that is around today," he said.
"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … We accept our part in the fight against inflation. We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings."
Odds of Cup Day rate hike increase
Today's inflation figures confirm the glum prognosis of RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser, who last week warned that inflation was on track to be "materially worse" than the 3.5 per cent the bank forecast in August.
That forecast was for "underlying" inflation for the September quarter, the bank's preferred measure because it is smoother. The actual result was 3.7 per cent.
Economists responded by dialling up their expectations of a rate hike next Tuesday, which KPMG's Brendan Rynne called "locked and loaded" and Deloitte Access Economics' Stephen Smith called the "best bet on Melbourne Cup Day".
Markets also upgraded their expectations of a rate hike to 87 per cent next Tuesday, and fully "priced in" a hike by the end of the year, indicating a belief that a rate hike is a near-certainty in December, if not November.
Another rate hike of 25 basis points would take the rate to 4.85 per cent, its highest level since 2008.
Treasury secretary backs up budget
The Coalition pursued the government over spending levels in Question Time and in Senate estimates today, where Treasury Secretary Jenny Wilkinson backed up Mr Chalmers' assessment that the budget was not a main driver.
"We can only control what we can control," she said, adding that recent budget updates had "taken some pressure from the government out of the economy" by consistently reducing the size of the budget deficits.
"We have seen public demand coming off … The thing that we have been surprised by has been that private demand in the economy has been stronger than we expected."
Pressed by Liberal deputy Jane Hume about the overall level of government spending, which remains at levels rarely seen outside of recessions, Ms Wilkinson said it was important to consider the kind of spending, not just the overall amount.
A similar point was made by RBA Governor Michele Bullock, who maintained her policy of refraining from direct comment on the government's budgets, but named private sector activity, global pressures, and poor productivity as primary drivers of inflation.
"Continued weak productivity growth means that the economy cannot grow strongly without putting pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone's real spending power over the next few years," she said.
Further cost of living relief unlikely
Mr Chalmers downplayed any suggestion that the government would resume its fuel excise discount, despite the continue growth in fuel prices.
"The budget can't afford to do that forever," he said.
"We try to be up front with people and say we need to make sure that when we provide cost of living relief, it's not counterproductive.
"[We must] strike the most effective balance between the pressures on the budget, the pressures on people, and the pressures on our economy."
He labelled the Middle East war "disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and … around the world" and said it was "absolutely turbocharging" inflation.
"From an economic point of view, the end of the war in the Middle East can't come soon enough."
Speaking in Question Time, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said economic difficulties were "not going to be solved overnight" but that the government would "continue to do everything we can to shield Australians from the worst of the impact."
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said government spending had made Australia "completely vulnerable to international factors" and reiterated calls for a fuel discount offset by further spending cuts.

'Cognitive erosion' has become a new target of disinformation – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:08:00 UTC
14:08:00 KST

'Cognitive erosion' has become a new target of disinformation – expert
Paolo Cesarini, Chair of the Executive Board of the European Digital Media Observatory (EDMO), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
According to the expert, the ultimate goal of such attacks is not persuasion but to push audiences into a state of apathy in which they stop believing in any facts or sources of information.
"Classic disinformation operations, like classic influence operations, had been known to be designed to persuade people. More and more, especially after AI took a huge role in the production and distribution of information online, you see that the strategy is no longer persuasion or motivation. Now it is cognitive erosion," the expert said.
In his opinion, this leads to disengagement, cynicism, and the defiance of any form of state authority or government institutions.
Cesarini also outlined EDMO's three-layer methodology for countering these threats:
- The first layer involves targeted monitoring of fake news, artificially generated content, and individual disinformation "spikes" in the media.
- The second layer involves analyzing deeper propaganda narratives, including Russian claims about "corrupt" Ukraine.
- The third layer involves identifying the organizers and coordinators of networks operating across different countries by combining fact-checking with open-source intelligence (OSINT) tools.

Netanyahu, Eisenkot deadlocked as Israel election delivers no clear winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

Israel’s election has left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition challenger Gadi Eisenkot without a clear path to power, as exit polls showed their blocs deadlocked despite record turnout and significant gains by Arab Israeli parties.
Eisenkot, a 66-year-old former military chief, vowed Wednesday to move quickly to form a government, saying voters had rejected Netanyahu’s divisive leadership.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, called for a strong right-wing government and highlighted the prospect of renewed military action against Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump.
Neither leader claimed victory. Exit polls from Israel’s three major television networks showed the competing blocs close to evenly matched, with neither securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 projected a 51-51 tie, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc a narrow 52-49 advantage. Final results were expected Thursday or Friday, leaving the country facing potentially prolonged coalition negotiations or another election.
Speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said the public had delivered a vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and urged the longtime prime minister to retire from politics.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
He also warned Netanyahu against using national security to advance his political interests, raising concerns about the prospect of renewed military action against Iran while the government’s future remained uncertain.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu did not immediately address supporters after the initial projections. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, an ally of the prime minister, dismissed the opposition’s victory claims as premature.
Arab Israeli parties made some of the strongest gains, with exit polls projecting a combined 17 to 18 seats. Their increased representation could prove decisive in determining whether Netanyahu’s coalition returns to power.
Turnout reached 77.7%, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest in more than two decades and about 7 percentage points above the 2022 election.
The strong participation included a surge among Palestinian citizens of Israel, many of whom voted to prevent Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition from returning to government.
At the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters celebrated as exit polls were released. Faten Gattas, a candidate for the alliance, pledged continued opposition to occupation and racism.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” she said in Nazareth.
Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab Israeli political leader, said the right-wing camp had suffered a major defeat and indicated he was open to working with Eisenkot.
However, Eisenkot has largely ruled out forming a government with Arab lawmakers, complicating his route to power. Their parties could still support a minority government in parliamentary votes without formally joining a coalition.
Far-right leader Itamar Ben Gvir warned Netanyahu against forming a unity government with Eisenkot, calling such a move a mistake. Ben Gvir, a prominent supporter of Jewish settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich were projected to win a combined 13 seats, short of the gains some had expected.
Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said Ben Gvir’s polarizing campaign had helped mobilize Arab Israeli voters.
“Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won,” Rahat said.
The election was held in the shadow of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Israeli figures.
The attack triggered the Gaza genocide and wider regional conflicts involving Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran.
Netanyahu campaigned on his security record, arguing that Israeli military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iranian targets had made the country safer. He also emphasized his relationship with Trump as an opportunity to confront Iran.
Addressing Likud supporters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Netanyahu said Israel faced a historic opportunity to eliminate what he described as the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all,” he said.
Eisenkot, who joined Netanyahu’s wartime government after the Hamas attack before resigning about eight months later, challenged the prime minister’s authority to make major security decisions without a clear public mandate.
He urged the security establishment to resist attempts to put political interests ahead of national security.
Despite presenting himself as a centrist on domestic politics, Eisenkot maintains a hawkish position on Palestinian issues. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
He has described Israel’s campaign in Gaza as a failure because Hamas remains in control. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths during the war.
The exit polls suggested a major setback for Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition, which once held 68 seats but appeared far short of a majority.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 years across several terms and has repeatedly survived political crises. After four inconclusive elections in two years, his opponents briefly removed him from office in 2021. He returned to power in December 2022.
His latest campaign included sharp attacks on Arab Israeli voters. Netanyahu accused them of trying to “steal the election,” while his Likud party unsuccessfully sought to keep polling stations open beyond their scheduled 10:00 p.m. closing time.
The opposition accused him of seeking grounds to challenge the results. Netanyahu also alleged that three senior officials from the United Arab List had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes of cash. Election authorities described the incident as an isolated local case.
Netanyahu entered the election facing criticism over intelligence failures that allowed the Oct. 7 attack and longstanding corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant related to the Gaza war.
His government’s policies have deepened Israel’s international isolation amid the war in Gaza, expanding settlements and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, has drawn public sympathy after losing his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza, and two nephews during the war. Before voting, he privately visited his son’s grave.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would become Israel’s first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent if he forms a government.
The election’s outcome remains uncertain as votes are counted and smaller parties prepare to negotiate their role in the next government.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, described the exit polls as a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner.
The deadlock could allow Netanyahu to remain caretaker prime minister during lengthy negotiations. If neither camp can assemble a governing majority, another election may be necessary.
Some Israelis returned from abroad to vote. Eilana Zisblit, 55, who has lived in Canada for nearly three decades, traveled to Israel to support a center-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP), saying the situation affected Jews and Arabs in Israel as well as Jews abroad.
Eisenkot has urged political leaders to avoid another election, arguing that the record turnout demonstrated the public’s desire for change.

Digital currencies could become new payment tool for Russia, Africa — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:05:41 UTC
14:05:41 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Central bank digital currencies could become new instruments for facilitating cross-border settlements between Russia and African countries, according to the authors of a report titled "Russia-Africa: Routes for Capital, Goods, Information, and Specialists," prepared by Vedomosti business newspaper and members of the New Generation International Club of Young Economists with the participation of the Roscongress Foundation.
The report also noted that currency swaps and settlement facilities between the Bank of Russia and African central banks could serve as other effective instruments, with priority given to Egypt, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and South Africa.
The report’s authors point out that the shift away from currencies of unfriendly countries in settlements, along with the risk of secondary sanctions and the lack of direct correspondent banking relationships and ruble-denominated accounts, is keeping trade between Russia and African countries below its potential level.
Other challenges include high costs and delays associated with multiple currency conversions, the near-total absence of accessible direct currency conversion channels for small businesses, and a lack of hedging instruments for currency pairs.
Trade between Russia and African countries totaled approximately $27 bln in 2025. Under the pessimistic scenario outlined by the report’s authors, payments will continue to be routed through third countries at considerable cost through 2030, sanctions could tighten, and bilateral trade could reach $27-30 bln by 2030.

Ex-SC judge Justice Kaul flags ‘punishment’ of prolonged custody before conviction
NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said that the period before conviction or acquittal has become a "punishment" in India, commenting on the denial of bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. He said that prolonged legal proceedings can themselves become a form of punishment and that bail should generally be the norm.In an interview with news agency ANI, Kaul said he had generally taken a liberal view on bail, but acknowledged that certain laws explicitly restrict the granting of bail in specific cases."I have taken a generally very liberal view on bail. I feel the bail cannot be the punishment. The conviction is the punishment. In our system, unfortunately, the pre-conviction or acquittal period itself becomes a punishment. The process becomes a punishment," former Supreme Court judge said.Kaul said several judges had raised concerns about the issue. He also referred to a judgment written by Justice Sundaresh, with whom he had dealt with the question of bail and the principles governing custody."And many judges have been writing and talking about it. In fact, I, sitting with Justice Sundaresh, had dealt elaborately with the bail itself, trying to say, why are you people under custody? Justice Sundaresh wrote the judgment.
He's, to my mind, a liberal judge on this. And we tried to lay down norms, etc., which were already in existence, but trying to, you know, until this case. So in most cases, our view is, that bail should be the norm. But there are certain acts which prohibit bail," said Kaul.Kaul has co-authored an upcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, with Jay Vinayak Ojha. The book is scheduled for release on October 31.Khalid and Imam are accused under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in connection with an alleged larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots. He was not even in the news then," Justice Kaul said, explaining how the meeting came about.
"He was a journalist, maybe met me a couple of times. He was insistent that I must, at Diwali time, come. I was going somewhere else. I said, 'Okay, I'll drop in for ten minutes.' I told my wife, 'Have a cup of coffee, I'll drop in for ten minutes, and then we'll go.' That's all that happened," he said.Asked whether he had mentored Das at any point, Justice Kaul denied doing so, while acknowledging that he had advised the activist on his choice of words."I was not mentoring him, but once or twice he met me, I told him that, I will always tell you to taper down a little in your language," he said.Justice Kaul added that differences in language and expression across generations could sometimes cause discomfort, particularly among those accustomed to more civil forms of conversation.

14:01:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Alishan Forest Railway's campaign celebrating the full reopening of the century-old line has won Japan's 2026 Good Design Award, recognizing its use of contemporary design to promote Taiwan's railway heritage.
The Alishan Forest Railway and Cultural Heritage Office announced the award on Monday, saying the campaign combined visual design, cultural activities, and commemorative merchandise to present the railway's history to a wider audience, per a press release.
Judges praised the campaign for maintaining a consistent visual identity across its events and promotional materials while reinterpreting traditional railway culture through contemporary aesthetics. Elements included original dance performances, Japanese woodblock print-style visuals (ukiyo-e), and specially designed souvenirs.
The railway resumed full-line service on July 6, 2024, after a 15-year interruption caused by typhoon damage. The reopening restored direct train service between Chiayi and Alishan. Celebratory events included a completion ceremony for Tunnel No. 42, a full-line reopening ceremony, and a market combining railway culture, forestry products, and art.
The campaign also extended the railway's identity into everyday life through limited-edition “120,000 Happiness” iPASS cards, commemorative ticket gift boxes, and stamps featuring station landscapes. Searchlight Culture Lab carried out the marketing project, per the press release.
The Good Design Award was established in 1957 and is organized by the Japan Institute of Design Promotion. The 2026 competition received 5,111 entries, according to the railway office.
The Alishan Forest Railway, which has operated for more than a century, is a designated cultural heritage asset in Taiwan. The award highlights efforts to combine heritage preservation, tourism, and contemporary design.

He urged lawmakers to support continued budget allocations to Taipower and CPC Corp. to help stabilize energy prices and protect households and small businesses.
He said the two state-owned companies provide essential electricity and fuel while absorbing costs from rising international energy prices, which have contributed to their financial losses. Government funding has helped shore up their finances and maintain stable domestic supplies, he said.
Kung rejected opposition criticism that Taipower's losses stemmed from flawed energy policies, arguing that surging global energy prices had created similar challenges for other countries.
He said governments have responded in different ways, with some allocating public funds to subsidize state-owned energy providers and others freezing domestic energy prices to shield consumers from higher costs.
According to Ministry of Economic Affairs data, Japan and Indonesia have each allocated more than NT$500 billion (US$15.41 billion) to stabilize domestic energy costs, while South Korea has allocated about NT$130 billion for subsidies, per CNA.
Kung said Taiwan's subsidies were intended to balance the financial stability of state-owned enterprises with the need to keep energy affordable. Without government intervention, higher international prices would be passed on to households and businesses, increasing pressure on living costs and inflation.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said Tuesday that intellectuals with a conscience would support an online appeal reportedly signed by students at more than a dozen Chinese universities calling for an end to Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s indefinite tenure.

Chiu recalled meeting Chinese intellectuals during the 19th Communist Party Congress in 2017, Liberty Times reported. He said some scholars told him that 95% of Chinese intellectuals would oppose abandoning the leadership succession system and allowing Xi to remain in power beyond the customary transition.
Chiu said intellectuals’ ability to correct the party’s mistakes had disappeared after Xi consolidated power. He added that the appeal reflected the conscience of intellectuals and that, although its authenticity remained uncertain, “any intellectual with a conscience would support the appeal.”

Obra Blanca 2026 brought together more than 23,000 industry professionals in its seventh edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Direct contact with a material allows one to appreciate textures, compare finishes, and observe how its appearance changes under different lighting conditions. At an exhibition, these possibilities are complemented by exchanges with manufacturers and professionals, helping to understand applications and resolve questions about their use. This relationship between material exploration and architectural practice was one of the central pillars of the seventh edition of Obra Blanca, which drew more than 23,000 professionals to Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
Featuring 190 exhibitors across 13 pavilions and 28,620 m² of exhibition space, the event showcased finishes and products for architecture and interior design. The exhibition was accompanied by a program of conferences, forums, and technical talks, alongside a new digital tool designed to consult and organize product information both during and after the visit.
The exhibition spaces offered diverse ways to engage with the products, ranging from material sample exploration to installations showcasing combinations of colors, textures, and finishes. Their layout provided context for understanding how these elements could be integrated into a project and interact with other components of a space.
"The booths are looking increasingly professional, with highly designed, experiential layouts. So, I think it is highly worthwhile to come and experience it firsthand," commented Nadja Borrás of Gensler.
The event also succeeded in bringing suppliers and professionals together in one place to discuss the featured solutions. For architects and interior designers, this exchange complements the technical information found in catalogs and product spec sheets with discussions tailored to the specific needs of their projects.
Spaces for Professional Exchange
The program brought together 70 specialists and featured three international lectures, four national ones, four forums with international guests, and twelve technical talks. Developed in partnership with 32 strategic allies, the agenda expanded the gathering beyond a simple product showcase, creating spaces to share experiences and discuss industry challenges.
For Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily, the value of the gathering also lies in this professional dialogue: "Beyond presenting products and innovations, I believe one of the event's greatest strengths is the space it creates to discuss architectural practice and the challenges currently facing the profession."
Harrouk spoke with Paula Villar Pastor, co-founder of the Peruvian association Espacio Común, about the Main Floating Stage of Muyunafest 2025, which won first place in ArchDaily's 2026 Building of the Year Award. Their conversation explored how regional conditions, local knowledge, and community collaboration guide design decisions. "Our conversation addressed a broader challenge that architecture faces today: how to respond to increasingly complex social and environmental realities without losing sight of the practical realities of construction," Harrouk noted.
Fernando Lozano Assad, President of Obra Blanca and Director of TCNA Mexico (Tile Council of North America-Mexico), highlighted the collective effort behind the program: "At Obra Blanca, we have always championed knowledge and community spirit. Building an activities agenda like this is the result of the collaborative drive among our 32 partnerships."
The Espacio Obra Blanca, designed by Augusto Quijano Axle, hosted sixteen expert interviews and showcased the Obra Blanca 2027 CMF Dynamic exhibition, titled La tendencia es emocionar (The Trend is to Emotion). Organized in partnership with La Jabonera Centro de Diseño, this initiative brought together twelve architecture and interior design firms from Guanajuato, Querétaro, and San Luis Potosí to explore color, materials, and finishes.
From Exhibition to Specification
One of the key additions to this edition was OB ESPECIFICA, a free digital tool designed for architects, interior designers, and specifiers. Using QR codes, it allows users to access technical specifications for the exhibited products, save selections, and organize them by project.
The platform also offers options to share these selections with design teams and contact sales representatives. Its purpose is to streamline post-event product research, ensuring that information gathered during the visit remains easily accessible when returning to design and specification work.
In this way, the combination of physical samples, professional dialogue, and technical information formed the backbone of the various activities at Obra Blanca 2026. The next edition will take place from October 12 to 14, 2027, at Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
For more information, visit the official Obra Blanca website.

Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said at the 30th Belarusian Energy and Ecology Forum.

Elections in Israel: Up to 480,000 ballots remain to be counted, the equivalent of approximately 12 seats in the Knesset
The Israeli Central Elections Commission estimates that between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double-envelope" ballots were cast in the parliamentary elections, a figure significantly lower than the 600,000 initially reported. These votes came primarily from soldiers, police officers, prisoners, and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as other voters who cast their ballots outside their usual polling stations. The ballots are counted separately after verification to prevent double voting. According to the Commission, these estimates remain provisional and could still change. With each Knesset seat representing approximately 40,000 votes, these ballots are equivalent to about a dozen seats and could alter the political balance. At this stage, Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is credited with 53 seats, compared to 48 for the predominantly Jewish opposition parties. ====================================================================================================

The billion-dollar cancer bill Australia's sunscreen overhaul may not fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:48:51 UTC
13:48:51 KST

in brief
- The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing.
- But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution.
Australia's sunscreen regulator is planning tougher rules after concerns some products failed to deliver the sun protection promised on their labels.
But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution, with boosting awareness on how Australians need to apply and reapply sunscreen also critical to preventing skin cancer.
In a report published last year, consumer group CHOICE tested 20 popular sunscreens and found that only four met their labelled sun protection factor (SPF), raising questions about the reliability of products Australians rely on to protect themselves from UV radiation.
The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) later recalled several sunscreen products after identifying batches that didn't deliver their advertised SPF protection.
The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing, improve ingredient-quality requirements, and clarify the SPF claims cosmetic products can make.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What are the proposed reforms?
The TGA is proposing several reforms to address sunscreen quality, with the goal of reducing instances of skin cancer.
Australia has the highest rate of melanoma incidence in the world, with an estimated 17,443 new cases diagnosed in 2025 according to Cancer Australia.
The reforms are:
- Strengthen sunscreen testing requirements
- Develop specific ingredient quality requirements
- Provide a consistent limit for SPF rating that can be claimed for all secondary (cosmetic) sunscreens
- Review sunscreen good manufacturing practice guidance
- Consider labelling for SPF ratings
Professor Terry Slevin, CEO of the Public Health Association of Australia, told SBS News that treating skin cancers costs the country almost $2.5 billion each year.
"We need to invest more in preventing those cancers rather than having to treat them at the tail end," he said.
The TGA told SBS News: "The proposed reforms are intended to provide greater assurance through stronger testing requirements, increased oversight of testing laboratories, testing of finished products and periodic testing over a product’s lifecycle, and improved access by the TGA to SPF testing evidence."
Improving testing
Improving how sunscreen is tested is one way the TGA wants to improve quality and reliability of SPF claims.
Slevin explained that a small number of labs in Australia produce the nation's sunscreen, supplying multiple brands.
Sunscreens can then be tested on volunteers who use the formula and are then exposed to UV radiation; the rate at which skin reddens can then be used to determine the product's quality.
While this method is common, it can also be imprecise.
"People have different skin types, and the amount of product being applied can vary a lot. So having consistent SPF levels relies on a lot of unpredictable variables," Slevin said.
These variations can lead to inconsistent product application and to sunscreens having marginally different SPF than advertised on their packaging.
Should you be worried about SPF levels?
The TGA reforms are looking to ensure that sunscreen manufacturers have clearer guidance and expectations, but SPF levels could still slightly vary from bottle to bottle according to Slevin.
However, variations would be minimal and would have little impact on the sunscreen's efficacy.
"The difference between SPF 50 and SPF 30 may sound significant, but the difference in the amount of UV that’s filtered out is only 3 per cent, a small change," he said.
"The vast majority of sunscreens serve a very useful and effective purpose; these reforms will only strengthen this."
But the main way to achieve the TGA's goal may not be reforming testing, but educating people on how to use sunscreen products best.
Dispelling confusion
Anna Wang, an associate professor in the School of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney, said that improving consumer understanding and behaviour is the best way to improve sun safety.
"What is going to make a bigger impact isn’t whether a sunscreen tests SPF45 using one method and SPF40 using another, but how often we reapply, and whether we put the recommended amount on," she told SBS News.
Experts recommended applying sunscreen generously to all exposed skin every two hours, seeking shade, and wearing a hat and sunglasses.
Towelling off after a swim, or wiping water or sweat off your body, can also remove some sunscreen.
Some cosmetic products, including foundations and moisturisers, also advertise SPF protection.
The TGA is considering a consistent limit on the SPF ratings these secondary sunscreens can claim, aiming to make it easier for consumers to distinguish products designed primarily for sun protection from those intended mainly for cosmetic use.
"In Australia, we have several hundred formulations to choose from so it can be confusing," Wang said.
She supported the TGA's reforms to clarify the distinction between primary and secondary sunscreens.
Investigation ongoing
In the meantime, the TGA confirmed to SBS News its investigation into sunscreens with disputed SPF results is ongoing.
"The TGA is considering the available evidence and providing sponsors with an opportunity to provide additional data or evidence before regulatory decisions are made," it told SBS News.
The regulator said it will issue product recalls or cancellations as needed while it develops the new reforms.
"The TGA intends to publish its findings and learnings and provide further guidance to sponsors and manufacturers to clarify expectations around SPF evidence and testing."
Clarification: This story has been revised to reflect the estimated $2.5 billion cost of skin cancer annually.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

France minerals envoy says rare earths diversification from China possible within 3-5 years

- China still dominates some rare earth magnets, with up to 90% of production, and its 2025 export curbs hit industries like carmakers.
- Projects in Europe, Australia, the US, Japan, Brazil and India are moving fast, but magnet output may limit progress; the G-7 wants reliance cut below 60% by 2030.
AI generated
SYDNEY – Western countries could achieve an acceptable level of rare earths diversification away from China within three to five years, France’s top envoy for strategic metals said on Oct 27.
Governments and manufacturers are racing to diversify supplies of metals vital to defence, technology and renewable energy, and reduce dependence on China, which accounts for as much as 90% of production of some specialised rare earth magnets.
Beijing rattled global markets in 2025 when export curbs on permanent magnets disrupted industries, including the automotive sector, exposing their reliance on a single source.
Some investors and analysts have questioned whether breaking China’s dominance is achievable, given the scale of investment and technical know-how required to produce the niche metals used in everything from cars and aircraft to electronics and weapons systems.
“You don’t need hundreds of rare earths mines around the world to cover the supply. It’s a limited market, it’s a limited quantity. We have already made some progress,” said Benjamin Gallezot, France’s Interministerial Delegate for Strategic Minerals and Metals Supply.
Expansion projects led by Belgium’s Solvay and France’s Carester, plus others in Australia, the US, Japan, Brazil and India, are developing quickly, he said.
“If you take all together, these projects, and you push to accelerate them, hopefully, you can have a good diversification in the next three to five years,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a mining conference in Sydney.
While rare earths mines and refining projects were progressing, the amount of magnet manufacturing could still be a limiting factor, he said.
“You don’t need a decade to solve this problem.”
Leaders of the Group of Seven nations agreed in June to step up coordination to cut their countries’ reliance on China for critical minerals.
They aim to reduce dependence on any one supplier outside the G-7 and its partner countries for rare earths and permanent magnets to below 60% by 2030, with an ultimate goal of 50% “as soon as possible”.
“We can do much more,” Gallezot said. REUTERS

Centre deputes a high-level team to investigate death of Cheetah, caused by firearm pellet injuries, in Madhya Pradesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Wednesday deputed a high-level team to investigation the death of a 19-month-old male Cheetah of Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, caused by firearm pellet injuries.The team has been tasked with undertaking a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to the death of the Cheetah, examining all available evidence and coordinating closely with the Madhya Pradesh forest department to ensure strict and swift action in the matter.The 19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25 in the territorial forests of Morena, outside the protected area of Kuno National Park. Preliminary medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the firearm pellets.The incident, the first reported casualty of a shooting since PM Narendra Modi launched Project Cheetah at Kuno in Sept, 2022, is being viewed quite seriously at the Centre, given the critical importance of Project Cheetah and the need to ensure the highest standards of protection for the reintroduced population of the Big Cat.
“As reported by the MP forest department, the injured cheetah was rescued from the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division the same day and provided intensive veterinary care and emergency surgery at the veterinary facility in Jabalpur. During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body. Despite the medical intervention, the Cheetah succumbed to its injuries on Oct 27,” said the Union environment ministry in a statement.It said, “The state govt has already constituted a Special Task Force (STF), comprising forest and police officers, to investigate the incident. The central team deputed by the Union environment ministry would work in coordination with the state machinery. It would also examine the implementation of security protocols, as well as monitoring and protection measures being undertaken to avoid any such incident in future.
“The central team would submit its findings and recommendations to the ministry for further directions to the state govt and field authorities.”The central team comprises the Inspector General of Forests, National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), Additional Director, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB), and Regional Deputy Director, WCCB.

Approximately 25% of global oil trade and around 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration subsequently effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran and a shift toward attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.
