China, 25 other countries sign UN convention on negotiable cargo documents
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:33 CST
11:35:33 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows the signing ceremony of the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents in Accra, Ghana. China, Ghana and 24 other countries on Monday became the first signatories to the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents at a signing ceremony in Accra. (Photo by Seth/Xinhua)
ACCRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- China, Ghana and 24 other countries on Monday became the first signatories to the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents at a signing ceremony in Accra, capital of Ghana.
Chinese Vice Commerce Minister Jiang Chenghua signed the convention on behalf of the Chinese government at the ceremony.
Jiang said the institutional innovation fills a gap in international rules and provides an international legal framework for financing transactions involving cross-border transport documents.
It will effectively ease the financial pressure on enterprises engaged in international trade, reduce transaction costs in cross-border overland trade, and inject new momentum into the high-quality development of global trade, he added.
China is ready to work with all signatory states to complete their domestic approval procedures as soon as possible, Jiang said, expressing China's hope that more countries will join the convention so that its benefits can reach more nations and contribute to global trade prosperity and the well-being of people around the world.
Anna Joubin-Bret, secretary of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), said the convention would help reduce uncertainty, enhance resilience, facilitate trade finance, support trade digitalization and improve the efficiency of international supply chains.
She thanked the Chinese government for bringing the convention project to UNCITRAL. "Since the adoption by the United Nations General Assembly, we have greatly benefited from China's steadfast support to the convention and its efforts to promote the broader understanding of this framework," she said.
Around 400 representatives from more than 60 countries and regions attended the signing ceremony.
Initiated and spearheaded by China, the convention was adopted by the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in December 2025. ■

The former Dortmund forward pulled a goal back from the penalty spot in the 65th minute after Ryerson fouled Mick Schmetgens inside the area.
Fullkrug struck again four minutes later, dispossessing Waldemar Anton near halfway before beating an opponent and driving home the equalizer.
Mitchell Weiser then threatened to complete Bremen's comeback, but Dortmund regained control in the closing stages.
Amos Pieper blocked Daniel Svensson's effort in the 89th minute before Sabitzer curled a free kick into the top corner in stoppage time to send Dortmund into the third round.
"We must be relieved in the end. We are happy we managed to avoid extra time," Dortmund captain Nico Schlotterbeck said.
"We played a good first half but had some problems afterward. We became nervous after they pulled one back. It was a 50-50 game that we ended up winning."
Elsewhere, Augsburg beat Sonnenhof Grossaspach 4-2, while RB Leipzig edged Rot-Weiss Essen 2-1 and Bochum defeated Mainz 2-0.
Eintracht Frankfurt won 3-1 away to Hamburg, Cologne thrashed Union Berlin 5-0, Borussia Monchengladbach beat Karlsruhe 2-0 and Darmstadt defeated Elversberg 2-0. ■

“Ukraine is about to enter another wartime winter. To ensure the most stable energy supply possible and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is crucial that Ukraine receives funding to purchase equipment to strengthen and restore critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombing,” Energy Minister Terje Aasland said.
During a visit to Kyiv on Tuesday, October 27, Aasland announced that Norway would provide 500 million Norwegian kroner (NOK) to support Ukraine’s energy sector.
The funding is being provided under the Nansen Support Programme, which runs through 2026. The assistance will be channeled through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund (UESF).
This mechanism allows funds to be quickly directed toward repairs, the purchase of new equipment, and investments where they are most urgently needed.
In particular, the Ukrainian side emphasized the need for new power cables to ensure a stable energy supply.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Norway has allocated more than 16 billion Norwegian kroner ($1.72 billion) for gas procurement, repairs to energy infrastructure, and investment in new solutions.
As previously reported, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Norway would maintain its military, humanitarian, and financial assistance to Ukraine at around $9 billion in 2027.

UN nuclear inspectors see no evidence Iran repaired US-bombed sites
NEW YORK – The United Nations nuclear watchdog said it has not detected any efforts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes over the past two years, even as Tehran continues to block inspectors’ access to most of its atomic sites.
“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026,” International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi told the UN Security Council on Oct 27.
Grossi’s remarks undercut US President Donald Trump’s narrative that launching a new war against Iran in late February was necessary to halt its nuclear weapons ambitions.
The President has repeatedly said he Is weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
The assessment echoes a conclusion that former US director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard included in written testimony before a congressional committee earlier in 2026.
She wrote that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “obliterated” in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, and that there “has been no efforts since then to try to rebuild their enrichment capability”.
At the same time, the IAEA’s ability to assess Iran’s nuclear activities remains constrained by its lack of access to most of the country’s atomic sites.
Grossi reiterated that inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s nuclear material – including the previously declared 440kg of uranium enriched up to 60% – and called on Tehran to grant renewed access.
“As at today the IAEA has not been able to verify that there has been no diversion of nuclear material required to be safeguarded,” he said.
The Trump administration has repeatedly claimed it had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but offered little evidence to back up its claims.
Trump started the current war against Iran because he said he needed to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, something that most experts said the Islamic Republic was years away from.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has offered other explanations for the war, including that Washington had to act before Israel struck Iran and sparked retaliation against the US.
He’s also said Iran was building up its ballistic missile and drone capability as a conventional “shield” around its nuclear programme. BLOOMBERG

Putin gave 90-minute "history lecture" during call with Norwegian and Finnish leaders
During a phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Russian leader Vladimir Putin spent almost the entire conversation discussing the "initial reasons for the conflict" with Ukraine instead of discussing how to end the war.
Source: Financial Times
Quote: "Vladimir Putin used most of his call with the leaders of Finland and Norway to lecture them about medieval Slavic history, underscoring the difficulties Europe faces in asserting itself in upcoming peace talks with Russia."
Details: Stubb told Finnish media that the call, which was supposed to last less than half an hour, dragged on for 90 minutes.
According to three sources familiar with the conversation, instead of discussing the key issues involved in ending the war, Putin delivered a lengthy monologue to the Nordic leaders about the "initial reasons for the conflict", as the Kremlin calls them.
By contrast, the prospect of an immediate ceasefire – Ukraine's main demand for starting the peace process – was barely discussed, according to the FT's sources.
One source said that the Nordic leaders had decided not to interrupt Putin during his "historical asides" so that they could gauge how seriously he was approaching dialogue with Europe.
It was the first conversation between the Kremlin leader and any of Ukraine's European allies since July 2025, when Putin spoke to French President Emmanuel Macron.
Background:
- On 27 October, Stubb and Støre held a phone call with Putin.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that during the conversation, the leaders of Norway and Finland discussed steps to de-escalate the war, particularly in relation to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
- The Kremlin's account of the call said that Putin had, among other things, reminded Stubb and Støre of the "root causes" of the war against Ukraine.
- Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen later said she was highly sceptical about the outcome of the call, which had allegedly not been coordinated with other European countries.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that the call had been coordinated with the Ukrainian side.
- During a meeting with US President Donald Trump in Alaska in 2025, Putin delivered another lengthy "historical" speech about Ukraine. This did not go down well with Trump, who became angry and even threatened to walk out.

OpenAI plans to buy Google’s chips as part of its AI build-out
- OpenAI plans to buy Google’s AI chips to boost its computing power, according to a person familiar with the matter. The deal terms are still unknown.
- The move is part of OpenAI’s wider push to build AI infrastructure fast. It also plans to use its own chips in 2026, including Jalapeno chips made with Broadcom.
- Google’s TPUs, first built for search, are now a rival to Nvidia’s chips. Oracle will also offer TPUs in its cloud, as Google says AI needs “a diverse range of compute”.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI intends to buy artificial intelligence computing chips from Alphabet’s Google, according to a person familiar with the matter, part of broader efforts by the ChatGPT maker to build out its AI infrastructure.
The final terms of any deal are not yet known, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. OpenAI and Google declined to comment.
The move reflects OpenAI’s multi-pronged bid to quickly add more AI processing power.
The company has already announced plans to start using its own chips to support its artificial intelligence models later in 2026.
It joins a stampede of companies working to develop home-grown AI chips and challenge Nvidia’s dominance in the field.
OpenAI’s in-house Jalapeno chips, developed with Broadcom, were created with help from Google veterans. Richard Ho, who runs the OpenAI internal chip team, was previously involved in the development of Google’s semiconductors – known as tensor processing units, or TPUs.
Google began working on its TPUs more than a decade ago. Initially, the processors were used to speed up the company’s web search engine and improve efficiency.
But the chips soon proved valuable for handling AI work and have emerged in recent years as an alternative to Nvidia’s prized graphics processing units.
Oracle also announced on Oct 27 that TPUs would be available through its cloud-computing infrastructure.
“The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute,” Google executive Amin Vahdat said in a statement announcing that deal.
The Information previously reported that OpenAI was planning to buy Google chips. BLOOMBERG

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The ruling DPP is gaining ground ahead of November's local elections, while the opposition KMT faces growing challenges, Japanese political analyst Ogasawara Yoshiyuki said Tuesday.
Ogasawara, an honorary professor at National Tsing Hua University, said the DPP could win races in Chiayi, Changhua County, and Yilan County, CNA reported. He also saw opportunities in New Taipei and Hsinchu County, although the party could lose Penghu County.
Ogasawara identified New Taipei as the most important race in the Nov. 28 elections. He said DPP candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) had steadily gained on KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), drawing level in the spring before taking a narrow lead after September.
He said winning either Taipei or New Taipei would be a major victory for the DPP. Even if the KMT won 13 or 14 of Taiwan's 22 mayoral and county leader seats, losing New Taipei would still amount to a political defeat, he said.
In Taipei, Ogasawara said DPP candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had gained ground since September and was now running neck and neck with incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安). He said Shen had stronger momentum but cautioned that the race remained too close to call.
Ogasawara linked the DPP's improving prospects to growing public frustration with the KMT's actions in the legislature. He said opposition efforts to block government spending had delayed approval of this year's central government budget until August, a record 266 days late.
He also cited a dispute over cuts and freezes to the Presidential Office's budget, which forced it to cancel orders for mooncakes from workshops employing people with disabilities. Ogasawara said the controversy had fueled criticism that the opposition had gone too far.
Ogasawara said the KMT may have become overconfident after defeating efforts to remove its lawmakers from office in last year's recall votes. However, he said recall votes and regular elections involve different political dynamics.
Meanwhile, Ogasawara said the DPP had shifted its campaign strategy toward local issues and everyday concerns. Rather than focusing on its message of resisting China and defending Taiwan, the party was paying greater attention to voters' daily needs.

Incorrect or non-functional contact numbers create unnecessary difficulties for candidates. We will also raise the matter in a meeting and seek a resolution.”
The issue assumes significance for candidates who have opted for the float option in counselling. Those choosing freeze accept the allotted seat, while candidates choosing float wish to retain their current allotment while remaining eligible for an upgrade in subsequent rounds. Candidates who have to complete online reporting and submit documents are seeking timely verification and clear communication from their allotted institutes.The MCC portal itself displays a message stating that document verification is pending at the allotted institute and advises candidates to contact the nodal officer for admission-related queries. But when the listed contact details do not work, candidates are left without a clear channel to resolve their concerns.
A social media post by a former J&K nodal officer for the Diplomate of National Board (DNB) programme also raised questions over outdated contact details. He said an MCC allotment letter dated October 23 listed his name and personal mobile number as the J&K nodal officer despite his having retired.Candidates say delays or confusion over document verification can leave them uncertain about whether their joining formalities have been completed within the prescribed timeline. They want the MCC and participating colleges to ensure that contact details are current, officials are reachable and admission-related queries are addressed promptly.The complaints raise questions about who is accountable for coordinating online joining during counselling, and what recourse candidates have when neither the college nor the helpline can resolve their queries.

Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Meta, Snap head to trial in another case about social media’s harms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:06:00 UTC
11:06:00 KST

Meta, Snap head to trial in another case about social media’s harms
SAN FRANCISCO – Jury selection is expected to begin on Oct 28 in Los Angeles for another landmark trial about the alleged harms of social media on young users, with Meta and, for the first time, Snap as defendants.
Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.
The cases – the first of which went to trial earlier in 2026 in Los Angeles – have taken twists and turns.
Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier in 2026, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined US$6 million (S$7.7 million) penalty.
Meta said at the time that they “respectfully disagree” with the verdict.
Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.
Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August. That plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.
TikTok and YouTube were previously named as defendants in the new case, but both companies reached settlement agreements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, before the start of the trial, their lawyers said.
Meta reached a settlement agreement with one of the plaintiffs, SJ, but not KDB, according to their lawyers.
A California state judge consolidated both cases into a single trial.
If no additional settlements are reached before opening statements kick off on Nov 4, the new trial will move forward with both Meta and Snap as defendants.
Star witnesses are expected to testify beginning mid-November, including Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel.
Earlier in October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A New Mexico jury previously found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million.
In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys-general several days into a trial held in California.
Part of that settlement hinged on YouTube and TikTok making similar changes to their own products, such as limiting daily screen time.
‘Addictive and problematic’
As regulators around the world grapple with reining in, or even banning, social media use for teens, American lawsuits have focused on allegations of addictive design and deceptive practices by social media companies.
In November, lawyers for the two plaintiffs in Los Angeles – SJ and KDB – will argue that their clients were exposed to “addictive and problematic” social media apps when they started using them at 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.
SJ, a teen in Illinois, began to use Snapchat, the app created by Snap, compulsively and subsequently experienced mental health issues, an eating disorder and self harm, her lawyers claim.
KDB, now an 18-year-old from Mississippi, similarly developed compulsive use of both Meta and Snap, leading to worsening mental and physical health, according to her lawyers.
Meta has previously denied such claims.
“We will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits,” Meta told AFP in July.
Snap intends to argue that it is different from other apps like Meta’s Instagram and Facebook because of Snapchat’s focus on primarily being a messaging platform.
“We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement. AFP

UN chief appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action and police
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has announced the appointment of Russian ambassador Gleb Desyatnikov as Assistant Secretary-General for Mine Action and Police in the Department of Peace Operations.
Source: the UN Secretary-General's office
Details: Desyatnikov will lead the division responsible for coordinating the UN's mine action activities and police contingents serving in peacekeeping missions around the world.
The organisation said the diplomat has "more than 35 years of experience in international relations, political affairs and security issues across government, multilateral diplomacy and conflict-affected regions".
He has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018. Before that, from 2010 to 2018, he was deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Department of Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Earlier, he worked as a senior adviser on Middle East and North Africa affairs at the Permanent Mission of the Russian Federation to the United Nations in New York from 2004 to 2010. Between 1994 and 1997, he was seconded to the UN Special Commission on Iraq (UNSCOM). Desyatnikov graduated from the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and speaks English and Arabic.
Background:
- In April 2017, António Guterres appointed another Russian representative, Alexandre Zouev, as Assistant Secretary-General for Rule of Law and Security Institutions (OROLSI) in the UN Department of Peacekeeping Operations. Zuev's portfolio included key areas such as the UN peacekeeping police, justice reform, prison systems and the UN Mine Action Service (UNMAS).
- In March 2022, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and called for the immediate withdrawal of Russian troops. At the time, Ukrainian diplomats urged the UN Secretariat to remove Russian citizens from senior and sensitive security-related positions.
- In March 2023, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. That same month, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry posted a report documenting evidence of widespread torture, executions of civilians and sexual violence committed by Russian forces in Ukraine.
- In addition, Russian military structures and private military companies have repeatedly contributed to the closure of UN peacekeeping missions in Africa, including in Mali and the Central African Republic, where they support military juntas and have been named in human rights reports concerning mass killings of civilians.
- In April 2024, UN bodies and the Ukrainian government stated that Ukraine had become the most heavily mined country in the world. As a result of the actions of the Russian military, more than 156,000 sq km of Ukrainian territory require surveying and clearance of mines and unexploded ordnance.

Global study counts almost 3 million climate change-related deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:52:40 UTC
10:52:40 KST

Global Lancet study counts almost 3 million climate change-related deaths
In short:
A new Lancet report has found the number of heat-related deaths has been growing since the 2015 Paris Agreement, despite real gains from the climate pact.
It says climate action is not keeping pace with increasing health impacts as the world keeps burning fossil fuels.
What's next?
Researchers are calling for climate change to be declared a global health emergency to enable a coordinated global response.
The latest global study on climate change-related health risks has found that 3 million deaths between 2016 and 2023 can be attributed to a warming planet.
Published ahead of the world's COP 31 climate conference in Turkiye, this year's Lancet Countdown report noted significant progress had been made on key climate goals that could reduce heating by 2100 from up to 3.5 degrees Celsius to 2.6C.
It found the growth of energy from renewable sources had "vastly exceeded expectations", but that global action on climate change was "grossly insufficient", and that this had already led to significant harm to human health.
Almost 3 million climate-related deaths
It is the first time the authors of the Lancet Countdown study have quantified heat-related deaths directly due to human-caused climate change.
The authors estimate more than half a million deaths per year between 2016 and 2023 were linked to heat and that 68 per cent of those deaths were caused by climate change.
Developing countries had the highest proportion of heat-related deaths, which the authors found "reflected the disproportionate adverse impacts of climate change on those least responsible for it".
Study co-author and Macquarie University climate health expert Professor Paul Beggs said vulnerable people were most at risk from climate change globally, but no-one was immune.
"Even here in Australia, we know people do die from heatwaves, people do die from bushfire smoke exposure and things like that," he said.
"So I think it doesn't matter where you live; climate change is already having an impact on health, and that's only going to increase."
According to recently released peer-reviewed studies, severe heat killed more than 50,000 people across Europe during this year's Northern Hemisphere summer, which was marred by rolling heatwaves and fires.
The scientists attributed about two-thirds of these deaths to human-caused climate change.
The Lancet report tracks 54 indicators of how climate change and efforts to tackle it affect health, but warns that wider, system-wide risks could be far greater than the individual measures suggest.
"A severe El Niño threatens to compound the impacts of climate change and trigger unprecedented climate-related humanitarian crises globally," the report states.
"Climate change has become a global health emergency. Addressing it requires urgent course correction."
More heatwaves, droughts
The study authors noted that the past 11 years had been the hottest on record, accompanied by more frequent heatwaves and droughts.
Climate change has increased the risk and intensity of droughts, which affected more than 50 per cent of global land in 2025 for at least a month.
At the same time, extreme rainfall has also increased, resulting in a higher flood and landslide risk. The report found the world's exposure to very high or extremely high risk of wildfire had also increased.
Climate change was also affecting productivity, according to the researchers.
"Globally, heat exposure caused the loss of 573 billion potential work hours in 2025, resulting in US $1.07 trillion in income losses," the report found, with low-and middle-income countries most affected.
Western Sydney physician Aditya Vyas co-authored a separate Lancet climate health report due to be released on Oceania.
He said health workers had recorded a 13 per cent increase in emergency presentations during heatwaves, which he described as a "silent killer" in the community.
"The impacts are worse now than they were before, but also they're worsening, and for the next generation this is going to have a real impact on their health status," Dr Vyas said.
'Vested interests' obstructing progress
The Lancet authors found fossil fuels continued to supply about 80 per cent of global energy, pushing energy-related emissions to a record high in 2024.
"Unequal access to clean energy and the persistent use of polluting fuels are not only exacerbating climate change risks, but also directly harming health and increasing vulnerabilities through air pollution," the report states.
The authors also cited "vested interests", in the form of "lobbying and disinformation by fossil fuel interests and political allies", as an obstruction in the effort to transition towards clean energy.
This was "countering the growing body of scientific literature on the links between health and climate change."
The authors singled out the USA for promoting fossil fuel expansion and withdrawing from the Paris Agreement.
"The growing political support for fossil fuels from the USA and other countries threatens to lock the world into a future of irreversible damage and mounting risks to health and survival."
Air quality preventing deaths
The authors also provided cause for hope in the form of growth in renewable energy sources and its effect on human health.
They estimated that 400,000 deaths were prevented in 2023 compared to 2016 due to improved air quality from switching to cleaner energy sources.
Electricity use in transport had increased by 427 per cent from 2016 to 2023 globally, the report's authors noted, which, together with air pollution control and active travel promotion, had "prevented 85,000 deaths across 75 countries".
Scaling up access to off-grid renewables would prevent another 2 million deaths annually, which could be "attributable to household air pollution from solid-fuel use".
Professor Beggs said the report was an urgent call to prioritise human health over fossil fuels.
"Australia is the president of COP this year," he said.
"We're really hoping for big things in terms of progress on mitigating climate change, and that means reducing fossil fuel emissions."

In brief
- Star Entertainment has been fined $260 million over historical money laundering failures.
- The penalty leaves Australia's biggest listed casino operator facing an uncertain future.
Australia's biggest listed casino company is on the brink of administration after being fined $260 million for historical money-laundering violations.
The Star Entertainment Group was fined in the Federal Court on Wednesday, four years after financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC launched legal action against the company.
The agency previously argued a $400 million penalty was necessary to punish what it said were "manifest failures" at Star.
But the stockmarket-listed company, which has a market value of $763 million, argued any penalty over $100 million would send it into liquidation.
Justice Cameron Moore determined a $260 million penalty was appropriate for the significant harm Star's conduct has caused.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"In effect, Star put profit ahead of compliance," the judge said.
Star will have 19 months to pay the fine in four equal instalments.
Shares in the casino giant closed at 13 cents on Tuesday.
It is in a trading halt for up to two days to give management time to publicly address the fine's impact on the business.
The court previously heard that one man was allowed, alongside many other high-risk gamblers, to funnel hundreds of millions of dollars through the casinos, despite his known criminal links.
These concerns fell on deaf ears of senior management, who failed to impose adequate anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism-financing controls, it heard.
Star, which owns casinos in Sydney and the Gold Coast and operates one in Brisbane, has been dealing with a raft of scandals and license suspensions involving years of money laundering, organised crime infiltration and governance failures.
US gaming giant Bally's Corporation saved the business from administration in April 2025, allowing its chair, Soo Kim, to step up to the same position at Star.
Speaking at the group's annual general meeting on Tuesday, Kim predicted that the "fire is out".
"I didn't come here to say 'mission accomplished'," Kim said.
"I came here to say, the fire is out, and now the rebuilding starts."
The vast majority of customers weren't involved in malfeasance or unwanted behaviour, and the company should welcome them, Kim added.
Star's ex-head Matthias Beikir was fined $700,000 in June for failing to inform the company's board of suspicious conduct committed by Chinese junket operator Suncity in 2018 and 2019.

Hackers target US FEC system, disrupting campaign finance disclosures days before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:43:00 UTC
10:43:00 KST

Hackers target US FEC system, disrupting campaign finance disclosures days before midterms
NEW YORK – The US Federal Election Commission’s website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an e-mail seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system a week before the Nov 3 elections.
The hack comes as so-called super political action committees (PACs) and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races.
The elections will determine whether US President Donald Trump’s Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.
In a statement, the FEC said, “at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service”.
The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports.
A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10pm local time on Oct 26 (10am Singapore time on Oct 27).
Around 8pm on Oct 26, a new status message said the issue “has been identified and a fix is being implemented.” The FEC did not immediately return a message seeking comment and a notice on its website said its filing system remained offline.
The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots.
The outage prevents organisations from filing the FEC’s 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races.
“I’ve never seen this in 26 years,” said Steven Mele, president and chief executive at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group.
“The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections” until it is fixed, he added.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.
The FEC posted the notice after campaign finance officers could not file mandatory reports late on Oct 26.
“We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in the e-mail to several campaign compliance firms that night.
The midterms are the most expensive US election in history, with roughly US$11.21 billion (S$14.4 billion) spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact.
It has surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when US$11.2 billion was spent on all races, including US$3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former US Vice-President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said.
Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions.
The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds.
Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over US$50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at non-partisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets.
More than US$250 million in spending was reported on Oct 20 alone, he added.
“It’s a big deal,” he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online.
“These are the key reports that tell us what is happening,” Glavin said.
“In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money’s being spent” and who is spending it, he added. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Bangladesh’s Persisting Mob Violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:43:00 UTC
10:43:00 KST

Since the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on August 5, 2024, mob violence has assumed serious proportions in Bangladesh. Incidents range from individuals being beaten to death over allegations of religious blasphemy to attacks driven by personal vendettas or attempts to seize property. Mobs have indulged in vandalism and attacked shrines, newspaper offices and cultural organizations, national monuments, and memorials related to the 1971 liberation war, even exhuming bodies from graves.
The recent killing of 38-year-old Wahiduzzaman Shamim in Satkhira in southwest Bangladesh on allegations of blasphemy and attacks on a charitable maternity clinic in the capital, Dhaka, have only deepened these concerns.
After the exit of the Awami League government, the interim administration under Dr. Mohammad Yunus (August 2024-February 2026) failed to act effectively amid the deteriorating law and order situation. Since February, Bangladesh has an elected government led by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). However, mob violence persists.
According to data from the Human Rights Culture Foundation, 537 incidents of mob violence occurred in Bangladesh between January 1 and October 17 this year, resulting in 256 deaths and 575 injuries, compared to 428 incidents in 2025 and 169 in 2024. Data from Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), a rights organization, indicates that 171 people were killed in mob violence from January 1 to September 30 this year; the figures for 2024 and 2025 were 128 and 198, respectively.
While methodologies for data collection and calculation may vary across different organizations, the data points to a similar scenario — mob violence has become a grave public security crisis for Bangladesh. And it is not stopping.
There are allegations that leaders and activists from the ruling BNP are involved in incidents related to the seizure of property. The most significant BNP-related incident in the past eight months was the attack on a 50-year-old government-run maternity center in Dhaka, the sole medical facility serving local slum women. A group of local shopkeepers allegedly carried out the attack with the intent to seize the hospital’s land. The BNP has expelled several local leaders in this incident and forced a parliamentarian to resign.
Meanwhile, questions have been raised about the role of the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh’s largest Islamist party, and its associates in mob violence linked to religious issues. The killing of 38-year-old Shamim in the name of protecting Islam is just one example.
Shamim, who suffered from a mental illness, was beaten to death by a mob. The violence was triggered by audio clips that allegedly contained derogatory remarks about Islam. Although the police initially rescued Shamim and admitted him to a local hospital, a frenzied mob of approximately 250 people attacked the hospital that same night. He subsequently died. The family members of the deceased have alleged that members of the Jamaat were involved in the incident.
Jamaat-e-Islami has denied these allegations, claiming that it is a political organization that believes in the rule of law, justice, and democratic values.
Determining the veracity of allegations requires impartial investigations and concrete evidence. It is as unjust to treat mere allegations as proven facts as it is dangerous to exempt individuals from investigation simply because of their political affiliation.
Hence, if allegations are levelled, it is the police’s duty to register complaints and the courts’ responsibility to try the alleged perpetrators under the law. But this isn’t happening in Bangladesh today.
Leaders of the ruling BNP and the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami routinely blame each other in incidents of mob violence. Neither party is committed to putting an end to such mob actions.
Over the past two years in Bangladesh, most instances of mob violence have occurred in the name of the “Tawhidi Janata“ (the devout masses).
Prior to the incident at Satkhira, a Jamaat activist and its student wing leader in Kushtia were involved in attacking a shrine and exhuming the body of a deceased “pir” (spiritual leader) from his grave and burning it. Jamaat activists were also accused of similar actions at a major shrine in Dhaka. Yet, the Jamaat has not expelled any of them. They simply dismissed allegations of the party’s involvement.
When members of any political party face such allegations, it is not enough for the party in question to simply evade responsibility; they must cooperate with impartial investigations and take necessary organizational action against those accused. This responsibility applies equally to all political parties, whether they are in power or in the opposition.
The BNP government has repeatedly claimed that it is dealing firmly with mob violence. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that since the BNP took office, mob violence has declined. Regarding allegations of political involvement, he said that these must be verified through investigation.
Whether the number of violent incidents is down or not, the bigger question is whether the law enforcement agencies responded swiftly when someone was beaten on the streets, or a mob vandalized an institution. If they did not arrest perpetrators, launch an impartial investigation, and punish them under the law, warnings from authorities would be seen as empty rhetoric. It is important that justice is done on the basis of the crime committed, and not the identity of the person committing the crime.
Bangladesh police are still not fully operational since the July-August 2024 protests. According to the U.N. OHCHR Fact-Finding Report, 450 out of the 639 police stations across Bangladesh were destroyed or damaged during the protests and the subsequent retaliatory attacks. Hundreds of police personnel were forced into retirement. Many police officials say they hesitate to make decisions that could later become politically controversial.
Importantly, mob violence cannot be addressed unless political parties allow the police to do their work and politicians rein in their supporters

Trump drastically loosens oil and gas methane rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:42:00 UTC
10:42:00 KST

Trump drastically loosens oil and gas methane rules
- Trump announced a rollback of methane rules for oil and gas producers, saying it will save consumers and energy firms “US$45 billion” and “unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas.”
- The EPA says Americans need cheaper energy, but critics call the new rules “toothless” and warn they let companies keep leaking and flaring methane.
- The changes target the “Super Emitter Programme”, “marginal wells”, and routine flaring, even as the US remains the world’s biggest methane emitter from oil and gas.
AI generated
LUBBOCK, Texas – US President Donald Trump announced on Oct 27 a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas super pollutant.
Trump made the announcement at a rally in support of Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton, who faces a tough battle for a US Senate seat in Nov 3 midterm elections.
The regulations were put in place by Republican Trump’s Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers US$45 billion (S$57.66 billion),” Trump said at the rally in Lubbock, Texas.
To cheers from the crowd, Trump added that the move would “unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas”.
Texas is by far the country’s leading fossil-fuel-producing state.
An Environmental Protection Agency statement earlier in October gave the same US$45 billion figure in cost savings, without offering a detailed breakdown of the number.
“Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work,” said EPA administrator Lee Zeldin. “They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens.”
Trump is pushing ways of bringing down energy costs ahead of the midterms, amid voter anger over soaring oil costs caused by his war on Iran.
Polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress to the Democrats in next week’s vote.
Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming behind carbon dioxide – responsible for about a third, or 0.5 deg C, of total planetary heating since the pre-industrial era.
A molecule of methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, but persists in the atmosphere for only seven to 12 years, whereas carbon dioxide can last for hundreds of years.
‘Toothless’
The changes take aim at rules to curb methane emissions from oil and gas operations.
Emissions occur at every stage, from extracting gas held underground, to processing, transmission and distribution.
“Lee Zeldin’s EPA is giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they’ve long wanted: a toothless methane standard they can use to pretend they’re well-regulated, all while they continue to knowingly leak and flare dangerous amounts of the heat-trapping gas,” said Julia Kane, a researcher at oil and gas watchdog Fieldnotes.
The US is the world’s leading emitter of methane from its oil and gas sector, followed by Russia, according to the International Energy Agency.
The new changes include proposing to kill off the “Super Emitter Programme”, a provision that allows EPA-approved observers to report major leaks with a rate of over 100kg per hour.
Another will weaken regulation against so-called “marginal wells” that produce 15 barrels or less of oil equivalent a day.
Yet another will relax rules around the routine flaring of “associated gas”.
In places like the Permian Basin where oil is the main product, the associated gas that comes up is considered a by-product, with the cost of capture exceeding its market value, leading operators to often burn it off or flare it. AFP

Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba passes away at 87
Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, best known for the "Ashita no Joe" series and the first manga artist to receive the Order of Culture, died of myelodysplastic syndrome at a Tokyo hospital Thursday. He was 87, JIJI Press reported.
Born in Tokyo in 1939, Chiba was taken by his family to the Korean Peninsula as an infant and then to Japanese-controlled Manchuria in present-day northeastern China when he was 2. He experienced the end of World War II there and endured the ensuing chaos of violence and looting before returning to Japan in 1946.
He developed an interest in manga around that time and joined a manga magazine group before making his debut as a professional manga artist at age 17.
Chiba won a children's manga award sponsored by publisher Kodansha Ltd. in 1962. He went on to release hits including "Shiden-kai no Taka," about the struggles of a wartime pilot, as well as the sports manga "Harris no Kaze," which turned into a hit television anime.
In 1968, Chiba teamed up with comic artist Asao Takamori, also known as Ikki Kajiwara, to create "Ashita no Joe," a series about a protagonist named Joe Yabuki who devotes his life to boxing.

The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:40:35 UTC
10:40:35 KST

The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
Scientists discover that mysterious “jumping genes” may have helped ants take over the world after the dinosaurs disappeared.
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- University of Münster
- Summary:
- The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.
- Share:
Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck Earth and brought the age of the dinosaurs to an end. The mass extinction that followed created opportunities for countless other animals to evolve and spread. Ants were among the groups that eventually became remarkably successful, and scientists have now identified a surprising genetic factor that may have helped fuel their rise.
Today, ants are the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found around the world. New research published in Science Advances suggests that their extraordinary evolutionary success was partly driven by mobile segments of DNA known as transposable elements, or "jumping genes."
The international study was led by Dr. Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity (IEB) at the University of Münster (Germany).
How "Jumping Genes" Helped Ants Evolve
Jumping genes are pieces of DNA that can move to different locations within a genome and produce additional copies of themselves. Scientists once viewed them primarily as "genomic parasites" because, much like viruses, they can multiply without providing any clear benefit to their host. In some cases, their activity can even contribute to disease.
More recently, however, researchers have begun recognizing that these mobile genetic elements can also create opportunities for evolutionary change. The new findings suggest they played an important role in the remarkable diversification of ants.
When the scientists compared different groups of ants, they discovered that lineages containing the greatest numbers of jumping genes also tended to have the most species today.
Even more revealing was the timing of these genetic changes. The researchers found that several major ant lineages experienced separate surges in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene (about 66 million years ago). These bursts occurred shortly before the groups began expanding into the thousands of species that exist today.
"The asteroid impact had dramatic consequences for the environment. We have now found the genomic mechanism that connects these ecological upheavals to the subsequent rapid diversification of the ants: transposable elements," explains Lukas Schrader.
Ants are not the only animals showing this evolutionary pattern. Previous studies have also identified periods of increased jumping gene activity associated with the emergence of new species in other groups, including primates and bats.
A Genetic Boost to Ant Communication
The researchers also discovered a connection between jumping genes and the expansion of gene families that allow ants to communicate through chemical signals.
Of particular importance were genes responsible for odorant receptors, which enable ants to detect and respond to smells. These receptors are essential to nearly every aspect of ant social behavior. Ants depend heavily on chemical cues to find their way through the environment, identify members of their own colonies, and coordinate activities with other ants.
The findings suggest that jumping genes may have contributed to the expansion of these sensory systems, potentially improving the ability of ants to detect and interpret the chemical messages that make their complex societies possible.
Tracing 100 Million Years of Ant Evolution
To investigate how jumping genes influenced ant evolution, the international research team examined and compared the genomes of 163 ant species. These represented twelve of the 16 ant subfamilies that survive today, providing a broad picture of the genetic diversity found across modern ants.
Using these genomic comparisons, the scientists reconstructed how transposable elements evolved and changed in activity over the past 100 million years.
Their results reveal a striking connection between ancient bursts of jumping gene activity and the later diversification of ants, suggesting that DNA sequences once dismissed as genetic parasites may have helped one of Earth's most successful insect groups flourish.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Münster. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lukas Schrader, Janina L. Rinke, Mohammed Errbii, Scott J. Teresi, Esther van den Bos, Zijun Xiong, Joel Vizueta, Jacobus J. Boomsma, Jürgen Gadau, Guojie Zhang. Transposable elements as evolutionary catalysts of ant macrodiversity. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (39) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee0306

What Type of Country Should India Be? The Debate Over the Sharjeel Imam Interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:37:00 UTC
10:37:00 KST

Sharjeel Imam, an Indian Muslim student activist who has been in jail since 2020 on charges relating to his alleged role in instigating communal riots in Delhi that year, recently gave an interview to The Quint news outlet.
Imam’s interview has sparked much debate in India, particularly because it presents a vision of India that is starkly at odds with the project of the modern Indian state and its constitution. Whatever one may think about the circumstances of his arrest — he has been both denied bail and trial — his ideas on India’s constitutional and political arrangement are problematic and deserving of criticism.
At the heart of Imam’s vision is the need for the Muslim community to have “community rights.” Community rights refer to group or corporate rights, which is the notion that groups can have certain rights particular to their group rather than those possessed by society — and all the individuals belonging to it — at large. This idea is necessary, as per Imam, because Muslims are a separate nation apart from, and distinct from, the larger mass of Indians, who are majority Hindu. Imam’s preference is for a “constitutional arrangement in which Muslims will have full autonomy to administer their affairs, carry out those reform programs, etc without fear of violence and interference from the majority community.”
The reason given for this proposal is the assertion that Muslims have faced discrimination within the modern Indian state, something that is true in some times and places. But his definition of discrimination goes beyond combating bigotry and guaranteeing constitutional rights so every citizen of India is treated with equal dignity. Rather, he alleges Muslims are discriminated against by the very circumstance of living under a constitution “which gave no statutory guarantees to Muslims.”
As the pseudonymous Muslim writer Ibn Khaldun Bharati noted in ThePrint news portal, Imam essentially rejects the framework of liberalism, rather than criticizing the Indian state for not living up to liberalism. According to Ibn Khaldun, Imam “dismisses liberalism as a ploy for majoritarianism… he contemptuously rejects any suggestion of a difference between liberals and Hindutvadis. For him, both are simply Hindus. In his essentialist worldview, all Hindus are the same, for they are unanimous in denying Muslims the political power they claim as a divine right….” In other words, the liberal promise of constitutionally protected individual rights is problematic by its very nature in denying groups their corporate rights. It privileges the group — and its desire to preserve its own distinctive traditions, laws, and customs — over the larger body of citizens which form the Indian nation.
Imam’s arguments are not new, nor are they exclusive to him or his community. In fact, India has long had a problem of groups demanding group rights, quotas on the basis of caste and gender, disproportionate regional representation, and various other schemes to privilege the rights of communities at the expense of individuals. In each instance, despite very different historical justifications, the logic is similar: a belief that a community’s needs or importance entitle it to a special dispensation, reserved seats, or legal privileges.
On the subject of needs, one of Imam’s defenders, Asim Ali, notes in The Telegraph that Imam’s proposals lie within the tradition of radical democratic politics, arguing that communities should organize around their own particular demands before negotiating with other communities. Imam holds that various underprivileged communities like Muslims and Dalits must work together and fight for decentralization, autonomous institutions, and proportional representation, making it more difficult for the majority to exercise power over minorities.
At the heart of this issue is a question: should India’s constitutional model be that of a country of individual citizens and individual rights or a country of corporate communities, including various religious groups, regional ethnicities, and jatis (castes)?
As Muslim leaders gathered at Simla in 1906 suggested to the British Viceroy of India, Lord Minto, “any kind of representation, direct or indirect, and in all other ways affecting their status and influence, should be commensurate not merely with the numerical strength but also with their political importance.” Subsequently, separate electorates were established for the Muslims of British India. A separate electorate is different from a quota or reserved seat in that only members of a specific group, who have their own voter roll, can elect their own representatives.
This led to demands for separate electorates for other groups, such as Dalits (formerly “Untouchables”). Negotiations between Indian independence leader Mohandas K. Gandhi and Dalit leader Bhimrao R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact in 1932, in which Dalits gave up their demand for a separate electorate but retained seats reserved for members of their community that the entire electorate could vote for. This compromise is enshrined in India’s post-independence constitution, which adopted the classical liberal propositions of one man, one vote, and a single electorate undivided by caste or religion (Article 325), while also making an allowance for some reserved seats.
The demand for group rights, laws specific to certain groups, quotas, and reservations, though rooted in a desire to remedy past injustices, has morphed into ways for groups to acquire privileges and entrench their power. They are not about protecting the constitutionally guaranteed rights of Indian citizens — only strict adherence to the constitution’s guarantee of individual equality under the law would accomplish that.
Entrenching more group rights would help permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges. It would also help justify majoritarianism as well, because if minorities have group rights, why not the majority?
Ultimately, this line of thinking could inhibit the true emergence of a modern state and society because it keeps a large number of people trapped in zero-sum, communal competition. For, if one group can have certain special rights in how they manage their personal relations, why not another group? If one group has its own electorate or a certain quota, why not another group — that would seem fair, after all. One group securing favorable representation is another group’s loss because it decreases the latter group’s percentage of representation.
Sharjeel Imam’s interview engendered debate because his ideas are so combustible. By seeking to define the Indian Muslim community as a distinct nation, by seeing oppression in the denial of specific group rights, and by alleging that India’s modern nation-building project is illegitimate and fake — an oppressive construct rather than an attempt to build a nation-state that guarantees all its citizens equal rights as individuals — he lays the groundwork for his solution: the fragmentation of the Indian social body itself. This would potentially lead to the Balkanization of citizenship and endless internecine domestic conflict. His logic points to a state seen not as one body of equal citizens, but as a negotiated compact among separate communities. It is hardly a formula for a functioning nation-state.
The alternative is a polity guided by an electorate that at least can aspire to vote on the basis of seeking solutions to economic, developmental, and national security issues, the very issues that a strong, modern nation-state is constituted to handle. This is, after all, the raison d’être of nation-building. In the 1940s, a key philosophical difference between the Indian National Congress (INC) and the All-India Muslim League was between their visions. The INC sought a stronger, more centralized government inhabited by a diverse but undivided Indian nation. But the Muslim League saw India as a land inhabited by separate nations, which necessitated proportional representation, devolution, and eventually, partition. In an era characterized by swift technological change, economic challenges, and geopolitical threats, India seems wise to have gone down the path that it did, not a path similar to the one Sharjeel Imam is advocating.

Wired for War: Israeli spy-tech firm targeted Starlink users – researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:36:52 UTC
10:36:52 KST

Wired for War: Israeli spy-tech firm targeted Starlink users – researchers
An Israeli online advertising company implicated in spyware attacks targeting internet users was heavily active on SpaceX’s Starlink service, Japanese researchers have found, bolstering claims that the firm was running a “targeting and tracking” operation masquerading as a commercial advertising business.
Earlier this month, Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant published extensive investigations identifying Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising technology company, as a middleman helping spyware firms, including Candiru and Intelos, as well as a little-known US-linked operator known as Dark Cartographer, track internet users and potentially infect their devices without their knowledge.
Discover-Tech’s operation involved buying ad space on hundreds of thousands of websites and apps, using ads to gather information about the users that saw them, and selling this data to the spyware companies, who could then target specific users and install spyware on their devices via code concealed in Discover-Tech’s ads.
Despite presenting itself as a commercial operation, Discover-Tech concentrated much of its advertising spending on markets that would be of limited interest to conventional advertisers. Of 228 countries and territories examined, Palestine was the most heavily targeted, despite its population having severely limited access to Western goods and relatively little purchasing power.
In more than 100 countries, Discover-Tech was the leading bidder for advertising space targeting Starlink users, according to researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Japanese cybersecurity firm Trend Micro. The company was also the largest advertising bidder in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan, and the second-largest in Afghanistan.
TrendAI published its findings on October 15, identifying the suspicious advertiser only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79. Six people familiar with the research subsequently told Reuters that the codename referred to Discover-Tech.
Noting that “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero,” the researchers concluded that the company was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.”
The findings suggest that Discover-Tech may have been attempting to identify, geolocate, or monitor Starlink users. However, they do not establish that the company successfully infected Starlink users’ devices with spyware.
Who runs Discover-Tech?
Founded in 2020 by Israeli entrepreneur Dekel Boni, Discover-Tech appointed Eric Banoun as its director. Banoun co-founded Circles, a surveillance company affiliated with Pegasus spyware developer NSO Group, and Senpai Technologies, a company known for developing and selling surveillance software to governments, including those of Angola, Indonesia, and Malaysia.
Banoun also founded Intelos, which uses advertisements similar to those placed by Discover-Tech to surveil and geolocate individuals. He attempted to sell the technology to Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency, according to Haaretz.
Haaretz also identified Sara Hamou, through her holding company, as a shareholder in Discover-Tech. Hamou is a former manager at Intellexa, the company that marketed Predator spyware in Greece. Earlier this year, she was sentenced to eight years in prison for her role in the Predator scandal.
Is Discover-Tech linked to the Israeli government?
It remains unclear who Candiru, Intelos, and Dark Cartographer sold their services to, once they had obtained user data from Discover-Tech. However, as RT covered earlier in our ‘Wired for War’ series, Israel views its domestically-developed spyware programs as weapons, and retains the final say over where they may be exported to. 
According to a 2021 investigation by Haaretz, export licenses for Pegasus were often granted when sales were considered beneficial to Israeli foreign policy interests, including in connection with trade agreements or diplomatic support for Israel at the UN.
Other Israeli spy-tech companies covered in the series, including Black Cube, BlackCore, and Paragon Solutions, all worked to advance Israel’s interests, even when they were not directly hired by the Israeli state.
Discover-Tech’s advertising infrastructure was used to target at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera with Candiru spyware in 2024 and 2025, according to Citizen Lab. Researchers confirmed that some devices were infected through malicious advertisements that required no interaction from users.
The attacks occurred during a period of heightened tensions between Israel and the Qatar-based broadcaster, which the Israeli authorities have accused of threatening national security. Candiru was founded by two Israel Defense Forces (IDF) intelligence veterans and operates under Israeli defense export controls.
While the Israeli government has not been accused of ordering Candiru to surveil Al Jazeera journalists, the targeting raises questions about whether the company’s clients shared interests with the Israeli authorities. The investigations have not identified the government or client responsible for commissioning the attacks.
Is Discover-Tech still operating?
Following the investigations by Citizen Lab and Confiant, several major advertising companies took action against Discover-Tech. Google, Comcast-owned Beeswax, and Eskimi blocked the firm from their platforms, while Vungle suspended its access pending a review. Industry association IAB Europe also suspended Discover-Tech from its list of approved vendors.
Discover-Tech’s website, which markets the company as a “tailored digital advertising agency,” remains active. The firm has not publicly responded to the findings reported by Citizen Lab, Confiant, or TrendAI.

Ukrposhta cuts network to 7,211 branches over three years, Lubinets says
The ombudsman reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
“Imagine: the post office in your village has closed. Where do you go now to collect your pension? How do you pay your bills? Will the mobile post office come, and when can you expect it?
These questions arise for a reason. I’ve been receiving complaints about the closure of post offices and the operation of the mobile postal service. That’s why I decided to look into what’s happening and whether people are losing access to essential services,” he wrote.
According to Lubinets, over the past three years, Ukrposhta has reduced its network from 10,000 to 7,211 branches. At the same time, the ombudsman noted, mobile branches accounted for about 28% of the network in 2024–2025.
“The number of mail carriers in 2023–2024 nearly halved—from 12,505 to 6,658. But it’s something else that raises the most questions. During the Ombudsman’s Office’s monitoring, we found that Ukrposhta does not keep separate records of settlements where a stationary branch has been replaced by a mobile one, and those where there is no post office at all. “This means we cannot fully assess where mobile postal services are actually solving the problem, and where people risk being left without services,” he noted.
The Ombudsman stated that Russia’s war against Ukraine is affecting the postal service’s operations. According to his data, from the beginning of 2022 through July 1, 2026, 1,070 postal facilities ceased operations or changed their operating hours due to security concerns.
“I have provided Ukrposhta with recommendations to improve tracking and monitor how the mobile branches are operating and whether people have access to services. It’s not enough to simply close a branch and replace it with a mobile one. We need to ensure that people can actually get what they used to come to the post office for,” Lubinets wrote in his post.
As reported by Ukrinform, city branches of JSC “Ukrposhta” will prioritize processing incoming and outgoing parcels.

US Justice Department sues Maryland school district over transgender policies

US Justice Department sues Maryland school district over transgender policies
WASHINGTON – The US Justice Department sued a public school district in Maryland on Oct 27 over transgender policies that it alleged had violated federal law, the latest attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to limit transgender rights.
The Trump administration has launched federal probes against educational institutions and threatened to freeze their federal funding over transgender policies.
The Justice Department complaint filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland alleged that Anne Arundel County Public Schools violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA).
The school district said it “disagrees with the allegations and stands by its compliance with FERPA and PPRA”, saying it has been in regular contact with the Justice Department in “good faith” and found the department’s decision to pursue litigation “regrettable”.
The school system covers 128 schools serving more than 84,000 students, according to its website.
Trump has cast the gender identity of transgender people as a lie, issued a series of executive actions targeting their rights and stated in a directive that the US government will recognise only two sexes: male and female.
The US Education Department previously accused the school district of being in violation of federal law by classifying information about a student’s gender identity as “confidential medical information” that cannot be shared with parents.
“Schools should not discuss preferred pronouns or ‘gender identity’ with a student without parental notification and consent,” Assistant Attorney-General Harmeet Dhillon of the Justice Department’s civil rights division said on Oct 27.
Trump has also targeted educational institutions over other issues like climate initiatives, pro-Palestine protests against US ally Israel’s assault on Gaza and diversity programmes, leading to concerns about academic freedom, free speech and due process. REUTERS

“I feel better,” Kalanit Sharon, 37, told AFP as cheers erupted in the Tel Aviv hall packed with backers of Eisenkot and his Yashar party.

Anat Margolin, a 49-year-old engineer, was less confident.

“We expect a trilateral format in November, with Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives,” Zelensky said in his evening address.
“It is important that Europe also take part in all diplomatic moves. Ukraine has always insisted that Europe must be present and must have a say in the decisions,” he said.

The Ukrainian president’s comments underscored Kyiv’s position that any settlement must address not only Ukraine’s future but also the security interests of European countries affected by Russia’s war.
The anticipated negotiations are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, according to statements from Moscow. Discussions are being prepared at the level of negotiating teams, rather than as a summit of the three countries’ presidents.

Zelensky’s appeal followed a rare phone call on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Zelensky Urges US to End Month-Long Patriot Missile Delay as Russian Strikes Kill Civilians
The call, conducted from Helsinki, was initiated by Finland and Norway in consultation with Ukraine and followed diplomatic discussions held in Oslo on Oct. 20.

“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said, emphasizing that the outcome of the war would directly affect European security.
“Ending the war requires direct discussions,” he added.
Støre stressed the war’s human and economic consequences and said the leaders had called for de-escalation.
Both leaders reaffirmed their continued support for Ukraine.
Zelensky briefed after Putin call

Zelensky thanked them for coordinating the initiative with Kyiv and supporting efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations.
The leaders also discussed preparations for the November trilateral meeting and possible formats for broader European participation.
Finland and Norway, both of which share borders with Russia, have a particular interest in reliable security arrangements, Zelensky noted.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, said the participants had welcomed plans to resume trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.
Moscow reiterated its position that any lasting settlement must take account of what it describes as Russia’s security interests.
Kyiv seeks united European approach ahead of negotiations

“These days, we are doing our best to secure new support packages,” he said.
“Coordination with our partners is also ongoing to ensure diplomacy and meetings as soon as possible.”
Zelensky also confirmed that Kyiv would remain in contact with Washington as preparations continued.
The renewed diplomatic push follows talks in Oslo involving Zelensky, European leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Following those contacts, both Kyiv and Moscow expressed support for resuming trilateral negotiations, which had stalled after earlier rounds produced limited progress beyond prisoner exchanges.

DUYI HAN turns SHANGHAI RESIDENCE INTO TEXTILE LISTENING GARDEN
Staged within the domestic interior of VILLA tbh in Shanghai, ‘it’s raining outside, it’s raining inside’ is a solo exhibition by designer and artist Duyi Han. Developed following a multi-week residency in the residence, the site-specific installation configures a ‘Listening Garden’ composed of textile sculptures, hand embroidery, objects, and acoustic elements. Drawing visual and atmospheric references from rainfall, cinema, fashion, and pop music, the project investigates how soft furnishings and narrative materiality alter spatial perception within a historic home.
Rain-ripple carpets and embroidered textiles shape the exhibition
At the core of the installation by artist Duyi Han, a custom carpet printed with concentric rain-ripple motifs grounds a cluster of pleated, translucent organza sculptures. The domestic rooms feature varied contextual interventions: a sheer, tailored garment suspended within a timber vitrine, embroidered sneakers arranged as static sculptural accents, resin water droplets suspended over the kitchen sink, and backlit textiles softening the bathroom surfaces. Graphic fragments of song lyrics and film dialogues are embroidered across the woven fabrics, embedding typographic narratives directly into the decorative textiles to link sound, light, and interior form throughout the residence.

dates: October 24th – November 22nd, 2026

US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:16:40 CET
10:16:40 KST

By Phil Stewart
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.
(Reporting by Phil Stewart; Editing by Tom Hogue and Stephen Coates)

Israeli Arab parties claim kingmaker status in extra-tight vote
