UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres speaks at a Security Council open debate at the UN headquarters in New York, Oct. 27, 2026. Guterres on Tuesday called for efforts to carry forward the women, peace and security agenda. (Manuel Elias/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday called for efforts to carry forward the women, peace and security agenda.
Women's participation in peace and security is not symbolic. Peace processes are more likely to endure when women participate meaningfully in advancing them, said Guterres.
"Stability is more achievable when women have equal opportunity to shape the future of their communities. And societies are stronger and more resilient when women and girls can live free from fear and violence," he told a Security Council open debate on women, peace and security.
Guterres called for urgent action in three areas.
First, there is a need to deliver on the promise of the landmark Security Council Resolution on women, peace and security: women at every peacemaking table and their needs reflected in every peace agreement, he said.
Women represented just 5 percent of negotiators across 57 peace processes last year. And less than one-fifth of global peace agreements last year included at least one reference to women, girls, gender or sexual violence, he noted.
"Twenty-six years after Resolution 1325, this implementation gap is unacceptable. Durable peace must reflect the leadership, aspirations and contributions of all people, including (those) of women and girls," he said.
All peace processes, dialogues, ceasefires, and peace agreements must reflect the diverse needs of women and girls, without exception, he added.
Second, there is a need to scale up funding.
The need is especially urgent for women's organizations in conflict-affected areas and those working to address forced displacement, where women and girls are especially vulnerable, he said. "I call on all countries to live up to their official development assistance commitments, and urgently restore funding to organizations that support women and girls in conflict settings."
Third, it is time to enforce zero tolerance for violence against women and girls -- from victims of gender-based violence to those women who are on the front lines of peace as peacebuilders, community organizers, human rights defenders and humanitarian workers, he said.
"I call for full accountability for those responsible for any acts of violence against women and girls. The UN will continue doing our part, including by securing commitments to cease such acts, documenting violations and advocating for justice," he said. "And I renew my call for the lifting of all restrictions on women humanitarian workers -- and their full protection -- as they carry out their lifesaving work."
These three priorities are not the only areas where action is urgently needed. States must also work harder to strengthen accountability for gender-based violence; anchor commitments on women, peace, and security in domestic laws and policies; ensure women's economic security; step up support to women's organizations in conflict settings; and close information gaps through a gender data revolution, said Guterres.
Equality is not a dream. It's a decision. The UN decision on gender equality has made it a stronger organization. The world must make the same decision when it comes to including women at the peacemaking table and across all political processes, budgets and policies; when it comes to standing up for the rights and bodily autonomy of women and girls in all situations, including in conflict; and when it comes to building the peace and security our world needs, he said. ■

Pic story: volunteers bring warmth to quake-hit Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:01:18 CST
09:01:18 KST

Abdu (1st L), Zhe Jiaxin (2nd L) and Alimjan Haliq (1st R) serve stir-fried rice noodles at a temporary shelter in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 26, 2026.
In the wake of the earthquake that struck Baqen County on Oct. 22, several volunteers rushed to the quake-affected zone to serve hot meals, sending warmth to those affected who are facing high-altitude cold in late October.
Among them was Alimjan Haliq, a volunteer from northwest China's Xinjiang. Knowing how difficult it is to cook at high altitude, he brought two pressure cookers with him all the way to the quake zone. Zhe Jiaxin, a young woman from Xinjiang, spent nearly 48 hours on a bumpy journey through multiple cities before finally reaching the epicenter. Abdu, who runs a Xinjiang restaurant in Lhasa, quickly rallied his friends, gathered supplies, and rushed to the disaster area. Their paths were different, but they converged on the snow-covered plateau for the same purpose.
"There is strength in numbers," Alimjan Haliq said, voicing the thoughts of every volunteer. Upon arriving in the quake zone, the rows of tidy tents and prefab houses, ample supplies, and locals helping one another deeply moved the volunteers. Zhe Jiaxin said with emotion, "I want to do all I can to help the children here feel more comfortable."
The unceasing cook fires and hot food from the volunteers did more than fill empty stomachs -- they let the affected people feel be cared and supported. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)

Lula calls Flavio Bolsonaro's departure from Brazil "shameful"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:01:12 CST
09:01:12 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Tuesday criticized defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro for leaving the country following the election, calling the move "shameful."
"I regret that he left Brazil ... And his decision to leave Brazil is shameful," Lula told supporters who gathered outside the Alvorada Palace, the presidential residence in Brasilia, to celebrate his 81st birthday.
Federal lawmaker Mauricio Marcon of the Liberal Party said Tuesday that Flavio Bolsonaro had left Brazil and was heading to the United States.
Brazil's Supreme Federal Court on Monday barred Flavio Bolsonaro from leaving the country. According to Brazilian media reports, the judicial order is related to a money-laundering investigation by the court in which Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz are both under investigation.
Bolsonaro's departure has not been officially confirmed.
Brazilian media reported that there was no record in the country's immigration control system indicating that he had left Brazil through regular border controls. The Federal Police were investigating whether and how he might have left the country.
Lula defeated Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential runoff, winning 51.79 percent of the valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.21 percent. ■

Jennifer Lawrence revealed how her husband threatened to send her to a hotel because of an unpleasant smell
Kyiv • UNN
Jennifer Lawrence said that after four days of wearing a hair mask, her husband complained about a fishy smell. The actress is developing her own brand, Mes.
Hollywood actress Jennifer Lawrence shared an amusing story from her family life. The 36-year-old star admitted that while testing cosmetics, her husband Cooke Maroney threatened to send her to live in a hotel because of the unpleasant smell of her hair. E! News reported this, citing the actress’s interview with The Cut, writes UNN.
Details
Lawrence said that she personally tested the products while developing her own hair-care brand, Mes. One of the experiments turned out to be particularly unsuccessful.
According to the actress, she left a fragrance-free hair mask on for four days, after which it began to smell like fish.
My husband said to me: "If you don't wash your hair, you'll have to get a hotel room"
The actress spoke candidly about motherhood and her attitude toward her appearance
The star of "The Hunger Games," who is raising two sons, explained that after having children, she began to view her appearance differently.
According to Lawrence, she wants to look well-groomed even when she has just woken up and is not at all ready to leave the house
The actress also admitted that a good hairstyle helps her feel more confident.
If my hair looks good, no one will notice anything else on my face, clothes, or body. I can also use it to hide
Lawrence, who previously deliberately took a break from public life because of excessive attention to her persona, is now trying to balance her career, motherhood, and the development of her own business.

Middle Powers and the Illusion of a Post-America Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Middle Powers and the Illusion of a Post-America Middle East
Gulf diplomacy fuels claims of a middle-power moment, but the Iran war exposes limits to strategic autonomy and enduring US supremacy.
Intensifying US–China rivalry, the erosion of post-Cold War certainties and recurring doubts over the durability of American leadership on the global stage have helped propel one of the more fashionable ideas in contemporary foreign policy debates – the rise of the world’s ‘middle powers’ into more autonomous and consequential actors, capable not merely of hedging between great powers but of shaping the regional orders around them. Nowhere does the thesis appear more compelling than in the Gulf region, where states have converted energy, capital, geography and increasingly active roles in mediation into influence far beyond their size. These states have diversified their relationships, expanded their diplomatic reach and have become more willing to resist the preferences of the US, even as Washington continues to maintain the post-Cold War security architecture in the region.
Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia engage China and Russia, working closely with both countries on mutual economic and security interests, while retaining their longstanding alliance with Washington. Qatar mediates conflicts involving actors Washington cannot easily reach or engage directly and has expanded ties with China, even as a Major Non-NATO Ally to the US. These states are less wholly dependent on the US, more autonomous and more active than they were during much of the post-Cold War period.
Their greater agency and diplomatic reach can be read in two ways: a transformation from bystanders to consequential players in the global international order or as evidence that a more contested system has simply created greater room for manoeuvre beneath the level of great-power primacy.
The Myth of American Retreat
The idea of the middle-power moment has been driven in large part by the perception of American retreat. As Washington has increasingly looked to allies and partners to shoulder more of the burden for addressing challenges to international security, those states have gained greater room to hedge and pursue their own agendas. However, this shift has been mistaken for a transfer of power, rather than a change in how American power is exercised.
The shocks supposedly driving the rise of the middle powers have, therefore, simultaneously established their continuing dependencies
A principal reason for caution is that the apparent retreat of American power can be deceptive. The US can reduce troop numbers, transfer greater burdens to regional partners and redirect strategic attention elsewhere, while retaining the bases, intelligence networks, logistical infrastructure, naval and air power that allow it to re-enter a crisis at scale. The war on the Islamic State demonstrated this under Obama following America’s pivot to Asia, and Gaza illustrated this under Biden; the Iran war has done so under President Trump, who has exercised American military supremacy across multiple theatres.
Diversification is, therefore, not strategy, and accumulating partners is not the same as acquiring autonomy. In addition, periods of geopolitical transition routinely create openings for ambitious actors. Pakistan’s role in mediating between the US and Iran is a case in point: Islamabad gained diplomatic relevance precisely because the crisis created an opportunity for actors who could bridge otherwise hostile camps. This was the central lesson of previous regional inflections, which were effectively litmus tests that either exposed the difficulty of displacing American supremacy or highlighted the limitations facing actors that saw themselves as emerging alternatives.
Russia exploited American indecisiveness in Syria and used its military intervention to become the predominant external actor in the country until the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. China has used trade, infrastructure and investment to deepen its regional presence. Yet even these two states, great powers, proved opportunistic rather than transformative actors. China’s shortcomings will have proved the most acute for a region and international community that has long vaunted its role as an alternative to the US. Beijing’s much-heralded 2023 brokering of the Saudi–Iran rapprochement was treated as evidence that China could begin to arbitrate regional order but the Houthi escalation, Hormuz crisis and Iran war demolished that proposition, even as Saudi Arabia turned to Beijing to press Tehran over Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
Lessons from History
Mediation, summitry and strategic partnerships signal autonomy, relevance and influence but can also be largely performative. During the Cold War, Egypt, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Turkey all learned to extract economic, military and diplomatic concessions by playing Washington and Moscow against one another but their activism did not amount to a redistribution of systemic power. It reflected the opportunities created by competition between powers. During the 1973 oil embargo – a useful warning against overreading BRICS de-dollarisation efforts – Arab producers demonstrated that control over a strategic commodity could impose significant costs on far stronger states but it proved difficult to sustain, divisions emerged among producers, consuming states adapted and the political demands attached to it were only partially realised.
The current debate on so-called middle powers risks making the same analytical mistake: extrapolating from successful episodes of bargaining or mediation to a much larger claim on the distribution of power. Europe offers a useful comparison. Even with their economic scale, industrial base and institutional architecture, European countries have not yet converted calls for strategic autonomy into a genuinely independent pole of power and are divided over what such autonomy should mean, how far it should extend from the US and who should provide the political and military leadership required to sustain it.
Most recently, the 7 August 2026 Mecca pact established a collective-defence arrangement that has the potential to become a pillar of the regional security architecture, particularly if it can give operational meaning to its core provision that an attack on one signatory is an attack on all. However, that provision was tested, and then failed to live up to its intended purpose, almost immediately by renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and again on 10 October by the deadly Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Turkey and Pakistan signalled support and the three states began discussing intelligence sharing and military coordination, and on 5 October the signatories moved to activate their collective-defence commitments, agreeing to provide military forces and capabilities for rapid deployment to Saudi Arabia. However, we have not yet seen collective military action on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.
The Middle East is no stranger to ambitious collective security arrangements. The 1955 Baghdad Pact developed into an anti-Soviet containment effort linking Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and Britain. Yet divergent interests, limited institutional integration, the unwillingness to absorb costs for another and domestic political upheaval prevented it from becoming anything like a Middle Eastern NATO.
The Test of War
The more revealing test, however, has come in war rather than institutional designs. The war with Iran has underscored vulnerabilities that portray the extent to which regional actors are still tethered to US military supremacy, from missile-defence dependence to their own limited coercive capabilities. Since the war began in February, Iran has fired more than 7,000 missiles and drones at Gulf Cooperation Council states. The UAE alone has faced more than 550 ballistic missiles and 2,265 drone attacks, while the attacks have wiped out 17% of Qatar's liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity, causing an estimated $20 billion in lost annual revenue for up to five years. To the credit of the Gulf states, their air defences intercepted the majority of those threats but the scale of the assault placed extraordinary pressure on interceptor stocks, command-and-control systems and critical infrastructure.
In 2021–25, Saudi Arabia and Qatar were the world’s third- and fourth-largest arms importers; the US supplied 77% of Saudi imports and 48% of Qatar’s, while more than half of all major arms imported into the Middle East came from the US. Iranian attacks revealed the limits of procurement as a substitute for strategic depth: integrated air and missile defence, intelligence and surveillance, logistics, munitions reserves, command integration and, ultimately, credible external deterrence. In addition, the formidable arsenals at the disposal of the Gulf states remain deeply embedded in Western supply chains and maintenance systems.
From Buying to Building
The shocks supposedly driving the rise of the middle powers have, therefore, simultaneously established their continuing dependencies. However, even amid such vulnerabilities and limitations, we may still be witnessing the acceleration of strategic autonomy among the Gulf states. The UAE is attempting to move beyond buying advanced weapons towards producing more of the underlying systems at home, including drones, autonomous platforms and propulsion technology. Saudi Arabia is pursuing the localisation of its military capabilities, targeting more than 50% by 2030 and expanding into components for missile-defence systems. Qatar is pursuing the same direction using joint ventures and technology-transfer agreements to build domestic production and technical expertise.
The war with Iran may accelerate the investment in domestic manufacturing and supply chains needed to make autonomy more credible and durable. These domestic capabilities have the potential to move the Gulf states beyond diplomatic activism and towards a more substantive form of strategic independence, built on an indigenous military-industrial base capable of underpinning diplomatic reach and reducing the extent to which regional objectives remain conditioned by external suppliers and security providers.

Turkish parliamentary committee approves defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
A Turkish parliamentary committee approved a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Tuesday, as tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels grow.
The defence agreement commits the sides to regard an armed attack against one as an attack on all three. The foreign affairs committee approved it with votes from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party and its allies, despite objections from the opposition.
The agreement now goes to the full assembly for a debate and a vote. No date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defence Agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, according to the agreement published by Turkish state media.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice, in Istanbul and Riyadh, while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran on Monday to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials say they are considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, but that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Ruling Justice and Development Party legislator Fuat Oktay, who heads the committee, urged fellow members to approve the pact, arguing that it aims to increase deterrence and cooperation, does not target other countries and is likely to contribute to peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries," Oktay said.
"On the contrary, our nation is a party to defence agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability."
Opposition parties warned the agreement could put Turkish soldiers in harm's way and embroil the country in other nations' conflicts.
"Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Turkey in the wars of other nations?" asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party.
Pointing to conflicts between Pakistan and India and tensions along Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, she continued: "What are the limits of the responsibility Turkey might assume in the face of these challenges?"
The opposition has also criticised the parties for holding meetings before parliament has ratified the pact.

====================================================================================================

Access to the pill and UTI treatment is changing. Is it a win for women?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:47:21 UTC
08:47:21 KST

How is access to UTI treatment and the pill changing? And is the policy backed by evidence?
From February 2027, eligible women will be able to consult a pharmacist at a participating community pharmacy for treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs) or hormonal contraception, with no out-of-pocket consultation fee.
If the pharmacist prescribes a medicine, it will cost no more than $25 per prescription.
Health Minister Mark Butler has promoted the initiative, which will be trialled for 12 months, as a win for women's health.
But what's actually changing? And does the evidence support expanded roles for pharmacists?
What can pharmacists already prescribe for women's health?
Queensland introduced pharmacist-initiated treatment of uncomplicated UTIs in 2020. Similar schemes now operate in every Australian state and territory.
But rules around patient eligibility, medicines prescribed and training requirements vary.
Since 2023, some of these schemes have extended to hormonal contraception. Some states only allow repeat prescriptions (resupply). Others allow pharmacists to initiate a prescription.
Currently, pharmacist prescribing consultation fees vary across Australia. Some state governments subsidise this cost. Elsewhere, patients might pay more out of pocket for both the consultation (talking to the pharmacist) and the medication itself.
The new federal initiative aims to address these differences by covering consultation fees at participating pharmacies. It also caps the costs of certain medicines — such as the pill — at rates equivalent to a Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription.
What's an 'uncomplicated' UTI?
Common UTI symptoms include pain or discomfort when urinating, and needing to urinate more frequently or urgently.
An "uncomplicated" UTI is a bladder infection in an otherwise healthy person, without factors that increase the risk of complications.
Some mild cases may recover without antibiotics. However, treatment can shorten symptoms and reduce the risk of uncommon but serious complications.
Pharmacists can start antibiotics based on symptoms when the patient meets the relevant eligibility criteria.
But people who have symptoms suggesting a more serious infection, or are pregnant, get frequent UTIs, are male, or have other risk factors may need to be assessed by a doctor or nurse practitioner.
What about hormonal contraception?
Access to contraceptive options allows people to make informed choices about whether and when they have children. In addition to preventing pregnancy, the pill can also help manage conditions such as endometriosis and acne.
For those already taking the pill, a pharmacist-issued repeat prescription can prevent interruptions in treatment, reducing the risk of unintended pregnancy.
Where pharmacists can initiate contraception, they must assess whether the medicine is appropriate, considering factors such as medical history and personal circumstances.
Pharmacists can initiate a limited range of hormonal contraceptives, including the pill, vaginal ring and depot injection.
But for many people, long-acting reversible contraceptives, such as an implant or intrauterine device (IUD), may be a more suitable option. These are more effective at preventing pregnancy but require an appropriately trained health practitioner for insertion.
Contraceptive consultations with a suitably trained health practitioner can also provide opportunities for people to talk about their broader sexual and reproductive health needs, which may otherwise go unnoticed.
Does the evidence support these expanded roles?
It's challenging to evaluate changes to health care delivery. Evaluations often lack a comparison with usual care, making it difficult to determine whether these services lead to better health outcomes.
Evaluations of pharmacist-led UTI treatment in Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory found high rates of symptom resolution and positive patient experiences.
A NSW and ACT trial of contraceptive resupply reported high patient satisfaction and few safety concerns.
These findings are encouraging, but not definitive.
There's a lot of debate about what outcomes to measure when deciding whether a health service is good quality. Patient satisfaction is important, but one concern is that it incentivises a customer service mindset rather than better long-term health outcomes.
It's important that women feel heard and comfortable seeking care, especially with many having experienced dismissal of their pain. But we also need more solid evidence about the quality, effectiveness and appropriateness of these services.
International research supports the feasibility of pharmacists initiating hormonal contraception, but this evidence is also limited.
There is little evidence examining how these services influence informed contraceptive choice, including access to long-acting reversible contraceptives.
A recent report commissioned by the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners highlighted continuing gaps in evidence about safety, effectiveness and broader impacts on the health system.
What does it mean for women's health?
Improving access to medicines doesn't necessarily improve access to quality health care. While community pharmacies are widely accessible, not every pharmacy offers these services, and not every woman will be eligible.
Pharmacists are registered health practitioners expected to act in their patients' best interests. But community pharmacies are also businesses. Critics argue that prescribing and supplying medicines in the same pharmacy creates potential conflicts of interest. This could favour medicine supply over referral to a GP clinic or other treatment.
Professional codes of ethics are important, but they aren't enough. Pharmacists need appropriate training and support to recognise when prescribing isn't appropriate. This includes evidence-based guidelines, appropriate remuneration and systems that support collaboration and referral.
The government's new policy funds consultations regardless of whether a prescription is issued. This could help. Reassurance, advice or referral can be just as valuable as supplying medicine.
Lauren Cortis is a senior lecturer in pharmacy practice and Hilary Bowman-Smart is a research fellow at the Australian Centre for Precision Health, both at Adelaide University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 28. /TASS/. Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the country’s presidential election, arrived in the United States on Tuesday with his wife and daughters after fleeing Brazil, CNN Brasil reported, citing sources.
The senator followed in the footsteps of his father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who also traveled to the United States after losing to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election, the broadcaster noted.
The politician left the country in defiance of an explicit court order. The previous day, Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports to the police and barred him from leaving the country as part of a criminal investigation into money laundering allegations
Earlier, Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that the senator may have secretly crossed the border into Argentina before flying to the United States aboard a private jet, although immigration authorities in neither country had recorded his legal passage across the border.
Brazil held the second round of its presidential election on October 25. According to the final results released by the electoral commission, incumbent President Lula da Silva won with 51.79% of the vote, while Flavio Bolsonaro lost with 48.21%. The politician’s secret flight from the country caused deep disappointment among his political allies, who had expected the senator to personally lead the opposition to the new government in the National Congress.

Kyiv • UNN
Nova Poshta units confirmed the first Shahed shoot-downs as part of the private air defense system. Nearly 100 companies have already joined the project.
The company "Nova Poshta" confirmed the first successful interceptions of Russian Shahed-type attack drones by its own air defense units. Nova group co-owner Vyacheslav Klimov said this during the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum, Defense Express reports, as cited by UNN.
Details

Nearly 100 enterprises have joined the private air defense initiative

Aid to Ukraine from allies outside the EU may decrease nearly fivefold in 2027 — FT
Kyiv • UNN
The aid promised to Ukraine by partners outside the EU may decrease from €19 billion to €4 billion in 2027. The shortfall is estimated at €70 billion.
Financial support for Ukraine from international partners that are not members of the European Union may sharply decline in 2027. According to preliminary estimates by the European Commission, the amount of promised aid stands at just €4 billion, compared with €19 billion in 2026. Financial Times reports this, writes UNN.
Details
Thus, the allies’ stated commitments for next year are currently almost five times smaller. At the same time, these are preliminary funding pledges, rather than the final amounts that Ukraine will receive during the year.
Brussels is concerned about the situation, as Ukraine’s overall funding shortfall for 2027 is estimated at approximately €70 billion.
EU calls on international partners to increase support for Ukraine
The European Commission is calling on the United Kingdom, Canada and Japan to increase financial assistance to Kyiv. At the same time, Brussels does not plan to cover the entire funding shortfall on its own.
In parallel, the European Union is seeking additional mechanisms to finance Ukraine. Joint borrowing by EU countries is being considered as one possible solution.
The issue is expected to be discussed at a summit of European leaders at the end of November.

General medicine leads NEET-PG 2026 Round 1 allotments with 51 of the first 100 seats
NEW DELHI: General medicine accounted for more allotments than radiodiagnosis among top entries in the first round of NEET-PG 2026 counselling, highlighting the competing career attractions of the two sought-after PG specialties, reports Anuja Jaiswal.An analysis of Medical Counselling Committee’s Round 1 allotment list shows 51 allotments in general medicine as against 28 in radiodiagnosis among the first 100 entries. Dermatology was a distant third with six allotments, while paediatrics and general surgery had three each. Doctors say the choices reflect different career priorities. Radiology attracts candidates because of its good work-life balance.
General medicine appeals to those who enjoy clinical challenges
Radiology attracts candidates because of its prospect of earning well early in their careers. General medicine, on the other hand, remains an evergreen specialty, offering opportunities to pursue super-specialisation and earn more in the long run. However, financial settlement can take longer, as candidates must complete a DM course and then build their practice, which could take another two to three years.
“General medicine appeals to candidates who enjoy clinical challenges, patient interaction and managing complex diseases.
While the financial rewards may take longer to materialise, the scope for super-specialisation and professional growth is immense. Ultimately, the choice should be guided by what fulfils you as a doctor, not just by how quickly you can start earning,” said Prof Neeraj Nischal, internal medicine, AIIMS.According to a senior doctor, radiology is attractive because it offers good earning potential early in one’s career. However, with AI advancing rapidly, some candidates may also be weighing the technology’s long-term impact on the specialty.While this does not mean that human expertise will not be needed, the growing role of AI could influence how students assess radiology as a career choice.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Were Florida police called over a 3-year-old's soccer skills? Here's what police body cams show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:37:04 UTC
08:37:04 KST

Were Florida police called over a 3-year-old’s soccer skills? Here’s what police body cams show
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The internet exploded with fury after the parents of 3-year-old soccer superstar Nevada Pierre claimed on Instagram that someone called the police on their son during a youth league match because he was too talented.
“Nevada was escorted out ... for being the best 3 year old in the world today,” read the video caption, which included a police officer emoji, raised hands and reference to a Bible chapter. The video shows Nevada skillfully dribbling the ball and scoring, before cutting to the preschool prodigy looking at the cops with confusion.
Now, body camera recordings have shed light on what took place during the viral incident at Martin Luther King Jr. Park in Winter Park, Fla., on Saturday.
According to a statement from the Winter Park Police Department, officers were contacted by a soccer league official requesting a response to a disturbance between the parents of a player and league staff.
In the body camera recordings released Monday, the league official tells the officers that Nevada’s parents are “creating a big scene, arguing with the other parents” and says “I just want them out immediately.”
The league official also says the little boy is playing much better than the other players and pushing them, which concerned him.
Videos shared by Nevada’s parents on Instagram show the precocious dynamo masterfully weaving between taller players and delivering powerful kicks driving the ball into the goal.
When the officers approach Nevada’s mother, Martasia Griffin, she says she is upset because she saw parents huddled together talking about her son. She says she doesn’t believe he should be penalized for being good.
“I’m a little baffled because I signed my kid up for soccer,” she tells the officers, “so they are literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer.”
As she and her husband talk to the police, 3-year-old Nevada can be seen standing wide-eyed in the background.
“At just 3 years old, Nevada could not understand why he was being taken away from a game he loved,” Griffin wrote in a GoFundMe statement Monday. “What should have been a happy childhood moment became heartbreaking and distressing for him and deeply painful for our family to witness.”
In the body camera footage, Griffin says she is concerned the league will not provide her family a refund. The officers reply that they have no control over that and relay the league’s request that the parents leave the park, which they do.
“The incident was a civil matter between those parties and not criminal,” the department said in a statement. “No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park.”
On social media, Nevada’s family continued to voice their frustrations, posting clips from the game and writing “where is the pushing?” They also wrote that Nevada was taken out of a 30-minute game three times, but nonetheless managed to score 10 goals in approximately 10 to 15 minutes of playing time.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who has represented the families of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor and Trayvon Martin, weighed in Monday on social media, saying, “If this child was punished for excelling, what message does that send to every young athlete?”
Some on social media speculated that there was racial motivation behind the incident, as Nevada is Black and several kids he was playing against were white. The body camera recordings show that the league official who spoke with police is also Black.
Early childhood educator and child welfare activist Ms Rachel highlighted the encounter on her Instagram, calling what took place “racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting” and inviting Nevada to come on her show and showcase his skills.
Reels of his astonishing skills routinely receive millions of views, and his fame has only risen in the wake of the viral police encounter.
On Monday, Nevada’s mother started a fundraiser to cover registration fees, training, equipment, uniforms and travel expenses for him to continue developing his talent in a “more supportive setting.” Within 24 hours, the GoFundMe had raised $35,000.
“This fundraiser is about more than one painful experience,” Griffin wrote. “It is about protecting Nevada’s passion for soccer and making sure this moment does not define his journey.”
The family also shared a screenshot on Instagram revealing the sports league had issued them a refund. The company, i9 Sports, did not immediately respond to The Times’ request for comment. A spokesperson told the Orlando Sentinel that the organization reached out to Nevada’s family and was reviewing the incident.
“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” the spokesperson said. “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us.”

Charles tackles thorny legacy of slavery on Caribbean trip

Charles tackles thorny legacy of slavery on Caribbean trip
- King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas and acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” over slavery, while facing calls for an apology and reparations.
- He will visit the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda, meet young people, and raise colonial issues and climate threats at the Commonwealth summit.
- Leaders and protesters want more action, with Guyana’s president calling apology “the next step” and Commonwealth chiefs set to discuss reparations, climate resilience, trade, and investment.
AI generated
NASSAU, Bahamas – King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas on Oct 27, where he acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” in the face of pressure to apologise for the slave trade.
The 77-year-old British monarch, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer, will also highlight climate threats facing low-lying islands during the visit to three countries in nine days.
He will first make solo visits to the Bahamas and Guyana, before being joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda, where he will address a Commonwealth heads of government (CHOGM) summit.
“We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness,” he said at a youth rally.
“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said leaders of “affected” Commonwealth nations would be discussing the issue in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where the issue of reparations for slavery will be on the table, according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.
Several of the former colonies have demanded the King take a new step towards making amends for colonisation and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.
As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where the Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading “pay what you owe us”.
In September, Jamaica – where Charles remains head of state – filed a petition in an appeals court in London “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement”.
Charles has previously called slavery the “darkest days” of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.
Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.
Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet Charles during the visit, told ITV News the King’s recognition of the “darkest days” was just the first step.
“Now, moving to the apology is the next step,” said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said “exploited the region”, “destroyed lives” and “created under-development”.
Modern monarchs have in various degrees expressed remorse for Britain’s central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologised.
The debt-laden British government has baulked at the idea of financial compensation.
Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from Nov 1 to Nov 4, that it “wouldn’t hurt” for the King to apologise.
Botchwey also said the “time has come” to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.
Climate resilience
Buckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the King to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.
In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat low-lying islands face from climate change.
“In an island nation where 90% of the land sits below 2m, there is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth,” he said.
“Our world cries out for healing.”
According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the King at its helm, is an important anchor in a “world that is almost spinning out of control”.
“This CHOGM is going to be one like never before,” the secretary-general told AFP in an interview, with the meeting in St John’s set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.
Charles, who has long championed environmental causes, will meet organisations working in the field, including a coral restoration project in Antigua and Barbuda, and rainforest conservation in Guyana.
“Many of these countries that are affected by climate are not polluters, and yet they feel the brunt of the effects of climate,” said Botchwey, adding that the CHOGM summit will also touch upon climate resilience schemes.
While she refused to elaborate on whether the British government and royals should pursue slavery reparations, she said the issue would be on the table in St John’s. AFP

Valencia Basket held off a spirited fourth-quarter comeback by Fenerbahce Tarfin to secure an 86-78 home victory Tuesday in Round 8 of the EuroLeague.

The Spanish side held on for an 86-78 victory, despite Fenerbahce scoring 32 points in the final quarter, seven more than their entire first-half total.
TJ Shorts led Valencia with a game-high 23 points, while Kameron Taylor and Brooks contributed 16 points apiece.
Wade Baldwin paced Fenerbahce with 19 points, followed by Shavon Shields with 18 and Will Clyburn with 15.
The victory lifted Valencia to second place in the standings with a 6-2 record, while Fenerbahce dropped to third with the same record.

Gaza’s women filmmakers turn pain into cinema as new academy launches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:35:51 UTC
08:35:51 KST

Gaza’s women filmmakers turn pain into cinema as new academy launches
Al-Bureij, Gaza Strip – A Sack of Flour, an 11-minute documentary by the emerging filmmaker Mona Abu Qass, draws on her personal experience to examine Israel’s use of starvation against Palestinians in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
The film is one of five documentaries by Palestinian women screened Monday at the opening of the second Gaza International Women’s Film Festival, which also marked the official launch of the Gaza Cinema Academy.
The event took place at the site of the al-Nakheel Hall in al-Bureij, central Gaza, under the slogan “Women Creating Life from Death”. The hall is destroyed, like the majority of buildings in Gaza, after three years of Israel’s war, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
The film captures Palestinians’ struggle to find food in Gaza, the dangers at aid distribution points and the lives lost while trying to obtain flour.
Through Abu Qass’s own experiences, A Sack of Flour explores how the trauma of hunger continues to affect families even after food becomes available again.
Those experiences have renewed relevance as Israeli restrictions on goods entering Gaza and cuts to food assistance have caused shortages and fears of a return to famine.
“The idea for the film stems from a personal experience and a true story,” Abu Qass told Al Jazeera. “It documents daily life in Gaza, weighed down by bombardment, destruction, siege, hunger, and loss.”
“I want to capture details that reveal suffering and people’s determination to hold on to their life,” she added. “I seek to show reality as people experience it and help viewers understand what the war has done to their relationships, dreams, and hopes.”
Highlighting struggles of the disabled
Another film, Beyond Silence, by emerging filmmaker and journalist Raghda al-Buhaisi, explores wartime struggles in Gaza for people with disabilities through the story of a deaf artist who never learned to read, write or communicate through sign language. His art studio in southern Gaza’s Rafah was destroyed by Israel, and his parents and several family members were killed.
After being displaced to Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, another family took him in and set up a modest studio by the roadside. His paintings reflect loss and displacement, expressing what words cannot through colour and line.
“I want to highlight the additional challenges people with disabilities face during war, including displacement, family loss, and the destruction of livelihoods,” al-Buhaisi told Al Jazeera. “Art can cross barriers of language and silence, turning an individual experience of pain into a visual message that conveys Gaza’s suffering to the world.”
Alongside those films were three others by emerging Palestinian women filmmakers – Soso: The Lifeline, Remnants of Light, and Dandana. The films document life in Gaza and the suffering brought by war.
Soso: The Lifeline follows an orphaned child and his donkey, who help people survive in Gaza. Remnants of Light follows a filmmaker struggling with the loss of her family and home, while Dandana tells the story of a mother whose eight children were killed, and who turns to Palestinian songs with her surviving family to cope with her grief.
The five documentaries were produced through a filmmaking diploma programme that began in March and brought together 25 young Palestinian women.
Preserving Gaza’s stories
Festival director Ezzedine Shallah said the films draw on experiences women and girls lived through during the war, offering visual testimony to daily life and giving women space to tell their stories in their own voices.
“Though their subjects differ, the films turn individual pain into broader human stories, revealing war’s psychological and social scars,” he told Al Jazeera. “They preserve stories that might otherwise never reach the screen, transforming suffering into cinematic testimony and bringing Gaza’s stories to audiences beyond its borders.”
The festival, which runs until October 31, features 73 films from 24 countries and offers a broader platform for filmmakers from Gaza and beyond.
But even with events like the festival, filmmaking in Gaza comes with formidable challenges. The destruction of cultural institutions, scarce equipment, limited funding, power and internet outages, and the pressures of war and displacement have severely restricted opportunities for film production. Women filmmakers also struggle to access training, production opportunities and international festivals.
Filmmaker Rima Mahmoud, a co-founder of the festival, said that war and the Israeli siege on Gaza – which predates 2023 – have hindered young women’s filmmaking, pushing some to use simple methods, self-fund projects and document Gaza’s reality even with the difficulties.
“Despite limited resources, these films deserve international exposure,” Mahmoud said. “Their makers need technical and financial support, translation, and partnerships with festivals and platforms.”
Resisting attempts at erasure
Palestinian filmmaker Mai Masri, based in Lebanon and another co-founder of the festival, said the films help young women tell their own stories, resist erasure and preserve collective memory, while building skills and accessing work in Gaza or through digital platforms.
The academy has also developed a filmmaking diploma in cooperation with al-Quds Open University and accredited by the Palestinian Ministry of Education.
Masri said that the academy is also now trying to help directors reach international festivals.
“We are seeking agreements with distributors to screen these films in educational and cultural institutions outside Palestine, and through international platforms and festivals focused on women’s and human rights,” she said.
“This would bring the voices of Palestinian women to a global audience, shed light on their human experiences and artistic creativity, strengthen the presence of Palestinian cinema internationally, and open new horizons for young female directors to reach global screening platforms and film festivals,” Masri added.

WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An FBI agent who helped lead the case against two former senior bureau officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigations testified on Tuesday that he feared the probe would look “political”.
The testimony came at a hearing to decide whether the case against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former senior counterintelligence officials, can go forward. It adds to defense claims that the Trump Justice Department brought the case for political reasons, which prosecutors deny.
FBI special agent Bryan Witt said his concerns were based on the fact that the probe began in July, the day after President Donald Trump gave a primetime speech in which he directed the FBI and other agencies to investigate whether the US intelligence community suppressed information about foreign meddling in the 2020 election.
One of the former FBI officials who was charged, Nikki Floris, sought to discredit an FBI intelligence report that said China sought to influence the 2020 election in favor of Biden. FBI Director Kash Patel directed the FBI’s field office in Kansas City, Missouri, where Witt is based, to investigate following Trump’s address, Witt testified.
“I had concerns this would be viewed as political,” Witt said.
The testimony revealed concerns within the FBI about a probe into two of the FBI’s most senior counterintelligence officials whose actions Trump and Republican lawmakers had condemned for years. The case is the latest brought by the Trump Justice Department to face claims of political bias.
Justice Department officials have argued the former FBI officials should be held accountable for misleading a congressional investigation. Spokespeople for the Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Prosecutors called Witt to testify as the agent who outlined the allegations in a criminal complaint.
Asked by Floris’ defense lawyer, Margaret Donovan, if he viewed the investigation as a “witch hunt,” Witt denied making that statement but said “people generally viewed it as that around the office.”
The direction of the probe eventually changed from foreign election influence to 2023 testimony by Floris and Benavides before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee. Both were charged last week with making false statements about their knowledge and involvement in Hunter Biden investigations.
Hunter Biden was charged during his father’s administration with tax and gun crimes. Former President Joe Biden pardoned his son shortly before leaving office.
Floris and Benavides were both supervisors on the FBI’s foreign influence task force ahead of the 2020 election. A criminal complaint accused them of lying to the House panel in denying or downplaying their role in Hunter Biden probes, citing internal FBI records and witness interviews.
JUDGE CRITICIZES PROSECUTORS
Attorneys for Floris and Benavides have disputed the allegations and accused the Trump administration of bringing the case to drive a political narrative.
US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, who presided over the hearing, said their claims had some credibility as he condemned prosecutors for filing a new criminal complaint early on Tuesday that added an obstruction charge against both defendants without seeking a judge’s approval. Faruqui said he was aware of no previous instance of prosecutors filing a criminal complaint that had not been approved by a magistrate judge.
Prosecutors denied doing anything improper and argued they were not legally required to seek a judge’s sign-off.
Faruqui told prosecutors their conduct bolstered defense claims that “everything here is atypical and bizarre and that is because this is not an appropriate case.”

By Maayan Lubell, Lili Bayer and Tamar Uriel-Beeri
JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Israel’s wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu’s coalition and potentially weeks of political wrangling to form a government, though the deadlock could allow Israel’s longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.
“The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics,” Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv.
More than four hours after polls closed, party faithful were waiting for Netanyahu to address his Likud party’s headquarters in Jerusalem.
“We need to be patient, to wait. It’s too early to celebrate,” Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Likud lawmaker Amichai Chikli told reporters. “One thing we know for sure. Those who said that Netanyahu is over celebrated too early. That is for sure.”
Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 showed Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp taking a narrow edge over Eisenkot as the night progressed. None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu’s bloc.
Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power.
Voter turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Final results could take days, and Israel’s fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers in coalition negotiations that have run to weeks or months after past elections. If neither bloc can form a government, another vote may need to be held, something Eisenkot opposed.
“In an election with such a high turnout it would be a mistake to go to another election,” he said.
Tuesday’s vote was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu’s coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.
NETANYAHU SETBACK, NO CLEAR WINNER
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister’s leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu’s leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel’s response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. He told Israel’s defence establishment that Netanyahu had lost the people’s faith and warned the prime minister not to subject Israel’s security to his own political interests.
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped high Arab turnout would allow them to play a decisive role in blocking Netanyahu’s coalition from returning to power.
A WARTIME VERDICT
Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel’s deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticised for the country’s biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel’s international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel’s foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing long-standing corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.
(Additional reporting by Rami Ayyub in Jerusalem; Writing by Tom Perry, Michael Georgy and Lincoln Feast; Editing by Howard Goller, Joe Bavier, Peter Graff and Kevin Liffey)

LISBON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Thousands rallied outside Portugal’s parliament in Lisbon on Tuesday to protest against a deepening housing crisis and recent police operations against housing activists, while lawmakers debated the government’s draft budget for 2027.
Portugal faces one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, with prices more than doubling since 2017 and new-lease rents nearly doubling, hitting young people hardest, as wages have not kept up.
Tuesday’s protest followed baton-charging police operations to dismantle tent camps set up by housing activists in Lisbon and Porto on Sunday, sparking allegations of excessive force.
Rally organisers said several thousand people packed the area. Police gave no crowd estimate.
The Portuguese protests echo recent demonstrations in Spain and elsewhere across Europe over housing shortages and surging rents.
Erica Rodrigues, 39, an actress, said the crisis affects young people and older generations because the “cost of living in Portugal is very high for what people earn. It is unbearable.”
“My congratulations to this government for the clown show it has put on in recent times. It has done a terrible job,” she said.
Protesters demanded the minority centre-right government scrap a bill that would speed up evictions and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first reading with the far-right Chega party abstaining.
Joao Martins, 39, unemployed, said protesters were “fighting for decent and affordable housing for everyone” and for a “state budget that genuinely reflects the interests of the majority of the population, rather than just a few privileged people”.
He said they were also demonstrating “for the right to protest, which has been seriously threatened in recent days”.
Portugal’s internal affairs watchdog, the IGAI, opened an inquiry into the police operations, while prosecutors launched a separate investigation into officers’ conduct.
Police reported 11 minor injuries, including 3 officers, in the two operations on Sunday, while activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 were hurt.
Speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said police acted in line with the principles of “necessity, proportionality and adequacy”.

By Mikhail Flores and Karen Lema
CEBU, Philippines, Oct 28 (Reuters) - US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth sought to reassure Southeast Asian counterparts on Wednesday of Washington’s commitment to the Indo-Pacific, pledging that Washington would defend its interests and those of its allies and partners.
Hegseth, who is participating in the two-day ASEAN defence ministers and related meetings in Cebu, Philippines, said the US would back that commitment with practical cooperation, including stronger maritime domain awareness, greater interoperability and cooperation among navies.
“These are not symbolic things. They are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do,” he said. “Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict.”
Hegseth is visiting the region as governments in Southeast Asia and the wider Asian region weigh Washington’s ability to stay focused on the Asia Pacific as the Iran war strains US military resources and creates political pressure at home.
The defense secretary described the US approach as “strong, quiet and clear,” saying it would be “strong enough to deter coercion and aggression,” quiet enough to avoid “needless escalation or public theatrics,” and clear enough that friends and potential adversaries understood Washington’s position.
“We will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners. That is, by definition, peace through strength,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth also proposed developing a US-ASEAN framework for defence cooperation to guide ties during what he said would be the “critically important next several years,” as the two sides mark half a century of formal relations next year.
ECONOMIES GRAPPLING WITH IRAN WAR IMPACT
Southeast Asia is grappling with the effects of the Iran war, while tension between the Philippines and Beijing has added another source of friction to a forum meant to promote dialogue and practical cooperation on security.
The Iran war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, has disrupted global shipping and oil markets, exposing Southeast Asia’s vulnerability to imported-fuel shocks and pushing energy security further up ASEAN’s agenda.
Greg Poling, director of the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, which tracks developments in the South China Sea, said Hegseth would get an opportunity at the gathering to tackle aspects regarding China, the South China Sea and Washington’s commitments to its treaty allies.
The topic is critical for the Philippines, a US treaty ally whose ties with Beijing have soured amid repeated confrontations in the disputed South China Sea, Chinese sanctions and, more recently, a summoning of the Chinese ambassador.
China claims almost the entire South China Sea while other countries in Southeast Asia, including the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia, claim parts of it.
China’s defence attaché in the Philippines will attend the meeting, its defence ministry said on Tuesday.
Days before the meeting, the Philippine military said it monitored and shadowed China’s Liaoning aircraft carrier group as it passed through waters off the southern Philippines toward the Celebes Sea.
Stronger signals were more likely to figure in talks among like-minded partners, added Poling.
Such partners include the “Squad”, an informal grouping of the United States, Japan, Australia and the Philippines, whose defence chiefs are set to meet on October 28. Hegseth will also join an expanded defence ministers’ meeting on October 29, bringing together ASEAN’s 11 members and eight partners, including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea and Russia.
EVENTUAL CHAIRMAN’S STATEMENT SEEN AS RESTRAINED
The eventual chairman’s statement was likely to be more restrained than talks behind closed doors and would employ familiar ASEAN language, said Collin Koh, a security scholar at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
Manila’s position as ASEAN chair while embroiled in a dispute with China was “particularly sensitive”, he added.
Poling said the Philippines had to balance “aspirational cooperation” on issues such as energy connectivity, the digital economy and coast guard cooperation against rising tension with China and stalled progress on a South China Sea code of conduct.
“For the Philippines, the whole ASEAN chair year has been a difficult balance,” added Poling, who is also a fellow with the Southeast Asia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“I’d expect tactical cooperation on the ADMM workstreams … but no strategic alignment on the South China Sea or other thorny issues,” he said, referring to the bloc’s effort to tackle issues such as maritime security and counter-terrorism.

Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week. Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Despite months of campaigning by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful nations.
Sudan’s war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
“She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts — that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General,” Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organized by online campaigns group Avaaz.
Last month, a UN fact-finding mission said foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks — including individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, among others — are helping sustain Sudan’s conflict.
“This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General,” Roth told the webinar titled “Call To Stop UAE Minister’s Bid for UN Top Job Amid Sudan Genocide”.
The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre, on their concerns about Nusseibeh’s candidacy and its implications for the UN’s commitment to protect civilians, according to the organizers.
“Electing (the UAE’s) senior diplomat as Secretary-General would hand leadership of (United Nations) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable,” said Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV.
Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Tuesday, Nusseibeh said: “If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history.”
“The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice,” she added.
Nusseibeh told the media at the UN after the dialogue that, as a secretary-general, she would work to be a “risk-taker” and “prime mover in mediation efforts.”
She has also separately said she would “put the UN’s full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people.”
Nusseibeh served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade. She previously led the UAE’s successful campaign for election to the Security Council as a non-permanent member in 2022-23. She is widely known by diplomats working in New York, who say she is a competent manager, skilled negotiator and clear communicator.
An informal council poll this month had placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body’s declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

- Villa Vie is now reviewing restructuring and recapitalisation options over the next 60 days as high oil prices hit cruise and airline costs worldwide.
AI generated
PHNOM PENH – Passengers on a luxury ship touring the world were unexpectedly stranded in Cambodia after the cruise company suspended operations, citing “extraordinary increases” in fuel costs.
Villa Vie Residences is now “working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements”, it said in a statement on Oct 27.
While the company is covering lodging and local transportation, it has not provided funding for passengers to depart Cambodia, where the 650-passenger Odyssey is now moored, Villa Vie founder Mikael Petterson said during a telephone interview.
The company’s fuel costs have risen over 300% since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the company said, with per-cabin fuel costs that have historically averaged about US$1,800 (S$2,300) a month surging to as much as US$8,000.
The Odyssey, which has been at sea since October 2024, is not like a typical cruise line.
The vessel departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for a “continuous” voyage around the world, according to the company’s website, and its passengers either rent, own or rent-to-own cabins on the ship.
The price of a cabin for permanent residency ranges from just under US$130,000 to as much as US$440,000 for a suite, with monthly fees of US$2,000 to US$10,000, according to a brochure.
Passengers baulked at a request to pay more to cover the cost of fuel to depart Cambodia.
The company is now proposing an additional US$500 a month fee, on top of a surcharge, as long as prices remain elevated, Petterson said, adding monthly operational costs have climbed by about 50% to US$3 million.
Villa Vie is also seeking financing in order to depart the area “quite quickly”, Petterson said.
The cost to travel – whether by plane, car or ship – has surged since the Iran conflict spiked the price of oil and the products made from it, including diesel, petrol and jet fuel.
Those elevated costs are hitting companies’ bottom lines, feeding into inflation and rippling through the global economy.
Cruise ships run on the same fuels that keep much of the world’s fleet moving, but marine gasoil, which powers the Odyssey, has been particularly hard hit.
Marine gasoil has surged to US$1,321 a tonne in Singapore – the world’s largest bunkering hub – almost double what it cost before the Iran war, according to data provider ClearLynx.
Odyssey had made stops in 2026 in ports from Tonga to Australia and had been due to end 2026 in India, according to its itinerary.
“As you flip through these pages, envision yourself sailing on a continuous odyssey where every day promises new horizons, cherished memories, and heartfelt connections,” the company wrote in a brochure for prospective residents.
Since the Iran war began in late February, the ship has tried to reduce fuel consumption by slowing its itinerary and spending more time in port, but the measures did not offset fuel costs, it said.
The company is evaluating restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days.
Villa Vie is far from alone in feeling the brunt of the global fuel crisis.
High jet fuel prices helped spell the demise of Spirit Airlines in the spring of 2026, while Royal Caribbean reported on Oct 27 that an otherwise strong quarter was dampened by elevated oil costs.
“It’s been abundantly clear for at least two months that cash flow was a significant concern,” said Kelly Kosmin, 57, who travelled on the ship for some segments of the journey before disembarking in Australia in March.
She had planned to rejoin the cruise in Sri Lanka in early 2027.
“The concept of affordable residential cruising has never been done until this ship,” Kosmin said.
She would be happy to pay the additional US$500 a month, as well as the fuel surcharge, to return to the boat.

In Russia, the authorities monitor millions of social media accounts every day because of criticism of the war against Ukraine

Details

Russians are held accountable for posts opposing the war
