Rubio joins Trump on campaign trail days before US midterms
Corpus Christi, United States - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made a rare appearance on Oct 27 alongside President Donald Trump on the midterms campaign trail, visiting an oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude just days before the crucial vote.
Rubio and Vice-President JD Vance are widely viewed as top contenders to carry the Republican Party into its post-Trump era in the 2028 election.
But while Vance has been crisscrossing the country in recent weeks to rally support ahead of the Nov 3 polls, it is very unusual for the top US diplomat to engage in such domestic political trips.
On Oct 27, Trump called Rubio on stage at his campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, remarking: “He’s so popular.”
“We love Marco,” he added, beckoning Rubio to join him at the podium as the crowd chanted Rubio’s name.
A State Department official said Rubio was travelling with Trump in his capacity as National Security Advisor. He is the first person to hold both key foreign policy jobs since Henry Kissinger.
“He needs time with the President on all kinds of issues. The president will be on the go, so being on the plane with him gives (Rubio) a chance to talk to him about these items,” the US official added on condition of anonymity.
While the official did not elaborate on the nature of these issues, their comments come against the backdrop of wars in the Middle East and Ukraine – as well as elections in Israel and the upcoming vote in the United States.
Rubio, who made a run for president in the 2016 election, has yet to say if he would throw his hat in the ring again in 2028.
Trump remains a dominant figure in the Republican party, and the 80-year-old has yet to endorse a successor.
Until now, Rubio, the first Hispanic and first fluent Spanish speaker to be the top US diplomat, has steered clear of the campaign trail.
He has instead focused on a series of international trips – including visits to Uzbekistan and India last week.
He is also set to host a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, Georgia, on Oct 30-31.
Venezuelan oil
Trump and Rubio’s showcasing of an oil tanker carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan crude comes as affordability remains a top worry for American households grappling with steeper costs of gasoline and other goods.
The oil, Trump said, is set to be processed at Texas refineries.
Relations between Washington and Caracas have warmed after the United States toppled longtime leader Nicolas Maduro in a military operation in January.
Maduro’s vice-president Delcy Rodriguez took power after his ouster, and has been complying with Trump’s demands for Caracas to open its energy industry to American companies.
Trump is hoping this showcase of supply from Venezuela will bolster support from voters, vowing that gasoline and diesel costs will soon cool.
Global oil prices have surged since US-Israel strikes targeting Iran in late February triggered Tehran’s retaliation in blocking off a key route of energy transit, the Strait of Hormuz.
This has translated into higher costs at the gasoline pump and sparked a surge in transportation fees for businesses, threatening further spillover into consumer prices.
Republicans are wary that voter anger over inflation, stoked by Trump’s launch of war on Iran, could trigger a “blue wave” of Democrats winning in the midterms.
The US leader has since been working to rally loyal supporters who often stay home when he is not on the ballot, as Republicans push to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump has held near-daily rallies across the country over the past month.
His third visit to Texas in the past month reflects Republican concerns, as polls show a close senate race in a state that has stayed solidly Republican for more than 30 years. AFP

Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:16:00 UTC
08:16:00 KST

Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
October 28, 2026
An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a license.
Attalah, one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine.
The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated.
Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country.
What happened during Lina Attalah's trial?
Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo.
According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team.
"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP.
The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah.
She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order.
During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds.
That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11.
Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr?
Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017.
The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022.
Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind.
Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation.
How have press freedom groups reacted?
The ruling drew widespread international condemnation.
A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."
"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful."
"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime."
What is the state of press freedom in Egypt?
The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism.
Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses.
Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests.
The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations.
On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years.
According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work.

The energy truce and Trump’s agreements helped Russia increase oil refining by 25%
Kyiv • UNN
Russian refineries increased processing to 700,000 tonnes per day at the end of October after Ukrainian attacks ceased. Diesel fuel production rose by 50,000 tonnes.
Russian oil refineries increased their throughput by 25% at the end of October compared with the beginning of the month. This became possible amid the cessation of Ukrainian strikes on refineries following agreements between Washington and Moscow and the "energy truce" announced by U.S. President Donald Trump. The Moscow Times reports this, citing Reuters, writes UNN.
Details
According to estimates from three sources in the oil industry, in the second half of October Russian facilities processed about 700,000 tonnes of oil per day, or approximately 5 million barrels. This is one million barrels more than at the beginning of the month.
At the same time, diesel fuel production increased by approximately 50,000 tonnes per day, to 225,000 tonnes. Of this volume, Russian companies will be able to export about 80,000 tonnes daily.
Russian refineries get a respite after months of Ukrainian attacks
Since mid-March, Ukrainian drones have regularly attacked Russian oil-refining facilities. This caused a fuel shortage on the domestic market, forced the Kremlin to restrict petroleum-product exports, and even to begin importing them by sea.
However, in October, after the conclusion of a diesel agreement between Russia and the United States, Trump announced an "energy truce." When the attacks continued, the U.S. president publicly expressed his dissatisfaction on October 16.
According to the Russian authorities, the latest attacks included strikes on a refinery in Ryazan on October 15 and a facility in Surgut on October 16. After the strikes ceased, Russia's oil-refining industry gained the opportunity to significantly increase production.

BRASILIA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Central Bank said Tuesday it sees no "significant risk" to the country's financial stability, noting that the financial system maintains adequate levels of capitalization and liquidity, and the capacity to withstand adverse scenarios.
The bank's financial stability report for the first half of 2026 published on Tuesday pointed to a slowdown in credit for households and businesses, a trend consistent with high interest rates and a more moderate economic activity, as financial institutions have become more cautious in granting loans.

The bank's estimates suggest the pressure on consumers' ability to make payments will persist throughout the second half of the year.
Despite this outlook, the bank concluded that the country's financial system remains resilient and the provisions held by financial institutions are sufficient to cover expected losses. ■

French Senate weighs Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:12:00 UTC
08:12:00 KST

French Senate passes Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
- French Senate passes a Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage, after violence linked to protests and earlier riots. The Senate backed it 229 to 105, and the National Assembly will now debate it.
- The Bill could force people to pay up to €10,000 and may seize welfare and housing aid. Critics call it a threat to the right to protest and warn of “collective punishment.”
- Ministers say the law is needed to stop vandals and chaos. The Senate also approved fast removal of social media posts calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state” within 24 hours.
AI generated
PARIS – The French Parliament’s Upper House on Oct 27 passed a Bill that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations, despite warnings from critics that it could curb the right to protest.
The Bill was drafted in response to riots that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the UEFA Champions League final in May.
But it has taken on added significance after weeks of protests over inequality and soaring prices culminated in some of the worst violence France has seen in years on Oct 17, when thousands of businesses across the country were damaged and looted.
The Senate passed an expanded version of the Bill by 229 votes to 105, backed by a right-wing and centrist alliance which holds a majority.
The legislation has been sent to the National Assembly, which is split between France’s political factions, for debate and voting.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the front runner to succeed Emmanuel Macron in next spring’s presidential election, supports the legislation.
Speaking in Parliament, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stressed the “urgency” of responding to the damage and scenes of chaos seen on Oct 17. “We can no longer allow the vast majority of our fellow citizens to pay for a minority of vandals,” he said.
‘Legal travesty’
Under the legislation, protesters could be ordered to pay up to €10,000 (S$14,260) for damage caused during street demonstrations. But critics argue that people who took no part in vandalism could nonetheless be held liable if they were deemed to have been associated with those responsible.
The Bill introduces joint financial liability for anyone found to have “knowingly participated” in a group formed with the intent of carrying out acts of vandalism. It would also apply to individuals who “voluntarily” continued to take part in a gathering likely to disrupt public order after two police dispersal warnings.
Welfare benefits and housing assistance could also be seized to help cover the cost of damages under the scheme, a provision that has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing parties and advocacy groups.
In the second reading, senators toughened the measure to include other social benefits such as the family supplement, back-to-school allowance and the employment bonus.
Left-wing lawmakers accused the government of an “authoritarian drift” at the expense of the freedom to demonstrate.
Communist senator Fabien Gay denounced what he called a “legal travesty that deliberately conflates protesters and rioters”. Green senator Melanie Vogel accused the government of responding to social demands with “collective punishment”.
Supporters of the Bill sought to reassure critics. “We must not give the impression that this Bill would criminalise a passer-by or a peaceful protester,” said Olivier Bitz of the centre-right Horizons party.
‘Disastrous consequences’
The government has proposed introducing protest bans targeting the most violent individuals.
Late on Oct 27, the Senate approved a Bill allowing the authorities to demand the rapid removal of social media content calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state”.
“As we speak, there are calls circulating for next Saturday that are calls for insurrection. Those are the kinds of content we want to remove,” the interior minister told senators.
Platforms would be required to remove such content within 24 hours, or they could face “blocking” or “delisting”.
In an op-ed published in French daily Le Monde last week, a coalition of trade unions and student groups warned of a “serious infringement on the freedom to demonstrate”. They argued the measures would disproportionately affect “the poorest families” and encourage “arbitrary police action.”
Amnesty International also urged the government to abandon the Bill, warning the measures could push “already marginalised families further into poverty”. Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said on Oct 26: “If passed, this Bill would be a deeply regressive step.” She added: “Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people.” AFP

FBI agent says he feared case against ex-FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden probes would look political

FBI agent says he feared case against ex-FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden probes would look political
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 - An FBI agent who helped lead the case against two former senior bureau officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigations testified on Tuesday that he feared the probe would look "political".
The testimony came at a hearing to decide whether the case against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former senior counterintelligence officials, can go forward. It adds to defense claims that the Trump Justice Department brought the case for political reasons, which prosecutors deny.
FBI special agent Bryan Witt said his concerns were based on the fact that the probe began in July, the day after President Donald Trump gave a primetime speech in which he directed the FBI and other agencies to investigate whether the US intelligence community suppressed information about foreign meddling in the 2020 election.
One of the former FBI officials who was charged, Nikki Floris, sought to discredit an FBI intelligence report that said China sought to influence the 2020 election in favor of Biden. FBI Director Kash Patel directed the FBI’s field office in Kansas City, Missouri, where Witt is based, to investigate following Trump’s address, Witt testified.
“I had concerns this would be viewed as political,” Witt said.
The testimony revealed concerns within the FBI about a probe into two of the FBI’s most senior counterintelligence officials whose actions Trump and Republican lawmakers had condemned for years. The case is the latest brought by the Trump Justice Department to face claims of political bias.
Justice Department officials have argued the former FBI officials should be held accountable for misleading a congressional investigation. Spokespeople for the Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Prosecutors called Witt to testify as the agent who outlined the allegations in a criminal complaint.
Asked by Floris’ defense lawyer, Margaret Donovan, if he viewed the investigation as a “witch hunt,” Witt denied making that statement but said “people generally viewed it as that around the office.”
The direction of the probe eventually changed from foreign election influence to 2023 testimony by Floris and Benavides before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee. Both were charged last week with making false statements about their knowledge and involvement in Hunter Biden investigations.
Hunter Biden was charged during his father's administration with tax and gun crimes. Former President Joe Biden pardoned his son shortly before leaving office.
Floris and Benavides were both supervisors on the FBI’s foreign influence task force ahead of the 2020 election. A criminal complaint accused them of lying to the House panel in denying or downplaying their role in Hunter Biden probes, citing internal FBI records and witness interviews.
JUDGE CRITICIZES PROSECUTORS
Attorneys for Floris and Benavides have disputed the allegations and accused the Trump administration of bringing the case to drive a political narrative.
US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, who presided over the hearing, said their claims had some credibility as he condemned prosecutors for filing a new criminal complaint early on Tuesday that added an obstruction charge against both defendants without seeking a judge’s approval. Faruqui said he was aware of no previous instance of prosecutors filing a criminal complaint that had not been approved by a magistrate judge.
Prosecutors denied doing anything improper and argued they were not legally required to seek a judge’s sign-off.
Faruqui told prosecutors their conduct bolstered defense claims that “everything here is atypical and bizarre and that is because this is not an appropriate case.” REUTERS

No clear mandate projected in Israel election: What’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:06:47 UTC
08:06:47 KST

Israel election results: No clear winner projected, what’s next?
President Isaac Herzog will task the strongest candidate with forming government once results are finalised.
Exit polls from Israel’s legislative elections have come in, with no party or bloc projected to secure a clear mandate to form a new government.
According to The Times of Israel, the partial results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 56 seats and the opposition alliance 48.
That could leave neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat parliament, setting the stage for weeks or months of political jockeying to form Israel’s next government.
The results also show the Arab-led parties, which are not part of either coalition, on course to secure 16 seats. This means the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if other parties agree to join forces with them.
Here’s what comes next:
What are the exit poll projections for the Israeli parties?
Here’s the breakdown, according to The Times of Israel, with over 66 percent of ballots counted.
Netanyahu’s ruling bloc is leading on 56 seats:
- Likud – 28
- United Torah Judaism – 8
- Shas – 7
- Otzma Yehudit – 7
- Religious Zionism – 6
The opposition alliance is ahead on 48 seats:
- Yashar – 21
- B’Yachad – 11
- Yisrael Beytenu – 8
- The Democrats – 8
Arab-led parties are on course to win 16 seats:
- Joint List – 12
- Ra’am – 4
How have parties reacted?
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to the incumbent prime minister, said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu, while Yair Lapid, the current opposition leader, said the prime minister’s bloc has suffered a “crushing defeat”.
“This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home,” Lapid said.
But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said the opposition’s celebrations were premature.
In a social media post, he said: “Likud is the largest party in Israel. It is always good to learn something from the past.”
Netanyahu, who heads Likud, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher based in Israel, told Al Jazeera that early exit poll projections show “a clear weakening of Netanyahu’s bloc” but expressed caution about “declaring either a Netanyahu victory or the end of his political career”.
“The exit polls suggest that his bloc has lost its majority, but they also suggest that his opponents face a difficult task in building one,” he said. “If neither side can form a government, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker while the negotiations continue.”
Who will the president nominate to form a government?
It remains to be seen.
Once the final vote tally is announced on November 4, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That will not necessarily be the leader of the party that won the most seats in the Knesset.
With Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties emerging as the strongest, the two are viewed as leading contenders.
How much time will the invited leader have to form a coalition?
Up to 42 days. The candidate initially has 28 days, but the president can extend it by 14 days.
During this time, parties could engage in intensive negotiations and dealmaking, seeking policy concessions or potential ministerial portfolios, as the designated candidate tries to cobble together enough support to govern.
If the candidate cannot assemble a coalition with at least 61 seats, they could also try to form a minority government by relying on support from smaller parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
To be sworn in, a new government must win a parliamentary confidence vote by a simple majority, which can be fewer than 61 votes if a number of parties abstain.
What if negotiations fail?
If the first candidate fails to form a government, Herzog has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
If the Knesset remains at an impasse, it would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days. In the meantime, Netanyahu’s government would remain in office as a caretaker government.
Has this happened before?
Yes.
Prolonged gridlock in the Knesset forced Israelis into three rounds of elections between April 2019 and March 2020. The result was a power-sharing agreement between Netanyahu and his then-chief rival, Benny Gantz, under which they were supposed to rotate the prime ministership.
That government collapsed a year later after failing to pass a budget.
Will the opposition form a coalition with the Arab-led parties?
While the exit polls suggest the Arab-led parties could become kingmakers, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with them, citing a lack of shared values.
Asaf Ronel, an Israeli political analyst, said that while exit polls suggest an end to Netanyahu’s “nightmarish government”, there are serious questions about whether other leaders can overcome their “racism and refusal” to collaborate with the Arab-led groups.
“The question now is whether they can let go of their racist election promise, otherwise the most likely scenario is that we are back to another round of elections in the next few months,” he said.
Mohamad Bazzi, director of the Hagop Kevorkian Center for Near Eastern Studies at New York University, said ignoring Arab-led parties will prove a difficult stance to maintain as negotiations continue.
“The numbers are going to make it difficult without that block, that large block, of seats for the Arab parties. It’s going to be difficult to get to that magic number,” he said, referring to the 61 seats required for a majority.
Bazzi also foresees an arrangement where the Arab parties could come to a compromise with Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
“They could be invited in a form where they don’t actually have any ministries and where they don’t really have power in the governing coalition, but they would provide their support in the Knesset,” he explained.

India increased ammunition sales to Ukraine's allies in Europe nearly 18-fold
Kyiv • UNN
Since the beginning of the invasion, India has exported $872 million worth of ammunition to Europe, compared with $49.2 million previously. The main buyers were Eastern European countries.
India has sharply increased its exports of ammunition to European countries that are actively supporting Ukraine with weapons. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, the volume of such supplies has reached at least $872 million. Bloomberg reports this, citing data from India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, writes UNN.
Details
For comparison, in the four years before Russia’s invasion, Indian manufacturers exported only $49.2 million worth of similar products to Europe. Thus, sales volumes increased 17.7-fold.
The exports include artillery shells, mortar rounds, explosives, and rocket propellant. About 75% of exports went to 13 Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland, the Czech Republic, Romania, and the Baltic states.
India has become one of the largest ammunition suppliers to Europe
According to Trade Data Monitor, India rose from 28th to second place among suppliers of ammunition and components for it to Central and Eastern European countries, surpassed only by South Korea.
Even if Indian ammunition was not transferred directly to Ukraine, European states could have used it to replenish their own stocks while transferring their weapons to Kyiv.
Walter Ladwig, an expert at King’s College London, said that Russia’s invasion had created new demand, which Indian defense companies had taken advantage of. At the same time, New Delhi seeks to develop its own weapons production and reduce its dependence on imports, particularly from Russia.

AI generated
NEW YORK - An American woman who joined the Islamic State (IS) group before being caught by anti-IS forces in Syria was found guilty on Oct 27 of receiving military training from the jihadists.
Halima Salman, 27, was one of hundreds of foreign women who went or were taken to the territory controlled by the Islamic State, and who then married jihadist fighters before being captured and detained pending their repatriation.
The fate of these women and their children has proven a sticking point for the Western countries from where some originated, with many trapped or stripped of their citizenship by their former homelands.
Salman’s mother is an American, and her family travelled from the United States to Syria when she was young.
Salman was convicted of receiving military-type training from IS when she was 18, prosecutors said in a statement, a crime that could carry 10 years of imprisonment. She will be sentenced at a later date.
At 17, she travelled to an IS-controlled area of Syria in late 2016 or early 2017, via Russia and Turkey.
“While in Syria, Salman was trained to use an assault rifle and received ammunition from an ISIS military battalion when she was 18,” prosecutors had alleged, using another acronym for the group.
While there, she married German-Afghan IS fighter Abu Ali, according to court documents.
In early 2019, she was taken into custody by Syrian forces opposed to IS and was placed in a relocation camp until 2024, when Salman returned to the US and was arrested.
“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said United States Attorney Joseph Nocella.
“ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”
Salman’s defense attorney had claimed she was “the victim of her (mother’s husband) bringing her as a child to ISIS territory in Syria”.
The attorney added that Salman was unaware of the man’s pro-IS beliefs.
A US-led coalition was deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group, which had seized large swathes of territory, committed massacres, and forced thousands of women and children into slavery.

Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:03:55 UTC
08:03:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Israelis went to the polls on Tuesday in the highest turnout in decades, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning whoever can cobble together a coalition will form the next government.
The country's main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and ICC fugitive Netanyahu's bloc to win 50.
Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing they won 17 or 18 seats combined.
Here are four possible scenarios:
Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate with the best chance to form a government, not necessarily the party with the most seats, which initial exit polls showed was Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab parties, particularly Raam, have said they are open to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, seeing their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious way to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold to enter parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
After the November 2022 election, Benjamin Netanyahu took 58 days to form his government.
Minority government
If no bloc secures 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority, instead relying on ad hoc support from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab parties, whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian, could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, said it is unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout "indicates a strong desire for partnership".
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
"Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results," Elovitz said.
National unity government
Given Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government may seem fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused about a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies and ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on 16 October found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot, a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the current situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu and casting him as unfit to lead.
Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 because politicians could not forge a lasting coalition.
The president-designated candidate will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although other procedural measures can prevent new elections from being called immediately.

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:00:42 UTC
08:00:42 KST

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce
US tech giant Microsoft is moving to shrink its workforce through a buyout program covering some 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global staff, the company has announced.
The move follows thousands of job cuts earlier this year and comes as Big Tech companies seek to slash payroll costs while ramping up AI investment.
Microsoft unveiled the program on Monday, saying that it would cover roughly 27% of its 223,000 employees across selected divisions in the US, Canada, UK, and India, including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, finance, and human resources.
Microsoft has described the initiative as a voluntary exit program, under which employees can leave with severance packages. The company has not disclosed how many workers it expects to accept the offer.
In a memo to employees, Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman said that the initiative would give eligible staff considering a departure an opportunity to leave with financial support.
The latest move follows several rounds of workforce reductions at Microsoft. In July, the company announced plans to eliminate 4,800 positions, including approximately 3,200 in its Xbox gaming division. It had already launched a voluntary exit program in April covering roughly 8,750 US employees, or about 7% of its American workforce, with around 30% reportedly taking the offer.
The cuts come as Microsoft commits enormous sums to AI infrastructure, including data centers and computing capacity, putting pressure on the company to remove other expenses.
Other Big Tech giants have also been cutting jobs while pouring billions into AI. Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts earlier this year, following another 14,000 layoffs in 2025. Meta has also slashed jobs while ramping up AI investment, while Google has repeatedly launched voluntary exit programs to reduce its workforce.
The trend has fueled concerns that the technology being promoted as a driver of economic growth could also eliminate large numbers of jobs, particularly in administrative, technical, and other white-collar occupations.
The threat extends beyond the tech industry. The Netherlands announced plans on Monday to eliminate around 25,000 government positions by 2035, partly through the adoption of AI, in a drive to save €3.5 billion ($4 billion) annually. The cuts will be phased in over several years, with police and security services exempt.
Denmark has also announced plans to use AI to free up 50 million working hours annually by 2035, equivalent to roughly 30,000 full-time positions, although it has not committed to corresponding layoffs.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has warned that AI could cause major upheaval in the labor market, while arguing that certain professions, including caregiving, should remain “human reserved” even if machines become capable of performing them.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in July that AI would eventually outperform humans in any job, describing the transition as “a bumpy road.” His warning comes amid growing fears of AI spiraling out of human control following incidents involving systems defying instructions. Musk, whose company xAI develops advanced AI models, also predicted that the technology could surpass humanity’s combined intelligence within five years, potentially escaping human control within a decade.

Kazakhstan proposes closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:57:17 UTC

Kazakhstan proposes closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at UN
The Permanent Mission of Kazakhstan to the United Nations, in cooperation with the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA), hosted a forum entitled “Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones: From the Comprehensive Study to Practical Cooperation," Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh MFA.
The event marked the 20th anniversary of the signing of the Semipalatinsk Treaty and the publication of the new UN comprehensive study on nuclear-weapon-free zones – the first in 50 years. Discussions focused on implementing its recommendations, strengthening cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones and engaging with nuclear-weapon States.
Participants included UN Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu, Deputy Permanent Representative of Mexico to the United Nations Porfirio Thierry Muñoz Ledo, Vice President of the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI) Paul Dean, as well as permanent representatives and diplomats of UN Member States, representatives of international organizations, and experts in nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. Dr. Ryan Musto of William & Mary (United States) moderated the discussion.
In his opening remarks, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Kairat Umarov, stressed that rising nuclear risks made it particularly important to strengthen cooperation mechanisms that had proven effective. He called for the recommendations of the new UN study to serve as a basis for concrete joint initiatives, highlighting Central Asia’s contribution to regional security and the nuclear non-proliferation regime.
Ms. Nakamitsu commended the longstanding partnership between the United Nations and Kazakhstan and the country’s sustained efforts to advance cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones. In particular, Kazakhstan and UNODA jointly organized international workshops in Astana in 2019 and 2024 to strengthen interzonal cooperation and improve consultation mechanisms. Highlighting the Semipalatinsk Treaty as an example of successful regional diplomacy, the UN Under-Secretary-General emphasized that the study’s lasting value would depend on the practical implementation of its recommendations and reaffirmed UNODA’s readiness to support this work.
Mexico’s representative advocated strengthening the institutional capacity of nuclear-weapon-free zones while taking their regional specificities into account, and continuing dialogue with nuclear-weapon States on legally binding security assurances.
The NTI representative highlighted the potential of nuclear-weapon-free zones to reduce nuclear risks, drawing particular attention to the experiences of Kazakhstan, South Africa, Brazil and Argentina. He also outlined plans to convene an interzonal meeting in Vienna and develop a dedicated online learning resource for diplomats.
During the open discussion, the ambassadors of Brazil and the United Kingdom emphasized the importance of regular consultations among nuclear-weapon-free zones and constructive dialogue with nuclear-weapon States. Experts and civil society representatives proposed strengthening coordination, information-sharing and educational cooperation, including through youth engagement. A representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted the complementary nature of nuclear-weapon-free zone treaties and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
Concluding the forum, Mr. Umarov proposed closer coordination among the five regional nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia, including to advance shared priorities in dialogue with nuclear-weapon States.
As a practical follow-up to the forum, Kazakhstan, with UNODA’s support, will prepare a concise summary of the discussion outlining participants’ key proposals and possible areas for further cooperation.
Earlier, it was reported that foreign ministers of Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates had a telephone conversation. The sides expressed satisfaction with the dynamic development of Kazakhstan-UAE cooperation, reaffirming their mutual interest in further deepening political dialogue and expanding practical cooperation in areas of common interest.

Thousands rally outside Portugal’s Parliament over housing crisis, police operations
- Thousands protested in Lisbon over Portugal’s worsening housing crisis and police raids on activist camps, as Parliament debated the 2027 draft budget.
- Housing prices and rents have nearly doubled since 2017, hitting young people hardest. Protesters called for fair housing, rent caps and protection of the right to protest.
- Watchdogs and prosecutors opened inquiries into police conduct after the Oct 25 operations. The police said 11 people were injured, while activists claimed 60 were hurt.
AI generated
LISBON – Thousands rallied outside Portugal’s Parliament in Lisbon on Oct 27 to protest against a deepening housing crisis and recent police operations against housing activists, while lawmakers debated the government’s draft budget for 2027.
Portugal faces one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, with prices more than doubling since 2017 and new-lease rents nearly doubling, hitting young people hardest, as wages have not kept up.
The Oct 27 protest followed baton-charging police operations to dismantle tent camps set up by housing activists in Lisbon and Porto on Oct 25, sparking allegations of excessive force.
Rally organisers said several thousand people packed the area. The police did not give a crowd estimate.
The Portuguese protests echo recent demonstrations in Spain and elsewhere across Europe over housing shortages and surging rents.
Actress Erica Rodrigues, 39, said the crisis affects young people and older generations because the “cost of living in Portugal is very high for what people earn”.
“It is unbearable,” she said. “My congratulations to this government for the clown show it has put on in recent times. It has done a terrible job.”
Protesters demanded the minority centre-right government scrap a Bill that would speed up evictions and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first reading with the far-right Chega party abstaining.
Joao Martins, 39, who is unemployed, said protesters were “fighting for decent and affordable housing for everyone” and for a “state budget that genuinely reflects the interests of the majority of the population, rather than just a few privileged people”.
He said they were also demonstrating “for the right to protest, which has been seriously threatened in recent days”.
Portugal’s internal affairs watchdog, the IGAI, opened an inquiry into the police operations, while prosecutors launched a separate investigation into officers’ conduct.
The police reported 11 minor injuries, including three officers, in the two operations on Oct 25, while activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 were hurt.
Speaking in Parliament on Oct 27, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said the police acted in line with the principles of “necessity, proportionality and adequacy”. REUTERS

Trump ally flees to US after Brazil election defeat – media
Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fled to the US following his election defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Reuters and Brazilian news outlet Jovem Pan reported on Tuesday, citing sources.
A senior US State Department official told AP on Tuesday that Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of US President Donald Trump, narrowly lost Sunday’s runoff to Lula despite receiving more votes in the first round earlier this month.
He is under investigation for money laundering and currency evasion involving financial ties to lawyer Willer Tomaz and businesses linked to online gambling. Bolsonaro also faces a separate investigation into suspected irregularities in the financing of ‘Dark Horse’, a biographical film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.
His brother Eduardo, also a politician, moved to the US in February 2025, citing fears of political persecution and arrest. He was subsequently convicted of attempting to interfere with judicial proceedings against his father by lobbying Washington to impose sanctions on Brazilian officials. Eduardo, who remains in the US, was sentenced to four years and two months in prison in June 2026.
Flavio Bolsonaro initially refused to recognize the election results and vowed to seek annulment, citing a two-hour extension of voting.
“They will not silence me. They will not intimidate me. Let’s hold our heads high and keep fighting for our Brazil, whatever happens,” Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Monday, although he later dropped his demand for annulment.
Later on Monday, Bolsonaro was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of the investigation involving Tomaz. The documents were reportedly canceled on Tuesday after he missed the deadline. Bolsonaro, who could face prosecution in lower courts when his Senate term ends on January 31, said on Monday that he had no plans to flee.
Trump also questioned the election results. “It had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” he told reporters on Monday. “The extension given was very strange.”
Both campaigns requested a two-hour extension of voting on election day, citing difficulties for voters, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The elder Bolsonaro also traveled to the US following his defeat before returning to Brazil. He denied wrongdoing and argued that the case was politically motivated.
Lula previously served two presidential terms from 2003 to 2010. He was barred from running in the 2018 election after being convicted on corruption charges and imprisoned. Brazil’s Supreme Court later annulled his convictions, restoring his political rights and allowing him to run in 2022, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro. Lula has also denied wrongdoing and maintained that the corruption case against him was politically motivated.

United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese has warned that the systematic targeting of journalists across Gaza constitutes a deliberate campaign to conceal atrocities, presenting her latest investigative findings as an exposure of truth that has been "buried under the rubble".
"What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional," Albanese said during a virtual press briefing addressing the genocide in Gaza.
She termed the phenomenon "mediacide", characterising it as "the systematic destruction of the media's public function".
"In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime," Albanese added, underscoring that silencing witnesses forms a core mechanism of mass atrocities.
Impunity and legal accountability
Questioned on the status of inquiries into Israel's 2022 killing of Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, Albanese noted: "Nothing, nothing happened. So, the update is impunity".
She emphasised that this culture of unaccountability was fostered not solely by Israel but also represented "impunity by the United States".
Rejecting the broad application of the terrorist designation, Albanese argued that the term "has been the label to kill everyone, to bring famine upon everyone in Gaza, to destroy Gaza".
She maintained that even where a state invokes self-defence under international law, "Israel doesn't have and cannot claim the right to wage a war against Gaza".
Addressing concerns over whether the International Criminal Court had failed Palestinians, Albanese asserted that "the complementarity of international criminal investigation can be triggered", calling for immediate proceedings "starting now with activating domestic courts".
She stressed that citizens of Britain, France, the United States, and Belgium who served in the Israeli military must face immediate legal scrutiny under national jurisdictions, warning that action "cannot be delayed".
Albanese also highlighted the noticeable absence of Western legacy media from the briefing, suggesting it reflected possible solidarity with news organisations scrutinised in her report.

Ukraine’s Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive

Oct 27 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv’s troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv’s battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
“It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions,” Zelenskiy said.
“Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine’s Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called “fortress belt” of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin’s presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia’s General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow’s forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
Ukraine’s military dismissed the Russian statements.

In his remarks on Monday at a campaign event in Michigan where Republican Mike Rogers is running for the US Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the US health secretary falsely claimed that Arabs had not won major international awards and “don’t produce” science and literature.
“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” the US health chief said.
Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with the US health chief’s comments.
The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US rights advocates have raised concerns over escalating rhetoric against Muslims, Arabs, immigrants and ethnic minorities by President Donald Trump and his allies during the ongoing midterm election campaign.

Israel Election: Four Scenarios as Opposition Edges Netanyahu but Falls Short of Majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:37:59 UTC
07:37:59 KST

Israelis went to the polls in the highest turnout for decades on Tuesday, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning the next government will be formed by whoever can cobble together a coalition.
The country’s main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu’s Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Following the previous election in November 2022, it took Benjamin Netanyahu 58 days to form his government.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
“Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel’s extreme polarization, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the center, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

Netanyahu began calling coalition party leaders after the initial projections, according to Israeli media. His Likud party asked members to suspend media interviews, Yedioth Ahronoth reported.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid called the projected outcome a “crushing defeat” for Netanyahu’s bloc.
“This is a complete collapse, and the public told them to go home,” he wrote on the US social media platform X.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot said the initial projections showed a “complete lack of trust in Netanyahu” and his government.
He said that if the projections were confirmed, he would act immediately to carry out voters’ wishes, replace Netanyahu’s government, and form one that would prioritize military conscription.
Democrats party leader Yair Golan also declared that voters had rejected the government.
“The public has spoken. It has fired Netanyahu’s government,” he wrote on X.
“We have a historic opportunity to form a government that brings real change in Israel, and we will not give it up,” he added, pledging to work with his partners to bridge their differences.
Exit polls by the public broadcaster and Channel 13 each projected 50 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 53 for Eisenkot’s and 17 for Arab parties in the 120-seat Knesset.
Channel 12 projected 50 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 52 for Eisenkot’s and 18 for Arab parties.
Neither bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Channel 12 also reported that turnout among Arab voters reached 80%, describing the projected gains for Arab parties as historic.
Overall turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 election, the Central Elections Committee said.
Vote counting began after polls closed at 10 pm local time (2000GMT). Exit polls are projections, not official results.

Speaker Mike Johnson calls election-transfer concerns ‘absurd’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:35:25 KST

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., committed Tuesday to a peaceful postelection transfer of power, calling concerns that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans could contest the results if Democrats win control of Congress "absurd."
"We're going to follow the Constitution," Johnson said in Orangeburg, New York during a campaign stop with Republican Rep. Mike Lawler one week before the Nov. 3 midterm election. "The Constitution says when a state certifies the election of members of Congress, then they're administered the oath. That's what I'll be doing on Jan. 3 to everybody who's there," Johnson said in response to a question from MS NOW.
"I may not like some of those outcomes, but that's our system," he said. "And for anybody to suggest otherwise is absurd."
Democrats and voting rights advocates are bracing for potential challenges if control of the House flips, as is widely projected to happen, or control changes in the Senate, which is more closely contested. Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress.
Trump, who has continued to falsely claim that widespread fraud cost him the 2020 election, has fueled those fears by calling to "nationalize" elections earlier this year and repeatedly questioning the security of mail voting, while also suggesting noncitizens could vote in large enough numbers to skew results. His administration sued California on Oct. 15 in a fight over noncitizens voting.
The Department of Justice also sued Alaska on Oct. 22 to block the certification of its results in the event of voter confusion. GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan will appear on the ballot beside Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Republicans have said is on the ballot only as a spoiler candidate.
Johnson, who in the wake of the 2020 election was a key congressional ally of Trump's in his quest to overturn results, on Tuesday said questions about a peaceful transfer were "a little silly."
"Of course we'll have a peaceful transfer of power. But it will not be transferring, because we are going to keep the majority and I'm going to be the speaker of the House and I will keep steady hands at the wheel," Johnson told reporters.

Alexander brothers each get 30 years for sex trafficking in US
- Alexander brothers Oren, Tal and Alon each received 30 years in prison for sex trafficking after a five-week trial in New York.
- Victims said they were drugged and raped at luxury events, while prosecutors said the brothers used wealth and status to lure and abuse women.
- The judge called their conduct “monstrous”, rejected life terms as too harsh, and the brothers said they will appeal.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The Alexander brothers, two of whom were once among the US’ top luxury real estate brokers, were each given 30 years in prison for using their wealth and glamorous lifestyles to traffic women for sex.
Oren and Tal Alexander and their non-broker brother Alon were sentenced on Oct 27 by US District Judge Valerie Caproni. The three were convicted in March of sex trafficking and other charges after a five-week trial in which a number of their victims testified.
Caproni told the brothers: “Your conduct was monstrous.”
Tal, 40, and Oren and Alon, both 39, maintained grim expressions during the sentencing but otherwise had little reaction. The prison terms, while lengthy, were less than the life behind bars prosecutors sought. Lawyers for the brothers told the judge they would appeal.
The prosecution was one of the highest-profile sex-trafficking cases to go to trial in recent years.
Oren and Tal were brokers on some of the most expensive residential property sales ever in New York and Miami, claiming US$8 billion (S$10.26 billion) in sales and dubbing themselves the “0.1% of brokers that really sell to the 0.1% of clients”.
At trial, several women testified that they were drugged and raped after being lured to parties, music festivals and other events in glamorous locations such as the Hamptons and Aspen, Colorado.
In requesting life sentences, prosecutors said the Alexanders “spent years designing, executing and perfecting their playbook of luring victims with promises of luxury, drugging victims so they could not resist, and then forcibly raping them”.
Before sentencing the brothers, Caproni allowed 12 victims to speak. Many addressed the brothers directly, who showed no visible reaction during the statements. One woman said their “wealth, power and social standing cannot shield them from the consequences of their actions”.
Lawyers for the brothers had asked that they be given no more than 15 years behind bars. They claimed that all the encounters were consensual and accused the government of trying to criminalise the behaviour of successful young men seeking to enjoy their lives as bachelors.
The Alexanders also addressed the court. They maintained their innocence and characterised their actions as youthful partying and womanising that often involved recreational drug use and excessive drinking.
Tal described himself as having a “work hard, play hard mentality”.
“I sometimes behaved in ways I’m not proud of,” he told the judge.
Caproni suggested that the brothers might have been better off remaining silent. “You didn’t have to say anything this afternoon. You did not have to stand up and say you never drugged or raped a woman,” she said.
“In my view, that’s entirely a lie.”
But the judge also said she regarded sentencing them to life in prison as a “draconian penalty” and that she did not believe the brothers were “beyond redemption”.
In a statement, Manhattan US Attorney Jamie McDonald, whose office prosecuted the case, said: “Today’s sentence makes clear that this craven, sinister conduct is extraordinarily serious and will be met with serious punishment.”

Israeli exit polls show deadlock, setback for Netanyahu
Israel’s wartime election appeared deadlocked on Oct 27, exit polls showed, a potential setback for veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the projections hold, with neither side having a clear path to power but rival Gadi Eisenkot’s larger bloc potentially giving him the first chance to form a government.
The stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu’s favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.
Israel’s three major networks updated their exit polls, giving Eisenkot’s bloc a two-seat edge over Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp, at 52-50 respectively. The remaining 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls.
Trump will respect US midterm results ‘if they’re honest’
President Donald Trump said on Oct 27 he would respect the results of the US midterm elections “if they’re honest,” in what appeared to be a fresh bid to sow doubt ahead of next week’s crucial vote.
Trump has ramped up his baseless, years-old claims of mass voter fraud as polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress in the Nov 3 elections.
“I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump told reporters when asked if he would respect the results of the midterms, as he headed on a campaign trip to Texas.
Flavio Bolsonaro, family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing the Oct 25 presidential election, three sources said on Oct 27, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Ukraine, Russia say US-brokered Oleshky truce holding
A local truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3am local time (9am in Singapore).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Pope’s cancer a ‘gamechanger’ for papacy
Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis and surgery has affected how Catholics view his health and papacy, the Vatican’s foreign minister said on Oct 27.
“It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery on Oct 13. His doctors have said the cancer was localised and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.

Russian District in Siberia to Cut 37% of Administrative Staff as Budget Gap Widens
Authorities in Russia’s Irkutsk region have begun cutting public-sector jobs as a widening budget deficit forces local governments to reduce spending, The Moscow Times reported on October 27.
The layoffs have begun in the Nizhneilimsk municipal district, where 37% of administrative staff are expected to lose their jobs by the end of the year, district head Pavel Berezovsky stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have major budget problems, and we are cutting our expenses,” Berezovsky noted. He added that the financial strain was affecting not only his district, but the wider region and other parts of Russia.
Among the first positions targeted are night guards at schools, kindergartens, and cultural centers, as well as workers at municipal companies responsible for local infrastructure.
Technical staff at social institutions in the Chunsky district are also expected to be cut. District head Nikolai Khrychov stated that several institutions would each lose four guards and four boiler-room workers.
“We feel very sorry for the people. But otherwise, we will not even have money for electricity at the same facility,” Khrychov was quoted as stating.
An updated 2026 budget proposal submitted to the Irkutsk regional legislature last week showed the deficit had widened to 11.8% of expenditures, up from 8.3% before the latest amendments.
Irkutsk is the second-largest economy in Russia’s Siberian Federal District by gross regional product, behind only Krasnoyarsk region, according to official data cited by The Moscow Times.
The cuts in Irkutsk come as financial pressure spreads across Russian regional budgets. UNITED24 Media reported that around 65 regions were preparing to reduce investment and infrastructure spending between 2027 and 2029, while Russia’s Finance Ministry projects a combined regional budget deficit of about $10.5 billion in 2027.

Porsche posts earnings rebound but expects lower vehicle sales in 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:25:04 CST
07:25:04 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A senior executive at German sports carmaker Porsche said Tuesday that 2027 was expected to mark a low point for the company, with vehicle sales and operating profit likely to decline, despite a sharp rebound in earnings in the first nine months of 2026.
Porsche chief financial officer Jochen Breckner attributed the expected downturn to gaps in the company's "product portfolio," noting during a quarterly earnings presentation that the combustion-engine Macan was no longer available following the end of its production earlier this year.
According to financial results released Tuesday, Porsche's global vehicle deliveries fell 16 percent year-on-year to 178,532 units in the first nine months, while revenue declined by a smaller 5.9 percent to 25.28 billion euros (28.17 billion U.S. dollars). The company said a higher proportion of high-margin models helped cushion the impact of lower sales volumes.
By contrast, operating profit surged to 1.74 billion euros (1.94 billion dollars) from just 40 million euros (44.6 million dollars) a year earlier, lifting the operating profit margin to 6.9 percent from 0.2 percent.
The Volkswagen-owned carmaker attributed the sharp rebound largely to lower special charges, which fell to around 500 million euros (557 million dollars) in the first nine months from 2.7 billion euros (3 billion dollars) a year earlier.
The charges were mainly related to changes in its electric vehicle strategy and battery operations, alongside workforce restructuring.
In 2022, Porsche announced an ambitious electrification target, aiming for fully electric vehicles to account for more than 80 percent of its sales by 2030.
However, the company revised its strategy late last year amid weaker-than-expected demand for electric vehicles, delaying some electric vehicle projects and extending plans for combustion-engine models. The changes resulted in substantial one-off charges that weighed heavily on last year's earnings.
Alongside the shift in its product strategy, Porsche has also moved to cut costs and reduce its workforce. In July, the company announced plans to cut another 5,000 jobs in Germany by 2035, bringing its planned workforce reductions to around 9,000 positions in the country. ■

JERUSALEM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot said Tuesday night that exit polls showing his bloc ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's ruling coalition reflected a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu's government, vowing to move swiftly to replace it, as the projections pointed to a parliamentary election deadlock.
Exit polls by public broadcaster Kan and commercial TV Channel 13 projected 53 seats for Eisenkot's bloc against 50 for Netanyahu's, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot's bloc 52 seats and Netanyahu's 50. Neither bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a majority.
"If these are the final results, this is a victory for Israel's mainstream Zionist majority," Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, said in a statement.
He pledged to act immediately to "implement the people's decision, replace Netanyahu's government and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible."

Yair Lapid, the current opposition head, said in a statement that the Netanyahu bloc has suffered "a crushing defeat" and "a total collapse."
Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and the Muslim Ra'am party, were projected to win 17 to 18 seats in the 120-member Knesset or parliament, potentially holding the balance of power. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out forming a coalition with them.
With no outright majority, the results point to potentially prolonged coalition negotiations and political instability.

07:24:56 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Nineteen pathogens cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year, according to an updated report released by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Tuesday.
The 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report is the CDC's most comprehensive estimate to date of the impact of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi, as well as Clostridioides difficile, the CDC said.
The report classifies 19 pathogens according to their threat to public health in the United States: four as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats and two as concerning threats.
The four urgent threats are Candida auris (C. auris), carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, and drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the report said.
Drug-resistant C. auris infections have increased tenfold since 2019, and some strains are resistant to available classes of antifungal drugs, according to the report.
The report also highlighted the rapid spread of resistance genes, which can make infections harder to treat and more deadly.
"Antimicrobial resistance threatens modern medicine and puts millions of Americans at risk every year," CDC Director Erica Schwartz was quoted as saying by U.S. media outlets. "High-quality data help drive action, and CDC is committed to providing easily accessible information to help protect people from drug-resistant infections." ■

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- U.S. aerospace giant Boeing on Tuesday reported a sharp reduction in its third-quarter net loss, while revenue rose 4 percent year on year to 24.19 billion U.S. dollars, driven by stronger defense and services businesses.
For the quarter that ended Sept. 30, Boeing posted a net loss of 116 million dollars, compared with 5.34 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted loss per share narrowed to 26 cents from 7.14 dollars, while core loss per share, a non-GAAP measure, narrowed to 34 cents from 7.47 dollars.
Operating profit reached 354 million dollars, reversing a 4.78-billion-dollar loss, while operating margin improved to 1.5 percent from negative 20.5 percent.
Commercial airplanes revenue fell 3 percent to 10.7 billion dollars, reflecting a less favorable delivery mix. The division's operating loss narrowed to 697 million dollars from 5.35 billion dollars, while deliveries edged up to 161 aircraft from 160.
Boeing said higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and increased supply chain costs weighed on the division's performance. The year-earlier results were affected by a charge related to the 777X program.
Defense, space and security revenue rose 15 percent to 7.94 billion dollars, with operating profit increasing to 492 million dollars from 114 million dollars, partly reflecting a 252-million-dollar gain from the sale of HRL Laboratories.
Global services revenue grew 4 percent to 5.57 billion dollars, while operating profit reached 1.02 billion dollars.
Operating cash flow rose 33 percent year on year to 1.5 billion dollars, while free cash flow, a non-GAAP measure, reached 464 million dollars. Total order backlog rose to a record 745 billion dollars, including more than 6,300 commercial airplanes.
Boeing also reported progress in its aircraft certification programs. The 737-7 received amended type certification from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration during the quarter, while the 737-10 obtained certification in October. The company said the 777X program remains on track for its first delivery in 2027. ■

Unknown Publisher
