Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."
Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."
Mr. Trump told reporters early Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., though he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
"It would be OK with me," Mr. Trump said.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.
"This is what the Bolsonaro family is like: Brazil is their second nation, the U.S. is the first," Lula said Tuesday, according to Reuters.
Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.

what can looking at earth from space teach us about how we live on it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:35:48 UTC
06:35:48 KST

what can looking at earth from space teach us about how we live on it?
bringing together more than 50 artists, astronauts, scientists, and cultural thinkers, 'inploration: art exploring space to understand earth' by richelle ellis and lawrence azerrad explores how art can turn the perspective of space exploration into a deeper understanding of our planet.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
inploration brings the overview effect down to earth
‘We are not observers of this world. We are participants in it. We always were.’ In an interview with designboom, artist Richelle Ellis and creative director Lawrence Azerrad discuss the thinking behind Inploration: Art Exploring Space to Understand Earth, a book published by DelMonico Books. Bringing together more than 50 artists, scientists, astronauts, ecologists, and cultural thinkers, the publication examines how exploring space can change our understanding of Earth, and how art can turn a sense of planetary wonder into a more active form of environmental responsibility.
The book takes its starting point from Earthrise, the photograph captured by Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders on Christmas Eve 1968. Not included on the shot list of the mission, the image was captured spontaneously, revealing Earth as a blue and white sphere suspended against the darkness of space, without visible borders. Its impact extended beyond the space program, offering a new perspective on the planet as a shared and vulnerable home. Nearly six decades later, Ellis and Azerrad return to that image asking how the Overview Effect can resonate with people who may never leave Earth. In a culture saturated with photographs, videos, and digital feeds, the challenge is not simply to reproduce the sense of wonder that Earthrise inspired, but to connect that perspective to the ways people live, make decisions, and care for the world around them.
looking outward to understand what is at home
For Richelle Ellis, the relationship between space and Earth extends beyond the astronaut’s view. Her artistic practice moves between deep space, the deep ocean, remote terrestrial environments, and analog space missions, including projects that send artworks beyond Earth. These different settings share a central question: what happens to our understanding of home when we leave the environments we know? The farther we travel from familiar surroundings, Ellis argues, the more apparent our dependence on Earth becomes. Space makes borders seem arbitrary, while the deep ocean reveals worlds that remain largely invisible despite their importance to planetary health. Both environments challenge the assumption that what cannot be seen or directly experienced is somehow separate from everyday life.
Art can bring distant or unfamiliar environments closer, helping people connect with ideas that might otherwise remain abstract. In Inploration, this is where art and science meet. The book brings together people from both fields to explore how we understand the world, what remains unknown, and how looking at things differently can change our perspective. While their methods may differ, artists and scientists share a willingness to ask questions, look more closely, and explore the unfamiliar. Among the contributors is Amber Straughn, deputy project scientist for the James Webb Space Telescope, whose work helps communicate the significance of images made by the observatory. As she puts it, ‘Astronomy can lead us to think about bigger things rather than just the facts’. The telescope’s images allow viewers to reconsider time, scale, and humanity’s place in the universe. As Straughn explains, ‘we’re literally seeing them as they were further back in time.’ The publication also responds to changing ways of seeing. Its cover and back cover were updated at press time to include images from the Artemis II mission, many taken by crew members using their iPhones. Placed alongside the Hasselblad film photography associated with the Apollo era, these contemporary images point to how space exploration is documented and shared across generations. The tools change, but the challenge remains: how can an image of somewhere remote alter our understanding of where we are?
from the voyager golden record to a new earthrise
Azerrad brings another perspective to the project through his work as a creative director and his involvement in the 40th-anniversary edition of the Voyager Golden Record. Launched aboard NASA’s Voyager spacecraft, the record was designed as a message to potential extraterrestrial life, assembling images, sounds, music, and information intended to communicate something about humanity. Its audience may be unknown, but its message also turns back toward Earth. The act of selecting what to send into the cosmos requires a decision about what matters enough to represent us. The Golden Record is as much an exercise in collective self-understanding as it is an attempt at interstellar communication. Azerrad approaches Inploration in a similar way, as an attempt to prompt new ways of seeing Earth. His creative process begins with listening and asking questions, allowing different perspectives to sit alongside one another.
The work of artist Cai Guo-Qiang offers another perspective on humanity’s relationship with time and the planet. His pyrotechnic works exist only in the moment of their creation, demanding the viewer’s attention before disappearing. Reflecting on his practice, Ellis and Azerrad share that it reminds them that ‘our only true relationship with the planet exists in the finite moment we are in. The past and the future are really just ideas.’ The observation connects Cai’s ephemeral works to the book’s broader argument: planetary awareness begins with paying attention to the world as we experience it now.
whose cosmology, whose responsibility?
The section on Indigenous knowledge and cultural cosmologies expands the book’s exploration of how different ways of understanding the universe shape our relationship with Earth. Rather than treating the cosmos solely as something to observe and measure, these perspectives connect knowledge to relationships among people, land, other living beings, and future generations. The difference is not simply between scientific and spiritual understandings, but between the ways knowledge informs our responsibilities to the world. Where some Western approaches have treated nature as a resource to study and extract, many Indigenous cosmologies emphasize reciprocity, care, and the obligations that come with being part of a living world.
Artist Cannupa Hanska Luger expresses the relationship between cultural knowledge and scientific understanding directly. ‘The stories are the cosmology. The cosmology is the science,’ he notes. Here, storytelling is not an alternative to knowledge but a way of transmitting an understanding of how the world works and how people should live within it. Other contributors bring the discussion back to the scale of everyday responsibility. Artist Tavares Strachan asks us to reconsider the geography of care: does responsibility extend to someone twenty miles away, or only to the person next door? Artist Rebeca Méndez poses a more fundamental question: ‘What does the Earth need from us?’ These questions complicate the familiar image of Earth as a single, unified home. Seeing the planet as a whole can produce a sense of collective belonging, but that feeling must extend beyond the photograph. It requires attention to the unequal ways environmental harm is experienced, to the knowledge held by communities whose relationships with land have endured across generations, and to the consequences of decisions made in the present. Physicist and systems thinker Fritjof Capra also highlights the importance of slowing down enough to recognize relationships that are otherwise easy to miss.
MAKING THE FUTURE TANGIBLE
Inploration: Art Exploring Space to Understand Earth also asks how we move from understanding environmental crises to feeling able to respond to them. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and the complexity of planetary systems can be difficult to grasp on a personal level. Faced with a constant stream of alarming information, it is easy to feel overwhelmed rather than empowered to act. Art and design offer another way to engage with these challenges by translating complex ideas into images, sounds, and experiences. As musician and artist Beatie Wolfe observes, data alone cannot always convey the emotional weight of an issue. Art can help people connect with information that might otherwise feel distant. Astronomer Janna Levin captures this role succinctly: ‘The point is to move people with the knowledge.’
For artist Lita Albuquerque, understanding our place in the universe begins with locating herself within it. She describes her cosmic address, tracing her position from a specific date and time through the Solar System to the Laniakea Supercluster. ‘I don’t feel overwhelmed,’ she says, adding, ‘I feel connected.’ Her perspective suggests that looking beyond Earth can reveal the connections that make life possible. Design offers another way to consider our relationship with the future. Designer Forest Young notes that ‘any brief is an exercise in futuring,’ describing the act of creating as an exercise in imagining what comes next. He follows this with a question: ‘What is the thing we’re steering away from?’ His approach asks us to consider the choices shaping the future now. Activist Van Jones makes a similar point: ‘The future is not something we enter. The future is something we create together.’ The book carries this thinking beyond its contributors through a series of self-directed exercises that invite readers to reflect on their own relationship with the planet. A related program is planned for MASS MoCA in November 2027, alongside a companion LP to be released through Magnolia Record Store.
NO ROCKET REQUIRED
For Richelle Ellis and Lawrence Azerrad, the Overview Effect is not limited to astronauts looking back at Earth from space. It can start with looking up at the night sky or noticing details of the world we often take for granted. As they suggest throughout Inploration, we do not need to leave the planet to see it differently. The harder part is carrying that perspective into how we live. How do we account for the generations that come after us? Who do we include when we talk about humanity, and what do we owe the planet we share? The Earthrise photograph changed how millions of people saw Earth, even though most would never experience that view for themselves. With Inploration, Ellis and Azerrad hope art can prompt that same sense of recognition today, by paying closer attention to the world we already call home.

MusicSA chair on 'post-apocalypse' industry ahead of Good Music Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:35:46 UTC
06:35:46 KST

MusicSA chair on 'post-apocalypse' industry ahead of Good Music Month
Australian music is caught in a paradox.
Original acts are pumping out excellent music with an edginess fitting of a troubled era, yet local offerings account for only 8.5 per cent of what is being streamed in the country.
APRA-AMCOS reported this month that 91 per cent of the music we streamed in the 2025-26 financial year was imported, with Australian music down 37.5 per cent in five years.
It has previously blamed the situation on global algorithms preferencing music from countries such as the US.
This is despite an original music scene bursting at the seams with excellent rock, indie, blues and psychedelic acts in a revival that's been underway for most of the decade in pockets across Australia.
South Australia is riding the same wave.
At small venues such as The Hotel Metropolitan, Jive, Ancient World and Memphis Slim's House of Blues, as well as at mini-festivals at locations like the Fleurieu Peninsula and Adelaide Uni Bar, young people are regularly packing rooms to see local acts they know well enough to sing along to.
A difference from golden ages like the 1990s, however, is that this scene is mostly being ignored by larger media outlets.
One needs to tune into stations like 3D Radio in Adelaide, Triple R in Melbourne or RTRFM in Perth to get a real finger on the pulse, pick up a street magazine for a gig guide, then get out the house to hear it in person.
In fact, the APRA-AMCOS 25-26 Year in Review pointed out, in a major study with Monash University, that 1.6 million Australians discovered local acts via community radio, and 1.5 million then looked them up on a streaming platform.
APRA-AMCOS has called for audio streaming to be treated the same way as radio and broadcast, as "critical cultural infrastructure", with local content obligations introduced that act in a similar way to commercial radio quotas to ensure Australian music is heard.
It's into this arena that Adelaide songwriter and lawyer Adrian Tisato has entered as the new chairperson of MusicSA, the not-for-profit organisation charged with promoting, supporting and developing the state's contemporary music sector.
"We are in the post-apocalypse,"
he said.
"Whether the apocalypse was Napster, or the post-Napster rollout of the delivery of music to consumers through digital streaming, whether it was COVID-19 or the combination of these events, it's the metaphorical apocalypse.
"But the truth is, we're still here, making music."
An 'electric buzz'
Mr Tisato has replaced John Glenn, who retired as MusicSA chair after nearly six years.
He believed Adelaide was in the midst of a "very important time as a music city" — one with an "electric buzz" that was attracting young and older music lovers to intimate live venues.
"The quality of music that's happening in small venues on the streets of Adelaide, in our regions and in mini-festivals, is outstanding, on a global level," Mr Tisato said.
Live shows have become more or less the only way local musicians can make money since the large-scale digital disruption of the industry and streaming left artists earning very little income from recorded music.
Much of it will be on show during Good Music Month, an open access program featuring local, national and international acts that kicks off with a street party at Hyde Street on Friday night, and runs at venues in Adelaide and across the state until November 30.
Wednesday to Friday will also see the national Regional and Remote Music Summit take place in Mount Gambier, a conference hosted by MusicSA that takes a "deep dive" into the state of music in Australia.
The not-for-profit organisation will also present the annual SA Music Awards on November 10 to "celebrate those South Australian artists who are excelling".
"The calibre of the finalists for each of our awards is extraordinary," Mr Tisato said.
A background in music
The son of Italian migrants, Mr Tisato grew up a Roman Catholic in Woodville and said his home was the meeting place for neighbours, friends and extended family, who would gather around after dinner and play Italian card games.
"They would sing Italian folk songs that had been handed down in the oral tradition, funny little melodic tunes that were sweet and poignant, sometimes containing ribald innuendo or telling tragic tales," he said.
"They'd be sitting there singing in two, three or four-part harmonies while we, as kids, would run around the house absorbing this music into our minds and bodies.
"Once I started to learn the guitar as a 15-year-old, I got involved in the church music group as a singer and guitarist."
Mr Tisato soon began songwriting and ultimately formed a trio with members from the church group. The band started playing parties and then performed in pubs and Adelaide venues.
Named Lookout Joe, the band was one of many enjoying Adelaide's vibrant live music scene throughout the 1990s.
Like the 1970s and 1980s, it was an era, Mr Tisato said, when people didn't question whether they were going out to see live music or not.
"They were going to see a band. It was just a question of which venue or venues they were going to,"
he said.
Mr Tisato also founded and ran an indie record label in the 2000s, and songs he has co-written in the last decade have been licensed to US and Australian television series.
Like most Adelaide artists, however, it was necessary to pursue a day job for financial security and Mr Tisato has been a commercial lawyer for more than 30 years.
A former Adelaide Fringe deputy chairperson and People's Republic of Animation chairperson, he has been actively involved in arts governance and is the current Art Gallery of South Australia Foundation chairperson and a gallery board member.
He has also served on the boards of the South Australian Film Corporation and the Motor Accident Commission.
'Quality trumps all'
Mr Tisato wants to see Adelaide continue to present itself to the world as a "global city of art and culture" and says he will bring his passion for music, business, governance and legal skills to the role.
With so much to on offer from homegrown artists, Mr Tisato urged commentators not to get stuck on whether or not the city attracted every big act that came to Australia.
"Over the years there's been an insecurity in Adelaide about the fact that certain artists don't come to Adelaide," he said.
"We need to let go of that. I actually think it's much more important to ask ourselves whether our own artists in intimate venues are great and thriving.
"Go see them perform live. They're brilliant."
Mr Tisato points out that despite the challenges in a post-digital disruption age, "quality trumps all".
"For musicians, for songwriters, however difficult it may be to make a living from this, the opportunity remains to find a way," he said.
"It starts with being great at what you do and writing extraordinary songs and performing them to audiences, and I still believe that for those who are doing that, the future is bright."

More Than 3% of Russian Men Aged 40–50 Have HIV as Epidemic Spreads in 27 Regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

- Category
- World
More Than 3% of Russian Men Aged 40–50 Have HIV as Epidemic Spreads in 27 Regions
The HIV epidemic in Russia has reached a generalized stage in 27 regions, Vasily Akimkin, director of Rospotrebnadzor’s Central Research Institute of Epidemiology, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta, as reported by The Moscow Times on October 26.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A generalized epidemic means the virus no longer threatens only high-risk groups but is spreading among the broader population. In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women.
The most affected regions are Kemerovo, Irkutsk, and Sverdlovsk, where more than 2% of residents are infected.
Among Russian men aged 40 to 50, the virus is present in more than 3%, stated Natalya Ladnaya, a leading researcher at the institute’s department for HIV/AIDS prevention and control. She noted that the average age of infected people has risen from 32 to 44 over the past 15 years. About two-thirds of new transmissions occur through heterosexual contact, Ladnaya added.
An infographic illustrates the scale of Russia’s HIV. (Data: Rospotrebnadzor via Nezavisimaya Gazeta and The Moscow Times)
Insufficient treatment coverage remains a central problem. Only half of the people living with HIV in Russia have a suppressed viral load, Ladnaya explained, meaning at least 600,000 people continue to transmit the virus. Among patients receiving antiretroviral therapy, viral load is suppressed in about 77–78%, compared with the 95% target set by the World Health Organization.
In 2025, Russia also recorded the highest number of bloodborne infections in medical facilities in 15 years, mostly HIV and hepatitis C, reported Elena Igonina, head of Rospotrebnadzor’s Department of Epidemiological Well-Being of the Population.
Investigations are ongoing into 11 clusters of such infections across ten regions. In 2026, authorities also identified two cases of HIV transmission through blood component transfusion, the first in six years.
Igonina attributed the infections mainly to violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules, including the use of the same catheters and glucometers for multiple patients.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, 30,000 to 34,000 people have died of HIV annually in recent years, an extremely high figure. For every death, there are 1.5 new infections. The draft federal budget for 2027 provides additional medication for 30,000 HIV patients.
That funding falls short of the number of new diagnoses, which stood at about 52,000 in 2024 and 45,000 in 2025.

As I see it
For its autocratic African ally, Taiwan bites its tongue and opens its wallet
Democratic values don’t stop Taipei from offering aid and debt-trap loans to eSwatini – its sole remaining diplomatic partner on the continent and Africa’s last absolute monarchy
3-MIN READ3-MIN
18
 Listen
Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs. 
Eswatini probably does not register on most people’s mental maps. Its relatively recent name might sound unfamiliar as many people still know it as Swaziland.
That it demands attention from pundits like yours truly has much to do with it being the only African country that still formally recognises Taiwan. It is also the continent’s only absolute monarchy. The two facts are closely connected. Recognising Taipei makes little sense when every one of eSwatini’s neighbours recognises Beijing, but it makes perfect sense for the only system of government this kingdom of about 1.2 million people has known since independence from Britain in 1968.
King Mswati III is the son of King Sobhuza II, the first post-independence ruler, and one of his 70 wives. The kingdom briefly made headlines in 2023 when human rights lawyer Thulani Maseko, who had spent years agitating for an end to absolute monarchy, was shot dead in his home. The government denied that its security forces were responsible. While major governments condemned the killing, Taipei stayed silent.

Trump touts Venezuelan oil at Texas rally ahead of US midterms
US president seeks to underscore Latin American military operation, as Iran war causes midterm affordability threat.
United States President Donald Trump has featured a ship he said is carrying Venezuelan oil during a visit to Texas, where he will hold two rallies one after the other in the hopes of boosting Republican chances in a make-or-break Senate race.
Speaking at Corpus Christi on Tuesday on his fourth trip to the state this campaign season, Trump pointed to a ship in the distance.
“It’s got 1 million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela,” he said, adding the cargo was “thanks to our big victory in our recent war with Venezuela”.
The emphasis on the oil comes as US consumers have wrestled with high fossil fuel prices amid the US-Israel war with Iran, a key issue in the upcoming midterm elections.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said.
It was not immediately clear under what pretext the oil had been shipped or whether the details Trump gave were correct. The US had received crude oil shipments from Venezuela before the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro on January 3, but those transfers have increased this year.
In August, the Trump administration announced a deal giving the Pentagon a 35 percent stake in North America Blue Energy Partners, a new company overseeing 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. The White House said in September that the first shipment from the deal would likely hit US reserves in November, although experts have cast doubt on whether the deal will have any short-term impact.
Speaking to reporters earlier in the day, Trump referred to the shipment as a “gift” from Venezuela. The country’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez, has not commented on the specific shipment.
At the rally, Trump also floated making Venezuela the “51st state”.
Key race
Trump’s frequent visits to Texas underscore the state’s significance for Republicans.
Trump endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Republican primary over incumbent Senator John Cornyn. The scandal-ridden Paxton now faces a punishing contest against Democrat James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian.
Polls have regularly shown Talarico leading Paxton, although that lead has largely remained within the margin of error. A RealClearPolitics average of polls had Talarico leading Paxton by 1.7 points.
Talarico’s victory would mark a sea change in a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994.
It would also represent a major rebuke to Trump, whose Republican Party is fighting to maintain its narrow control of the Senate. Democrats are widely projected to take control of the US House of Representatives in the November 3 vote.
Talarico has used the final stretch of the race to focus on years of corruption allegations against Paxton, while drawing a contrast to voters’ affordability concerns.
“Ken Paxton represents everything that’s wrong with this broken, corrupt system,” he said during an event in Houston last week.
Paxton has sought to portray Talarico as too “radical” for Texas, saying his policies would hurt a state known for its pro-business policies.
Trump and other administration officials, notably Vice President JD Vance, have regularly focused on cultural issues, distorting Talarico’s past comments on transgender rights and border security.
Speaking in Corpus Christi, Trump repeated those attacks and urged his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot.
“If you go out, and if you all vote, we win in a landslide,” Trump said.

WASHINGTON - The US State Department’s policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, said on Oct 27 he was leaving his role after nearly two years in which he helped lead an overhaul of US foreign assistance and implemented President Donald Trump’s policies towards Venezuela and Cuba.
Lewin, a top adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, said on social media he was leaving to return to the private sector.
“President Trump has put decades of post-Cold War malaise behind us – permanently transforming US foreign policy to put Americans first, keep them safe, and drive peace and shared prosperity in key regions,” Lewin said on X.
The 29-year-old joined the government as part of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and played a leading role in closing the US Agency for International Development.
Trump and Musk justified the move by accusing the agency of waste, fraud and abuse.
Some programmes were later restored or revamped under the State Department.
Lewin oversaw that process as acting under-secretary of state for foreign assistance, humanitarian affairs and religious freedom.
In late August, Lewin began his stint as the department’s director of policy planning, in which he focused on US policy towards Venezuela and Cuba, according to his State Department biography.
The biography says Lewin is the only person under 30 to serve in the policy planning role.
The US military captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January.
Washington has since controlled the sale of Venezuelan oil and holds the proceeds, and Trump has said no Venezuelan oil will go to Cuba.
That move cut off the main source of oil for Communist-run Cuba. REUTERS

Moscow was attacked by drones during the summit attended by Putin: around 150 flights were canceled or delayed
Kyiv • UNN
During the gas summit in Moscow, authorities reported intercepting 16 drones. Around 150 flights were canceled or delayed, and mobile internet access was restricted.
On Tuesday, October 27, Moscow came under a drone attack during an international gas summit at which Russian dictator Vladimir Putin spoke. Due to the threat of strikes, airports in the Russian capital restricted their operations, while passengers faced widespread flight delays. The Moscow Times reports this, citing Russian authorities and local media, writes UNN.
Details
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that over the course of two hours, until 6:30 p.m., Russian air defenses allegedly intercepted 16 drones approaching the city. The Russian Defense Ministry reported that 71 drones had been shot down in various regions during the day.
Residents of western Moscow and the Moscow region reported explosions, loud rumbling, and car alarms going off. In particular, explosions were heard in the areas of Barvikha, Rodniki, and Govorovo.
The attack caused chaos at Moscow’s airports
Due to the drone threat, operations at Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Vnukovo airports were restricted. According to estimates by Russian media, around 150 flights were delayed or canceled, while some aircraft were diverted to alternate airfields.
At that time, Putin was speaking at the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum at Moscow’s World Trade Center.
Mobile internet was shut down in central Moscow
Russian authorities also restricted mobile internet within the Third Ring Road, citing security measures.
According to Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development, the restrictions will remain in effect on October 28–29. In addition, some streets in the city center were partially closed.
There is currently no independent confirmation of the Russian authorities’ claims regarding the number of drones shot down.

====================================================================================================

Boeing Bullish on Defense Sector After Fighter Wins, Shunning Fixed-Price Deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:24:29 UTC
06:24:29 KST

Fresh off Boeing’s victory in the competition to build the Navy’s sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter, CEO Kelly Ortberg on Oct. 27 expressed confidence that the darkest days of the company’s beleaguered defense sector are in the past.
A year ago, Boeing expected its Defense, Space, and Security division to see revenue growth in the low single digits, Ortberg told investors in an earnings call. Now, the company is projecting defense revenue growth in at least the mid-single digits or higher.
Ortberg pointed to Boeing’s Sept. 29 win of both the $20 billion F/A-XX contract and a $2.38 billion Air Force contract for 22 more F-15EX Eagle II fighters as examples of the tailwinds boosting Boeing’s defense portfolio. The F/A-XX win followed the Air Force’s March 2025 selection of Boeing to build its F-47, putting both the U.S. military’s sixth-generation fighter programs in its portfolio.
In the first three quarters of 2026, Boeing’s defense sector brought in $23 billion in revenue, with earnings of $710 million. That’s up from $19.8 billion in revenue and $379 million in earnings a year earlier.
Ortberg also said the company’s decision to swear off risky contracts—such as the fixed-price contract for Boeing’s KC-46 Pegasus program, which has lost the company billions—has helped put its defense sector back on course.
“The important part is, all these programs are also being underwritten with the right contract type,” Ortberg said. “So not only are we booking more orders, we’re booking more orders that won’t result in some of the challenges we’ve had.”
The F-47 contract is a cost-plus deal, Ortberg said. He declined to identify what type of contract Boeing signed for F/A-XX, but said it is “an appropriate contract type.”
In 2022, Boeing put executive Ted Colbert in charge of its defense sector, who pledged to not agree to further fixed-price contracts with the Pentagon. A few months into the job, Colbert told reporters in London that Boeing had passed on competing for the Air Force’s Survivable Airborne Operations Center, or SAOC, in part because it would have required agreeing to fixed-price elements in the contract.
Colbert also said fighters remained an important part of the company’s business, even though the firm then had not landed a contract to create an entirely new fighter in years. Later in 2022, Colbert reorganized Boeing’s defense sector in an effort to stop it from bleeding revenue and fix persistent quality problems.
Two years later, Boeing Defense appeared increasingly troubled. Financial losses piled up, and the company fired Colbert in September 2024. Labor troubles between Boeing and its machinists led to a massive strike in 2024, and a smaller one a year later, further complicating the firm’s outlook and slowing its F-15EX delivery pace.
But this year, Ortberg said he saw more reasons for optimism. Boeing’s T-7 Red Hawk trainer for the Air Force and MQ-25 Stingray for the Navy both achieved their Milestone C approvals and moved into low-rate initial production this year as well, which Ortberg said was a positive sign for the company.
“We’re not done with the development programs until we’re done,” Ortberg said, adding that the defense team is “doing a really good job of finding win-win scenarios with our customers to get these projects moved forward.”
“So the outlook is strong, our products are in strong demand, and the budget supports additional growth,” Ortberg said. “I think our defense portfolio is a little bit of a sleeper.”

SC: Cannot let pharma industry ‘run amok’ in name of free market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:21:54 UTC
06:21:54 KST

SC questioned the Centre over pharma companies pricing medicines at over 1,000% of cost, saying the industry can't "run amok" in the name of free market.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday said the pharma industry cannot be allowed to “run amok” in the name of free market to fix the maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines at an exponentially high level, which in some cases happens to be over 1,000% of the price at which they are sold to retailers.Expressing anguish over the suffering of the common man who had to pay the price, a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said the court is “pained by the loot” and repeatedly asked Centre to explain the rationale behind allowing a high MRP and who ultimately benefits from the policy. It reserved its order on plea to bring all non-patented medicines and medical consumables under price control mechanism like scheduled drugs.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, who had to face a volley of questions from the bench, tried to convince the court that govt was aware of the problem and that was why it recently decided to cap the price of anti-cancer drugs. But the court responded that govt “woke up” only after it intervened and passed harsh observations on the prevailing system.She, however, said the deliberation was already on and SC’s intervention expedited it.
“People are living in a daydream that someday they will benefit from the drugs prices control order (DPCO)... The policy is only to give benefit to the corporate. We are thinking from the point of view of poor patients,” SC observed. Bhati, thereafter, submitted that medicine prices in India are among the lowest in the world due to free market and govt cannot take control of the entire pharma market, but the bench told her, “You are either not aware about the problem or not keen to solve the problem.
.. Why is the entire system working for the benefit of few people?”“Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. It is not that the govt has left the market unregulated but the complete control of the market is not feasible,” Bhati said, adding that the issue pertains to economic policy and commerce and the court should desist from interfering. Not convinced by this, the bench said, “Should they (pharma companies) be allowed to run amok? What is the justification for the difference in prices? You are not able to come with an answer. We have asked you 30 times. Do not talk about control... You are talking about economic policy and commerce. Is commerce more important than the life of citizens and be given precedence?”

Satellite images confirm damage at Russia’s largest known air defense storage base after Ukrainian drone strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:20:46 UTC
06:20:46 KST

Satellite images show signs of fires at the 75th Arsenal facility in Serpukhov in the Moscow Region, around 60 miles south of the Russian capital, Greenpeace analysts who examined the imagery told The Insider. The site was struck by Ukrainian drones overnight into Oct. 22. The target was the largest known Russian storage base for air defense equipment.
Satellite images from Oct. 26 show changes compared with earlier imagery. Greenpeace experts who analyzed the data told The Insider that burn marks are visible in the upper left of the image. Additional signs of fire can be seen in the center near a hangar and in the lower left.
The Ukrainian open source intelligence (OSINT) project Oko Hora ✙ News and Analytics claims that the strikes hit workshops No. 24 and No. 25, which specialize in repairing and restoring components for Russia’s S-300V and Buk surface-to-air missile systems, its Tunguska-M air defense systems, and radar equipment. The site, formerly an arsenal of the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate (GRAU), only became the largest known storage base for air defense equipment in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
OSINT analyst Jompy wrote in March 2024 that researchers had identified an air defense equipment storage base at the 75th Arsenal site in Serpukhov, adding that the facility had originally served as an artillery depot before being repurposed to store air defense systems. Satellite images show numerous hangars at the site that may contain systems including the Buk or S-300. The analyst said it appeared to be the largest known storage base for air defense and surface-to-air missile systems in Russia.
Another OSINT analyst, Athene Noctua, wrote in June 2024 that the 75th Arsenal base held about 60% of the identified reserve of Russian Ground Forces air defense equipment — 574 out of 950 units.

German special forces have begun preparing for a possible war with Russia – the military is changing tactics and combat scenarios
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:18:00 EET
06:18:00 KST

German special forces have begun preparing for a possible war with Russia – the military is changing tactics and combat scenarios
Kyiv • UNN
The KSK has changed its training to confront Russia, focusing on prolonged operations and battles against heavy weapons. The unit numbers around 1,500 personnel.
Germany is redirecting the training of its elite KSK special forces unit toward a possible military confrontation with Russia. The soldiers are being trained for prolonged operations, countering heavy weaponry, and conducting combat operations in extreme conditions. BILD reports this, citing KSK commander Andreas Kühne, UNN writes.
Details
According to the general, the German command has already changed its approach to training special forces. Whereas previously they mainly practiced short operations lasting approximately three days, they must now be ready to remain in the field for significantly longer.
We are very specifically orienting ourselves toward Russia as the adversary
German special forces are being prepared for confrontation with the Russian army
The new training program provides for operations against an adversary equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and modern electronic warfare capabilities.
Particular attention is being paid to preparing for prolonged stays directly in the combat zone, when servicemen cannot count on a swift return to their permanent bases.
The special forces are also practicing carrying out missions in extremely low temperatures. This is connected with the possible conditions of combat operations on NATO's eastern flank, particularly in the Baltic states.
According to Kühne, during exercises in the Baltic states, German servicemen have already demonstrated the capabilities of their special forces units. Such training is intended to show Moscow that an attack on NATO would have serious military consequences.
What is known about the elite KSK unit
The KSK Special Operations Command is based in the city of Calw near Stuttgart. The unit's total strength is approximately 1,500 servicemen.
Approximately one-third of the personnel carry out combat missions directly. The remainder provides training, command, and operational support.
Selection for the KSK is considered one of the most difficult in the Bundeswehr. According to the data cited, only about 15% of candidates can successfully pass it.

War update: 178 clashes on front line, Pokrovsk sector remains hottest
As reported by Ukrinform, this was stated in a report by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on the situation as of 22:00 on Tuesday, October 26.
“A total of 178 combat clashes have taken place since the beginning of the day. The enemy launched one missile strike and 46 airstrikes, dropping 171 guided aerial bombs. In addition, they used 5,942 kamikaze drones to strike targets and carried out 1,563 shelling attacks on settlements and the positions of our troops,” the report said.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, Russian forces carried out 27 attacks on the positions of Ukrainian troops and settlements, one of them using multiple rocket launchers.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, the enemy attacked Ukrainian positions five times toward the settlements of Okhrimivka and Mala Vovcha. Two of these attacks are still ongoing.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces made three attempts to improve their positions, conducting assault operations toward Radkivka. Fighting is ongoing.
Four attempts by Russian forces to advance were repelled in the Lyman sector, toward Nove, Stavky, and Lyman.
In the Sloviansk sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces stopped two attempts by Russian troops to advance near Yampil and toward Orikhuvatka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces launched one assault toward Malynivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, Ukrainian Forces repelled 13 Russian assaults near Kostiantynivka as well as toward Raiske and Pavlivka. One enemy assault is ongoing.
Russian forces launched 24 attacks in the Pokrovsk sector. They attempted to advance near Sofiivka, Vilne, Vodianske, Vasylivka, and Molodetske, as well as toward Toretske, Kucheriv Yar, Dobropillia, Hannivka, Novohryshyne, Hulive, and Serhiivka. One combat clash is ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 23 Russian troops were killed and eight wounded in the sector today. Ukrainian forces destroyed five vehicles and one piece of special equipment. Three vehicles, one electronic warfare system, one UAV command post and 39 enemy shelters were damaged. A total of 173 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled 16 enemy attacks toward Ternuvate, Dolynka, Hirke, Charivne and Yehorivka. Fighting is ongoing.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Orikhiv and Dnipro River sectors.
No significant changes in the situation were reported in other sectors of the front.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Vivaldi operation by the Ukrainian Defense Forces pushed Russian troops back and liberated significant areas north of Lyman, but the threat to the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration still remains.

Dream postponed: Hebron groom caught in Israeli military lockdown

Dream postponed: Hebron groom caught in Israeli military lockdown
Israel’s military operation in the West Bank’s Hebron has disrupted Palestinian life, including a postponed wedding.
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Haidar Yahya Tamimi had finished preparing his home, bought new furniture, chosen his wedding suit, and sent invitations to around 1,000 people. After four months of preparations, the 27-year-old was due to marry his fiancee, Ruba, on Friday.
Instead, he has been forced to leave his home in the al-Jalada neighbourhood, and the wedding has been postponed indefinitely.
Haidar is among thousands of Palestinians displaced by an Israeli military operation in Hebron that began after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint at the western entrance of the West Bank city on October 23. Both gunmen were killed by Israeli forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered an immediate lockdown in Hebron, and Israeli bulldozers destroyed buildings in the vicinity of the area where the attack took place, as well as going house to house in the neighbourhoods of al-Jalada and Ein Deir Baha, where the attackers lived.
By Monday, more than 3,100 Palestinians had been forcibly displaced, according to Hebron’s municipality.
Wedding put on hold
Haidar has worked as a radiology resident doctor at the Palestine Red Crescent Society Hospital in Hebron for about a year. He had been preparing to celebrate his wedding on Friday, with a feast scheduled for Thursday evening.
He and his fiancee had chosen the furniture for their new home together, as well as his wedding suit, a photograph of which he showed Al Jazeera.
But on the evening of October 23, as Hebron was declared a closed military zone after the attack, Haidar and his family were ordered to leave their homes along with other residents of al-Jalada and Ein Deir Baha. They departed in the middle of the night, taking only what they could carry.
Everything the couple had prepared for the wedding was inside the house, out of their reach. Haidar says they don’t know when they’ll be able to go back.
The groom was able to get to a spot nearby where he could see the house, but wasn’t able to get any closer due to the presence of the Israeli military.
“I looked at the house and saw that my dream was supposed to happen here, but it has been postponed indefinitely,” Haidar said.
He saw Israeli soldiers around the house, and says that relatives showed him security-camera footage of the soldiers entering his home. The current condition of the house is unknown.
As for the wedding, the couple have yet to set another date. First they need to know when they can return home.
Passports trapped inside an office
Locals estimate that more than 100 businesses have been affected by the Israeli lockdown.
Consider the al-Jalada offices of Rukn al-Asala, a travel agent specialising in Muslim pilgrimage services. Agency manager Kamal al-Sharif, 35, has been unable to reach the office where he has worked with his father for 16 years.
The agency was organising an Umrah religious pilgrimage to Saudi Arabia for 15 people, set to depart on Wednesday. With the prospective travellers’ passports still in the office, and locals uncertain when the lockdown will end, that trip is likely to be postponed or cancelled.
Among the documents also inside the office are seven passports that Kamal says arrived from the Chinese embassy on October 22, the day before the lockdown. They belong to traders who had planned to travel to China on October 26.
The traders have their visas, but not their passports, and have been unable to travel, Kamal said.
One of the traders, a man in his 30s who did not wish to be named for security reasons, said he had been preparing to attend an exhibition in China where he could source equipment for his family business.
His flight and hotel bookings have now been cancelled – and the trader is stuck, not knowing when he’ll be able to get the products his business needs.

Israel opposition holds narrow edge over Netanyahu in first projections
Israeli voters on Tuesday gave opposition parties a narrow edge over ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, initial projections showed, after a decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the outbreak of the genocidal war in October 2023.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for nearly two decades, had run on promises to fight enemies from Hamas to Iran and had spent election day raising fears of the strength of Israeli Arab voters.
Early projections broadcast by Israeli television networks showed that the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief, had a narrow edge over Netanyahu's bloc, which includes the far-right.
Early exit polls showed Arab parties made sweeping gains, likely giving them a critical role in the next parliament.
With no single party winning a majority, Israeli politicians will likely spend weeks in high-stakes negotiations to cobble together a coalition.
The country's main pollsters, Channels 11, 12 and 13, projected the opposition bloc to win 52 to 53 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win around 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.
In a dash to secure as many votes as possible, Netanyahu had charged that Israeli Arabs were out to "steal the election" and his Likud party unsuccessfully asked election authorities to keep polls open past 10:00 PM (2000 GMT).
His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.
"We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," a visibly tense Netanyahu told supporters as he tried to bring up turnout in a Likud stronghold.
Nationwide turnout as of 8 PM stood at nearly 75 percent, the highest in decades.
Arab minority in spotlight
Some 7.3 million people were eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
Throughout his career, he has repeatedly raised the spectre of Arab voters as a threat. He warned Tuesday of Arabs voting by the busload, writing on social media that Israel could wake up to a "government of the left wing and Muslim Brotherhood".
Netanyahu said that three senior officials of the United Arab List had been arrested with envelopes full of cash in the south.
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had "caught individuals who tried to bribe voters", adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.
He said the matter was a localised case and under investigation.
United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, who could emerge as a kingmaker in a close election, accused Netanyahu of "lying and inciting" to mobilise his voters.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
In Tel Aviv, left-wing party The Democrats, which is part of Eisenkot's opposition bloc, said police had arrested a man with a knife who had moved threateningly towards its leader Yair Golan.
"Incitement and violence will not intimidate us," Golan said in a statement, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" of Netanyahu.
Netanyahu last returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket and have aggressively championed settlements in the West Bank.
In the last days of the campaign, he posted an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv and talked up his endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who is also fond of alleging election fraud.

Israeli election exit polls show race headed toward stalemate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:10:00 UTC
06:10:00 KST

No clear winner in Israeli election as polls show race headed toward stalemate, negotiations on forming government
No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections on Wednesday with the vote count still under way. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to exit polls on Tuesday night.
With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Each would need 61 seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."
"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.
If the opposition breaks their pre-election vow — a common occurrence in Israeli politics — they could take power and remove Netanyahu. A central tenet of Netanyahu's election campaign was keeping the Arab parties out of power.
Another possibility given the current stalemate, analysts say, is a unity government between the pro-Netanyahu and opposition blocs without the Arab parties or the ultra-Orthodox. The question in this scenario is who would be prime minister or whether Eizenkot or Netanyahu could rotate out of the position.
This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis headed to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multifront war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for renewed strikes.
For many Israelis, after three years of war on multiple fronts, the election is seen as existential, and voter turnout appeared to be high.
Netanyahu vs. the "change bloc"
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.
Netanyahu is telling voters that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.
President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of parties with different ideologies but one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.
The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.
"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister," Eisenkot said in a rally late Tuesday, according to Reuters. "A worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics."
Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.
What happens next?
In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in the Knesset, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.
One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.
Another possibility is the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than the 50% of the 120 available.
Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.

The leaders also welcomed the launch of the Canada-UAE Strategic Partnership, which will establish a framework for deeper cooperation across shared priorities, including trade and investment, energy, innovation, defense and security, and sustainable development.
To advance the partnership, Canada and the UAE signed several memoranda of understanding to strengthen cooperation in key areas, including energy, defense, and diplomatic learning and development.
Carney and Sheikh Khaled also welcomed progress toward the UAE’s historic commitment to invest $70 billion in Canada, including opportunities to advance major investments in energy, transportation infrastructure, and technology.
The leaders exchanged views on regional and global developments, including in the Middle East and issues relating to maritime security and international peace and security.
They reaffirmed their commitment to "dialogue, regional stability, freedom of navigation, and effective multilateral cooperation," the statement noted.
The two leaders agreed to remain in close contact.

Ukraine has launched its own communications satellite – it will become the foundation of an independent network to replace foreign systems
Kyiv • UNN
HIMERA and GomSpace have placed OBRIA NANO into orbit to test a Ukrainian satellite network. Production is planned to be relocated to Ukraine.
The Ukrainian company HIMERA, together with Denmark’s GomSpace, has placed the first OBRIA NANO test satellite into orbit, which will become the foundation of a future independent Ukrainian satellite communications network. The spacecraft has already begun operating in space. HIMERA reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The satellite was launched on October 1, 2026, as part of the SpaceX Transporter-18 space mission. It is currently undergoing scheduled tests that will help verify the technologies needed to create a fully operational satellite system.
The main goal of the OBRIA project is to provide Ukraine with its own satellite communications channels and reduce dependence on foreign operators. Such a system is particularly important during wartime, when stable communications are critically important for the country’s defense.
Ukraine plans to produce its own satellites and terminals
OBRIA NANO is operated by a Ukrainian operator. The results of its tests will be used for the further development of the satellite constellation.
In the future, the developers plan to create a network that will provide communications coverage across the entire territory of Ukraine and complement the capabilities of European satellite systems.
The next stage will be to relocate the production of satellites and ground terminals directly to Ukraine. This will enable the development of domestic space technologies and the gradual expansion of production capacity.
HIMERA is already developing secure communications systems for the Ukrainian military. Its Danish partner GomSpace specializes in developing small satellites and satellite technologies.
At the same time, OBRIA NANO is currently only a test spacecraft, not a ready-made alternative to Starlink. A fully independent network will require the launch of additional satellites and the deployment of ground infrastructure.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has branded European leaders “political masochists,” accusing them of sacrificing their own citizens’ welfare in pursuit of Russia’s defeat in Ukraine.
Speaking to editors-in-chief of African media outlets in Moscow on Tuesday, Lavrov accused Western governments of pressuring their populations to accept declining living standards to secure Ukraine’s victory in conflict with Russia. 
“They are trying to keep public opinion in a position where people must sacrifice everything: salaries, jobs, healthcare services and social benefits in general, so that Ukraine defeats Russia,” Lavrov said. “People can feel how their situation is deteriorating in European countries,” he added.
He singled out German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as one of the politicians advocating such an approach. “These are masochists, political masochists, if you like,” the foreign minister said.
Merz has defended Germany’s growing military spending and continued support for Kiev while warning that the country can no longer afford its existing welfare system.
The German government has tightened welfare rules, introducing benefit reductions of 30% for repeated violations and, in some cases, complete withdrawal. Berlin’s proposed 2027 budget also envisages billions of euros in savings from pensions, healthcare and other social programs.
Germany has meanwhile earmarked €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027, alongside plans to raise defense spending to record levels.
Britain, another major backer of Kiev, has also reduced welfare payments, nearly halving health-related benefits for most new claimants under Universal Credit, a program supporting low-income households and people unable to work.
In September, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for further welfare cuts to fund increased military spending. “We need to fund our defence, not spend all our money on welfare,” she said. The government, however, rejected her proposal.
France has likewise pursued spending restraint, including a proposed public-sector pay freeze, while increasing military expenditure. The measures have faced opposition from trade unions protesting declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
Public discontent has fueled widespread protests across Europe in recent weeks, with hundreds of thousands demonstrating in France over rising living costs, education funding and inequality. Tens of thousands have also taken to the streets in Spain and Portugal over soaring housing costs, while Italy has seen protests over declining living standards.
European NATO members have committed to substantially increasing defense expenditure, citing the perceived threat from Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin last week rejected repeated claims that Moscow was preparing for war with Europe, describing them as part of an ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. “They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. Israeli exit polls show deadlock, setback for Netanyahu
- Israel’s wartime election looked deadlocked, with exit polls giving Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc a narrow lead over Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp and no clear route to a majority.
- Turnout hit 77.7%, the highest in more than 20 years, as voters faced the trauma of the Oct 7 attacks and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
- The result could still let Netanyahu stay on as caretaker prime minister, while coalition talks and smaller parties may decide who forms the next government.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israel’s wartime election was deadlocked on Oct 27, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu’s coalition, though the deadlock could allow Israel’s longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.
“We must establish a strong, right-wing government,” Netanyahu told Likud party supporters after 3am during a speech in Jerusalem, highlighting Israel’s military successes and what he described as a historic opportunity to “remove the Iranian threat.”
Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 showed Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp taking a narrow edge over Eisenkot as the night progressed.
None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
“The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister... a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics,” Eisenkot earlier told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv.
Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu’s bloc.
Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power.
But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power.
Voter turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Final results could take days, and Israel’s fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers in coalition negotiations that have run to weeks or months after past elections.
If neither bloc can form a government, another vote may need to be held, something Eisenkot opposed.
“In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another election,” he said.
The Oct 27 vote was the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu’s coalition, but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.
Netanyahu setback, no clear winner
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you. The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Eisenkot, 66, a hawkish former military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu’s war Cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the Prime Minister’s leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu’s leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish security views that have become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack.
He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel’s response – a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities – was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.
“Dear Democrats, a decision was made,” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party and a Netanyahu rival, said at a party rally after polls closed.
“The nation has given us a sacred duty: to translate the trust they have placed in us into action, to fortify democracy, to save Israel and to provide true defence for the state.”
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released at the close of voting, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth.
Candidates hope that high Arab voter participation would allow them to play a decisive role in preventing Netanyahu’s coalition – the most far right in Israel’s history – from returning to power.
A wartime verdict
Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel’s deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticised for the country’s biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by assassinating top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel’s international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel’s foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.
His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing longstanding corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.
Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran, who has said they should “finish the job”. REUTERS

The 2027 US defence bill, covering more than US$1 trillion in proposed defence spending, will be one of the most closely watched pieces of legislation when Congress returns after the midterm elections, with efforts to counter China running through nearly every corner of the text.
The US House of Representatives passed its version of the bill, known as the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA), in July. The bill faces a tougher path in the US Senate, where a July procedural vote to begin consideration failed after Democrats objected to US President Donald Trump’s military actions involving Iran.
Whatever happens to the bill, competition with China looms large across the legislation. Provisions targeting “foreign adversaries” and “entities of concern” would curb Pentagon purchases of Chinese-made technology and materials, while restricting the use of defence funds to buy certain used foreign-built vessels.

The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear-powered submarines capable of launching nuclear-armed missiles.

This unusual deployment of the majority of the British fleet of strategic nuclear submarines may indicate an increase in their operational readiness.
In recent years, maintaining adequate readiness has been a challenge for the Royal Navy’s submarine force.
The Vanguard-class strategic nuclear submarines include:
All four submarines are equipped with Trident II D5 ballistic missiles with nuclear warheads and provide Britain’s nuclear deterrent.
The constant presence at sea of at least one submarine armed with Trident missiles is considered one of the most important guarantees of the United Kingdom’s security.
“Such action could be used to send a signal to opponents,” the publication notes.
One of the Vanguard-class submarines — HMS Victorious — is currently at the Devonport naval base, where it is undergoing maintenance.
Last year, HMS Vanguard was on combat patrol at sea for over 200 days.
This was likely one of the longest deployments in the submarine’s entire service history. Such a lengthy deployment placed a significant strain on both the crew and the submarine itself.
The longest known deployment of a British nuclear submarine lasted 207 days. It was carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.
In total, the British Navy has nine nuclear submarines: attack submarines and strategic missile submarines.
Last year, the United Kingdom commissioned its sixth Astute-class submarine—HMS Agamemnon.
Astute-class submarines are designed to conduct covert operations, reconnaissance, protect aircraft carrier strike groups, and deliver precision strikes.

US says it killed five people in strike on alleged drug boat
Unknown

US says it killed five people in strike on alleged drug boat
Latest strike brings death toll of campaign decried as extrajudicial killings to 243 people since September 2025.
The United States military has said that it has killed five people in a strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the eastern Pacific, continuing a campaign condemned by legal scholars and rights groups as extrajudicial killings.
US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), which oversees military operations in Latin America and the Caribbean, said on Tuesday that five people were killed in the strike.
“On October 27, under the direction of SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific,” it said in a social media post. “Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed five narco-terrorists.”
The administration of President Donald Trump has previously killed at least 238 people in 68 reported strikes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific since the campaign first began in September 2025, according to a tracker from the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), a US-based research group that promotes human rights and democracy.
Tuesday’s strike appears to bring the reported total to 243 people. SOUTHCOM has often accompanied its announcements with videos that purportedly show vessels being struck.
The government has rarely shared details to substantiate its claims that those targeted are involved in drug trafficking, and relatives of some of those killed have said that they were fishermen or workers who were not involved in the drug trade.
The Trump administration has designated numerous criminal groups in Latin America as foreign “terrorist” organisations. Legal experts reject that framing and say that drug trafficking is a criminal activity against which military strikes are not permitted.
“This is the 6th lethal boat strike in the past 4 months,” Adam Isacson, an analyst at WOLA who has tracked the strikes, said in a social media post in response to SOUTHCOM’s announcement on Tuesday.
“The pace is slower than before, but the administration and its commanders persist in grinding out illegal killings every few weeks, with no discernible impact on the drug trade. A bleak pre-midterms message.”

Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Vatican's secretary for relations with states and international organizations, said Tuesday that the Holy See would continue to firmly support a two-state solution in the Middle East, despite some losing faith in the prospect.
Speaking to journalists at the Foreign Press Association in Rome, Gallagher responded to questions on a range of international issues.
Asked about the Vatican’s support for a two-state solution despite opposition to the proposal among some Israeli opposition figures during Israel’s election campaign, Gallagher said the Holy See would continue to firmly advocate for the establishment of two states.

Gallagher said the Vatican had the opportunity to convey its views to both during the visit.
He noted that neither side wanted the Vatican to act directly as a mediator or facilitator, but rather preferred it to assume a supportive role.

His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.
"We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," a visibly tense Netanyahu told supporters as he tried to bring up turnout in a Likud stronghold.
Nationwide turnout as of 8:00 p.m. stood at nearly 75%, the highest in decades.
Israelis cast their ballots in the shadow of Oct. 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.
The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the genocidal military attacks in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.

Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Eisenkot called on Israelis to vote to replace "the worst government since the state was established."

"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.
The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore".
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
