The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had "caught individuals who tried to bribe voters", adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.

German soldier led local branch of Putin-linked Night Wolves biker club for years, The Insider finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:43:49 UTC
05:43:49 KST

A Bundeswehr serviceman spent several years leading the German branch of the Night Wolves motorcycle club, and he continues to hold a leadership position with the group. The Insider found a ruling by a German military disciplinary court dismissing the soldier from service. His name was withheld in the ruling, but The Insider identified him as Alexander Sautner, a dual German-Russian citizen. Sautner initially served as vice president of the club’s “Roads of Victory” division, where he was responsible for organizing international motorcycle rallies. In early 2023, Sautner became vice president of the independent German chapter of the biker club: Night Wolves MC Germania. Despite a disciplinary investigation against him, Sautner continued directing the club’s activities and maintaining contacts with its Russian leadership.
A Bundeswehr soldier
The German military court’s ruling describes in detail how a Bundeswehr serviceman came to hold a leadership position in the Night Wolves.
The soldier is not named in the document, but the charges list the actions that formed the basis of the case against him. They include his participation on April 11, 2022, in a Rossiya Segodnya video conference featuring a Soviet flag in the background, several links to RT and Sputnik material that he posted in 2015, and criticism of Polish authorities for refusing to allow a Night Wolves motorcycle convoy to cross their border. According to publicly available information, the only German participant in the aforementioned April 2022 news conference was Alexander Sautner, and the same posts cited in the ruling can be found on Sautner’s Facebook page (1, 2).
According to the court, Sautner was born in Kazakhstan, moved to Russia with his parents at the age of 2, and relocated with his family to Germany in 1994. He holds both Russian and German citizenship.
Sautner joined the Bundeswehr in July 2007 as a noncommissioned officer candidate and attended the German Air Force’s NCO school. After completing his training, he served in transport units, working in vehicle logistics. In February 2010, he was promoted to Stabsunteroffizier, a junior noncommissioned officer rank, and in January 2013 he was transferred to a logistics battalion.
From July to November 2013, Sautner took part in the International Security Assistance Force mission in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, receiving the Bundeswehr’s bronze deployment medal for his service. He was also awarded the gold-level military service badge.
A September 2013 performance review described Sautner as an experienced, motivated, and results-oriented noncommissioned officer. His commanders praised his openness, honesty, good relations with fellow soldiers, and overall strong performance. In August 2018, at his own request, Sautner transferred to another unit within the logistics battalion.
Sautner’s Bundeswehr contract was not due to expire until June 30, 2032. However, even before the 2018 transfer, Sautner had begun participating in the activities of the Night Wolves motorcycle club — infamous for its longstanding ties to Vladimir Putin, including its role in Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea. According to Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service, known by its German acronym MAD, Sautner had been a club member since around 2016 and had taken part in its motorcycle rallies even earlier than that.
Sautner later became the first German member of the Night Wolves to achieve “full color” status, meaning full membership in the motorcycle club. In biker culture, “colors” are patches bearing a club’s name and emblem that members wear on their vests. The right to wear the complete set signifies that a person has progressed from supporter and prospective member to a full member of the club.
Sautner later became vice president of the Roads of Victory division, replacing his wife’s uncle in the role. The court ruling does not specify exactly when that happened, but MAD describes him as a longtime vice president and says that until the spring or summer of 2022, he played a key role in organizing and running international motorcycle rallies.
Roads of Victory is a themed Night Wolves division that organizes annual motorcycle rallies around May 9, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany in World War II. Before an independent German chapter was established, Night Wolves activities in Germany were carried out through Roads of Victory, which was headed by Andrei Bobrovsky. Bobrovsky, for his part, is an associate of Night Wolves founder Alexander Zaldostanov, who came under European Union sanctions in 2022. As vice president, Sautner effectively headed Roads of Victory activities in Germany.
The Night Wolves motorcycle club itself was founded by Zaldostanov in 1989. MAD documents say the organization has about 45 chapters in different countries and operates under a strict hierarchy. According to the counterintelligence agency, members are required to follow the club leadership, while Zaldostanov can issue instructions directly to members of foreign chapters.
The Night Wolves and several of the club’s leaders are under EU sanctions for supporting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. The sanctions justification says the organization spreads Russian propaganda, supports pro-Russian armed formations in Ukraine, and maintains close ties to the Kremlin.
German military counterintelligence regards the Night Wolves’ activities as one instrument of Russia’s hybrid warfare efforts against Germany. MAD assesses that the annual motorcycle rallies are used not only as commemorative events, but also to spread pro-Russian political messages.
How the investigation into Sautner began
The first suspicions among Bundeswehr commanders emerged in 2020, when Sautner’s battalion commander and a security officer noticed a Night Wolves emblem sticker on the rear window of Sautner’s car while it was parked on military premises. At the time, Sautner was working primarily as part of the Bundeswehr’s assistance to civilian health authorities. However, after his links to the Russian motorcycle club were discovered, his commanders concluded that he could no longer be assigned to perform work involving classified information.
Sautner’s former direct superior, whose name was withheld in the ruling, testified that the soldier was primarily assisting civilian health authorities at the time, but the restriction on deploying him to posts requiring security clearance created problems for a unit that had commitments to NATO’s rapid-response forces. The situation was compounded by Sautner’s military specialty, which was in short supply, making him difficult to replace.
Sautner also told the court about the circumstances that prevented him from passing the security vetting required for access to classified information, saying that he had retained Russian citizenship because renouncing it would have involved significant expense. He also refused to sign a pledge not to visit certain countries that were considered potential security risks. The ruling does not identify those countries. Holding a second citizenship is not itself prohibited for Bundeswehr service, and the court documents do not indicate that Sautner concealed the existence of his Russian passport from his commanders.
On Feb. 4, 2021, the Bundeswehr’s logistics command formally opened disciplinary proceedings against Sauter, and in December of that year, he was informed of the main findings, which centered on four Facebook posts he had made between 2015 and 2019. Sautner was offered the opportunity to respond, but declined.
On Jan. 27, 2015, Sauter commented on a Sputnik report about Ukrainian military losses in the Donetsk region, writing that Ukrainians could now try out their crematorium. Military disciplinary prosecutors interpreted the remark as incitement to violence and hatred.
On April 27, 2015, Sautner criticized Polish authorities for refusing to allow Night Wolves participants in a motorcycle rally to transit the country on their way to Berlin. He complained that the bikers were being prevented from honoring those killed in World War II and called the Polish authorities “dirty U.S. vassals.”
On Sept. 4, 2015, Sautner shared an article from the German magazine Compact describing the country as an occupied American colony. He posted another article, this time from RT Deutsch, on June 26, 2019. It concerned historical memory and relations between Russia and the West.
The Insider found the first two posts, which were described in detail in the court ruling, on Sautner’s Facebook page. The court ultimately did not consider the four posts in its final judgment, and they were not brought up during Sautner’s disciplinary hearing because they were unlikely to materially affect the type or severity of the punishment.
Notably, despite the investigation, Sautner continued participating in Night Wolves activities. On May 9, 2021, during one of the Roads of Victory rallies, he was seen carrying the flag of the self-proclaimed “Luhansk People’s Republic.” MAD assessed that displaying the symbol of the unrecognized Russian-backed statelet demonstrated how commemorative events were being used to promote Russian political messages.
Instructions from Night Wolves leaders and a pro-Russian demonstration in Berlin
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, German military counterintelligence uncovered evidence of direct interaction between Sautner and the club’s Russian leadership. MAD materials cited in the court ruling say Sautner maintained direct contact with Alexander Zaldostanov and Andrei Bobrovsky and received instructions from them, including while members of the club leadership were in the war zone in Ukraine.
One such episode occurred in early March 2022, mere days after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24.
In club correspondence from March 4 and 5, counterintelligence officers found discussions of a demonstration in Berlin that was to be held under the stated aim of opposing alleged persecution of Russian-speaking residents of Germany. According to MAD, Sautner received a personal message containing instructions from Roads of Victory president Bobrovsky, who was referred to as Hauptkommandant, or “commander in chief” in the correspondence. Participants were urged to fight on the “information front.”
Sautner then sent a voice message to the German Roads of Victory group chat strongly urging other club members to attend. On March 5, 2022, Sautner appeared with other Night Wolves members at a demonstration at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, where he posed with a Russian flag bearing state symbols and the word “Russia.” Photographs from the event were later reviewed by the court.
Sautner said he attended the demonstration to protest discrimination against Russian-speaking people in Germany, adding that he was particularly concerned about his own children. The court, however, viewed the event as a public display of solidarity with Russia staged against the backdrop of the start of its invasion of Ukraine.
The court ruling also mentions another public appearance by Sautner. On April 11, 2022, he participated by video link in a news conference organized by the Russian state media group Rossiya Segodnya. A Soviet flag with a hammer and sickle was visible behind him. MAD interpreted the episode as a further demonstration of Sautner’s senior position within the Night Wolves leadership.
Raising money for Donbas
During the investigation, German military counterintelligence also examined messages from a WhatsApp group called NW DP GERMANY, which was found on Sautner’s phone.
One message asked club members to contribute 1,000 rubles (around $13 at the time) each by Feb. 1, 2022, and then another 500 rubles per month to support Night Wolves chapters in Donbas. The appeal was posted by Denis N., whom German counterintelligence described as a close confidant of Sautner. The person was Denis Nalyotov, who later became head of the club’s German branch.
MAD assessed that the collected funds could have been used to purchase equipment suitable for armed operations against Ukraine. On Feb. 27, 2022, after the full-scale invasion had begun, Sautner himself called on members of the German Roads of Victory organization to send 13 euros each to a person named Badja. According to the message, the money was intended for humanitarian aid to Donbas.
On March 1, Denis Nalyotov discussed the collection with another club member, Thorsten M. He said the money could be sent by PayPal but that it would be better to wait for an in-person meeting and hand it over in cash so the transfers would leave no record.
On April 26, Sautner said in a WhatsApp voice message that around 1,000 euros had been collected. He said the money had been transferred to a fund called “Humanitarian Aid for Donbas.”
MAD materials also cite correspondence from March 2, 2023, in which Badja again called for donations for humanitarian aid. A Roads of Victory representative in Germany replied that fundraising was already underway.
The court ruling does not establish that Sautner personally purchased military equipment or that the funds collected were in fact used for armed activity against Ukraine. The possible military purpose of the money appears specifically as an assessment by MAD.
How Sautner became vice president of Germany’s Night Wolves
In the spring or summer of 2022, Sautner stepped down as vice president of the German Roads of Victory organization, being replaced by Denis Nalyotov. Сounterintelligence assessed that Sautner may have given up the title because of pressure from German law enforcement. Disciplinary proceedings against him were already underway, and MAD documents also refer to an investigation by Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office. The court ruling does not disclose details of that investigation.
The formal transfer of the post, however, did not mean Sautner stopped playing a leadership role. According to MAD, he continued coordinating all major decisions with Nalyotov, with the two generally making and implementing them together.
In early 2023, the Night Wolves established an independent German chapter, Night Wolves MC Germania. Nalyotov became president of the new organization, while Sautner became vice president.
The two informally divided Germany into two zones. Nalyotov ran the northern chapter from Hanover, while Sautner oversaw the south from Bad Mergentheim in Baden-Württemberg. Flight records reviewed by The Insider also indicate that Sautner and Nalyotov traveled to Moscow together after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. (Nalyotov flew from Kaliningrad to Moscow on Jan. 15, 2023, and returned on Jan. 21.)
Sautner therefore obtained a new formal leadership position in the Night Wolves’ German structure after the Bundeswehr’s disciplinary proceedings had already begun. MAD assessed that Sautner’s appointments as club president and vice president indicated a particularly high level of trust from Alexander Zaldostanov. MAD also found that the Russian leadership continued to control foreign chapters, including the organization of propaganda events in Germany.
At the court hearing, Sautner confirmed that he remained a full member of the Night Wolves and continued to serve as vice president of the German chapter.
Why Sautner was not dismissed from the Bundeswehr until 2026
On March 9, 2022, the proceedings were suspended pending additional disciplinary charges. The Bundeswehr’s Federal Office of Personnel Management later considered dismissing Sautner under a law allowing the expedited removal of soldiers involved in anti-constitutional activities without lengthy court proceedings. Sautner was temporarily suspended from official duties in April 2022, and the hearings continued for several more years. On May 26, 2025, the agency determined that there were insufficient grounds execute Sautner’s expedited removal, and the disciplinary case against him continued.
Then on Oct. 10, 2025, Sautner was served with an amended charge sheet. In addition to the earlier Facebook posts, the case now included three new allegations: participation in the pro-Russian demonstration on March 5, 2022; serving as vice president of the German Night Wolves chapter from at least early 2023 through July 29, 2025; and sending an insulting email to a fellow soldier.
The final incident occurred on April 19, 2025. During the night, Sautner emailed a senior NCO in his unit complaining that he had not been informed about the death of a former fellow serviceman. Sautner said the man had died by suicide and accused the command of inaction. The email contained numerous insults directed at members of the unit.
At the court hearing, Sautner apologized to the recipient. The court nevertheless found that he had deliberately violated his duty to treat fellow soldiers with respect.
The court also heard testimony from Sautner’s former commanders, who described him as an experienced, calm, and reliable soldier widely respected by his colleagues. One commander said he had been surprised by the allegations against him.
At the same time, Sautner’s former superiors said that given his actions, they no longer considered his return to the Bundeswehr possible. According to the court ruling, Sautner had openly discussed his Night Wolves activities on his Facebook page, meaning his links to the club were known within his unit.
When Sautner was asked during the hearing whether he even wanted to remain in the Bundeswehr, he was unable to answer immediately. Ultimately, the judges concluded that Sautner had deliberately violated his soldierly duties to remain loyal to Germany, to uphold its constitutional order, and to refrain from conduct that could undermine trust in the Bundeswehr. The court separately stressed that Sautner’s leadership role in an organization closely linked to the Russian state was incompatible with service in Germany’s armed forces.
The ruling also noted that Sautner did not end his Night Wolves activities after the investigation began. On the contrary, while disciplinary proceedings were already underway, he assumed an even more prominent position in the club. The court considered that to be an aggravating factor.
“He can no longer be the servant of two masters,” the ruling said. The judges were quoting wording used by Sautner’s own defense, although the document does not explain the context in which his lawyer used the phrase.
The judges ruled that the Bundeswehr’s trust in Sautner had been irreparably destroyed. On Jan. 28, 2026, Germany’s military disciplinary court found him guilty of disciplinary violations and ordered his dismissal from service. Sautner was also denied special transitional payments following his dismissal and ordered to pay court costs.
The judgment became final on Feb. 5, 2026. The decision was based on Sautner’s leadership role in an organization that German counterintelligence links to the Russian state, his public participation in a pro-Russian demonstration after the start of the full-scale invasion, and his violations of military duties.

PAC-3 Missiles To Be Maintained in Poland — First Such Center Outside the USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:43:04 UTC
05:43:04 KST

Poland will host the first maintenance center outside the U.S. for PAC-3 anti-aircraft missiles, which are used in Patriot air defense systems.
This was announced by Poland’s Deputy Minister of National Defense, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka.
According to her, four countries — Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway — competed for the right to host the center. Poland’s proposal received the highest rating as early as the initial selection stage.
The decision was made by the U.S. government in cooperation with the American defense contractor Lockheed Martin, which manufactures the PAC-3 missiles.
According to an official statement from the company, the new facility will carry out the repair, refurbishment, maintenance, and recertification of the interceptor missiles.
The center will service missiles for NATO countries that operate Patriot systems. Its establishment will significantly reduce the time required to return missiles to service, as previously they had to be transported to the U.S. for such work.
Polish Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz previously noted that transporting the missiles to the United States, servicing them, and recertifying them could, in some cases, take up to two years.
According to Reuters, the cost of establishing the center will amount to approximately PLN 1 billion ($253 million). It is expected that it will take about a year or slightly longer to bring the facility into operation.
On July 7, Poland, the United States, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden signed an agreement on the establishment of a European maintenance center for PAC-3 missiles during the defense-industrial forum at the NATO summit in Ankara.
In July, Militarnyi reported that Poland plans to cooperate with Ukraine in the production and maintenance of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
That same month, Warsaw also proposed to the U.S. that they launch a trilateral format for the production of these missiles with Ukraine’s participation.

UK Defense Chief Calls on NATO to Brace for Potential Confrontation With Russia
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting warned that Western allies must prepare for a scenario where the United Kingdom and NATO could find themselves in a direct military confrontation with Russia.
Speaking alongside Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz in Warsaw, the official stressed the necessity of strengthening deterrence capabilities across Europe, as reported by The Guardian.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Addressing joint defense efforts, Streeting pointed to historical precedents regarding official assurances from Moscow prior to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“We must be prepared for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the NATO alliance find themselves at war with Russia. Not because we want war—we have no quarrel with the Russian people and do not seek war with Russia; NATO is a defensive alliance—but when Putin assures that he has no intention of provoking a war with NATO, we remember what he said about Ukraine just a few days before the invasion,” he noted, The Guardian reported.
The defense minister reaffirmed the alliance’s readiness to defend all member territories while maintaining active support for Kyiv.

On May 27, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a historic Security and Defense Partnership Treaty in London, officially designating Russia as the primary threat to European stability.
The agreement was designed to elevate bilateral military cooperation to its highest level and enable rapid, direct defense responses in the event of a regional crisis without awaiting unanimous consensus from NATO’s 32 members.
Tusk underscored that while Poland remained fully committed to the transatlantic alliance, building swift, bilateral mechanisms with key allies like the UK and France was essential to counter regional aggression effectively—particularly as Washington prepared to gradually reduce its military footprint on the continent.

The medical negligence case is being delayed: should the victims turn to the European Court of Human Rights?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:40:12 EET
05:40:12 KST

The medical negligence case is being delayed: should the victims turn to the European Court of Human Rights?
Kyiv • UNN
Systematic postponements of court hearings in medical negligence cases may violate victims’ rights. Roman Yedelev, an associate professor at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, explained when it is possible to apply to the ECHR, how the expiration of the limitation periods affects the case, and whether a closed criminal proceeding can be reopened.
In Ukraine, hundreds of criminal proceedings are registered every year under Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by medical or pharmaceutical workers. According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, 409 such proceedings were registered in 2025, and another 305 in the first eight months of 2026. Some of these cases concern the deaths of patients whose families have spent years trying to establish the circumstances of the tragedy and obtain justice. Instead, they face protracted expert examinations, regular adjournments of court hearings, and some cases are closed because the limitation periods have expired. Can such delays constitute grounds for applying to the European Court of Human Rights? Associate Professor of the Department of International Law at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv Roman Yedelyev told UNN in an exclusive blitz interview.
Photo: Roman Yedelyev, Associate Professor of the Department of International Law at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
- Can the systematic postponement of court hearings in medical negligence cases violate victims’ rights and constitute grounds for applying to the ECHR?
- Yes, it can. But it is important to understand that not every postponement of a court hearing constitutes a violation of the Convention. If a patient’s death resulted from possible medical negligence, Article 2 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to life, obliges the state to ensure an effective and timely examination of the case that will make it possible to establish the circumstances of the death and clarify the issue of responsibility. If court hearings are systematically postponed without proper justification, the proceedings make no progress for years, and the delays create a risk that the limitation periods will expire, this may indicate a violation of the Convention.
Such case law of the ECHR also exists in relation to Ukraine. In particular, in the case of "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the Court found a violation of Article 2 due to shortcomings and delays in proceedings concerning the deaths of patients. Similarly, in "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025), the Court found the investigation into the circumstances of a patient’s death, which lasted many years, to be ineffective.
To apply to the ECHR, it is important to prove not merely the fact that hearings were postponed, but that the delays were unjustified and negatively affected the possibility of an effective examination of the case. In certain circumstances, prolonged ineffectiveness of the proceedings may justify an application even before their conclusion.
- If criminal proceedings in a medical negligence case are closed because the limitation periods have expired without a judgment on the merits, will the victims be able to challenge this before the ECHR?
- Yes, victims may apply to the ECHR even after criminal proceedings have been closed because the limitation periods have expired. However, it is important to understand that the mere fact that the proceedings were closed does not necessarily mean that the Convention was violated. The ECHR will primarily assess whether the state ensured an effective investigation and judicial examination. If the limitation periods expired as a result of unjustified delays, inaction by state authorities, or numerous procedural shortcomings, this may constitute a violation of Article 2 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to life.
The case of "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025) is illustrative. In that case, criminal proceedings concerning a patient’s death were closed because the limitation periods had expired after more than ten years of investigation. The ECHR found a violation of Article 2; moreover, even the compensation received by the victim in civil proceedings did not remedy the shortcomings of the investigation. In "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the Court also confirmed the state’s responsibility for the ineffectiveness of proceedings concerning possible medical negligence.
At the same time, the Convention does not guarantee victims a mandatory conviction. The key requirement is that the state ensure a genuine opportunity to establish the circumstances of the incident and obtain legal protection, including compensation for damage.
- What practical results can victims achieve through the ECHR? Can its judgment contribute to the resumption of the examination of the case and the adoption of a decision on the merits?
– First and foremost, victims may obtain official recognition that the state violated their rights, as well as monetary compensation. For example, in the cases of "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025) and "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the ECtHR found violations of Article 2 of the Convention on account of the ineffectiveness of proceedings concerning medical negligence and awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary damage. However, the significance of an ECtHR judgment is not limited to compensation. Under Article 46 of the Convention, the state is obliged to comply with the Court’s judgment, including, where necessary, by taking measures to remedy the consequences of the violation.
Could this lead to the reopening of the criminal proceedings? Theoretically, yes, but not automatically. Ukrainian legislation provides for the possibility of reviewing judicial decisions after the ECtHR has established a violation of the Convention. However, everything will depend on the nature of the violation established, the circumstances of the particular case, and the existence of relevant legal grounds.
- What legal steps should victims take now to protect their rights and minimize the risk of the proceedings being closed due to the expiry of the limitation periods?
- First and foremost, I would advise victims not to remain passive participants in the proceedings, especially if the expiry of the limitation periods is approaching. It is important to use the available legal mechanisms to seek the timely consideration of the case.
First, it is worth submitting written applications to the court requesting compliance with reasonable time limits for consideration, drawing attention to the risk that the limitation period may expire. Article 28 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine provides for this possibility. If hearings are systematically postponed, it is necessary to demand a proper explanation of the reasons and, where possible, propose alternative ways for the accused to participate, including via videoconference.
Second, it is important to document all instances of delays in the proceedings, including the dates of postponed hearings, the reasons for adjournments, the applications submitted, and the court’s decisions. This may be crucial if it subsequently becomes necessary to apply to the ECtHR.
Third, I would recommend not limiting oneself exclusively to the criminal proceedings, but assessing the possibility of filing a separate civil claim for compensation for damages. Even if the criminal case is closed, the possibility of civil-law protection may, under certain conditions, remain. At the same time, it is important not to miss the time limits for bringing such a claim.
Ultimately, the most important thing is not to wait until the limitation periods expire. An active procedural position does not guarantee that the proceedings will not be closed, but it may help protect the victims’ rights at the national level and create an adequate evidentiary basis for a possible application to the ECtHR.
In cases involving medical negligence, time is of particular importance. The longer the proceedings last, the more difficult it becomes to establish the circumstances of the incident, gather appropriate evidence, and ensure that those responsible are held accountable. Therefore, the ECtHR assesses not only formal compliance with procedural rules, but also the actual effectiveness of justice.

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin
Russia and the US are exploring opportunities for cooperation in the Arctic, President Vladimir Putin said, stressing that Moscow is ready to work with partners genuinely interested in joint projects.
Speaking at the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin highlighted growing global demand for natural gas and Russia’s efforts to expand production, particularly in the Arctic.
Natural gas already accounts for a quarter of the global energy mix, and Russia, which holds the world’s largest reserves, is investing in infrastructure and technologies designed to operate in extreme northern conditions, the president stated.
“Russia is systematically strengthening its technological sovereignty,” Putin said. “We have also taken a major step forward by creating our own proprietary LNG technologies, which are already being deployed in the harsh conditions of the Arctic.”
Moscow is “open for cooperation” in technology and other areas, he said, adding that it is “actively working with many nations” in the Arctic. “We are now exploring avenues for joint work with American partners.”
Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Moscow and Washington were discussing a potential venture to use Russian technology to extract natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it.
The proposed company, called Polar LNG, was reportedly discussed last month by Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to the NYT, Russian gas producer Novatek has helped finance the venture through a UAE-based firm and is considering taking a minority stake.
Western energy companies have largely scaled back their Russian operations since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. US energy giant ExxonMobil withdrew from the Sakhalin-1 oil and gas project, although the Wall Street Journal reported last year that it is considering a return.
ExxonMobil and Chevron nevertheless retain stakes in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which transports Kazakh oil through Russia to the Black Sea.
Several major European energy companies have also exited Russia, although France’s TotalEnergies retains stakes in Novatek and the Yamal LNG project.
The EU has adopted an increasingly militaristic approach to the Arctic. Its latest Arctic strategy identifies the region as a potential flashpoint for confrontation with Russia, while declaring that the EU “is part of the Arctic” and outlining a range of military objectives.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that the EU is seeking to turn the Arctic into a new “hotbed” of tensions. He accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization” through its military buildup, while stressing Moscow’s commitment to “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation.”

Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:35:18 UTC
05:35:18 KST

Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Editor Lina Attalah was freed once a $53,400 fine was paid, only to learn of a one-year sentence passed in her absence
An Egyptian court has ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, three million Egyptian pounds ($53,400) for running a website without a licence.
The New Cairo Misdemeanour Court also ordered the confiscation of the outlet’s equipment and devices. Attalah was taken into custody after Tuesday’s ruling. She was released several hours later, after Mada Masr paid the fine in full.
During the release procedures, Attalah learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. Mada Masr said Attalah’s lawyers have challenged that ruling, and a retrial hearing is scheduled for November 11.
In an editorial published hours after the verdict, Mada Masr said it had entered court “with a measure of faith in the law and the justice system”. It added: “But what we found in court left none of that faith intact.”
The outlet said the court refused its lawyers’ requests to review the case file, submit additional evidence and call witnesses. According to Mada Masr, the judge then appointed “an unknown party” to act as Attalah’s defence lawyer, even though eight of her own lawyers were in court and she herself objected. The editorial said the judge wrote that lawyer’s requests himself “before issuing a verdict carrying the maximum penalty, with no review and no defence”.
Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, attended the hearing. According to Mada Masr, he said the court went ahead with the appointment despite Attalah’s own objection to being represented by a court-appointed lawyer. Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari, told the Egyptian outlet Zawia3 that the court rejected the defence’s requests and then appointed a lawyer, a step Attalah and her team objected to.
Egypt’s website laws
Tuesday’s ruling is based on Article 105 of Egypt’s 2018 media law, which sets fines of one to three million Egyptian pounds ($17,800–$53,400), plus closure and confiscation, for operating an unlicensed website.
Mada Masr says it applied for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and again in 2020, without a reply. It says it learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised it during a previous case in 2022. In 2023, an administrative court upheld the council’s refusal, citing the absence of proof that the outlet’s trademark was registered, although Mada Masr’s lawyer said he had submitted a trademark registration certificate. A new application has been pending since June 2023.
There was no immediate official comment on the verdict.
The head of the Journalists’ Syndicate, Khaled el-Balshy, said the union would take legal action to appeal the ruling.
Mada Masr was founded in 2013 and has been blocked inside Egypt since 2017. It says it has faced six cases in six years, and rights groups say this is the first to reach trial.
“We tried to defend the law,” the outlet wrote, “just as we tried to defend ourselves.”
Amnesty International’s senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said in a statement, “Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.”
“This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent media voices,” Ahmed added.
The verdict came on the same day that Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution, which investigates national security cases, renewed the detention of six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash for another 15 days.

The $9 billion fuel bill raising questions about Australia's energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:32:19 UTC
05:32:19 KST

In brief
- Australia paid a higher price for imported diesel than any other nation during the fuel crisis.
- New analysis linked billions in extra fuel costs to energy security risks.
Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.
The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.
The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6 billion for petrol imports.
The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.
The council's report, called Crude Awakening, analysed Australia's energy security, its exposure to rising global fuel prices, and policies and progress towards electric transport and renewable energy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It found Australia was the world's largest seaborne importer of diesel, with imports responsible for 90 per cent of its supply.
Diesel use in Australia had also more than doubled since 2000 to 33 billion litres in 2025, with about a quarter used in mining.
Australia paid $9 billion in additional costs to import diesel between March and August, compared to an extra $3.5 billion in Brazil and $3 billion in the UK.
The nation also paid an additional $1.6 billion for petrol, or $56 per person.
Climate Council spokeswoman and economist Nicki Hutley said those costs had a widespread impact.
"We're seeing costs (rise) right through the economy, whether it's in inflation at the supermarket or all the way through the supply chain," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.
"If we keep relying on imported oil, that is leaving our energy security in somebody else's hands, and we're seeing that this year."
Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.
Australia was still slow to adopt electric trucks, with the vehicles representing 0.7 per cent of new sales compared to nine per cent worldwide, and had one public charging point for every 41 electric cars, compared to the global average of one for every 11 EVs.
Electrifying more vehicles and removing diesel fuel tax credits could help to protect Australia from future fuel shocks, Hutley said, and state and federal policies should support the transition.
"Every crisis should be seen as an opportunity, and we shouldn't waste that opportunity," she said.
"The best time to do this was yesterday, as they say, and the next best time is today to say what will set us up for a long-term future of energy security at lowest cost to Australian taxpayers."

Verkhovna Rada Simplified Conditions for Legalizing Foreigners Serving in Ukrainian Defense Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:28:30 UTC
05:28:30 KST

The Verkhovna Rada passed a law extending the deadlines for issuing temporary residence permits to foreigners and stateless persons performing military service in Ukraine.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
On October 27, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 16094. The resolution was approved by 282 members of parliament.
The bill extends the deadline for applying for a temporary residence permit from six months to one year for foreign military personnel who signed a contract by May 10, 2026.
Thus, they will have until May 10, 2027, to apply for a permit.
The Ministry of Defense explained that due to undergoing basic military training and carrying out combat missions, foreign volunteers are not always able to apply to the migration service in a timely manner.
The law also provides for a number of other changes. In particular, foreigners and stateless persons who sign new contracts will be able to legally remain in Ukraine from the date of signing until they receive their residence permit, but for no longer than three months.
For military personnel who signed contracts after May 10, 2026, but were unable to complete the necessary paperwork in a timely manner, a transition period is provided through May 10, 2027.
At the same time, foreign military personnel who have been discharged from service without having obtained their residence permits will have three months to establish legal grounds for their continued stay in Ukraine.
The law is currently awaiting the President of Ukraine’s signature and will take effect the day after its official publication.
In May, the Cabinet of Ministers simplified the procedure for issuing temporary residence permits for foreign volunteers.
In addition, in September, the Ministry of Defense established an interagency working group to improve the conditions of service for foreign volunteers.

Trump weighs lifting sanctions on Russian fund once described by U.S. Treasury as Putin’s ‘slush fund,’ NYT reports

Trump weighs lifting sanctions on Russian fund once described by U.S. Treasury as Putin’s ‘slush fund,’ NYT reports
President Donald Trump’s administration is considering lifting sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), sources familiar with talks between Russia and the United States told The New York Times.
Russia is pressing for sanctions relief for RDIF so the fund can take part in supplying Russian diesel fuel to the United States, the sources told the Times.
The U.S. Treasury Department is reviewing the fund’s application for sanctions relief under its standard procedures, one source said. RDIF will have to prove that the reasons it was sanctioned no longer apply.
RDIF is headed by Kirill Dmitriev, a key participant in the talks between Russia and the United States. He is leading the Kremlin’s push for possible joint business ventures between the two countries.
RDIF was established in 2011 to attract foreign investment to Russia. The best-known project it helped develop was Russia’s Sputnik V coronavirus vaccine. Dmitriev and his wife, Natalya Popova, are believed to be close to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s younger daughter, Katerina Tikhonova.
President Joe Biden’s administration imposed sanctions on RDIF on February 28, 2022, four days after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “While officially a sovereign wealth fund, RDIF is widely considered a slush fund for President Vladimir Putin and is emblematic of Russia’s broader kleptocracy,” the U.S. Treasury Department said at the time.

UN rapporteur says impunity prevails for killing journalists in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:07 UTC
05:23:07 KST

Merve Aydogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese said Tuesday that the targeting of journalists in the Gaza Strip is part of a deliberate effort to conceal atrocities, describing her latest report as an examination of "truth" that has been "buried under the rubble."
"What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional," Albanese, who briefed reporters virtually, said about the genocide in Gaza.
She said she provocatively called the phenomenon "media side," describing it as "the systematic destruction of the media’s public function."
"In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime," she added.
Asked for an update on the investigation into Israel’s 2022 killing of Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, she said: "Nothing, nothing happened. So, the update is impunity."
She noted the impunity was not only by Israel but also "impunity by the United States."
Rejecting the terrorist label, Albanese said it "has been the label to kill everyone, to bring famine upon everyone in Gaza, to destroy Gaza."
Even if Israel has a right to self-defense under international law, she said: "Israel doesn’t have and cannot claim the right to wage a war against Gaza."
Responding to a question on whether the International Criminal Court (ICC) had failed Palestinians, she said "the complementarity of international criminal investigation can be triggered," urging prosecutions "starting now with activating domestic courts."
She said citizens of France, Britain, the US and Belgium who served in the Israeli army could face scrutiny, stressing it was "something that cannot be delayed."
Albanese also pointed to "the absence of so many media, especially legacy media" from Western countries, saying she read it as "possibly an act of solidarity" toward outlets named in the report.

Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead, but no majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:21:00 UTC
05:21:00 KST

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 12:30 p.m. local time, just over 84.5% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."

Key Event
Rio Tinto boss likely to make $18.5m after 56% pay hike
Speaking of inflation, news just in from London is that Rio Tinto's board has proposed increasing CEO Simon Trott's target remuneration package by 56% to £9.8 million ($18.56 million), according to four people familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Reuters.
If Mr Trott hits all his KPIs, his remuneration could be closer to $35 million.
Surging pay at defence, aerospace and energy transition firms has left mining companies scrambling to compete for top talent, Reuters said.
According to an investor presentation seen by Reuters, Rio Tinto's board has expanded the list of companies it compares itself to when calculating executive compensation ranges.
Among other companies, it added US energy majors Chevron and ExxonMobil, as well as GE Aerospace, to its peer benchmarking group.
Ben Wyatt, who chairs Rio Tinto's remuneration committee, said the miner was consulting investors ahead of a policy update.
He told Reuters Mr Trott's fixed pay would remain unchanged, but incentives tied to multiyear business outcomes and shareholder returns would be adjusted.
"This is designed to drive business performance in the interests of shareholders, support the delivery of Rio Tinto's long-term strategy, and attract and retain strong leadership in a competitive global market," he said in a statement.
Appointed in July 2025, Mr Trott delivered a 43% jump in first-half underlying earnings this year while pursuing restructuring and asset sales.
Reflecting a compensation overhaul weighted to performance, Trott's maximum remuneration is proposed to grow 63% to £18.3 million ($34.58 million), the briefing documents showed.
Short-term incentives would rise to a maximum of 300% of base salary from 200%, while long-term targets would jump to 900% from 500%.
Mr Trott's new package would apply to the next three years of his compensation.
To come into effect, the expanded framework will require shareholder approval at next year's annual meeting.

AUSTRAC says it won't tolerate companies putting profit over compliance
AUSTRAC has responded to the Federal Court's decision to fine casino operator Star $260 million for historical breaches of anti-money laundering laws.
AUSTRAC chief Brendan Thomas said the penalty reflected the seriousness of Star's contraventions and built on previous state and Commonwealth fines to provide ongoing deterrence value.
"The Court found The Star did not simply fail to complete the right checks. It allowed high-risk customers to gamble without properly establishing where their money came from and put profit over compliance on a large scale," Mr Thomas said.
"AUSTRAC will not tolerate companies putting profit over their obligations to the Australian community.
"It permitted a private casino within its casino to operate without appropriate oversight and continued courting customers who had been excluded from gambling in another state.
"The Star allowed junkets to engage in highly suspicious incidents without intervening controls and despite its concerns about these activities, and the known risks associated with junkets, it allowed ongoing access to its private gaming rooms.
"Due to The Star's admitted deficiencies in monitoring we cannot know how much money high-risk customers pumped through its casinos."
"But we do know the risks involving significant amounts of money and instead of closing the door to those risks, The Star's operations exposed the casino and Australia's financial system to them."
