Key Event
Have the Kiwis given Aussie borrowers hope?
A lot of Australian borrowers will be looking eastwards across the ditch and thinking wistfully, "maybe there is a chance the RBA won't hike rates next Thursday".
After all, the RBNZ board just thumbed its collective nose at the markets and economist expectations with a surprise interest rate hold today. (Markets had priced in a 100% chance of a NZ rate hike, making the market's punt of a 90% chance for an RBA hike look attractive.)
This is despite NZ inflation heading towards 4% and a very accommodative cash rate of 2.75%.
It was a split decision (4-3) in favour of holding, and that's all Aussie borrowers want.
However, there was an implied threat that the rate-setting committee maintained a hawkish bias and "agreed that tighter monetary policy is likely to be required but remains conditional on the economic outlook".
JP Morgan economist Tom Kennedy said the decision to pause despite markets seemingly green-lighting further tightening is surprising in a global context.
"The RBA has taken a more front-footed approach, hiking on risk-management concerns and pushing the cash rate into restrictive territory despite clear weakening in the local activity data.
"In contrast, the RBNZ is taking a gradualist path while policy remains accommodative and below the central bank's estimate of neutral."
Kennedy said while the RBNZ governor emphasised that inflation remains elevated, he said the broader environment is still favourable for inflation to return to target in the medium term.
"Again, this is quite different to the risk bias shown by some other central banks," Kennedy said.
If the RBA hikes as expected on Tuesday, perhaps Aussie borrowers could offset some of the pain with a cheap holiday in NZ.
In the aftermath of the RBNZ's decision, the Aussie dollar jumped 2% against the Kiwi to hit the highest point since early 2013 at $NZ1.2602
RBNZ narrowly votes to hold rates amid 'abrupt' global downturn fears
If the Anthropic IPO flops and the AI bubble bursts before the end of this year, then a couple of Reserve Bank of New Zealand board members are going to look like geniuses.
This was from the RBNZ's post-meeting statement, after it voted 4-3 today to leave its overnight cash rate (OCR) on hold at 2.75%:
"Members noted that the increase in global long-term yields may partly signal a higher global neutral interest rate, due to higher inflation expectations, war destruction and demand for capital to support AI investment. Higher global interest rates could bring forward a potential global downturn, and the neutral interest rate could decline rapidly in the event of an abrupt global adjustment.
"Prasanna Gai and Anna Breman attached material risk to the possibility that the global environment could shift abruptly. It was therefore appropriate to account for such risks when judging neutral rates and the stance of monetary policy rather than relying on most likely or mid-point measures.
"Members reflected on potential trade-offs associated with increasing the OCR at this meeting or waiting until the December MPS.
"Members discussed that information arriving over the next six weeks could meaningfully change the appropriate policy stance in either direction. There is a risk that inflation becomes entrenched before conventional expectations measures respond, despite the previous two OCR increases. In addition, the world economy could tip abruptly into a downturn causing weaker inflation over the medium term. It is also possible that geopolitical escalation could drive fuel prices higher while weakening global economic activity at the same time."
If the RBA hikes rates next week, for a fifth time this year, and it turns out that the global economy does fall in a heap before the end of the year, the local central bankers are going to have a fair bit of egg on their faces.

With Reuters
Supply shocks, longer-term inflation expectations, and the RBA's models
In the RBA officials' Senate estimates testimony, Greens senator Nick McKim asked some questions about supply shocks that led to an interesting discussion.
Senator McKim:
"Recently we've seen impacts of COVID on the supply chain, Ukraine, Trump's tariff shocks, Iran, the bond yield leap, we've got our climate system crumbling around us, we've got a record El Niño heading our way.
"These are obviously, or would you agree, that these have a compounding impact on the bank's inflationary outlook in the medium to long term?
"And if you do agree with that, what do you think is going to happen to interest rates as these things continue to compound?
"And how's the bank going to respond to that? And is monetary policy equipped to respond to that?
RBA governor Michele Bullock:
"The first thing is, you've highlighted a number of supply shocks that have occurred, starting with COVID, and [then] continuing.
"Now, what supply shocks do, negative supply shocks, is they basically worsen the trade-off between inflation and unemployment. So for any given unemployment rate or given the state of the economy, inflation is higher.
"A traditional way of thinking about this is that — and all central banks talk about this — is that you would try to 'look through' the supply shock.
"So, if it's a shock, you let it flow through and then once it's flowed through, prices will settle down again, and inflation will settle down again.
"That works, I think, if you've got a one-off shock … [but] if you've got compounding shocks, and they are continuing to raise the level of inflation, then there is a concern that people start to think that inflation is just going to be higher permanently, and if that is the case, then I think it's very difficult for central banks … to completely look through these shocks because it might become embedded in inflation expectations."
Governor Bullock then said fuel price shocks have their own specific problems:
"Something like a fuel price shock is a little bit more difficult because it underlies costs that are embedded in businesses, and if it's a very quick shock, goes up and it comes down again, businesses might think 'Well, I'll just wear it', but the longer it goes on, the more they might think, 'Well, actually, you know what? The fuel price isn't coming down, transport costs aren't coming down, I've just got to start passing this on'.
"So it does make it more challenging for central banks."
And she said the RBA was working hard on updating its models to adapt to a world with more supply shocks:
"We are working very hard on adjusting, adapting our models to try to get better at recognising supply shocks and how to respond to them.
"But I think the bottom line remains that there are going to be a lot of supply shocks, but there are also going to be demand consequences of interest rates, and central banks still need to be involved in setting interest rates to try to make sure that inflation remains low and stable."

Key Event
CBA shifts call to a November hike
One of the more interesting notes out on the inflation figures comes from the CBA's economics team, who have shifted their call from "hold" to "hike" at next week's RBA meeting.
As we posted some hours ago, CBA said an "in line" 1.0% rise in the trimmed mean quarterly figure, delivering a year-on-year 3.7% increase, would likely mean an unchanged rate next week — although there was an important caveat about the composition that kept the decision "live".
CBA's head of Australian economics, Belinda Allen, says there has been a shift in focus by the RBA being driven by a rethink on domestic capacity pressures.
"The labour market has been described as tighter than initially thought. Productivity is an ongoing challenge, and the RBA is clearly worried about anchoring longer run inflation expectations," Allen said
She said offshore factors are also playing a role in the change in RBA thinking.
"The conflict in the Middle East is more prolonged than expected, leading to a sustained shock from energy prices and the global capex boom led by AI is creating inflationary pressures.
"As a result, we see the hike in November as an insurance hike to protect against these forces.
"Acting early and acting decisively should manage the risk of inflation being higher for even longer."
Key Event
Rate hike 'locked in': ANZ
The ANZ's economic team says today's inflation data "cements the case for the RBA to hike rates 25bp in November".
Quarterly trimmed mean inflation printed in line with expectations, rising 1.0% over Q3, while the annual growth in underlying inflation was slightly stronger than expected at 3.7%.
"It appears the upside inflation risks the RBA has been focussing on — around oil prices, the AI tech boom and domestic capacity constraints — are materialising and will see a 25bp rate hike in November," ANZ's head of Australian economics Adam Boyton and economist Madeline Dunk wrote.
"We also expect to see upward revisions to the RBA's inflation forecasts which will be published in the November SMP [Statement on Monetary Policy]," the pair said.
"The monthly underlying inflation 'pulse' is tracking at around 4% and market services inflation recorded its strongest annual growth since 2024."
They also highlighted a key component of the inflation data the RBA will likely focus on.

Westpac's Luci Ellis says rate hike next week is very likely
Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis says today's inflation data, and the RBA's Senate testimony, have reaffirmed her expectation that the RBA will increase the cash rate again at its November meeting (next week).
"Today’s inflation data and Senate testimony are the final pieces of information before the RBA Monetary Policy Board (MPB) meets next week," she writes.
"Recent data and communication have consistently pointed to the staff recommending an increase in the cash rate. We expect a majority of the external members to agree, though some members might dissent.
"Inflation is above target, and above what the RBA's August forecasts implied. Some upside risks identified in August have partially materialised, particularly energy prices. The RBA is especially worried that above-target inflation will become embedded in people's expectations and pricing decisions. It will therefore deem that further policy tightening is needed.
"The RBA has made it clear that it is down-weighting the recent easing in the labour market, even though this was more than it forecast. It is also relatively sanguine about the current downturn in the housing market.
"The question then turns to the future beyond November.
"While we still expect a hawkish tone in the RBA's communication until inflation has clearly turned down, further hikes beyond next week are not currently our base case.
"Clearly, the risks of another hike — most likely in February — have increased.

RBA: Unemployment will rise further, but we don't expect a recession
The RBA officials were asked about the prospect of Australia's economy experiencing a recession.
They said they expect unemployment to keep rising a bit from here, but they're not forecasting a recession.
Greens senator Nick McKim:
"How worried are you about the pace of the increase in the unemployment rate and what pace of increase in unemployment would give you cause for concern that we may be heading towards a recession?"
Governor Michele Bullock:
"We're not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage. We do forecast that it has to gradually move up, [but] that is very different from saying that people have to lose their jobs. In fact, we are forecasting that employment continues to grow. It just means that the supply of labour is growing a bit more quickly than jobs can keep up with, and I can't be specific about what that number is. What I can say is we think that it's probably above where the unemployment rate is at the moment. So the unemployment rate, in order to ease some of these capacity pressures, probably will be rising a bit further, and that's what will be in our forecast."
The RBA's chief economist Sarah Hunter then jumped in, to add to Bullock's answer.
Sarah Hunter:
"I might just add to the governor's response. In the context of a recession, if you're defining that through the usual sort of technical definition, which is two quarters of negative growth for GDP, we're obviously monitoring a very wide range of indicators across the real economy, including the labour market, but also spending trends across all of the major categories, and there's various sorts of sets of lead indicators and real-time indicators that we can track to look at that.
"And just to reiterate what the governor says, at the moment our assessment is that none of those indicators are suggesting that the economy is in, or heading into, a recession in the near term.
"So that's not what we're seeing or expect to see over the forecast horizon."

RBA keeping a keen eye on employers' inflation expectations
RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser has spoken a little bit about inflation expectations.
He said one of the surprising things about the post-COVID era is how well anchored inflation expectations have actually been, "not just in Australia, but around the world".
And he said most of the measures of long-term expectations "remain pretty well anchored" still.
But he said the RBA was keeping a very keen eye on them, because it was concerned that more employers were beginning to question whether inflation would return to more typical levels:
"One thing we are looking at, and I think has taken our interest, is what companies are beginning to think about the outlook for inflation, given the cost pressures they face, both through our liaison and through a survey that we've been involved with with Macquarie University, called the Boss Survey.
"There's just some signs that some companies might be thinking, 'You know what? Maybe prices aren't going all the way back, and if they're not, we're going to have to take that into account in our pricing decisions'.
"It isn't a klaxon. It isn't my nightmare yet, but it is something we're watching quite closely.
"And obviously, consumer confidence measures are at historical lows, and people are very angry about the cumulative effect of inflation over the recent past. That's not unique to Australia. That is true right around the world," he said.
When does exuberance become irrational?
RBA officials are covering a lot of different topics in their conversation at Senate estimates.

"The question here is not: is this tech going to be transformative?" he said.
"It's whether the financial markets have just gotten ahead of themselves in pricing in a lot of good news. That's really the issue at hand.
"It's not for us to, I think, to suggest that there's an irrational amount of exuberance, but there's clearly been exuberance in this space, if you look at earnings expectations and the amounts of debt that is now starting to be deployed to fund some of this expansion.
"So at the moment we're not at DEFCON One on AI-related imbalances in the financial markets, but it's a clear watch point because we are seeing risk appetite increasing in a pretty notable way around the world," he said.

Key Event
Housing the largest contributor to inflation rise, followed by fuel
Here's a breakdown on the key components in the Q3 (headline) inflation data from ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck:
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2%.
"Annual inflation of 5.2% for housing reflected rising costs for both new dwellings and electricity.
"New dwelling prices rose 4.7% in the 12 months to September as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour.
"This is down from 5.4% in the 12 months to August.
"Transport was the second largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 8.7%, due to higher automotive fuel prices.
"On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 9.4% in September, compared to a rise of 14.8% in August. This was driven by higher world oil prices.
"When prices for some items change significantly, measures like the trimmed mean can give more insights into how underlying inflation is trending without the impact of temporary shocks.
"In September, automotive fuel was excluded from the trimmed mean and this was a key driver of the difference between headline and trimmed mean inflation.
"Trimmed mean annual inflation was 3.6% in September. Trimmed mean annual inflation in August, as released last month, was 3.6%, but a change in seasonal factors has seen that revised down to 3.5%."

Star's money laundering breaches were 'not mere oversights'
Justice Cameron Moore did not mince his words when handing down Star Entertainment Group's penalty this morning.
He said its conduct caused "significant harm", and that the business relied on the funds that were being funnelled through its casinos.
"A significant part of Star's business relied on facilitating the movement of money from overseas."
In the Federal Court this morning, Justice Moore handed down a $260 million penalty to the entertainment giant, made up of a $195 million fine for Star Sydney and a $65 million fine for Star Brisbane.
"A significant part of Star's business relied on turning a blind eye to customers who were a [money-laundering or terrorism-financing] high-risk."
In his ruling, he said that revenue from high-risk customers alone was more than $1.3 billion, based on Star's own calculations.
"Star caused not insignificant damage to the Australian community and financial system," Justice Moore said.

Government spending not the main driver of inflation: Treasury
Inflation has been driven by global events and the private sector, not by government spending, Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson tells Senate estimates.
There's a fair bit of talking at cross-purposes as Liberal deputy Jane Hume tries from a few angles to extract an admission that spending is fuelling inflation.
Hume is focused on the overall level of government spending, which is high by historical standards. But Wilkinson says it's better to look at the change in the level.
And by simply tracking the budget balance, she says, you can see that the government has delivered consistent improvements — smaller deficits and less inflation pressure.
Hume's not impressed and points out that if you focus simply on the government's new policy decisions, they haven't always improved the bottom line.
But Wilkinson says the main drivers of inflation's recent resurgence have been strong private-sector investment (AI and some other things) and the Middle East war fallout.

Star Entertainment conduct 'egregious', judge says
Star Entertainment Group, Australia's largest listed casino company, has been fined $260 million for historical money-laundering charges brought by AUSTRAC.
The court heard that hundreds of millions of dollars were funnelled through the casino by a man with known criminal links.
Justice Cameron Moore called facilitating the movement of money overseas a "significant part of Star's business", and called the conduct "egregious".
"They were not mere oversights from time to time."
The company operates casinos in Sydney, Brisbane and the Gold Coast, and has argued that any penalty above $100 million would send it into liquidation.
In June, Star's former CEO and lawyer were also collectively fined more than $1.1 million for breaches of the Corporations Act, and were disqualified from holding corporate office for six and seven years respectively.
Key Event
Breaking: Casino giant Star fined $260m for money laundering breaches
Star Entertainment Group has been fined $260 million for repeated breaches of anti-money-laundering laws that led to the suspension of its casino licences in NSW and Queensland.
Financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC launched legal action against the company in 2022, arguing for the Federal Court to impose a penalty of $400 million.
But the company had argued that any penalty over $100 million would send it into liquidation.
Justice Cameron Moore handed down his judgment on Wednesday morning, a day after shareholders gathered for the casino operator's annual meeting in Sydney.
He said in his judgement in landing on the final penalty that proposed fines of $400 million would be too high and $100 million would be too low.
"It is important that Star be deterred … " from breaching anti-money-laundering laws, he said, adding it was also necessary to consider the casino's financial position.
US gaming giant Bally's Corp and the Mathieson family put forward a $300 million rescue package that saved the business from administration in April 2025.

To hike or not to hike? And will today’s CPI answer the question?
The old joke goes: "Ask five economists and you'll get five different answers — six if one went to Harvard."
For the sake of blogging brevity, we'll keep it binary. Here are two different takes on the same result — the trimmed mean CPI coming in at 3.6% yoy.
Pause: CBA senior economist, Trent Saunders
CBA's economics team, which is tipping the consensus result of the trimmed mean CPI coming in at 1.0% over the quarter (3.6% yoy), is leaning towards the RBA holding next week even with a result that is a fair bit higher than the RBA's forecast.
CBA senior economist Trent Saunders says it's not all about inflation, noting that the recent easing in the labour market and subdued consumption growth also come into play.
Saunders points out the oft-quoted RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser last week was suggesting the board faces hard choices — a difficult trade-off between responding to persistent inflation pressures and avoiding unnecessary further weakness in activity and employment.
He says while the November meeting will be "live", that is a hike is possible, a pause is more likely.
"While our baseline remains for the RBA to leave the cash rate unchanged, the decision will depend heavily on the outcome and composition of [the] CPI print."
Hike: UBS senior economist Stephen Wu
The UBS belief that the RBA will hike next week is also strongly influenced by Hauser's comments last week but is more focused on the "inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report" bit.
UBS senior economist Stephen Wu says Hauser was effectively conceding that absent a big downside surprise in the monthly CPI for September, the quarterly for Q3 inflation will be higher.
"Overall, UBS still expect a 25bps hike to 4.85%, most likely in November 26. The likely trigger remains a 1.0% q/q Q3 trimmed mean, alongside upgrades to the RBA's inflation profile," Wu said.
How's the Aussie dollar tracking ahead of the decision?
CBA's FX team has just fired in its morning note saying the AUD/USD consolidated about 0.7030 during the overnight trading session as markets positioned ahead of key risk events.
"Domestically, the Australian Q3 26 CPI is under the spotlight today. With the market pricing an around 60% chance of a 25bp increase in the cash rate next week, the CPI will make or break the case to increase the cash rate."
CBA's Australian economics team has pencilled in a trimmed CPI slightly lower than consensus.
"The upshot is AUD/USD could move sharply down today, possibly testing support at 0.6951," the CBA FX strategy team wrote.
CPI — the numbers that matter
Just a quick primer ahead of the consumer price index (CPI) inflation release at 11:30am (AEDT).
While the CPI is essentially backwards-looking — measuring the price changes of a basket of goods and services in the three months to the end of September (Q3) — the real significance is next week's RBA meeting.
Too high and there's a very strong likelihood of another interest rate hike.
A lower-than-expected result may keep the RBA on hold.
Before the CPI release, the market is pricing in a 60% chance of a hike.
Trimmed mean CPI
The most "policy-relevant" number to look out for is the trimmed mean CPI.
The consensus is it will have increased by a firm 1% over the quarter, taking the year-on-year figure to 3.6%.
If the consensus figure is delivered, that would be the fifth consecutive quarter of the trimmed mean being between 0.8% and 1.0%.
It would also be well above the RBA's August forecast of 0.8%.
A rate hike trigger? Perhaps.
It's worth noting that since the August forecasts were published, deputy governor Andrew Hauser noted last week that the inflation outlook now looks "materially worse".
A surprise on the downside is always possible.
A trimmed mean CPI below 0.8% may be good enough for the RBA to keep its powder dry.
September CPI
As well as the quarterly data, the most recent September numbers will be broken out.
The trimmed mean is expected to come in at 0.3% over the month.
Headline inflation is expected to have accelerated in September, largely due to a jump in fuel prices, which are thought to have been up around 10% on ABS measures.
A 0.7% jump in headline inflation in September would deliver a 4% year-on-year result.

Exit polls from Israel’s election show no clear winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:18:18 UTC
05:18:18 KST

Partial results show no clear winner in Israel election
Israel’s first election since October 7 attack appears deadlocked, with neither Netanyahu or Eisenkot on track for a majority.
Partial results and exit polls from Israel’s parliamentary election show no clear winner, with neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, on a clear path to a governing majority.
With just over 57 percent of votes counted at 8am (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition was on track to win 56 seats in the 120-seat parliament, with Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 49 seats, according to tallies published by Israeli media.
Either side would need 61 seats to form a majority government.
Arab parties were projected to win 16 seats, which could give them significant leverage in forming the next government.
The election is largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s handling of the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks and Israel’s ensuing genocidal war on Gaza, as well as the attacks on Lebanon and Iran.
An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo, allowing Netanyahu to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
‘Crushing defeat’
According to two exit polls published by Israeli media after Tuesday’s vote, the two blocs were deadlocked on 51 seats, while a third exit poll showed Netanyahu’s bloc was three seats ahead.
Netanyahu was defiant early on Wednesday, aiming to position himself to remain the country’s longest-serving prime minister.
“We must establish a strong, right-wing, nationalist government,” said Netanyahu. “We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties.”
Eisenkot said the exit polls showed a “lack of confidence” in the current prime minister.
Yair Lapid, the current opposition leader, echoed the sentiment.
“Don’t let anyone confuse you,” he said. “The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home.”
Yair Golan, the leader of the opposition Democrats, meanwhile said Israeli voters have “fired the Netanyahu government”, pledging to work with political partners to form a new administration.
“We have received a historic opportunity to establish a true government of change in Israel and we have no intention of giving it up,” he wrote on X.
But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said the opposition’s celebrations were premature.
In a social media post, he criticised the “pronouncements of biased commentators” and said: “Likud is the largest party in Israel. It is always good to learn something from the past.”
Netanyahu, the 77-year-old head of Likud, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years.
Meanwhile, at the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters erupted in whistles and applause as the exit polls were published, capping a night of historic turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, called the election a “historic day” and said voters had delivered a “clear and sharp” message. “The ‘government of bloodshed’ must go!” he said in a statement.
“We have proven that we are a political force that cannot be ignored, and that a future here cannot be built without our voice.”
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, also hailed the projected results. “We will transform the mandate we received into a new reality in the country,” Abbas told reporters, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
While the exit polls suggest the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with the parties, citing a lack of shared values.
‘Difficult task’ ahead
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that early exit poll projections show “a clear weakening of Netanyahu’s bloc” but cautioned against “declaring either a Netanyahu victory or the end of his political career”.
“The exit polls suggest that his bloc has lost its majority, but they also suggest that his opponents face a difficult task in building one,” he said. “If neither side can form a government, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker while the negotiations continue.”
Polling stations had closed at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT).
The Central Elections Committee said some 77.7 percent of eligible voters – or more than 5.69 million of about 7.33 million voters – cast their ballots in Tuesday’s election.
The figure is about 7.1 percentage points higher than the 70.63 percent recorded in the 2022 election and the highest turnout in a Knesset election since 1999, when 78.7 percent of eligible voters participated.
Earlier in the day, the committee rejected a request from Netanyahu’s Likud party to extend voting hours.

Firefighters brought the main blaze under control Tuesday after a fire broke out in Guryong Village, a shantytown in Seoul’s southern district of Gangnam, officials said. No casualties have been reported, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Yonhap.
The fire broke out at around 3:50 p.m. at a makeshift building in the village, prompting 39 residents to evacuate, according to fire authorities.
Authorities issued a Level 1 emergency response at 3:59 p.m. and later raised the response level by one notch as the fire spread, before downgrading it to Level 1 again.

Australia clawed its way back into the third Test, but big challenges await
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:16:44 UTC
05:16:44 KST

It was, in the final analysis, close to the perfect day of Test cricket: ebbing, flowing, intriguing, with 10 wickets falling and 329 runs-worth of enterprising batting fulfilling Les Favell's trusty old criteria for an entertaining day on the hill.
There was a six-fer for Mitchell Starc, another bundle of tantalising, shot-filled knocks from South Africa's underappreciated batting stars and a pair of remarkable sequences in which Australia took 5-29 and 4-2. Both sides will, in some ways, feel they got the better of the other for telling periods.
The nagging doubt, after day one of the third and deciding Test, is how badly Australia's chances had been damaged before a ball had even been bowled. Not sufficiently recovered from his neck injury, Steve Smith withdrew. Not sufficiently superior to his colleagues in most facets of the game a week ago, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon.
Then there was the toss. The minute Pat Cummins won it and elected to bowl first under sunny skies, on a perfect-looking pitch — not exactly a ringing endorsement of Australia's remade top six — it was hard to stop one's mind from wandering away from Newlands and back through time in search of precedents.
The obvious destinations were Edgbaston in 2005, the scene of Ricky Ponting's ill-fated decision to bowl first in that classic nailbiter, and Brisbane three years earlier, when poor old Nasser Hussain got it even more horribly wrong.
By lunch at Cape Town, Cummins's Australians were fighting an unwelcome omen: South Africa's domineering 0-140, obtained with a procession of boundaries off the most credentialed bowling attack in world cricket, comfortably shaded both England's 1-132 at Edgbaston in '05 and Australia's 1-125 in Brisbane in '02. Was Cummins coming similarly a cropper?
Cricket history tends to write inconvenient facts out of these stories. Few remember that in the immediate aftermath of Nasser's nightmare, for instance, Australian skipper Steve Waugh admitted he probably would have bowled first, too, albeit with a caveat. "The significance of the toss is overrated," Waugh explained. "Whatever you do first, you've got to do it well."
To say Australia didn't bowl or field well in the first session of this crunch game is an understatement. The vaunted quicks misfired early. To staunch the bleeding, Lyon had to be deployed in just the 11th over. Normally apt to suffocate opponents with sharp fielding, tight lines and partnership bowling, Australia managed only two maidens in the first 25 overs.
Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, who'd never batted at the top of the order in first-class cricket until his Test debut last week, attacked the bowling like prime David Warner, clubbing 12 fours and two sixes in his run-a-ball, thrill-a-minute 95. With Aiden Markram, he raced to South Africa's first 150-run opening stand in nearly a decade.
Of particular concern for Australia was the captain's bowling performance, the tone of which was set in his first over when Markram freed his arms, swivelled into position as though the ball was travelling in slow motion and cross-batted Cummins over the fence at cow corner. Cummins would finish the day with 0-73 from 18 overs, having extracted almost nothing from the pitch he'd so liked the look of in the morning. South Africa played him as though intent on showing a competitive disrespect.
But at first, slowly, and then in two manic bursts, Australia did pull things out of the fire somewhat from their dismal early position.
Lyon, whom Ackerman had taken a particular liking to, kept his head amid the onslaught and had the left-hander stumped, later roaring back into the game at a critical juncture and sneaking one past Temba Bavuma to bowl the Proteas skipper for a duck. Australia stemmed the flow of easy runs — from 5.18 an over in the first session, down to 3.11 in the second.
Reprieved on 39 when Travis Head dropped a sitter at short cover, Markram had doubled his score but looked set for even bigger things when he fell into a trap set by Hazlewood to be caught on the fine leg boundary. Matthew Breetzke was too casual against Cooper Connolly's spin, the left-armer reviewed an LBW shout cannily to claim his first Test wicket.
In the above-mentioned half-hour of head loss, South Africa lost 3-13 and squandered its momentum. Immediately after tea, the Proteas were even more culpable for failing to resist what appeared to be a very obvious temptation: an outer ring of catchers scattered around the boundary from fine leg to deep mid-wicket and Starc banging it in short.
David Bedingham, who'd reached 50 without much trouble, was the first to fall for it, hooking recklessly to be cleverly caught on the fine leg rope by Hazlewood. Two balls later, Wiaan Mulder tried an equally daft hook and feathered an edge to Carey behind the stumps.
If South Africa is destined to win this match and with it the series — and unfortunately for Australia, there is an air of destiny about that result at the moment — perhaps the Proteas' 97-run seventh-wicket partnership will be looked back on as a critical period. Ryan Rickelton, out of form with the bat until that point, contributed a patient 42 as all-rounder Marco Jensen battered a typically confident half-century.
The latter fun, which threatened to take the game back away from Australia entirely, ended when Starc took the second new ball. Calling it a clinical demolition of the tail would undersell him: with 4-2 in the space of seven ruthlessly full and straight deliveries, the Australian paceman took his 20th Test five-wicket haul and finished with 6-72 from 16.3 overs.
Once the day's surges of chaos were done with, a comment by Cummins before play seemed worth revisiting. Boland's omission, the Australian captain claimed, was that great cliché of cricket team selection: "a good problem to have".
But is it? Perhaps Cummins was implying something else, that Australia's other selection problems — replacing three of its top-six batters with players assuredly not in the same class as Boland — are bad ones to have. Ones that may shape this game more than what happened on day one.
Which brings us to another of cricket's enduring clichés: don't judge a pitch until both teams have batted on it.

Iraqi court jails French nationals for belonging to IS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:14:52 UTC
05:14:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraqi court jails French nationals for belonging to IS
An Iraqi court on Tuesday jailed seven French nationals for belonging to the Islamic State group, after they were transferred along with dozens of others from Syria last year.
Six of the defendants were handed life sentences, which under Iraqi law are equivalent to 20 years in prison.
They were found guilty of belonging to IS and "of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror", according to an AFP journalist at the court.
The judge told the defendants the court had "commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, given that you are young, to offer you a chance...to get your life back on track".
The court sentenced a seventh French national to 15 years in prison. The now 24-year-old had been taken to Syria by his mother, who joined IS more than a decade ago.
All seven were part of a group of 47 French citizens transferred from Syria last year.
The larger group includes Adrien Guihal, who claimed responsibility for the 2016 Nice attack for IS.
"These sentences offer a certain form of relief, especially for the families, because the death penalty was legitimately feared," said Matthieu Bagard, the French lawyer for four of the seven defendants sentenced on Tuesday.
He told AFP, however, that it "did not make a difference to everything we have denounced".
"There are French citizens being judged without a fair trial," he said, mentioning "the torture they suffered and the forced confessions".
Marie Dose, the lawyer for the now 24-year-old, reproached France for accepting "that this fate should be reserved for children who have become adults, who bear no responsibility whatsoever for their parents' choices".
The jihadist group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery.
Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces ultimately defeated the group in Syria two years later.
Iraq is nonetheless still reckoning with the group's legacy, with mass graves still being uncovered and testimonies of IS brutality yet to be investigated.
For years, its courts have handed down hundreds of execution orders and life sentences to those convicted of terrorism offences, including foreign fighters.

Storied Paris department store BHV Marais seeks bankruptcy protection

- The store was already under strain from payment delays to brands, then anger over its 2025 deal with Shein caused several brands to leave.
- New owners said delayed funds hurt their revamp plans, while Brookfield denied owing money and labour inspectors said payments may not have been made.
AI generated
PARIS - Paris department store BHV Marais, which courted controversy in 2025 with a partnership with Asian fast-fashion giant Shein, said on Oct 27 it had sought bankruptcy protection to protect its operations and jobs.
The bankruptcy procedure “is part of BHV’s relaunch, not its failure,” the company said, adding that the landmark store opposite Paris City Hall that employs 700 people will remain open.
The store’s previous owner already had problems with brand-name boutiques it hosted over payment delays before it sparked controversy in 2025 by announcing that BHV Marais would host Shein’s first physical permanent store.
The announcement struck a raw nerve in a French public concerned about the disappearance of local jobs amid a flood of Asian imports, and triggered the departure of a number of brands.
The owner finally sold the business to a number of its managers in June, who promptly parted ways with Shein.
The new owners said that as part of that deal the ownership of part of the building was transferred, but they had yet to receive the funds, which adversely impacted their plans to revamp the business.
The owner of the building, the Canadian asset manager Brookfield, rejected that assertion, saying it does not have any outstanding sums due to BHV Marais.
French labour inspectors believe that BHV Marais has not been making payments, which its management has denied. AFP

Ukraine Holds Its Strongest Frontline Position in a Long Time, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:10:53 UTC
05:10:53 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, Oct. 27, that Ukrainian forces had recaptured significant territory in three major offensive operations this year, strengthening their frontline positions and disrupting Russia’s battlefield plans.
In his evening address, Zelensky highlighted an Air Assault Forces campaign that liberated more than 800 square kilometers (309 square miles), Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk region, where Ukrainian troops reported recapturing 277 square kilometers (107 square miles), and Operation Veles near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian forces turned Russian underground infiltration tactics against Moscow’s troops.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is important to note that this year, Ukraine’s positions on the front line remain the strongest they have been in a long time during this war,” Zelensky said, noting that Ukraine would be in a much better diplomatic position if partner support was equally strong, particularly in the field of air-defense systems.
Air assault gains and Operation Vivaldi
According to Zelensky, the offensive led by Air Assault Forces (DShV) has liberated more than 800 square kilometers (309 square miles). The campaign ran through Jan. 29 through Aug. 12, liberating 26 settlements spanning across three regions – Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia.
The second, Operation Vivaldi, was carried out by the 3rd Army Corps near Lyman in Donetsk region from July until mid-October. According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s Defense Forces liberated more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) there, in an area where Russia had concentrated its assaults.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 27, 2026
When the operation ended on Oct. 14, 3rd Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky said his forces had retaken 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) and more than 16 towns and villages, while inflicting at least 8,000 casualties on Russian troops.
The offensive, he said, pushed Russian forces back from the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk highway, a key supply route for both cities.
In an interview with ArmyInform on Oct. 19, Biletsky, who is also commander of Ukraine’s Center Grouping of Forces, said Operation Vivaldi had disrupted Russia’s broader plan to encircle the strategically important cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
According to the general, Russian forces intended to advance from a bridgehead along the Chornyi Zherebets River, bypass Lyman and approach Sloviansk and Kramatorsk from the north, while another Russian grouping advanced from the Dobropillya direction.
The commander said Ukrainian forces eliminated the Russian bridgehead, forcing Moscow to abandon its planned northern advance.
Biletsky also reported more than 8,000 Russian personnel losses and approximately 270 soldiers captured, including more than 20 officers.
He emphasized that the operation’s most significant achievement was not the territory liberated but the disruption of Russia’s strategic plans to capture the remaining Ukrainian-held strongholds in Donetsk region.
Turning a Russian tactic against Moscow
In a separate statement earlier on Tuesday, Zelensky said he had been briefed on the operation’s results by Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa and Brig. Gen. Ihor Oboliensky, the Khartiia Corps commander.
According to the report, Russian forces had previously tried to use underground gas pipelines to slip past Ukrainian positions and launch assaults. Ukraine’s Defense Forces then adopted the method and refined it, making it “far more thought-out and technologically advanced,” Zelensky said.
Repeating figures Khartiia’s Corps first released on Oct. 22, Zelensky confirmed that more than 30 Russian soldiers have been captured, while Russian losses exceeded 100.
At the time, it was reported that more than 30 Russian prisoners were captured, with the maneuver described as the world’s first full-scale underground counteroffensive.
Without any GPS or daylight, Ukrainian troops pushed through more than 15 kilometers (9 miles) of underground infrastructure before emerging behind Russian positions overhead.

Shackled, shaved and in uniform: first inmates arrive at Costa Rica mega-prison
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:07:19 CET
05:07:19 KST

SAN JOSE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Costa Rica has locked up the first 123 inmates in a new mega-prison, built with the help of the Salvadoran government in the outskirts of capital San José, the country’s justice ministry said on Tuesday.
The ministry shared images showing rows of inmates dressed in orange, seated with shaved heads bowed and their hands behind their necks, in poses resembling photographs from El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), the mega-prison where President Nayib Bukele’s government holds tens of thousands of gang members and suspected gang affiliates.
Costa Rica’s maximum security prison, which it calls the High Containment Center against Organized Crime (CACCO), has been presented by the government of President Laura Fernandez as a symbol of a new “tough on crime” approach championed by her administration in response to a security crisis facing Costa Rica, once one of the most peaceful countries in the Western Hemisphere.
“Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history,” Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement. “CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation.” Aguilar has said the new facility will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system.
The prison has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, equivalent to 20% of the country’s prison population.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organized crime. The country recorded a record number of homicides in 2023, although figures have since stabilized. Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets.
(Reporting by Álvaro Murillo; writing by Stefanie Eschenbacher, editing by Cassandra Garrison and Rosalba O’Brien)

EU burying its own economy – Putin (VIDEO)
The EU is burying its own economy by rejecting Russian energy supplies, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said.
European nations have faced soaring energy costs since imposing sweeping sanctions on Russia and its hydrocarbon exports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Brussels has pledged to eliminate Russian gas imports entirely by 2027, despite opposition from several member states.
Speaking at the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin warned that efforts to push Russia out of the global gas market were hurting European industries and households.
“[Europe] is dealing a blow to its own industry and social sector by abandoning Russian energy supplies and tearing up long-term contracts,” he said.
There is a saying in Russia: ‘Don’t dig a pit for someone else, or you might end up there yourself.’ In my view, that is precisely what has happened today in the countries of the European Union.
Putin also accused European nations of hypocrisy over their approach to fossil fuels, arguing that they had built their own prosperity on resources they now discourage developing countries from using.
“The economy of modern Europe was built precisely on coal and hydrocarbons,” he said.
Yet those same countries reopened coal-fired power plants “when they found it more difficult to address their own energy challenges,” Putin added.
European gas prices surged to their highest level since December 2022 on Monday, briefly exceeding €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour as supply disruptions linked to the Iran war and forecasts of colder weather rattled markets, according to Trading Economics.
Germany, Europe’s largest industrial economy, has been particularly hard hit by the loss of Russian gas. The country suffered two consecutive years of economic contraction in 2023 and 2024, while its energy-intensive industries, particularly chemicals and metals, have struggled with higher production costs.
German industry is shedding around 15,000 jobs a month, Tanja Goenner, head of the Federation of German Industries, warned in July, citing structural weaknesses, US tariffs and mounting competition from China.
Economic pressures have also fueled public anger across Europe. Rising living costs, stagnant wages and government policies have triggered protests in France, Belgium, Italy and other countries this month, with demonstrators demanding relief for struggling households.

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. UralChem Group plans to supply at least 1 mln tons of fertilizers annually to African countries in the coming years, with the intention of eventually increasing shipments to 2 mln tons per year, the company told TASS.
"UralChem plans to supply at least 1 mln tons of fertilizers to Africa annually in the coming years. We plan to boost sales volume to 2 mln tons in the foreseeable future," the company said ahead of the Russia-Africa forum, adding that this can be achieved as effective distribution systems and logistics infrastructure are developed within the continent.
Uralchem ranks among the top five fertilizer suppliers to the African continent, having increased its sales from 100,000 tons in 2018 to around 1 million tons by 2025. Moreover, the company supplied about 135,000 tons of fertilizers to African nations free of charge between 2022 and 2024, while also covering the transportation costs associated with these humanitarian shipments.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

African leaders attending the Russia-Africa summit must call on the Russian authorities to immediately end the coercive and deceptive recruitment of African nationals into Russia’s military forces to fight against Ukraine, Amnesty International’s African section directors said in an open letter ahead of the summit, which takes place from 28 to 29 October in Moscow.

Putin holding talks with Equatorial Guinea president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:03:01 UTC
05:03:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding talks with visiting President of Equatorial Guinea Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, a TASS correspondent reported.
The meeting is being held on the sidelines of the 8th summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum. Earlier in the day, the Russian leader supported Nguema Mbasogo’s proposals related to cooperation in the gas sector.
Diplomatic relations between the former Soviet Union and Equatorial Guinea were established on December 7, 1968. From the 1990s through the 2010s, bilateral dialogue was maintained at the level of the foreign ministries. In June 2011, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has been leading the country since 1979, visited Russia for the first time. In July 2013, he participated in the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, and in October 2019, he attended the Russia-Africa Summit in Sochi. On both occasions, he met with Putin. In November 2023, he paid an official visit to Russia.
According to Russia’s Federal Customs Service, trade between Russia and Equatorial Guinea was $1.7 million in 2021 (further updates are unavailable). Meat and meat products accounted for 86% of Russia’s exports, which also included cardboard, paper, and timber. Timber and charcoal accounted for 100% of imports.
Currently, Russia and Equatorial Guinea are discussing Russian companies’ potential participating in the Central African gas transmission system project. This refers to an agreement reached in September 2022 by seven oil-and gas-producing countries, namely Angola, Gabon, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Chad, and Equatorial Guinea, to build a network of major oil and gas pipelines, oil refineries, and power plants to reduce dependence on the refining capacities of developed countries.

EU urges swift formation of Serbia's new parliament, government following elections

Melike Pala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The EU on Tuesday called for the swift formation of Serbia's new parliament and government following the certification of early parliamentary election results, stressing the need for an orderly transition of power.
In a joint statement, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said the certification of the results should pave the way for a smooth transition and the formation of new institutions without delay.
"The Parliament and government to be formed without delay in order to begin addressing the key challenges Serbia is facing," the statement said.
Citing preliminary findings by an international election observation mission, the EU acknowledged generally efficient preparations and positive assessments of voting procedures at most polling stations.
However, the observers also raised concerns about advantages enjoyed by the ruling party, including alleged misuse of state resources, media bias, voter intimidation and pressure on candidates and civil society.
They also reported disruptions to campaign activities and incidents of physical violence.
"The EU remains ready to work closely with the incoming Serbian government on the fundamentals of the EU accession process," the statement said, referring to democratic standards, judicial independence and fundamental rights.
"The EU stands ready to offer support with the reforms and to turn these into opportunities for the people of Serbia," it added.
Serbia's student-backed opposition won 52.71% of the vote in the Oct. 25 snap parliamentary elections, securing 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly, according to the election results provided.
President Aleksandar Vucic's "United Serbia" received 39.17% of the vote, with a projected 104 seats.

New Taiwan cultural office unlikely in Perth
Australian officials have hinted that the government is unlikely to green light a new de facto consulate for Taiwan.
Taiwan has signalled that it would like to open a new trade and cultural office in Perth — on top of their existing offices in Canberra, Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne.
But there's enormous sensitivity around this topic, because China — which claims Taiwan as part of its territory — would likely respond furiously to any attempt by Taiwan to expand its informal diplomatic presence in Australia.
Senior DFAT officials Michael Growder and Elly Lawson wouldn't even confirm whether or not a request to open a new office had been lodged.
Growder told Senate Estimates that Australia "would consider any requests of this nature, if they were made, in accordance with national interest".
But he also suggested that Taiwan's current presence was sufficient.
"Under Australia's One China policy we have a strong and productive unofficial relationship with Taiwan," he told Liberal Senator Jess Collins.
"It's appropriate for Australia to advance this unofficial engagement through the TECO offices already in Australia that is in Canberra, Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane in accordance with our One China policy."
Josh Burns and Dave Sharma join Afternoon Briefing political plan
Labor MP Josh Burns and Liberal senator Dave Sharma have joined the Afternoon Briefing political panel where they're discussing today's inflation update.
The Coalition continues to pressure Labor to make cuts to government spending, with Sharma arguing there are "too many subsidies".
The Coalition has proposed scrapping home battery programs, electric vehicle discounts and net-zero advisory bodies to save roughly $9.4 billion from the budget's bottom line.
Sharma claims subsidies like the one for households installing batteries provide taxpayer money to those that can afford it.
"They're overwhelmingly favouring higher income households. There's nothing progressive about them. They're regressive measures," Sharma says.
"I think the battery program has been a huge success, but you know, these are the decisions that we have to look at," Burns says in response.
Asked whether the government was considering scrapping the battery program, Burns denies that's what he's saying.
"I think that the battery program is really important. It's important for our grid, it's important for households," he says.
"But right now we've got inflation at a too high. So, we have to face it honestly."
Former immigration minister says migration should be separate from Home Affairs
Philip Ruddock, former immigration minister during the Howard era, has said the immigration portfolio should be divorced from the super-portfolio of Home Affairs.
Ruddock joined Afternoon Briefing to share his view amid increasing debate over Australia's migration policies, with Labor, the Coalition and One Nation all vowing to bring down net overseas migration.
"I don't regard the numbers as being so significant, it's the composition of the program that is fundamental to me," he said.
He said Home Affairs included issues like customs, and people with expertise in that field weren't always well equipped to decide who should migrate into the country.
"Getting those skills is absolutely crucial to being able to have an economy that will grow and be more prosperous," he said.
"You don't chose people based on the basis of their religion, their cutlure or their race."
Ruddock said Australia was still a generous country when it came to taking refugees, and we should "take those people who have the greatest need for support".
Should basic grocery prices be capped?
Labor MP Ed Husic suggests the government should consider price caps on basic groceries like milk, bread and eggs to help Australians with rising costs.
Speaking to Afternoon Briefing, Husic says people shouldn't have to choose between paying rent or buying groceries while major companies continue to make a profit.
He points to caps on gas and coal prices in 2022 after the Russian invasion of Ukraine as an example of government intervention at time of crisis.
"I believe that is the type of action we have to absolutely consider to give people some sense of comfort and relief," he says.
"The thing that gets me about the interest rate increases is it's not wages that's driving up inflation. It's not people buying the essentials that's driving up inflation."
Opposition slams government spending as inflation rises
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has weighed in on the latest inflation figures and said the blame lies squarely with the government's "out-of-control spending".
Headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent in the year to September, compared to 4.0 per cent in August. Underlying inflation was 3.6 per cent.
Taylor said Australians were paying more for "absolutely everything".
"It's not only a dreadful set of circumstances, it's a government now that will not admit that there's a problem," he told 2GB.
Taylor said his solution was to "stop spending money at the rate that the government's been spending it".
He highlighted the Coalition's costings from earlier this week, that promised $31 billion in savings by making cuts to climate-related policies, some housing measures and cutting welfare for non-citizens.
Government facing pressure to detail spending cuts to curb inflation
Assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino has refused to be drawn on where the government will make spending cuts as it grapples with inflationary pressures.
Earlier today, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government's budget is not the main driver of inflation, but acknowledged inflation figures are still "too high".
Australia's inflation rate rose to 4.3 per cent in September, compared to 4.0 per cent in August.
Speaking to Afternoon Briefing, Mulino says the government will make savings in the next budget update.
"I can guarantee that it will be a responsible, economic document," he tells Afternoon Briefing.
"I just don't want to get into the particulars of the different parameters, but we will have savings in there and we will do it in a way that is responsible."
'Mind-blowing' bonus was actually a decrease for Australia Post boss
Last night Senate estimates heard about a generous bonus given to Australia Post's chief executive Paul Graham.
Graham disclosed he received a $1.2 million executive bonus — on top of his $1.64 million base salary — which Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson described as a "mind-blowing amount of money".
It turns out that bonus is actually a decrease compared to his bonus last year, which was $1.58 million.
Communications Minister Anika Wells has said she will continue to discuss the matter with the Australia Post board and has urged them to "exercise restraint" when handing out bonuses.
"The government expects the Board to exercise restraint in the use of performance bonus payments," she said in a statement.
"I have raised concerns about the size of these bonuses before and welcome the decrease this year."
Wilson argues Coalition tax plan not inflationary
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson has joined Afternoon Briefing and rejected assertions that a Coalition plan to automatically index personal income tax thresholds to inflation would be inflationary.
The Coalition has proposed indexing the bottom two income tax thresholds to inflation to combat bracket creep, a plan that they say will provide $250 in relief in its first year.
"I don't accept that all, inflation is about the aggregate demand across the entire economy. It's not specific to one tax policy," he says.
Wilson says he thinks the Coalition's plan will address inflationary challenges.
"The labor government, for instance, cut fuel excise. We call for them to do that, but we provided inflation offsets they did without inflation offsets. So it became inflationary," he says.
"And we want to provide offsets to address exactly these sorts of challenges. Because I don't want more inflation."

Update on Australian allegedly kidnapped in Cambodia
Officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade have just given their most detailed statement yet on Hiep Tran, the Australian man who was allegedly abducted in Cambodia before turning up in a prison in Vietnam.
Tran’s supporters say he told consular officials last month that he was kidnapped before being bundled across the border.
Human rights groups say it was a textbook case of transnational repression by Vietnam’s government, accusing President To Lam of intensifying his efforts to target political critics overseas.
Senior DFAT official Elizabeth McGregor told Senate estimates this afternoon that Australia was “deeply concerned” by Tran’s allegations and says the federal government has sought “urgent clarification” about what happened from both Cambodia and Vietnam.
She also said Australia had raised his case at “senior levels” pressing for an “expeditious resolution” to his case – as well as monthly consular visits, humane treatment and access to legal representation for Tran.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong also said that the government took “any allegation that an Australian may have been deprived of liberty and moved across an international border against their will very seriously.”

Aged care algorithm under scrutiny
The aged care algorithm has been a huge focus in health estimates this morning, after yesterday's damning report from the Commonwealth Ombudsman about the Health Department's administration of the scheme.
The classification algorithm was launched on November 1 last year and is used to assign people a level of funding to stay at home with support, but as my colleague Anne Connolly has reported, it has been mired in controversy since its introduction.
The report says the department put the classification algorithm in place "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making" and recommended instating a human override.
In estimates today, it was revealed the department had received the Ombudsman's draft report in September, but proceeded with a different model, rather than giving assessors the power to override the algorithm.
What isn't clear is whether the recommendations in the draft were identical to those contained in the final report, however Health Department boss Blair Comley conceded that it was "probably true" to say it was unusual for recommendations to change substantially from a draft report to a final report.
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston put to him "you still proceeded with an alternative mechanism and disregarded the recommendation"
"I wouldn't say we disregarded it," Comley replied.
"Clearly we were aware of the recommendation from the draft recommendation from the Ombudsman, but there are other views as to what should constitute a process for determining a human override."

Centrelink compliance regime resumes after system unlawfully cancelled payments
More than 50,000 welfare recipients could now get compensation after the government unlawfully stopped their payments, claiming they had failed to meet "mutual obligation" requirements.
That scheme, which was partially paused in July 2024, when concerns it may have been operating unlawfully first arose, has now restarted, with advocates warning the problems have not been fixed.
A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation last year found 964 payment cancellations were not made in accordance with the law.
The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) said it had fixed the issues identified by the Commonwealth Ombudsman through IT system changes, system testing, improved participant communications and additional training for decision-makers.
But advocacy groups fear not enough has been done to fix the underlying issues, with questions set to be put to the government over the scale of the payment cancellations and what evidence it relied on before resuming the program.

The changing face of youth extremism
What drives a 12-year-old child from a loving, stable home to absorb violent online propaganda? That is a core challenge facing the Australian Federal Police amid new data tabled to Senate estimates.
The AFP analysed the histories of 55 radicalised youths and found online extremism is impacting children who show no history of family trauma or obvious vulnerability.
Every subject studied was male, aged between 12 and 17, and radicalised at least in part online. But while violent jihadism and white supremacy dominate, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett warns that investigators are seeing a messy shift toward "mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/incoherent ideologies … and ideological fluidity."
While some of the radicalised youths faced trauma or lacked stability, Barrett notes that others came from completely secure family environments.
The AFP's deep dive into youth radicalisation did highlight a few common threads: 13 per cent were suspended in primary school, over one-third were kicked out of high school, and three in five had received mental health treatment.
With no single profile or predictable pathway, the AFP hopes this data will help police, educators and parents spot early warning signs, long before an online rabbit hole turns into real-world violence.

US nuclear-powered submarine arrives in Australia
It's full steam ahead for AUKUS following the arrival of a US nuclear-powered attack submarine — USS Colorado — at HMAS Stirling yesterday for scheduled maintenance.
The visit serves as a trial run of sorts for the Submarine Rotational Force–West (SRF-West) plan.
What is that? Well, starting in late 2027, SRF-West will establish a permanent presence of up to five US and UK nuclear subs in Western Australia.
This will essentially boost the US and UK's military presence in the Indo-Pacific while giving Australian crews and technicians crucial hands-on experience with nuclear submarines before Australia acquires its own fleet in the 2030s.
Defence officials confirmed the Colorado will return as the inaugural vessel under that arrangement.
This week's maintenance work is basically an opportunity for Australian and allied technicians to show they're up to the task of servicing these high-tech submarines. But while Canberra points to the operation as proof of growing domestic capability, some sources I've spoken with remain concerned about Australia's ability to rapidly scale up local infrastructure and workforce numbers in time. It's a huge undertaking!
The Australian Submarine Agency chief Jonathan Mead said in a statement: "This is the fourth maintenance period since 2024. Export hurdles and visa waits for Ukrainian companies force Pentagon to slow its drone contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:01:15 UTC
05:01:15 KST

Export hurdles and visa waits for Ukrainian companies force Pentagon to slow its drone contest
A soldier holds a remote controller near a GARA unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) at an unnamed location in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
One morning in June, the head of export at Ukrainian drone company Stellarion found himself unexpectedly in need of a U-Haul outside the Detroit Metro Airport in Michigan.
Stellarion was set to test its drones in front of American soldiers at a competition organized by the Pentagon at Camp Grayling, a military base three hours away. But while many of its 48 invited competitors were American companies that had had weeks to modify, prepare, and fit warheads onto their drones, Stellarion was facing a last-minute scramble.
The company's drones had landed that very morning, slowed by Ukrainian export controls and lengthy shipping times, Stellarion's head of exports, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
Stellarion performed strongly enough to advance in the competition, but the Ukrainian company's ordeal reflects a broader problem.
Interviews with Ukrainian manufacturers competing in the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program (DDP), a contest to procure drones for U.S. defense, revealed the companies’ struggles with export controls, shipping times, and visa approvals, sometimes resulting in late product arrivals and rapid turnarounds before competition.
The obstacles to Ukrainian companies are serious enough that, in early October, the Pentagon announced it was pushing back the next phase of the competition, Phase 2.5, which focuses on bomber drones, to November. About half of the 17 companies invited to participate are Ukrainian, a sign of how much the U.S. procurement strategy now depends on drones made in Ukraine.
read also
It is the first time the program has been so visibly forced to accommodate its rules and timeline to meet the needs of Ukrainian companies.
In a statement to the Kyiv Independent, the Pentagon said that "Ukrainian companies have the most battlefield-tested Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems products in the world, and have scaled. We have a responsibility to give American soldiers and Marines the benefit of the best materiel."
The DDP, initiated by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a July 2025 memorandum, is the U.S.’ flagship effort to procure drones at a time when Russia and Ukraine each plan to produce 7 million in 2026 for their respective war efforts. The program is funded to the tune of $1.1 billion and initially aimed to procure 340,000 drones, according to the Request for Solutions released in December 2025.
The Pentagon has prized speed, stating in February in a press release: "We are buying what works — fast, at scale, and without bureaucratic delay."
In the spring, Phase I tested classic one-way attack first-person view (FPV) drones. Over the summer, Phase II tested long-range strike drones and those that operate in close quarters. Other than the U.S. itself, no country sent more competitors to those initial phases than Ukraine. Other competing countries included Israel. Croatia, the U.K., among others.
In July, the Pentagon announced the names of the 17 companies that would be invited to compete in Phase 2.5, spending $30 million to acquire up to 1,200 bombers, according to the Request for Solutions released in July.
Unmanned bombers, which can carry heavier payloads, have played a crucial role in Russia's war against Ukraine. These drones have increasingly been used for logistical, resupply, and rescue missions, with one drone airlifting a 42-kg E-bike to a wounded soldier in July of 2025.
Eight or nine of the companies invited to Phase 2.5, according to the Inside Unmanned Systems blog, have Ukrainian origins: UFORCE, Gurzuf Defence, Skycutter-Skyfall, Meta Bureau, Grim Tech, and F-Drones are publicly Ukraine-based. Two other companies, listed as Achiever UA and UA Defense Tech, have no public presence, nor does the Areya corporation. Ukrainian companies need a registered legal entity in the U.S. to enter the competition.
read also
Ukrainian companies have long struggled with the DDP’s tight turnarounds. In late July, the DDP put out a "Request for Solutions," or an invitation for companies to pitch the Pentagon on participating in Phase 2.5. Responses were due by Aug. 10. Invitees were announced publicly on Sept. 21, and given until mid-October to ship six ready-to-test bomber drones — which can cost up to $20,000 per unit to produce — to Camp Grayling.
But the export obstacles that Stellarion faced in June are still present.
Ukraine has worked to streamline its export approvals, aiming in July to shorten the approval process to 30 days, but it can still take weeks to approve drone exports. Phase II of the DDP required a special deal to get Ukrainian drones out fast.
But shipping the drones to the U.S. can add another two or three weeks, leaving Ukrainian companies with practically no time to make needed modifications or prepare in an on-base testing environment.
A number of Ukrainian companies therefore considered or decided to withdraw from the competition. One is Skycutter-Skyfall, a partnership between a British defense tech startup that works closely with SkyFall, which produces drone hardware in Ukraine.
Skycutter-Skyfall placed first in Phase I of the DDP in March, earning an order of 2,560 of its one-way-attack FPV drones, according to the DDP’s online leaderboard. Yet, Skycutter was the last of 11 companies to deliver its drone contract, the leaderboard shows.
Gurzuf Defence told the Kyiv Independent that it had notified the Pentagon of its withdrawal from Phase 2.5, while another Ukrainian company told the Kyiv Independent, on condition of anonymity, that it considered pulling out of the competition before ultimately deciding to attend.
As of Oct. 13, at least four companies — a quarter of all those invited — declined to audition their drones at Camp Grayling, according to the DDP website. Two of the four were Ukrainian companies.
Now, the Pentagon is postponing Phase 2.5 to November "to best position all participants for success," according to the Drone Dominance website. The Pentagon reached out to companies that had withdrawn to ask them back to the competition. Gurzuf, for its part, still declined, telling the Kyiv Independent it would take them until December to be fully ready.
The Pentagon told the Kyiv Independent that Ukrainian export controls and shipping times were not "in themselves a factor" in the decision to postpone Phase 2.5. Instead, they emphasized that the decision "included a recognition of the time-consuming U.S. visa processes."
The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv does not process traditional business visa applications, meaning Ukrainian applicants need to travel elsewhere to complete the process, which can take weeks or months, depending on the location.
The Pentagon maintains that it holds Ukrainian companies to the same standards as all competitors. In the first two phases of the program, run between February and August, multiple Ukrainian companies, on condition of anonymity, said the Defense Department’s attitude to supply chain challenges could be boiled down to: "These are the rules. You knew them in advance."
The Pentagon’s decision to postpone signals a shift in approach, suggesting the DDP cares more about encouraging Ukrainian participation than preserving its initial, rapid timelines.
The DDP is the largest drone procurement initiative in the world outside Russia and Ukraine. It is a central part of the U.S. defense modernization effort.
A Grim Tech representative, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told the Kyiv Independent: "If you want to access the American market, you need to be there." In its request for Fiscal Year 2027, the Pentagon has asked for $54 billion for drone warfare and procurement. Companies that succeed now stand to benefit from large future American contracts.
Ukrainian companies also know domestic wartime demand will not last forever. Some have begun to modify their products and form new partnerships to make themselves attractive to foreign governments, the Pentagon most of all.
In March, Ukrainian drone producer General Cherry announced a partnership with American military producer Wilcox Industries to produce hardware in New Hampshire. F-Drones, another Ukrainian company, announced in June a major production project in Ohio. Both General Cherry and F-Drones advanced in earlier phases of the DDP.
But these partnerships don't come cheap. As Grim Tech’s representative put it, "We are finding reliable partners in the U.S., but we're still thinking about what we can do. Because it's a high cost. It's a big investment to set up."
Stellarion’s head of exports put it similarly: "Companies that already have some strong representation in the U.S., some U.S. partners, are in a much better position."
"We had to navigate challenges on our own."
