Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ends brief hunger strike
Lissu, who faces treason charge carrying a possible death sentence, refused food after being denied access to lawyers.
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu has ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his lawyers, his lawyer has said.
Lissu, who leads the opposition’s Party for Democracy and Progress (CHADEMA) and came second in the 2020 presidential election, began refusing food on Monday after his lawyers were denied entry to the prison where he is being held, party spokesperson Brenda Rupia wrote on X.
“Lissu did not take his tea, breakfast or lunch,” his lawyer Rugemeleza Nshala told The Associated Press on Tuesday. Nshala said Lissu ended the strike after lunchtime, following the meeting with his brother.
His detention, along with the alleged abductions of government critics, has led to scrutiny of the human rights record of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who won a 2025 election.
The government has rejected accusations of widespread abuses and said it is committed to respecting human rights. It ordered an investigation into reports of abductions in 2024, though no official findings have been made public.
‘Treason’
Accounts of Lissu’s protest have differed. While CHADEMA spokesperson Rupia said on X that Lissu began refusing food on Monday, Nshala told AP that the strike began on Tuesday morning, after promised private consultations failed to take place.

Could tomato paste help your brain? A three-month trial points to modest gains in attention and memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:00:07 UTC
05:00:07 KST

Eating concentrated tomato paste every day for three months was linked to better performance on tests of selective attention and face-name memory in healthy middle-aged adults, according to a clinical trial published in Antioxidants. A small brain-imaging subgroup also showed changes in how certain brain networks communicate, and levels of a protein involved in brain cell growth showed a borderline increase. The findings suggest that a single, common food may help support cognitive performance during midlife.
Dietary patterns rich in plant-based antioxidants, such as the Mediterranean diet, are often linked to healthier brain aging and a lower risk of cognitive decline. A primary component of the Mediterranean diet is the tomato, which serves as the main dietary source of a natural pigment called lycopene. Lycopene belongs to a family of fat-soluble plant compounds known as carotenoids, which give red, orange, and yellow fruits and vegetables their bright colors.
Among all dietary carotenoids, lycopene is especially effective at neutralizing unstable oxygen molecules in the body. It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier, a protective layer of tightly packed cells that prevents harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering the brain. Once inside the brain, lycopene is thought to help reduce brain inflammation and oxidative stress, which is cellular damage caused by a buildup of reactive molecules.
Animal and laboratory experiments have helped clarify how this compound protects neural tissue. For example, a 2018 study in mice found that lycopene supplementation prevented inflammation-induced memory loss and reduced the buildup of harmful amyloid proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Lycopene is also thought to support neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to adapt and form new connections, by regulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Often referred to by the acronym BDNF, this protein acts like a growth factor for the nervous system, helping existing neurons survive and encouraging the growth of new ones.
In human populations, several observational studies have connected higher blood levels of carotenoids to better mental performance. In a 2019 neuroimaging study of older adults, higher blood concentrations of lycopene and other nutrients were linked to better memory and more efficient communication across brain networks. Similarly, a 2019 clinical trial in young adults indicated that taking daily supplements of lutein and zeaxanthin, two carotenoids other than lycopene, for six months boosted circulating BDNF levels and improved cognitive scores.
Despite these encouraging connections, direct clinical trials testing the cognitive impact of tomatoes in humans have been rare. Past trials typically combined tomato extracts or lycopene with several other vitamins, herbs, or berries, and they focused mostly on older adults. Because these studies mixed multiple ingredients together, scientists could not tell whether the cognitive benefits came from the tomatoes or from the other substances.
To isolate the effects of tomatoes alone, Ricardo López-Solís, Marina Corrado, Rosa M. Lamuela-Raventós, and their colleagues at the University of Barcelona designed a randomized clinical trial focusing on healthy middle-aged adults. By studying people between the ages of 40 and 55, the researchers aimed to see whether eating tomato paste could support brain health before age-related cognitive decline typically becomes noticeable. They used a crossover design, meaning that every participant completed both the tomato diet and the control diet at different times, allowing each person to serve as their own comparison.
The researchers recruited 47 healthy, non-smoking adults from the Barcelona area who had no history of chronic diseases or cognitive impairment, and 42 participants completed the full study. The participants had an average age of about 47, and two-thirds of the sample were women. Nearly 93 percent of the participants had completed higher or postgraduate education.
Each participant completed two three-month dietary phases separated by a one-month break, known as a washout period, during which they mostly returned to their normal eating habits before avoiding lycopene-rich foods in the final week. During the tomato phase, participants ate concentrated commercial tomato paste containing only tomatoes and salt every day alongside their regular meals, either raw or cooked. The daily dose was tailored to each person’s body weight at 0.5 grams of paste per kilogram of weight, which worked out to an average of about 35 grams of paste (roughly two tablespoons) containing 38.4 milligrams of lycopene per day.
During the three-month control phase, participants followed a low-lycopene diet that restricted tomatoes, watermelon, papaya, pink grapefruit, guava, and any food products made from those ingredients. To help participants keep the rest of their diet consistent, the researchers provided a recipe booklet offering paired meal options, such as dishes made with tomato paste for the active phase and similar tomato-free dishes for the control phase. Throughout the trial, the researchers monitored participants’ broader diet, sleep, body composition, and physical activity using food questionnaires and wrist-worn activity trackers.
At the beginning and end of each three-month period, participants provided fasting blood samples to measure their blood levels of lycopene and BDNF. They also completed three standardized cognitive tests measuring different mental abilities. One paper-and-pencil test evaluated selective attention and visual processing speed by asking participants to scan rows of letters under time pressure and mark only specific target letters with two dashes.
A second test measured associative memory, the ability to learn and remember the relationship between unrelated items, by showing participants 12 pairs of faces and names and testing their recall 15 minutes later. A third test used a card-sorting game to measure executive function, which includes mental flexibility and the ability to adapt when rules change unexpectedly. In addition, a smaller subgroup of 14 participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, a type of brain scan that measures how different regions of the brain communicate while a person is lying still and not performing a specific task.
Blood tests indicated that lycopene levels responded to the diets as intended on average, while participants’ overall calorie intake, sleep, and exercise habits remained unchanged. Based on a blood-lycopene cutoff, however, the researchers judged that 14 of the 42 participants had not fully followed the diet in at least one phase. During the control period, average blood lycopene levels stayed flat at 0.40 micromoles per liter, whereas during the tomato paste intervention, average blood lycopene levels more than doubled, rising from a baseline of 0.32 micromoles per liter by an average of 0.40 micromoles per liter.
Cognitive testing showed that eating tomato paste improved selective attention and one aspect of associative memory compared to the low-lycopene control diet. On the attention test, concentration performance started at an average baseline score of 171.0 points and increased by 7.8 points after the tomato phase, yielding an adjusted difference of 7.2 points over the control phase. Visual processing speed improved by a similar margin, rising from a baseline average of 188.3 points by 8.5 points after the tomato diet, for an adjusted gain of 8.3 points compared to the control period. These attention gains amounted to roughly 4 percent of baseline scores; in standardized terms, the authors describe the effects as moderate.
When the researchers excluded participants whose blood tests suggested they had not strictly followed the diet rules, these attention gains grew roughly twice as large, reaching a 13.7-point advantage in concentration and a 14.7-point advantage in processing speed. On the associative memory test, participants improved their ability to match faces with the correct names from a baseline average of 9.4 out of 12 points by 0.8 points over the control diet. The overall associative memory score, which combined all three parts of the face-name test, did not differ significantly between the two phases, however. In addition, the card-sorting test showed no meaningful changes in executive function during either phase of the study.
Although the trial’s sample size was originally calculated to detect changes in BDNF, blood levels of the protein showed only a borderline increase after the tomato intervention, with an adjusted average difference of 15.2 nanograms per milliliter compared to the control period (relative to baseline levels of 26.5 to 32.2 nanograms per milliliter).
The researchers noted that participants who completed the tomato diet first still had elevated BDNF levels when they started the control period a month later. An analysis restricted to the first phase, which avoids this carryover problem, found a consistent difference of 11.0 nanograms per milliliter. The authors suggest that this lingering carryover effect may reflect sustained biological changes triggered by tomato consumption that last longer than the four-week break between phases.
In the subgroup of 14 participants who underwent brain scans, the tomato diet was linked to reduced communication within two brain systems: the right frontoparietal network, which helps direct attention toward goals, and the auditory network, which processes sound. Larger drops in connectivity in these networks correlated with larger gains on the face-name matching task.
The authors suggest that this reduction in cross-network chatter may reflect greater neural efficiency, helping the brain filter out distracting background noise and sensory interference during visually demanding tasks. These brain findings came from 14 people and did not pass the study’s strictest statistical correction for multiple comparisons, so they are best treated as preliminary.
During the low-lycopene control diet, brain scans showed weakened connectivity within the dorsal attention network, a brain system responsible for sustaining focus. Across the study, bigger increases in blood lycopene levels were moderately correlated with stronger connectivity in the dorsal attention network and modestly correlated with faster cognitive processing speeds. The findings are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which linked higher blood levels of carotenoids and other nutrients to slower brain aging and better cognitive performance in older adults, rather than directly testing a tomato intervention in middle-aged adults.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because participants were eating actual tomato paste rather than swallowing an identical-looking pill, they knew which dietary phase they were in, and so did the staff who administered the cognitive tests. Expecting benefits could have boosted participants’ motivation during testing. The authors argue that the parallel changes in blood lycopene and brain scans make a purely expectation-driven explanation less likely.
The design of the control phase also introduces a question about what drove the differences between the two periods. Because participants had to actively avoid tomatoes and several red fruits during the control phase, the authors note that the restriction itself, rather than only the added tomato paste, may have contributed to differences between the phases, such as the weaker dorsal attention network connectivity seen during the control period. In addition, while lycopene was the primary compound tracked in the blood, tomatoes contain other beneficial nutrients like vitamin C, beta-carotene, and plant polyphenols that may have worked together to produce the observed effects.
The study sample was also relatively small, especially the 14-person brain imaging subgroup, and more than 90 percent of the participants had a university or postgraduate degree. Future studies will need to test larger and more diverse groups of people to see if the results hold true across the broader population. Longer trials with extended washout breaks and brain scans conducted while participants actively perform mental tasks could help clarify whether daily tomato intake provides lasting protection against age-related cognitive decline.
The study, “Tomato Intake Improves Cognitive Performance and Modulates Functional Brain Networks in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Crossover Clinical Trial,” was authored by Ricardo López-Solís, Carolina Donat-Vargas, Patricia Ramírez-Carrasco, Rocío M. Gutiérrez-Romero, Maria Pérez, Magda Castellví, Beatriz Bosch, Camila Arancibia-Riveros, Alejandro Hinojosa-Moscoso, Carlos Laredo, Emma Muñoz-Moreno, Ana Maria Ruiz-Leon, Rosa Casas, Ramon Estruch, Anna Vallverdú-Queralt, Marina Corrado, and Rosa M. Lamuela-Raventós.

Ukraine, Russia say US-brokered truce holding in ravaged city of Oleshky
- A US-brokered local truce in occupied Oleshky appeared to hold, with Ukraine and Russia reporting no violations as humanitarian aid and evacuations were planned.
- The city is badly damaged and nearly empty, with residents facing hunger and no medicine; former residents welcomed the chance to leave.
- Fighting continued elsewhere in Ukraine, with strikes on Kyiv and other areas, while talks may resume in November and leaders sought new ways to end the war.
AI generated
KYIV - A local truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3am local time (9am in Singapore).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents told AFP in September that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
“The possibility of evacuation from Oleshky is very good news for me and for the people who are trapped there,” Olga, a former resident whose last name AFP is withholding for security reasons, told AFP on Oct 27.
“My acquaintances are ready to leave,” she said.
Announcing the truce on Oct 23, US First Lady Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require”.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
AFP was not able to immediately verify details about the humanitarian mission or whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
The Russian military does not routinely grant international media, including AFP, access to areas under Russian occupation.
Right-leaning US cable network Newsmax said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city on Oct 29.
‘Biggest de-escalation since 2022’
David Arakhamia, a Ukrainian lawmaker who took part in peace negotiations with Russia in 2022, described the ceasefire as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”.
Both sides were adhering to the truce as of 5.30pm (10.30pm in Singapore), Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said in a post on Facebook, adding that it was scheduled to remain in effect until 10.59pm on Nov 1.
Russia also reported the truce was holding.
A staffer for Lubinets said the truce applied to the entire Kherson region.
Oleshky, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.
The population has since dropped from about 24,000 to around 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Former residents told AFP in September that some of those remaining in the city were hunting pigeons to survive and had “forgotten what bread is”.
The Ukrainian military has released drone footage of the town showing rows of empty apartment blocks, some charred by fire or partially destroyed by fighting.
Vladimir Saldo, a Moscow-installed official in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, told Russian media that those wishing to evacuate could go to Russian-occupied Crimea or Rostov in southwestern Russia, but would need to wait until the heavily-mined road from the city had been cleared.
Air barrages elsewhere in Ukraine
Outside the Kherson region, Russia continued to pummel the rest of Ukraine with air strikes, officials said.
Ballistic missiles struck a university campus in Kyiv on the evening of Oct 26.
Another overnight strike hit the capital’s Southern Bridge – a major road-and-rail artery crossing the Dnipro river.
Images posted on social media showed a gaping hole in between subway tracks and a mess of twisted metal.
In Russia, two people were killed “as a result of explosive devices being dropped” on the western city of Bryansk, the regional governor said.
Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-occupied Luhansk region killed four people, the region’s Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said.
Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed and millions forced to flee their homes since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, a conflict that has spiralled into Europe’s deadliest since World War II.
Russia, which denies targeting civilians, now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour: the Crimean peninsula, which it invaded and later claimed to have annexed in 2014, most of the eastern regions of Donetsk and Luhansk – collectively referred to as the Donbas – and large parts of the southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume in November, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister held a surprise call with Putin on Oct 27 aimed at ending the war, which they described as “frank and substantive”. AFP

UN chief urges greater role for women in peace processes as conflicts, sexual violence rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:53:27 UTC
04:53:27 KST

Diyar Guldogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday urged governments to strengthen women's participation in peace negotiations, restore funding for women-led organizations and ensure accountability for gender-based violence.
Addressing a UN Security Council open debate on women, peace and security, Guterres warned that gender inequality continued to undermine peace efforts despite international commitments to women's participation.
He cited Security Council Resolution 1325, adopted in 2000, which recognized the importance of women's involvement in conflict prevention, resolution and peacebuilding.
"But let's face facts: too often, it has resulted in a lot of talk, and not enough action," Guterres said, referring to the implementation of the women, peace and security agenda.
Guterres said the world was experiencing its highest number of conflicts since World War II, citing crises in the Gaza Strip, Ukraine, the Sahel, Sudan and Myanmar.
He warned that women and girls faced increasing exposure to armed conflict, sexual violence, displacement and restrictions on their fundamental rights.
"The number of UN-verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence has sharply increased, reaching over 9,700 last year – with the actual number certain to be much higher," he said.
Women and girls also faced growing risks from explosive weapons used in densely populated areas, including in Myanmar, Sudan and the occupied Palestinian territory, he said.
Guterres also raised concerns about rising maternal mortality in crisis zones, disruptions to girls' education and attacks on women leaders, journalists and human rights defenders.
3 priorities for governments
Guterres said women remained largely excluded from formal peace negotiations despite evidence that their meaningful participation could strengthen peace agreements and improve prospects for lasting stability.
Women accounted for just 5% of negotiators across 57 peace processes in 2025, he said.
Fewer than one-fifth of peace agreements concluded globally that year included at least one reference to women, girls, gender or sexual violence, he added.
Guterres urged governments and other participants in peace processes to introduce binding targets and quotas to ensure women's meaningful participation in negotiations.
He outlined three immediate priorities: securing women's representation in peace talks, increasing funding for women's organizations in conflict-affected areas and enforcing zero tolerance for violence against women and girls.
"Of course, these three priorities are not the only areas where action is urgently needed," he said.
Guterres called on governments to fulfill their official development assistance commitments and restore funding to organizations supporting women and girls in conflict settings, particularly those affected by forced displacement.
He also demanded full accountability for perpetrators of gender-based violence, including conflict-related sexual violence.
The UN chief urged authorities to remove restrictions on female humanitarian workers and strengthen protections for those delivering aid.
Beyond those priorities, Guterres called for stronger domestic laws addressing gender-based violence, improved economic security for women, greater support for grassroots organizations and better collection of gender-related data.
"Equality is not a dream. It's a decision," he said.

Voter turnout at Israel’s elections exceed 74% two hours before end of voting — TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:53:16 UTC
04:53:16 KST

TEL AVIV, October 27. /TASS/. Voter turnout at the elections to Israel’s Knesset, or parliament, reached 74.3% two hours before the closure of polling stations, TV Channel 12 reported.
According to it, this figure is a record for any election held in Israel since 1988. Furthermore, it has already surpassed the final turnout figure from the previous parliamentary elections, held in November 2022, when 70.63% of voters took part.
More than 12,000 polling stations opened on Tuesday at 7:00 a.m. local time (5:00 a.m. GMT) and will close 10:00 p.m. (8:00 p.m. Moscow time). Shortly after they close, exit poll results will be announced and the vote count will begin. The elections are taking place amid heightened security measures; according to Israel’s Channel 12, a total of 20,000 police officers, border police, and volunteers are maintaining order. For its part, the army announced a blockade of the Palestinian territories and the closure of all checkpoints in the West Bank.
Parliamentary elections in Israel are held on party lists, with 36 parties vying for seats in parliament. The electoral threshold is 3.25%. AS many as 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote. The Central Elections Committee is expected to announce preliminary vote counts on October 29, and the final results of the elections are to be officially released no later than November 4. Once the official results are received, the president will begin consultations with representatives of the parties that have won seats in the Knesset, following which he will task one of the lawmakers with forming a new governing coalition.

Mongolia Eyes a Non-Permanent Seat on the UNSC – in 2048
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:53:00 UTC
04:53:00 KST

In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), the Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa announced Mongolia’s official candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for the 2048-2049 term. With Mongolia’s track record in contribution to the U.N. global missions and its growing commitment, Ulaanbaatar believes that it may have the qualification to gain such an opportunity. That’s not unusual; what’s odd is the lengthy timeline involved.
During his speech to the UNGA, Khurelsukh reflected on and reiterated Mongolia’s multipilared foreign policy objectives. He noted that Mongolia supports United Nations reform, peacekeeping operations, sustainable development goals, and has a special interest in landlocked developing countries.
This year, Mongolia’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Ambassador Ankhbayar Nyamdorj served as one of the vice presidents of the 81st UNGA. Mongolia also chaired the Asia-Pacific States Group this June for the election of the General Assembly.
Despite Mongolia’s many contributions to the United Nations, as Khurelsukh pointed out, the country is “one of the 58 states that have never served as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.”
At first glance, announcing Mongolia’s candidacy for a seat more than two decades away may seem unusually distant. But the announcement serves to promulgate Mongolia’s deeper commitment to international engagement as an active and responsible player on the world stage. The goal of serving on the UNSC in 2048-2049 cements Mongolia’s longstanding multilateral diplomacy as a concrete, long-term objective.
Mongolia’s contributions to the United Nations have been growing since gaining membership status in 1961. Mongolia’s engagement with the U.N. and U.N.-led missions have diversified and expanded over time, making Ulaanbaatar an unquestionably active member of the global organization.
Since 2002, Mongolian “Blue Helmets” – U.N. peacekeepers, including both military, and police contingents – have served in diverse conflict zones around the world: Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC), South Sudan (UNMISS), Abyei Region (UNISFA), Western Sahara (MINURSO), Lebanon (UNIFIL), Central African Republic (MINUSCA), and Cyprus (UNFICYP). In total, Mongolia has deployed 21,000 peacekeepers.
As of July 2026, the latest data update from the U.N., Mongolia had 548 active military and police personnel deployed to U.N. peacekeeping operations. That makes Mongolia the 24th largest contributor of peacekeepers in the world. It’s even more impressive given Mongolia’s relatively small population. On a per capita basis, Mongolia is the third largest contributor, behind only Rwanda and Uruguay.
In June, Mongolian peacekeepers and contingents received U.N. medals for their contribution in civilian protection and safety in conflict zones. Mongolia is planning to host international conference on women in UN peacekeeping in 2027.
In recent years, Mongolia has also adopted and actively promoted the U.N. Sustainable Development Goals. With issues of climate change taking center stage in the U.N., Mongolia stepped up its game and hosted COP17 to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) this summer.
Moreover, Mongolia’s continued commitment to its nuclear-weapon-free status has received recognition through the U.N. General Assembly. Mongolia’s Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on Northeast Asian Security serves as a recognized platform for regional and global actors to discuss nuclearization and proliferation issues.
Taken individually, none of these initiatives would guarantee Mongolia a Security Council seat. Taken together, with Mongolia’s track record of U.N. contributions, they form the foundation of the case. These active engagements within the U.N. framework serve as an important element for Mongolia’s multilateral diplomacy, opening diverse cooperation mechanisms that are supported by Mongolia’s multi-pillared foreign policy.
The choice of 2048-2049 as a target date may appear unusually distant, but UNSC candidacies are often planned far in advance. Mongolia will compete for one of the seats allocated to the Asia-Pacific Group, which holds two of the Council’s 10 rotating non-permanent seats. One Asia-Pacific seat normally comes up for election each year.
Unlike some regional groups, however, the Asia-Pacific Group does not have a formally established rotation system for its Security Council seats. Therefore, countries have to plan their candidacies around other declared and anticipated candidates. Each would-be UNSC member must make an assessment of when they have the highest chance of being selected.
For Mongolia, 2048-2049 emerged as the first viable opening in that longer-term regional calendar. The distant date thus illustrates how far ahead states must think when seeking representation on one of the U.N.’s most consequential bodies. Even so, Mongolia’s attempt to “reserve” a seat may not work. The competitive landscape could change considerably over the next two decades, as any country could throw its hat into the ring.
Under the U.N. Charter, non-permanent Security Council members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms, with attention given both to contributions to international peace and security and to equitable geographical distribution. Election requires a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. To reach that goal, Mongolia must continue building the substance behind its candidacy.
As of now, it’s not clear what agenda Mongolia would like to highlight in its candidacy. For comparison, Kyrgyzstan was elected to its first non-permanent stint on the UNSC in July. Its campaign, as Oliver Fisk noted for The Diplomat at the time, “prioritized four key areas of focus: conflict prevention; promoting the sustainable development of mountainous, less developed, and small-island states; nuclear disarmament; and support for U.N. reform.”
The basis for a Mongolian campaign can already be guessed at. Its consistent support for U.N. peacekeeping missions and its call for nuclear disarmament will likely bolster Mongolia’s diplomatic identity. In addition, Mongolia can be expected to highlight issues that already form the focal points for its U.N. engagement, such as advocacy for landlocked countries; issues related to the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda; climate and desertification issues; and regional dialogue. Mongolia’s track record on these issues will bolster Ulaanbaatar’s bid to gain a non-permanent seat at the UNSC in 2048-2049.
There are risks involved with a seat on the U.N.’s most powerful body. Mongolia has spent much of its post-Cold War foreign policy attempting to preserve room for maneuver between its two large neighbors while expanding relations with “third neighbors” and multilateral institutions. A seat on the Security Council would place Mongolia directly inside difficult debates over wars, sanctions, and geopolitical disputes involving major powers.
If elected to the UNSC, Ulaanbaatar could face pressure to take visible positions on issues concerning Russia, China, the United States, or their respective partners. The same membership that would expand Mongolia’s international influence could therefore make its traditional balancing act considerably more challenging.
Khurelsukh launched Mongolia’s candidacy, but he will be long out of office when the election takes place more than 20 years later. That said, Mongolia’s approach to the United Nations is not dependent on changing governments but rather a foreign policy strategy that is approved by Mongolia’s legislative branch and executed at the government and agency level. Since Mongolia jointed the U.N. in 1961, its relationship with the U.N. has moved on the same trajectory, toward deeper contributions and engagement. The long-term test will be whether Mongolia can convert its international initiatives into sustained institutional influence and durable partnerships across successive governments.
Mongolia will have more than two decades to build support and strengthen its diplomatic record, but the campaign will also have to survive several presidents, governments, and foreign ministers, as well as shifting geopolitics and competing domestic interests.
As a relatively small, landlocked state situated between Russia and China, Mongolia has limited ability to shape the strategic environment around it through hard power. International institutions, a diverse set of diplomatic partners, and participation in multilateral initiatives have provided Ulaanbaatar with additional political space beyond the constraints of its geographic location. The bid for a Security Council seat fits naturally within this approach.

Russia emerging as leading supplier of fertilizers to Africa with 20% share — UralChem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russia is becoming a leading supplier of fertilizers to Africa, having increased the share of its supplies to the continent to 18-20% of total imports, up from 4% in 2018, UralChem Group told TASS.
"Russia is steadily emerging as a leading supplier of fertilizers to Africa. For instance, the share of Russian supplies in African imports has grown from 4% in 2018 to 18-20% in 2025," the company stated ahead of the Russia-Africa forum.
This means that Moscow acts as a guarantor of the stability of the continent’s agri-food markets, UralChem said. "This is a highly responsible role, and we recognize that part of our function is to help maintain the stability of this market," the company added.
Uralchem ranks among the top five fertilizer suppliers to the African continent, having increased its sales from 100,000 tons in 2018 to around 1 million tons by 2025. Moreover, the company supplied about 135,000 tons of fertilizers to African nations free of charge between 2022 and 2024, while also covering the transportation costs associated with these humanitarian shipments.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:49:18 UTC
04:49:18 KST

Legendary musician Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit against President Donald Trump's campaign committee for infringing Young's copyright by playing his song "Rockin' in the Free World" just before the president took the stage to speak at an Oct. 12 rally in Youngstown, Ohio.
The Trump 47 Committee has caused that song, without the musician's permission, "to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections," Young's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Richmond, Virginia, alleges.
Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license," the suit filed Monday says.
Young, 80, in 2020 sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump for President Inc., in Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement of "Rockin' in the Free World," and another song written by Young, "Devil's Sidewalk," for having played the songs without permission at campaign rallies.
In that first case, Trump's corporation "asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use 'Rockin' in the Free World' without a license and permission from Young," the new suit said.
CNBC has requested comment from the Trump 47 Committee about the suit, and from Young's lawyers.
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the Republican National Committee, which did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Young, who was born in Canada, is a naturalized U.S. citizen. He is a two-time inductee in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: in 1995 as a solo artist, and in 1997 as a member of Buffalo Springfield. Young was also a member of the folk rock supergroup Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young.
Young released "Rockin' in the Free World" in 1989.
His lawsuit describes the tune as a "blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten."
The lyrics include descriptions of a mother discarding her baby, addiction, and "garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn't shared by all," the suit notes.
"In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for," the suit says.
In addition to the Trump 47 Committee, the suit lists five other defendants, identified by the pseudonym "Doe," whom Young believes are liable for infringing on Young's copyright.
The Oct. 12 Trump rally that is referenced in the lawsuit was also the scene of an incident that has drawn attention from local law enforcement. Videos from the rally show several attendees apparently attacking and beating a woman, Blake Miley, who had repeatedly yelled 'fascist" at Trump while wearing a shirt bearing the message "Release the Epstein Files."
Mahoning County, Ohio, Sheriff Jerry Greene reportedly is investigating three individuals in connection with the incident.

Ceasefire takes effect in Russian-occupied Oleshky ahead of planned civilian evacuation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:46:37 UTC
04:46:37 KST

A ceasefire has taken effect around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, located in Ukraine’s Kherson Region, as part of an agreed humanitarian operation to evacuate local residents. The ceasefire was announced by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and the Russian Defense Ministry.
Ukraine’s ombudsman wrote on Telegram:
“Today, at 3 a.m. Kyiv time and 4 a.m. Moscow time, a ceasefire was introduced in designated areas connected with the humanitarian mission.
This is taking place as part of a humanitarian mission that we are carrying out jointly with Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, with the mediation and coordination of U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
The parties are observing the agreements that Yana Lantratova and I reached.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry also confirmed the ceasefire:
“In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of the settlement of Oleshky in the Kherson region, the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation have ceased fire on the Kherson front and introduced a ‘regime of silence’ starting from 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27, 2026.”
As Lubinets previously said, before the evacuation begins, demining teams will first clear roads of explosives. Humanitarian aid will then be delivered to the city, and registration will begin for residents who want to leave Oleshky. The evacuation is expected to start only after those steps are completed.
The agreement on a ceasefire in Oleshky became public on Oct. 23. The White House announced it first, after which officials in Moscow and Kyiv confirmed the arrangement.
According to the latest estimates from Ukrainian authorities, about 2,000 people remained trapped in Oleshky under a complete blockade — without food, medical care, or a stable electricity supply. In addition to Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV had also joined the efforts to secure a humanitarian corridor for residents of the occupied city, calling Vladimir Putin from a hospital and asking him to halt the fighting in Oleshky as soon as possible.
In late September, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty called for an immediate ceasefire in occupied Oleshky in order to allow unhindered access for humanitarian organizations and the safe evacuation of civilians. He said the humanitarian crisis in the city was rapidly worsening and that civilians, including children, were trapped without adequate food, medical care, running water, or electricity.
In early October, Ukrainian officials reported that the country’s National Guard had carried out a successful operation to deliver humanitarian supplies to Russian-occupied Oleshky. Drones delivered about 400 packages weighing nearly 4 metric tons in total. The shipments contained food, medicine, and supplies for children.

Australia's police chief has a warning about where online hate can lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:54 UTC
04:44:54 KST

In brief
- The AFP warned threats against politicians reflected a deeper social problem.
- The recent attack on MP Helen Haines has renewed concerns about safety in public life.
No single measure can undo the shift in social attitudes that is driving political threats, according to the head of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), as it grapples with how to keep parliamentarians safe.
AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett began her late-night appearance at the Senate estimates hearing, noting "a heaviness that hangs across Australia" after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
The federal member for Indi lost both her legs and remains in a serious but stable condition in a Melbourne hospital after being struck repeatedly by a four-wheel drive outside her Wangaratta office.
State authorities are leading the ongoing investigation into the motive behind the attack, with the police chief confirming the alleged offender was not known to federal police.
As the nation comes to grips with the attack, Barrett said it has aligned with a global trend of violence emerging with little or no warning from individuals largely unknown to authorities.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievances, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns," she told the Senate estimates hearing on Tuesday night.
"What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and far-away criminals, has been impacted by fully integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence."
Barrett said technology has enabled an "instant pipeline of hate" delivered to people's homes, including teenagers, and workplaces because of the ubiquity of devices.
"Our investigators are charging almost one person a week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians or high office holders," she told senators.
The AFP received 785 protective security reports containing "adverse content" about federal parliamentarians in the first half of the year, Barrett said, with 394 directed at male MPs and 371 at female MPs.
She added that while all reports were taken seriously, the "adverse content" sometimes did not meet a criminal threshold.
An AFP psychological analysis of Joint Counter Terrorism Team youth cases from 2020-2025 showed the 55 boys aged between 12 and 17 were entirely or partially radicalised online, Barrett said.
The ideological presentation of those youths had shifted over the past two years away from jihadist extremism or white supremacist ideology, she said, with an increasing number having hybrid or unclear beliefs and displaying "ideological fluidity".
"In three out of five cases, the youths had received support, treatment or intervention for a mental health condition," she added.
Individuals who believe threats and violence are tolerable if their cause is noble are taking to social media, corroding community and normalising violence, creating a fundamental shift, Barrett said.
"It continues to impact on many, most notably the Jewish community. Antisemitism is often the early warning sign of a decay in our society, and the poisoning of our compact with each other," she said.
"Our collective consciousness must be awake to this threat, and acknowledge there will always be another target group of hate if we do not recognise where it can start.
"There is not one single measure alone that will stop the threats, because this goes to a wider societal problem Australia is facing," Barrett said, pledging to work with the home affairs and finance departments to ensure the security of electorate offices and the homes of parliamentarians.
Barrett reiterated she did not seek to judge how parliamentarians "do politics," police free speech or intervene in political discourse.
The federal police commissioner will meet her state and territory counterparts soon to discuss the issue of democratic and parliamentary security.

Three Russian Diesel Tankers Head to US, Including One Sanctioned in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:39 UTC
04:44:39 KST

- Category
- World
Three Russian Diesel Tankers Head to US, Including One Sanctioned in Europe
Three tankers carrying around 140,000 tonnes of Russian diesel, including one vessel sanctioned by European authorities, are heading to US ports, the Financial Times reported on October 27.
The shipments are the first licensed by US authorities under President Donald Trump’s recent agreement with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, to exempt Russian diesel from sanctions. The vessels are expected to arrive shortly after the November 3 US midterm elections.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Germany rejected the easing of restrictions, arguing that pressure on Moscow should be increased rather than reduced. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned that lifting sanctions without enforceable Russian de-escalation would signal weakness and allow Moscow to prolong the war. Czech President Petr Pavel later argued that the diesel decision weakened Western leverage over Russia and made a ceasefire harder to achieve.
According to the Financial Times, the vessels include the Hong Kong-owned, Sierra Leone-flagged tanker Leruo, which is sanctioned by the UK, EU, and Canada. Ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic showed the vessel signaling an arrival on the US Atlantic coast on November 11.
Leruo departed St. Petersburg on October 17 and was in the North Sea off Norway on October 26. European authorities sanctioned the tanker in 2025 over Russian cargoes and practices including disabling location technology and conducting ship-to-ship transfers.
The vessel was also accused of violating the G7 price cap on Russian oil cargoes, according to OpenSanctions .
Its planned arrival could create legal complications for companies handling the cargo in the US. Jeremy Paner, a partner at Washington-based law firm Hughes Hubbard, told the Financial Times that a tanker sanctioned by the EU, UK, and Canada entering a US port would be “highly problematic” because their financial and maritime systems are closely interconnected.
The US banned imports of Russian oil and refined petroleum products in March 2022. Washington later joined other G7 countries in imposing a price cap on Russian diesel exports.
Trump’s administration has issued a temporary license permitting Russian diesel imports under the new agreement with Moscow. However, members of Congress have challenged whether the administration can authorize the imports without violating restrictions enacted into US law.
On October 26, senior Democrats and Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned US banks, port authorities, and fuel distributors that companies involved in importing Russian diesel could face congressional investigations and legal action.
“Any importation of Russian diesel into the US raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” the lawmakers wrote, according to the Financial Times.
They added that companies violating US law could face criminal and civil liability and argued that the transactions raised national security concerns because revenue from the fuel could support Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The first tanker scheduled to reach the US is the Greek-owned Agioi Fanendes, which is carrying around 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel and is expected in New York on November 7, according to ship-tracking data cited by the Financial Times.
If unloaded as indicated, the shipment would be the first Russian gas oil or diesel cargo tracked by commodities platform Kpler to arrive in the US since July 2023.
A second vessel, the 20-year-old Russian tanker Talisman, is scheduled to reach the US East Coast on November 9, followed by Leruo two days later. The Financial Times noted that ship destinations can change and tracking data is not always definitive.
The shipments come as US diesel prices average $6.34 per gallon, compared with $3.66 a year earlier. The Trump administration has presented the Russian diesel agreement as part of its effort to reduce fuel prices.
The Financial Times also reported that legal uncertainty and relatively small shipment volumes could deter major companies from participating. One oil trader told the newspaper that most large firms were likely to avoid handling Russian diesel because of the associated legal risks.
Before the first US-bound cargoes emerged, Russian diesel had already begun returning to its established overseas markets. UNITED24 Media reported that Türkiye accounted for about 34% of Russian diesel shipments in 2026, followed by Brazil at 24% and Morocco at 10%, as exports resumed following the October policy changes.

China's Alibaba wins injunction against Pentagon contract restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:32 UTC
04:44:32 KST

(Reuters) -- A U.S. federal judge on Monday granted Alibaba Group Holding's request for a preliminary injunction, ordering the U.S. government not to deny Pentagon contracts to companies because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries do business with firms that engage in lobbying activities for the e-commerce giant.
Alibaba sued the U.S. government in June after the Pentagon added it to a list of companies allegedly aiding China's military, alongside internet search provider Baidu, EV maker BYD and other major Chinese manufacturing and technology firms.
Monday's ruling means Alibaba will be able to retain U.S. lobbyists who also represent Pentagon contractors, removing a potential obstacle to the company's efforts to challenge its designation as a Chinese military company.
Alibaba fired dozens of its Washington lobbyists after the Pentagon action in June, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter who was not authorized to speak to the media.
The designation does not impose formal sanctions, but restricts Pentagon contracts with listed companies and, from 2027, purchases of their products or services through third parties.
Other listed Chinese tech firms were also concerned about the designation's impact on international lobbying activities as well as the indirect procurement ban, which would completely remove Chinese products from US defense contractors' supply chains, the source added.
Alibaba has denied any military ties, saying its products and services are built for retail, logistics and enterprise technology rather than defense or intelligence.
"The determinations have no basis in fact or law," Alibaba said in its lawsuit in June, seeking its removal from the list.
Monday's injunction does not remove Alibaba from the Pentagon list, which the company is continuing to challenge in court.
Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
Alibaba is one of several Chinese firms taking legal action to challenge their placement on the Pentagon's list.
Last month, two subsidiaries of the world's largest electric vehicle maker, BYD, sued the U.S. Department of Defense over a federal law banning any Pentagon contractors from hiring lobbyists that also work with blacklisted firms, arguing that it breached BYD's First Amendment rights.
In August, DJI, the world's largest drone maker, appealed its inclusion on the blacklist with the court finding merit in its argument that unclassified records did not support the conclusion that the company contributed to the Chinese defense industrial base.
The appeals court ordered the lower court to reconsider its decision to reject DJI's bid to be removed from the Pentagon list, and the case is ongoing.
The same month, biotech firm WuXi AppTec also won a preliminary injunction from a U.S. federal court, which blocked its inclusion on the list. WuXi said the Pentagon designation was politically motivated.

Protesters storm pro-Vucic TV station in Belgrade (VIDEO)
Supporters of Serbia’s student-led opposition have stormed the Belgrade offices of Informer, a broadcaster supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic, as celebrations of their election win turned violent. Vucic condemned the attack as an assault on media freedom and accused the EU of turning a blind eye.
The incident came a day after the Student List movement defeated Vucic’s United Serbia coalition in a snap parliamentary election, ending 14 years of rule by his Serbian Progressive Party and its allies.
According to Informer, demonstrators smashed windows and forced their way through the entrance before damaging offices and threatening journalists. Employees reportedly hid in bathrooms and the basement before police arrived and evacuated staff.
Editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic said attackers destroyed cameras, computers and other equipment worth tens of thousands of euros. Some demanded access to the control room to disconnect cables, he said.

Russian diplomat Desyatnikov appointed UN Assistant Secretary General

UNITED NATIONS, October 27. /TASS/. United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres has appointed veteran Russian diplomat Gleb Desyatnikov as Assistant Secretary General for Mine Action and Police in the Department of Peace Operations (DPO).
"Mr. Desyatnikov brings to the position more than 35 years of experience in international relations, political affairs and security issues across government, multilateral diplomacy and conflict-affected regions," the Office of the Spokesperson for the United Nations Secretary General said in a press release.
Since 2018, Desyatnikov has served as Russian Ambassador to Jordan. Prior to that, from 2010 to 2018, he was Deputy Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Middle East and North Africa Department.
In 2004-2010, he served as Senior Adviser on Middle East and North Africa affairs at the Russian Permanent Mission to the United Nations in New York. In 2000-2004, he worked at the Russian Foreign Minister as Chief Officer for the Iraq and Jordan Political Desk. In 1997-2000, Desyatnikov served in the Russian Embassy in Jordan. And between 1994 and 1997, he also undertook several seconded deployments with the United Nations Special Commission on Iraq (UNSCOM).

EU divided over 'associate membership' for Canada ahead of Montreal summit: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:42:50 UTC
04:42:50 KST

Melike Pala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
EU member states remained divided over whether to offer Canada "associate membership" status, with at least four countries opposing the term's inclusion in a joint summit statement, Politico reported on Tuesday.
EU ambassadors failed to reach an agreement on the wording during talks Monday, according to the report.
A subsequent attempt to approve the statement through a so-called silence procedure also failed after Germany and at least three other countries raised objections before Tuesday's midday deadline, two EU diplomats told Politico.
The issue is expected to return to the agenda at another meeting of EU ambassadors Wednesday, a day before the EU-Canada summit begins in Montreal.
Germany is leading efforts to remove the term "associate membership" entirely from the proposed text, the diplomats said.
The disagreement reflects divisions within the bloc over the proposed status, which European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg last month.
Four EU diplomats previously told Politico that von der Leyen had not consulted member state capitals before putting forward the proposal.
Von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and several European commissioners are expected to travel to Montreal for the Oct. 29-30 summit.
The talks are expected to focus on strengthening EU-Canada relations and expanding cooperation in trade, energy, education and the Arctic.

GECF member states call for ensuring creation of fair gas price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:42:10 UTC
04:42:10 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member states of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) have called for ensuring a fair price for natural gas, according to the declaration adopted following the summit in Moscow.
The member countries of the association call for "ensuring the creation of a fair price for natural gas, including through the use of long-term contracts and diversified pricing mechanisms, such as oil-price adjustment, in international gas trade in order to achieve an objective distribution of risks, enhance price predictability, reduce market volatility, and attract necessary investment in gas infrastructure, including underground storage facilities and liquefied natural gas storage," the document reads.
This also refers to ensuring stable gas supplies.
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal are observer states. GECF members hold roughly 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, account for 38% of global gas production and 42% of global gas exports, and represent 47% of global exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

Shackled, shaved and in uniform: first inmates arrive at Costa Rica mega-prison
SAN JOSE, Oct 27 - Costa Rica has locked up the first 123 inmates in a new mega-prison, built with the help of the Salvadoran government in the outskirts of capital San José, the country's justice ministry said on Tuesday.
The ministry shared images showing rows of inmates dressed in orange, seated with shaved heads bowed and their hands behind their necks, in poses resembling photographs from El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), the mega-prison where President Nayib Bukele's government holds tens of thousands of gang members and suspected gang affiliates.
Costa Rica's maximum security prison, which it calls the High Containment Center against Organized Crime (CACCO), has been presented by the government of President Laura Fernandez as a symbol of a new "tough on crime" approach championed by her administration in response to a security crisis facing Costa Rica, once one of the most peaceful countries in the Western Hemisphere.
"Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history," Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement. "CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation." Aguilar has said the new facility will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system.
The prison has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, equivalent to 20% of the country's prison population.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organized crime. The country recorded a record number of homicides in 2023, although figures have since stabilized. Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets. REUTERS

Russian authorities track 6 million  social media profiles critical of the war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:40:36 UTC
04:40:36 KST

Almost half of the 12.5 million social media accounts and profiles monitored daily by Russia’s Federal Agency for Youth Affairs (Rosmolodezh) are critical of Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to the agency’s deputy head Denis Ashirov. Ashirov presented the data on Oct. 26 at a meeting of the expert council of the State Duma committee on family protection, saying that the agency is tracking 6 million profiles criticizing the “special military operation” and the Russian army. Rosmolodezh classifies such publications as “destructive and unlawful information.”
In addition, the agency links another 1.1 million monitored profiles to political violence and criticism of the authorities, 1.5 million to drugs and drug-related content, and 906,000 to the promotion and rehabilitation of Nazism. It is unclear from Ashirov’s remarks what criteria the agency uses to determine the presence of criticism of the war and the authorities, whether the listed categories overlap, and what share of the accounts belongs to minors. It is also not specified how many unique users stand behind these profiles.
The figures were cited in the context of protecting children from dangerous online content. State Duma family protection committee chair Nina Ostanina noted that existing mechanisms for blocking content do not make it possible to fully restrict the spread of banned materials, and teenagers continue to use digital tools to bypass restrictions. At the same time, the lawmaker acknowledged that bans alone cannot solve the problem — as Ostanina herself explained, restrictions can pique heightened interest in banned content among underage users.
At the same meeting, a representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russian law enforcement authorities identified 62,300 people suspected of committing crimes on the internet; 4,220 of them (6.8%) were minors. Another 692 minors were held liable for fraud.
How Rosmolodezh monitors social media users
Rosmolodezh has a Center for the Study and Network Monitoring of the Youth Environment (CISM), created on Vladimir Putin’s instruction. The organization searches the internet for information that the Russian authorities consider dangerous to minors.
As The Insider previously reported, the center takes part in identifying “socially dangerous” schoolchildren and students. According to Rosmolodezh head Grigory Gurov, thanks to the center’s work, Russia opened approximately 500 criminal and several hundred administrative cases in 2024. In addition, thousands of people were subjected to “preventive measures” aimed at countering the spread of banned information.
In August 2026, DOXA reported on the center’s work. Journalists studied the court system and found 48 rulings from 2025 and the first half of 2026 in which information supplied by the center served as the basis for prosecution. Among them is the case of Magnitogorsk resident Sergei Sokolov, who was fined 30,000 rubles ($373) after the center reported him to the prosecutor’s office over his VKontakte comments criticizing the Russian army. In Novosibirsk Region in 2025, the most common category of “destructive” content identified by Rosmolodezh was criticism of the war in Ukraine. Anarchist ideas and drug propaganda came in second and third.
The center has also been mentioned in investigations by international law enforcement agencies. In December 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that, according to the charging documents, several CISM employees were members of the pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16), which carried out DDoS attacks on government institutions, banks, and infrastructure facilities in various countries. According to the U.S. investigation, center employees also took part in creating the network infrastructure for those attacks. Vot Tak previously linked the center’s leadership to the development of the DDoSia program used by the group to attack the websites of European states.
Earlier, media reports also covered Russia’s development of a system called Generation Index. Its closed part is designed to track the ideological attitudes of young people, including their views on the West, LGBT people, and the war in Ukraine. In particular, the system is designed to assess the share of young people who believe in Russia’s war effort, and low figures are supposed to serve as grounds for the authorities to take “urgent measures.”

Anthropic Says It Will Revolutionize Biology—Some Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:39:04 UTC
04:39:04 KST

AI giant Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have repeatedly claimed that the company’s models will revolutionize biology and drug discovery. But in its IPO filing Monday, Anthropic struck a humbler note, acknowledging its lack of experience in physical experimentation and the potential pitfalls of drug development. Wherever it’s going, it seems, it will take some time to get there.
Two years ago, Amodei wrote that he was “open” to the idea that AI systems could produce a thousand years of progress in biology in just five to 10 years. In August, he said on X that “Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine.” In the same post, he predicted that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in the next five to 10 years and promised a “deluge of AI-accelerated drugs.” The company also promoted the discovery of a “Crispr-like” enzyme by Claude in September.
While the new IPO filing still touts AI’s ability to “profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine” and compress “decades of scientific progress into years,” it’s reserved about how it will turn the potential into the actual.
The company says that its teams “need first-hand experience doing scientific research and drug discovery” and that its life sciences activities will require it “to engage in activities outside our historical experience as a software and research organization.” That includes handling potentially hazardous materials, operating laboratory equipment, and complying with a bevy of regulations.
Anthropic also toned down its language about its enzyme discovery, saying it “might have the potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool, perhaps for gene editing.” (Italics added for emphasis.) Researchers previously told WIRED they were skeptical of the enzyme discovery’s value and utility, and one scientist who had been studying these exact enzymes became suspicious that Claude used his research. (The company said neither its model nor its molecular biology team would have had access to this material.)
The IPO filing indicates that Anthropic no longer sees itself solely as an outside provider of AI tools to the biotech industry; it sees biotech discovery as a core part of its business model. And like all biotech companies, it faces the long timeline of drug development. Any AI-assisted discoveries still have to be researched in a test tube, then in animals, and eventually in people. Even if AI could help sort out which new drugs or targets will work in humans versus those likely to be duds, it will still take years of testing to prove their safety and efficacy.
Anthropic recognizes these challenges in its filing. “Any drug candidates or other discoveries resulting from these efforts would face the lengthy, costly, and uncertain development and regulatory pathways characteristic of the life sciences industry, and may never generate revenue,” the filing says. (For his part, Amodei made the case in his August X post for streamlining regulations for the coming wave of AI-generated drugs.)
US Securities and Exchange Commission filings are generally more cautious than statements made by companies or their executives, given the legal risks of overstating claims to would-be investors. And the IPO makes clear that the company believes its technology will drive revolutionary advancements.
But as Anthropic pushes further into biological discovery, it will face the same conundrum as other biotech companies: proving their worth in trials that can’t be hastened simply by adding computers.

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reportedly heads to US despite travel ban after election defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:38:29 UTC
04:38:29 KST

Laura Gamba
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Brazil's defeated presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has reportedly left the country for the United States despite a judicial travel ban, with conflicting accounts of his whereabouts emerging Tuesday as authorities investigate a possible escape through Argentina.
Brazilian news outlet Globo cited sources close to Bolsonaro that it said confirmed he had left Brazil with his family, while official channels have not officially confirmed his departure or established his route.
The reports by came after Brazil's Federal Police canceled Bolsonaro's regular and diplomatic passports Tuesday when he failed to comply with a court order requiring him to surrender the documents within 24 hours.
Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the order Monday, a day after Bolsonaro lost the presidential runoff to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
The ruling also prohibited the 45-year-old senator from leaving Brazil.
The restrictions stem from an investigation into suspected money laundering and currency evasion involving financial transactions linked to attorney Willer Tomaz, an associate of Bolsonaro.
The senator is also under investigation in a separate case involving the financing of Dark Horse, a biographical film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro. Authorities are examining alleged payments connected to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of the now-defunct financial institution Banco Master.
Bolsonaro, who denies wrongdoing, said Monday that he had no intention of leaving Brazil.
“I have never thought about leaving the country. I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” Bolsonaro said, describing the judicial order as “a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
He made the remarks after visiting his father, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest in Brasilia.
Speculation about his whereabouts intensified Tuesday after Argentine media reported that he had crossed into Argentina by land using his national identity card and planned to board a private flight to Miami with his wife and daughters.
The reports centered on a Gulfstream G400 private jet, registered as LV-JQW and operated by Argentine charter company Baires Fly SA, which arrived at Puerto Iguazu airport near the Brazilian border from Buenos Aires late Monday.
The aircraft had been expected to depart for the US with four passengers and three crew members but remained on the ground Tuesday.
Argentine media reported that aviation authorities had withheld departure clearance over regulatory issues, while other reports indicated that the planned passengers never arrived and the flight was canceled.
However, Argentina's National Directorate of Migration said it had no record of Bolsonaro entering the country and that no flight plan had been submitted listing members of his family.
The agency said authorities had inspected the aircraft and its crew and found the company's documentation in order.
Brazilian federal police also found no record of Bolsonaro leaving the country through an official immigration checkpoint and began examining border crossings and flight records to determine whether he had departed.
Bolsonaro's campaign coordinator, Sen. Rogerio Marinho, initially denied that he had left Brazil, while his brother Eduardo, who lives in the US, dismissed the reports as a "lie."
Bolsonaro's reported departure comes two days after Lula defeated him in Sunday's presidential runoff to secure a fourth term in office.
The senator initially called for the election result to be annulled, although his Liberal Party has acknowledged Lula's victory.

GECF to establish mechanisms to respond to crisis situations on gas market
Unknown

04:37:38 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member states of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) intend to establish mechanisms for responding to crisis situations on the gas market, according to the declaration adopted following the summit in Moscow.
"We declare our shared determination to establish mechanisms to respond to crisis situations on the gas market, including the expansion of high-level consultations to assess the impact of external shocks, coordinate actions to ensure reliable gas supplies, and develop effective tools to support energy security," the document reads.
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal are observer states. GECF members hold roughly 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, account for 38% of global gas production and 42% of global gas exports, and represent 47% of global exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

01:36:24 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said that Turkish investors were ready to acquire a stake in the Akkuyu nuclear power plant in southern Türkiye, as Moscow seeks partners for the multibillion-dollar project.
“We are building, operating and owning the plant. Some Turkish companies ... are ready to acquire a stake. We would welcome that,” Putin said on Wednesday, according to Interfax news agency, valuing the project at around $25 billion.
The plant is being developed by Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom and is financed by Russia.
Rosatom seeks partners to share investment burden
Russia and Türkiye signed an agreement in 2010 to build the plant, which will feature four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors. Construction began in 2018.
Rosatom, the plant’s sole owner, can sell up to a 49 percent stake to a partner, potentially helping distribute the substantial investment costs.
In April, Rosatom said it had opened new talks with Turkish companies on joint ownership of Akkuyu.
Earlier in October, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev said the negotiations were making progress.
First reactor target remains in focus
The project’s original commissioning target was 2023, but the schedule has been pushed back several times.
Rosatom now expects the first reactor to achieve its first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction before the end of this year, marking a key milestone towards bringing the plant into operation.
Akkuyu is a major element of Turkish-Russian energy cooperation, and potential Turkish investment would give local companies an opportunity to take part in a project currently financed by Russia.

Canada, UAE sign major trade deal amid tensions with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:35:00 UTC
04:35:00 KST

Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a comprehensive trade agreement Tuesday aimed at reducing trade barriers and attracting investment, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to diversify economic partnerships amid strained relations with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-U.S. trade over the next decade as President Donald Trump's tariffs have rippled through Canada's economy. Subsequent attempts for a deal with Washington have broken down, and that has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
"Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE. That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators," The Prime Minister's Office said in a statement.
"The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors," it said, adding CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
"We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing - all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” UAE's Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart Maninder Sidhu.
UAE is the largest Middle Eastern market for Canadian exports and is a big buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery. Two-way trade between the countries was worth C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) last year. It has been growing at 10% annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE last year also committed up to $50 billion in investment in Canada.
The signing is the last step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement, a Canadian government source said.
