====================================================================================================

How a 20-Point Lead Became 2.8: Reading Bulgaria’s Presidential First Round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:05:25 UTC
04:05:25 KST

A month before Sunday's vote, every major pollster had Iliana Yotova at least 17 points ahead of Andrey Gyurov and some had her within reach of 50 percent. When the Central Election Commission announced the official result, the incumbent president had 528,951 votes, or 34.76 percent, against Gyurov's 486,232, or 31.95 percent. The gap between them is 42,719 votes, a margin of 2.8 points, and both tickets go into the runoff on November 1 with the race effectively open.
Kostadin Kostadinov of "Revival" came third with 190,910 votes, or 12.55 percent, followed by Radostin Vassilev of MECH with 4.61 percent, Ivelin Mihaylov of "Greatness" with 3.79 percent and Ivan Hristanov with 2.39 percent. Another 67,353 people, 4.43 percent, chose the "I do not support anyone" option. Only 1,525,034 of the 6,584,025 registered voters took part, a turnout of 23.16 percent and the lowest of any national election since the fall of communism.
The headline numbers hide a more interesting story. The result was shaped less by voters changing their minds than by which voters bothered to show up and the biggest group that stayed home was the one that had handed Rumen Radev a parliamentary majority six months earlier.
Radev's Voters Did Not Come Back
In April, Progressive Bulgaria won 1,444,920 votes and 131 of 240 seats. On Sunday, the candidate it backed received just over a third of that. According to Alpha Research, only about 29 percent of Progressive Bulgaria's April voters took part in the presidential vote. Alpha's exit poll found that 74 percent of those backed Yotova, 11 percent Kostadinov and 9 percent Gyurov. Trend's exit poll puts her share among them slightly lower, at 71.2 percent, with 12.3 percent going to Gyurov.
Relatively few of Radev's voters defected to her rivals and most of them simply stayed at home. Several explanations are in circulation and they are not mutually exclusive. Six months in government have dented Radev's standing, with Bulgaria among the three EU countries with the highest inflation and the cabinet's cautious line on the Black Sea drone strikes drawing criticism. Polls showing a comfortable lead may have persuaded many supporters that their vote was not needed. And several commentators, from DW's Emiliya Milcheva to Ivan Bedrov in Svobodna Tochka, have questioned how hard Radev himself fought for his former vice president. They point to the case of Sonya Koltuklieva, a reporter for PIK who was knocked to the ground and injured by a National Service for Protection guard escorting Speaker Mihaela Dotsova on October 22. Yotova demanded the resignation of the service's chief, General Emil Tonev, who submitted it, but his dismissal requires the government's agreement and Radev declined to give it until an investigation is complete. Tonev remains in post.
Yotova's own campaign did not help. The "Petrich Escobar" pardon followed her throughout, as she first leaned on the medical commission's findings, then had to explain why a prisoner released on health grounds was again under investigation for drug trafficking and finally sent the file to the prosecutors, after which further questions could be refused on the grounds of investigative secrecy. Her refusal to debate before the first round and her pledge that no Bulgarian soldier would go to Ukraine, a decision that belongs to parliament, which ruled out such participation in February 2025, gave her opponents easy targets. As Novinite's profile put it before the vote, she ran as the status quo, and the status quo turned out to be less popular than the polls suggested.
How Gyurov Closed the Gap
Gyurov did the opposite. We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria won just over 400,000 votes in April, and Gyurov finished on more than 486,000, which means he mobilized his own camp and then reached beyond it. Trend's exit poll shows him taking 86.2 percent of PP-DB voters and, more significantly, 47.6 percent of the GERB voters who turned out, against 22.9 percent for Yotova. Alpha Research puts the GERB split at 39 percent to 22 percent. Whichever figure is closer, a sizable share of Boyko Borissov's electorate voted for Gyurov without any instruction from party headquarters.
His map was the map of urban, younger and educated Bulgaria. He won all three Sofia constituencies, taking 88,681 votes to Yotova's 35,767 in the 23rd alone, and carried Plovdiv city. Trend found him ahead among every age group under 40, with 42.5 percent among 18 to 29-year-olds, and among university graduates by 39 to 31.7 percent. Abroad he won 45.8 percent to Yotova's 22.8 percent, leading in Germany, the United Kingdom, Spain, France, Italy and the United States, while Yotova carried Turkey and Kostadinov topped the small count in Russia.
Yotova's strength lay where Radev's had in April: smaller towns, villages and older voters. She won 56.8 percent of the over-70s and almost every province outside the big cities, and in places like Haskovo, Pleven and Vratsa she polled more than double Gyurov's vote. Varna was closer, at 33,199 to 31,364. DW noted that Gyurov also benefited from being a comparatively new face, unworn by years in politics, which made him an easier choice for voters looking for an alternative to the governing camp without wanting to return to the old parties. Novinite's pre-election profile called his offer the balance, and a third of those who voted took it.
A Record Low Turnout and a Boycott in Plain Sight
Turnout of 23.16 percent is the lowest for any election since 1990, far below the previous low of 34.41 percent at the October 2024 parliamentary vote. Only the 2013 referendum on the Belene nuclear plant, at 20.22 percent, drew a smaller share of voters. In April, by comparison, 51 percent of voters had turned out. Pollsters had expected between 36 and 40 percent, and the gap between that forecast and reality explains much of why they misjudged the margin: their samples of likely voters included a large group of Progressive Bulgaria supporters who never arrived.
The drop was steepest in the strongholds of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS). Delyan Peevski's DPS did not field a candidate and in the week before the vote prosecutors arrested the DPS mayors of Belitsa and Sungurlare on corruption allegations and Kardzhali mayor Erol Mumun was taken in for questioning. Local party structures in Belitsa and Sungurlare called for a boycott. By 4 p.m. turnout stood at 5.65 percent in Belitsa, 5.91 percent in Yakoruda and 6.76 percent across the Kardzhali region. In Turkey, home to many Bulgarian citizens of Turkish origin, it fell to 15.95 percent from 34.63 percent in April. Mumun spent the day posting photos from a farmers' market. Alpha Research estimates that only about 15 percent of April's DPS voters, roughly 40,000 people, took part nationwide.
The boycott can be read as a demonstration of control, with Peevski showing that he can keep his voters at home as reliably as he can bring them out. Radev offered his own explanation for the low turnout, blaming PP-DB, GERB and DPS for convincing people through their constitutional changes and conduct in government that voting changes nothing.
Kostadinov's Partial Revenge
For Kostadinov, the result was a qualified success. Pro-Russian and nationalist Revival won 4.19 percent in April after Radev's new party swept up much of its electorate and on Sunday its leader took three times that share, finishing on 12.55 percent, above every pre-election poll. He fell well short of his prediction of reaching the runoff, finishing more than 295,000 votes behind Gyurov, but the score confirms that part of the nationalist vote Radev borrowed in April is drifting back. Novinite's profile described his campaign as the vengeance, and he has now collected part of the debt.
Together with Vassilev's 4.61 percent and Mihaylov's 3.79 percent, the three candidates can be grouped as the "nationalist vote," sharing a distrust of the EU and a closer view to Moscow's on the war in Ukraine, took almost 21 percent. That bloc is now the largest pool of votes in play and its first move has already complicated both finalists' plans, as the runoff preview explains.
What the First Round Tells Us
The clearest lesson is for Radev. A prime minister who won 1.44 million votes in April could not turn even half of them out for his chosen candidate six months later and whatever the mix of complacency, disappointment and lukewarm campaigning behind that, the government goes into the runoff weaker than it looked a week ago. Lyuben Obretenov wrote in Club Z that "political logic" had returned to Bulgaria after April's surprise, while Bedrov called the result a yellow card for the prime minister.
It is clear that the round exposed two strategic blunders. Yotova's team believed the 20-point leads in the polls and barely campaigned, counting on Radev's April voters and the Bulgarian Socialist Party and falling back on the familiar attacks that tied opponents to the Petrohan case and to warmongering. Moscow might have made the bigger mistake, striking ships off Romania and Bulgaria in the hope of frightening Bulgarians into backing a candidate seen as closer to the Kremlin. If that was the aim, the exit polls suggest it failed: fear appears to have moved mainly Revival's voters, toward Kostadinov, while pro-European voters rallied behind Gyurov. There is no evidence that the attacks were timed to influence the vote and Sofia has not formally attributed them, although EU leaders blamed Russia on October 16. The broader point stands on firmer ground. Neither the comfort of incumbency nor the language of fear produced the result the governing camp expected and a large part of the country showed it is not willing to hand every institution to a single political force without a contest.
For the opposition, Gyurov showed that a pro-Western candidate can expand beyond the PP-DB base when the alternative is a single camp controlling every institution and that GERB voters will act on their own when their party gives them no direction.
The turnout also leaves a problem for whoever wins. Fewer than one in four registered voters took part in choosing the two finalists and unless participation rises sharply on Sunday, the next president will take office with the votes of well under a fifth of the electorate. That is a thin mandate for an office whose main authority rests on being the one official the whole country elects.
This article is part of Novinite's editorial coverage of Bulgaria's 2026 presidential election. It was not commissioned or paid for by any candidate, party or initiative committee, and it does not endorse anyone.

Italy Delaying Transfer of Aster 30 Missiles to Ukraine Due to Political Disputes — Italian Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:01:14 UTC
04:01:14 KST

The Italian government is postponing approval of the 13th package of military aid to Ukraine, which is to include Aster 30 anti-aircraft missiles for the SAMP/T systems.
This was reported by La Repubblica, citing sources in Italian government circles.
According to the newspaper, the aid package has already been prepared, but its final approval is being delayed due to internal political disputes within Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s governing coalition.
La Repubblica’s sources claim that the Italian government may postpone the decision until the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, in order to assess the Trump administration’s future policy toward Ukraine.
The document is to be signed by Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
According to the publication, the delay is also linked to the position of the Lega party, led by Matteo Salvini, which opposes further arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Journalists note that approval of the package had already been postponed from July to September, and later to October. At the same time, according to La Repubblica, the last delivery of Italian military aid to Ukraine took place in December 2025.
Despite the delay, on October 26, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told ANSA that the new military aid package is already ready.
“We stand with Ukraine and will continue to help it for as long as necessary. The next military aid package is already ready, and we will send it to Kyiv as soon as possible,” Tajani said.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto also emphasized that Italy’s position on supporting Ukraine will not change, as Russian aggression poses a threat to the security of all of Europe.
In August, Militarnyi reported on Italy’s preparation of the 13th military aid package, which was to include Aster 30 missiles from the Italian Army’s stockpiles.
These missiles are used in the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense missile systems, which Ukraine employs to defend against Russian air attacks.
In July, France and Italy agreed to expedite the delivery to Ukraine of the previously agreed-upon number of Aster 30 missiles by October of this year.
In addition, Ukraine received licenses from France to manufacture a range of weapons, including Aster 30 anti-aircraft missiles, SCALP cruise missiles, and AASM Hammer air-to-ground bombs.

Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to leftist Lula.
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, leading to his documents being canceled.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
Jair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former U.S. President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
His son has yet to officially concede defeat - saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities - but his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.
It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
"If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

The 'very uncomfortable' issue at the heart of Australia's national identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:00:15 UTC
04:00:15 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Ahead of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's appearance at Australia's national multiculturalism conference earlier this month, expectations were high.
It had been decades since a sitting prime minister had addressed the conference, which is run annually by the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia (FECCA) and brings together hundreds of community leaders, researchers and advocates to discuss policy and shape national conversations about migration, social inclusion and cultural diversity.
At a time of heightened community tensions, some hoped the prime minister would use the moment to deliver strong action in support of multiculturalism.
Instead, they were left feeling underwhelmed, describing his keynote address as a missed opportunity.
At the conference, which SBS covered as a media partner, the prime minister spoke positively about cultural diversity in his electorate of Grayndler, which spans parts of Sydney's inner west and has been home to many migrant communities over the years, including Greek, Italian, Portuguese, Lebanese, Islander and Vietnamese.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It means that you can walk around the streets of Marrickville and get groceries from the Filipino shop … [and eat] the best lamb you have ever had in your life [at a restaurant across from my old electorate office]," Albanese said in his speech.
Sociology professor Andrew Jakubowicz from the University of Technology Sydney says it's important that Albanese agreed to speak at the conference, "particularly as situations in Australia seem to be getting more tense and even violent", but he noted the prime minister made no tangible commitments.
"There was nothing said that suggested there was actually a strategy, and we're in an extremely difficult time," Jakubowicz tells SBS News.
[This is a] lost opportunity to make a significant statement about government commitments going forward.
Many of the experts SBS News has spoken with, including Jakubowicz, believe racism is on the rise in Australia, although this is largely based on anecdotal evidence.
There is no single body that consistently collects and reports on race and racism at a national level, so available data tends to be fragmented or infrequent.
A new report released today by the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) is calling for a nationally coordinated approach. It follows a similar recommendation made in 2024 as part of FECCA's Anti-Racism Framework, also commissioned by the AHRC.
Jakubowicz points out that recommendations from the framework, as well as a separate government-funded review on multiculturalism titled Towards Fairness, largely remain unactioned.
The failure to implement most of the significant elements of [the multiculturalism] review means that there is a level of disappointment and cynicism in the multicultural community.
"The government is quite comfortable about making the right noises, and very uncomfortable about doing anything to implement significant change."
Advocates are concerned that, without action, Australia's successful multicultural society may begin to fray.
'Disappointing' response to racism
According to the AHRC's Race Discrimination Commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, Australia has "clearly got a problem" with racism. He points to recent examples of "horrific racist violence", including an antisemitic attack at Bondi Beach that claimed the lives of 15 people, and an alleged act of terrorism at an Invasion Day rally in Perth.
He believes racism has increased online too, particularly following the failure of the Indigenous Voice referendum in 2023.
"When people talk about a lone wolf or a lone actor … that person is never alone," he says.
"They usually have been plugged into an online ecosystem that … taught them how to be violent.
"And it's led to the violence we see on the streets."
Sivaraman says he frequently hears about acts of racism that go unreported, including Muslim women having their hijabs ripped off, Jewish students being screamed at in the street, and young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders being chased by people in cars.
But he says it's difficult to know the extent of the problem because there's no centralised system to collect data on racism in Australia — something the AHRC is pushing for as one of 16 recommendations in its Data for Change report released today.
The same recommendation was among those included in AHRC's anti-racism framework in November 2024, which Sivaraman says no level of government has endorsed, let alone implemented or funded.
"That is disappointing because it indicates they don't see it as a priority," he says.
He says an AHRC-commissioned audit of government responses to racism found it often involved knee-jerk reactions that pit communities against each other and increase racism or anger.
"There's no monitoring or evaluation of anti-racism work either," he says.
"That is not an effective way to deal with racism."
Jakubowicz says a lack of strategy to encourage intercultural engagement has meant that antagonism between different groups, fuelled in part by social media, has also been allowed to "fester and deepen".
He says much of the significant opposition to multiculturalism often stems from Islamophobia, including from those belonging to migrant communities.
It's one of the reasons some multicultural communities are signalling support for Pauline Hanson's One Nation, which has openly criticised Islam and broadly opposes Muslim immigration.
"One wouldn't necessarily expect to see people who have experienced racism being so strongly supportive of [One Nation], yet we're seeing that occur," he says.
"I think that's partly a consequence of the failure of government to engage meaningfully with the wider Australian population, [to build] cultural links and [address] questions of racism both within and between different migration communities."
Jakubowicz believes there's a need for a national multicultural commission, as well as a research and policy strategy to provide both policymakers and the public with credible, accessible information.
Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly says the government is taking action by strengthening hate crime laws, funding a national anti-racism campaign and establishing the Office for Multicultural Affairs.
"We’re taking a coordinated multi-faceted approach to combating racism, with action underway across a range of portfolios, so we can deliver practical, lasting change," she tells SBS News.
Multiculturalism at risk
Many experts, both at the FECCA conference and beyond, are calling for a similar kind of systemic change to address racism.
Sivaraman says this will ultimately benefit all Australians because it ensures systems and institutions become more transparent, responsive and accountable.
"It means that irrespective of race, gender, sexual identity, class, age [or] disability, a system or institution is inclusive."
He says racism can impede people at every step of their life journey, and dealing with it is critical to Australia being a successful multicultural country.
Racism is affecting kids who go to school, people who want to progress at work, people who are accessing health services, [and] those that encounter the justice system.
Mario Peucker, an expert in place-based anti-racism and associate professor at Victoria University, says data provides a foundation for identifying organisations where racist incidents occur, so pressure can be applied on them to take action.
He believes Australia's failure to address racism adequately is holding it back from achieving genuine multiculturalism — a state in which diverse racial, ethnic and cultural groups co-exist harmoniously.
"There is the need for reckoning with historic injustices, especially because they have ongoing implications for First Nations and multicultural communities."
Whole-of-government approach needed
Bulent (Hass) Dellal is a former director of SBS and chair of the panel that produced the multicultural review. He explains its aim was to identify ways to support a cohesive society in Australia following the COVID-19 pandemic.
The government endorsed the review's recommendations and acted in 2025 to elevate the position of minister for multicultural affairs to cabinet for the first time in Australia's history.
It also announced $85 million in reforms to better recognise the skills of migrants.
Dellal says the review's 29 recommendations are ambitious and acknowledges that full implementation will take time.
"But … one thing that has given communities less confidence is the lack of communication between government and communities about the next steps," he tells SBS News.
In particular, Dellal is concerned about progress on implementing a whole-of-government approach to multiculturalism, which he says has "remained limited".
It shouldn't be just one department being responsible for the reality of who we are — which is a multicultural Australia — it crosses over every department [and] every service provider.
"So, it is important that there is a level of coordination between governments and institutions … [as well as] accountability mechanisms, and these are still often unclear."
Australians need shared civic identity
Dellal says Australia's problem isn't that it doesn't support multiculturalism, but that it hasn't yet built a strong shared civic identity around it.
He points out that 83 per cent of Australian adults agree that "multiculturalism has been good for Australia" according to the Scanlon Foundation's 2025 Mapping Social Cohesion report, but many don't feel like they belong.
Only 46 per cent felt a sense of belonging in Australia "to a great extent", compared to 63 per cent in 2020.
But addressing this rift does not mean Australians of different ethnicities and backgrounds need to become "culturally identical", Dellal says.
He believes a shared Australian identity should be built around fairness, freedom, democracy and equal citizenship. These principles must be applied equally in everyday life for multiculturalism to thrive.
"Fairness must be visible in the workplace," Dellal says.
"Democracy must include the opportunity to be heard, to disagree and to help shape decisions.
"That shared civic identity is credible only when people can see the principles at work."

Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:57:45 UTC
03:57:45 KST

Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo, which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy, Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing, in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

Money for shifting electricity consumption: how Ukrainians will be able to receive a reward
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:57:44 EET
03:57:44 KST

Money for shifting electricity consumption: how Ukrainians will be able to receive a reward
Kyiv • UNN
The NEURC approved an aggregation project that provides for a reward for changing the consumption schedule. The system will operate after the rules are approved.
Ukrainians and businesses are being offered payments for changing their electricity consumption schedule—for example, shifting appliance use from peak hours to another time. To participate, it will be necessary to conclude an agreement with an aggregator—a company that represents consumers in the energy market. On October 27, the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission of Ukraine (NEURC) approved a draft of amendments to the retail market rules. UNN explains how to participate in such a project, what to know about the compensation, and how to receive it.
How the mechanism will work
The NEURC explains the two-zone electricity consumption mechanism as follows: demand for electricity changes throughout the day. When people switch on household appliances at the same time, the power system needs additional capacity. Changing the operating schedule of appliances will help distribute the load on the system more evenly.
The aggregator will combine participants’ capacities to change their consumption and provide the relevant services on the market. A consumer will be able to receive compensation by meeting the conditions. It should be noted that the project provides both for shifting consumption and for temporarily reducing or increasing the load at the aggregator’s command in response to market needs.
Who will be able to participate in the program
The regulator lists households and businesses among the potential participants. For an apartment or house, an example could be changing the operating times of household appliances; for a business, shifting some production processes. Having one’s own solar power plant is not identified as a mandatory condition in the NEURC’s announcement. However, participation will depend on the final rules, the technical possibility of metering, and the aggregators’ offers.
We emphasize that participation is voluntary. Current legislation allows consumers to join an aggregated group without the consent of their electricity supplier. There is no need to change the company supplying the electricity: the supply agreement and the agreement with the aggregator are separate.
How to receive compensation: a step-by-step plan for Ukrainians
After the rules are approved and offers become available, the following steps will need to be completed in sequence in order to receive compensation.
First, find an aggregator. To do this, determine whether the company works with household customers or the relevant type of business and what terms it offers. You can check the company in the NEURC’s licensing register via the link. At the same time, it is worth remembering that the law provides for cases in which a separate aggregation license is not required.
Second, clarify metering issues. Ask the aggregator and the distribution system operator whether the existing meter is suitable, whether additional equipment is needed, and who will pay for it. A meter that shows only total consumption will not indicate how much electricity was used during specific hours. Most likely, a two-zone meter will be needed to participate in the project.
The next step is concluding an agreement. The draft resolution provides for a written agreement specifying the equipment, management procedures, settlements, and payments. It is worth clarifying how commands will be delivered, whether they may be disregarded, how the result will be determined, and what costs the consumer will bear.
After that, it will be necessary to notify the supplier if the final rules require this. A written notification can be sent to the authority’s postal or email address, or submitted through the electronic account within three business days after concluding or terminating the agreement. The notification must specify the relevant electrical installations and metering points.
Afterward, the person will only need to comply with the conditions and check the calculations. The project provides that the aggregator will inform the participant of the results at least once per settlement period. The payment information must specify the cost of services, incentive payments, and the deadlines and methods of settlement.
What compensation will be available
It is not yet possible to name an amount, since the NEURC has established neither a single rate per kilowatt-hour nor a guaranteed monthly payment. Under the project, the procedure for calculating the results and payments will be determined by the agreement in accordance with the market rules.
Therefore, before taking part in the program, it makes sense to find out exactly what the payments will cover, how changes in consumption will be measured, and whether there are aggregator service fees or equipment costs. In addition, expenses and possible taxes should be taken into account. The latter will depend on how the payments are formalized and on the recipient’s status.
Which appliances can be used at other times
First of all, attention should be paid to appliances whose operating schedule can be changed without harming household activities or production:
-  washing machines and dishwashers; 
-  water heaters, if their control system allows it; 
-  charging electric vehicles and storage systems when the appropriate equipment is available; 
-  some production processes, if they can be safely and technologically shifted. 
The hours will depend on the contract and the situation in the energy system. For example, on October 27, Ukrenergo asked people to limit the use of high-power appliances from 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
In addition, refrigerators or medical equipment should not be switched off if they need to operate continuously. After power is restored, all high-power appliances should not be turned on at the same time — this could overload the grid.
Nighttime tariff: how to save money already
Aggregator remuneration and a two-zone tariff are different mechanisms. In the first case, the payment is for an agreed change in load; in the second, it is a lower electricity price at night when a two-zone meter has been installed and programmed.
For most household consumers, the price is UAH 4.32 per kWh. With two-zone metering, from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m., half of this price applies — UAH 2.16 per kWh. The current prices for households have been extended until April 30, 2027. For certain categories, including consumers entitled to a preferential tariff for electric heating, the calculation may differ. If 100 kWh of monthly consumption is shifted from daytime to nighttime hours, the difference in payment under the general tariff will be UAH 216.
When the system will start operating and how it will help the energy sector
As of October 27, 2026, the NEURC had approved only a draft of the amendments. It is planned to put it up for discussion, but the regulator has not yet announced a specific date for adopting the new rules and launching payments.
According to the NEURC’s plan, Ukrainians’ participation in the aggregation program will help reduce peak loads and maintain the balance between generation and consumption. However, energy-sector experts are already warning that the outcome will depend on the number of participants and the remuneration terms.

Poland to Host €227M Patriot Missile Service Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:54:13 UTC
03:54:13 KST

Poland has announced that it will be hosting a European service center for US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles, aiming to cut repair times for weapons that are already in short supply worldwide and critical to Ukraine’s defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who led Warsaw’s negotiations, called the decision “historic” in a statement on Tuesday, Oct. 27. Three other countries had competed to host the facility, she said, naming Germany, the Netherlands and Norway.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This success was not a given. It is the result of many months of negotiations and the hard work of the entire team,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote, noting that the Polish bid had been the highest rated since the application stage.
According to TVP World citing Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, the hub would be the only one of its kind outside the United States. Its cost would be roughly 1 billion Polish zlotys (about $253 million) and would take about a year to become fully operational.
In her statement, the defense minister thanked Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who appointed her chief negotiator.
The outcome showed what was possible when the government and the country’s President Karol Nawrocki pulled in the same direction, she added.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
Short repair times for scarce interceptors
PAC-3 missiles, used in US-made Patriot air-defense systems, are currently shipped to the US for servicing, which led Washington to seek a European site to cut turnaround times, TVP World reported.
The US, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden signed an agreement with manufacturer Lockheed Martin in July, in an aim to explore setting up such a hub.
According to the broadcaster, Warsaw has long pursued the project with hopes that it would eventually lead to Patriot missile production in Poland.
Plant near Warsaw seen as likely site
Although the government did not officially name a location at the time of the report, TVP World reported that the WZE electronics plant in Zielonka, located about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) northeast of Warsaw, is widely seen as the leading candidate.
In September, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka toured the plant with US Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno. At the time, the US Embassy in Warsaw noted that the visit highlighted bilateral cooperation on critical Patriot components.
Under a 2019 agreement with Lockheed Martin, the plant already produces and services key PAC-3 MSE components, TVP World reported.
Ukraine facing critical shortage
As of Oct. 15, Ukraine has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
The shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
According to CNN’s exclusive, Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots as the Air Force shot down four Russian ballistic missiles during that same attack.
Around the same time, the US aerospace giant Starlink tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), crippling Kyiv’s drone operations, including interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US over tripled demand, as countries seek to rebuild their stocks amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
For much of the year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western partners for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically, after backtracking on the previous July commitment.

dobedo studio develops ehho!², a portable micro-pavilion that reinterprets the traditional japanese kago, hand-carried by two people.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DOBEDO builds PORTABLE PAVILION FROM DEMOLISHED JAPANESE BARN
Designed by DOBEDO STUDIO, EHHO!² is a portable micro-architecture engineered from materials salvaged during the deconstruction of an agricultural barn in Gunma Prefecture, Japan. The mobile timber structure draws functional and formal inspiration from the traditional Japanese kago (palanquin), carrying architectural remnants of rural infrastructure into the urban public realm. Upcycling weathered corrugated iron sheets, structural logs, reclaimed timber boards, and hand-woven ropes, the project translates rural material memory into a compact, deployable social pavilion carried by two people.
CORRUGATED METAL AND TREE-BRANCHES DETAIL LOW-TECH ASSEMBLY
The tectonic assembly by DOBEDO STUDIO balances low-tech mechanics with site-adaptive details. The rusted corrugated metal sheets are bent to form a protective curved roof, utilizing decades of atmospheric weathering as a natural, textured exterior skin. Hinged timber side panels fold downward to function as exterior benches, exposing a contrasting crimson-painted interior inspired by the seasonal bloom of local red spider lilies (higanbana). To secure the folding benches during transport, the studio integrated small wooden branches as tactile latch pins. If misplaced during transit, these fasteners can be replaced using fallen twigs sourced directly from nearby urban trees, establishing an intuitive, maintenance-free locking mechanism.

Rada withdraws bill that threatened journalists' work – MP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:53:13 EET
03:53:13 KST

Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration by the Verkhovna Rada, according to MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak (the Holos faction).
"Yes, I would like to report that following constructive negotiations with Andriy Motovylovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction, and the parliament's leadership… Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration – both for tomorrow and for the rest of this week," Zhelezniak said on his Telegram channel.
The bill in question provides for amendments to Articles 361 and 361-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, increasing penalties for acts involving unauthorized access to electronic systems and the dissemination of restricted information.
According to media reports, the bill was proposed for the agenda by Andriy Motovilovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction.
The bill had already been considered in 2024 – on December 4, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not support the bill in its second reading and sent it back for a repeat second reading. Prior to that, on December 2, media and human rights organizations called on the Rada not to support the bill due to threats to freedom of speech, the work of journalists, and the protection of journalistic sources and whistle blowers in Ukraine.
Chair of the Committee on Freedom of Speech Yaroslav Yurchyshyn called on his colleagues in the Verkhovna Rada to remove Bill No. 10242 from the agenda and draft a new one that takes into account the rights of whistle blowers. However, two weeks later, the bill reappeared on the agenda. On December 17, Media Rukh, along with media and human rights NGOs, appealed to lawmakers for a second time, urging them to withdraw their support for the bill and noting that the revised version had not eliminated the risks. Proposals to introduce effective protection mechanisms for individuals who disclose confidential information in the public interest-particularly journalists and whistleblowers – were not taken into account.
On December 18, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not consider the bill, but it was not withdrawn from consideration.
In January 2025, the bill was once again added to the agenda of the Verkhovna Rada sessions without consultation, even though the Committee on Freedom of Speech had previously sent a list of editors and media experts who would be proposed for a meeting to reach an agreement. Shortly thereafter, the bill was again removed from the agenda, as some members of parliament emphasized during the discussion that they were unwilling to support the bill until it had been agreed upon with the media community.

Yehor Perelyhin, who served as deputy minister of economy and environment from July 2025 until October 20, has joined the team of investment group BGV Group Management as deputy CEO and a member of its board of directors, the investment group said in a statement on Tuesday. The group is active in the mining sector and was founded by Hennadiy Butkevych, co-owner of ATB, Ukraine's largest retail chain.
"Essentially, this is a Chief Mining Officer position, using the Western equivalent and terminology. There are many plans and objectives. They include establishing and developing production and businesses in the critical minerals and other strategic materials sector, developing a commercially viable business model, structuring new investment and commercial agreements, attracting capital for strategic projects, establishing and overseeing the relevant operational processes, and implementing a very ambitious strategy," Perelyhin wrote on Facebook on Tuesday.
He said he was pleased to join the team led by Oleksandr Naumik, which was among the first in Ukraine to recognize the strategic importance of mining and processing critical minerals and had consistently invested financial resources and expertise in geological exploration, laboratory work, processing technology development, project preparation and reserve assessments in accordance with Western standards.
As reported, at the Ministry of Economy, Perelyhin was responsible for coordinating and overseeing the work of the Investment Attraction and International Organizations Cooperation Department, the Financial Policy and War Risk Insurance Department, and the Subsoil Use Directorate.
Perelyhin received his higher education in France (ISEG, ISG) and the United States (St. John's University) and holds an MBA. Before his appointment to the government, he held senior positions in the banking sector and headed Petro-Consulting (now European Lithium Ukraine LLC). He also served twice as head of United Mining and Chemical Company JSC (UMCC) in 2021–2025, bringing it to the privatization stage. In April 2025, he was appointed deputy minister of environmental protection and natural resources. Following the reorganization and merger of the ministries, he was the only deputy to move to the position of deputy minister of economy, environment and agriculture.
Perelyhin was also delegated as an authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF). After he left his position as deputy minister, former Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko replaced him in that role.
In early October, URIF approved the creation of a joint investment platform with BGV Group Management to develop a portfolio of critical minerals projects in Ukraine. The arrangement provides for the possibility of investing up to $30 million in individual projects, as well as attracting Ukrainian and international co-investors, financial institutions, technology companies, industrial companies and strategic partners to specific projects.
According to the company, BGV Group Management's investments in mining already exceed $125 million. After 10 years of operating in the sector, the company has the largest portfolio of specialized projects in Ukraine across six critical minerals segments involving graphite, beryllium, zirconium, titanium, molybdenum and rare earth elements.
BGV Group Management was founded in 2015. It develops five main business areas: mining, energy, real estate development, retail, and education and sports.

Even American Monsters Need Mechanics: Ukraine Reveals What’s Under the MaxxPro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Even American Monsters Need Mechanics: Ukraine Reveals What’s Under the MaxxPro
Ukrainian military mechanics have revealed what lies beneath the massive armor of the US-made International MaxxPro, sharing rare close-up photographs of the heavy-duty suspension and mechanical systems that keep the mine-resistant vehicle operational on the battlefield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 27, Ukraine’s 146th Separate Repair and Recovery Regiment released photographs showing its specialists maintaining and restoring armored vehicles used by Ukrainian forces.
The images show a MaxxPro positioned over an inspection pit inside a military repair facility, where two Ukrainian servicemembers are working beneath its front section.
With the undercarriage exposed, the photographs provide a detailed look at the vehicle’s enormous suspension springs, reinforced control arms, and other components designed to support several tons of armor.
Despite its imposing appearance, the MaxxPro relies on complex mechanical systems that require regular maintenance, particularly after operating on damaged roads and difficult terrain.
Modern versions of the vehicle, including the MaxxPro Dash, use independent suspension systems designed to improve mobility, stability, and handling over uneven ground.
Another notable feature visible in the photographs is the additional metal mesh protection installed around the vehicle’s body. Similar screens are widely used on Ukrainian military equipment to provide an extra layer of defense against Russian FPV drones.
The International MaxxPro belongs to the Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected (MRAP) family of military vehicles, developed to protect personnel against mines, improvised explosive devices, and ambushes.
One of its defining features is a V-shaped armored hull, which helps redirect the force of explosions away from the crew compartment, reducing the impact on personnel inside. Depending on the configuration, MaxxPro vehicles can transport troops, support frontline operations, and evacuate wounded servicemembers from dangerous areas.
The vehicle’s protective capabilities have already proven critical during combat operations in Ukraine. In November 2025, soldiers from Ukraine’s Syla Svobody Battalion survived an anti-tank mine explosion while traveling in a MaxxPro to evacuate fellow servicemembers.
Earlier, in June 2025, a Canadian-made Roshel Senator MRAP was filmed evacuating wounded Ukrainian soldiers in the Donetsk region despite losing a wheel in a mine explosion. The armored vehicle continued moving on just three wheels, highlighting the importance of mine-resistant designs in protecting troops and maintaining mobility under battlefield conditions.

Italy Delays 13th Military Aid Package for Ukraine as Meloni Waits for US Midterms
Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine is ready but remains frozen as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government waits for the outcome of the US midterm elections, La Repubblica reported on October 27.
The package has already been delayed several times, first from July to September, then until after the League party congress, and now potentially until after the November 3 US vote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to La Repubblica, the government had previously assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the package would be approved by the end of October. With four days remaining in the month, however, Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee, Copasir, had still not been called to review the decree.
Italy has not sent a new military aid package to Ukraine since December 2025.
The new package is expected to include Aster 30 missiles, which Ukraine needs to strengthen air defenses protecting Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks. Italy and France are the only countries able to supply the missiles, according to the report.
Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto has continued to publicly support military assistance to Ukraine and is pressing for approval of the package.
The interministerial decree requires signatures from Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti. La Repubblica reported that Giorgetti has been hesitant amid concern over opposition from Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, though the final political decision rests with Meloni.
Crosetto has privately told colleagues that a political obstacle still needs to be resolved, according to the newspaper. Government officials interpreted this as a lack of final approval from Meloni’s office.
La Repubblica reported that some government sources now favor waiting for the US midterms to assess the direction of President Donald Trump’s next two years and calibrate Italy’s policy accordingly.
Domestic politics are also weighing on the decision. Salvini’s League has opposed further military support for Ukraine, while former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte has continued campaigning against weapons deliveries.
Italian officials have informally urged Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to La Repubblica, arguing that an immediate confrontation over the package could create additional political difficulties for Meloni.
Italy and France had committed to supplying the missiles by the end of October. With Copasir still not convened to examine the decree, another postponement remains possible.
Earlier, UNITED24 Media reported that Italy’s 13th military aid package was expected to include four SAMP/T NG air defense batteries, Aster 30 interceptor missiles, and seven long-range radars, with part of the Aster 30 stockpile planned for transfer by October.

- Taura air base in Ecuador has become a growing hub for US anti-drug operations, with around 20 military flights, new construction and signs of a longer-term presence.
- President Noboa backs closer US cooperation, but a former air force chief warned it may be illegal or unconstitutional, and he was removed two days later.
- Local people say the area feels unsafe and neglected, with cartel violence, no drinking water and anger over military abuses, while some welcome foreign troops.
AI generated
TAURA, Ecuador - An isolated Ecuadoran air base has quietly become a key hub in Washington’s expanding war on drug trafficking, according to flight records, satellite imagery, witnesses and military documents uncovered by AFP.
Hidden among shrimp farms and teak plantations about an hour from Guayaquil – the Pacific port that has become the biggest gateway for Latin American cocaine bound for the United States – the Taura complex plays an increasingly prominent role in President Daniel Noboa’s security alliance with Washington.
AFP observed significant works at the decades-old facility, identified around 20 US military flights between June and mid-October, and obtained documents referring to the presence of US troops at the base.
The buildup comes less than a year after Ecuadorans voted against allowing foreign military bases, and has prompted questions from even within the highest ranks of Ecuador’s armed forces.
In a letter obtained by AFP dated Sept 8, then Air Force commander Mauricio Salazar warned the top brass at Joint Armed Forces Command that hosting US troops at Taura, supporting the US Air Force and receiving ongoing flights by US personnel might be illegal or unconstitutional.
His letter states that the US Air Force would “use and modify infrastructure at the base” and operate “temporary support flights” from there.
Two days later, he was removed from his post.
Flight records reviewed by AFP show repeated arrivals at Taura by US military aircraft, including C-130 Hercules and C-17 Globemaster transport planes, V-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and Black Hawk helicopters.
Several of the flights connected Taura with facilities in the United States, including the Cherry Point Marine Corps Air Station in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.
Satellite imagery also shows the base undergoing significant construction work in recent months.
Several hectares of vegetation have been cleared, new operational areas have appeared around the airfield and dozens of structures consistent with rapidly deployable military tents have been installed inside the complex.
A larger structure measuring roughly 40m by 20m resembles a retractable aircraft maintenance hangar.
Outside the facility, guarded by camouflaged soldiers, AFP observed three construction trucks entering and leaving the base within 10 minutes.
Taura is the only Ecuadoran air base reserved exclusively for military use and boasts a runway of more than 3,000m, longer than that of Guayaquil’s international airport.
President Noboa announced in September that he was working with the United States so that “any type of cooperation” between countries could be carried out there.
“I think it is much more appropriate to move everything to Taura,” he said.
The Ecuadoran Air Force did not respond to a request for comment.
The Pentagon said to contact US Southern Command, which did not immediately answer questions from AFP.
Details on security cooperation closely guarded
Details of the cooperation between Quito and Washington remain closely guarded, with only occasional announcements about the arrival of aircraft and equipment.
The flights detected by AFP arrived as President Donald Trump has expanded military support for anti-cartel operations across Latin America and the Caribbean.
Ecuador’s defence minister announced in August that the United States would deploy three Black Hawk helicopters as part of bilateral security cooperation.
The following month, Noboa said Ecuador would operate two MQ-9 Reaper drones, a platform used extensively by the United States for surveillance and strike missions in conflicts in the Middle East and Africa.
Retired Air Force colonel Roberto Marchan told AFP the aircraft and facilities observed at Taura suggest preparations for a long-term operational presence.
The transport aircraft identified by AFP would allow troops and equipment to move rapidly across the Andean region, he said, while some of the newly installed structures appear suitable for aircraft maintenance and logistical support.
“The US military is establishing a capability there,” Marchan said.
He also argued the growing American presence “diminishes sovereignty.”
“There is some discontent among the rank and file, but they keep it to themselves out of respect for the institution and fear of losing promotions,” he added.
‘Nobody comes around here’
Outside the perimeter fence, daily life bears little resemblance to the military activity unfolding inside.
A few kilometres from the base lies the town of Taura, a community of around 9,400 people connected by dusty roads and surrounded by shrimp farms.
Despite its proximity to one of Ecuador’s most strategic military installations, the town lacks access to drinking water.
Residents say the area has become increasingly associated with cartel violence.
“Nobody comes around here. They think it’s dangerous because sometimes bodies are found dumped,” community leader Fidela Martinez said.
In 2025, the bodies of four boys were found in scrubland near the town after they were tortured, killed and burned by soldiers in a case that shocked Ecuador.
Others have noticed more immediate effects from the expansion of the base.
Alma Goya, 40, runs a small food stall nearby. She said a medical centre inside the military installation no longer serves the public.
“They told us it was because of the state of emergency,” she said.
Not everyone opposes a foreign military presence, in a country that recorded South America’s highest homicide rate in 2025, with 51 killings per 100,000 inhabitants.
“I saw a big plane coming in to land,” said 68-year-old resident Tito Henriquez, who owns a small restaurant, adding that it would be “wonderful” to see foreign troops arrive.
As C-130 transport planes continue to arrive, bulldozers are clearing new sections of land inside the Taura complex. AFP

Ukraine intercepting more Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones, General Staff says

Ukraine's air defenses have intercepted nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with interception rates reaching 80% during some attacks, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces said.
Fighter jets, including F-16s, Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29s, play a significant role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, according to the General Staff.
It did not mention interceptions rates of the more advanced Geran-5 drone.
Ukraine is also working to strengthen its short-range air defenses amid a shortage of surface-to-air missiles.
These defenses include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft systems, newer platforms such as Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups operating across Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped with machine guns and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), which Ukrainian troops have successfully used to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.
The General Staff said Ukraine is also seeking cheaper ways to counter the threat, including testing new interceptor drones. Some of the systems being tested have already shot down dozens of Russian jet-powered Geran drones, according to the military.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones to attack Kyiv and the surrounding region since late summer, adding to the threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles.
The newer Geran-5 drones fly higher and faster than other drones, making them significantly harder to intercept. Their growing numbers have also challenged Ukraine's existing interceptor drones, which have proved effective against slower Russian drones.
Ukraine is racing to develop faster interceptors to counter the evolving threat, while Russia is expanding production of jet-powered drones.
Ukraine previously achieved interception rates of around 95% against conventional Shahed-type drones.
