====================================================================================================

Russian satellites help Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:55:57 UTC
02:55:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Russian satellites help Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia
Iranian-backed militias carried out a precision strike last month, hitting the pumping stations of Saudi Arabia’s most important oil pipeline. Days later, another attack hit a Saudi military air base, damaging an Italian fighter jet inside a hangar.
Crucial to the strikes' success was what was happening in the skies overhead: For days beforehand, a constellation of Russian spy satellites converged over the pipeline and the air base to gather intelligence.
A private geospatial intelligence firm said it examined 40 missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and militias in Iraq between July 1 and Oct. 19. In every case, the firm found the same pattern of Russian government and military satellites orbiting above the areas for days before and after.
"What we found is a 100% match" between the satellite activities and strikes, said Nawaf Obaid, founder of Geneva-based AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence.
The findings illustrate how Russia is believed to be helping Iran and its allies in the region target Saudi Arabia’s oil and military infrastructure in attacks that have helped raise global energy prices.
Three officials, including one from Saudi Arabia and another in the top ranks of the Houthis, as well as a private intelligence analyst, told The Associated Press that the Houthis and other Iranian allies have benefited from Russian intelligence, as well as Chinese capabilities. Iranian advisers in the field analyzed and transferred the intelligence to their allies, according to AP reporting.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, told reporters last week that Iran and the Houthis receive intelligence from "elements in Russia and China, even commercial elements sometimes."
"We do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so," he said.
Russian officials had no immediate comment when asked about the allegations, including AURORAH’s findings.
Russia and Iran have a longstanding military cooperation arrangement, including transferring drone technology. While Russia has not been directly involved in the wars in the region, U.S. and European officials have said Russia has shared intelligence with Iran.
Iranian-backed groups were able to carry out pinpoint strikes 
On the morning of Sept. 10, multiple drone strikes from Iraq hit three critical pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, immediately interrupting the flow of oil. The 1,200-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline across the kingdom has been a vital alternative route for getting its crude to market amid Iran’s attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The pumping stations are vital to moving oil through the pipeline, which rises more than 1,100 meters (3,608 feet) in altitude as it goes from eastern Saudi Arabia across the Najd Plateau then back down to the kingdom’s western coast on the Red Sea, said Obaid, a fellow at King’s College Department of War Studies who also served as an adviser to various Saudi officials from 2004 to 2016.
"This is where the militias out of Iraq decided to strike," he said.
Beginning in July, his firm observed 11 of Russia’s Cosmos 2600 series satellites concentrating on those three sections of the pipeline. Flybys increased in the weeks leading up to the attacks and in the hours around the strikes, showing reconnaissance before and after, he said.
A week later, King Fahd Air Base in Taif, Saudi Arabia, was hit with multiple projectiles fired by the Iranian-backed Houthis. Along with hangars at the base, an Italian air force Eurofighter Typhoon jet was damaged, according to the Italian Defense Ministry. The Italian military has had assets deployed in Saudi Arabia for years as part of the U.S.-led coalition’s campaigns in Iraq and Syria.
In both those cases, Obaid's firm monitored a 50% increase in the number of Russian satellites orbiting above the targets during a 72-hour period before and after the strikes, compared with July.
Notably, the Taif attack precisely hit the Italian warplane rather than Saudi ones stationed at the same base, suggesting "highly specialized intelligence support that the Houthis and Iranians simply don’t have," Obaid said.
The Houthis have warned foreign powers not to help Saudi Arabia.
A clear pattern of satellites is visible 
AURORAH used open-source information as well as other intelligence sources to identify 72 Russian reconnaissance satellites out of more than 11,000 spacecraft orbiting the Earth, Obaid said. It then tracked their trajectories and maneuvers while comparing them to military activity on the ground.
The firm has not intercepted actual transmission of intelligence to Iran or its allies, Obaid said. Instead, the firm has established a definitive pattern of Russian satellite positions and reconnaissance activity around strategic targets ahead of strikes, indicating that intelligence is being collected and transferred for Houthi and Iraqi militia targeting, he said.
Obaid said the same satellite patterns also occurred in connection with Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Middle East during the U.S.-Iran war that began in February.
“That is the fundamental transformation in the regional military balance: The intelligence system behind the weapon is becoming as important as the weapon itself,” he said.
Adam Marsh, vice president of technological solutions at California-based Leolabs, an orbital intelligence firm, said the massing of satellites is what one would expect to see for purposes of collecting intelligence. The Russians can deny they are doing it, he said, but he noted there is only a general policy and no regulatory body: “How would you stop anybody?”
Satellite intelligence has also helped Houthis in their fight inside Yemen 
An official briefed on investigations in Saudi Arabia into recent attacks said intelligence showed that Russian satellites had helped Houthis and Iraqi militias strike sensitive targets, including the pumping stations on the East-West Pipeline. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to journalists.
The satellites also helped strikes by Iran in March on Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, where a U.S. surveillance aircraft was severely damaged, and on a CIA unit inside the U.S. Embassy complex in Riyadh, the official said.
The investigations found that missiles and drones used by the Houthis in their strikes had Russian- and Chinese-made components, the official said.
Russian satellite intelligence has also helped the Houthis in the dramatic advances they made against Saudi-backed opponents in Yemen’s civil war, according to Obaid and a Houthi leader.
AURORAH identified satellite configurations over targets in connection to an Oct. 15 Houthi strike on the presidential palace in Yemen’s southern port city of Aden and a nearby command center used by the Saudi-led coalition, as well as a strike on a government recruitment center in the province of Shabwa that killed 75 new recruits, Obaid said.
Iranian advisers on the ground in Yemen have been providing the rebels with data based on Russian satellite intelligence to help in targeting, a senior Houthi leader told the AP. The leader spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the confidential role of the advisers.
Mzahem Alsaloum, a security analyst who has followed Iranian-backed groups for nearly a decade and now runs a private intelligence firm, said the advisers use Russian spy satellite information to provide Iranians with target lists and operational information.
The Houthi leader also said the Iranians provided the rebels with more advanced equipment, including systems for piloting drones and for helping missiles evade air defenses.
The equipment was developed by the Iranians, bought commercially or provided by Russia and China, he said, though he did not know whether those countries were aware the equipment was being used in the Yemen war.

The leftist incumbent eventually won by a clear margin of more than 4 million votes.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election results, pointing to the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results, but the senator has not yet conceded victory.
His refusal to accept the results mirrors how his father Jair disputed his election defeat to Lula four years ago.
Jair is serving a more than 20-year prison sentence for plotting a coup to overthrow Lula after the 2022 election.
How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?
The Argentinian Migration Department on Wednesday said Flavio Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered Argentina before taking a private plane to Ecuador.
The department added that Bolsonaro and his family had entered the country through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in Misiones Province.
It also said that they were holding valid travel documents and that there was "no legal impediment" blocking their entry, despite a court order banning Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil.
Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.
Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts were unclear, with some reports claiming that he had landed in the US, while others said he was in Ecuador or still en route.
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he "would approve" of the far-right senator coming to the US.
"I think they're fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews.
Trump also repeated his belief that Flavio's father, Jair, was the victim of persecution by Brazil's judicial authorities.
"The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn't involved," Trump added. "That's Brazil. It's a different country."
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.
Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.
What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?
The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was taken from government pensions for senior citizens.
A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."
Bolsonaro will lose his immunity from prosecution once his senate term ends in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.

CIUS awards over 800 grants, scholarships to scholars, institutions in Ukraine over past 50 years
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:54:23 EET
02:54:23 KST

The Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies (CIUS) at the University of Alberta is celebrating its 50th anniversary and has announced an international symposium to mark the occasion, titled "Recentring the Humanities: Ukraine and the World."
According to CIUS, over the past 50 years, the institute has awarded at least 1,742 academic honors, grants, and scholarships, of which 883 – or about 51% – were awarded to Ukrainian scholars and institutions.
CIUS currently comprises 11 research centers and programs that study the Holodomor, medieval and early modern Ukrainian history, contemporary social processes, the Ukrainian language and methods of teaching it, as well as the history of Ukrainians in Canada and other countries. One area of focus concerns the history of Ukrainian statehood. Among the institute's long-term projects is the English-language Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine. Crimean Tatar studies constitute a separate area of focus.
The CIUS was founded in 1976 with the support of the provincial government, the University of Alberta, and the active participation of the Ukrainian community in Canada. The institute made its first payment to an institution in Ukraine in 1987-1988, and as early as 1989-1990, KIUS became one of the hubs through which Ukrainian researchers established contacts with the academic community in North America. The collaboration also encompassed legislative reforms and the development of democratic institutions, a significant portion of the funding for which was provided by the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA).
A symposium marking the institute's anniversary will take place October 28-30 in Edmonton, with the option to participate online upon prior registration.
Among the announced participants are Oleksandra Matviychuk, head of the Center for Civil Liberties; Refat Chubarov, Chair of the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People; historians Serhiy Plokhy and Yaroslav Hrytsak; philosopher Volodymyr Yermolenko; and Metropolitan Borys Gudziak. Participants will discuss how Ukraine's experience – particularly its resistance to Russian aggression – is shaping international debates on history, human rights, democracy, and cultural identity.

Poland selected for new PAC-3 missile maintenance center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:51:38 UTC
02:51:38 KST

- Lockheed Martin plans to establish a PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility in Poland, in coordination with the U.S. government, to repair and recertify Patriot interceptors.
- Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Poland and the United States signed the original agreement in July, and the facility’s location, cost and opening date remain undisclosed.
Lockheed Martin plans to open a dedicated maintenance facility in Poland for Patriot PAC-3 interceptors, the company announced Tuesday.
The PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility is being set up in coordination with the U.S. government and will serve NATO allies that operate the interceptors. The site will repair and recertify the missiles. According to the company, that will let allies get them back faster for resupply and testing.
Recertification is a periodic check that confirms a stored missile is still fit to fire. Allies keep PAC-3 interceptors in inventory for years, and each one has to go through that process to stay available for combat.
The company did not say where in Poland the facility will be built, when it will open or how much it will cost.
The plan dates to July, when five NATO countries, Poland among them, agreed to explore a European maintenance site for PAC-3 missiles at the alliance’s summit in Ankara. At the time, U.S. Under Secretary Michael Duffey told reporters that the host country had not been decided. Tuesday’s announcement names Poland.
Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden also signed that agreement and will help supply the facility, the company said.
The facility will be tied into Poland’s existing defense industry, creating skilled jobs and work for local suppliers, the company said. It gave no figures.
Polish industry already has a role in the PAC-3 program. In September 2025, state-owned Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne completed validation of its production line for the missile’s attitude control section and attitude control motor, which steer the interceptor in flight.
“Lockheed Martin is a permanent part of Europe’s security landscape,” said Jay Pitman, president of Lockheed Martin International.
The facility is expected to service both PAC-3 models in allied use. The newer Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) has a dual-pulse rocket motor that gives it more range and altitude than the earlier Cost Reduction Initiative missile. Both destroy targets by hitting them directly.
The Polish site will maintain missiles, not build them. New PAC-3 MSE interceptors are assembled at Lockheed Martin’s plant in Camden, Arkansas, where output is set to grow. In July, the U.S. government raised the value of a seven-year PAC-3 MSE production contract to $58.62 billion, building on a $4.7 billion first-year award in April. The funding is meant to triple production capacity by the end of 2030.

The Mecca Pact courts Iran: Containment comes full circle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:50:37 UTC
02:50:37 KST

For nearly half a century, Iran’s adversaries have tried to isolate it, intimidate it, sanction it into submission and bomb it into irrelevance. Now, in a remarkable inversion of regional power politics, three countries historically invested in its containment have arrived in Tehran to discuss their security with the very state they were supposed to marginalise.
The country they could not defeat is becoming the country they cannot afford to ignore.
Yesterday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın met Iranian officials in an encounter whose diplomatic courtesies barely concealed its strategic significance.
The Mecca Pact, the joint defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed in Mecca in August, was supposed to consolidate a formidable Sunni-led defence alignment. Yet its representatives have come to Tehran confronting an inconvenient reality: Iran cannot be excluded from regional security merely because Washington and its partners find its independence intolerable.
Apparently, the Islamic Republic has become considerably more respectable since demonstrating that it cannot be conveniently eliminated.
This is the distinction between military destruction and strategic defeat that Washington and Israel persistently confuse. Overwhelming firepower can devastate infrastructure, assassinate officials and inflict enormous suffering. It cannot manufacture political submission.
Iran has survived military confrontation, retained retaliatory capabilities and forced neighbouring governments to reconsider the potentially catastrophic consequences of another war.
Survival becomes strategic victory when your adversaries must reorganise their calculations around it.
For Saudi Arabia, the reckoning is particularly humiliating. Riyadh spent decades treating American military supremacy as an insurance policy against Iranian influence. Yemen exposed the bankruptcy of that assumption.
Ansar Allah, Yemen’s Houthi movement, demonstrated that superior arsenals cannot guarantee security against an adversary capable of imposing disproportionate costs. The Saudi monarchy possesses spectacular weaponry, immense wealth and powerful patrons. Yet none of these has eliminated its vulnerability to Yemeni retaliation.
Now Riyadh finds itself seeking Tehran’s cooperation to manage a conflict that its military superiority has failed to resolve.
Evidently, purchasing American weapons is considerably easier than purchasing strategic security.
Pakistan’s predicament is scarcely less revealing. Munir presides over a military establishment accustomed to presenting strategic dependency as diplomatic sophistication. Islamabad’s defence commitments to Riyadh now threaten to entangle Pakistan in confrontations with Iran and Yemen that serve neither its geography nor its national interests.
The Mecca Pact promises collective security. Its less advertised feature is collective exposure to somebody else’s strategic miscalculations.
Munir must now reconcile his obligations to Saudi patrons with the inconvenient realities of Iranian power. It is an awkward assignment for an establishment that has repeatedly mistaken proximity to foreign power for genuine strategic independence.
Türkiye confronts a different calculation but reaches a similar conclusion. Ankara understands that NATO membership, military capabilities and regional ambitions cannot abolish geography. No credible security architecture can be constructed by pretending Iran is dispensable.
The deeper contradiction, however, lies within the Mecca Pact itself.
Its members seek the reassurance of collective defence while attempting to avoid being dragged into another American-Israeli confrontation. An attack on one may formally constitute an attack on all. But such commitments become considerably less attractive when Iranian retaliation, Yemeni escalation and vulnerable Gulf infrastructure enter the equation.
Collective defence sounds magnificent until someone presents the collective bill.
Iran’s achievement is not that its neighbours have embraced its revolutionary worldview. They have not. Saudi Arabia remains deeply connected to Washington, Pakistan continues its elaborate balancing act, and Türkiye remains embedded in NATO.
The significance runs deeper: these governments increasingly recognise that excluding Iran from regional security may expose them to greater dangers than engaging it.
That realisation strikes at the foundations of the American security paradigm.
For decades, Washington cultivated regional dependence on American protection while organising strategic anxieties around Iranian power. Now those same governments are exploring cooperation with the country they were encouraged to regard as an existential threat.
The irony is devastating. Decades of attempting to contain Iran may have helped establish its indispensability.
And Tehran, displaying the composure of a state conscious of its diplomatic leverage, has welcomed its visitors graciously. No triumphalist declarations are necessary. The spectacle speaks adequately for itself.
The Mecca Pact arrived ostensibly to discuss regional stability. What it encountered was the strategic consequence of its own failed assumptions.
Iran did not have to join the alliance. The alliance had to come to Iran.

How Would China Actually Govern Taiwan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:49:00 UTC
02:49:00 KST

On September 12, the University of Hong Kong’s Beijing Center held a low-profile symposium at which Chinese scholars discussed the institutional design and governance arrangements that would follow unification with Taiwan. The participants reached 12 points of consensus on how the “One Country, Two Systems” principle should be implemented in Taiwan.
All of Taiwan’s power would derive from authorization by Beijing; Taiwan’s armed forces would be disbanded and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops stationed on the island. All this while still upholding the central government’s policy on Taiwan: “peaceful reunification.” The blueprint, however, also accounts for the scenario of achieving “reunification through non-peaceful means,” which would involve a transition period of “quasi-military governance for a duration of three to five years.”
The symposium built on Xi Jinping’s 2019 speech marking the 40th anniversary of the “Message to Compatriots in Taiwan,” in which he called for exploring a “Two Systems” solution for Taiwan. The symposium was not an isolated event. Chinese scholars regularly debate and publish on how Beijing should approach unification.
This article puts the 12-point consensus in context and compares it with the 2022 white paper “The Taiwan Question and China’s Reunification in the New Era,” to assess how part of China’s scholarly community envisions governing Taiwan after unification, and where that vision departs from the contemporary official line.
One Country, Two Systems
More than 20 Chinese scholars who participated in the symposium drew on the post-handover experience Beijing has from Hong Kong and Macao, both Special Administrative Regions (SARs) that operate under the principle of “One Country, Two Systems.”
Hong Kong was transferred from British to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years of British rule following the First Opium War (1839-1842). During the negotiations, Beijing promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and pledged to maintain its capitalist system and way of life unchanged for 50 years. Macao, where Portuguese traders settled in the 1550s, was handed over to Beijing on December 20, 1999, becoming China’s second SAR.
The “One Country, Two Systems” principle was initially designed with Taiwan in mind. In September 1981, Ye Jianying, a top military leader and chairman of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, set out a nine-point proposal for peaceful unification, which became known as “Ye’s Nine Points.” At that point, it was proposed that Taiwan would maintain a “high degree of autonomy” as an SAR.
In 1982, Deng Xiaoping, China’s paramount leader after Mao’s death, developed these ideas into the “One Country, Two Systems” formula. The principle was first applied to Hong Kong and later to Macao. The recent symposium attempted to spell out what a Taiwan version would involve.
The Symposium Consensus
According to the 12-point consensus, the “One Country, Two Systems” principle would be implemented whether the unification came by peacefully or via “non-peaceful means.” In a “non-peaceful” scenario, the scholars envisioned a post-conflict transition period of “quasi-military governance,” which could be implemented for a duration of three to five years, during which the central government would crack down on “Taiwan independence elements,” or (in Beijing’s terminology) “Taiwan independence separatists.” China uses the term to refer to anyone who advocates or promotes the de jure independence of Taiwan.
The symposium’s direct discussion of the use of force against Taiwan – and what would follow – is an outlier. “Peaceful reunification” remains Beijing’s official discursive approach to Taiwan, reflected in many official documents of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Force is left as a last resort aimed at external interference and a “very small number of separatists,” as stated in the 2022 white paper.
The possibility of a military conflict across the Taiwan Strait is widely regarded as one of the most serious geopolitical flashpoints today. In the last decade, China has been steadily intensifying military pressure on Taiwan through a combination of large-scale military exercises and gray-zone operations around the island.
However, many analysts argue that a large-scale military conflict across the Taiwan Strait – particularly if the United States, Japan, or other regional actors were drawn in – would carry serious risks for the CCP’s primary goal: maintaining its monopoly on political power and ensuring the regime’s survival. As a professor at MIT and China researcher M. Taylor Fravel argued, China is even more aware of such a risk since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Following the “reunification,” all existing Taiwanese armed forces would be disbanded, their weapons “collected and turned over” to the central government, and the island’s defense would become Beijing’s responsibility. The central government would station troops in Taiwan, following the practice in Hong Kong and Macao, where PLA garrisons have been present since 1997 and 1999, respectively. The 2022 white paper did not mention anything about the future of Taiwan’s military, but the 1993 white paper on “reunification” stated that Taiwan would keep its own military and the mainland would not send troops or administrative personnel to Taiwan.
According to the symposium’s 12-point plan, Taiwanese people would also be allowed to voluntarily enlist in the PLA. The PLA is the armed force of the CCP, which commands it through the Central Military Commission, chaired by Xi Jinping, following the principle that “the party commands the gun.” Taiwan’s armed forces, by contrast, are constitutionally required to stand above party affiliation, as stated in Article 138 of the Constitution of the Republic of China (ROC).
Matters of security, defense, and foreign affairs involving Taiwan are expected to be the sole responsibility of the central government in Beijing following unification.
In terms of law, the Chinese scholars proposed a “de-nationalization” and “de-centralization” of the old legal system, transferring the whole body of law to the SAR regulations. They called for ensuring that “patriots govern Taiwan,” while the existing political parties could be retained under the new constitution. This diverges from the 2022 white paper, which was silent on this topic.
Taiwan is a fully functioning democracy with a pluralistic, multiparty electoral system. Since the democratization in the 1990s, the two dominant parties at the national level have been the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), both holding the presidency and controlling parliament at different times. The KMT generally favors closer cross-strait relations and engagement with China, while the DPP generally emphasizes Taiwan’s distinct identity and supports maintaining Taiwan’s de facto independence and autonomy, while officially calling for the preservation of the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.
China, on the other hand, is a one-party state with the leadership of the Communist Party embedded in the PRC Constitution. Alongside the CCP, however, exist eight other legally recognized political parties, all of which accept the CCP’s leadership. While China holds no elections these parties can contest, they participate in the state advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
The 12-point consensus also covers a complete reorganization of Taiwan’s administrative divisions and electoral system. The scholars also called for a thorough reform of Taiwanese textbooks to align with the “patriotic and national” education of China.
Post-unification, Taiwan and the mainland are expected to undergo deeper economic integration. Commerce and cultural ties would continue as usual. Taiwan is expected to become a key economic node in the new “Zhejiang-Fujian-Taiwan Greater Bay Area,” which would serve as an Asia-Pacific economic operations center and high-tech industrial base.
From a geopolitical perspective, the scholars envision Taiwan becoming an “eastern bulwark of national security.” Taiwan has a pivotal position in the First Island Chain, a strategic line of islands from Japan, through Taiwan to the Philippines, that limit China’s direct and uninterrupted access to the Western Pacific. Taiwan is geopolitically perceived as both the gateway for China’s expansion into the Pacific and as a frontline for external interference in China’s mainland.
Perspective From Taiwan
According to commentary on the symposium, no participants from Taiwan took part, including Taiwanese figures who favor closer cross-strait ties or eventual unification. One online commentary offered two explanations. First, it claimed that Taiwanese scholars were not invited out of concern for their safety. Due to the sensitivity of the topics discussed – especially unification through “non-peaceful means” – the article argued that attendance could expose pro-unification figures to repercussions at home. Separately, however, the author bluntly stated that Taiwan’s interests should not constrain China’s national interests. The absence of any Taiwanese voices at the symposium nonetheless raises the question of how much decision-making power Beijing would be willing to grant to Taiwanese people post-unification.
In late August 2026, shortly before the symposium took place, Ci-Ze Li, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education, published three essays on what a Taiwan-specific version of “One Country, Two Systems” might involve. His proposal, according to his words, was a conditional exercise, not a claim that Taiwanese society had accepted unification.
Assuming a single sovereign state for the sake of discussion, Li argued that Taiwan should retain democratic elections, judicial authority, financial autonomy, and locally controlled defense forces. He also proposed constitutional safeguards that would make it harder for Beijing to withdraw these guarantees unilaterally. Specifically, he called for a Taiwan-specific chapter in the PRC Constitution, a Basic Law, and a charter endorsed by Taiwan’s voters.
His proposals differed sharply from the symposium’s consensus. Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office nonetheless welcomed discussion of such proposals in Taiwan, with spokesperson Zhu Fenglian stating that engaging earlier and more broadly would bring Taiwan greater benefits.
In response to these discussions, Liang Wen-chieh, the deputy minister of Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), stated that Beijing would not accept Li’s conditions, since China’s approach to “One Country, Two Systems” amounts to replicating the Hong Kong model in Taiwan. Liang added that as long as the CCP retains absolute leadership, any guarantees offered by Beijing would lack credibility, and that Taiwan would not accept the formula on any terms. These statements reflect the position of the government in Taipei.
The latest public opinion survey commissioned by Taiwan’s MAC and conducted by National Chengchi University in August 2026 found that 81.2 percent of respondents opposed Beijing’s “One Country, Two Systems” proposal, while 83.9 percent agreed that Taiwan’s future should be decided by its 23 million citizens. Furthermore, 65.8 percent of respondents considered Beijing’s attitude toward the Taiwanese government unfriendly, and 51.1 percent expressed the same view regarding its attitude toward the Taiwanese people.
Support for eventual or immediate unification dropped among Taiwanese respondents from 23.2 percent to 7.8 percent between 2000 and 2026. The decline in support for unification is consistent with a stronger, distinct Taiwanese identity and with a growing share of people who see Taiwan as their primary political community and democracy as a defining feature of that community.
Taiwan’s Contested Status
The unification of Taiwan with China is portrayed by Xi as nothing less than an “inevitable requirement for the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” The CCP today holds that Taiwan has been part of China since antiquity, that it was ceded to Japan in 1895 during what official Chinese narratives call the “century of humiliation,” and that it was returned in 1945 under the Cairo and Potsdam declarations. It also holds that the PRC, as the successor to the ROC in 1949, holds sovereignty over the island.
The CCP position on Taiwan has not always been consistent, however. In their analysis in the Pacific Affairs journal from 1979, Frank S. T. Hsiao and Lawrence R. Sullivan found that in a number of official documents dated between 1928 and 1943, the CCP described Taiwanese as a distinct nation or nationality (minzu) and Taiwan as a colony entitled to self-determination. Today, by framing Taiwan as an inseparable part of China, the CCP reinforces an idea of shared national identity and mobilizes patriotic sentiment.
Supporters of Taiwan’s independence point to the growing Taiwanese identity and argue that Taiwan meets all legal criteria of statehood and is entitled to self-determination, a principle embedded in the international system and recognized in Article 1(2) of the United Nations Charter. Beijing argues that self-determination does not override territorial integrity that was broken during the 19th century, when the administration of Taiwan was transferred from Qing China to imperial Japan after the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895).
The legal and historical claims on which Beijing and Taipei rest their position remain contested. The facts of administration are, however, not disputable: The PRC has never exercised jurisdiction over Taiwan.
The 12-point consensus offers a window into how China might approach the governance of Taiwan post-unification. This is a scholarly consensus, not official policy. The consensus from the symposium is nonetheless unusually detailed, answering some questions the 2022 white paper left open, and dropping earlier assurances such as the pledge not to station troops in Taiwan. Whether official statements adopt these specifics are indicators to watch.

“Ukrainian forces have successfully adapted this tactic, updated it, and made it far more deliberate and technologically advanced. We are protecting the lives of our people, inflicting losses on the occupiers, and achieving our objectives on the Kupiansk axis,” Zelensky emphasized.
As previously reported, the Khartiia Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine released details of Operation Veles, an underground counteroffensive being conducted in the Kharkiv region.

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
The Central Election Commission (CEC) has confirmed that Bulgaria’s October 25 presidential election failed to produce a winner, with only 1,525,034 of the country’s 6,584,025 eligible voters casting ballots, or nearly 23%, according to the final results announced by the Commission.
“No president or vice-president of the Republic was elected in the elections held on October 25, 2026, as less than half of the eligible voters participated, and none of the candidates received more than half of the valid votes cast,” the CEC said.
The two presidential tickets with the most votes will face each other in a runoff on November 1. Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, backed by an Initiative Committee and listed as ballot number 4, received 486,232 valid votes. Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev, also nominated by an Initiative Committee and listed as ballot number 25, secured 528,951 valid votes. A total of 67,353 voters selected the option “I do not support anyone.”
The first round recorded the lowest turnout in Bulgaria’s modern electoral history, raising questions about whether the candidates can mobilize more voters for Sunday’s runoff and how supporters of the different political parties will vote.
Communications expert Natalia Dimitrova and Yulian Angelov of VMRO discussed the prospects for the second round on Nova TV.
Dimitrova said voters who had supported Progressive Bulgaria in April did not turn out in comparable numbers this time, while the core supporters of the parties backing Gyurov appeared to have mobilized more effectively. She added that the choices of GERB and DPS voters remained uncertain.
Angelov predicted that participation would increase on November 1, suggesting that some voters had stayed away because they expected Yotova to win the first round. He also expressed the view that voters of Revival would support her in the runoff.
Turning to the candidates’ policy priorities, Dimitrova highlighted foreign policy and argued that Gyurov and Kandev offered the right approach. “No one is in favor of war,” she said, calling on both presidential tickets to participate in a debate focused specifically on foreign policy.
Angelov, by contrast, argued that domestic political issues would play a greater role in voters’ decisions. He said Yotova and Valchev were offering a patriotic platform that could help bridge divisions in society.
Angelov also called for a debate, claiming that Georgi Kandev had declined to face his opponent, Kiril Valchev. He said he hoped Yotova and Valchev would win because they could defend Bulgaria’s national interest.
“We, from VMRO, will push for the President’s powers to be strengthened, as they were curtailed by the 'assembly arrangement'. We want the Head of State to have the sole authority to appoint the caretaker Prime Minister, to be able to propose legislation on specific topics, and to have the power to call for a vote of no confidence in the government or the parliament,” Angelov said, adding that the president should serve as a check on Bulgarian politics.
Dimitrova said her support for Gyurov and Kandev stemmed from the fact that they were backed by political forces outside the current government. “They need to win so that this check on the authorities can exist,” she said.
The first round drew slightly more than 1.5 million voters, with turnout estimated at around 23%. By comparison, nearly 4 million people voted in the first round of the 2016 presidential election, while approximately 2.5 million participated in 2021.
Presidential elections in Bulgaria generally attract more voters in the first round than in the runoff. One notable exception occurred in 2001, when the second-round contest between Georgi Parvanov and Petar Stoyanov drew more voters following an unexpected first-round result.
The only vote with lower participation was the referendum on the Belene Nuclear Power Plant, in which fewer than 1.5 million Bulgarians voted. Since that was a referendum rather than a political election, the 2026 presidential first round represents the lowest turnout in modern Bulgarian history for an election to the National Assembly, the presidency or the European Parliament. European Parliament elections, in particular, generally record participation below 35%.
Analysts have attributed the low turnout to a negative campaign, the widespread expectation that the outcome was already decided and a lack of confidence in the political class. The absence of two major political formations, GERB-SDS and DPS, was also cited as an important factor.
The 2013 referendum on the Belene Nuclear Power Plant remains the record-low participation vote, with turnout at 20.22%. A boycott by opponents of expanding nuclear power was among the reasons for the low participation, although 1,405,463 people still cast ballots.
Turnout in the 2007 European Parliament elections was 28.60%. Participation in the next two European elections was also relatively low, reaching 32.64% in 2019 and 33.78% in 2024.
Repeated parliamentary elections and unstable governing coalitions in recent years have also contributed to voter disengagement. In 2024, parliamentary turnout fell to a record low of 34.41%. The second round of the 2021 presidential election also remained below 35%, with participation at 34.84%, although it was not among the five elections with the lowest turnout.
The highest participation rates were mostly recorded in the early years of Bulgaria’s transition to democracy. The record since 1989 was set in June 1990, when Bulgarians elected the Seventh Grand National Assembly, which was tasked with drafting a new constitution. Turnout reached 90.79%, a level that has not been surpassed. A total of 6,976,620 people voted, exceeding Bulgaria’s current total population.
High participation continued in 1991, when 83.9% of eligible voters took part in the parliamentary elections.
The presidential election in early 1992 recorded turnout of 75.39% in the first round and 75.9% in the second. The 1994 parliamentary election was the last to attract more than 75% of voters, with turnout at 75.3%. Participation in the 2001 parliamentary election reached 67%.
By comparison, turnout in Bulgaria’s most recent parliamentary election, held on April 19, 2026, was 51.11%.
The Bulgarian National Television (BNT) will air the only televised presidential debate between candidates Iliaana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov on October 29 at 9 p.m., the public broadcaster announced

Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
Unknown

2026-10-27
17:44:11 UTC

Breadcrumb
Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
A drone was shot down near the US embassy in Baghdad on Tuesday, triggering three loud explosions near the heavily fortified Green Zone, Iraqi security officials said.
Iraq's Security Media Cell said in a brief statement that the explosions were caused by the interception of a drone near the Green Zone, which houses the US embassy and several government institutions.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that two surveillance drones had approached the US embassy compound before being intercepted by its C-RAM air defence system.
The sources said Iraqi authorities had launched an investigation but had not yet established where the drones were launched from.
The incident comes as the Iraqi government continues efforts to persuade armed factions to surrender their weapons and bring all military capabilities under state control.
Several factions have agreed to hand over their weapons, but others have refused, including four groups operating under the umbrella of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
They are Kataib Hezbollah, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, Harakat al-Nujaba and Harakat al-Awfiya.
Security sources told The New Arab that they suspected the drones belonged to factions opposed to disarmament, although no group had claimed responsibility.
The sources said the factions continued to regard the US embassy as an occupation base and possessed surveillance and drone capabilities unmatched by other local Iraqi groups.
Last week, the four factions accused Washington of violating Iraqi sovereignty and failing to honour its commitments to Baghdad.
In a joint statement, they criticised restrictions on airports and border crossings with Iran, arguing that such decisions were being dictated by the United States.
They also questioned whether Iraq could exercise genuine sovereignty while major national decisions remained subject to foreign influence.
Earlier, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced that three of five armed factions that had agreed to surrender their weapons had already done so, while negotiations continued with the remaining two.
"Five factions agreed to hand over their weapons, and three have already done so, while dialogue continues with the others," Zaidi said during a meeting with tribal leaders, according to his office.
Iraqi researcher Mujashaa al-Tamimi told The New Arab that the use of surveillance drones could be intended to signal to Washington that armed factions remained active and capable of carrying out operations.
However, he stressed that this interpretation depended on whether the drones had actually been launched by those groups.
Tamimi warned that the renewed use of drones could signal another period of heightened tensions in Baghdad.

EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:44:00 UTC
02:44:00 KST

EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers
October 27, 2026
The European Commission on Tuesdayunveiled a new proposal to beef up the powers of the EU border agency in order to empower it to support the return of irregular migrants.
The proposed legislation gives the agency, called Frontex, more resources to act beyond EU territory.
The plan would give the agency the power to support non-EU countries to return migrants to their countries of origin.
The proposal comes as EU member states increasingly focus on returns, saying too many people who are asked to leave the bloc remain.
EU border agency to be beefed up after Ceuta humanitarian crisis of summer
The new role for Frontex comes after the humanitarian crisis in Ceuta this summer.
The tragedy in the Spanish exclave was seized upon by some EU member states as an example of where the EU could do more to block people from reaching the EU.
Italy, for example, placed some temporary border controls on travel from Spain.
Spain's prime minister at the time criticized several EU member states for their "selfish" response to the influx of migrants to Ceuta.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
Frontex to be given wide powers to support deportation of irregular migrants
The ability to deport migrants from non-EU countries means that Frontex could, for instance, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya, where many migrants start the final leg of their journey into the bloc.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers within the next 15 years.
Those officers would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would also create a new EU Return Coordination Center within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process.
It would also include a new online monitoring center to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
Frontex reform criticized by rights groups
Frontex has been responsible for guarding the external borders of the EU as well as ensuring the rights of new arrivals.
It has been criticized for its lack of accountability in the past.
The planned reform shrinks the scope of the agency's internal rights watchdog, with complaints to be referred to national authorities.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said.

Whose interests does the ceasefire serve?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:44:00 UTC
02:44:00 KST

A new report released yesterday by the UN Commission of Inquiry states that Israel is still committing genocide in Gaza after the ceasefire agreement which was reached on 10 October 2025. Referencing earlier reports concluding that Israel had committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide in Gaza, the report goes on to state “The cases investigated for this report … show that the Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
In the occupied West Bank, the report notes, there was an increase in the number of Palestinians killed by Israeli airstrikes: from six between 2008 and 6 October 2023, to 254 between 7 October 2023 and 30 September 2026.
Whose interests does the ceasefire serve, if Israel is still committing genocide against the Palestinian people?
Since the ceasefire, discourse has mostly centred on humanitarian aid, rebuilding Gaza, the Yellow Line and forced displacement. Taken together, including the farce of rebuilding Gaza when Israel has repeatedly said it will not withdraw from the territory it occupied, the report reflects the Commission of Inquiry’s statement regarding genocide. The only change has been the vocabulary – with the ceasefire, genocide is rarely spoken of by world leaders. Instead, the focus is once again on separate human rights violations, limiting the context of Israel’s genocide and completely obliterating colonialism from the equation.
Such rhetoric served Israel well throughout the decades. In his final UN General Assembly speech, Secretary General Antonio Guterres referred to the International Court of Justice’s reference to genocide but spoke of “raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing” in his UN role. “We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes,” Guterres said. What better way to ensure Israel’s impunity than to talk of saving the defunct two-state paradigm?
Under the diplomatic shelter provided by the ceasefire, world leaders can pretend to restore the status quo and use the same discredited framework to whitewash their conduct. There is no international opposition to this equation. There is Gaza, of course, which bears the full consequences of the genocide, including the impunity the international community has granted Israel and, by extension, itself.
Gaza also pays the price of the failed ceasefire, which the international community uses as cover to avoid confronting the evidence of genocide. That evidence is well documented, yet governments prefer to describe Israel’s actions as a series of separate violations of international law rather than as genocide.
Israel did not stop its genocide during the ceasefire; it scaled it back to a level the international community finds acceptable. The only ones who benefit are those complicit in it. Beyond periodic calls on Israel to respect the ceasefire, the international community has made no real move to hold it accountable. On the contrary, it is relieved to return to the language it used before, when diplomats did not have to confront an open genocide and ethnic cleansing could be dismissed as isolated cases of forced displacement. This is what the ceasefire has achieved. It will likely rescue the rhetoric of a two-state solution before it rescues Palestinians in Gaza.

IOC previously-imposed sanctions against Russia, Belarus

Following the IOC’s recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations decided to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.

Dozens of people killed and 150 injured in Sudanese Armed Forces' Nyala drone strike
Share
Crisis Update27 October 2026
Yesterday, 26 October, at around 8 p.m. local time, a drone strike by the Sudanese Armed Forces struck a busy market in the west of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, Sudan, causing complete devastation among the people gathered there. A second strike also hit a civilian neighbourhood. The Médecins Sans Frontières- (MSF) supported Nyala Teaching hospital has so far received the bodies of 36 people, 21 of whom were wearing civilian clothing. The hospital’s medical teams reported seeing over 150 wounded patients in the emergency room.
Dale Koninckx, MSF project coordinator in Nyala, describes the scene at Nyala Teaching hospital.
“My colleagues saw patients arrive at the hospital with shrapnel injuries, blood on their faces, and severe burns. People were carried to the hospital on tuk-tuks and donkey carts from the market where the drone struck.
“Medical staff worked around the clock treating patients, including women and children. They’re all very shaken. The question everyone is asking is, ‘Why are markets being targeted? The places where people need to access food, where a lot of civilians gather?’
“This is appalling. Markets, homes, and key civilian infrastructure are not targets. All parties to the conflict must protect civilians.”
This attack follows a similar incident in Nyala on 16 October when a drone struck Al-Mawashi market in Nyala, killing at least four people and injuring many more. These incidents, among others, are exposing civilians to direct violence and people’s access to food and supplies, at a time when malnutrition is a growing concern.
Both sides in the conflict are targeting civilian areas and infrastructure. In recent days, the Rapid Support Forces reportedly carried out drone strikes targeting electricity infrastructure in Khartoum, Al-Jazirah, Gedaref, Sennar, and White Nile states.

Rania R.a. Abushamala

Voter turnout in Israel’s hard-fought parliamentary (Knesset) elections reached 66.7% as of 6 pm on Tuesday, the highest figure recorded for that hour since 1973, the Central Elections Committee said.
The figure marked an increase of approximately 9% compared with the same time in the previous elections, according to an update reported by Ynet.
“We have surpassed the number of voters on the night of the previous elections,” in 2022, said Din Livne, the committee’s acting director. “We will discuss extending voting hours.”
According to Israel’s private Channel 12, the turnout beat the previous record of 65.2%, set in the 1973 and 1988 elections.
Turnout stood at 55.7% at 4 pm, when over 4.08 million voters had cast their ballots, up from 44.9% at 2 pm, according to earlier figures from the committee.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party requested an extension beyond the scheduled 10 pm closing time (2000GMT) of polling stations, with Justice Noam Solberg, the committee chair, set to decide on the request.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party opposed the request, saying no exceptional event had occurred to justify an extension. But Otzma Yehudit sought to join Likud’s petition, citing congestion and unusually long waits at polling stations.
The committee has clarified that anyone arriving at a polling station by 10 pm will be allowed to vote, even if they cast their ballot after that time.

Bulgaria Warns North Macedonia: EU Progress Depends on Protecting Bulgarian Rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Bulgaria Warns North Macedonia: EU Progress Depends on Protecting Bulgarian Rights
Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said she sees no escalation in relations with North Macedonia over Iva Mihailova’s stay in Bulgaria, stressing in an interview with bTV that Skopje must fulfill its commitments to the European Union and improve conditions for Bulgarians living in the country.
Petrova discussed bilateral relations following Mihailova’s arrival in Bulgaria, noting that she and North Macedonian authorities had given conflicting accounts of how Mihailova crossed the border.
The deputy minister said she had met with North Macedonia’s foreign minister at a forum focused on Corridor VIII, where Bulgaria reiterated that fulfilling existing commitments was necessary to build trust between the two countries.
“Bulgaria reaffirmed its position that, in order to build trust between the two countries, they must fulfill the commitments they have undertaken,” Petrova said.
Asked whether her North Macedonian counterpart had expressed grievances against Bulgaria or whether the discussion had become tense, Petrova said the meeting had remained constructive.
“The tone was one of dialogue. And when we have a clear position, there is nothing further that needs to be expressed,” she said.
Petrova clarified that the meeting took place before Mihailova entered Bulgaria, so her possible return was not discussed. At that stage, the only issue concerning Mihailova was ensuring she could access medical treatment in North Macedonia.
Petrova said she did not anticipate further deterioration in relations between Sofia and Skopje because of Mihailova’s stay in Bulgaria.
“I do not see such an escalation at the moment. For me, the key priority is ensuring that their commitments are fulfilled,” she said.
She stressed that the commitments were not simply conditions imposed on North Macedonia’s European integration, but were also essential to improving the lives of ethnic Bulgarians in the country.
“These commitments are not merely some arbitrary requirement for them to continue on their European path; rather, they are a crucial part of guaranteeing a better quality of life for the Bulgarians living there - which is our primary objective,” Petrova said.
Petrova also discussed Bulgaria’s preparations to host a connectivity summit in 2027, an initiative announced by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during her annual address.
She said Bulgaria’s selection as host demonstrated confidence in the government and contradicted claims that the country had become internationally isolated.
Petrova described the summit as an important opportunity to present Bulgaria’s infrastructure and transit projects within a wider European and regional framework.
“The Connectivity Summit itself is extremely important for Bulgaria, as it achieves several objectives. On one hand, it demonstrates a vote of confidence in the Bulgarian government; on the other, it provides an opportunity to position our own infrastructure and transit projects,” she said.
She acknowledged that Corridor VIII and other infrastructure projects had been long-standing ambitions that remained unrealized. Petrova attributed the delays partly to their failure to be strategically incorporated into international transport corridors that could benefit both the European Union and the region by creating opportunities for diversification.
“They have been a long-held dream, yet they have not materialized. This is because they were not strategically integrated into the framework of international corridors - corridors that would benefit both the Union and the region by creating opportunities for diversification,” Petrova said.
She emphasized that diversifying transport and energy connections was particularly important under current international conditions, pointing to Russia’s war in Ukraine as an example of how military conflicts can disrupt trade and specific energy links.
Petrova said hosting the summit could strengthen Bulgaria’s position as a major regional player and help secure financing for the country’s infrastructure priorities.
“This summit will position us as a key regional player and, hopefully, secure funding for the specific projects we need - enabling Bulgaria to become better connected and ensuring its commercial security,” she said.
The government has already started preparations for the summit and drawn up a list of priority infrastructure projects, Petrova confirmed.
Separately, Bulgaria reiterated its support for North Macedonia’s EU integration while insisting on the full implementation of commitments under the 2017 Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation and the 2022 European consensus.
The position was conveyed at a meeting between Bulgarian Deputy Foreign Minister Ivanka Tasheva and North Macedonia’s newly appointed ambassador to Bulgaria, Krum Efremov.
Tasheva welcomed Efremov and pointed to progress on the cross-border railway tunnel between the two countries, part of Corridor VIII. The project is based on an agreement between the two governments covering the facility’s preparation, construction and operation, and was cited as an example of what political will can achieve.
The deputy minister emphasized that better transport links would support regional economic development and strengthen connections between people on both sides of the border. She described these human ties as the most valuable asset in bilateral relations, saying they required sincere dialogue, mutual respect and the rejection of provocations and hate speech.
Tasheva reaffirmed Bulgaria’s constructive support for North Macedonia’s European integration while underscoring that the commitments undertaken must be fully implemented. The 2017 treaty and the 2022 European consensus remain key benchmarks for bilateral progress and Skopje’s European prospects.
Efremov expressed his intention to develop relations through constructive dialogue and closer cooperation in several areas, particularly trade, tourism and infrastructure.
At the end of the meeting, Tasheva wished Efremov success in his diplomatic assignment in Bulgaria and expressed hope that the issues discussed would produce tangible progress.

Protesters storm Serbian pro-Vucic TV station after his loss at polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:37:51 UTC
02:37:51 KST

Protesters storm Serbian pro-Vucic TV station after his loss at polls
On his personal Instagram account, President Vucic called the incident an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
Protesters stormed a Serbian television station supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the streets for a second night of post-election celebrations late Monday after his defeat at the polls.
Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed about 30 people entering its newsroom on Monday evening and surrounding editor-in-chief and owner Dragan Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted, “This is how it is in free Serbia!” and “Where is Vucic now?” Others called for Vucicevic’s arrest.
On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the crossed-out word “sorry”, called the incident an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
Serbia’s Student List, born out of a student-led anticorruption protest movement, defeated Vucic’s alliance in a historic election on Sunday, bringing to an end his party’s 14-year grip on power. Vucic, who became prime minister in 2014 and president in 2017, previously served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and maintained tight control over the media during his rule.
Call for calm
Celebrations erupted across Serbia, with fireworks lighting the sky almost immediately after Vucic made an announcement conceding defeat.
“It means freedom from a dictatorship that has lasted for 12 years, that I cannot remember a time before,” voter Jana Vasic told Al Jazeera.
The student movement has no clear leader, and Serbians are waiting to see whom it will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions. The leading candidate on its election list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, called for calm.
“We ask of you to stay calm and dignified until the end of the electoral process, just like you have been until now,” he said in a video posted on his Instagram account. “Don’t resort to any form of violence. Your Student List and your student movement urge you on this.”
The Independent Association of Journalists of Serbia said in a statement that it would submit an application on Tuesday to have Informer TV’s broadcasting licence revoked, citing systematic violations of law and programme obligations.
Public broadcaster apology
Meanwhile, Informer’s Vucicevic released a statement saying, “On the very first day of [Student List] power, they want to ban the media. They have said everything about themselves, and nothing about us.”
In a separate development, a group of people also gathered outside the private pro-Vucic Pink TV station in Belgrade on Monday evening, which was cordoned off by police.
Earlier, public broadcaster RTV in the Vojvodina region began its evening news bulletin by apologising to viewers for failing to fulfil its role, citing uncritical, one-sided reporting.
Serbia was ranked 104th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders, its lowest position ever and worst in the European Union-Balkan region.
The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (Crta) election monitor said last week that television stations with national reach gave three-quarters of the time allotted to politicians to government representatives. The Student List was portrayed negatively more than 80 percent of the time it was discussed, Crta added.

Starving residents of Oleshky must not become props in Russian propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:37:40 UTC
02:37:40 KST

Starving residents of Oleshky must not become props in Russian propaganda
Russian President Vladimir Putin addresses the Russian public, the country’s armed forces and law enforcement agencies amid the Wagner Group’s armed rebellion on June 24, 2023. (Artem Priakhin/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Peter Pomerantsev
Executive Editor of The Reckoning Project
For months, desperate civilians remaining in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky have been blockaded inside, as Russia severed food and medicine supplies to the city amid constant shelling, food shop closures, and reports of looting; many of the city's elderly and less mobile residents have been forced to forage for weeds and eat grass in order to simply survive.
Oleshky is starving. The stories of the residents have been well documented.
Now, there seems to be light at the end of the tunnel: U.S. First Lady Melania Trump has helped to broker a temporary, localized ceasefire agreement, which, in theory, should take place from Tuesday, Oct. 27. Much-needed aid could finally be delivered, and residents evacuated.
But this city of weak, hungry, and vulnerable people will face a new danger as Oleshky slowly opens: under the pressure of living on the brink of death, they could become props for Russian propagandists attempting to rewrite the history of what happened in the city.
Russia has a long track record of attempting to blame Ukraine for its own atrocities, and who better to use than Ukrainian civilians themselves? 
Ukraine is well aware of the danger. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha have already raised concerns about how Russia will likely manipulate the ceasefire.
Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there," said Zelensky. Sybiha has noted that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos in occupied Oleshky.
"Then they would ask a question, turn off the camera, tell her what to answer, and then turn the camera back on to record the 'required' response. Armed soldiers were present the entire time together with the journalists, standing behind their backs."
"Local residents will be forced to say on camera that they are happy, well-fed and grateful to the Russian occupiers," he stated. Ukraine's Security Service noted that one Russian unit has been specifically tasked with preparing "a series of 'compromising' interviews with the residents” in which they should accuse Ukraine's defense forces of "constant shelling."
At The Reckoning Project (TRP) — a global team of journalists and lawyers documenting and publicizing atrocity crimes and helping build cases to hold perpetrators accountable — we also know that this is a tried-and-tested Russian method based, among many other reasons, on the testimonies of several of our interviewees: Ukrainian civilians in the temporarily occupied territories who have previously been forced to participate in Russian propaganda campaigns against their own nation.
"Russian disinformation campaigns frequently pave the way for future aggressive Russian actions, with propaganda operations coordinated with military operations."
As these testimonies reveal, Russians exploited every opportunity to coerce civilians into becoming actors at gunpoint, serving in the Russian military, or, as one interviewee recounted, even producing and editing propaganda footage themselves if Russian forces discovered they had the necessary skills.
"They interviewed my mother-in-law. At first, they asked her name, age, and where she had lived," one witness, Viktoria, told TRP (name changed for security reasons). "Then they would ask a question, turn off the camera, tell her what to answer, and then turn the camera back on to record the 'required' response. Armed soldiers were present the entire time together with the journalists, standing behind their backs."
Russia has a long track record of creating propaganda videos to prop up its military objectives.
In July 2014, for example, after Russia's catastrophic destruction of a civilian plane carrying 298 people, Russian media and officials began promoting claims that Ukrainian forces shot down Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 traveling from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur.
The subsequent investigation established that the Buk, the missile launcher used in the attack, was transported from Russia before the attack and smuggled back immediately after the attack.
Russian disinformation campaigns frequently pave the way for future aggressive Russian actions, with propaganda operations coordinated with military operations.
For example, prior to Russia's full-scale invasion, the U.S. stated that it had intelligence that Russia planned to release faked footage of a supposed Ukrainian attack on Russian speakers to use as a pretext for its invasion, including plans to excavate fake "mass graves."
The same playbook could well be used today — and we are seeing the first signs — during the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky.
Key Russian media figures are already starting to spread the narrative that Russia is "rescuing" the residents that it has been terrorizing.
Kremlin propagandist Margarita Simonyan recently posted a video on her Telegram channel claiming that Ukrainians had been responsible for creating a "living hell" there.
Simonyan is notoriously unreliable: in February 2022 she stated that Russia "is not going to start a war with Ukraine, and this will not happen in any way." She also received a state award for her role in the annexation of Crimea in 2014.
As TRP has previously documented together with law firm Global Rights Compliance, Russia has also relied on preparing "information alibis" to publish cover stories for attacks even before they take place.
"The Kremlin's propaganda style has a decades-long track record, and we’ve seen these tactics even well before the war in Ukraine."
We established how Russia had started laying the groundwork to blame Ukraine for its own deadly assault on Kramatorsk railway station, stating a week beforehand that Ukraine was planning to use civilians as "human shields" in the area. Dozens were killed on April 8, 2022, but Russia gave itself away when state outlet RIA Novosti tweeted about the attack three minutes before it took place.
Russian officials, online media, and pro-war Telegram channels also spread stories that hospitals and a theater in Mariupol were full of Ukrainian military as a pretext for hitting civilians — accusations that have been debunked by journalists who were in the city, as well as eyewitnesses, UN groups, and OSINT specialists.
Similarly, Russian propagandists accused Ukrainian forces of planning the Kakhovka dam explosion and the bombing of POW camps (under the orders of U.K. intelligence) — all before Russia committed these acts itself.
The Kremlin's propaganda style has a decades-long track record, and we've seen these tactics even well before the war in Ukraine.
In Syria, Kremlin media would accuse the Syrian opposition of "gassing" civilians to cover for Putin's ally Assad's use of chemical weapons against his own people. Or going back to Soviet times, the Kremlin cynically organized a mass media campaign aimed at Western correspondents in order to make it look like their mass murder of some 14,700 Polish officers and prisoners of war at Katyn was actually the work of the Germans.
The German philosopher Nietzsche once argued that there are "no facts (...) only interpretations."
Kremlin propaganda has long followed that idea to a triumphantly cynical extreme.
At moments like this, it's important that news media do not slide into bothsideism which credits well-known sources of disinformation with the same valency as more reliable sources.
We are entering a fierce cognitive battle, where propagandists know how to play the media to whitewash their regimes' crimes.
The siege, we hope, is ending — but the assault on truth and perception is just beginning.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Trapped without food, electricity, or medicine, civilians in occupied Oleshky finally have a chance to escape. But even those wishing to go to Ukraine will reportedly be taken to Russia first.
Source: Meduza
- A ceasefire took effect early on October 27 in Oleshky (called Alyoshki in Russian) in Ukraine’s Kherson region. Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt fighting to evacuate civilians and deliver humanitarian aid to the Russian-occupied city, where a humanitarian catastrophe has unfolded. U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped the two sides reach the agreement.
- The ceasefire will last until 10:59 p.m. on November 1, said David Arakhamia, who heads the Servant of the People faction in Ukraine’s parliament and is a member of Ukraine’s negotiating team. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the timing. Arakhamia called the ceasefire in Oleshky “the biggest de-escalation since 2022.”
- Melania Trump said the ceasefire had begun two days ahead of schedule and had been extended beyond Oleshky to allow humanitarian convoys to pass safely. She said Valery Gerasimov, chief of Russia’s General Staff, had confirmed this.
- Ukraine and Russia said on the evening of October 27 that both sides were fully observing the ceasefire. The Kremlin also said the humanitarian operation in Oleshky was “going according to plan.”
- Many details of the humanitarian operation remain unclear: which roads will be cleared of mines, where residents will be taken and how they will be evacuated, whether they will be allowed to go directly to Ukraine or stay in Oleshky, and where families with children will be allowed to go. The Financial Times reported that even those wishing to go to Ukraine will first be taken to Russia. The operation will be carried out in several stages.
- Petro Andriushchenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for the Study of Occupation, said the evacuation from Oleshky is scheduled for October 30. Information about residents who want to leave is being gathered in a rush, he said, adding that details of how the evacuation will proceed remain confidential for now. Andriushchenko suggested that departures would depend on how the roads are cleared of mines. He said Ukraine expects a route across the Dnipro River to be arranged so Oleshky residents who want to go to Ukraine can travel directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
- Oleshky residents may be evacuated to Russian-annexed Crimea or Rostov-on-Don, said Vladimir Saldo, the Russia-installed “governor” of the Kherson region. He said transportation and temporary accommodation had already been arranged for them. Saldo also said those wishing to go to Ukraine would receive help.

Poland to host European Patriot maintenance centre, government says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:36:48 CET
02:36:48 KST

WARSAW, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A maintenance centre for Lockheed Martin’s Patriot interceptor missiles will be established in Poland, Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on Tuesday.
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have strained stocks of air-defence interceptor missiles and caused delivery delays, prompting countries to seek maintenance and production capabilities closer to home.
“Four countries competed for the European location of this investment: alongside Poland — Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote on social media platform X. “This success was not a given,” she said.
The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the United States, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
The Pentagon said, in a statement on its website, that the European Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Maintenance Facility (MMF) “will be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden.”
“By establishing regional maintenance, repair, and overhaul capabilities directly within the European theater, the MMF will dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines,” the statement said.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told reporters during a briefing in Brussels that the value of the investment would be around 1 billion zlotys ($253 million) and that it would take a dozen or so months to make the centre operational.
($1 = 3.9462 zlotys)
(Reporting by Karol Badohal, Anna Wlodarczak-Semczuk, Pawel Florkiewicz; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Tomasz Janowski)

MADRID, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A Spanish judge investigating July’s mass migrant crossing into Ceuta from Morocco told the government on Tuesday to declassify further intelligence documents and reports related to the deadly border rush, a court ruling showed.

• Tardon requested declassification of all notes and reports produced by the CNI after July 30 concerning the border surge and Morocco’s role, including classified reports on Moroccan authorities’ conduct
• The judge also sought the full recipient list for two already-declassified CNI intelligence notes dated July 27 and July 30, with timestamps confirming their delivery
