Soccer-From ‘Mobut’ to Mao, Mbappe dictator meme turns self-mockery into China storm
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:36:33 CET
02:36:33 KST

By Fernando Kallas
MADRID, Oct 27 (Reuters) - France and Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe has drawn public lines against extremism and police violence in his home country, but a joke about his own power in football carried him across a different boundary on Tuesday and forced him to apologise to China over an apparent reference to Mao Zedong.
The “dictator Mbappe” memes began as caricatures of his influence at Paris St Germain, not statements of political allegiance. By apparently laughing at an image depicting him as Mao, however, the France captain entered territory in which self-mockery could be perceived as an insult to a country’s founding leader.
Mbappe said the funniest meme he had seen of himself depicted him as “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. Chinese brands subsequently cut ties with him, turning an apparently casual remark into a major commercial setback.
The sensitivity goes beyond disapproval of an unflattering description. Mao founded the People’s Republic of China and remains central to its official history. Jokes about him are still taboo, and what Mbappe apparently treated as a comic disguise carries a very different significance in China.
That was far removed from the football grievance behind the original caricature.
The memes took off around Mbappe’s 2022 PSG contract extension, exaggerating supporters’ perceptions that he could decide who played, who was sacked and who was sold by the club. They gathered momentum around his acrimonious 2024 departure and followed him to Real Madrid, with artificial intelligence helping multiply the edits.
A recurring figure was former Zaire ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, complete with his distinctive leopard-skin hat. The nickname travelled from supporters into France’s dressing room, where team mate Ousmane Dembele called Mbappe “Mobut” in footage posted by the French FA during the World Cup.
Mbappe was not oblivious to the uncomfortable history behind the humour. He told France Football last month that Dembele had picked it up from social media and accepted their exchange as “just a joke”, while saying other versions showed “a lack of political and human awareness among people”.
That distinction fits a player who has repeatedly used his public position to say where he believes acceptable behaviour ends.
DIFFERENT POLITICAL STORM
The controversy puts Mbappe in an unfamiliar position after public interventions against political extremism, racism and police violence.
During France’s 2024 parliamentary election campaign, Mbappe declared himself “against extremes, ideas that divide” and urged young people to vote.
Asked about team mate Marcus Thuram’s opposition to the far-right National Rally, Mbappe endorsed Thuram’s values of tolerance and respect. After the first round of voting, he said the country could not be left in the hands of “these people”.
His response to the police killing of teenager Nahel M. in the suburbs of Paris in 2023 combined solidarity with restraint: he called it an “unacceptable situation”, then shared a team statement acknowledging the anger while rejecting the violence.
This year, Mbappe demanded a Champions League ban for Benfica’s Gianluca Prestianni over an alleged racist insult towards his Real teammate Vinicius Jr, saying he heard it five times. Prestianni denied the allegation, saying Vinicius had misheard, but UEFA handed him a six-match suspension for homophobic conduct.
For a player accustomed to taking public positions, Mbappe’s apparent attempt at self-mockery has become a controversy with consequences reaching far beyond himself.

The meme got out of control: in China, people took offense at Mbappé over jokes about Mao Zedong
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:36:24 EET
02:36:24 KST

The meme got out of control: in China, people took offense at Mbappé over jokes about Mao Zedong
Kyiv • UNN
Chinese companies terminated advertising deals with Mbappé over a joke about a meme featuring Mao Zedong. The footballer and La Liga apologized.
An ill-fated joke by France captain and Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé cost him advertising deals in China and triggered a diplomatic crisis in the football world. A remark about a meme featuring Mao Zedong outraged Beijing, forcing not only the footballer himself but also the leadership of Spain’s entire La Liga to apologize, UNN reports.
Background
In 2022, Kylian Mbappé extended his contract with PSG instead of moving to Real Madrid. However, information later appeared in the media that the club had granted him significant privileges; in particular, the Frenchman gained influence over the club’s transfer policy and the appointment of head coaches, which led to the dismissal of Mauricio Pochettino and sporting director Leonardo.
For this reason, people on social media began jokingly calling Mbappé a "dictator," and humorous videos also began appearing online depicting Mbappé in military uniform as a dictator.
The meme gained popularity after Xabi Alonso’s departure from Real Madrid, which, according to media reports, was prompted by the players led by Mbappé. The meme became especially popular during the 2026 World Cup, which was held in the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
Mbappé was also compared not only to a dictator but to Chinese political leader Mao Zedong.
What preceded the scandal
Recently, during preparations for the French show The Bridge, Mbappé was asked which meme was his favorite.
Mbappé replied: "There are plenty of them. The one that made me laugh the most was when they posted a video of 'some guy'; I think he was a Chinese dictator, and they put my... in there. I use it very often with my friends online, on PlayStation."
Mbappé’s statement immediately drew a negative reaction from China. In particular, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV also removed advertisements featuring Mbappé, while several Chinese companies announced that they were ending their cooperation with the footballer.
Photo: Tribuna.ua
Beverage producer Dongpeng, dairy giant Mengniu, and cheese producer Milkground also published similarly worded statements on Tuesday, announcing the termination of their agreements with the football star and stating that they oppose "any words or actions that hurt national feelings."
The Chinese Football Association said it had "lodged a strong protest" with Real Madrid and demanded that both the player and the football club "publish a public and official apology."
Mbappé apologized on social media platform X, writing: "During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of me that had been placed in a particular scene. This statement was inappropriate, and I now understand that it offended many people in China and in the Chinese community around the world. I apologize to everyone who was hurt by my words. That was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I sincerely regret this."
La Liga president Javier Tebas also became involved in the matter.
LALIGA deeply regrets the offense caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments. These comments were expressed as a personal opinion and do not reflect LALIGA’s position. As part of our institutional responsibility, we apologize on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs
Javier Tebas said: "I want to personally apologize to Chinese fans for the offense caused. I have deep respect for China, its institutions, and its people, and I value the trust with which they have supported our football for so many years. As president of LALIGA, I take responsibility for working with our clubs and players to strengthen awareness and respect for different cultures. We want to develop these relations through concrete actions and will take specific measures to prevent similar situations from recurring in the future. This commitment will be embodied in an awareness and communication protocol that we will develop jointly with the clubs and players. Its implementation will complement the work we are already carrying out together with our partners and institutional counterparts in China to address this situation."
Why China Took Offense
In May 2018, China’s special "Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs" came into force. It prohibits defaming, insulting, or denying the deeds and achievements of national heroes and revolutionary leaders, foremost among them Mao Zedong.
Under the law, it is prohibited to refute the official version of the history of the revolution, while internet platforms and media outlets are required to immediately remove any such content and report violators to the police.

KYIV, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 million) to water crossings over the River Dnipro which bisects the city, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Tuesday, after a spate of Russian attacks on bridges.
Russia has disrupted transport for Kyiv residents by hitting bridges this month, part of a significant step up in drone and missile strikes on logistics in and around the Ukrainian capital in recent months.
The Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge, one of Kyiv’s six main bridges, was hit overnight by four Iskander ballistic missiles, a Ukrainian military source told Reuters, an attack decried by President Volodymyr Zelenskiy as a “serious escalation”.
Disruptions to bridge traffic could become a critical issue for Kyiv residents who live and work on opposite sides of the wide river and have to commute across daily.
One of the city’s metro lines runs over Pivdennyi bridge that also carries road traffic. Russia has targeted other bridges in the city with drones.
Klitschko said on Telegram that the city’s defence council had discussed a “project to build combined water crossings over the River Dnipro and the access roads leading to them.”
He did not give further details.
Water crossings come in various forms, including pontoons, fords and other low-lying structures that enable people and vehicles to cross.
Such structures have not been used in Kyiv since Russia’s February 2022 invasion.

Pope’s cancer is a ‘gamechanger’ for papacy, Vatican foreign minister says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

02:36:22 KST

By Joshua McElwee
ROME, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis and surgery has affected how Catholics view his health and papacy, the Vatican’s foreign minister said on Tuesday, an unusually frank assessment by one of the Church’s most senior officials.
“It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery earlier this month. His doctors have said the cancer was localized and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.
Gallagher said that given Leo’s relatively young age for a pope and his physical fitness, some Catholics had thought he was a “Superman” pope.
The illness revealed that Leo “is a poor mortal like the rest of us,” said the archbishop.
“I think that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” said Gallagher, a Briton who has served in his Vatican role since 2014.
POPE EXCITED ABOUT LATIN AMERICA TRIP
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in an operation on October 13.
The pope has been gradually resuming his schedule since returning to the Vatican on October 18 and has appeared energetic at public events, speaking in a firm, clear voice.
The Vatican confirmed on Monday he would go forward with a three-country, November 6-17 visit across South America, one of the most intense foreign tours arranged for a pope in decades.
“All of the medical advice is very positive … so he feels he can go,” Gallagher said in response to a question about why the pope is travelling only 24 days after his surgery.
“I think he’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go on it,” said the archbishop. “It was obviously quite advanced in the planning.”
UKRAINE CEASEFIRE, PAPAL VISIT TO US
Separately, Gallagher also addressed the recent ceasefire agreed by Russia and Ukraine to allow aid into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
He said that while Leo had recently spoken with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, he did not believe the Vatican was involved in arranging the ceasefire.
“I don’t think we were,” said Gallagher.
He also spoke about the Vatican’s ongoing agreement with China on the appointment of Catholic bishops in the communist state, and acknowledged “imperfections” with the accord.
The deal, first signed in 2018, gives Chinese officials some input into whom Leo appoints as bishops in the country.
“It’s not easy, the dialogue is not easy. The imperfections of the agreement are evident, but there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue … and that is what will continue to happen,” said Gallagher.
The archbishop also said he expects Leo, the first US-born pope, to visit the United States “in the not too distant future.” But he said the visit might not occur in 2027, depending on the pope’s commitments.

LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - British comedian and actor Russell Brand told police that he had never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity despite encounters in countless locations and scenarios, a London court was told on Tuesday.
Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters and the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial at London’s Southwark Crown Court over accusations of sexual offences against six women between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old has denied all the allegations.
BRAND CLEARED OF ONE COUNT, NEW CHARGE BROUGHT
He is accused of three counts of rape and three of sexual assault and, on Tuesday, the judge instructed the jury to return a verdict of not guilty over an allegation of indecent assault. However, he will now face a new charge of attempted indecent assault over that alleged incident.
The jury had previously been told how all the women came forward to detectives after a documentary was broadcast in 2023 along with a number of newspaper articles about him.
The prosecution has set out its case that Brand was a ruthless predator and the former comedian is expected to set out his defence on Wednesday.
But on Tuesday the court was told for the first time of his responses to the allegations.
Prosecutors read prepared statements Brand gave to police during four interviews held between September 2023 and July 2025 following those allegations.
In these statements, he said that “defamatory and fictitious” documentary and newspaper reports which contained “false, anonymised allegations” against him had led to the media and police inviting other allegations against him.
This, he said, had paved the way for “further incidents to be reinvented or reimagined”.
“I have never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity,” his statement said.
He said he had repeatedly stated that he had been very promiscuous in the past, behaviour he now denounced. He said he had had sex in toilet cubicles at parties, and had engaged in sexual encounters in “countless locations and scenarios often with people I have just met”.
“Those encounters were always consensual,” he said.
The jury has heard accusations that Brand raped a woman after meeting her at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in 1999, forced a woman to give him oral sex in toilets at a London bar in 2004, and had molested another woman at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.
He is also accused of trying to pull a woman into the male toilets at MTV Europe, in London, where she was working in 2001, and that in 2009 he anally raped a woman who had agreed to consensual sex at his home.
The final allegation is that he assaulted a woman who was working at the Channel 4 TV station where they were involved in a recording project. She says she was forced into giving him a massage during which he put his head between her legs.

Rights monitors raise concerns over senior UAE diplomat bid for next UN boss

By Antoni Slodkowski
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Human rights monitors criticized senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s candidacy to be the next UN chief on Tuesday, citing her role in championing the country’s foreign policy and denying the UAE’s role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan.
Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week. Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Despite months of campaigning by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful nations.
Sudan’s war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
“She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts — that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General,” Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organized by online campaigns group Avaaz.
Last month, a UN fact-finding mission said foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks — including individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, among others — are helping sustain Sudan’s conflict.
“This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General,” Roth told the webinar titled “Call To Stop UAE Minister’s Bid for UN Top Job Amid Sudan Genocide”.
The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre, on their concerns about Nusseibeh’s candidacy and its implications for the UN’s commitment to protect civilians, according to the organizers.
“Electing (the UAE’s) senior diplomat as Secretary-General would hand leadership of (United Nations) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable,” said Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV.
Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Tuesday, Nusseibeh said: “If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history.”
“The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice,” she added.
Nusseibeh told the media at the UN after the dialogue that, as a secretary-general, she would work to be a “risk-taker” and “prime mover in mediation efforts.”
She has also separately said she would “put the UN’s full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people.”
Nusseibeh served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade. She previously led the UAE’s successful campaign for election to the Security Council as a non-permanent member in 2022-23. She is widely known by diplomats working in New York, who say she is a competent manager, skilled negotiator and clear communicator.
An informal council poll this month had placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body’s declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski; Editing by Aurora Ellis and Lincoln Feast.)

Brazil wonders: Where on earth is Flavio Bolsonaro?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:36:00 CET
02:36:00 KST

By Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery and Luciana Magalhaes
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election, three sources said, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Argentina’s migration department said on Wednesday that Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered the country’s Misiones province on Tuesday night through a road crossing, with valid travel documents, before boarding a private plane bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador at 11:30 pm local time (0230 GMT).
Argentina cited the flight plan, for the plane operated by air charter company Baires Fly, as the source for the aircraft’s destination. The Ecuadorian foreign ministry did not respond to an emailed request for comment outside regular hours.
The current location of Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear.
Speaking to reporters late on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump had said that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
“The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States,” a senior State Department official said.
BRAZIL-US RIFT GROWS
Bolsonaro’s departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday’s election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the United States.
“Well, I would approve. I think they’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It’s gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market”, Trump said.
“I think it’s so terrible to see it. I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well. The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn’t involved. That’s Brazil. It’s a different country”, he said.
Trump has previously alleged Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. The elder Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
On Monday, Trump had said the Brazilian vote “looked like another rigged election.”
Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence.
Bolsonaro had been favored to win Sunday’s presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result.
ORDERED TO HAND OVER PASSPORTS
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports, which were canceled after the deadline lapsed, two sources said. In a court ruling seen by Reuters, the Supreme Court cited the risk of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and his “significant financial resources” in ordering his passports seized.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, had said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
“I have never thought about leaving the country,” he said. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
His departure appeared to have caught his campaign manager off guard.
“We are surprised by the news because, just yesterday, we discussed the need for Flavio — given the 60 million votes he received — to take on this role as leader of the opposition,” Senator Rogerio Marinho told reporters.
FOLLOWING FATHER’S PATH
Although Bolsonaro has yet to officially concede defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula’s victory.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro’s younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
“If my brother does not win, I’m in favor that he would leave the country,” he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.
(Reporting by Ricardo Brito and Luciana Magalhaes; Additional reporting by Lucinda Elliot, Brendan O’Boyle, Oliver Griffin, Simon Lewis, Chandni Shah and Shivani Tanna in Bengaluru; Editing by Gabriel Stargardter, Aurora Ellis and Raju Gopalakrishnan)

Canada introduces bill to allow people to be euthanized after they lose capacity to decide
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:35:55 CET
02:35:55 KST

By Maria Cheng
OTTAWA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Canadian government will introduce a new bill on Tuesday to allow people to request being euthanized at a later date when they have lost the mental capacity to make that decision, in a potential further expansion of one of the world’s most liberal assisted dying programs.
• Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the new legislation will allow adults to consent to being euthanized in advance “so their wishes could be respected if they are diagnosed with an incurable illness that could take away the ability to make this decision.”
• Fraser said the government would work with provinces and territories on implementation, with “rigorous safeguards to protect people and ensure the decision remains voluntary and free from external pressure.”
• Making an advance request will not mean euthanasia is automatically provided later, the government said. New safeguards will be introduced and people will have to be experiencing “intolerable suffering” at the time when they are killed.
• Canada first legalized euthanasia in 2016 for people who were terminally ill and broadened its law in 2021 to allow people with incurable but not terminal conditions to seek death.
• If the bill passes, provinces and territories will still have to decide whether to make advance requests available in their jurisdictions; it is already allowed in Quebec.
• Advance requests for euthanasia are also legal in countries including the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain.
• Krista Carr, CEO of Inclusion Canada, a disability rights charity, has raised concerns about advance requests for euthanasia, saying that a person consenting to their death “is the most basic protection a person has” and that “Parliament should not take it away.”

JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners made a last-ditch push on Tuesday to get their supporters to the polls, warning of surging Arab voter turnout, a tactic Arab politicians denounced as racist and inflammatory.

Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said strong turnout among Israel’s Arab minority would “pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality”.

NETANYAHU HAS REPEATEDLY DESCRIBED ARAB VOTERS AS A THREAT
Netanyahu’s warnings echoed previous election campaigns in which he sought to mobilise right-wing supporters by portraying strong Arab participation as a threat, drawing accusations of racism from opponents.
The election is the first since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack and the subsequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Four years of Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition have coincided with a surge in violent crimes in Israel’s Arab communities, including many murders linked to organised crime.
Polls suggest Netanyahu’s coalition is on course to lose its parliamentary majority, although opposition parties may also struggle to secure the 61 seats needed to form a majority government.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has overseen a policy of destroying homes of Arabs that were built illegally, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has promoted “Judaizing” areas in northern and southern Israel where many Arabs live. Both ministers have been sanctioned by Western countries over accusations they incited violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
In a statement, Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout as “crazy”, urging supporters to vote for his Jewish Power party if they wanted the country to be Jewish and Zionist.
Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party said the finance minister had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what it described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters.
(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell, additional reporting by Steven Scheer & Lina Obeid; Editing by Ros Russell)

Cologne has drawn the most online pledges, with more than 12,000, followed by Frankfurt with just under 11,000, Hamburg and Berlin with more than 8,000 each, and Munich with nearly 7,000, the organisers reported.

In major cities, water cannons and armoured vehicles are expected to be on standby, with several hundred officers deployed, it reported.
Demonstrations are to be monitored from the air by helicopters and, if needed, police drones. Plans also include intercepting violence-prone extremist groups at train stations and separating them from travel groups, according to the report.

Zookeeper dies after she was attacked in leopard enclosure, Dutch safari park says
A keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park announced on Tuesday.
The woman was attacked while caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility at the Beekse Bergen park in the south of the Netherlands.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure as there are no cameras. The animals were inside due to bad weather and staff are usually kept away from the leopards.
She sustained serious injuries to her head and neck, according to local media. She underwent emergency surgery but died on Tuesday, the zoo said in a statement.
"The keeper started at the Beekse Bergen Safari Park at the age of 17 and worked here, with only a few short interruptions, for nearly 40 years," the park said in a statement on social media. "Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends, and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss."
An independent investigation will be launched to establish the circumstances of the incident, the zoo added.
The leopards were behaving naturally, a park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet.
"They are, and remain, predators," Brabant said.
According to the zoo, the leopard is "a solitary predatory cat found in Africa and Asia" and primarily hunts animals such as deer, monkeys and antelope at night.
Big cats have killed caretakers at other parks around the world in recent years.
Last year, a zookeeper was killed in a lion attack after he stepped out his vehicle at a safari park in Thailand.
In October 2024, a group of lions mauled a zookeeper to death in Crimea after a door inside their enclosure was left unlocked.
In 2020, a 55-year-old keeper at Zurich's zoo was killed by one of the park's Siberian tigers.
In 2018, a lion escaped its enclosure and killed a recent college graduate at a North Carolina conservatory during a routine cleaning.
A Malayan tiger killed a zookeeper at Florida's Palm Beach Zoo in April 2016 after a door that was supposed to be locked was left open and she was attacked.

Shuford had previously served as Texas’s chief state epidemiologist and an infectious disease medical officer, as well as being an infectious disease physician in private practice.
Citing a desire to spend time with her family, Shuford confirmed her departure to the Washington Post late on Monday. Sources told the Post that she had clashed with the administration over its attempts to overhaul the U.S.’s vaccine guidance and that this reportedly factored into her leaving.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A CDC spokesperson confirmed to Scientific American that Shuford's last day would be Nov. 12.

The agency has come under fire from infectious disease experts for its responses to a series of ongoing measles outbreaks, including for seemingly disputing several recorded deaths from the disease in Pennsylvania. And for the first time in years, the agency has not held a flu vaccine awareness campaign ahead of flu season, leaving independent organizations to issue their own guidance. Public confidence in the CDC, meanwhile, has plummeted, with a recent survey showing only half the country trusts health recommendations from the agency.
The departure is a sign of continuing dysfunction at the CDC, said Yolanda Jacobs, president of American Federation of Government Employees Local 2883, which represents many CDC workers, in a statement.
"When the agency’s own leadership can’t build a lasting, cohesive team, imagine the damaging effects this has on the employees they’re charged with leading," she said. “The theatrics happening in and around CDC are continuing to cause ripple effects on the health and wellbeing of CDC employees and, ultimately, it is the public that will pay the price.”

Germany’s Special Operations Forces Are Reorienting for War with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:31:01 UTC
02:31:01 KST

The Bundeswehr’s Special Operations Forces Command (KSK) is reorienting its training toward a potential war with Russia and preparing its units for prolonged operations on NATO’s eastern flank.
KSK Commander Brigadier General Andreas Kühne told the German newspaper BILD about this.
According to him, typical special forces operations were previously planned to last about three days, after which the unit would return to base to rest and replenish supplies.
In the event of a war with Russia, the command assesses that this format would be unsuitable.
“We are very specifically focused on the enemy—Russia,” Kühne stated.
He noted that units will have to remain in the field for much longer periods without the ability to quickly return to a secure base.
“Perhaps initially with no end date at all,” the KSK commander noted.
In this regard, special forces are practicing operations against an adversary equipped with armored vehicles, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare systems.
Special attention is being paid to operating in the low temperatures characteristic of a potential theater of operations on NATO’s eastern flank.
According to Kühne, if a real threat emerges, KSK units must begin carrying out their missions before the main ground forces are deployed.
He cited the Bundeswehr’s 45th Tank Brigade, deployed in Lithuania, as an example.
“When the 45th Tank Brigade in Lithuania actually starts its engines in a real-world scenario, we want our work to already be done,” the KSK commander explained.
According to him, upon receiving an order, the unit can depart Stuttgart by air within four hours, carrying the necessary equipment to carry out the mission.
This includes, in particular, reconnaissance deep within enemy territory, special operations, and other tasks designed to create conditions for the main forces to operate.
Küne also said the Russian military leadership must know the capabilities of German special forces.
During exercises in the Baltic states, Germany has already demonstrated its special forces’ capabilities.
The KSK commander called this a kind of “price” for potential aggression, intended to make an attack on NATO countries too costly for Russia.
The KSK’s reorientation comes amid broader changes in the Bundeswehr’s preparations to defend Germany and NATO’s eastern flank.
The German military regularly conducts exercises involving force deployment, the protection of critical infrastructure, the defense of allied nations, and operations against a technologically advanced adversary.
Heimatschutz reservists also participate in these scenarios; in the event of war, they are tasked with protecting key military and civilian facilities, troop movement routes, logistics hubs, and rear-area infrastructure.
Special attention is paid to making training conditions as close as possible to those of an actual battlefield.
During the Taurus 2024 series of exercises, specialized paratroopers from the 2nd Company of Fallschirmjägerregiment 31 practiced trench warfare, countering armored vehicles, airborne assault operations, and searching for enemy forces in their own rear.
One element of the exercises involved engaging a real, demilitarized Soviet-designed BMP-1 used as a moving armored target.
According to the scenario, a reconnaissance drone first detected the vehicle, after which groups of paratroopers advanced to positions to engage the armored vehicle with anti-tank weapons.
To ensure the vehicle’s safe reuse during training, an additional steel plate was installed on its rear.
During other phases of Taurus 2024, paratroopers were deployed by NH90 and CH-53 helicopters; they practiced urban combat and operations against an enemy that had penetrated the rear and could attack bridges, warehouses, airfields, and railway junctions.
Such exercises demonstrate the Bundeswehr’s shift from scenarios involving short-term expeditionary operations to preparing for a protracted, high-intensity conflict in Europe.
Currently, approximately 1,500 military personnel and civilian employees serve in the Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK).
Of these, about one-third belong directly to the special operations units, while the rest provide command, logistics, and other functions.
According to Kühne, the KSK’s staffing level is approximately 70–80%.
The selection process remains rigorous—only slightly more than 15% of candidates successfully pass it.
The command expects that an increase in the Bundeswehr’s overall strength will allow for an expanded pool of candidates for selection into the special forces unit.
Training at the KSK center in Calvi includes marksmanship drills, close-quarters combat, physical training, swimming, martial arts, and operations in harsh climatic conditions.
According to BILD, the units use up to 500,000 rounds of ammunition during the course of a year of training.
The KSK was established in 1996 to carry out the most complex special operations, including hostage rescues, countering terrorist groups, evacuating people from crisis regions, and conducting reconnaissance behind enemy lines.
In particular, the unit has carried out combat missions in Afghanistan against the Taliban.

====================================================================================================

Paolo Cesarini, Chair of EDMO Executive Board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

The European Digital Media Observatory (EDMO) is an independent, multidisciplinary observatory that serves as the EU’s largest network to combat online disinformation. Operating through a central hub and 15 national and transnational hubs across Europe, including regional centers like F.A.C.T. for Ukraine and Moldova, EDMO brings together independent actors, researchers and practitioners, as well as media organizations, with its core mission being to detect and analyze disinformation campaigns, support independent fact-checking, promote media literacy, and assist public authorities in evaluating how online platforms mitigate risks to the information ecosystem.
Ukrinform sat down with Paolo Cesarini, Chair of the Executive Board of EDMO, to reflect on the current challenges Europe is facing in terms of information manipulation, dwell into cognitive warfare nuances, and discuss the instruments and platforms that are being used to make sure both the societies and policymakers have in hand the solutions to address the ever-growing problem of malign influence on people’s minds, mindsets, and, ultimately, electoral processes and decision making.
EUROPEAN INSTITUTIONS AND INDEPENDENT FACT-CHECKERS MUST ACTIVELY EXCHANGE INFORMATION
- How does EDMO envisage its operational role within the European Commission's proposed democracy shield, particularly in bridging the gap between independent academic fact-checking and rapid policy responses by EU bodies?
- Edmo is very proud of being and remaining a network of independent factchecking organizations, academic bodies, and media-literacy practitioners. Of course, we are collaborating, and we are eager to collaborate even more in the future with the European institutions and also with member states’ authorities. And we envisage this role as a two-way exchange of information, possibly in real time, to improve overall abilities to detect hybrid threats, disinformation operations, while at the same time remain completely independent regarding the editorial treatments of disinformation from our side.
I think that approach is beneficial for both the partner and the civil society sides of this equation. Public authorities would not be in a good position if they were left alone controlling the information space. On the other side, the civil society organizations still have rather limited means for developing a thorough media and social media monitoring, which of course influence its ability to operate as a network that raise situation awareness towards the larger public.
So the two sides of the question are equally important. Each of the two sides needs to respect the prerogatives of the actors that are involved in this common cause, including situational awareness. And I would say from the side of EDMO, as an organization that is multidisciplinary and multifaceted in a way, because we have not only factcheckers and academic researchers but also people involved on the ground in educational programs, is that the real bridge that needs to be crossed now it is to translate situational awareness into actual society resilience. The question to address is how to speak to people, how to make people more aware of the risks that occur online, and what are the most prominent threats that emerge from time to time.
- With multiple actors involved in monitoring informational threats, how can Europe create a unified data-sharing framework without compromising academic independence and the autonomy of fact-checkers?
When I said before that facilitating a two-way exchange of information is an important factor that can contribute to a better awareness, we know very well that there are limits as to what public authorities can actually share. And there is also a need for the factchecking and academic side to carry out independent verifications around the hints and leads that may be shared within the hub of European resilience.
- It’s like an army unit that is on a mission without seeing the full battlefield picture.
- Ideally, it would be great to see the whole “battlefield picture” but here we are facing a situation where nobody is actually able to fully grasp the forces that undermine the integrity of the information space. I don't think that the intelligence agencies have the full picture either, because what you need to have is also a direct touch with the editorial agenda of the mainstream media and how they tell the story to their audiences.
And there is a disconnect between a purely security-driven approach in guaranteeing information integrity, and the one that looks more at the narratives and how they influence the public discourse.
THERE ARE THREE LEVELS IN THE METHODOLOGY FOR ASSESSING COGNITIVE INFLUENCE
- How is EDMO updating its analytical methodologies to measure and counter the deeper psychological impacts of modern cognitive warfare?
- We have, first of all, a first layer, an observation standpoint that looks at disinformation in individual stories. What is this disinformation? We intercept what is AI generated, what is a fake, what is a blatant misrepresentation of facts… That is the classic methodology that factcheckers apply. They look for the so-called spikes. These spikes are normally very much linked to what topics media cover. They tend to piggyback on audience attention that is created by the media.
Then there is another layer, the narratives. To understand the narratives, you need to compound different false stories into broader pictures. For instance, looking at Ukraine, you may extract the main recurring themes that depict Ukraine, from the Russian perspective, as a corrupt, post-Nazi state, that portray Zelensky as the one embezzling money for his own benefit. All these stories concur into creating a general sentiment that we call narrative.
The third layer is about connecting the narratives to the targets, to the objectives, and to the actors. To detect the actors, in EDMO we are combining factchecking capabilities with OSINT. We are combining the narrative analysis with the structural analysis of the disinformation distribution dynamics.
Sometimes it’s a result of informal collaboration with national agencies. Think about Russia’s Pravda network, which has been initially been identified by a public open source intelligence agency in France as Portal Combat network of outlets coordinated by the Kremlin. And then EDMO and some other organizations have extended that investigation to other countries and languages beyond France, and found out that the same network, now called Pravda, of false media, cloned accounts, were operating in fact in 15 languages in different countries.
- How has the strategy of disinformation operations changed lately?
- Classic disinformation operations, like classic influence operations, had been known to be designed to persuade people. More and more, especially after AI took a huge role in the production and distribution of information online, you see that the strategy is no longer persuasion or motivation. Now it is cognitive erosion.
- Confusing the public?
- Yes, it is about confusion. It is about leading people not to believe in anything, which leads to disengagement, cynicism, and basically defiance of any form of state authority or state organization. That is the main risk that the EU, Europe as a whole is facing today. It is a profound gap between the role of the European institutions and people’s perceptions that little by little are shaping the public opinion in a way that it is not rational, but simply the result of the drip-dropping of narratives that erode the capacity of people to think critically about what is going on.
The problem is that, while we do have a methodology to better understand disinformation campaigns, applying them to individual situations in individual member states is very costly. There’s lack of resources so it’s if we slam our heads against the closed door.
MAJOR SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS WILL NOT COOPERATE IF THEIR PROFITS ARE AT STAKE
- Is the EU doing enough to address the underperformance of very large online platforms in fixing the issue of disinformation spread and radicalization of users?
- I spent a lot of time in the relevant enforcement agency within the European Commission, and I know how heavy any investigation is when you're trying to attack big companies.
But much depends also on the political will and the way you evaluate tahe evidence that you have at your disposal in order to open and conclude an investigation, bring the investigation to fruition, take a decision, and levy a fine.
As long as you do not touch these platforms’ business model, they play along. But if the mitigation implies a profound reconsideration of the architecture of their own algorithms and the re-equilibration of the content that is prioritized in social media feeds, they won’t cooperate. Because this is about their profits.
RUSSIANS ARE TRYING TO TURN THE FIGHT AGAINST FACT-CHECKING ON ITS HEAD
- What lessons can European institutions learn from the Ukrainian information battlefield?
- The war in Ukraine has been quite a classroom for seeing how AI can be weaponized. Take the latest examples. During these months we have been seeing AI-generated images of civilians being forced onto trains to go to combat on the frontlines.
So in that sense, Ukraine is offering a range of examples of how both new technologies and also new techniques in terms of coordinated networks can operate on real life battlefields and how hybrid threats are implemented in support of kinetic operations.
And then you can see another phenomenon, that the same techniques like LLM grooming, for instance, or AI slops, are increasingly used domestically. The line is being blurred between FIMI and DIMI, which is domestic manipulation. If you have a foreign state that tries to interfere with elections, this is pretty clearly an attack on the integrity of the democratic process. But let's not forget that the same techniques are used by internal actors... as you are now seeing regarding the riots that have been inflamed across Europe these days.
And then, say, Russian actors use social networks like TikTok, X, or Telegram to radicalize them.
- How effectively do you think Russia's national news agency TASS and other major networks are used to push Kremlin-backed narratives, and also what is your opinion on the clone of the international fact-checking network Russia has come up with?
The problem with Russian media is their circumvention of the sanctions imposed by the EU – on outlets like Russia Today, Sputnik, and so on. That circumvention is in the open. They create hundreds of websites that reproduce exactly the same content. The other element is, indeed, their mimicking of the counter-disinformation activities. They put things upside down, basically, shifting the roles. They are claiming that propaganda comes from fact-checking in Western countries and saying that, because there is a censorship machinery in the West, Russia reacts by creating their own fact-checking network. It is like in the Commedia dell'arte, where the ambiguity was consistent in switching the roles between characters and thus creating for a moment the confusion about who does what, and who is what.
- When it comes to media literacy and preparing the public to withstand these sophisticated information campaigns, what are the most effective avenues EDMO is exploring, and where are the biggest hurdles?
- That is the most difficult area. There’s very little progress in member states in terms of planting media literacy in schools. You may also reach people in the out-of-school environment, but it is not easy. Gamification is one approach. You reach people online where they, through games, could develop critical thinking or critical interpretation of the information that they receive online.
This is experimented at the level of the hubs, because you need to operate close to the citizens, you need to understand your environment through proximity. But it is very resource-intensive, and still the fragmentation of the civil society organizations that deal with these activities still represents an enormous cost and an enormous barrier.
Ievgen Matiushenko, Brussels
Photos provided by the author

The Finnish president’s office said the call was meant “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin” ahead of meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi. It was Putin’s first contact with European leaders supporting Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.
The Kremlin confirmed the call, saying Putin “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine and reminded participants of the “root causes of the conflict.” Putin also pointed to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting,” the Kremlin’s press service said.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Stubb and Støre briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelensky said. He added that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between negotiating teams from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia.
Stubb’s office said the call “was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine.” The Norwegian capital hosted talks that day between Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky, with Støre and Stubb also taking part. Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg to meet with Putin before returning to Oslo and flying home to the United States.
Those trips produced an agreement on a trilateral meeting between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia, to be held in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will take place after November 4, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said. The day before, on November 3, the United States will hold midterm elections in which Republicans could lose their congressional majority.
Announcing the timing, Ushakov said the peace talks would also have to involve “all of Europe.” Europe has long sought a negotiator to represent the European Union’s interests in talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Stubb has repeatedly been named as a candidate for the role, having built a good relationship with Trump, including on the golf course, and emerged as one of Trump’s main points of contact with European leaders. The Telegraph has also named Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and Czech President Petr Pavel among the candidates.
After Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, Frederiksen criticized the initiative, saying she was “skeptical” and that the talks had not been coordinated with other European leaders. She added that she sees no sign that Russia wants peace with Europe, either in the hybrid war that continues every day or in Ukraine.
The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily says contacts between European leaders and the Kremlin amount to “a significant shift in position.” European leaders had “mostly preferred not to talk to Putin at all” since the war began.
However, a source close to the Kremlin said that “events are moving toward escalation, including an intensification of hybrid warfare with Europe.” According to the source, Putin is convinced NATO is waging a hybrid war against Russia and blames Ukraine’s European allies for “comprehensive assistance” in attacks on Russia, including helping identify targets and guide strikes.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of capturing all of the Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary, the source added.

Ukraine Moves Closer to Its Own Satellite Network as Test Craft Reaches Orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:25:51 UTC
02:25:51 KST

Ukrainian communications company Himera and Danish satellite manufacturer GomSpace have sent Obria nano, a test satellite, into orbit as the first step toward an independent Ukrainian communications network.
Himera told Ukrainska Pravda on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that the satellite reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1, and is reportedly already operating.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The technical trials should provide the practical experience needed for the project’s further development into Ukrainian national infrastructure,” Himera said.
While the launch relied on a SpaceX rocket, the satellite itself will be controlled by a Ukrainian operator and will serve Ukraine’s strategic security needs. The project comes as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on SpaceX’s Starshield service amid recent disruptions and diplomatic tensions with Washington.
Reducing reliance on foreign technology
Ukraine’s dependence on foreign-made technology creates strategic risks, especially during wartime, Himera argued. Building capabilities domestically, the company said, would widen the country’s communication options and strengthen its security.
In the long term, the company plans to deploy a satellite constellation covering all of Ukraine’s territory.
The network would also complement existing European satellite systems and form the basis of a sovereign Ukrainian communications system.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
Moving production of satellites and ground terminals to Ukraine is Himera’s next priority, as this could help Kyiv build its own expertise in satellite communications, while gradually expanding domestic manufacturing.
Ukraine also signed seven agreements with Finland on Oct. 22, including deals to expand Kyiv’s use of Finnish satellite capabilities through Nokia and ICEYE.
“We agreed that we will make greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier. “This is important for our defense and for Ukraine’s resilience.”
Radios field-tested by military intelligence
A unit of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) had tested Himera’s tactical radios – HIMERA G1 PRO radios and HIMERA B1 repeater – in real combat conditions, the company said in a statement on Oct. 15.
HUR testers reportedly praised the devices’ durable casing, simple setup, compact repeater and a long battery life.
According to Himera, the radios ran for up to four days on a single charge, even in low temperatures and high humidity.
However, the main improvement users requested was much better sound quality for the G1 PRO. At the time, Himera said it had already sent some users a beta version and reported collecting their feedback for the next update.
Russia’s own domestic Starlink: Rassvet
Meanwhile, Russia is working on its own, domestic alternative to Starlink.
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020 told Interfax-Ukraine that Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time.
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites, arguing that the network could later be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against Europe.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
According to Pavlenko, Russia is also moving its jet drone factories underground, which could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones.

In Kyiv, the increase in taxi prices during alerts will be limited — Koretskyi
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:24:40 EET
02:24:40 KST

In Kyiv, the increase in taxi prices during alerts will be limited — Koretskyi
Kyiv • UNN
Bolt, Uklon, Uber, and OPTI have limited fare increases in Kyiv to 75% during alerts and transport stoppages. The limit will remain in effect for at least two hours after the all-clear.
Ukraine’s Ministries of Economy and Infrastructure signed a memorandum with the digital platforms Bolt, Uklon, Uber and OPTI to prevent a critical rise in transportation prices in Kyiv during an air raid alert or a suspension of public transportation services. This was reported by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, according to UNN.
Details
In particular, in the event of the metro or other force majeure circumstances related to logistics in the capital. For example, as happened after today’s attack on the Pivdennyi Bridge.
According to Koretskyi, the memorandum with the operators provides for setting a ceiling on how high prices may rise under such circumstances. This is a maximum of 75% above the base fare.
That is, if the base fare under normal conditions—without air raid alerts, traffic jams, and so on—from point A to point B is, say, 200 hryvnias, the maximum charge will be 350 hryvnias. If it is 300 hryvnias, the maximum will be 525 hryvnias. Passengers will retain the ability to regulate the price themselves, but upper limits will also be established. This price restriction will remain in effect for at least two hours after the all-clear for a red-level alert or until normal public transportation services and bridge traffic are restored. It is often precisely then that demand for rides is highest, while people need to get home
We would like to remind you
At the beginning of the new workweek, diesel and autogas prices surged. The average price of diesel fuel at Ukrainian filling stations currently stands at 103.40 hryvnias per liter, A-95 gasoline at 90.93 hryvnias, and autogas at 54.45 hryvnias.

US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:13 UTC
02:22:13 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries.
The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.
Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.
Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8
— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026
The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”.
His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.
Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.

Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland.
The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre.
“The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.”
Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine.
The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles.
In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”.
Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026
Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted.
After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles.
Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026
The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states.
Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers.
Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles.

Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea.
Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision.

Feature: Tanzania's Zanzibar seaweed farmers pin hopes on China's import expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:17:51 CST
02:17:51 KST

Women sort harvested seaweed in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- After more than two decades of growing seaweed off Tanzania's Zanzibar, Bahati Issa Suleiman is looking to China for better prices and new opportunities for her family.
The 51-year-old mother of eight hopes the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), which opens in Shanghai on Nov. 5, will help Zanzibar's seaweed reach more Chinese buyers and gain wider recognition in the international market.
For Suleiman, seaweed farming has long been a vital source of income, helping her family cover daily expenses and pay school fees. She has also seen fellow farmers use their earnings to buy land and build houses.
"When our seaweed reaches China, we will announce ourselves to the world," Suleiman said, hoping greater market exposure would encourage more people to return to seaweed farming and strengthen household incomes.
Her aspirations reflect Zanzibar's broader efforts to turn its marine resources into a stronger driver of economic growth by moving beyond raw-material exports toward higher-value products.
Zahor Kassim El-Kharousy, deputy principal secretary in Zanzibar's Ministry of Blue Economy and Fisheries, said the CIIE and similar international exhibitions offer an opportunity to connect local producers with buyers and investors, addressing a major challenge facing the seaweed industry.
"Currently, 99 percent of the seaweed that we export outside the country is raw," he said, describing the transition to value-added products as a key government priority.
El-Kharousy said stronger links between producers, processors and markets could encourage investment in processing facilities, expand the range of seaweed-based products and enable Zanzibar to capture a greater share of the value generated along the supply chain.
For farmers, this could translate into more reliable markets and better prices. For local businesses, it could create opportunities in processing, packaging, transportation and export logistics, while generating employment, particularly for women, who dominate seaweed cultivation in Zanzibar.
China is already an important destination for Zanzibar's marine products, including seaweed and sea cucumber, El-Kharousy said.
He added that the ministry was also promoting the production of value-added sea cucumber products to expand the sector's contribution to the blue economy.
The size of the Chinese market offers opportunities for Zanzibar to expand exports, but the ministry official emphasized that businesses must understand consumer preferences and meet prospective buyers' requirements.
Companies participating in the Shanghai expo should therefore use the platform not only to showcase their products but also to establish commercial partnerships and identify opportunities to develop products suited to Chinese market demand, he said.
For Zanzibar, the potential benefits extend beyond immediate export orders. Business contacts made at the expo could attract investment, facilitate technology transfer and help local enterprises improve product quality, processing capacity and access to international supply chains.
China's decision to remove tariffs on eligible imports from Tanzania could provide additional opportunities for exporters, although the benefits will depend on the applicable product coverage and compliance with Chinese import requirements.
Suleiman, meanwhile, said farmers need support to improve production and post-harvest handling. In her village, some seaweed is dried directly on the ground, while cultivation in shallow waters near the shore can damage crops.
She hopes stronger international interest will encourage improvements in farming methods and post-harvest practices, helping farmers supply more consistent, higher-quality products.
Ultimately, she believed, expanding the Chinese market could motivate farmers who have abandoned the activity to resume cultivation, increasing production and strengthening the industry's economic contribution.
"Once our seaweed arrives in China and gets promoted, I believe the price will increase," she said. ■
Zahor Kassim El-Kharousy, deputy principal secretary in Zanzibar's Ministry of Blue Economy and Fisheries, speaks during an interview in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
Bahati Issa Suleiman, a seaweed farmer, displays harvested seaweed in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania's northeastern Arusha Region has stepped up measures to prevent the spread of Ebola, training more than 100 health workers, designating an isolation and treatment facility, and intensifying health screening at the Namanga border post following an outbreak in neighboring Kenya, an official said Tuesday.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are nine confirmed cases and two deaths in Kenya, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
Arusha Regional Administrative Secretary Toba Nguvila said the measures aim to strengthen early detection and prompt management of suspected infections at the busy crossing linking Tanzania and Kenya.
Nguvila outlined the preparations after inspecting screening procedures and staff readiness at the Namanga One-Stop Border Post in Longido District.
He said more than 100 health workers from all seven district councils in the region had received training on Ebola preparedness and response, adding that a facility had been designated to isolate and treat suspected patients.
Nguvila urged border officials to screen every traveler, including conducting preliminary health assessments and temperature checks, and refer suspected cases for further testing.
He warned that infected travelers entering Tanzania could expose others while traveling to Arusha and other destinations, calling for continued vigilance and strict implementation of preventive measures.
The Ministry of Health has also strengthened screening at the country's points of entry, including health declarations, temperature checks and 21-day monitoring of travelers considered at high risk. ■

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

VATICAN CITY - Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis and surgery has affected how Catholics view his health and papacy, the Vatican’s foreign minister said on Oct 27, an unusually frank assessment by one of the Church’s most senior officials.
“It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery on Oct 13.
His doctors have said the cancer was localised and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.
Gallagher said that given Leo’s relatively young age for a pope and his physical fitness, some Catholics had thought he was a “Superman” pope.
The illness revealed that Leo “is a poor mortal like the rest of us,” said the archbishop.
“I think that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” said Gallagher, a Briton who has served in his Vatican role since 2014.
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in an operation on Oct 13.
The pope has been gradually resuming his schedule since returning to the Vatican on Oct 18 and has appeared energetic at public events, speaking in a firm, clear voice.
The Vatican confirmed on Oct 26 he would go forward with a three-country, Nov 6-17 visit across South America, one of the most intense foreign tours arranged for a pope in decades.
“All of the medical advice is very positive... so he feels he can go,” Gallagher said in response to a question about why the pope is travelling only 24 days after his surgery.
“I think he’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go on it,” said the archbishop. “It was obviously quite advanced in the planning.”
Ukraine ceasefire, papal visit to US
Separately, Gallagher also addressed the recent ceasefire agreed by Russia and Ukraine to allow aid into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
He said that while Leo had recently spoken with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, he did not believe the Vatican was involved in arranging the ceasefire.
“I don’t think we were,” said Gallagher.
He also spoke about the Vatican’s ongoing agreement with China on the appointment of Catholic bishops in the country, and acknowledged “imperfections” with the accord.
The deal, first signed in 2018, gives Chinese officials some input into whom Leo appoints as bishops in the country.
“It’s not easy, the dialogue is not easy. The imperfections of the agreement are evident, but there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue… and that is what will continue to happen,” said Gallagher.
The archbishop also said he expects Leo, the first US-born pope, to visit the United States “in the not too distant future.”
But he said the visit might not occur in 2027, depending on the pope’s commitments. REUTERS

Russia’s Oil Revenue Hits Highest Weekly Level Since 2022 as Diesel Exports Return
The value of Russia’s seaborne crude exports surged to $2.76 billion in the latest week, marking the highest level recorded since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 27.
During the week ending October 25, the estimated value of Russian crude shipped by sea jumped by roughly $430 million to $2.76 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The increase came despite falling prices for Russia’s flagship Urals crude. The decline was more than offset by a sharp rise in export volumes and continued gains in the price of ESPO crude, which has now risen for eight consecutive weeks.
Ship-tracking data and industry reports showed that about 37 tankers loaded 26.93 million barrels of Russian crude during the week ending October 25.
That was a substantial increase from the previous week, when 31 tankers loaded approximately 21.87 million barrels.
China and India remain by far the largest buyers of Russian crude, maintaining a wide lead over other importers.
However, the final destination of many Russian oil cargoes is often unclear when tankers first leave port. Some vessels list intermediate destinations such as Suez, Port Sudan, or Singapore and only reveal their ultimate destination after traveling much of the route.
The surge comes as Russian diesel exports are also beginning to return to major international markets following a temporary easing of US sanctions and the lifting of a Russian export restriction.
US President Donald Trump recently said he had spoken with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement covering Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets.
Under the arrangement described by Trump, Russia is expected to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and international markets, followed by another 500,000 tons during November and an additional 1 million tons later.
Shipping data from Kpler and LSEG also indicate that Russian diesel cargoes are already moving back toward traditional destinations. At least two tankers have recently signaled routes toward Türkiye and Brazil.
The renewed diesel flows add another layer to Russia’s energy exports at a time when its seaborne crude business is already generating record wartime revenue.
Previously, US President Donald Trump blocked the implementation of sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia and buyers of Russian energy under a law championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, just weeks after signing the legislation himself.

One Russian Warship Down, Another on the Way? Moscow’s New Baltic Dilemma
