One Russian Warship Down, Another on the Way? Moscow’s New Baltic Dilemma
Russia may be preparing to send a newly launched missile-armed corvette to the Baltic Sea, potentially replacing a warship previously targeted by Ukrainian drones, despite the vessel originally being intended for the Pacific Fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 26, citing Polish defense outlet Defence24, Russia’s new Project 20380 corvette Grozny has raised questions about its future deployment after appearing with a tactical number associated with vessels operating in the Baltic Sea.
The corvette, launched in October 2026, is officially intended to join Russia’s Pacific Fleet once construction and outfitting are completed. However, Polish analysts identified a detail suggesting that Moscow could have other plans.
Grozny carries the tactical number 551, while vessels assigned to the Pacific Fleet’s 114th Surface Ship Brigade typically have numbers beginning with 3. By contrast, several Russian Baltic Fleet corvettes use numbers beginning with 5, including Steregushchy (550), Soobrazitelny (531), and Boyky (545).
The numbering discrepancy has led Polish analysts to question whether Grozny could eventually be deployed to the Baltic rather than the Pacific. Defense Express further suggested that the vessel could replace Boyky, another Project 20380 corvette that was struck by Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces in June 2026.
However, the outlet emphasized that the potential replacement of Boyky was its own assessment, while the Polish analysis focused on Grozny’s possible reassignment to the Baltic Fleet.
A precedent for changes in Russian naval assignments already exists. The Project 20380 corvette Mercury was initially intended for the Baltic Fleet under tactical number 535 but was later formally assigned to the Black Sea Fleet with number 735.
Despite its official assignment, Mercury has remained in the Baltic Sea because restrictions on passage through the Turkish Straits have prevented its transfer to the Black Sea.
Grozny is equipped with eight Kh-35 anti-ship missiles, a 100-mm naval gun, two AK-630 close-in weapon systems, 324-mm torpedo launchers, and a Redut air defense system with 12 missile launch cells. The 104-meter-long vessel has a full displacement of approximately 2,200 tons and can carry a Ka-27 anti-submarine helicopter.
Despite speculation surrounding its deployment, Defence24 analysts believe Grozny is unlikely to enter operational service for several years. As a result, even if Moscow ultimately redirects the corvette to the Baltic Fleet, it would not provide an immediate replacement for Boyky.
On June 3, 2026, operators from Ukraine’s 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces struck the Russian corvette Boykiy with a long-range drone while it was undergoing repairs at a dry dock in Kronstadt, near St. Petersburg.
The strike was confirmed by Ukraine’s military, while subsequent satellite imagery revealed extensive fire damage and the apparent destruction of the ship’s superstructure.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that a reported diesel deal between Russia and the US was a "purely business arrangement" without political or security-related conditions.
Speaking at a meeting with chief editors of African media outlets in Moscow, Lavrov described the arrangement as a "pragmatic approach" by leaders concerned about their countries' economies and the global economy.
He said the interests of citizens were being prioritized over geopolitical objectives.
"There were no conditions – such as 'we’ll buy diesel fuel from you, provided you take certain actions on the political or security front, whether in the Strait of Hormuz or anywhere else' – there were no such linkages whatsoever," Lavrov said. 
Lavrov criticizes European approach to negotiations
Commenting on a phone call involving Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr, Lavrov said he had not seen a detailed account of the conversation but believed it had produced "nothing new."
"This merely demonstrates a desire on the part of the Europeans to insert themselves into the negotiation process – though with what positions they intend to do so remains a big question," he said.
"We do not yet see any change in Europe's approach," Lavrov added. 
Russia accuses Western countries of involvement in Sahel sabotage
Turning to Africa, Lavrov accused Western countries, including France, of involving Ukrainian military personnel in what he described as terrorist operations and acts of sabotage in the Sahel region, particularly in Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.
"There is growing evidence that certain Western capitals, including Paris, though not exclusively, are bringing in Ukrainian military personnel to carry out terrorist tasks. They are being brought there and used to organize acts of sabotage," Lavrov claimed.
He said Russia was assisting Sahel countries in their fight against terrorism, with the Russian Defense Ministry's Africa Corps operating in the region.

Immigrant detainee dies at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:13:54 UTC
02:13:54 KST

Immigrant detainee dies at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A record number of people have died in ICE custody under the Trump administration, including a person who died Saturday at the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego.
- CoreCivic, the private prison company that operates the facility, said staff attempted lifesaving measures after finding Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, 43, from Guatemala unresponsive.
- Immigration and Customs Enforcement said his death is under investigation.
WASHINGTON — An immigrant detainee died Saturday morning at the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego, marking the 61st such death under the Trump administration.
The death of Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, 43, from Guatemala is under investigation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed Tuesday. The cause was not immediately clear.
In a news release, ICE wrote that facility staff found Jimenez Gutierrez unresponsive at around 11:31 a.m. in his assigned safety cell — a segregation cell typically used for people who are suicidal or under psychological observation. The staffers attempted to wake him, contacted medical personnel, declared an emergency and called 911.
Medical personnel began CPR about seven minutes later, the news release states. After paramedics arrived, they continued lifesaving measures but pronounced Jimenez Gutierrez dead at about 12:23 p.m.
ICE wrote that San Diego agents arrested Jimenez Gutierrez on Oct. 9 during an enforcement operation in Escondido, reinstated a prior final removal order and transferred him to the Otay Mesa facility pending his removal to Mexico. The agency did not immediately explain why he would be sent to Mexico despite being a Guatemalan citizen.
Jimenez Gutierrez was convicted in 2024 of selling liquor to a minor, ICE said.
In an emailed statement, an unnamed spokesperson with CoreCivic, the Tennessee-based private prison company that operates the facility, confirmed the death.
“We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” the spokesperson wrote, adding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was immediately notified.
The death was first reported by Daylight San Diego.
ICE said it had notified Jimenez Gutierrez’s family and the Consulate of Guatemala. The agency added that it provides comprehensive medical care and is committed to ensuring safe, secure and human environments for those in its custody.
Terra Lawson-Remer, chair of the San Diego County Board of Supervisors, said the county medical examiner was notified on Saturday, conducted an autopsy Monday and is still working to establish what happened.
“We do not yet know what caused his death, but we know a family has lost someone they love,” she said during a news conference. “They deserve answers.”
Lawson-Remer said she and Supervisor Paloma Aguirre sent a letter Tuesday to the Trump administration and CoreCivic demanding their cooperation with an independent examination and investigation. She said CoreCivic has refused to sign an agreement that would allow public health inspections inside the Otay Mesa facility despite a 2025 state law that allows local public health authorities to inspect ICE facilities.
Aguirre said she asked the county public health officer to determine what kind of follow-up is possible under that state law. She added that county leaders are also asking ICE and CoreCivic to preserve records tied to Jimenez Gutierrez’s detention, care and death, including requests for medical help.
Jimenez Gutierrez is the seventh person to die while in ICE custody in California under this administration, and the first to die at the Otay Mesa facility since 2023.
Deaths have increased as the Trump administration detained record numbers of people, with the population at one point ballooning past 70,000 nationwide.
The most recent death reported by ICE was that of Luis Sandoval, 48, a Salvadoran immigrant who died of apparent suicide Friday. Staff at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center in Georgia found Sandoval with a ligature around his neck, according to an ICE news release.
ICE policy is to notify the public and Congress within two business days of a detainee’s death. More extensive reports about each death, which were typically three pages, must be released within 90 days, though those have been reduced to several paragraphs.

French slam Macron’s riots response – poll

French slam Macron’s riots response – poll
French voters overwhelmingly disapprove of President Emmanuel Macron’s handling of weeks of violent nationwide protests, with just 12% backing his response, according to a new Ipsos-BVA-CESI poll.
Around 80% of respondents said Macron’s response to the unrest has been inadequate, according to the poll for Le Parisien published on Saturday. The riots also sparked widespread anger, with 58% of respondents expressing outrage.
Macron’s overall approval rating fell to 16%, the lowest since January and down seven percentage points from last month, according to a monthly CSA poll for Le Journal du Dimanche published on Sunday.
The unrest began last month with student demonstrations over teacher shortages, school funding, and deteriorating facilities before spreading nationwide. As trade unions and opposition parties joined the movement, the protests grew into broader demonstrations against soaring living costs, inequality, and cuts to public services.
The unrest escalated sharply on October 17, when around 550,000 people joined the demonstrations nationwide, spilling out into clashes with the police, arson, and widespread looting in several cities.
Immigration also emerged as an issue in public perceptions of the violence. Around 55% believe there is a link between immigration and the October 17 riots, according to a CSA survey published last Thursday.
Last week, Macron responded by announcing a crackdown on public gatherings. Protests deemed unauthorized were banned and limits on marches were imposed – even those organized by recognized groups.
Opposition leaders blamed Macron’s policies for the unrest, accusing him of failing to maintain public order.
Despite the restrictions, the demonstrations continued, drawing around 410,000 people on Saturday, according to Interior Ministry data.
Similar protests took place elsewhere in Europe, with demonstrators in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal voicing concerns about living costs, housing shortages, and public services.
After Western media outlets reported that several EU governments suspected Russia of involvement in the unrest, President Vladimir Putin dismissed the allegations.
“To claim that we are provoking mass protests in major European cities is really going too far,” Putin said, arguing that the accusations reflect European leaders’ inability to address the crisis.

Nearly 5,000 Palestinians displaced in Israel's Hebron siege
Unknown

2026-10-27

Breadcrumb
Nearly 5,000 Palestinians displaced in Israel's Hebron siege
Nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes in Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank as Israeli military operations entered their fifth consecutive day, while raids and settler attacks continued across the territory.
The Israeli army has closed all entrances and exits to Hebron while carrying out operations in the neighbourhoods of Deir Baha and al-Jilda, the hometowns of two Palestinians who carried out a shooting attack on Friday that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded others. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to carry out collective punishment against the neighbourhoods following the shooting.
Ola al-Qawasmi, a spokesperson for Hebron Municipality, told The New Arab that municipal records showed 780 families, comprising 4,969 people, had been displaced from their homes.
Those displaced include 336 infants under the age of two, 441 people aged 60 and above, 216 pregnant or breastfeeding women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people with chronic illnesses, al-Qawasmi said.
She added that displaced families had sought shelter with relatives, while the municipality had opened temporary shelters in preparation for further displacement as the Israeli operation and siege continued.
Military raids and settler attacks
The United Nations said on Tuesday that more than 3,000 people had been displaced by Israeli forces in Hebron since Friday, as humanitarian organisations supported local authorities in responding to the needs of affected residents.
Elsewhere in the West Bank, settlers attacked the village of Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, and set fire to three cars, according to village council head Marwan Sabah.
Settlers also stormed the courtyards of Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque compound on Tuesday morning under Israeli police protection and performed Talmudic rituals. Israeli officials and far-right settlers have increasingly challenged the longstanding status quo at Islam's third-holiest site, under which non-Muslims may visit but are not permitted to pray.
In Nablus governorate, a 44-year-old Palestinian was shot in the foot by Israeli forces at the Huwara checkpoint south of the city. The Palestinian Red Crescent said troops had initially prevented its medical teams from reaching the scene after receiving reports that a vehicle had come under fire. They later allowed medics to enter and evacuate the wounded man to hospital.
A 50-year-old Palestinian was also injured in a settler assault in the town of Burqa, northwest of Nablus, according to the Red Crescent.
Israeli forces also bulldozed memorials erected in honour of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the villages of Beita, Rujeib, Azmut, Madama and Iraq Burin, as well as the town of Beit Furik, east and south of Nablus.
Troops raided several communities across the West Bank, turned homes into military barracks and carried out arrests and house searches in multiple governorates on Tuesday and overnight. Israeli forces also tightened restrictions at checkpoints and roadblocks at the entrances to towns and villages.
In the village of Burin, south of Nablus, Israeli forces had been carrying out a raid since around 2am on Tuesday, according to village council head Ibrahim Omran, who spoke to The New Arab.
Omran said troops had seized a building and converted it into a military barracks while conducting widespread raids on residents' homes. Around 20 Palestinians had been detained, he said, with all but two released by the time he spoke. The raid was still ongoing.
Olive harvest disrupted by settler violence
Settler attacks have also targeted Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest.
In Madama, south of Nablus, a settler uprooted electricity poles, damaging the village's power network and obstructing residents' access to their land. An armed settler also forced four Palestinian families to leave while they were picking olives.
Elsewhere, settlers attacked olive harvesters in several villages around Nablus and Ramallah, smashing a vehicle and stealing harvested olives.
In other incidents, settlers closed off the al-Himma spring in the northern Jordan Valley and fenced off privately owned Palestinian land, cutting off a water source used by residents and livestock, according to Hasan Malihat, director of the al-Baydar Human Rights Organisation.
Israeli forces and settlers also prevented farmers from harvesting olives in Barta'a and Turmus Ayya.
In Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces raided a Palestinian home after settlers attacked the property and assaulted family members, forcing the family to leave. Troops later arrested the homeowner and his son, according to activist Osama Makhamreh.
In Beita, south of Nablus, settlers attacked Palestinian homes and fired live ammunition at residents' vehicles as young men confronted them. No injuries were reported.

I've been singing the praises of merino wool in these pages for over five years. Most people have come around to the fact that merino wool is a super fiber; it's both sustainable and quite remarkable in its capabilities. Merino wool somehow manages to be comfortable in 95-degree heat, and it'll insulate you against below-freezing temperatures. Unlike synthetic fibers derived from petroleum, merino wool resists odors and is naturally breathable. What's not to love? The price.
Merino wool isn't cheap. That's why I love these merino T-shirts from Quince: They're just $42.
The Quince All-Season T-shirt is 100 percent extra-fine merino wool with a 165-gsm weave, which is perfect even on the warmest summer days where I live. (Admittedly, I think the hottest it got this summer was 92 Fahrenheit). I like the relaxed fit here as well. It's neither skintight technical nor overly loose and baggy. It fits like a T-shirt is supposed to. That's what Quince does well in a number of categories: offer a solid, no-nonsense, competitively priced merino wool T-shirt that fits well and feels great. As an added bonus, Quince offers free shipping and free returns for 365 days. I haven't actually tested either—I haven't needed to, my Quince T-shirt is still going strong after two years of use. But there are plenty of customer reviews on Reddit suggesting the company does honor that offer.
Not sold on the idea of a wool T-shirt? I understand. When I started testing merino, I too had visions of lumberjacks in plaid and itchy sweaters someone's grandma had knitted. None of that is merino wool. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool, which has evolved to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures and is comfortable to wear next to your skin.
One wool myth that's not just a myth is care. Merino isn't cotton. Quince's care instructions for the All Season T-shirt say to wash it in cold water and lay flat to dry. The latter is important, as hanging merino wool to dry will stretch it out (because of the water weight). Can you throw it in the dryer? Yes. I have, for testing purposes only. It will shrink, and it will wear it out much, much faster, but you can do it.

Kernel yields: wheat up 9%, sunflower up 18%, rapeseed up 48%, corn down 13%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:11:08 EET
02:11:08 KST

Net wheat and sunflower yields at Kernel's agricultural operations increased by 9% and 18%, respectively, year over year, reaching 6.4 tonnes per hectare and 3.1 tonnes per hectare, the company said in a stock exchange filing last week.
"The Group's total acreage under operations increased by 48% y-o-y to 530,000 hectares, following the expansion and optimization of its farming footprint during FY2026," Kernel said.
The company specified that wheat acreage increased by 13%, to 106,000 hectares, while sunflower acreage rose by 90%, to 88,000 hectares. This is expected to translate into increases in their respective harvests of 22.3%, to 678,400 tonnes, and 2.2 times, to 272,800 tonnes.
At the same time, the company noted that sunflower harvesting remains to be completed on 4% of the area allocated to the crop.
As for corn, harvesting has so far been completed on 28% of the planted area. Taking this into account, the net yield is expected to reach 8.1 tonnes per hectare, down 13% from last year, "primarily reflecting the impact of summer heatwaves and insufficient rainfall during key stages of crop development, which severely affected corn yields in one of the Group's clusters," Kernel explained.
However, given that corn acreage increased by 48% this year, to 254,000 hectares, the harvest is expected to rise by 28.6%, to 2 million 57,400 tonnes.
In addition, Kernel increased its rapeseed acreage from 3,000 hectares to 43,000 hectares. Combined with an increase in yield from 2.4 tonnes per hectare to 3.5 tonnes per hectare, this resulted in a 20.9-fold increase in the rapeseed harvest, to 150,500 tonnes.
The company also allocated 39,000 hectares to other crops, compared with 43,000 hectares last year.
Before the war, Kernel ranked first globally in sunflower oil production, accounting for about 7% of worldwide output, and exports, with a share of around 12%. It is one of Ukraine's largest producers and sellers of bottled sunflower oil. The company also grows and sells agricultural products.
In FY2026 (July 2025-June 2026), Kernel increased EBITDA by 20%, to $558 million, and net profit by 35%, to $322 million, while revenue rose 7%, to $4.404 billion.

Spain deports migrants from Ceuta in move criticised by rights group

Spain deports migrants from Ceuta in move criticised by rights group
The deportation was the first of its kind since a mass border crossing into the territory from Morocco in July.
Spain has deported more than a dozen migrants from its North African enclave of Ceuta, prompting criticism from Amnesty International, which said Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s left-wing government was endangering their human rights.
It was the first deportation of its kind since a mass border crossing into the territory from Morocco in July.
The Spanish Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that it had deported the migrants from Ceuta after their asylum applications were rejected, and that Morocco had agreed to receive them.
Nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) told the Reuters news agency that 16 people from African, Middle Eastern and Asian countries had been deported.
About 80,000 people entered from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July. At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.2sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.
The crisis has evolved into a major political challenge for Sanchez, who is seeking re-election in snap polls scheduled for November 29.
Tens of thousands of protesters have gathered across Spain in recent months to denounce the government’s handling of the situation. Meanwhile, right-wing parties have used the crisis to attack Sanchez.
The leader of the far-right Vox Party, Santiago Abascal, has branded the prime minister a “traitor”.
Human rights guarantees
Amnesty International has warned that the human rights of those deported from Ceuta on Tuesday could be at risk.
“Spain, despite its [progressive] speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” said Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher.
“Morocco does not respect many human rights.”
However, Madrid disputes the rights group’s accusations. In a statement, the interior ministry told Reuters that the European Union considers Morocco to be a safe country, adding that deportations are carried out “with all the necessary safeguards”.
Most of those who entered Ceuta in late July left within days. However, about 8,000 migrants still remain. Some are sleeping on the streets, while others are being housed by Spain, charities and civil society groups.

Türkiye presents Digital Sovereignty Strategy to Cybersecurity Board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:08:55 UTC
02:08:55 KST

Seyit Şamil Kurt
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Türkiye's Digital Sovereignty Strategy, aimed at strengthening the country's sovereignty in the digital sphere and reducing dependence on foreign technologies, was presented to the Cybersecurity Board on Tuesday, according to the country's Communications Directorate.
The board met under the chairmanship of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and discussed the implications of global and regional geopolitical developments for the cybersecurity environment, as well as recent cybersecurity incidents worldwide and evolving threat dynamics, the directorate said in a statement.
The board was briefed on how developments in artificial intelligence are affecting the nature, scale, and speed of cyber threats.
It also assessed the effects and risks of algorithmic manipulation and cognitive influence activities carried out through digital platforms on national security and societal resilience.
The meeting stressed the importance of digital sovereignty for national security, identifying the protection of critical infrastructure, strengthening national cyber resilience and deterrence capabilities, and achieving technological independence as strategic priorities in Türkiye's security and development policies.
Against this backdrop, the strategy was presented to the board with the aim of "strengthening Türkiye's sovereignty in the digital sphere, reducing dependence on foreign sources in critical technologies, and developing national technology capacity," the statement said.
The board decided that measures taken in line with the strategy's objectives would be implemented by relevant institutions and organizations within their respective spheres, while implementation processes would be effectively monitored and progress regularly assessed.
The meeting also focused on strengthening interagency coordination, developing joint risk assessment capabilities, and ensuring consistency in implementation, given the ability of cyber threats to spread rapidly and affect multiple sectors simultaneously.
The board reaffirmed its commitment to deepening cooperation among public institutions, the private sector, and academia and developing a comprehensive cybersecurity ecosystem, the statement added.

UN nuclear watchdog demands access to Iran's 440kg stockpile of highly enriched uranium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:08:41 UTC
02:08:41 KST

The head of the UN nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to provide the information and access needed to verify its previously declared nuclear material, including 440 kilogrammes of highly enriched uranium, warning that outstanding safeguards issues remain unresolved.
Addressing the UN Security Council, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said on Tuesday that the agency continued to engage with Tehran to resolve questions concerning its nuclear programme and verify material at facilities covered by safeguards agreements.
“One area of particular concern is Iran’s previously declared nuclear material, which includes 440kg of High Enriched Uranium,” Grossi said, adding that the issues had remained outstanding for more than five years.
IAEA seeks access to nuclear facilities
Grossi said the agency had withdrawn all its inspectors from Iran by the end of June 2025 for safety reasons following the start of military attacks.
Although inspectors had been available to return for months, he said Iran had not provided the information and access required to verify previously declared nuclear material at safeguarded facilities, including sites affected by military attacks and those that were not.
The Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant remains an exception, with IAEA inspectors currently conducting verification activities there.
Grossi also said Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization had engaged constructively with the agency to arrange the delivery of safeguards equipment needed to verify spent nuclear fuel before its transfer to a new dry storage facility, expected early next year.
“I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions,” Grossi said, stressing that providing access was Iran’s legal obligation.
Security Council adopts agenda amid divisions
The Security Council opened its session by adopting the agenda with 11 votes in favour, two against from Russia and China, and two abstentions from Pakistan and Somalia.
Grossi highlighted the scale of the IAEA’s global verification work, saying its inspectors spent more than 14,000 calendar days in the field last year, carrying out verification activities at more than 1,400 facilities and locations outside them.
The agency was able to draw safeguards conclusions for 179 states, he said, underscoring the role of inspections in monitoring compliance with nuclear safeguards obligations.
The dispute over access in Iran remains a key challenge for the agency as it seeks to establish the status of previously declared nuclear material and resolve outstanding questions about Tehran’s nuclear activities.

Nearly 100 fighters have been killed in renewed clashes between Yemen's Houthis and government forces in southwestern Yemen, military sources from both sides told AFP on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Yemen's government launched a counter-offensive with Saudi air support to try to reclaim the territory lost to the Houthis.
But the campaign has faltered, while the Houthis have ramped up deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia that shuttered its capital's airport for two weeks and disrupted daily life.
Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in 2015 in the conflict, which has devastated Yemen and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The US selected Poland to host a new European maintenance facility for Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missile systems, a move aimed at strengthening NATO’s air and missile defense capabilities and improving military readiness on the alliance’s eastern flank, the Pentagon said Tuesday.
The announcement was made on the sidelines of a meeting of NATO’s Conference of National Armaments Directors (CNAD), with the US government coordinating with defense contractor Lockheed Martin and European allies on the initiative.
Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will lead critical supply-chain integration for the facility, which will establish regional maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities for PAC-3 missiles within Europe, the Pentagon said in a statement.
"Today's announcement puts partnership into action. By investing national resources to establish this critical sustainment capability on NATO's Eastern Front, Allies are sending a clear message: the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action," said Michael Duffey, under secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment.
The Pentagon said the initiative advances defense-industrial commitments made at the NATO summit in Ankara in July under the framework it described as “NATO 3.0.” The broader objective is to increase European allies’ ability to assume primary responsibility for their conventional defense while maintaining close cooperation with the US.

In Armenia, archaeologists found a coin of Emperor Octavian Augustus
Kyiv • UNN
Archaeologists near Metsamor discovered a coin of Octavian Augustus, gold earrings, and a bronze dagger. The tomb dates to different eras.
A coin of the Roman emperor Octavian Augustus, gold earrings, a bronze dagger and other artifacts were discovered by archaeologists during excavations near the Metsamor Historical and Archaeological Museum-Reserve in Armenia. Armenian media report this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Service for the Protection of the Historical Environment and Historical and Cultural Museum-Reserves, the finds date to different historical periods, including the Late Bronze Age, the Iron Age and antiquity.
Excavations at the site under investigation began in 2024 and continued in 2026. The work is being carried out on privately owned land. The structure under investigation is a stone burial chamber surrounded by a circular stone structure.
During excavations in previous years, a burial from the ancient period, dating to the 1st century AD, was discovered in the upper layer of the tomb. Among the objects found were gold ornaments, a coin and other artifacts.
In the lower part of the burial chamber, near its base, archaeologists discovered the main burial, which, according to the preliminary dating of the materials found, dates to the 14th–13th centuries BC.
This layer contained a concentration of horse bones, numerous pottery fragments, a dagger of the Lchashen type, fragments of a belt, pieces of bronze objects and bell-shaped pendants.

An EU country has reopened the Russia channel. What brought it back?
On October 26, 2026, the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission resumed its work. The announcement was made during Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s visit to Moscow for WWII Victory Day celebrations. The timing of the meeting is particularly favorable for the ruling coalition led by Fico’s SMER party. The only event that somewhat dampened the occasion was the defeat of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s party in snap elections in Serbia. Vucic’s foreign policy has often been likened to Fico’s approach in Slovakia. Below, we explore why these stories are fundamentally different and what is really happening in the context of Russia-Slovakia relations, as well as in Slovakia itself, ahead of the election on September 26, 2027.
Perfect timing
Although the resumption of the intergovernmental commission was announced in May, the talks did not take place until six months later. On the Slovak side, they were led by a close ally of Fico and the current foreign affairs minister, Juraj Blanar. The lists of negotiators on both sides were not disclosed until the last moment. The date of the negotiations was also shrouded in secrecy and was not revealed until last week during an EU summit, which, according to reports, was marked by a “terrible” atmosphere and was “unworthy of a meeting of the European Council.”
Fico’s attendance was uncertain right up to the last minute, with Bratislava skillfully playing this card. Slovak diplomats maintained suspense, suggesting that Fico’s visit depended on the “substantiality of concessions,” keeping the EU on its toes regarding a possible geopolitical demarche. Ultimately, Fico stayed in Bratislava, crafting a perfect political alibi before Brussels while sending a full government delegation to Moscow to tackle pressing political and economic challenges. He skillfully employed this maneuver, illustrating that in today’s landscape, ‘glitch-art diplomacy’ – characterized by protocol breaches, unpredictability, and exploiting systemic errors – remains effective. Though not large in size, Slovakia is a critical node through which the East and West continue to exchange signals.
The timing of this event strikes a perfect balance for the ruling authorities, both in terms of domestic political dynamics and the wider European context. First, municipal elections held in Slovakia over the past weekend confirmed the strength of the current coalition. Fico and his allies demonstrated their dominance across regions and industrial hubs, leaving the pro-Western opposition confined to Bratislava. This electoral victory has secured a solid backing for the prime minister, giving him the freedom to pursue bold foreign policy initiatives.
The external context vividly illustrated to the Slovak audience the validity of the ruling coalition’s stance. The recent EU summit only deepened the rift among allies. The European Commission attempted to impose new climate quotas, but the countries of the Visegrad Group clearly expressed their dissent, with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis openly criticizing Ursula von der Leyen for her ‘green transition’ dogmas. This unfolded against the backdrop of a shocking report from Eurostat, revealing that most EU countries are facing budget deficits, with the highest figures recorded in Hungary (7.2%) and Romania (9.2%).
Amid this dismal European landscape, news from Slovakia underscores the looming threat of deindustrialization. German automotive giant Porsche recently announced its decision to shift production of its Cayenne model from Bratislava back to Leipzig, aiming to salvage its parent company’s facilities in Germany, which are struggling due to the energy crisis. The risk of German capital flight poses an existential threat to the national industry, considering the fact that businesses depend heavily on accessible energy resources.
In light of these developments, Fico’s rejection of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s proposal for a €1.5 billion compensation package in exchange for halting gas transit appears to be a rational choice. For the Slovak public, which is opposed to prolonging the conflict, there’s no clear way to survive without supplies of hydrocarbons from the East. By refusing the offer, Fico has made it clear that virtual ‘paper’ funds from Kiev won’t heat factories or convince foreign automotive companies to remain in the country.
Not a time for half-measures
The defeat of Vucic’s team in Serbia during the early parliamentary elections is unpleasant news for Bratislava. Many Western analysts predict a similar fate for Fico in the upcoming parliamentary elections in September 2027. However, a fundamental difference between Belgrade and Bratislava must be noted. The Serbian scenario demonstrated that, in turbulent times, success goes to those who can balance the loyalty of the silent majority with pressure from the crowds.
Fico is purposefully venturing into this precarious territory. Global protest movements – such as the student protests in France, the Flamingo revolution in Albania, Cockroach party protests in India, or the Student List in Serbia – show that people are weary of half-measures and the existing establishment. The paradox of Fico lies in his unique strategy. He manages to remain the foremost systemic critic of Brussels’ supranational doctrines while being a key player in European politics. Fico deftly harnesses protest potential before it can turn against him.
This position is driven by a need to protect the country’s real economy. Slovakia relies heavily on exports, which account for around 90% of GDP, with the automotive industry being the cornerstone of the economy. This sector employs over 230,000 people, meaning that nearly 1 in 10 Slovak families depends on it directly. This established industry cannot be sustained by illusions of a green transition or even by Slovakia’s own nuclear power, since its costs remain tightly linked to fluctuating gas prices.
This is why Fico demonstrates remarkable flexibility in foreign policy matters, except when it comes to energy supplies from the East. This sets him apart from Vucic, who tried to maintain a delicate balance and compromise with Brussels, ultimately trapping himself in a web of sanctions, losing legitimacy among his patriotic electorate, and facing a significant electoral defeat. Fico learns from the mistakes of others and avoids half-measures entirely. Amid the wave of protests and strikes sweeping across Europe, his overt refusal to follow the EU’s general approach of replacing Russian energy resonates with ordinary Slovaks. People see Fico as a leader who is ready to defend national industries rather than abstract EU directives.
The glitch art of Slovak diplomacy
On October 26, a Slovak delegation arrived in Moscow, illustrating Fico’s commitment to defending national interests. Behind the closed doors of the 22nd meeting of the intergovernmental commission, Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar and Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov focused exclusively on practical and vital issues for Bratislava.
As anticipated, energy security and the nuclear sector took center stage. Blanar signed final protocols ensuring stable resource supplies for Slovak energy companies and factories. Additionally, both sides strengthened cooperation in pragmatic areas such as agriculture and ecology, while also addressing culturally sensitive topics relevant to conservative Slovak voters, such as humanitarian issues and military memorials.
“We reject the construction of a new Iron Curtain between the EU and Russia, and we consider it of utmost importance – even during this challenging period – to maintain open lines of communication,” Blanar said in Moscow.
In summary, the resumption of the work of the intergovernmental commission should not be viewed as a concession to Russia. Fico understands that his political survival, along with that of his party in the September 2027 election, hinges not on the approval of the European elites or the slogans of Bratislava’s liberal street protesters. His fate will be determined in the factories of automotive giants and in the kitchens of ordinary Slovak families, where heating bills and job security take precedence over the geopolitical ambitions of Brussels.
The recent talks in Moscow can be seen as an effort to establish a protective shield over industry before the European energy crisis completely devastates Eastern Europe’s automotive sector.
Unlike Serbia, where the government fell victim to its own half-measures, Bratislava is betting on clarity. By turning down ‘paper’ compensation from Kiev, Fico offers his electorate tangible results. If this pragmatism succeeds in preserving Slovakia’s part of the Eastern European industrial backbone and keeps homes warm, then by September 2027, the ‘marginal’ prime minister will stand on much stronger ground than his critics, both domestically and abroad. Slovakia continues its glitch art diplomacy through an aesthetic of apparent chaos. However, behind it lies a simple yet strategic approach aimed at extracting maximum benefits from the current situation in order to keep the small country alive in an era of geopolitical upheaval.

US midterms — Here are the five issues shaping the November 3 elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:00:53 UTC
02:00:53 KST

Americans voting in the November 3 midterm elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency, along with dozens of governorships and thousands of state offices.
The campaign is playing out against an unusually combustible mix of economic anxiety, war on Iran, immigration battles, corruption concerns and unease over rapidly expanding artificial intelligence.
Polls asking voters about priorities use different methodologies, but they broadly agree on the dominance of pocketbook concerns.
An October Pew survey found economic issues easily topped voters' worries, while a September Emerson poll put the Iran war, jobs, tariffs, gas prices, immigration and AI regulation among the most important factors in voting decisions.
Here are five issues shaping the midterms:
It's the economy
Affordability remains issue number one.
Inflation was running at 3.7 percent in September, but the political problem goes beyond the headline rate, with voters paying more for gasoline, housing, electricity, groceries and borrowing.
Pew found that 65 percent of Americans see Trump's economic policies as hurtful to the economy.
Another survey, from the Joseph Rainey Center for Public Policy, found 57 percent placing groceries, gas or utilities among their top three issues.
Trump's tariffs feed directly into the debate, with opponents blaming them for higher costs while the administration argues they protect American industry and raise revenue.
US war on Iran
A foreign war has become a domestic pocketbook issue.
The conflict with Iran, underway since February, has driven energy costs higher and become deeply unpopular.
Emerson's September survey rated the Iran war the single most important issue among those it tested, while Reuters/Ipsos found only 34 percent approving of Trump's handling of the conflict.
Republican candidates in several competitive races have called for the fighting to end, and four Republican senators joined Democrats in a September vote seeking to rein it in.
Immigration
The strength of Trump's signature political talking point has become more complicated.
The president returned to office promising mass deportations, but support has eroded following controversy over deaths during arrests and detention, and aggressive ICE operations.
Reuters/Ipsos found 55 percent disapproved of Trump's handling of immigration. Marist, meanwhile, found Democrats and Republicans essentially level on which party voters trusted more on the issue — a striking change from the clear Republican advantage of 2024.
The shift is particularly notable among Latinos. A survey across competitive House districts found 62 percent of Latino voters disapproved of the administration's deportation and immigration enforcement.
Money and power
The president himself is a poll plank — including how he uses the office.
Trump has explicitly asked voters to behave as though he were on the ballot, making the election partly a referendum on his second term.
Government ethics ranked second behind the economy in Pew's open-ended survey, cited by nine percent of voters.
A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found 97 percent of Americans believed there was at least some corruption in the federal government.
AI comes to town
Artificial intelligence has jumped out of the laptop and onto the campaign trail.
Voters worry about job losses, safety and regulation — but increasingly also about the giant data centers needed to power AI.
Half of Americans told Pew they were very concerned about AI's role in the economy, while 59 percent said they disliked political leaders supporting data centers in the respondents' localities.
AI regulation scored surprisingly highly in Emerson's September survey, just behind immigration and gas prices. Data centers themselves ranked lower nationally, but have become major campaign issues in states including Ohio as communities battle over electricity, water and construction.
Congress even spent some of its final pre-election days arguing over who should pay the electricity costs created by them — proof that, in 2026, even the server farm has become political.
Other fault lines
Not every familiar American culture-war issue has dominated the 2026 campaign, but several remain potent dividing lines.
Health care is a perennial election concern, encompassing the cost of insurance and medicines, and access to coverage.
These issues have not necessarily driven the national midterm campaign as strongly as affordability, Iran or immigration, but they remain powerful mobilisers for parts of both parties' coalitions.

'A celebration for democracy': Israeli voters speak of change, unity and the importance of voting
From voters demanding political change to those backing Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir, Israelis expressed different visions for the country's future but shared a belief in the importance of democracy
As Israelis headed to the polls on Tuesday, voters spoke to i24NEWS about the importance of democracy, the need for political change and their hopes for the country's future.
For some, the election represented an opportunity for a fundamental change in direction, while others emphasized the importance of maintaining Israel's Jewish identity and security.
Nita, who has lived in Israel for 54 years and worked as a teacher for four decades, told i24NEWS that the country needed significant reforms so she's backing the Democrats.
"Because this country has to change and has to change radically," she said, pointing to education, healthcare and social issues, particularly those affecting Israel's Arab population.
"I do believe there can be some kind of change. Yes. And I do believe that education is the key to change."
Despite expressing disappointment at the number of Arab voters she had seen near polling stations in Jaffa, Nita remained optimistic.
"I still see a lot of people and a lot of hope in the air," she said.
The importance of participating in democracy also motivated Israelis living abroad to return home to cast their ballots.
One voter who traveled from the United States told i24NEWS that the election's significance justified the journey.
"It's a critical election and many of us flew in to try and make a change," she said.
Another voter emphasized the importance of teaching younger generations to value their democratic rights, regardless of political affiliation.
"It's a privilege that they get to vote and you know, and be a part of this," the voter said.
Describing the atmosphere at the polling station, the voter added that elections should be "a celebration for democracy."
Despite the country's political divisions, another voter argued that Israelis remained more united than political discourse suggested.
"Truth is, I think we're much more united than many times we see, you know, in politics," the voter said.
For supporters of the political right, security and Jewish identity were central motivations.
One young Netanyahu supporter explained that Israel's democratic character must coexist with its Jewish identity.
"We are in a democratic country, but we are also a Jewish country," she said, emphasizing the importance of having a safe place to practice Judaism.
She also called for greater youth participation in politics, saying, "It's important for everyone to listen to our voice because we are not heard enough."
Another voter, who backed National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, described him as "a strong leader."
The voter, who had served in the military and lived abroad, acknowledged the divisive nature of the election campaign, comparing it to American politics.
"Like every campaign, dirty. Even in the United States, the last campaign was dirty. And over here it's dirty too," he said.
He argued that military service influenced political preferences, claiming that "most of the soldiers, they tend to go to the right to Bibi and Ben-Gvir."
He also pointed to Israelis returning from the United States to vote as evidence of the election's importance, saying, "They care about what's happening over here."
Asked to predict the election's outcome, he answered simply: "Bibi."
While voters disagreed over the country's political direction, their interviews reflected a shared conviction that participation in the election mattered, whether to bring about change, preserve national identity or strengthen Israeli democracy.

France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:57:51 UTC
01:57:51 KST

France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
France is working with 10 other European countries to establish a new nuclear deterrence framework aimed at Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The initiative, which President Emmanuel Macron called “forward deterrence,” was unveiled in March 2026. It calls for deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets to other European countries. Participants also intend to create a joint system for early warning and intelligence sharing.
The United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have joined France in the initiative. The three Baltic states, which are most vulnerable to Russian aggression, are not part of the project, while Italy declined to participate. Finland said it would like to take part but does not plan to host nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime.
French officials believe the new deterrent could be more credible because the security of France’s European neighbors matters far more to Paris than to Washington.
European officials also emphasize that the new system should supplement, rather than replace, the American “nuclear umbrella” over the continent and create further strategic uncertainty for Russia.
Experts say the French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale fighters are more effective in modern warfare than American B-61 nuclear bombs. The American bombs were developed in the 1960s, and advances in Russian air defenses limit their use.
Macron also said France plans to resume producing nuclear weapons for the first time in decades. The country currently has about 290 nuclear warheads but will no longer disclose information about its arsenal.
In practice, however, France will retain full control over its nuclear forces. “The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” said a minister from one of the countries involved in the project.
France is holding bilateral talks with its partners and has set up 10 separate groups for those discussions. Defense officials across Europe have had to hold frequent calls to keep one another informed about the negotiations, military officials said.

Defence Safety Management System (JSP 815)
Joint Service Publication 815 provides the Defence Safety Management System framework, enabling Defence organisations to develop and implement tailored safety management systems.
Documents
Details
Joint Service Publication (JSP) 815 is the Defence Safety Management System (SMS) and provides the framework, direction and guidance to enable Defence organisations to develop and implement their own safety management systems tailored to their business.
Purpose and Structure
JSP 815 is comprised of Defence SMS Framework and Defence SMS Direction and Guidance.
Defence SMS Framework
Defence SMS Framework provides the elements, expectations and performance statements that must be achieved to move Defence to a highly resilient and proactive organisation. The policy has been developed to align with ISO 45001 requirements.
Defence SMS Direction and Guidance
Defence SMS Direction and Guidance provides the direction and guidance which is to be used by all Defence organisations to assist them with the successful implementation of the requirements set out in the corresponding 12 elements.
Defence Safety Function Operating Model
The Directorate of Defence Safety and Support page holds the latest version of the Defence Safety Function Operating Model (1 September 2026) which should be read alongside JSP 815.

Weighing dependence on Washington: Trump between Zelensky and Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:55:14 UTC
01:55:14 KST

Within eight days in October, US President Donald Trump made two statements about two wartime leaders that, placed side by side, read like a confession. On 10 October, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, he said of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” He accused Zelensky of passing up the chance to settle the war with Russia “many times, many many times” and of driving up diesel prices by striking Russian oil refineries: “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
On 18 October, Trump posted a letter on his Truth Social platform describing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace.” In the letter, he gave Netanyahu his “Complete and Total Endorsement” nine days before Israel’s general election on 27 October.
Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu was expected, given Washington’s long record of backing Israel. His remarks on Zelensky, by contrast, shocked many. They revealed the real logic of the Trump administration: politics driven by calculations of interest rather than by allegiances or alliances. Together, the two statements hold an important lesson for anyone who believes American support is a promise rather than a calculation. They also expose Zelensky’s own strategic failure: he relied on a foreign power with its own interests instead of honestly weighing his own capabilities in the conflict with Russia.
A card that no longer plays
Zelensky’s fall from grace was triggered by a dispute over diesel. On 9 October, after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal under which Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and larger volumes after that. The Kremlin said Russia was ready to supply “the American and global markets.” Zelensky condemned the agreement as “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” and warned that Russia would “repay” the diesel “with further terror and perfidy.”
Trump responded with fury. For weeks, he had pressed Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian refineries, which had cut Russian diesel output and pushed up global fuel prices. A US official told Axios that Trump struck the deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests. Driven by his own political calculations, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop unilaterally and made no matching demand of Moscow. “We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries,” Trump told reporters. “So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries.”
The domestic context was decisive. The US was just over three weeks away from the midterm elections on 3 November. Diesel prices were close to record highs, driving up the cost of almost everything. Trump’s approval rating had fallen to the lowest point of his presidency amid the war on Iran, which the US and Israel launched in February. That war, and to a lesser extent the Ukrainian drone strikes, lay behind the energy crisis. By blaming Zelensky, Trump sought to shift responsibility for rising prices onto a foreign leader at a moment when American voters were preparing to punish the party in power.
The episode shows that Zelensky’s abandonment is not tactical but structural. He is no longer a useful card in American domestic politics, where Ukraine has no lobby to match the influence of pro-Israel groups. The Trump administration, along with other Western political circles, appears to have concluded that the war against Russia cannot be won.
Behind Trump’s insult lie facts about this war that are hard to deny. Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 was an act of aggression in breach of international law. Yet even if Western countries encouraged Kyiv to keep fighting, the choice to pursue the conflict on the battlefield rather than at the negotiating table was ultimately Zelensky’s, and he bet everything on Western support. His former spokeswoman Yulia Mendel has claimed that he undermined around seven attempts to end the war, an allegation his office rejects as baseless. In October 2022, he also signed a decree declaring negotiations with Putin “impossible”. The result is plain: having relied heavily on foreign powers, he is now stuck in a quagmire, with foreign support shrinking and no prospect of gains on the battlefield.
A war criminal who remains indispensable
Netanyahu is a different calculation entirely. In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The warrant remains in force even though Washington has sanctioned the court’s judges and deputy prosecutors and its president. He is a fugitive from international justice. Yet a sitting American president has endorsed his re-election in the most personal terms available.
Why? Because Trump needs him, both for his war on Iran and for electoral calculations shaped by pro-Israel lobbying networks in American politics. The most prominent of these is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which a US senator says plans to spend $233 million to defeat candidates critical of Netanyahu’s government. If Trump abandoned Netanyahu now, he would be abandoning his own decision to go to war with Iran. He believes the Israeli leader is central to the future of the US confrontation with Iran, and he does not want to carry on alone, which would become far more complicated if Netanyahu loses. Trump spelt this out himself: “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.” The endorsement was not moral; it rested on political calculation and self-interest.
The lesson: interest, not values
The contrast between Zelensky and Netanyahu is not one between good and bad. It is a practical lesson in how far a leader can rely on a foreign power. Netanyahu remains indispensable not because the case against him has gone away, but because he remains useful to the man who endorsed him. Zelensky was discarded because, at least in Trump’s view, he had become useless, with no domestic constituency in the US to protect him.
The difference is not between two leaders or their conflicts. It is between an asset and a liability. It is Zelensky’s own fault, not anyone else’s, that he failed to recognise the limits of American support when he chose to continue the war rather than settle it through direct talks. He believed a foreign leader would back him without exacting a price. Trump sees Netanyahu as an asset he would like to keep in power, while Zelensky was traded for a diesel deal that carries electoral value for Trump and his party in the upcoming midterms.
Return, finally, to the two men. One is a wanted war crimes suspect who received a presidential endorsement in a public letter. The other is a wartime president who was told publicly that his country should find someone else. The contrast is not an anomaly to be explained away; it is an instruction manual. Those who place their fate in Washington’s hands should study Zelensky’s path and adjust their expectations of a foreign power, whose support will never come at the expense of its own interests. That is American politics today.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza never stopped – UN commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:54:21 UTC
01:54:21 KST

Israel’s genocide in Gaza never stopped – UN commission
Israel has continued committing “genocide” in Gaza despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, while also perpetrating crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, the UN Commission of Inquiry has concluded.
The October 10, 2025 truce was meant to end Israel’s Gaza offensive, which was launched after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack in which around 1,200 people were killed and around 250 were taken hostage. The retaliatory campaign has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza’s population. Israel, however, has continued the strikes, accusing Hamas of ceasefire violations.
In a report published on Monday, the UN Commission of Inquiry accused Israeli forces of deliberately targeting Palestinian civilians, including children, under “discriminatory” rules of engagement and with near-total impunity.
Since the ceasefire and by September 30, it claimed, Israeli attacks killed 1,431 Palestinians in Gaza, including 300 children and 130 women. Israeli forces also killed 1,080 Palestinians and injured 10,940 in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since October 2023. The overall Palestinian death toll across the occupied territories, according to the report, now exceeds 75,000, including at least 21,500 children and 11,000 women.
“While Israeli authorities and security forces continue to commit genocide in Gaza, the situation in the West Bank has deteriorated drastically,” the commission said. It described military operations and settler violence as a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians. They also documented rape, torture, and sexual violence intended to “fracture, expel, humiliate, and subjugate” Palestinians.
The findings build on the commission’s initial September 2025 conclusion that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians, citing four of the five genocidal acts under the 1948 Genocide Convention. International bodies, including Israeli rights groups B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights-Israel, have also accused Israel of genocide.
Israel in denial
Israel has rejected the allegations of genocide and war crimes. Responding to the new report, its Geneva mission demanded the UN commission’s dissolution, accusing it of a “misinformation campaign to demonize the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal.” Ambassador Daniel Meron said the panel seeks “to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself.”
Meanwhile, members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition have called for control over Palestinian territory to be expanded. Earlier this month, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Israel to seize Gaza and launch a similar operation in the West Bank.
“Yes, we need to wipe out Gaza, for example. Not commit genocide, God forbid,” he said, calling the enclave a “terror entity with 1.8 million Nazis” raised to hate Israel.
What happened to the ceasefire?
More than a year after the truce took effect, its next phase – reconstruction, governance arrangements, and further Israeli troop withdrawals – remains deadlocked over Hamas disarmament.
Hamas has said it will not surrender its weapons without a complete Israeli withdrawal and an end to strikes. Netanyahu has demanded full disarmament and the dismantling of Hamas infrastructure before further withdrawals.
The prime minister also acknowledged expanding military control beyond the original Yellow Line, which initially left Israel holding around 53% of Gaza. With Israeli forces now controlling more than 60%, Netanyahu has ordered the military to extend that to 70%.
Netanyahu faces election reckoning
The UN report came on the eve of Israel’s first parliamentary election since the October 7, 2023 attack, with Netanyahu facing growing scrutiny over security failures, a widening regional conflict, and legal troubles.
Over the past three years, Israel’s Gaza offensive has expanded into fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon and direct military clashes with Iran. Netanyahu has also faced allegations that he received advance warnings of the Hamas attack, which his office denies.
He is also on trial for corruption and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, adding to the pressures surrounding his bid to retain power.
Final polls show a tight race between Netanyahu’s Likud and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party, which are projected to win 18-30 and 21-23 seats respectively. Neither bloc is assured the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.

‘Inexplicable’ order by control centre investigated after Spain train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:53:27 UTC
01:53:27 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that "the whole of Spain is in mourning" following the accident and expressed his solidarity with the victims, their families and the injured.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente has said an “inexplicable” decision by a central control centre in Madrid is at the centre of the investigation into Wednesday’s high-speed train crash in Castilla-La Mancha, rather than the actions of the train drivers.
At least 68 people have died and 58 are receiving treatment in hospital, according to regional authorities.
Puente said an order he describes as "inexplicable" from the central control centre had allowed the high-speed Renfe-operated train to resume normal running after a safety system failed. He stressed that the train drivers were not to blame and said the investigation was now examining how that decision was made.
According to the minister, at around 8:30 am the LZB safety system failed along a 63-kilometre stretch of track because of a computer malfunction, automatically bringing around six trains to a halt. The control centre then took over management of the traffic.
At 8:36 am, the Renfe AVE high-speed train was authorised to resume normal running despite a red signal remaining active on the line. It then travelled around 25 kilometres before colliding with a stationary Iryo train at around 8:53 am.
Puente said the AVE should instead have been operating under the "marcha a la vista" procedure, a railway safety measure used when automated control systems fail. Under the procedure, trains must travel at reduced speed so that drivers can stop if they encounter an obstacle or another train on the line.
Authorities are still examining data to establish the train’s exact speed before the collision, although Puente said it could have reached up to 200 kilometres per hour on that section of track.
Puente described the incident as "one of the toughest moments anyone can face" and expressed his solidarity and sympathy with the victims.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that "the whole of Spain is in mourning" following the accident and expressed his solidarity with the victims, their families and the injured.
Sánchez said the government's immediate priority was to care for victims and their relatives, locate survivors and ensure those affected received material and psychological support.
He also praised the work of emergency and Civil Protection services and the coordination between the authorities involved in the response.
Sánchez warned that if failures in the safety systems were confirmed, the government would respond firmly.
The prime minister also announced three days of national mourning.
The collision was Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail crash this year, after 46 people were killed in another accident involving Renfe and Iryo trains in January.

Poland chosen to host €227m Patriot missile maintenance centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:58 UTC
01:51:58 KST

Poland has been chosen to host Europe's service centre for PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot systems. It will be the only such facility outside the US.
Poland is to host a European maintenance centre for PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot air defence systems.
The decision on where to locate the investment was taken by the United States authorities.
The project is estimated to be worth around one billion zlotys (€227 million). Poland competed with Germany, the Netherlands and Norway for the investment.
Poland comes out on top in international competition
Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka announced the decision in a post on X.
"A historic decision! A servicing centre for PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot systems will be built in Poland," she wrote.
She said the Polish bid received the highest score at the application stage. The final decision, however, followed months of talks with the US side.
Speaking at a press conference at NATO headquarters in Brussels, the deputy minister underlined that the investment is important not only in industrial terms but also strategically.
"This is a clear guarantee from NATO that the alliance is holding together and that all of NATO stands behind each of its partners, behind every element of the alliance," she said.
Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also commented on the decision. He said the choice of Poland confirmed its importance as a partner of the United States.
"Poland is a trustworthy ally and an extremely important place on the map of global security," the minister wrote.
Pentagon: investment in the alliance's defence capabilities
US defence official Michael Duffey, who is responsible for procurement, described the decision as confirmation of allied unity and commitment to deterrence.
"It is a signal that the alliance is united, takes deterrence seriously and is ready to act," he said.
The Pentagon said the project fulfils commitments on cooperation between defence industries made at the NATO summit in Ankara in July 2026 under the "NATO 3.0" concept.
According to the US department, the investment is intended to strengthen the region's resilience and allow European allies to assume greater responsibility for their own conventional defence.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose also welcomed the decision.
Negotiations first, construction of the centre later
The Polish side now faces further negotiations with American defence and aerospace manufacturer Lockheed Martin.
"It will take at least several months for such a centre to be able to operate," Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
According to the plans, the Polish facility will be responsible for technical servicing of the missiles, helping to keep them in proper condition and ready for use.
The Pentagon says Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will also take part in integrating key elements of the supply chain.
Patriot a key element of Poland's air defence
Patriot systems are among the most important components of modern air defence, and their significance has grown in connection with the war in Ukraine and threats from Russia.
For several years Poland has been building up its air defence capabilities. Under the Wisła programme the Polish Armed Forces have received two Patriot batteries, which reached operational readiness in December last year.
Around 200 PAC-3 MSE missiles were ordered in 2018, while the next stage of the programme includes six additional batteries and around 600 more missiles. Deliveries are due to be completed by 2029.
The ability to service the missiles in Poland could cut maintenance times, improve operational readiness and help develop domestic defence expertise.
Could Poland get a permanent US military base?
Poland and the United States are moving closer to a final decision on creating a fully fledged permanent US military base on Polish territory.
In June, the Polish government approved the start of formal negotiations, with Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz appointed to lead the talks.
President Karol Nawrocki has also called a meeting of the National Security Council for 3 November, with a permanent US base among the issues due to be discussed.
According to initial plans, the new permanent base would accommodate around 5,000 US soldiers, and its estimated cost could range from 15 to 17 billion zlotys (€3.41 billion to €3.86 billion).
Asked about the proposal on 1 October, US President Donald Trump said his administration was considering it. "It could happen," he said.
Around 10,000 US troops are currently stationed in Poland, mostly on a rotational basis.

kengo kuma’s brick towers frame open-air pools at copenhagen’s upcoming bathhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:55:25 UTC
01:55:25 KST

kengo kuma’s brick towers frame open-air pools at copenhagen’s upcoming bathhouse
swimmers can float beneath the open sky between brick towers at copenhagen's public bathhouse, set to open on december 5th, 2026.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
soon to open on copenhagen’s paper island
Kengo Kuma & Associates‘ KAI Water Culture House is set to open on December 5th, 2026, on Copenhagen‘s Papirøen (Paper Island). Bringing ten swimming pools to the city’s harborfront, the 5,800-square-meter spa introduces a new place for swimming and bathing along a waterfront that has gradually shifted from industrial use toward public recreation.
The building is recognizable at once by its five irregular brick towers, which rise above a continuous band of glass at ground level. Their sloping walls form a clustered silhouette along the quay, with spaces between the volumes opening toward the sky. From the harbor, the heavy masonry appears to hover over the transparent base. This lends the building an unusual sense of lightness, even with its monolithic presence.
five brick towers shaped around the water below
The towers in Copenhagen take their forms from the swimming pools beneath them, with each volume responding to its interior layout. Approximately 300,000 handmade bricks cover the angular surfaces, their varying gray tones relating to the city’s surrounding harbor architecture. The masonry is laid in a stepped pattern that gives the sloping walls a textured finish, particularly where the surfaces catch the changing daylight.
Across the brick facades, 403 windows of different sizes create small openings toward the city. Some bring daylight deep into the bathing areas, while others frame views across the harbor. Inside, the walls rise above the water at steep angles, creating tall bathing chambers where the enclosed architecture feels almost geological. The architects led by Kengo Kuma shape the building’s tallest volume, known as the Culture Tower, to house spaces for cultural activities and community gatherings.
an outdoor swimming pool sits between the towers
Perhaps the most unusual part of KAI is its Valley Pool, an open-air swimming basin positioned on the first floor between the five brick towers. Here, visitors can swim surrounded by the textured masonry, with the sky visible directly overhead. The arrangement creates a sheltered bathing space that remains exposed to Copenhagen’s changing weather, allowing swimmers to experience rain and even snowfall from the water.
On the same level, a heated outdoor onsen overlooks Copenhagen Harbour, drawing on Japanese bathing traditions while taking advantage of the waterfront setting. Both outdoor pools are designed for year-round use, supported by a ground-source heat pump system connected to ten boreholes extending 250 meters below ground. The architecture makes these contrasting experiences possible within the same building, moving between enclosed brick interiors and pools open to the elements.
from indoor swimming to the harbor
At ground level, KAI contains a 25-meter fitness pool alongside a teaching pool and three smaller pools for children. Upstairs, warmer bathing areas are joined by a cold plunge pool, while saunas and a steam bath provide additional facilities. The transparent lower level opens views toward the surrounding waterfront, connecting the swimming spaces visually with the harbor beyond.
Outside, a timber boardwalk will lead to designated harbor swimming and dipping areas overlooking the Royal Danish Playhouse and Opera Park. These public bathing facilities are expected to open in early 2027, following the building’s December inauguration. The project itself began with a city-led ideas competition in 2015, when Copenhagen residents submitted 160 proposals for the future of Paper Island, most of them calling for a public swimming facility.
Kengo Kuma & Associates won the subsequent architectural competition in 2017, working with Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture during the early design stages and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects through detailed design and construction. Nearly a decade later, the project brings that original public request to the harbor’s edge.
project info:
project: KAI Water Culture House
location: Papirøen (Paper Island), Copenhagen, Denmark
lead architect: Kengo Kuma & Associates
early design collaboration: Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture
executive architect: Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects
client: Paper Island Water Culture House Foundation
main contractor: MT Højgaard
area: 5,800 sqm
opening date: December 5th, 2026

German defense company Quantum Systems has announced the establishment of a subsidiary, Quantum Systems Japan G.K., and the opening of an office in Tokyo.
The company’s press service reported the development.
The opening of the Japanese office was announced during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Japan on October 28.
The company plans to expand industrial cooperation with Japanese corporations Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic, with which it has already signed memorandums of understanding.
The partnerships aim to combine Japan’s manufacturing capabilities with Quantum Systems’ expertise in developing unmanned systems, strengthen the local industrial base and reduce dependence on foreign supply chains.
Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said Japan had recognized the direction the defense industry was evolving, including unmanned systems, rapid innovation, and the industrial capacity for large-scale production. He added that Ukraine had demonstrated why this mattered and that technological superiority became decisive when personnel were in short supply and threats evolved rapidly.
The new office will focus on cooperation with Japanese customers and adapting unmanned systems to the needs of the Japan Self-Defense Forces.
In particular, the company will offer integrated air, land, and maritime solutions based on its MOSAIC UXS software platform, which enables different unmanned systems to operate in coordination.
The opening of the Japanese office marks another stage in Quantum Systems’ international expansion. In August, the company opened an unmanned systems development center in Huntsville, Alabama.
Quantum Systems is also expanding its operations in Ukraine. In October, Militarnyi was told that Germany would fund the production in Ukraine of tens of thousands of the company’s interceptor drones to defend against Russian strike UAVs.
